shigezane:525.title: Letter from Masamune Date, October 22, Tensho 17
shigezane:525.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, October 22, Tensho 17. The opening reads: "Regarding the matter at Obarada, I hastened forth for the purpose of replacing the witness; as I stated during our direct conversation yesterday, this is the primary concern. Aside from these instructions..."
shigezane:525.markdown:
Regarding the matter of Obarada, I hasten to report that I have departed promptly in order to replace the witness; as I stated during our direct conversation yesterday, this is the primary point of contention. Aside from these instructions, there shall be no summons; this must be handled with utmost care. Since this letter is being written, it must not be lost. Furthermore, I believe any informal drafts sent from that end are, first and foremost, unnecessary. Now, as for Obarada, I report that Suda is to be closely monitored. Regarding Suda, he has been a villain to our side for many years; thus, his devotion is beyond measure. This shall be the basis for our contention. With these matters repeated, I offer my humble and respectful words. Subsequently, regarding the matter of Fude, further reports have come from Soma □, and I find this unsettling. That is all.

(Tensho 17) October 22, Masamune (kao), to Goro-dono

shigezane:597.title: Letter from Masamune Date, January 7, Tensho 18
shigezane:597.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, January 7, Tensho 18. The opening reads: "As intended, the auspicious omens of the New Year's change have not fully passed. A folding fan has arrived; long live the realm. I have repeatedly read letters from Soma Nyosetsu. As stated, the south gate..."
shigezane:597.markdown:
As you intended, there can be no delay in welcoming the auspicious signs of the New Year. From this moment forward, I shall receive the folding fan; long live the realm. I have repeatedly read the letters from Soma Nyosetsu. As I understand it, given that the Southern Gate's bow and arrow are inexhaustible, it is only natural that one side be lacking. Furthermore, the lapses of Soma over the years are truly, truly, truly regrettable. Could it be that the disputes should proceed in this manner solely at the discretion of Nyosetsusai? It appears that, following consultations between Soma's superiors and subordinates, that single letter has been sent. Please be advised. As the timing is most opportune, I earnestly hope for this to be realized; it is my sole desire. I lack the discernment to judge further. Naturally, regarding the matter of the salt flavor, I shall now proceed with correspondence; first and foremost, I humbly submit these words.

(Tensho 18) January 7, Masamune's Seal

Lord Goro

shigezane:616.title: Letter from Masamune Date, February 14, Tensho 18
shigezane:616.summary: February 14, Tensho 18. Letter from Masamune Date. The opening reads: "I have carefully perused your kind letter; it is a most welcome sight. Regarding the matter of Soma, Nakai (Nakajima Ise) has also come to visit, and in detail..."
shigezane:616.markdown:
It is a great pleasure to have received your kind letter and to have examined it in detail. Regarding the matter of Soma, I have consulted Naka-i (Nakajima Ise) and engaged in detailed discussions; I humbly submit my views point by point. I have had the strategies for Soma carefully assessed. One must never afford any lapse in vigilance. Despite my youth, I offer these as my sole counsel, and I believe there should be no discrepancy in my judgment. As for the Shirakawa entrance, nothing of note has occurred to date. According to legend, Yoshinobu (Satake) is expected to march forth within a day or two. In truth, it remains difficult to predict. Next, yesterday the 13th, Hama-i (Hamada Izu) returned to Iwaki. In Iwaki (Iwaki), he devoted his utmost effort; particularly at the time of the departure, it is said that many men will be dispatched immediately. As for the matter of the discussions, there may be some delay or haste. It is now the time for my arrival in Japan. I offer these words with utmost respect and humility.

(Tensho 18) 14th day of mid-spring, Masamune (kao), to Goro-dono

※In Watari Date Family Historical Materials 7 (41) [Commentary], it is stated, "In this year, Masamune was encamped in Odawara...", but February was prior to his departure (Takemizu's note).

shigezane:692.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, May 8, Tensho 18. The opening reads: "I have carefully read your letter, which I welcome most heartily. As for the situation in Odawara, I understand that it remains unchanged and is firmly held. However, as for whether..."
shigezane:692.markdown:
It is a great pleasure that you have taken the trouble to visit and peruse these letters once more. As for the situation in Odawara, I understand that it remains unchanged and is firmly held. However, one wonders if a settlement can truly be reached. Regarding the journey up, we shall decide on the matter tomorrow, the 9th. May 8, Masamune (kao)

shigezane:699.title: Letter from Masamune Date, June 9, Tensho 18
shigezane:699.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, June 9, Tensho 18. The opening reads: "Having attended court today, the 9th, at the hour of the Snake, I am most fortunate beyond measure; it is truly beyond words. That the Kanpaku himself personally devoted so much heart and soul to the matter—I am utterly speechless. Truly..."
shigezane:699.markdown:
Having reported for duty today, the 9th, at the hour of the Snake, I am most truly fortunate; it is truly beyond words. That the Kanpaku-sama himself has personally devoted such heartfelt care is beyond description. One cannot possibly fathom how profoundly kind he is. Accordingly, tea service is scheduled for tomorrow, the 10th. The day after tomorrow, I shall return to him. The 54 districts of Oshu also appear to be largely settled. I am utterly satisfied and deeply moved. A copy of this letter shall be sent to various quarters; as the matter is urgent, I humbly submit these words in haste.

Postscript: As I am somewhat preoccupied, I have written this in my diary. Please find a copy of this letter here. I assure you that your kindness toward me is all the more profound than this letter suggests, though I have omitted □□ from the text. That is all.

June 9, Hour of the Horse, Masamune (kao)

Lord Goro

shigezane:756.title: Letter from Masamune Date, August 27, Tensho 18
shigezane:756.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, August 27, Tensho 18. The opening reads: "Atago also looks on; while I should now be speaking in person, I have interposed to convey this in detail; it is the utmost of my wishes. As for the matters of Asaka and Sukagawa, as..."
shigezane:756.markdown:
Atago also witnessed this; while I was about to state the matter in full, you interrupted me and provided detailed instructions—a most welcome outcome. As for the matters concerning Asaka and Sukagawa, how shall they be handled? In such cases, the matter of disposition in those matters should be firmly entrusted to Shigezane; thus, even as the days draw to a close, you may await further instructions. In any event, should things turn out poorly on your part, I believe it would not be appropriate to speak of it. Where my judgment falls short, it cannot be helped; I trust you will hear of this. Furthermore, as I shall report the matter upon your departure for battle, I write to you now. Respectfully and humbly.

Postscript: As the matter of that region has first and foremost fallen under my charge, I trust you will feel at ease. That concludes my message.

August 27: Masamune's Seal

Lord Goro

## Rough translation

Atago also witnessed this; while I should have contacted you sooner, I instead wish to thank you for everything. As for what will happen with Asaka and Sukagawa—that matter is under the jurisdiction of that office, but I intend to leave it firmly in Shigezane's hands, so please bear with me even if it takes a little while. In any case, I intend to ensure that Shigezane does not suffer any wrongdoing. If my judgment falls short, there is nothing I can do, so I hope you understand. Furthermore, I plan to discuss it with you when you set out for the campaign, so this will suffice for now.

P.S. Please do not worry about that region, as it will become Date territory. That is all.

## Personal thoughts

Shigezane held the domain of Nihonmatsu and served as the commander for the Asaka and Sukagawa areas. It seems Shigezane pressed Masamune on what would happen during the Ou Shioki. [On June 9, he wrote, "I have a sense that my holdings will largely be confirmed."](#/post/shigezane/699) However, it appears that by this time, there were signs that some of his lands were about to be confiscated. "If this is not granted, there is nothing I can do—please understand," Masamune wrote, his tone turning tearful. Somehow, his choice of words toward Shigezane also seems more polite than usual, perhaps out of consideration.

shigezane:759.title: Letter from Masamune Date, September 22, Tensho 18
shigezane:759.summary: September 22, Tensho 18. Letter from Masamune Date. The opening reads: "A letter from Chuzaburo-dono; I was invited to view it. I consider it a trivial matter. At the same time, I do not find it burdensome. Furthermore, the Sendo Diary has arrived via Asadan from some source. Nearby..."
shigezane:759.markdown:
I have received a letter from Lord Chuzaburo and have been invited to view it. I trust this finds you well. I wish you continued health. Furthermore, the Sendo Diary has arrived from Asadan via some unknown source. I shall peruse it shortly; the matter concerning Shirakawa pertains to two districts. In the meantime, I am personally satisfied. Asadan has also expressed his agreement. Additionally, regarding the matter of Rakui at this location, I beg your kind discretion. I shall likely remain in Omori for two or three days while ascending. At that time, I shall also proceed to Fujiyama. I shall report all matters at that time. I believe there will be no interference in the meantime. As for the repeated letters from Lord Danjo, I shall forward them in due course. With utmost respect.

(Tensho 18) 22nd day of the 9th month: Masamune's sealed letter

Lord Goro

## Rough translation

Have you seen the letter from Lord Gamo Ujisato in private? How presumptuous of him. But I shall let it go. The Sendo Diary has been brought to Asano Danjo from some unknown source. It seems he will be reviewing it soon; as for the matter of Shirakawa, it has been reduced to two districts. I am satisfied. Asano Danjo is also pleased. Now, regarding the settlement of this matter, he is still giving it serious thought. I hear he will be staying in Omori for two or three days, so I shall also go to Nihonmatsu at that time. I shall hear everything then. I do not expect any particular unnecessary work to arise. If another letter arrives from Lord Danjo, I intend to send it along in due course.

shigezane:762.title: Letter from Masamune Date, September 29, Tensho 18
shigezane:762.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, September 29, Tensho 18. The opening reads: "Regarding the matter of proceeding to the capital, I have received word that I may accompany you. Furthermore, regardless of how you may view the matter, it is clear that no special arrangements are necessary. I shall handle the arrangements for Fujiyama to the best of my ability. Please rest assured. Additionally, the gate was opened yesterday, the 28th, and I allowed the horse to enter. I shall report further details as they arise. Once matters are settled, I intend to send Kojuro to Tamura. With utmost respect.

September 29, Masamune's signature

Lord Goro

Regarding the matter of the journey to the capital, I have certainly received your offer to accompany me; as always, I find this most reassuring. However, it is clear that no matter how one arranges it, the undertaking will be exceptionally arduous, so there is no need for you to accompany me. I intend to do my utmost to arrange the matter in Nihonmatsu. Please rest assured. Furthermore, the inner quarters have settled, and I stabled my horse here yesterday, the 28th. Details will follow. Also, per your instructions, Kojuro will be assigned to Tamura. I humbly submit this in trepidation.

shigezane:769.title: Letter from Masamune Date, October 3, Tensho 18
shigezane:769.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, October 3, Tensho 18. The opening reads: "I write to you by way of this fortunate opportunity. This morning, I received a letter from Asadan as follows. It appears that a guide has been dispatched to Aizu and is reporting that things are proceeding favorably in various respects..."
shigezane:769.markdown:
I hereby submit the details of the matter. This morning, I received a letter from Asadan as follows. It appears that guides have been dispatched to Aizu and are making various arrangements to ensure everything proceeds smoothly; accordingly, those there have also sought out guides from Shirakawa and Shio, as well as individuals of appropriate age, to ensure that there are no shortcomings when Asadan ascends Omori—a matter for which I have long been thoroughly instructed. Should the arrangements be sound, I believe the timing will be appropriate. Regardless of the circumstances, it is my earnest hope that this matter may be settled. I shall now proceed with the formal correspondence. Furthermore, I am forwarding two letters—one from Asadan and another from Lord Chuzaburo's retainers to Lord Danjo. Please review them and provide a reply thereafter. With utmost respect.

Postscript: As I have arrived once again, I shall respond to you in whatever manner may be necessary. That is all.

October 3, Masamune's Seal

Lord Goro

## Statement of Purpose for the Publication of the Family Records

This morning, I received a letter from Lord Danjo Kohitsu as follows. In any case, it appears that there are guides in Aizu who will explain matters in various ways. There, too, elderly men have been sought out as guides for Shirakawa, Nihonmatsu, and Shiomatsu; they have prepared detailed instructions, word for word, to be delivered in full when Lord Danjo Kohitsu ascends to Omori. He believes that if even the local people are properly informed, the situation will be resolved in due course. Regardless of how things unfold, he earnestly hopes that this matter will be settled. Furthermore, both the letter from Lord Danjo Kohitsu and the letter from Lord Gamo Chuzaburo's retainer to Lord Danjo Kohitsu have been dispatched. Please review and reply. Additionally, it is stated that until further notice, one should exercise patience and remain in that location.

shigezane:772.title: Letter from Masamune Date, October 6, Tensho 18
shigezane:772.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, October 6, Tensho 18. The opening reads: "You have gone to the trouble of sending a courier; this is a most welcome occasion. I have heard that there should be no delay. I have neither the strength nor the means. Furthermore, please exercise all due discretion regarding Asaka..."
shigezane:772.markdown:
The courier has been deliberately sent ahead; this is a most auspicious occasion. I have heard that there should be no hidden accomplices. I am powerless to act. Furthermore, please exercise all discretion; even those in the Asaka area should be sought out and brought to justice. Tomorrow, the 7th, I shall make a great expedition; therefore, tomorrow or the day after, I shall certainly, most certainly, send out a force. Accordingly, those tasked with guidance must act with the utmost diligence. Have you not received the letter from Chuzaburo-dono? As I have lost track of it, I shall not send it. There is no substitute for this. It is precisely as I have previously stated. Simply put, in Aizu, it is said that various schemes have been employed to cultivate a few accomplices. Regardless of the circumstances, those who believe this to be the case are perfectly justified in seeking you out. That said—that said—that said—that said—that said—this matter shall be settled with this single point. Time and again, do not let your guard down. I write this in haste, as time is of the essence. I am unable to read the contents of this letter. I offer my most respectful and humble regards.

October 6, Hour of the Horse. Masamune (Seal)

Lord Goro

shigezane:818.title: Letter from Masamune Date, January 27, Tensho 19
shigezane:818.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, January 27, Tensho 19. The opening reads: "I hereby send this urgent message by courier. Furthermore, I arrived in Kiyosu yesterday, the 27th. The Lord is presently at Takano and is expected to return at the hour of the Rooster. That is, the envoy..."
shigezane:818.markdown:
I hereby report this via urgent courier. Furthermore, I arrived here in Kiyosu yesterday, the 27th. The Lord is presently out at Takano and is expected to return at the hour of the Rooster. Accordingly, I dispatched Kinoshita Hansuke and Fukuhara Umasuke as envoys; they hastened from far-off lands and were summoned before the Lord this morning and granted a meal. Regarding the various matters of this occasion, the Lord did not regard them as mere trifles but viewed them as matters of grave importance; He spoke to them directly, and the various expressions of His earnest goodwill are beyond words on paper. As for the dispatch to the relay stations in Kyoto and the direct report to the Chunagon, our reputation rests upon this matter. From the upper and lower townspeople, not a single word has been spoken suggesting that this journey to the capital is in any way improper. I have now briefly recorded my account; I hope it shall satisfy you. I shall ensure that Motoyasu, Shigemune, and the rest of the clan are informed of this repeatedly and without fail. With utmost respect and humility.

Postscript: It is unnecessary to write to each member of the family and clan. I regret that my words may seem curt. However, as I shall proceed in haste tomorrow and may pass by your respective lodgings, there is no need for such formality. That is all.

(Tensho 19) 27th day of the later month

shigezane:88.title: Letter from Masamune Date, December 15, Tensho 14
shigezane:88.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, December 15, Tensho 14. The opening reads: "Since then, there has been no word, and I am growing anxious. Now then, I hear that the construction at Ni (Nihonmatsu) is currently in full swing; I imagine the great effort involved by all ranks. Accordingly, shortly, Ta (Tamura)…"
shigezane:88.markdown:
Since then, there has been no word, and I remain uneasy. Now, as for the construction at Ni (Nihonmatsu), I hear it is currently in full swing; I imagine the great toil involved for both parties. Accordingly, word has come from the Tamura (Tamura) group that they require our services, and that Shinza (Shinkan Saemon) from Soma and Hashi-gyo (Hashimoto Gyobu) from Tamura shall proceed as far as the midpoint, so this is my private understanding. Regarding the arrangements from both houses, I have received word that Kojuro Katakura shall now proceed; though I am young and hesitant, I shall proceed in accordance with the arrangements. Furthermore, regardless of how matters turn out, I intend to approach you with courteousness, so I hope you will find it reassuring. Privately, I have been informed that five or six families are meeting to arrange the transfer of their assets to us, and that I have come forward for this purpose. Though this is a matter of internal affairs, I mention it here. Additionally, a courier was sent directly from Satake on the 24th. Having stated this, I felt there was no other choice and responded with utmost sincerity. As the matter was settled, the outcome was as originally discussed between the two of you; I hereby report this. With profound respect and humility.

Postscript. I have heard from Watari that the wedding will take place soon. I am delighted to hear this.

15th day of the 11th month. Masamune's seal.

Seyasu

shigezane:arisaka.title: A Biography of Shigezane Date Based on the "Arisaka Documents"
shigezane:arisaka.subtitle: Arisaka Documents
shigezane:arisaka.summary: Having read in a certain book regarding the matter of Arisaka Tanba Homare, I have extracted the relevant points and recorded them below. Several entries in the Masamune Record were written by Date Awa-no-kami Shigezane.
shigezane:arisaka.markdown:
A (46) Arisaka Documents

Regarding the matter of Arisaka Tanba Homare, I have extracted details from a certain text and recorded them below. Several entries in the Masamune Records were written by Date Awa-no-kami Shigezane. As Date Tanemune's sixth son, Date Sanemoto, was destined to be the [ ] of Uesugi Sadazane, a yamabushi named Dairaku was dispatched; he was provided with Usami Nagamitsu's waist-armor, the character "Sane" (実) from his personal name, and the bamboo-and-sparrow curtain crest. Just as he was about to move to Echigo, a conflict arose between Lord Tanemune and his son Lord Harumune, and a rebellion was imminent. Consequently, Sanemoto abandoned his hopes of becoming the heir to the great province of Echigo and sought reconciliation, thereby ensuring the stability of the Date house and allowing the Date to remain vassals in later generations. His son, Togoro Shigezane (later known as Awa-no-kami), from the age of 17, devoted himself wholeheartedly to serving the clan's descendant, Komon Masamune; it was known throughout the land that he fought with unparalleled loyalty whenever Masamune marched out. Nevertheless, Date Kozuke-no-suke Masakage and Ishikawa Yamato-no-kami Akimitsu, being of low rank, found this contrary to their true intentions and, filled with regret, withdrew from Fushimi to Koya. Akimitsu, Masakage, and others viewed this with ridicule; though they twice voiced their dissent through Kuwaori Tenryosai and Arisaka Tanba—both of whom were Lord Masamune's confidants—they did not return. When messengers were sent three times, their whereabouts remained unknown, leaving no choice but to proceed. Afterward, Haneda Uma-no-suke, a senior retainer of the Shigezane house, was ordered to expel the retainers; a messenger was dispatched to Kakuda, the residence of the Shigezane house, with instructions from Lord Masamune to Yashiro Kageyubei, the caretaker of Iwadeyama, to annihilate the entire Shigezane household. Upon consultation among Kanazawa, Uchizaki, Sawajiri, Shiranezawa, Ishikawa, and others, they agreed: "Lord Shigezane has sent a secret letter to Haneda Uma-no-suke alone, making us seem as if we did not exist; we find this most regrettable. This time, we shall submit a joint petition to Iwadeyama." While they were discussing this internally, Kageyubei led a force and pressed upon Kakuda, and the documents mentioned above were delivered to Kageyubei. Haneda Uma-no-suke shut himself in his private residence, and over 30 men and women were killed in action. Kanazawa, Uchizaki, Sawajiri, Shiranezawa, and others were summoned by Lord Masamune and granted fiefs. Those who agreed with Uma-no-suke fled and settled in Kakuda. As for Shigezane, he remained secluded in the Shimogori district of Odawara, where he was granted a stipend of 100 koku by Lord Ieyasu. He was later dismissed following a lawsuit brought by Lord Masamune. During the time of the Sekigahara campaign, he was told by Uesugi Kagekatsu that he should be retained with a fief of 50,000 koku; however, as he felt it contrary to his true intentions to serve the Uesugi house or oppose Masamune, he remained unconvinced. Subsequently, through the mediation of Akimitsu, Masakage, and Kagetsuna Katakura, he was recalled and added to the camp of Akimitsu as a prisoner at the Shiroishi camp. Upon his return, he was granted a fief of 1,000 kanmon in Watari District, and during the reign of Lord Tadamune, his holdings were increased to 20,000 koku. As he had no biological children, he succeeded the younger brother of Lord Tadamune, Jibu-daibu, and took the name Munenari. Later, Awa-no-kami Shigezane passed away on June 4, Shoho 3. His Buddhist name was Yuzan-ji Don Kyuzan Daikoji. He was 79 years old. His death poem was as follows: "The years I longed for in the past—even passing ninety—were but a dream." The sentiment of this death poem is based on a poem by the ancient Tang poet Du Fu, which states, "Since ancient times, it has been rare to live to seventy"—meaning it is rare to live to 70. Therefore, it is most fitting.

shigezane:awanosu.title: The Awanosu Incident
shigezane:awanosu.summary: The incident on October 8, Tensho 13, in which Terumune Date was abducted by Yoshitsugu Hatakeyama at Miyamori Castle, and both perished at Awanosu (Hiraishi Takada, Nihonmatsu City).
shigezane:awanosu.markdown:
The incident on October 8, Tensho 13, in which Terumune Date was abducted by Yoshitsugu Hatakeyama at Miyamori Castle, and both perished at Awanosu (Hiraishi Takada, Nihonmatsu City).

〈Awanosu Incident Map〉 Created using Electronic National Land. Black areas represent rivers.

## Overview

Following the fall of Kotemori Castle during the campaign against Ouchi Sadatsuna in Tensho 13, Masamune Date steadily subdued Shiomatsu. Unable to endure the situation any longer, Ouchi Sadatsuna abandoned his main stronghold, Obama Castle, and fled to Nihonmatsu Castle—held by his relative Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu—before seeking refuge in Aizu. When Masamune entered Obama Castle (lower residence), which had become an empty castle, Terumune Date, who had been in retirement, also entered Miyamori Castle (upper residence). Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu, who had formed an alliance with Ouchi Sadatsuna, offered his surrender to the Date clan, but was rejected; his request was eventually accepted after several petitions.

On October 8, Tensho 13, Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu visited Miyamori Castle, Terumune's camp, as a token of gratitude. The ceremony concluded without incident, but as he was taking his leave, Yoshitsugu suddenly abducted Terumune. At the time, Masamune was away on a falconry expedition. Shigezane Date and Masakage Rusu were also present at the ceremony, but powerless to react to the sudden turn of events, Terumune was taken away toward Nihonmatsu. After proceeding over ten ri along a country road from Miyamori Castle to Awanosu, the Date forces attacked the Hatakeyama forces, and both Terumune and Yoshitsugu were killed.

In the Taiga drama "Dokuganryu Masamune," a highlight is the scene where Masamune catches up with Yoshitsugu and Terumune on the banks of the Abukuma River and, after a period of inner conflict, tearfully orders the firing of muskets; however, the river is not visible from the presumed site of the Awanosu ancient battlefield. It remains uncertain whether Masamune, upon hearing the news, caught up with Yoshitsugu and Terumune at that time or whether he ordered the firing of the muskets, but many fictional works feature scenes similar to those in the Taiga drama. Among these, the following stand out:

- "The Sorrowful Tale of the Date Clan: Those Without Compassion" (Iwao Kashiyama, Soei Publishing, 1994). It states that Masamune was unable to catch up, and that Shigezane ordered the firing of muskets. (I've only seen this in this book, but...)
- "[The One-Eyed Dragon: Masamune Date](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/ASIN/4415077110/oysannohitori-22)" (Taiji Mizuno. Seibido Publishing) The Awanosu Incident itself was Kojuro's conspiracy.

shigezane:awayashiki.title: The Fire at the Date Awa Residence and Sakanamachi
shigezane:awayashiki.summary: On February 23, Kan'ei 11, after Shigezane hosted Masamune, a fire broke out at Shigezane's residence.
shigezane:awayashiki.markdown:
On February 23, Kan'ei 11, after Shigezane hosted Masamune, a fire broke out at Shigezane's residence.

The "Jike Kiroku" records: "Tonight, at the hour of the Tiger, a fire broke out at Awa-dono's residence; the entire house was consumed, and fires spread to the rear of Sakana-machi, one block in."

## Was the fire in Sendai or Wakabayashi?

Given the mention of "Sakana-machi" here, there appears to be an interpretation that this refers to a fire in Sakana-machi, one of the hereditary towns of Sendai. Indeed, Volume 7 of the *Gen Teishi Mimibukuro* reportedly contains an account of a great fire in Sakana-machi, Sendai, in February of the 11th year of Kan'ei. Maps of the Sendai castle town reveal that the Date Awa Residence once stood in what is now Nishi Park, to the northeast of Sakana-machi.

However, various sources state that the residence of Shigezane involved in this fire was the "Wakabayashi" residence. According to these sources,

> [Masamune-ki: Matters Concerning Shigezane's Conduct](#/post/shigezane/masamuneki10-1) > "Masamune, in the vicinity of Sendai in the Kokubun district of Miyagi... (omitted) ...named that area Wakabayashi... (omitted) ...Accordingly, plans were drawn up for Shigezane's residence, and applications were made three or four times... (omitted; the following continues with the account of the fire)... " > Kimura Uemon Memorandum 120 > "In the year [...], a new residence was completed for Date Awa Shikesane at Wakabayashi... (omitted) ...two or three blocks of the town where Shikesane lived were burned down..."

However, "Sakana-machi" does not appear here, creating a contradiction with the "Jike Kiroku."

Let us examine the climate of Sendai during this season—roughly corresponding to the second month of the lunar calendar, or March of the solar calendar. During this period, dry northwesterly winds frequently blow. Southeasterly and south-southeasterly winds occur on days when humidity is high before the weather deteriorates (and moreover, the sea lies upwind). For a great fire to break out in an instant from a location where there should have been little open flame, dry northwesterly winds would be most fitting; in that case, it is unlikely that the fire would have spread along the route from the Wakabayashi Shigezane residence to Sendai's Sakana-machi. [Wikipedia entry for "Aramachi"](http://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%8D%92%E7%94%BA) contains several accounts of great fires in Sendai, but those where the origin and spread of the fire are known all show the fire spreading eastward to southward. Furthermore, if the fire had spread from the Wakabayashi Shigezane residence to Sendai's Sakana-machi, there would naturally be no traditions of that fire in other gofudai-machi believed to have been affected. Assuming this fire was that of the Sendai Shigezane residence in Nishi Park, a spread to Sakana-machi would be natural, but it is unlikely that Shigezane or Kimura Uemon would have confused Sendai with Wakabayashi. While the Sendai castle town expanded toward Wakabayashi following the establishment of Wakabayashi Castle, the domain administration strictly distinguished between "Sendai" and "Wakabayashi." [The fire regulations in the Ishimoda Documents](http://shigezane.fc2web.com/majime/shokan/isimoda-486.html) state that those in charge of Wakabayashi must not respond to fires in Sendai; furthermore, in the "Joint Statement of Acknowledgment" included in the same documents, the guard of the Sendai residence responds that he "resides in Wakabayashi," indicating that Wakabayashi was not included within Sendai.

So, where is the "Sakana-machi" mentioned in the "Jike Kiroku"? Regarding the town name Wakabayashi, "Wakabayashi Kasumi-no-me-machi Yone-machi" is confirmed in Ishimoda Family Document 366, and "Wakabayashi Omachi" in Ishimoda Family Document 372. Since "Omachi"—another gofudai-machi—also exists in Wakabayashi, is it not possible that "Sakana-machi" was also located in Wakabayashi?

## Cause of the fire

On the day of the fire, Masamune visited the Shigezane residence, but a scandal occurred during the visit. A companion monk named Sobaku had unscrupulously praised the Noh performance of the young Hyobu Munekatsu (Masamune's tenth son), thereby incurring Masamune's wrath. Masamune struck Sobaku with a sword in its scabbard, resulting in bloodshed. Furthermore, throughout his stay, Masamune remained constantly fearful that a fire might break out and issued strict orders regarding the handling of fire.

The "400th Anniversary Commemorative Volume" offers an interpretation that this fire was a riddle—that Masamune's fear of the blaze was a command to "burn and purify, for you have stained a celebratory occasion with blood," and that Shigezane responded to it. It posits that the incident was overshadowed by the delicate relationship between Masamune and Shigezane, which had persisted since around the time of Masamune's flight.

Shigezane himself writes in the "Masamune-ki": "Between the upper and middle kitchens, among the debris beneath the veranda, a cigarette ember must have fallen, naturally spreading fire to both kitchens..."

shigezane:bohi.title: Yorin-ji Temple: Gravestone of Shigezane Date, Inscription
shigezane:bohi.summary: A stone monument erected by Kuninari Date, head of the Watari Date family during the Bakumatsu period, stands beside the grave of Jitsugen at Yorin-ji Temple. In the first year of Keio, on his return from the defense of Edo Castle, he visited Yorin-ji Temple and made a vow.
shigezane:bohi.markdown:
A stone monument erected by Kuninari Date, head of the Watari Date family during the Bakumatsu period, stands beside the grave of Jitsugen at Yorin-ji Temple. In the first year of Keio, on his return from the defense of Edo Castle, he visited Yorin-ji Temple and made a vow. The inscription follows.

Your name was Jitsugen; in childhood, you were called Tokimunemaru. You had already received the rank of Togoro. You belong to the Date clan of the Fujiwara surname. In the spring of Tensho (the year of the Wood Pig), you were appointed Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, and Assistant Minister of Military Affairs. You are the third son of Tanemune, the Lord of Sakyo-daifu of our domain; your mother was the daughter of Moritaka, the Shuri-no-daifu of the Ashina clan. Your maternal great-grandfather was Sadazane of the Uesugi clan, Lords of Echigo Province, who wished to raise you as his heir and agreed to do so. In June of Tenbun (the year of the Water Tiger), a certain Naoe, a senior retainer of that province, rebelled; you were given the henki name Jitsugen and were also granted the sword Nagamitsu and the bamboo-and-sparrow crest of the shogunate. Later, when the plot against my retainers Kuwaori Muneyasu and Nakano Munetoki was discovered, the agreement was not fulfilled. At this time, factional strife among my retainers gradually brewed into a crisis of disaster; seeking to drive a wedge between Tanemune and Harumune, you—while still at a young age—acted with caution and prudence, believing that by following your father's will, you would avoid losing your brother's heart. Consequently, you and several of your retainers traveled far and wide, seeking no worldly gain. At this hour, the realm was divided and warlords vied for power; for those aspiring to govern the state, this was the very moment to act. You rose in sudden resolve and conspired with Haneda, Ibano, and others to attack and capture Endo, Oki, and Omori Castles, where you then resided. You further attacked and captured Horikoshi, Noto, and Hachichome Castles; news of this spread through the nearby villages, and they came to submit. Thus, you were entrusted with the two castles of Omori and Hachichome. Lord Harumune was most cautious, and from then on, the bond between brothers grew deeper. In the early days of Genki, Nakano Munetoki again plotted rebellion, similar to the Tenbun Disturbance. You conspired with the Mogami, Iwase, and Iwaki clans to overcome the internal turmoil and bring peace to the province. Although you ultimately did not challenge the Uesugi clan, as your agreement had been established, the henki and crest granted to you by Sadazane were used for the rest of your life. Later, Lord Harumune specially decreed that the bamboo-and-sparrow crest would forever be the emblem of the Date clan. Furthermore, you were appointed head of the imperial clan to serve as the wing of the imperial house. In your later years, you retired and took the name Seiansai. You passed away on the 16th day of the 4th month of Tensho (the year of the Fire Pig), the 61st year since your birth in the 6th year of Daiei (the year of the Fire Pig). You are buried half a ri southeast of the ruins of Yorin-ji Temple in Ogura Village, within the Omori district of Shinobu County, Oshu, with pine trees planted as a marker. The posthumous name was Dokusho-in Kessan Goei. Your first wife of the Hatakeyama clan predeceased you; your second wife of the Date clan bore you a son, Shigezane, who succeeded the house and rendered great service to the domain's founder, receiving the fief of Watari and Uta districts. The family lineage continued to grow prosperous. You were a man of gentle and steady disposition, yet possessed far-reaching vision and the ability to accommodate great talents; thus, many generals and soldiers from all directions sought your counsel. During the Keicho era, the head of Yorin-ji (the character "bun" below "lin") built Daiyu-ji in Watari to serve as the shrine for your spirit. In the Tenpo era (the year of the Fire Monkey), a shrine was built to enshrine you. However, since Yorin-ji is located over ten ri beyond the provincial border and has no marker for your grave, it gradually fell into ruin. Thus, your 15th-generation descendant, Kuninari, fearing your sin of neglect, acted in October of Keio (the year of the Wood Ox) by order of the domain to guard Edo Castle. In June of the following year, upon completing your term, you returned to your domain. Passing by Yorin-ji, you visited the grave and resolved to erect a monument to preserve your memory forever. Your retainer, Ken'in, inscribed the epitaph, recounting these deeds. As I am unlettered, how could I possibly fully express your great virtue? Nevertheless, as you pursued the path of remembrance to return your kindness, I firmly agreed to do so, for I could not remain unlettered amidst such turmoil. I therefore humbly composed this inscription: "Externally, warding off invaders; internally, purifying the walls; with profound strategy and great vision, extending power and prowess; the son of the clan, the light of the house, a legacy for ten thousand generations; the family lineage flourishing, with pines growing lushly—this is your legacy." This monument was carved for the hopes of future generations. In the summer of the 4th month of Keio (the year of the Fire Rabbit), your 15th-generation descendant, Date Kuninari, inscribed the plaque. Your retainer, Maeda Sane-shi, respectfully wrote it.

shigezane:buhen109.title: Record of Military Anecdotes, Episode 109
shigezane:buhen109.summary: My ancestor, Sugihara Hitachi-no-suke Chikanori, was a meritorious retainer for generations, from Uesugi Kenshin to Kagekatsu. Having heard detailed accounts of the Uesugi clan, the bamboo-and-sparrow crest was originally the crest of the Uesugi clan.
shigezane:buhen109.markdown:
In the Tale of Sugihara Hikozaemon, a retainer of Sakai Sanuki-no-kami Tadakatsu,

My ancestor, Shigezane Date, was a distinguished retainer of the Uesugi clan, spanning generations from Kenshin to Kagekatsu. Having heard the details of the Uesugi family, I learned that the clan's crest—the sparrow atop a bamboo stalk—was originally the Uesugi crest. The Uesugi were descendants of Fujiwara no Kanshuji Naofuji, the Minister of the Inner Palace of the Northern House. The crest of Kanshuji was the sparrow atop a bamboo stalk. For this reason, the Uesugi also used the sparrow atop a bamboo stalk. However, it is said that during the campaign at Sekigahara, Kagekatsu and Date Masamune fought a battle and drove Masamune back, seizing the Uesugi banners; hence, the Uesugi family adopted the sparrow atop a bamboo stalk. This is a grave misunderstanding. While it is true that after the victory at Sekigahara, the entire realm aligned with Lord Ieyasu, the Uesugi clan remained in Aizu and refused to obey. Masamune fought them relentlessly, engaging them in battle until the following year. The date Masamune seized the Uesugi banners was April 26, Keicho 6, the year after Sekigahara. The Uesugi's holdings were Fukushima Castle and Yanagawa Castle. At Fukushima Castle, Honjo Echizen-no-kami Shigezane, his son Dewa, Amakasa Bingo, Iwai Bitchu, and Sugihara Hitashige were stationed. At Yanagawa Castle, Suda Oi-no-suke Nagayoshi, Kurano Tanba (a retainer of Satake who provided reinforcements at this time), Chikuchi Shuri, and Yokota Daigaku were stationed. This was the boundary between Masamune and Uesugi. At a distance of three ri from Fukushima Castle, there was a place called Segami. Nearby was a river called Matsukawa, a tributary of the Okuma River. Since this river was the first gateway (toguchi) to Masamune's territory, it was fortified by over five thousand men, including Honjo Dewa, Amakasa Bingo, Iwai Bitchu, Sugihara Hitashige, Kurio Mino, and Okano Sanai. Nevertheless, Kagekatsu's forces, accustomed to repeated victories, disregarded Masamune's side, treating them as mere nets to catch birds. Masamune had previously instructed the commoners at Segami and Matsukawa to "raise a signal if the Uesugi forces are careless." Consequently, upon seeing the Uesugi forces' negligence, the commoners raised straw mats or wide strips of cloth high on their poles. The Uesugi soldiers noticed this and replied, "If they look like flags, will they appear as numerous as the enemy?" The Uesugi soldiers agreed and left them as they were. Masamune's side, seeing this, sent word to his camp at Koyama Village. Masamune had advanced with Sendai, crossed the Kunimi Pass, and crossed the Segami River in Shinobu District, establishing a camp at Koyama. At dawn on April 26, he launched an attack with approximately twenty thousand men. However, he divided his forces, sending five thousand under Shibata Kohei, Nakame Daigaku, and Ishikawa Yahei to block Yanagawa Castle, while Masamune attacked Matsukawa with ten thousand five hundred men. Kagekatsu's elder retainer, Suda Oi, was at Yanagawa Castle. At Matsukawa's camp, the Uesugi side, unaware of this, sent scouts who returned saying, "Masamune has advanced to Koyama and is pressing toward Yanagawa." Nevertheless, Masamune also refused to be careless; the on-duty armored units, Kurio Mino and Okano Sanai, charged out across the Matsukawa stream. Upon reaching it, a merchant from the Koyama side arrived, saying, "Lord Masamune has advanced with about thirty thousand men; it is difficult to resist them in small numbers." Honjo Dewa and the other generals arrived one after another. Hearing the merchant's words, they debated whether to block the Matsukawa stream and wait for the enemy, or to let it pass and strike them halfway. Matsuki Takumi said, "Masamune is mindful of our surprise. However, if we wait for them, our numbers will surely be outmatched and our momentum will falter. We should cross the river." Kurio said, "This river is deep and like a whetstone. Crossing it is a grave undertaking. Moreover, Masamune's army is large. We should let Masamune cross the river first and strike them halfway." Okano advanced, saying, "Even if we block the enemy's inner ranks, we cannot gauge their strength; if they fear the great army and fail to advance, we shall suffer a later disaster. We shall cross the river and wait for Masamune." Kurio, displeased, said, "As the son said, the general cannot predict the enemy; he must match the small force with the large and strike the strong with the weak—this is the way of the North. Now, the strength of the great enemy is their captivity. Is this not foolish?" After repeated discussions with Sanai, Amakasa and Sugihara arrived. Sugihara said, "Long discussions are useless; we must present a plan and let Masamune see the situation for himself." Honjo then dispatched Honjo Dan'emon, Izutsu Kohaya, and Inomata Shuzen as scouts. Inomata returned and said, "Masamune has crossed the river." Honjo Dewa and Amakasa asked why. Inomata replied, "Masamune is approaching, taking advantage of our surprise. However, we shall seize the opportunity when he reaches the riverbank and withdraw. If we cross the river and pursue him, we shall turn the tables and strike them halfway." Then, Dan'emon and Kohaya charged out, saying, "We cannot let Masamune cross the river without delay." Dewa and Hitashige heard this, and Shuzen and Dan'emon had different opinions, so they asked why. Shuzen said, "Masamune has not removed the mud from the horses and has kept his spears and slings as usual. Furthermore, he has pulled the small baggage and foot soldiers away from the river, so the river cannot be crossed." Dan'emon and Kohaya said, "That is not the case. Why would Masamune not yet have reached the riverbank when preparing to cross? If he crosses, there will be no delay in preparation. Also, pulling the baggage and foot soldiers far downstream means the enemy is waiting for the battle. Masamune will cross the river and prepare for the crossing. Considering the timing, we believe it cannot be delayed." Everyone agreed. "Having come so far with a great army, should we withdraw without letting Masamune cross the river?" The Uesugi generals agreed. While they were preparing to strike them halfway at the riverbank, Okano said, "Let us not waste the words spoken earlier." He led his unit across the Matsukawa stream, positioning his forces with their backs to the river, waiting for Masamune. Amakasa and Kurio said, "If Masamune has positioned his cavalry upstream and his foot soldiers downstream, his plan is to charge upstream and push the foot soldiers downstream to cross the river. Now that the great army is about to cross all at once, we must not cross the river." Thus, Fuse Jiro, Kitagawa Tosho, Odagiri Shozaemon, Shiga Yosoemon, and Yasuda Kansuke—about twenty riders—were sent. Sanai was ashamed of his intentions and broke military law, crossing the river. Sanai joined his forces and pushed back the remaining troops, saying, "I shall not be ashamed of a few words and shall lose a great advantage. No one else shall cross the river." At that moment, Masamune's ten thousand five hundred men charged forward in full force. The vanguard, Katokuro Kojuro, was first, followed by Date Awa, and others, including Date Shigezane, Yashiro Kanageyu, Moniwa Iwami, Date Aki, Takano Iki, and Kuwaori Tenryo, who formed ranks and charged forward. Local villagers joined in, filling the riverbed with about twenty thousand men. The Uesugi vanguard, Okano Sanai, with only four hundred-odd men, formed a spear-head formation and defended the front. However, Masamune's great army overwhelmed them; Sanai was surrounded by about a hundred men, broke the encirclement, escaped, and crossed the river to retreat. Masamune pursued them rapidly. At that moment, Uesuki's Kitagawa and Odagiri attacked, saying, "Our allies are defeated and the battle is already critical; we must be killed. I do not know the safety of the fourteen-year-old son, who remains in Aizu. We must surely seize the opportunity and serve Lord Kagekatsu." He removed a scarlet haori (a short coat) from his armor and gave it to Odagiri, saying, "Take this as a memento and give it to your wife and children." Odagiri replied, "The customs of warfare dictate that I, too, must die. If I am unwilling to die, I shall give it to my son," and took the haori, tucked it into his waist. Kitagawa said, "I have no intention of forgetting this now," and retrieved it from the river, charging into the enemy. "I am the Uesugi Kagekatsu, a mighty warrior. Seeing you fall, I shall use you as a lesson to my soldiers," he shouted, raising his sword. He rode his horse into the center of the enemy, wearing the gold-colored official's standard, and after twelve or thirteen men were killed, he was slain. Fuse, Yasuda, Takariki Tosho, and others were the elite soldiers of the Uesugi family. Kitagawa followed, scattering sparks and fighting in fierce combat, killing many. The remaining Uesugi forces collapsed into the river; the number of those killed is unknown. Masamune also joined the vanguard and fought. Okano, wearing armor with horn-shell crests, had a decorative ornament on his neck and rode a scarlet haori on a deer-colored horse, retreating at the riverbank. Seeing Masamune as a strong enemy, Masamune mounted his horse. Sanai struck him with two thrusts; Sanai was startled, leaped back, and was cut clean through. Masamune struck him from the center of his armor, cutting through the chest armor and cutting the sash of the sword with a second thrust, cutting through to the right knee. Masamune's horse stumbled and he fell, breaking his arm. In that opening, Sanai charged into the river and retreated. Masamune pursued with about ten riders, shouting, "Return and settle this!" Sanai turned back and cursed, "Those who are sharp-witted do not return amidst a crowd!" and charged up the south bank. Because his armor and equipment were heavy, Masamune did not even realize it. He later heard that it was a regrettable loss. Okano's group and others later joined, all crossing the Matsukawa stream to retreat. Yasuda Hyozaemon, aged sixteen, was a renowned warrior on the opposite bank of the Matsukawa. Seeing his father, Minbu, ride his horse toward the camp of Masamune, he charged forward. Kurio saw this and shouted, "Minbu's group has repeatedly defeated others even after crossing the river; why do they cross the river to attack the enemy? You are the son of the great general Yasuda. Why do you speak so recklessly?" Minbu turned back and said, "Discernment comes from the heart. Look! My son Hyozaemon is on the opposite bank and is about to be killed; there is no need for my spirit to be shaken." He charged forward and brought Hyozaemon back with him. At that moment, Masamune's followers arrived. Minbu also joined with Okinoike Jingozaemon and Machino Shusui, fighting across the river; all three were renowned. Masamune's vanguard, Katokuro, charged across the river, but Katokuro's men pushed them back toward the river, pursuing them as they fled. Honjo, Sugihara, and Iwai followed and attacked. Masamune's second line, Date Awa and Katokuro, did not assist and withdrew slightly. Seeing this, Sugihara cautioned his soldiers, saying, "The enemy is not retreating in a straight line. We must not pursue them." Just then, as planned, Awa charged forward with Masamune's banners. As they bypassed the Uesugi side and attempted to cut off their retreat, the Uesugi army was completely defeated. The distance to Fukushima Castle was eighteen ri by country road (six cho and one ri, with a hundred and eight cho of main road and three ri). The Uesugi forces retreated toward there. Masamune pursued them urgently, and the number of Uesugi wounded and dead was unknown. Armor, weapons, and equipment were left scattered across the road. Many men and horses, exhausted, collapsed and breathed heavily. Furthermore, those with long poles and spears, even those one shaku long, were mostly abandoned. The Uesugi side—Imogawa Nuidono, Iwai Bunchu, Nagai Zenzaemon, Aoki Shinbei, Shiga Yosoemon, Odagiri Shozaemon, and Yasuda father and son—totaled fifty riders, riding in the rear. Among them, Aoki wore a black robe with a bird-feather staff, and Nagai wore a red robe with a gold-colored half-moon; they appeared particularly distinguished. Aoki, riding a small horse with a short, light spear, gained freedom and defended the terrain. Amakasa was a mighty general of the Uesugi family, specifically the lord of Shiroishi; he was considered Masamune's primary strategist. However, in June of that year, while he was away in Aizu, the castle warden, Nobukage Shikibu, rebelled and took Shiroishi. Masamune, feeling this grievous, retreated and fought repeatedly. This time, Honjo, Sugihara, Iwai, Tetsu, and Ueno fought several times, pushing back from the Matsukawa stream to Fukushima Castle. When they reached the bridge of Fukushima Castle, Masamune's forces, led by Masamune, rushed forward. Masamune's vanguard, Katokuro, charged across the river. shigezane:buhen110.summary: At Ippaku-dono in Echizen, there was a messenger named Oida Kanmono. He was originally a ronin of the Uesugi clan. According to what this Kanmono's grandson recounted,
shigezane:buhen110.markdown:
At Ippaku-dono in Echizen, there was a messenger named Oida Kanmono. He was originally a ronin of the Uesugi clan. According to what this Kanmono's grandson recounted,

The crest of a sparrow on bamboo is the hereditary crest of the Uesugi clan. The reason the Date clan adopted the sparrow-on-bamboo crest was that a request had been made by Lord Uesugi. Long ago, the lord of Echigo Province was known as Uesugi Fusanori, and he resided in his castle within the provincial capital of Echigo. His lineage, Uesugi Shigezane, was also the lord of Kamijo Castle in Echigo. In the fifth month of the sixth year of Eisho, Nagao Rokuro Tamekage, a senior retainer of the Uesugi clan, rebelled and slew his lord, Uesugi Fusanori, at a place called Amego. Among the many Uesugi retainers, Usami Suruga-no-kami Sadayuki, the lord of Biwajima Castle, was twenty-one years old, yet his name was renowned for his repeated military achievements. On this occasion, he gathered the forces of Chisaka, Saito, Honjo, Kanazawa, and Naoe, and planned a battle to strike down Fusanori. He appointed Uesugi Shigezane of the Kamijo line as general and immediately presented Sadayuki the sword Bizen Nagamitsu, a treasured heirloom of Usami. This sword was a magnificent piece; the fact that Usami possessed such a formidable blade filled Sadayuki with boundless joy. Consequently, he gave it the nickname "Usami Nagamitsu" and kept it as a private treasure. Thereafter, the unrest in Echigo was settled. However, although Uesugi Shigezane had daughters, he had no sons. His son-in-law, Date Hyobu—the second son of Date Uemune—was sixteen years old; it was said that Shigezane regarded him as his grandson and that the boy was exceptionally gifted. He was sent to Oshu, and Hyobu was formally adopted as Shigezane's son. At that time, Shigezane sent a character from his own name and the bamboo-and-sparrow curtain of Usami Nagamitsu as a gift of congratulations. Date Hyobu was renamed Uesugi Hyobu Saneyuki. During the Tenbun era, just as he was about to go to Echigo, a dispute arose between his father, Uemune, and his brother, Harumune; thus, Hyobu Saneyuki was unable to proceed to Echigo and remained in Shinobu. Ultimately, he did not go to Echigo. Nevertheless, as the crest had been passed down through his mother's line, he kept the sword of Usami Nagamitsu and the bamboo-and-sparrow curtain as private treasures, which he eventually handed over at the request of his brother, Harumune. It is said that the Date clan began using the bamboo-and-sparrow crest from this point. The sword of Usami Nagamitsu is also said to have been passed down within the Date clan. Furthermore, among the two men who took the bamboo-and-sparrow curtain at the Yanagawa front, Soda Uheiji possessed an exceptional horse; he was heard to be a master of the horsemanship of Tomomori, the Shimosa-no-kami of Ise Province. He studied the art of horsemanship by observing the horse's movements and, after serving for three years, returned to Aizu and became a master of horsemanship. When he was transferred to Uesugi Yonezawa, he became a ronin and served Hori Tango-no-kami Naoyori, the lord of Murakami Castle in Echigo. Among those who were proficient in operations from the Matsukawa-guchi to the Fukushima-guchi, Aoki Shinbei, Okano Sanai, and Nagai Zenzaemon were considered the finest.

Reference > [Buhen Wakigaki](http://www.konan-wu.ac.jp/~kikuchi/buhen/)

shigezane:buhen111.summary: Usami Sadayuka was known as his father, Etchu-no-kami Takatada. Takatada was a senior retainer to Uesugi Sagami-no-kami Fusasada Nyudo Jotai, the lord of Echigo Province.
shigezane:buhen111.markdown:
Usami Sadayuki was the son of Etchu-no-kami Takatada. Takatada was a senior retainer to Uesugi Sagami-no-kami Fusasada (who had entered the priesthood as Jotai), the lord of Echigo Province. In the first year of Eisho, when Fusasada's son Uesugi Akisada fought against Uesugi Asayoshi and Hojo Soun at Kawagoe in Musashi Province, Usami Etchu-no-kami Takatada and his son Suruga-no-kami Sadayuki marched to the front of Kawagoe with 18,000 troops to assist Akisada from Echigo. Battles occurred frequently. On one occasion, a single enemy scout armed with a spear emerged; Etchu charged, cut down the enemy, and while striking the spearman, he severed the oak shaft of the spear and sliced through the spearman's head down to the front teeth. This man was Usami Nagamitsu. Such incidents occurred frequently. Etchu eventually passed the leadership to his heir, Sadayuki. As noted above, in May of the sixth year of Eisho, at a place called Amamizo, Uesugi Fusanori was killed by Nagao Rokuro Tamekage. Although more than half the province sided with Tamekage, Sadayuki alone did not follow him. Since his lord Fusanori had no sons, he appointed a member of the Uesugi clan, Uesugi Hyogo-no-kami Shigezane, as general, mobilized the hereditary Uesugi troops—including those of Chisaka, Saito, Naoe, and Honjo—and barricaded themselves in Kamijo Castle and the castles of Honjo, Shibata, and Gosen to engage in battle with Tamekage. At that time, he presented the long-established sword of Naga**mitsu** to Shigezane. At this juncture, the Uesugi side had few soldiers, lacked provisions internally, and had no means of external defense. Usami Suruga-no-kami was twenty-one years old at the time; though young, he gathered the people and urged them with tears, saying, "To strike down the enemy of one's lord is the ultimate desire of a warrior—a matter of loyalty and righteousness. I shall die in battle this time and leave my name behind. Sadayuki, you too shall expose your corps to a righteous fight and share the same pillow as the others." Consequently, the troops were moved by his words and resolved firmly, declaring, "We shall certainly accompany him in death." While awaiting reinforcements from Hachigata, Fusanori's elder brother, Uesugi Akisada, invaded Echigo from Hachigata; Tamekage was defeated and retreated to the west coast of Echigo, opening the way for Kamijo. The following year, Tamekage conspired with Shinano warrior Takanashi Settsu-no-kami Masayori to invade Echigo and fought against Akisada. On the 20th day of the sixth month of the seventh year of Eisho, they fought at Nagamorihara in Tsumaari, Echigo Province, and Akisada was killed. He was fifty-six years old. Echigo once again fell to Tamekage. At this time, Uesugi Norifusa, the lord of Shirai Castle in Koshu (the father of Kanrei Norimasa), and Akisada were in the same camp; Norifusa subsequently retired to Koshu. At this time, Kamijo Shigezane was made the son-in-law of Nagao Tamekage and a peace agreement was reached, but Sadayuki did not follow this. Following Akisada's will, he petitioned for the son of Koga Kubo Takamoto to be appointed as Akisada's successor, taking the name Uesugi Shiro Akisada. He entered Hachigata, while Suruga-no-kami barricaded himself in Matsuyama Castle in Echigo; for fourteen years from the seventh year of Eisho to the first year of Daiei, he remained in conflict with Tamekage. In the first year of Daiei, through the mediation of Kanrei Norifusa, a peace agreement was reached between Tamekage and Suruga, and Echigo was brought under control. In the fifth year of Daiei, Kanrei Norifusa passed away. As his son Norimasa was four years old, he petitioned for Prince Kenju, the youngest son of Koga Kubo Takamoto, taking the name Uesugi Awa-no-kami Norihiro and succeeding the Uesugi line. At this time, the Koga Kubo granted Usami Sadayuki a military fan (gunbai-uchiwa). It was said that the succession of the Uesugi line was solely due to Usami's military achievements.

References > [Buhen Wa Kikigaki](http://www.konan-wu.ac.jp/~kikuchi/buhen/) [Wikipedia: Usami Sadamitsu](http://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%AE%87%E4%BD%90%E7%BE%8E%E5%AE%9A%E6%BA%80)

shigezane:castle.markdown:
**☆ [Exploring Ancient Castles of Ou](http://www.ne.jp/asahi/saso/sai/index.html)**

A database of castles in Ou, from ancient to early modern times, centered on Miyagi Prefecture.

**☆ [Oshu Castle Wall Customs](http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~EX8A-INYU/)**

A website focusing on medieval castles and fortifications in the Tohoku region, as well as related figures and battles. It also includes explanations of the Waga, Hienuki, and Asonuma clans.

**☆ [Old Castle Exploration Notes](http://jurosodoh.cocolog-nifty.com/j_catsles/)**

A blog about castle tours centered on the Tohoku region. In addition to keep castles, it also features medieval fortifications.

**☆ [Castling for Two](http://www.linkclub.or.jp/~juta/castling/)**

A castle exploration journal. This volume is incredible!

**☆ [Sakura to Oshiro](http://www13.plala.or.jp/sakushiro/)**

A castle exploration journal. The sheer volume is incredible! Highly recommended.

**☆[Miyagi Archaeological Information](http://www.miyagi-ann.org/index.htm)**

It provides detailed information on the excavation of the Sendai Castle stone walls.

**☆ [Association to Protect the Stone Walls of Sendai Castle](http://www.vegalta.net/%7Eishigaki/)**

A group of researchers examining the issue of preserving the stone walls of Sendai Castle.

shigezane:comic.markdown:
Listed in order of publication date. Older entries are at the bottom. Comics with two or more volumes are sorted by the publication date of the first volume.

**[Crying at the Moon ‐Masamune Date at the Keicho Dewa Campaign‐](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4041208173/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4041208173&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

2013.9.26 Yoshisada Tsutsumi, Kadokawa Shoten. "The Sekigahara of the North," beginning with the Bunroku Campaign. Wow! I think this might be the first work—whether a novel or a manga—to focus primarily on this era! I'm most drawn to this period.

**[The One-Eyed Dragon Masamune Date—The Fierce Dragon of the North Who Survived the Turbulent Era (SP Comics SP Pocket Wide)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4845841541/ref=as_li_tf_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4845841541&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

2012.3.12 Kenji Okamura, Reed Publishing

**[The One-Eyed Dragon Masamune](http://blog.kahoku.co.jp/dokuganryu-masamune/)**

Sept. 4, 2011– Mayumi Chiba: Currently serializing in the Kahoku Shimpo Kahopyon Children's Newspaper. No other work has depicted the parent generation with such care. Terumune, Masakage, and Sanemoto are wonderful!

**[Mikazuki Ryu Ibun 1—Masamune Date Koshi (Burai Comics)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4790123995/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4790123995&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

2011.6.28 Yoshisada Tsutsumi, Shobunkan. I think it might be hard to follow without some prior knowledge, but I'm glad that not only the Date forces, but also the Satake and Soma have distinct characterizations! So cool!

**[Valientes: Date's Demon Kojuro Katakura 1 (Zenon Comics)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4199800107/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4199800107&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

2011.4.20 Katsuki Tanaka, Tokuma Shoten Zenon Comics. Terumune, Sazuki, Shigezane, Satake—basically, all the characters are so cool. And the fact that Masamune is slightly pathetic is just great (lol).

**[Masamune Date—A New Take on the Sengoku Comic Anthology (Burai Comics)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4790123790/ref=as_li_tf_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4790123790&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

2010.12.28 Matsubunkan

**[The Demon of Date: Strategist Kojuro Katakura (BUNCH COMICS)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4107715310/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4107715310&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

2010.12.9 Katsuki Tanaka, Shinchosha Bunch Comics, Kirra Kira no Kojuro!

**[Sengoku Shuju Ibunroku, Vol. 4: Continued—Masamune Date & Kojuro Katakura (ID Comics DNA Comics)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4758005796/ref=as_li_tf_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4758005796&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

This is an Ichijinsha anthology from July 24, 2010.

**[Biographies of Sengoku Figures: Masamune Date (Comic Edition: History of Japan)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4591119661/ref=as_li_tf_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4591119661&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

July 2, 2010 Toru Sugita, Poplar Publishing, "Comic Edition: History of Japan" series

****

**[Dokuganryu Kai (Gangan Comics IXA)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4757528930/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4757528930&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

2010.6.18 Yuka Fujikawa, Square Enix. Was this the steampunk Masamune? (My memory is a bit fuzzy). I think Terumune was pretty cool.

**[The One-Eyed Dragon: Masamune Date](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/B00FBBIPPK/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=B00FBBIPPK&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

April 19, 2010 Kenji Okamura, Reed Publishing

**[Sengoku: Oda Nobunaga, Date Masamune, Sanada Yukimura, Uesugi Kenshin (Comic Edition: NHK History Secret Stories Historia)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4781603009/ref=as_li_tf_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4781603009&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

2010.2.10 NHK Production Team, East Press. A manga adaptation of the NHK program "Rekishi Hiwa Historia."

**[Sengoku Warlord BL Anthology: Masamune Date (Action Comics Boys Love Series)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/457594260X/ref=as_li_tf_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=457594260X&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

2009.12.21 Futabasha

**[Tono to Issho (MF Comics)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4840119503?ie=UTF8&tag=oysannohitori-22&linkCode=as2&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4840119503)**

2007.9.22 Kai Oba, Media Factory. A Sengoku-era 4-panel comic. Masamune also features prominently.

**[Sengoku BASARA 2 (Dengeki Comics)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4840240140?ie=UTF8&tag=oysannohitori-22&linkCode=as2&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4840240140)**

2007.8.27 Haibara Yaku: A manga adaptation of the game "Sengoku BASARA 2." The Date clan is a gang of delinquents, but the coolness of Masamune and Kojuro is outstanding. I actually really like this kind of thing.

**[Princess General Masamune's Tale: Bontan!!](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4344809904?ie=UTF8&tag=oysannohitori-22&linkCode=as2&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4344809904)**

2007.5.24 Abegawa Kineko, Gentosha. A princess raised as a man takes the name "Bontenmaru"... A gag manga. I was momentarily put off by the idea of a female Masamune, but once I started reading, I found it incredibly entertaining. While maintaining the style of a gag manga, it also takes great care in depicting Hatakeyama, Ouchi, and Mogami, faithfully following the historical record.

**[Girls Who Time-Traveled (Unification of the Realm Arc)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?path=ASIN/4063609286&link_code=as2&camp=247&tag=oysannohitori-22&creative=1211)**

May 12, 2005, Yumi Kayama, Kodansha Manga Bunko. Features a lovey-dovey shoujo manga about Masamune and his beloved wife.

**[Biographies of Sengoku Warlords: Masamune Date](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/ASIN/4845827948/oysannohitori-22)**

2004.12.25 Go Nagai & Dynamic Pro, Reed Publishing. Plenty of things to nitpick, but it's still undeniably entertaining.

**[The One-Eyed Dragon Masamune](http://www.sasappa.co.jp/publishing/book04.html)**

April 25, 2002. Mayumi Chiba. Sasagi Publishing. Believe it or not, a biography of Masamune in Italian-Italian parallel text! The red and yellow cards issued by Hideyoshi and Ieyasu are quite amusing. Since it's by Mayumi Chiba, it's also brimming with love for Hasekura. An English version is also available.

**[The Era of Princess Kubo](http://www.post.japanpost.jp/ikiiki/tohoku/iwaki.htm)**

March 19, 1996, published and edited by Iwaki City [Relaunch Vote](http://www.fukkan.com/vote.php3?no=3446). A manga adaptation of an original work by Iwaki City, created through a public call for entries. The modern-day Harumune and Princess Kubo are wonderful. It is somehow brimming with Christianity. It is full of love. It is also valuable as a manga depicting the Tenbun Disturbance.

****

**[The Fascicle Chronicles: Hasekura Tsunenaga—The Samurai Who Raced Across the Globe](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/ASIN/4832300512/oysannohitori-22)**

1992.1.10 Mayumi Chiba, Hobun-do. A masterpiece on Hasekura. A must-read! A must-read! Do not dismiss it as mere manga. Tsunenaga is wonderful—filled with pride even as he struggles between his identity as a Christian and his identity as a Date.

**[Dandy dragon & spring・tiger (Fan Fan Series)](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4812814014/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4812814014&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

1990.11.1 Nano Takahashi, Minori Shobo

A parody manga of a Taiga drama. I loved it, but it's out of print. It was later reprinted by Tsukasa Shobo. The link leads to the reprint.

**[Masamune Date](http://bookstore.yahoo.co.jp/shoshi-331177/)**

July 20, 1987, Masami Ishii, Keisei Publishing. True to its series title—"Behold the Lower-Body Affairs of the Sengoku Warlords in Their Fierce Battles!"—it's thoroughly adult. The lower-body affairs may have been interesting, all right...

****

**The One-Eyed Dragon Soars**

June 30, 1987. Written by Mamoru Sasaki, illustrated by Shigeru Tsuchiyama, Kobunsha. The Masamune figures are somewhat stoic. It might be unusual for it to end with the birth of Hidemune. A bit mature.

**[The One-Eyed Dragon Masamune](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4591025241&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

June 1, 1987. Keisuke Nishimoto (Author), Akio Ito (Illustrator). For children. Masamune is cute.

**[Masamune Date: The One-Eyed Dragon of the Sengoku Period](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4051025640&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

May 1, 1987. Koji Kawate. Gakken Manga Biography Series

**[The One-Eyed Dragon Masamune 1: The Era of Bontenmaru](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4893531387/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4893531387&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

April 1, 1987. Mayumi Kagawa. Fusosha. A manga featuring Fudoson and Kongara and Seika in prominent roles. The art is by Mayumi Chiba, though the PN is different. It had an exquisite energy and was entertaining.

**[Masamune Date—Educational Manga Story](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4893221884/ref=as_li_qf_sp_asin_tl?ie=UTF8&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4893221884&linkCode=as2&tag=oysannohitori-22)**

Feb 1, 1987, Ryo Yoshizumi, Koshobo. Beautiful artwork. Shigezane is cute. The level of detail is superb.

**[Masamune Date—The Brave General of Tohoku](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4051023222&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

Sept. 1, 1986. Tsunezo Murotani. Gakken Manga Japanese History Series. His art is strangely popular with my kids...

**[Masamune Date](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/406260339X?ie=UTF8&tag=oysannohitori-22&linkCode=as2&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=406260339X)**

Sept. 1, 1986. Mitsuteru Yokoyama. This is the go-to manga for Masamune. A manga adaptation of Sohachi Yamaoka's original work. But I prefer [Iga no Kagemaru](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/B00007C921&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211).

**The Fierce Warrior of Michinoku: Masamune Date**

1976 Goro Tonomura (Author), Shigeru Koido (Illustrator), Obunsha

1955 Jun Shibata. Tokyo Manga Publishing Co.

shigezane:dainihon940.title: Letter from Shigezane Date, January 16, Kan'ei 10
shigezane:dainihon940.summary: Letter from Shigezane Date, January 16, Kan'ei 10. The opening reads: "1. Should any difficult matters arise in the world, I inquire as to how many people I should bring along—specifically, I refer to you." "That is what I intend to state..."
shigezane:dainihon940.markdown:
1. Should any difficult matters arise in the world, I inquire as to how many men I should bring along. While this is a matter of formal report, as orders were issued in secret, the number of men for Kojuro was mentioned; furthermore, as people began to speak of inquiries and caused a commotion among the common folk, it would not be appropriate for you to do so. Moreover, as there is currently no pressing matter, I did not mention it during your ascent. Nevertheless, as the matter you inquired about remains as it stands, I hereby submit this written report. I request that you be informed. Has everything you inquired about been reported? If not, I fear that urgent inquiries may arise. Since things have not turned out this way and are as they are now, I believe it would be best to remain quiet from time to time. Even if we speak a little, it should be as you wish. This is a grave matter.

1. As is customary, we shall be stationed in a distant province. While I wish to bring as many men as possible, I cannot do so; and since there are no others available, I report this as it stands. Though this is our final service, we lack the strength. I speak this out of necessity. I offer this in all humility. Respectfully submitted.

Furthermore, as this is indeed the case, should it be possible, I intend to bring even a single additional person along; however, it is regrettable that this cannot be done. That is all.

(Kan'ei 10) January 16, Date Awa-no-kami Shigezane, kao

To Lord Ishimoda Daizen and all concerned

## Record of the Number of Retainers of Shigezane Date

Memorandum

1. 100 muskets: Ashigaru; 1. 50 muskets: Rural retainers; 1. 50 muskets: Non-retainers; 1. 50 bows: Ashigaru; 1. 100 spears: Ashigaru; 1. 50 spears: Non-retainers

50 Ashigaru as listed above

1. 70 mounted cavalry; 420 personnel; 1. 50 people; small arms and equipment; 1. 10 people; relay riders; 1. 40 people; baggage officers and attendants; 1. 10 horses; 10 people; 1. 70 horses; small baggage; 1. 50 people; as listed above

End

The above totals 1,169 personnel—both mounted and on foot—and 155 horses.

January 16, Kan'ei 10: Shigezane Date, Awa-no-kami (kao)

---

The above is from the Archives of Ancient Japanese Documents, Vol. 3: Date Family Documents, Part 2, 939.

shigezane:date-link.title: Date-related links
shigezane:date-link.summary: The library on Masamune is incredibly extensive. It's great that it includes book reviews.
shigezane:date-link.cover_alt: Illustration from the Reference and Archives
shigezane:date-link.markdown:
****

**[The One-Eyed Dragon of the Realm: Masamune Date](http://park6.wakwak.com/~masamune/)**

The library on Masamune is incredibly extensive. It's great that it includes book reviews.

**[Yume no Ato](http://www008.upp.so-net.ne.jp/yumeno-ato/)**

Masamune and the Shinsengumi. I'm looking forward to seeing the introduction of Masamune's letters.

**[Masamune@One-Eyed Dragon](http://www.ne.jp/asahi/gu-tara.web/gu-tara/)**

Plenty of travelogues about Masamune. Plenty of photos, too.

****

**[Miyagi History Tour: The Thirteen Successive Generations of Date](http://hb2.seikyou.ne.jp/home/fm/)**

A website introducing the successive lords of the Date clan's Sendai domain, from Masamune to Yoshikuni, as well as historical sites related to the Date clan.

**[Miura Family Documents Research Society](http://www.geocities.co.jp/CollegeLife-Club/6700/)**

A website focusing on the Miura family, who were retainers of the Uwajima Domain.

**[A Study of the Burial Grounds of the Watari Date Family, Retainers of the Sendai Domain](http://www2.nkansai.ne.jp/users/monmuse/wataridateke/top-mokuji.htm)**

This is a research study on the burial grounds of the Watari Date family. As expected of a curator, it's incredibly detailed. I'm looking forward to the whole thing being posted.

**[Date Masamune Museum: Date Family Memorial Society](http://datemasamune.com/)**

The website of Yasumune, the current head of the Date family in Sendai. It's rich in many ways. The photos are stunning.

**[Miihaa Edition: Heisei Date Family Records Annex](http://www008.upp.so-net.ne.jp/tomeas/)**

A chronicle of the Date clan, from their ancestors to the successive lords. I secretly use it as a reference guide (lol).

****

**[Akatombo Zuihoden Guide Journal](http://zuihoden.web.fc2.com/)**

Zuihoden Volunteer Guide Journal

**[Sengoku Library](http://sekirei.nomaki.jp/index.html)**

A site primarily focused on book reviews, centered on works related to Masamune.

****

**[“The Date and Isa Clans”](http://www.geocities.jp/venusandmars1975/)**

The history of the Date clan began when the sons of Hitachi Nyudo Nensai—who held territory in Isa District, Hitachi Province (now part of Chikusei City, Ibaraki Prefecture)—were granted Date District by Minamoto no Yoritomo and took the name “Date.” For Hitachi, the ancestral home of the Date clan, see the Isa clan website.

**[Kojuro Katakura](http://www.city.shiroishi.miyagi.jp/section/kikaku/m2k/index.html)**

The Kojuro Katakura site for Shiroishi City. Even though it's a local government site... it's packed with moe!!

**[Atsushi Takakura's Miyagi Local History](http://takakura.fd531.com/)**

That Mr. Takakura has launched a website! It's packed with photographic materials.

**[The Kunii Family Lineage and the History of Komagamine Castle](http://www.rak1.jp/one/user/kk9210kk/)**

The History of the Kunii Family—Retainers of the Miyauchi Clan of the Sendai Domain—and Komagamine Castle

**[Shigebe's DIY Armor Club & Tracing the Footsteps of Shigezane Date](http://sigechannohe.blog.fc2.com/)**

Exploring Historical Sites Related to Shigezane and Crafting My Own Armor, etc.

**[\[sd-script\]-Writing about him-Personal archive on Shigezane Date, a retainer of the Date clan](http://sd-script.hateblo.jp/)**

A research site on Shigezane Date

**[Rokkencho Medieval History Research Group](http://app.f.m-cocolog.jp/t/typecast?blog_id=1801983&user_id=1811374#top)**

Official blog of the Tohoku Gakuin University Medieval History Research Group. Also features introductions to back issues of academic journals.

Details unknown
