shigezane:datenikki-ver.markdown:
## Masamune-ki and Shigezane-ki

The biography of Masamune Date written by Shigezane Date is generally referred to as the "Masamune-ki" or the "Shigezane-ki." This biography is broadly divided into two lineages. Namely,

- Courtly letters, primarily military chronicles dating up to around Sekigahara.
- A work written in an archaic style that records Masamune's daily life and later years in addition to military chronicles.

These are the two lineages. While the former is written in the style of a memorandum, the latter is more systematically organized; it is believed that the latter was compiled by refining the content after the former had been established.

For convenience, this article will refer to the former as the "Shigezane-ki" and the latter as the "Masamune-ki," following the variations found in the Sendai Sosho edition.

The bibliographic information is summarized below. Note that in preparing this article, I drew heavily on [Shigezane's Works and Other Records of Masamune's Words and Deeds](http://sd-script.hateblo.jp/entry/2013/06/04/225040) and [The Distinction between the "Masamune-ki" and the "Shigezane-ki"](http://sd-script.hateblo.jp/entry/2012/12/20/133459) from Kei-san's site, [\[sd-script\]-Writing about him-](http://sd-script.hateblo.jp/). I add this note with gratitude.

## Published books (printed)

### "Shigezane-ki" lineage

- [“Shigezane-ki”](#/post/shigezane/shigezaneki-mokuji) Included in Volume 3 of the Sendai Sosho. Republished by Hobundo in 1974.
- "[Date Nikki](#/post/shigezane/datenikki)" is included in Volume 21 of the Battles section of the Gunsho Ruiju.

### "Masamune-ki" series

- "Masamune-ki," included in the Sendai Sosho Publication Committee's Sendai Sosho, Vol. 11. Republished by Hobundo in 1974.
- Included in "[Masamune-ki](#/post/shigezane/masamuneki-index)," Jinbutsu Orai-sha Sengoku Shiryo Sosho 10, "Date Shiryoshu Jo." Text is being progressively digitized at [\[sd-script\]"Masamune-ki," a private archive concerning Shigezane Date, a retainer of the Date clan](http://sd-script.hateblo.jp/entry/2012/06/24/132626).
- "Lord Masamune's Military Fan: Autograph Manuscript by Shigezane Date" (Date Family Related Materials 916・35-1–2) → (Transcription included in ["Watari Date Family Historical Materials"](http://www.funkawan.net/book/books.html). Autograph??)

### Lineage unconfirmed

- "Masamune-ko Gunki": Gunkirui San (Kokushi Sosho No. 24) / Edited by Kokushi Kenkyukai, 1920
- "Date Nikki": Sendo Gunki; Iwaiwa Gunki-shu / Rekishi Tosho-sha 1979 [\[sd-script\]The "Date Nikki" Sendo Gunki edition, a private archive concerning Shigezane Date, a retainer of the Date clan](http://sd-script.hateblo.jp/entry/2014/07/11/175254) is being progressively digitized.

## Items available to view or download online via digitization

- "Date Nikki" [Kyoto University Digital Library](http://ddb.libnet.kulib.kyoto-u.ac.jp/minds.html), held in the Tanimura Collection.
- Morioka Museum of History and Culture: 4 volumes of the "Masamune-ki" manuscript, Genroku 10. Micro/digital information 281-584-2, 312 frames. Available in the Japanese Rare Books/Micro/Digital Catalog Database held by the [National Institute of Japanese Literature](http://www.nijl.ac.jp/). Reproduced. Also available for online viewing.

Additionally, the Sendai Series is being uploaded sequentially to the National Diet Library's Modern Digital Library.

shigezane:dateshi0804.title: Letter from Shigezane Date, August 4, date unknown
shigezane:dateshi0804.summary: Letter from Shigezane Date, August 4, date unknown. The opening reads: "Regarding the residence there, since the moat on the Domachi side has been filled in, the estate has been encroached upon by about two ken. While this is indeed the case, when viewed from the west, the view..."
shigezane:dateshi0804.markdown:
Regarding the residence in question: since the moat in the Domachi area has been filled in, the property has been pushed back by about two ken. While this may have been requested in haste, looking from the west, if there were no fences along the town boundary, it would consist entirely of row houses and would appear unsightly. Regarding the moats and fences within the town, the situation is as described above; stables should also be constructed. From the Shoemon residence in Domachi, the houses and residences continued in succession, and no row houses were visible from the alleys. Therefore, I requested that the moat be filled in and that row houses be built on the embankment of the property; although Shoemon subsequently made such a request, it proved unsightly upon inspection and was therefore abandoned. As such, stables should be constructed within the space. Respectfully submitted.

August 4, Shigezane (seal)

shigezane:dentyuu.title: Lord Shigezane Date damages the pillar
shigezane:dentyuu.summary: The completed Sendai Castle. "The moon only waxes and wanes," Shigezane remarked, as he struck the main pillar with his axe. While the other retainers marveled, wondering if he had lost his mind, Masamune simply smiled and said, "Good."
shigezane:dentyuu.markdown:
The completed Sendai Castle. "The moon only waxes and wanes," Shigezane remarked, as he struck the main pillar with his axe. While the other retainers marveled, wondering if he had lost his mind, Masamune simply smiled and said, "Good."

From "Anecdotes 16: Lord Shigezane Date Damages the Main Pillar," included in *Masamune Date* by Shien Takahashi.

## Original text

After Masamune had completed the construction of Sendai Castle, he held a banquet to celebrate the castle's completion. At this time, Shigezane Date turned to Kagetsuna Katakura and said, "Generally, one shuns fullness. The moon waxes and wanes, and flowers bloom and fall. Now that the castle is complete, it bears the sign of fullness; therefore, one should damage a part of it." He then took up an axe and damaged a main pillar. The retainers stared in astonishment, deeming him mad. Masamune, seeing this, smiled and said, "This is quite well done."

shigezane:dousai.title: The Tale of Yamaguchi Dosai (Excerpt)
shigezane:dousai.summary: Memoirs of Yamaguchi Inonojo, a former retainer of Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu, compiled starting in 1981 for "History of Nihonmatsu City, Vol. 3: Materials on the Primitive, Ancient, and Medieval Periods." The base text is reportedly included in the Sendai Sosho.
shigezane:dousai.markdown:
Compiled from the memoirs of Yamaguchi Inonojo, a former retainer of Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu, from "History of Nihonmatsu City, Vol. 3: Primitive, Ancient, and Medieval Periods, Source Materials Edition," 1981. The base text is reportedly included in the Sendai Sosho. ※Partial excerpts. Kanji and kana have been rewritten for readability.

Around the 13th year of Tensho, Terumune Date was on friendly terms with Masamune Date and Yoshikuni Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu; during the conflicts between Soma and Date, troops were dispatched from Nihonmatsu to the Date side on two occasions. Through these personal ties, Date Hyobu-no-daifu Sanemoto—the lord of Hachichome Castle in Shinobu District (Masamune's uncle and father of Awa-no-kami Shigezane)—maintained close relations with Yoshitsugu, and there was constant correspondence between the two parties. Within Yoshitsugu's inner circle, Yusa Shimosa had long been on friendly terms with Hyobu-no-daifu and was frequently dispatched as a messenger.

(Omitted)

In August of Tensho 13, Masamune reached an agreement with Lord Tamura to attack and crush the Ouchi of Bizen; the Ouchi evacuated their castle and moved to Iwakado Castle, and from there entered Nihonmatsu before retreating to Aizu. Consequently, Masamune moved to the Ouchi's residence, the castle of Yokohama in Yohonmatsu; furthermore, at a castle called Miyamori, four or five cho away, resided Terumune (by Tensho 15, both Bizen and Sukeemon had entered Masamune's service). As Terumune shared a close relationship with Yoshitsugu, he felt for Yoshitsugu's plight and, wishing for him to reach a peaceful settlement, said to Yoshitsugu: "As things stand now, it shall not be possible for the world to remain at peace. Masamune's side will exert considerable effort to mediate, so please give your careful consideration and reply." When Terumune repeatedly sent detailed messengers, Yoshitsugu summoned his clan—including Shinjo Danjo and Yamato—as well as other senior retainers, beginning with Kanokoda, to consult with them, and said: "Though Terumune has repeatedly sent such messages, it is regrettable that a family lineage inherited for generations should fall to the Date in my generation. In the end, I believe there is no choice but to take up the cause of the Date, fight, and, if fortune fails, commit seppuku. However, if you have any particular views, please speak without hesitation." After a moment when no one spoke, Shin'an, Yamato, and the other senior retainers said: "We believe your words are most reasonable; however, Masamune has gained control of approximately 20 ri in all directions from Yonezawa to this area, and moreover, he has seized most of the small castles held by us. The Ouchi have also vacated their castles, and rumors have reached us that both the senior and junior retainers of the hereditary house have turned their hearts toward the Date. Furthermore, the castles we hold are utterly besieged. Terumune has sent repeated messages stating that, from the Sugita River above to the Aburaiya River below, five villages within that area shall be taken as vassal lands, while other castle-holders and manor-holders shall remain in their castles and manors as is now, and serve the Date by taking a stipend of one-tenth of their original landholdings; if this proves successful, it would be appropriate for you to concur. Since you currently cherish Aizu, you have not even sent witnesses; it is as if you were already under the banner of Aizu. As long as you occasionally send a small token of gratitude to Yonezawa, there should be no public gossip regarding your residence in this castle." When they repeatedly offered this remonstrance, Yoshitsugu also agreed to concur.

In Yoshitsugu's reply to Terumune, he wrote: "I am deeply humbled by the repeated and heartfelt messages of your kindness. Those who have served us until now were originally taken into service by Masamune; as a matter of leniency, we have been granted five villages within the district." Terumune was pleased that matters had settled peacefully and held talks with Masamune, who stated that Yoshitsugu had long maintained a close relationship with him and his father, and that this had been agreed upon among the senior retainers. Masamune replied, "I recall that during the time of the Soma conflict, you provided assistance twice. However, in recent years, the repeated reinforcements to the Ouchi and Ishikawa have been most regrettable." As Terumune explained various points, Masamune came to understand. The messenger was young, Shigezane Date-no-kami, but since he had a lineage of service to Yoshitsugu (his father, Date Sanemoto, was the lord of Hachichome Castle and maintained a close relationship with the Nihonmatsu region), he was able to serve. Yoshitsugu was pleased, and on the 7th day of the 10th month of the 13th year of Tensho (Year of the Rooster), at the hour of the Goat, he unexpectedly traveled from Nihonmatsu to Obama and visited the camp of Date Awa-no-kami. There, he expressed his gratitude for various matters. As time drew near evening, he announced, "I shall not be able to meet with Terumune tonight. I shall depart tomorrow." Upon hearing this, Yoshitsugu returned from Miyamori. On the early morning of the 8th, Yoshitsugu sent a messenger to Awa-no-kami, stating, "I finally arrive today to express my gratitude for all matters." When Awa-no-kami immediately reported this to Terumune, Terumune ordered him to depart promptly. At that time, Masamune had gone out for hawk hunting in the vicinity; two or three messengers were sent to fetch him, but he did not return. Date Ueno-no-suke and many other senior retainers visited Miyamori to report that the peace agreement at Nihonmatsu had been successfully concluded and was a cause for celebration. Yoshitsugu also departed for Miyamori promptly. Among Yoshitsugu's attendants were Takabayashi Naizen, Kanokoda Izumi, and Otsuki Nakatsukasa; these three were summoned to the reception room. As Izumi took his seat, one of Yoshitsugu's retainers whispered something to Izumi—a matter that would later come to light. It was then that the saying "evil arises from below" came to mind. Whether it was the work of the heavenly demon, it was a bitter and distressing experience. A low-ranking retainer accompanying Yoshitsugu went to the stables and saw a servant with the blade of his wakizashi drawn. A fellow servant said, "What are you doing? Today, Lord Nihonmatsu has returned in peace; there are no more arrows, and both parties are delighted—it is said there is a banquet in the reception room. What a foolish thing this is." To this, the servant replied, "Do you not know? When Lord Nihonmatsu returns, there was a secret order to kill every single person without exception. I, too, wish to become a renowned warrior and am making preparations for it." When the lower-ranking attendants heard this, they were greatly astonished. When they told the samurai, they exclaimed, "How regrettable, to have been deceived and slain!" They first called Kanokoda and informed him in detail, saying, "The lower-ranking men are making preparations for this." Izumi then informed Yoshitsugu, saying, "Please exercise your discretion." Terumune replied, "Both yesterday and today you have visited; it is truly a most auspicious occasion. As Masamune has gone to the hawk fields, I shall send people to fetch him. I intend to offer him a feast, but given the season, it would be difficult if you were to feel constrained. I offer this cup as a token of my celebration." Yoshitsugu expressed his gratitude for the prior and subsequent visits, and Terumune gave Yoshitsugu a cup, which Yoshitsugu then returned to Terumune. From there, the cup was passed to Kanokoda and then to the other two, and it was presented to the senior retainers of the Date. Afterward, there was no further idle chatter, and everyone departed. As they were being seen off casually to the entrance, Yoshitsugu struck the ground with his hand and said, "I consider your hospitality and kindness to be excessive, but I have now heard that you intend to kill us." He then grabbed Terumune's collar with his left hand, drew his wakizashi with his right, and seven or eight of his attendants moved behind him. The path was narrow, enclosed by bamboo and a fence; the Date retainers and others were helpless. As they called out, "Lock the gates!", the attackers suddenly emerged from the gate and surrounded him. The Date retainers, in a panic, all followed behind them bare-skinned, crying "Good heavens!" in astonishment. Hanzawa Gennai, an attendant of Yoshitsugu, held a spear, Yuzato Kuro held a bow, and the others, with drawn swords, surrounded Terumune. They advanced from Obama to a spot called Awanosu, within one and a half ri of Obama, where the Date forces fired two muskets simultaneously. Without any command, everyone was cut down in an instant. Yoshitsugu and his 36 attendants, along with over 50 other foot soldiers, were all slain without a single survivor. Masamune immediately rushed to the scene, but there was nothing to be done; that night, he established his camp at a place called Takada (15 cho from Nihonmatsu, a boat crossing on the Abukuma River). Yoshitsugu's corpse was crucified at the edge of Ogawa, at the head of the town of Obama. A pine tree was planted there. It is said that commoners suffering from smallpox can recover if they shave off a piece from this pine and drink it. Furthermore, the site of the massacre was named Awanosu, and about ten pine and willow trees were planted there. There are four or five private houses there, and it is said that fires are lit there in July.

While Shinjo Danjo was serving as the castle warden of Nihonmatsu Castle, two musket shots were suddenly heard. "This is alarming. While I go to fetch them, everyone put on your armor," he declared. The men prepared themselves and left the castle, proceeding south to a boat crossing called Takada. There, two friendly foot soldiers approached from the opposite direction, panting heavily, and said, "It is as you say—everyone, starting with the general, has been slain without a single survivor. We were ordered to return and report the news, so we have fled." Upon hearing this, Shinjo was shocked and ordered, "Go and check on the Awanosu." This messenger (whose name I have forgotten) hurried across the river and climbed a rock atop Mount Takada, known as the Observation Rock; looking down, he saw the dead strewn about like scattered counting rods.

shigezane:e4-26.title: Letter from Shigezane Date, November 4, Tensho 17
shigezane:e4-26.summary: Letter from Shigezane Date, November 4, Tensho 17. The opening reads: "I write to you urgently. Accordingly, within the camp, there has been a growing sense of estrangement among us. I am deeply concerned. Accordingly, messengers have been dispatched from Kurokawa and Sukagawa to deliver this to the camp..."
shigezane:e4-26.markdown:
I humbly submit this message. As for those within the camp, appearances suggest they have grown estranged from one another. This leaves me feeling uneasy. Accordingly, messengers have been dispatched from Kurokawa and Sukagawa to deliver this to the camp. As Motoyasu and Sessai are reportedly absent, while we remain in close contact, once the camp is disbanded, there will be no choice but to proceed. I understand that a letter has also been sent to them privately; since they have been informed of this, I leave the matter to their discretion and fully entrust the arrangements to them. I offer my sincerest and most respectful regards.

(Tensho 17※) November 4, Shigezane (seal)

To Endo Bunshichi

※ I think Takesui dates back to Tensho 13. Scroll down for details.

## Rough translation

I am writing in haste. While at the camp, we have remained estranged, and I am deeply concerned. Consequently, messengers were dispatched from Aizu and Sukagawa to deliver a message to your camp. Since neither Motoyasu nor Sessai—the intermediaries—were present, they turned to me; however, as the Master was away from the camp, there was nothing that could be done. They say they have also sent a private letter to him, so as the matter stands, I earnestly request your mediation on their behalf. I beg of you once again. With utmost respect and humility.

## A bit of idle chatter

In the source, "Documents of the Endo and Nakajima Families, Senior Retainers of the Date Clan: Sengoku Period Edition" (published by the Shiroishi City Board of Education), the note for the phrase "随而自黒河須賀川御陣へ" states: "This refers to the march from Aizu Kurokawa Castle to Sukagawa in Iwase District. In November 1585, Masamune Date attacked the Nikaido clan at Sukagawa and forced their surrender." Based on this note, it feels as though it should be read as "from Kurokawa to the Sukagawa camp." On the other hand, the reading version in the same book places a "・" between "随而自黒河" and "須賀川御陣へ." This makes it "from Kurokawa and Sukagawa to the camp."

Of course, since the original text contains no punctuation or "・" marks, we have no choice but to interpret it; therefore, this site has adopted "from Kurokawa and Sukagawa to the camp."

Wait—what? Tensho 17?? The Nikaido clan surrendered on October 26. This letter is dated November 4. Of course, it is entirely plausible that the post-war settlement was still dragging on until around this time.

While this contradicts the term "advance," since Masamune was in Sukagawa, one could interpret it as "Sukagawa Camp"—referring to Masamune's location—and suggest that the Kurokawa resident sent a messenger to him. However, given Shigezane's expressions of respect and his request to Munenobu to "intercede on his behalf," it seems more natural to me to consider this a messenger from another house. Furthermore, while it mentions "disbanding the camp," indicating that Masamune had vacated his position, he essentially remained in Sukagawa from the time he captured Sukagawa Castle on October 26 until his return to Aizu-Kurokawa in December (Jike Records). It also feels off that the Kurokawa resident would use such influential figures as Motomune Watari and Masakage Rusu as intermediaries.

A messenger arrived at Masamune's camp, but Watari Motomune and Masakage Rusu, who were supposed to relay the message, were absent. Shigezane had no choice but to receive them, but Masamune had vacated his camp just before that. In other words, Masamune and Shigezane had been in the same camp until just moments before this. If Masamune and Shigezane were in the same campaign from late October to early November, the possibilities are quite limited. One is Tensho 17, as identified in the "Documents of the Endo and Nakajima Families—Sengoku Period Edition" of the Date Clan Senior Retainers—specifically, the time when Sukagawa surrendered. In fact, there is another applicable year: Tensho 13, just before the Battle of Hitotoribashi. Moreover, at that time, Masamune, who had besieged Nihonmatsu, was blocked by snow and vacated his camp on October 21 to return to Obama.

Reading this as "from Kurokawa and Sukagawa to the camp" and dating it to Tensho 13, Aizu-Ashina and Sukagawa-Nikaido would be on the same side as Masamune, and "opening the camp" would also correspond to the camp evacuation on October 21, which also fits well.

For these reasons, Takesui believes that this document dates from Tensho 13.

However, one thing that doesn't quite add up is that Endo Munenobu was still only 13 years old in Tensho 13 (according to the theory he was born in 1572). In a document written by Endo Motonobu on October 11—ten days before his ritual suicide—he refers to himself as "Senkuma-dono," meaning he had not yet undergone his coming-of-age ceremony. As for "I have also written to you privately," even if a letter had been sent to Endo Motonobu, it feels a bit odd to tell a 13-year-old boy, "Just go along with it!" There is also a theory that Endo Munenobu was born in 1568; in that case, he would have been 17 in Tensho 13. While it wouldn't be unnatural for Shigezane to assign him work, this in turn raises the question: "Wait, he's 17 but hasn't had his coming-of-age ceremony??"...

shigezane:gakuyuu.title: Is the theory that Masamune and Date were schoolmates true?
shigezane:gakuyuu.summary: Since this has become something of an established view, it may be tactless of me to say this, but whether Shigezane was Masamune's schoolmate since the days of Bontenmaru is quite—quite doubtful.
shigezane:gakuyuu.markdown:
Since this has become something of an established view, it may be tactless of me to say this, but whether Shigezane was Masamune's schoolmate since the days of Bontenmaru is quite—very doubtful. There is no mention of this in primary sources, nor in the family records or genealogies of the retainers. While Terumune is cited as Shigezane's eboshi-oya (ritual sponsor) (in the commemorative volume), the location was Omori rather than Yonezawa, suggesting that Shigezane did not appear to have resided permanently in Yonezawa. Furthermore, the surviving letters from Masamune employ a style that reflects respect rather than familiarity toward Shigezane, making it unlikely that he was constantly in close attendance. While they may not have been strangers, it is highly probable that this is a later invention, given that Masamune and Shigezane were of the same generation.

shigezane:gusoku.title: Shigezane Date's Armor and Camp Jacket
shigezane:gusoku.summary: There are several items said to be the armor and camp coats of Shigezane Date.
shigezane:gusoku.markdown:
There are several items attributed to Shigezane Date, including armor and battle jackets. Since artifacts such as armor and battle jackets are prone to confusion regarding their provenance or subsequent repairs, please keep in mind that—unless the provenance is exceptionally well-established—they are generally marked as "attributed to" (伝), meaning "it is said to have been..." They will be introduced below. Click the photos to view enlarged versions. Please use your browser's back button.

## Armor and Equipment Attributed to Shigezane Date, Collection of the Date City Pioneering Memorial Museum

Quoted from the brochure of the Date City Pioneering Memorial Museum. When it comes to Shigezane's armor, this is the one: a Sendai-do armor featuring a caterpillar-shaped crest. This piece, passed down through generations as the armor used by Shigezane Date, was exhibited at the Pioneering Memorial Museum in 1958 and has been preserved ever since. For some reason, there have been occasional claims recently that Shigezane's crest is a "centipede," but it is actually a "caterpillar."

A detailed report can be found in [Shigebe](http://sigechannohe.blog.fc2.com/)'s [Shigezane Date's Armor — Date City Pioneering Memorial Museum — Part 2](http://sigechannohe.blog.fc2.com/blog-entry-201.html).

[The item at Yuri-kan in Watari Town is a replica of the armor crafted by Kozan-do](http://yoroinokozando.blog65.fc2.com/blog-date-20100312.html). Additionally, a [replica by Marutake Sangyo, commissioned by Watari Town](http://www.yoroi.co.jp/shige.html) was reportedly produced and donated to a museum in Aomori.

## Armor and Equipment Attributed to Shigezane Date, Collection of the Date City Pioneering Memorial Museum

The Date City Pioneering Memorial Museum also houses another set of armor, said to have belonged to Shigezane Date. According to [Shigezane Date's Armor — Date City Pioneering Memorial Museum — Part 2](http://sigechannohe.blog.fc2.com/blog-entry-201.html),

> They mentioned that the other suit of armor had a bulging midsection, and if it had been made to fit Shigezane's build, he might have suffered from middle-age spread in his later years.

End of quotation. The information is provided by the current head of the Date family of Watari.

Nanban-do? Not exactly, is it?? The relationship with the "Kosha armor" introduced below remains unconfirmed.

## "Shigezane Date Armor," held by Daiyu-ji Temple on Mount Iburi

Quoted from the brochure of Daiyu-ji Temple on Mount Iburi in Date City, Hokkaido. It is reportedly on display in the treasure house. Its provenance is unknown. It is not a Sendai-do. The lack of kusazuri is notable. And above all, the crescent-shaped maedate is striking.

However, according to information provided by a visitor, some also believe that, seeing the actual armor, it does not appear to have been used by Shigezane.

Speaking of crescent moons, the armor of Date Sanemoto (held by the Date City Pioneering Memorial Museum), featured in "Date Shigezane: 400th Anniversary of His Entry into Watari," also features a crescent moon on the maedate and on the okegawa-do of the armor.

Quoted from "Shigezane Date: 400th Anniversary of His Entry into Watari." This armor, featuring a crescent moon maedate, is also shown in the pamphlet for the "Shigezane Date Exhibition" held at the time of the Yuri-kan's opening. This armor is also featured in the [Pioneering Memorial Museum pamphlet shown above](http://shigezane.info/majime/nazo/gusoku/narumi-gusoku.jpg), but it is somewhat concerning that the maedate is not attached here. According to [a visit by Nekota-san in November 2010](http://ameblo.jp/nek-o-hal/entry-10712059236.html), the maedate was reportedly absent.

\------- Added 2012.6.19: I received [information from Shigebe-sama regarding the crescent moon maedate of Daiyu-ji Temple](http://sigechannohe.blog.fc2.com/blog-entry-113.html). Below is a quotation.

> Regarding the crescent moon, I received an email from someone at the Funka Bay Cultural Research Institute (judging by the name, perhaps a descendant of Shige-chan??) after I asked about that crescent moon maedate. > "Now, as for the armor owned by Daiyu-ji, only the maedate might be different. The texture suggests that the material is not from that period. > Since the crescent moon maedate has such a strong impact, it may have been made after the move to Hokkaido. > The caterpillar maedate in our collection is made of bear fur. > It doesn't feel fluffy to the touch; it's a bit firm."

End of quotation. The implication is that the maedate is from a later period than the armor. As noted in [the comment I received from Mr. Nozaki on my blog](http://shigezane.seesaa.net/article/275553921.html), it is often said that "in the Sendai Domain, the generals wore crescent moons and the hatamoto wore half-moons" (I have also read that "head of the clan" is used instead of "general," and "samurai general" instead of "hatamoto"). The crescent moon maedate of the Jitsumoto armor at the Pioneering Museum may also not be paired with it recently based on the judgment that it is a later addition.

## Kosha Armor, Collection of the Date City Pioneering Memorial Museum

Quoted from "Shigezane Date: 400th Anniversary of His Entry into Watari". Since it is said that Shigezane favored the incense-chariot mark (Watari Town Local History Museum Opening Commemorative Shigezane Date Exhibition Pamphlet), it appears that this piece is treated similarly to the armor used by Shigezane. The Sendai do-gusoku armor said to have belonged to Shigezane Date. The haidate is covered in incense-chariot marks.

## Incense-chariot jinbaori

Quoted from "Shigezane Date: 400th Anniversary of His Entry into Watari." A jinbaori said to have belonged to Shigezane Date. The ruffles on the cuffs and the bamboo-and-sparrow crest and incense-chariot motif on the back are striking. According to [Nekota-san's visit report from November 2010](http://ameblo.jp/nek-o-hal/entry-10712059236.html) on [“Tokiminari”](http://m-pe.tv/u/page.php?uid=tokiminari&id=1&guid=on), it is said to have a karakusa pattern on the collar. It is believed to be a set with the incense-chariot armor (Watari Town Local History Museum Opening Commemorative Shigezane Date Exhibition Pamphlet).

I have a feeling that the style of the jinbaori from Musui is from around the late Edo period (the cut from the hem to the back, the shape of the bamboo-and-sparrow crest, etc.)—what do you think?

## Scarlet Jinbaori, Collection of Kotoni Shrine

Quoted from [Kotoni Net "Tondenhei Village Festivals Across the City"](http://www.kotoni.net/event/eventnews/2005/0829/0829.htm). The Kotoni Tondenhei, who settled in Kotoni, Nishi Ward, Sapporo, hailed from Aizu and Watari; Takehaya Chio-no-Mikoto (Shigezane Date) is also enshrined at Kotoni Shrine. Among the artifacts housed at Kotoni Shrine is one said to have been used by Shigezane Date.

Meanwhile, according to [Nekota-san's visit report from November 2010](http://ameblo.jp/nek-o-hal/entry-10700035558.html)... Quoted below:

> I visited the library inside the "Nishi Ward Community Center." > It was a small library, but I was surprised by how many people used it! > Here are some notes from a book I read there. > ■ In 1875, Seisaku Makino of Kotsutsumi Village, Watari District, moved to the Kotoni Tondenhei Village with his family of nine, including his father, Gondayu. > Gondayu had served as a martial arts instructor to the lord of Watari; he used samurai speech—such as "shikaruni..." and "sayo-de"—and lived to the ripe old age of 101. > Seisaku was a man of sturdy, unpretentious build who served in the Satsuma Rebellion, the First Sino-Japanese War, and the Russo-Japanese War, becoming the only officer from Miyagi. > He also played a central role when Kotoni Shrine was built; at that time, he offered a scarlet jinbaori (camp jacket), a family heirloom passed down through the Makino family, which is now a treasure of Kotoni Shrine. > This jinbaori was granted to the previous generation (perhaps Gondayu, or someone before him) by the lord, who had worn it for distinguished service in the field. At the same time, they were granted the bamboo-and-sparrow crest, and the Makino family uses the same crest as the lord (the Watari bamboo crest?). > 【From the story of Seisaku's grandchild】 > ↓ > This is likely the bright red jinbaori that is said to have been worn by Shigezane...

End of quote. Ah, I guess... ^^; This one didn't look very Sengoku-esque either, so I was a bit puzzled.

shigezane:h127.title: Letter from Masamune Date, October 9, Kan'ei 6
shigezane:h127.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, October 9, Kan'ei 6. The opening reads: "Yesterday, I visited out of courtesy and was pleased to receive your hospitality. Accordingly, a tea jar has arrived from the Kamigata region. Privately, at the Nishi-kuruwa, I have been mindful of the opening ceremony, but the construction has not yet been completed..."
shigezane:h127.markdown:
Yesterday, I visited out of courtesy and was granted a welcome. Accordingly, a tea jar has arrived from the Kamigata region. Privately, at the Nishi-kuruwa, I intend to make the opening address, but the preparations have not yet been completed; first, I shall have a cup of tea at the enclosure on the morning of the 11th. Please wait for me. With utmost respect.

I have also dispatched word to Ibushu. Furthermore, Jibu-no-tasuke is also to accompany you. Respectfully.

(Kan'ei 16, Ka) 9th day of early winter, Masamune (kao)

Date Fushu's Residence

shigezane:h135.title: Letter from Masamune Date, January 4, Tensho 15
shigezane:h135.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, January 4, Tensho 15. The opening reads: "The day before yesterday, I sent a messenger to collect the items. In particular, I viewed the (gold radical plus shell) and was quite satisfied. At the start of the year, this is only fitting. Now then..."
shigezane:h135.markdown:
The day before yesterday, I dispatched a messenger to deliver the items. In particular, (金偏に貝) also viewed them and was quite satisfied. At the start of the year, this was an appropriate gesture. Now, having heard that there has been no news regarding swords and the like in Shibukawa, I present to you the swords I had previously been privileged to hold. Furthermore, though it be a humble offering, I enclose a single-layered kosode. I trust you may appreciate this gesture as one born of sincere devotion. Accordingly, regarding the matters of the southern region, I believe you will be satisfied and in agreement. In any case, I believe the handling of this spring's affairs will be most fitting. Truly, this should be as you stated. With utmost respect and humility.

Postscript: I shall offer my greetings once more at the New Year. At that time, all is well. That is all.

(Tensho 15, Ka※) January 4, Masamune's signature

Lord Goro

※ I think Takesui dates back to Tensho 14. Scroll down for details.

## Rough translation

The day before yesterday, I received a messenger and specifically viewed the (gold radical with shell). I am satisfied. It is fitting for the start of the year. Now, having heard that the swords and other items at Shibukawa were damaged, I shall return the swords I reluctantly entrusted there some time ago. Additionally, though they are separate pieces, I am enclosing a single-layered kosode. Please accept this as a small token of my appreciation. Furthermore, I believe you have heard and are satisfied with the arrangements regarding the southern region. In any case, one cannot over-consult regarding the handling of this spring. For further details, please refer to the messenger's account. I humbly submit this.

P.S. I believe I will accept the offer again after the New Year. At that time, various matters.

## A bit of rambling

The source, "Date Masamune Documents: Supplement (VIII)" (City History Sendai vol. 24), dates the document to Tensho 15, noting that Masamune's kao resembles Type 2 (February 16–August 24, Tensho 15).

Incidentally, this letter mentions the place name "Shibukawa." Consequently, on Twitter, Haru-san and Jin-san were discussing whether this might date to Tensho 14, when Shigezane was stationed at Shibukawa.

So, I cross-referenced the contents of the letter with the materials I had on hand.

The "Date Tensho Nikki" survives for January of Tensho 15. The diary provides detailed accounts of Masamune's daily activities and who visited and what transpired; however, there is no mention of a messenger from Shigezane visiting Masamune in the entry for January 2, nor is there any record of Masamune writing this letter in the entry for January 4. Within the Date clan, "matters of the southern region" refers to the situation along the Sendo, but I cannot think of any significant developments in the Sendo region during Tensho 15.

Let us consider Tensho 14. The passage "regarding the fact that there has been no news of swords, etc., at Shibukawa" suggests that Shigezane had been in Shibukawa in the relatively recent past. Shibukawa was a castle located roughly midway between Hachichome and Nihonmatsu, on the border between the Date and Hatakeyama clans. Shigezane operated out of Shibukawa from November of Tensho 13 until the Battle of Nihonmatsu in July of the following year, Tensho 14. While I am not entirely certain of the free translation of "no news of swords, etc.," I believe it carries the nuance that there was some issue with the swords. Since Shibukawa was burned down by accidental fire in December of Tensho 13, this could be interpreted as damage sustained at that time. On January 1, Tensho 14, the Battle of Shibukawa took place, and after the war ended, Shigezane sent the heads he had taken to Masamune. It would make sense if the messenger from "the day before yesterday"—January 2—was that very messenger. As for "matters of the south" and "the handling of affairs this spring," these could be seen as referring to the fact that some senior retainers in Nihonmatsu defected to the Date side in the spring of Tensho 14.

And so, like Haru-san and Jin-san, I also think it might be Tensho 14.

As for the character 付記 (the "gold" radical plus "shell"), a search brought up "barium." They must have based it on the sound... I hear that the very similar character （金偏に見） refers to a small spear.

shigezane:h62.title: Letter from Masamune Date, November 18, Kan'ei 6
shigezane:h62.summary: Letter from Masamune Date, November 18, Kan'ei 6. The opening reads: "I have delivered the tea caddy as promised. I delayed without taking advantage of this brief window. I have acted contrary to my original intention. Before my trip to Edo, had I secured even a moment's respite, I would have visited at once and met with my entourage..."
shigezane:h62.markdown:
I present the tea caddy as promised. I have delayed, failing to seize the opportunity. I have acted contrary to my original intention. Before my journey to Edo, should I find a moment, I intend to visit you at once and meet you in private. I humbly submit this letter.

Furthermore, I have something to report regarding Wakasa. Sincerely.

(Kan'ei 16, Ka) 18th day of mid-winter, Masamune (kao)

Date Fushu's Lodgings

shigezane:hajimete.title: For First-Time Visitors
shigezane:hajimete.subtitle: Shigezane Date and How to Navigate This Site
shigezane:hajimete.summary: What kind of warlord was Shigezane Date, and where can you read the 319 available documents? This is the introductory article for "Neo Shigezane Zanmai," providing a recommended reading order.
shigezane:hajimete.markdown:
This site, "Neo Shigezane Zanmai," is a restructured version of "Shigezane Zanmai" (administrator: TAKEMI Shigino)—a site dedicated to Shigezane Date—featuring 319 searchable entries. For those overwhelmed by the sheer volume of material and unsure of where to begin, we have provided a guide to get you started.

## Who was Shigezane Date?

Shigezane Date (1568–1646) was a military commander and cousin of Masamune Date. His father was Sanemoto Date, and his childhood name was Tokimunemaru. The Date family crest, "Sparrow on Bamboo," is known as the crest of Shigezane's lineage.

As Masamune's right-hand man, he stood at the forefront of both battles and negotiations; during the Battle of Hitotoribashi in 1585, he fought valiantly to protect Masamune, the commander-in-chief. In 1595, he clashed with Masamune and fled, wandering from place to place before returning to his service in 1600. He subsequently moved to Watari (present-day Watari Town, Miyagi Prefecture), where he became the founder of the Watari Date clan.

He is also known as the author of the *Shigezane-ki*, in which he recorded his own experiences, and was a military commander who excelled in both martial prowess and literary talent.

## Recommended Reading Order

### 1. Trace his life through a timeline

To get an overall picture, a timeline is your best bet. You can trace the period from 1539 to 1646 using a horizontal scroll axis proportional to time.

[Open horizontal scroll timeline](https://oosawak.github.io/neo-shigezane-zanmai/nenpyou-timeline.html)

Click here if you'd prefer to read a list of articles.

[Shigezane Date Chronology](https://oosawak.github.io/neo-shigezane-zanmai/#/post/shigezane/nenpyou)

### 2. Read the biography

[Shigezane Date: Brief Biography](https://oosawak.github.io/neo-shigezane-zanmai/#/post/shigezane/ryakureki)

This provides a summary of his life's trajectory and a guide to the historical sources used.

### 3. View highlights in the battle chronicles

[Battle of Hitotoribashi](https://oosawak.github.io/neo-shigezane-zanmai/#/post/shigezane/hitotoribashi)

This is the battle that made Shigezane famous. You can find other battles by following the "Battle Records" guide on the top page.

### 4. Shigezane as a Noh Performer

[Noh Play: Surigami](https://oosawak.github.io/neo-shigezane-zanmai/#/post/shigezane/noh-suriage)

These are the lyrics and commentary for a new Noh play based on the Battle of Surigami, featuring Shigezane as the protagonist (shite).

### 5. Shigezane's own writings and letters

[Shigezane-ki I](https://oosawak.github.io/neo-shigezane-zanmai/#/post/shigezane/shigezaneki-1)

The *Shigezane-ki* is included in the "Works" category, along with the *Masamune-ki* and *Date Nikki*. 119 letters associated with Shigezane and the Date clan are in the "Correspondence" category. You can filter them using the guide card on the top page.

## About the Materials

Each article includes a link to the original page and a clear citation. The content of this site is published under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 2.1 Japan (CC BY-SA 2.1 JP) license, based on the license of the original work, *Shigezane Zanmai*. Text and photographs contributed by third parties are not reproduced; they are replaced with links to the original pages.

**[Masamune Date and the Keicho Mission to Europe](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4882161869&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

Kazuo Takagi.

**[Masamune Date's Black Ships: Confessions of a Fabricated History](http://ck.jp.ap.valuecommerce.com/servlet/referral?sid=2285236&pid=874428061&vc_url=http%3a%2f%2f7andy%2eyahoo%2eco%2ejp%2fbooks%2fdetail%3faccd%3d31756395)**

Mitsuoki Sudo, September 2006. Why was "Ishinomaki Tsukiura"—where shipbuilding and departure were impossible—chosen as a shipbuilding and departure site? This work clarifies the circumstances under which the Sendai Domain concealed the facts to counter the shogunate—a process that continues to the present day—by exhaustively searching numerous documents and historical records, conducting on-site investigations, and performing verification from multiple perspectives.

**The Untold Story of Hasekura Tsunenaga**

Akira Nakamaru, May 10, 1994, Takarajimasha

**[Hasekura Rokuemon and the Western Envoys](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/ASIN/4621051105/oysannohitori-22)**

Hidemichi Tanaka, Jan. 20, 1994, Maruzen Library. A book that views the Hasekura mission to Europe in an overwhelmingly positive light. It puts you in a bright mood.

**A Long Journey to Rome: The Footsteps of Hasekura Tsunenaga, Keicho Envoy**

Yukihiko Takahashi, Kodansha, Dec. 5, 1981. A masterful work that faithfully traces Hasekura's footsteps. No other book has followed Hasekura in such detail.

**[The Samurai Who Vanished in the Land of Mexico](http://px.a8.net/svt/ejp?a8mat=O6BQH+XCANM+5WS+C28PV&a8ejpredirect=http%3A%2F%2Fitem.rakuten.co.jp%2Fbook%2F1670396%2F)**

There was a samurai who went abroad as an attendant to Kuratsune Naga and others of the "Keicho Mission to Europe" and settled in Mexico. He achieved success there, eventually becoming a wealthy merchant.

**[Samurai](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/ASIN/410112325X/oysannohitori-22)**

Shusaku Endo, June 25, 1986, Shincho Bunko. A novel based on Hasekura Tsunenaga. As someone who isn't a Christian, the overt Christian vibe is off-putting.

**[The Samurai Who Became Japon-san](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4754100344&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

With secret orders from Masamune Date to overthrow the shogunate, Hasekura Nagatsune and his samurai set sail for Spain once again. This epic saga depicts the ruthless reality that awaits them and the samurai racing forward, chasing their dreams in a foreign land.

**[Secret Envoy Hasekura Tsunenaga](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/ASIN/4167350041/oysannohitori-22)**

Hideo Osabe, Bunshun Bunko, August 10, 1989

**[Medaka no Umi](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/477333469X&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

Fumon Ishigaki, Kindai Bungeisha, Feb. 1992. Includes "The Castle with a View of the Sea," which depicts the six months leading up to the execution of Tsuneyori, the heir to Hasekura Tsunenaga.

**[The Fascicle Biography: Hasekura Tsunenaga—The Samurai Who Raced Across the Globe](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/ASIN/4832300512/oysannohitori-22)**

Mayumi Chiba, January 10, 1992, Hobun-do. A masterpiece of Hasekura stories. A must-read! A must-read! Do not dismiss it as mere manga. Tsunenaga is wonderful—filled with pride even as he struggles between his identity as a Christian and his identity as a Date.

**[Hasekura Tsunenaga: The Tragedy of the Keicho Mission to Europe](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/ASIN/4121014685/oysannohitori-22/ref=nosim/)**

Koichi Oizumi, Chuokoron-Shinsha

**[The Samurai Who Vanished in Europe](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4048835793&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

People with the surname "Japon" (Japan) living in a small town in Spain. Are they descendants of Hasekura Tsunenaga's mission? Hasekura Tsunenaga crossed to Europe, carrying the competing ambitions of Masamune Date, the shogunate, and the missionaries. Across 400 years, we uncover the full story of this mysterious mission.

**[The Truth Behind Hasekura Tsunenaga's Keicho Mission to Europe: The True Image Hidden in the Portrait](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4639019009&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

Hasekura failed to achieve his objective and barely managed to return to Japan. However, due to the exhaustion of his journey and illness, his appearance had transformed into that of a completely different person—his hair had thinned, and he had grown gaunt... Drawing primarily on precious original foreign historical sources, this work unravels the mystery of the "National Treasure" portrait.

**[Hasekura Tsunenaga](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4642052275&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

Yoshikawa Kobunkan People's Series

**[Hasekura Rokuemon and the Western Envoys](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4621051105&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

Maruzen Library. Unraveling the Mystery of Hasekura's Portrait.

**[A Distant Romance: The Struggle of Hasekura Tsunenaga](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4873410606&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

Plenty of photos

**[Shikura Rokuemon Tsunenaga: An Interdisciplinary Study of the Keicho Embassy to Europe](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4830943068&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

This work refines and re-evaluates previous overviews of the Keicho Embassy to Europe—regarded as a landmark event in both the history of Japan's foreign relations and the history of Catholicism—through the introduction of numerous new historical sources. It is a revised and expanded edition of "A Study of the Keicho Embassy to Europe" (published in 1994).

**[The Samurai Who Vanished in Europe](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4048835793&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

People with the surname "Japon" (Japan) living in a small town in Spain. Are they descendants of Hasekura Tsunenaga's mission? shigezane:hitotoribashi.title: Battle of Hitotori Bridge
shigezane:hitotoribashi.summary: In retaliation for the sudden death of Terumune, the various clans of the Sendo region formed a coalition against Masamune, who had begun the campaign to capture Nihonmatsu. Battles broke out around Takakura and Motomiya.
shigezane:hitotoribashi.markdown:
November 16, Tensho 13 (1585)

In retaliation for the sudden death of Terumune Date, the various clans of the Sendo region formed a coalition against Masamune, who had begun the campaign to capture Nihonmatsu. Battles broke out around Takakura and Motomiya. The Sendo forces, centered around Satake Yoshishige, numbered 30,000 men, including the Ashina, Ishikawa, Iwaki, and Shirakawa clans. In contrast, the Date forces deployed Masamune's main camp at Kannon-do. To the left and right of the main camp were Masakage Rusu and Harada Munetoki. Kokubun Morishige was stationed in front of and behind the main camp, providing cover for Nihonmatsu. Hamada Kagetaka and Munemi Shiroishi were positioned in the vanguard of the main camp, covering the Aotahara and Arai areas. Shigezane Date was stationed at Setogawa-kan as the left-wing mobile force. On the front line at Takakura Castle were Tomizuka Omi and Ito Hizen. Their total strength was 8,000 men. Due to the overwhelming disparity in numbers, the Date forces were swiftly defeated piecemeal. The route from Maedazawa to Hitori-bashi and Kannon-do came under attack by the Satake forces—the enemy's central power—and for a time, even the main camp was in peril; however, they barely managed to hold out thanks to the valiant fighting of Oniwa Satsuki and others. Consequently, Shigezane's forces at Setogawa-kan were left isolated. At the time, Shigezane's forces consisted of 100 mounted riders and 300 muskets (Saito Hoon-kai, Illustration of the Battle at Hitori-bashi). He had joined the campaign after leaving more than half of his forces at Iwakado and Motomiya. Shimokoriyama Uchi-no-ki, a retainer, had just mounted his horse when he declared, "The main camp at Kannon-do has fallen. Let us retreat immediately!" He then pulled out Shigezane's small flag and handed it to his foot soldiers. Shigezane laughed, snatched the flag back, and insisted, "Even if we retreat, defeat is inevitable. I shall choose this place as my final stand and die in battle." The veteran retainer Iba Totomi was 73 years old at the time. Disliking heavy armor, he served as the rearguard wearing only a headband. While fighting valiantly, he sustained severe injuries and died. Shigezane's forces, racing down the mountain, fought a seesaw battle but managed to deliver a devastating flank attack to the Satake forces attacking Masamune's main camp around Hitori-bashi. Amidst the fierce fighting, Masamune himself entered a river to provide water to his exhausted horse, only to be hit by enemy gunfire, which killed the horse's groom. At that moment, Shigezane arrived with 20 to 30 men and, using a fan, struck Masamune's horse's rump to drive him out of the river. Thanks to the valiant efforts of Oniwa Satsuki and others, the Date forces barely managed to defend the main camp, even as the gates were breached three times; however, their vanguard was completely overrun, and they were forced to retreat, with Masamune declaring, "Tomorrow's main battlefield will be Motomiya." For his actions that day, Shigezane received a letter of commendation from Masamune, who acknowledged his efforts and ordered him to move to Motomiya the following day along with Masakage Rusu. However, when dawn broke, the enemy was no longer on the battlefield. The Edo and Satomi clans had invaded the home territory of the coalition's commander, Satake Yoshishige. Satake Yoshishige readily withdrew his camp, and the coalition, having lost its leader, disbanded and returned home.

More additions planned.

shigezane:hokaidou.title: Addendum—Date City, Hokkaido
shigezane:hokaidou.summary: During the Meiji period, the Watari Date family settled in the Iburi region of Hokkaido—present-day Date City. The entire clan relocated together. Consequently, there are many documents and historical records preserved here.
shigezane:hokaidou.cover_alt: Illustrations of the residence and castle town
shigezane:hokaidou.markdown:
## Date City

During the Meiji period, the Watari Date family settled in the Iburi region of Hokkaido—present-day [Date City](http://www.city.date.hokkaido.jp/). The entire clan relocated together. For this reason, there are many documents and historical records passed down here. For an overview of the settlement, [visit this site.](http://homepage1.nifty.com/t-kubo/Japan/kaitaku/watari.htm) [And this one as well.](http://www.city.date.hokkaido.jp/rekisi/index32.html)

## [Daio-ji](http://homepage1.nifty.com/daiouji/index.htm)

A subsidiary temple of Daiyu-ji, the family temple of Shigezane. It was established in Date City in 1880 to facilitate the migration of the Watari Date family to Hokkaido.

## [Kotoni Shrine](http://www.geocities.co.jp/HeartLand-Momiji/1970/)

While the Date clan of Watari is well-known for their settlement in Hokkaido, they also settled in Kotoni (Sapporo City) as Tondenhei; there, they established a shrine to enshrine Takehaya Chiyoo-no-Mikoto (Shigezane) in remembrance of the virtues of the clan founder. Aside from the Watari Date clan, many former retainers of the Aizu Domain also settled in the area, where Tsuchizu Reishin (Hoshina Masayuki) is also enshrined.

shigezane:huku-94-7.title: Letter from Tsunetaka Iwaki, May 17, Tensho 18
shigezane:huku-94-7.summary: Letter from Iwaki Tsunetaka, May 17, Tensho 18. The opening reads: "I shall certainly convey this in person. Your great efforts while I am away in the capital are truly commendable. That said, I remain utterly vigilant. Therefore..."
shigezane:huku-94-7.markdown:
I shall certainly convey this in person, relying on my strength of leg. To bear the burden of your absence while you are in the capital is surely no small task. Nevertheless, I remain utterly vigilant. Accordingly, I have appointed Matsumoto Somi as my messenger, and have received the following letter from Lord Ishida Jibu-shofu. It arrived on the 15th (day). I submit a copy for your perusal. Today, on the 17th (day), a messenger has been dispatched, stating that you wish for us to consult with Soma regarding our journey to the capital. Previously, we received instructions that such arrangements should be discontinued. There is no further need for such matters. That said, as this concerns the Prince's affairs, we proceed with them without hesitation. There is not the slightest objection. I hereby inform you of this, as there is no other way to convey it. As you have been commanded to join the campaign, I shall ascend shortly. I simply request that there be no discrepancy regarding our borders. For further details, please visit us, and I will explain them to you at the camp. With utmost respect and humility.

(Tensho 18) May 17, Tsunetaka (kao)

Lord Nihonmatsu

shigezane:huku7-143-28.title: November 29, date unknown: Letter from Shigezane Date
shigezane:huku7-143-28.summary: November 29, date unknown. Letter from Shigezane Date. The opening reads: "As your esteemed letter indicates, we have not held discussions until recently; this is most unexpected. My elderly father (Sanemoto) remains encamped there to this day. Regarding that matter of reconciliation... the arrangements..."
shigezane:huku7-143-28.markdown:
## Reading based on the critical edition in "History of Fukushima Prefecture, Vol. 7"

As your esteemed letter indicates, we have not held any discussions until recently; this is most unexpected. My elderly father (Sanemoto) remains encamped there to this day. Regarding the matter of that reconciliation, I believe you must be aware of the arrangements. Accordingly, a letter was dispatched to the distant mountain pass, and has finally crossed over today. As your reply should reach us shortly, I trust this will put your mind at ease. I have omitted certain details, awaiting the appropriate time to discuss them. I offer these words with utmost respect. Postscript: Having departed for Nagai in the province of Han, I have been unable to provide a formal reply.

November 29, Munemi, Seal, To Tamura-dono

## Reading based on the transcription in "[Satake Historical Documents in the Senshu Bunko Collection](http://www.amazon.co.jp/%E5%8D%83%E7%A7%8B%E6%96%87%E5%BA%AB%E6%89%80%E8%94%B5%E4%BD%90%E7%AB%B9%E5%8F%A4%E6%96%87%E6%9B%B8-%E5%8D%83%E7%A7%8B%E6%96%87%E5%BA%AB/dp/488594211X)"

As your letter states, I have not spoken of the matter recently. It is most unexpected. My elderly father remains encamped there to this day. Regarding the matter of that reconciliation, I shall ensure it is handled appropriately. Accordingly, I have sent a letter to Toyama. I will certainly deliver it to you today. As your reply will arrive shortly, I trust this will put your mind at ease. I have omitted certain details, timing them for when future correspondence arrives. With utmost respect and humility. Postscript: As I have departed for Hain and Nagai, no reply is necessary.

November 29, Shigezane, Seal, To Tamura-dono

※ Toyama = Endo Yamashiro, Hain = Haneda Inaba? (Takemizu's note)

Quoted from "[Satake Historical Documents in the Senshu Bunko Collection](http://www.amazon.co.jp/%E5%8D%83%E7%A7%8B%E6%96%87%E5%BA%AB%E6%89%80%E8%94%B5%E4%BD%90%E7%AB%B9%E5%8F%A4%E6%96%87%E6%9B%B8-%E5%8D%83%E7%A7%8B%E6%96%87%E5%BA%AB/dp/488594211X)" p. 348

shigezane:isimoda-194.title: Kan'ei 2? February 6, Letter by Shigezane Date
shigezane:isimoda-194.summary: Kan'ei 2? February 6, letter from Shigezane Date. The opening reads: "I received the sealed letter dated the day before yesterday yesterday. Regarding Kokita Echizen, who returned to Nanbu, I stipulated a three-year deferment for Jiroemon, stating it would be like an overnight stay..."
shigezane:isimoda-194.markdown:
End

I examined the letter dated the day before yesterday yesterday. Regarding Kokita Echizen, who returned to Nanbu, I have been told that he is to be detained for three years at the residence of Jiroemon, as if staying overnight. When we inquired privately, we found it to be exactly as stated. I, too, find this most regrettable. I am well aware that I should have retained him. I intend to send further correspondence, but I understand that the chief officials have departed for the New Year and shall not return. Should there be any mistiming, I fear the outcome may be dire; therefore, I ask that you wait until those men have returned. I shall not be present in the least. Furthermore, I intend to notify the village and leave my wife and children in their care. With utmost respect and humility.

(Kan'ei 2?) February 6, Shigezane Date Awa, signature

Lord Ishimoda Daizen

Lord Moniwa Suo

Lord Okuyama Daigaku

Announcement

shigezane:isimoda-40.title: May 7, date unknown: Letter from Shigezane Date
shigezane:isimoda-40.summary: May 7, year unknown. Letter from Shigezane Date. It begins: "Having returned yesterday, I sent a letter, only to be informed that you were away, so I left it aside and returned. Therefore, here in the village of Umekibukuro, there is a man named Tsugiemon..."
shigezane:isimoda-40.markdown:
End

Having departed yesterday, I submitted a written report, only to be told that you were away and that I should hold it in reserve before returning. Accordingly, I rented the residence of a man named Tsugiemon in the village of Umekibukuro; he is a man from the Kanto region. He had been there for a year or two. Two days ago, he abducted the wives and children of two men and fled. He claimed to have gone to a place of great scenic beauty; having let my guard down and waiting too long, I pursued him, only to learn that he is staying with a man named Motegi Chikugo in Nanuka-machi, Yoshida Village, within Yokote, in Senboku. As he is a samurai, while it is not proper to fire arrows at him, I have taken note of the report and returned. I humbly request that you forward this letter and instruct him to return. Regarding various matters, since he has departed from Senboku, I humbly request that you inquire after him. Respectfully and humbly submitted.

May 7

Shigezane Date Awa-no-kami (kao)

To Lord Ishimoda Daizen

shigezane:isimoda-486.title: Kan'ei 11, February 28: Official Decree
shigezane:isimoda-486.summary: Kan'ei 11, February 28, official decree. The opening reads: "Matters hereby established regarding fires."
shigezane:isimoda-486.markdown:
Matters Concerning the Fire Having Been Determined

1. When on duty, the retainers of the guard shall be summoned, proceed swiftly to the fire source, assemble there, and await instructions. That is all.

1. It has been previously agreed that the Wakabayashi guards shall not attend, even in the event of a fire in Sendai.

(Kan'ei 11, Ka) February 28

Daigaku, Omi, Kanmono, Daizen

shigezane:jinbutusousi.title: Biography of Shigezane Date from the "Sendai-han Jinbutsu Soshi"
shigezane:jinbutusousi.subtitle: Biographies of Figures of the Sendai Domain
shigezane:jinbutusousi.summary: Shigezane Date, commonly known as Togoro and later as Awa, served Masamune Date and held the rank of Jojo; he was a man of fortitude and courage, embodying the three virtues of wisdom, benevolence, and bravery.
shigezane:jinbutusousi.markdown:
Shigezane Date, commonly known as Togoro and later as Awa, served Masamune Date and held the rank of Jojo. He was a man of fortitude and courage, possessing the three virtues of wisdom, benevolence, and bravery. It may be said that the great achievement of restoring the Date clan sprang from Shigezane's courage in leading the three armies and his strategic acumen behind the curtain. The Battle of Hitotori Bridge was indeed a turning point for the survival or downfall of the Date clan, and Masamune's army was nearly in peril. In this crisis, Shigezane led his own troops, fighting fiercely in every direction, and ultimately turned defeat into victory. In the Battle of Koriyama, the seven generals of the Sendo region, all of whom were formidable, faced Masamune. Shigezane, along with Kagetsuna Katakura, took charge of their defense and secured the final victory, demonstrating his remarkable bravery. Furthermore, his wisdom was evident in the way he brought the enemy's capable generals—Inawashiro Morikuni, Ouchi Sadatsuna, and Katahira Shigetsuna—to surrender without employing a single soldier; his act of not condemning a certain Shirasawa for his disloyalty, but instead recommending him as a unit commander to allow him to demonstrate his abilities, was a supreme example of benevolence. Later, after fleeing for certain reasons, Tokugawa Ieyasu invited him with generous stipends, but he did not comply; Uesugi Kagekatsu likewise offered him 50,000 koku, but he did not accept. When Masamune sought to persuade him from all sides, he eventually returned. He was granted 23,800 koku in Watari and remained among the ranks of the clan for a long time. He passed away on the 4th day of the 6th month of Shoho 3 (Year of the Fire Dog) at the age of 79.

## Relief Funds, Donations, and Shareholder Programs

### Donations going directly to disaster victims

- Japanese Red Cross Society
- Japan Community Chest (Red Feather)

### Direct support for the affected areas, fractional ownership programs, and more!

- Hometown Support Fund: Furu-Sapo!
- Oshika Peninsula Support Group: Supporting the resumption of fishing in fishing villages on the Oshika Peninsula. Support via pre-order of harvested seafood is 3,000 yen per share.
- One-Share Disaster Relief Fund: Tashirojima, Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture — Nyanko the Project. Tashirojima, famous as the "Cat Island" near the Oshika Peninsula, is also a hub for oyster farming. Support funds are 10,000 yen per share. Owners receive cat merchandise, an ownership certificate, and a shipment of oysters 4–5 years later.
- Sanriku Oyster Recovery: A project to support affected oyster-producing areas in Sanriku, including Karakuwa in Kesennuma and Mangokuura in Ishinomaki. At 10,000 yen per share, approximately 20 oysters are delivered per share. However, since even conventional aquaculture takes two to three years, it is expected to take three or more years before shipment.
- 10,000-Yen-per-Share Strawberry Farm Recovery Support Ownership Program: Support for strawberry farmers in the JA Watari area. A support system for farmers producing "Mou Ikko," a large-fruited strawberry variety special to Miyagi Prefecture. Shares start at 10,000 yen, and supporters are expected to receive 24 berries (35g or more) in a decorative box.
- Agricultural Revitalization Support Project: Seasonal Curated Vegetable Set Ownership Program. For 12,000 yen per share, a "Vegetable Set" featuring approximately 10 varieties of seasonal vegetables and fruits will be shipped three times during the ownership period. Organized by Furusato Farm Co., Ltd.
- Mizuyama Aquaculture Farm "Revitalization Owners & Supporters": A supporter program run by the Mizuyama Aquaculture Farm in Karakuwa, Kesennuma City. For 10,000 yen per share, a set of "Mizuyama Oysters + Scallops" (a total of 20 oysters and scallops) will be shipped once per share. As with the Sanriku Oyster Revitalization program, the shipping date is currently undecided.
- A small-scale revitalization project: selling "onagawa fish" wooden keychains and "onagawa fish stickers" handcrafted by staff in Onagawa Town. Support the local community by purchasing items made by local residents.
- Now accepting apple owner applications to support the Tohoku reconstruction!! An Aomori Prefecture program. For a yearly shareholder contract of 8,000 yen, you'll get hands-on work experience and 10kg of apples. 1,000 yen of the annual fee will be donated as relief funds to the disaster-affected areas.
- Sanriku Marine Products Revitalization Project: A project undertaken by the General Incorporated Association "Sanriku Marine Products Revitalization Project" to organize sponsoring seafood manufacturers and fishermen, aiming to create a new framework for the recovery of the seafood industry. The annual membership fee for individual members is 10,000 yen, and members receive products (seafood, canned goods, etc.) at special prices.
- Urato Seafood Revitalization Project: The Urato Islands are a remote island group located in Shiogama City, Sendai Prefecture. A "fractional ownership" system for marine products—such as oysters, nori, and wakame—is being implemented to revitalize the fishing industry. At 10,000 yen per share, funds are allocated to the purchase of fishing materials and equipment; once the marine products are ready for harvest, they are sent to the owners.
- Securite Disaster-Affected Area Support Fund: Companies in the affected areas are seeking investors. The fund's clear presentation of reconstruction plans and its unique investor benefits are also appealing. Per unit: Investment of 5,000 yen + support fund (donation) of 5,000 yen + administrative fee of 500 yen = 10,500 yen.
- Sanriku Wakame Ownership Program: ¥10,000 per share. A portion of the proceeds (70%) is used for materials, equipment support for producers' wakame cultivation, and procurement costs for producers. (The remaining 30% covers expenses such as shipping, communication costs, payment processing fees, and reporting costs for delivering the wakame). When wakame production in Ishinomaki resumes, salted wakame (approximately 5 bags of 200g each) will be sent.
- Onmaehama Reconstruction Support Project: Reconstruction support for Onmaehama, Onagawa Town, Miyagi Prefecture. ¥10,000 per contribution. The full amount, excluding credit card processing fees, is delivered directly to the representative, Mr. Aihara. 400g of salmon roe will be sent after reconstruction.
- Magenedo! Utatsu Irimae! Irimae Oyster Reconstruction Support "Yukko Fund" — Utatsu Irimae, Minamisanriku Town, Miyagi Prefecture. 10,000 yen per share. In the future, we plan to send back "Reconstruction Yukko Oysters" (including packaging, shipping, etc.) worth 5,000 yen—equivalent to 50% of the support funds.
- We are the Tairyo Project—a per-share reconstruction support fund to assist fishermen at Koamikurahama in Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture. 10,000 yen per share. For the reward, you can choose from four options: sea squirts in the shell, live abalone, Kinka toro mackerel, or a discount voucher for the recreational fishing boat Otoku-maru.
- One of Japan's Three Most Scenic Views Tourism Revitalization Project [Reverse Okumatsushima]: A fund to revitalize "tourism," the industrial and economic foundation of Okumatsushima. Options: 3,000 yen per unit with no owner benefits, or 10,000 yen per unit with the benefit of 100 sheets of premium roasted nori "Otakamori."
- Preserving Japan's traditional culture. The Reed Field Restoration Project! A fractional investment support system (ownership program) aimed at reviving the traditional industry of processing reeds harvested from the Kitakami River reed fields and improving employment opportunities for residents in the surrounding communities. 10,000 yen per share. Benefits include reed udon or a reed ballpoint pen.
- I want to eat those Yamada senbei again. The YAMASEN Project! Support for the revival of Yamada senbei, a specialty of Yamada Town, Iwate Prefecture. A rare, fresh-style senbei. 5,000 yen per bite (bonus: 3 bags of Yamada senbei) or 10,000 yen per bite (bonus: 3 bags of Yamada senbei + 1 senbei roll cake).
- Sanriku Ishinomaki Kinka Sea Squirt and Scallop Recovery Support Project: Recovery support for Sameura Bay, Sanriku Ishinomaki. ¥10,000 per share. Bonus set (8 sea squirts, 2 bags of shucked sea squirts + 5 scallops).
- Stand Up! Domannaka Otsuchi — Iwate Prefecture Otsuchi Town Local Product Revitalization Project. ¥10,000 per share. Perks include "one whole aramaki salmon," "Bounties of Sanriku," and more.
- Ishinomaki City Amijishima Reconstruction Sea Urchin Ownership Program: Support for the revival of sea urchin fishing on Amijishima. ¥10,000 per share. Sea urchins harvested on the island will be sent once fishing resumes.
- "Shareholder Program" to Support the Revival of Wakame and Kombu in Matsushima Bay. Operated by Kyoeimaru Fisheries in Matsushima Bay, Miyagi Prefecture. 5,000 yen per share. Benefits include wakame or kombu.
- Support Group for the Ogatsu Bay Fisheries Cooperative: Share Ownership Program. Support the Ogatsu Bay Fisheries Cooperative (Miyagi Prefectural Fisheries Cooperative, Ogatsu Town, Ogatsu Bay Branch). 10,000 yen per share. Approximately 20–30 live scallops in the shell, or equivalent seafood, will be sent.
- Inomataya Reconstruction Project: A reconstruction project led by Inomataya, a seafood processing and direct-sales business in Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture. ¥10,000 per share. After production resumes, an assortment of Inomataya products (planned to include "Hime-zukuri" and "Ryoshi-don" featuring "Kinka Platinum Mackerel" and "Kinka Autumn Saury") will be sent.
- Aranami Oyster Restoration Committee: Support for the revival of oyster farming in the open waters of Aranami—a rarity worldwide. ¥10,000 per share. Bonus: ¥5,000 worth of Aranami oysters.

### Each municipality

Each local government is accepting relief funds and donations directly. If there is a specific place you'd like to support, please do so directly. I've listed the prefectural contact points, but municipalities are also accepting them. Donations are used for disaster recovery and reconstruction projects, while relief funds are used for livelihood support for those affected. Additionally, for long-term support, please also consider using the **Hometown Tax Donation System**.

## Protection of Cultural Properties and Materials

The [NPO Miyagi Historical Materials Preservation Network](http://www.miyagi-shiryounet.org/) is calling for the protection of disaster-affected historical records and materials. Emergency response procedures are also provided.

You might think, "Why now?" but these items are not only a source of memories—they can also prove unexpectedly useful for establishing land boundaries or planning urban development during future land readjustments. On a personal note, when my home in Takesui caught fire, I found historical materials that were charred black or soaked in water, and they actually proved quite useful. If immediate emergency measures are difficult, simply "not throwing them away for now" can make a difference.

shigezane:k19-1-21.markdown:
Regarding the appointment of Uhyoe (name unknown), he was deeply grateful for the imperial decree. Upon learning that he would be granted a fief, he was most pleased. Accordingly, a single white swan was presented to him, for which he was deeply grateful. He immediately enjoyed it. Furthermore, a horse of exceptional quality was provided; moreover, a chestnut horse named Kinzaki had recently been presented by his father, which was a further stroke of fortune. He further stated that he would continue to report his progress.

shigezane:kakuda-jidai.cover_alt: Illustrations of the residence and castle town
shigezane:kakuda-jidai.markdown:
## Kakuda Castle

Kakuda-aza Ushitate, [Kakuda City](http://www.city.kakuda.miyagi.jp/), Miyagi Prefecture. Also known as Gogyu Castle. It stands on a hill surrounded by wetlands. It was built by the Tade clan during the Eiroku era. The site also flourished as a port for water transport on the Abukuma River. It served as the residence of Shigezane from 1587 until his flight. That said, even during this period, Shigezane was busy with missions to Fushimi and Korea. After Shigezane's flight, Masamune took control of the castle. A battle ensued with opposing retainers, in which over thirty people are said to have fallen. In 1607, Ishikawa Akimitsu moved in, and the castle remained in use until the end of the Edo period. Today, the castle site is a high school and junior high school, but the original castle gate has been relocated to Chosen-ji Temple.

## Fushimi

After returning from the Bunroku Campaign, Shigezane resided in Fushimi (*Seshin Kafu*). According to one account, he was granted a residence by Hideyoshi, though none can be found on the map of Fushimi Castle. Instead, three residences of the Date clan are visible. From the north, they are listed as the "Sendai Chunagon Lower Residence," "Sendai Chunagon Masamune," and "Date Mutsu-no-kami." The site of the northernmost lower residence still remains today under the place name "Masamune." While Masamune had already been granted a residence at Jurakudai, he was granted a Fushimi residence in 1562, before its completion. Since he held New Year's greetings at the Juraku residence in 1563–64, Masamune's primary base in Kyoto was the Juraku residence. As Shigezane's primary wife, Lady Watari, died in Fushimi in June 1564, it is believed that Shigezane himself was already in Fushimi by that time. In August 1564, following the Hidetsugu incident, Hideyoshi ordered the senior retainers of the Date clan, as well as their wives and children, to reside in Fushimi. Jurakudai was demolished, and Masamune also moved to Fushimi. In the autumn of that year, the wives and children of the senior retainers all entered the capital; however, in Shigezane's case, it appears he was an exception, having sent his wife to the capital first. Speaking of place names, "Fujigoro-cho" exists near Omiya Shimo-Chojamachi-agaru in Kamigyo Ward (the area surrounding Jurakudai); this is the site of the residence of Hasegawa Fujigoro Hideichi.

## Jurakudai

Prior to the Hidetsugu incident, this area served as the Toyotomi clan's stronghold. Masamune's residence was also located here. Given the relatively long gap between his return from the Bunroku Campaign and the Hidetsugu incident, it is reasonable to assume that he also resided in this castle town for a time.

[According to a study by Kunitatsu Kori of the Kyoto Historical and Geographical Society, "An examination of the locations of Juraku Castle and Uesugi Kagekatsu's residence suggests a high probability that Masamune's Juraku residence was in Matsunoshita-cho, Horikawa Ichijo"](http://siseki-kukan.way-nifty.com/heiankyokyoto/2008/10/post-cbe2.html).

## Nagoya

Shigezane also participated in the Bunroku Campaign, embarking on a long journey as far as Korea. While he likely stopped at numerous locations, he is believed to have stayed in Nagoya from early April of the first year of Bunroku (1592) until his departure by sea in February of the following year.

## Osaka

Since there was also a residence in Osaka, he must have visited at least once... Or rather, just a quick note for now. [Gansen-ji](http://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%A1%98%E6%B3%89%E5%AF%BA_%28%E5%A4%A7%E9%98%AA%E5%B8%82%29): 2-27 Daikoku 2-chome, Naniwa-ku, Osaka City. Masamune's residence and tea room in Osaka had been donated and designated as National Treasures, but they were destroyed by war damage. [Photo found here](http://www.sououan.sakura.ne.jp/003concept/03temple/)
