shigezane:kakudasesshuu.title: Takeover of Kakuda Castle
shigezane:kakudasesshuu.summary: This Kakuda seizure incident is perhaps the most misunderstood event concerning Shigezane Date. Specifically, the misunderstanding is—
shigezane:kakudasesshuu.markdown:
This Kakuda seizure incident is perhaps the most misunderstood event concerning Shigezane Date. Specifically, the misunderstanding is—

"After Shigezane's flight, Masamune ordered Kageyori Yashiro to lay siege to Kakuda Castle in armed force to seize it. More than 30 of Shigezane's retainers guarding the castle were killed in action, and Shigezane's wife and children were also killed in the process."

And so it goes. I believe this theory was popularized by the Taiga drama "Dokuganryu Masamune" and Katsuhiko Iida's "Masamune Date and His Warlords." Fierce battles raged at Kakuda Castle, and the surviving retainers were scattered. Shigezane, having lost his wife and children, was left utterly alone in the world... It is a tear-jerking scene. (That said, I think making him a peasant is a bit much for the Taiga drama's setting (^^ゞ)

The obvious error is the part stating that Shigezane's wife and children were killed. Since June of Bunroku 4—the year Shigezane's wife passed away—was prior to his flight, he was no longer of this world by the time Kakuda was seized. While it is not impossible that he had concubines or children born to them, there are no historical records that can prove their existence.

Furthermore, the claim that "over 30 retainers of the Shigezane household guarding the residence were killed in action" is not incorrect, as it is recorded in the *Jike Kiroku* and *Seshin Kafu*. However, the depiction of a fierce siege suggested by this account is merely a product of imagination. According to the *[Seshin Kafu](#/post/shigezane/sesinkahu-narumi)*, the primary resister, Haneda Umanosuke, took refuge in a "private residence"—namely, the Haneda residence in the castle town, not Kakuda Castle itself. Moreover, regarding the number of people in the Shigezane household at the time: the *Seshin Kafu* states that there were approximately 1,500 people during the Watari 20,000-koku period and over 30,000 during the Nihonmatsu period; thus, it is unlikely that the number during the Kakuda period was any smaller. In other words, only "30/1,500" of those who resisted were killed in action. Additionally, among Shigezane's retainers, the Aoki, Shiranezawa, and Ishikawa clans became retainers of the main Date house at this time and remained so until the end of the Edo period. It is likely that the actual situation was that "while there were skirmishes, the castle was surrendered without major incident."

Additionally, there is an alternative account regarding the circumstances of the takeover of Kakuda. This version, presented in the *Sendai Shiryo* ["Shigezane Flees to Koyasan"](#/post/shigezane/sendaishiryou-1), suggests that what occurred was not the "takeover of Kakuda" but rather the "punishment of Haneda Umanosuke." The reason was that Haneda had incited Shigezane to flee. Against this backdrop, Haneda's tyranny was evident among the guardians of Kakuda, and it appears there were conflicts among the retainers. Endo Shukei, who served as a guardian alongside Haneda, reported this to Yashiro Kageyu at Iwadeyama; Yashiro then ordered Kono Iki of Marumori to strike down Haneda. Among the forces that besieged Haneda's residence, many names from the Shigezane household appear. Their position was firmly that "Haneda is the rebel." It is believed that after Haneda was slain, the Shigezane household and Kakuda Castle came under the command of Iwadeyama—the main Date house—due to the absence of their lord. In other words, their status shifted from "retainers of Shigezane Date, the lord of Kakuda Castle" to "Kakuda Castle guards dispatched by Masamune Date."

There are other accounts indicating that while Haneda Umanosuke was isolated from the rest of the clan during this period, he enjoyed the full trust of Shigezane. In the "[Arisaka Documents](#/post/shigezane/arisaka),"

> Regarding the consultations between Kanazawa, Uchizaki, Sawajiri, Shiranezawa, and Ishikawa: > "Lord Shigezane sent a secret letter solely to Haneda Umanosuke, treating us as if we were not present, which we find most regrettable. This time, we shall submit a joint petition to Iwadeyama." > While these matters were being discussed internally, Kageyu Hyoe, accompanied by a number of men, pressed toward Kakuda; accordingly, the above items were delivered to Kageyu.

That is what it says.

There are no clear records regarding the timing of the takeover of Kakuda Castle.

shigezane:kanei15-4-20.title: Yoshiyama Koji Family Records, Entry for April 20, Kan'ei 15 (Extract)
shigezane:kanei15-4-20.summary: Excerpt from the Yoshiyama Koji Family Records, entry for April 20, Kan'ei 15. The opening reads: "Issuer: Tadamune; Recipient: Shigezane."
shigezane:kanei15-4-20.markdown:
Issuer: Tadamune; Recipient: Shigezane

I write to you intentionally via courier. Regarding last year's flood, we have now borrowed 5,000 kanme of silver from the Lord. As there is no need to express our gratitude to our relatives or the common folk, your close attendants have advised that you ought to come in person. While it goes without saying that your journey must be arduous, we await your prompt arrival. Given the long distance, others might also be inclined to accompany you, but as this is a substantial gesture of gratitude, I urge you to come. Indeed, indeed, you should come without burden and with few attendants.

1. In gratitude for the above, I entered the castle on the 19th of last month, where I was summoned close to the Lord, who told me in detail about the great flood at my residence last year. He found it utterly ridiculous. There are various humble words of gratitude regarding these words, yet I cannot put them into writing.

1. The Lord's displeasure has subsided considerably, and since my arrival in the capital, I have had the honor of appearing before him twice. The great joy felt by all, high and low, is beyond measure. I hasten to report this. Humbly and respectfully.

Furthermore, such good fortune has not befallen even those of you. I believe each of you should find this satisfactory. I hasten to report this. Indeed, indeed, you ought to ascend with ease. That is all.

April 20, Tadamune's Seal

Lord Awa Date

shigezane:kaou.title: Kao of Shigezane Date
shigezane:kaou.summary: While Shigezane Date's kao is well-known for being distinguishable by purpose and period, several variations of Shigezane's kao are also known.
shigezane:kaou.markdown:
While Shigezane Date's kao is well-known for being distinguishable by purpose and period, several variations of Shigezane's kao are also known.

- Illustrations provided by Yamabiko-sama
- Illustration cited from "[Satake Historical Documents in the Senshu Bunko Collection](http://www.amazon.co.jp/%E5%8D%83%E7%A7%8B%E6%96%87%E5%BA%AB%E6%89%80%E8%94%B5%E4%BD%90%E7%AB%B9%E5%8F%A4%E6%96%87%E6%9B%B8-%E5%8D%83%E7%A7%8B%E6%96%87%E5%BA%AB/dp/488594211X)," p. 348
- Illustration from Endo Family Documents and Nakajima Family Documents of the Date Clan Senior Retainers: Sengoku Period (published by the Shiroishi City Board of Education), Endo Family Documents 17 (E4-26)

The above is what I would like to present. I have also received guidance from Seido-sama regarding the types of kao. I would like to express my sincere gratitude.

This illustration is a digitized version of a plate provided by Yamabiko-sama. According to Yamabiko-sama, the distinctions in the use of kao A and B are as follows. Both date from the period when Yamabiko-sama was the lord of Watari Castle.

## Type A: Found in documents addressed to retainers

Instructions for Town Planning (Collection of the Date City Board of Education / Included in Plate 104 of Shinjinbutsu Orai-sha's "Masamune Date Graffiti")

Letter to Mokusuke Ushizaka (Collection of the Watari Town Central Community Center / Included in Plate 151 of the Sendai City Museum catalog "Masamune Date and His Retainers")

Letter to Bingo Shiga (Collection of Michiyoshi Shiga; six letters by Shigezane are said to remain in the Shiga family)

Letter to Kakubei Kurono (included in Kyodo Watari)

Letter to an unknown recipient (Collection of the Date City Board of Education / featured in Plate 105 of Shinjinbutsu Orai-sha's "Date Masamune Graffiti")

## Type B: Found in documents submitted to the domain

Memorandum on the Number of Shigezane Date's Retainers

[Letter to Hyogo Oeda](#/post/shigezane/ooeda) (Original Calligraphy and Paintings of Old Families of Sendai)

If one were to summarize it, Type A would be the seal for internal use within the clan, and Type B would be the official kao.

## The kao on the [Letter from Shigezane Date to Lord Tamura](#/post/shigezane/huku7-143-28) from the Satake Historical Documents held by the Senshu Bunko

Partially quoted from the illustration on p. 348 of "[Satake Historical Documents in the Senshu Bunko Collection](http://www.amazon.co.jp/%E5%8D%83%E7%A7%8B%E6%96%87%E5%BA%AB%E6%89%80%E8%94%B5%E4%BD%90%E7%AB%B9%E5%8F%A4%E6%96%87%E6%9B%B8-%E5%8D%83%E7%A7%8B%E6%96%87%E5%BA%AB/dp/488594211X)". The kao from Jitsumoto's youth, during his lifetime. While it differs considerably from Types A and B above, it remains unclear whether this is due to the era or whether there were other distinct uses.

## The kao from [Shiroishi City, Endo Family Documents: Letter by Shigezane Date](#/post/shigezane/e4-26)

Adapted and reprinted from the illustration in Endo Family Documents 17 (E4-26) of "Documents of the Endo and Nakajima Families, Senior Retainers of the Date Clan: Sengoku Period Edition" (published by the Shiroishi City Board of Education). So far, this is the only such example. It dates from just before the Battle of Hitotori Bridge in Tensho 13. (The catalog lists it as Tensho 17.)

shigezane:kasin.title: Retainers of Shigezane Date
shigezane:kasin.summary: Listed, for now, in alphabetical order by surname. The reason I say "for now" is that I'm not entirely sure of the readings. This list includes retainers whose activities are recorded during Shigezane's lifetime.
shigezane:kasin.markdown:
Listed roughly in alphabetical order by surname. The reason I say "roughly" is that I'm not entirely confident in the readings. This list includes retainers whose activities are recorded during Shigezane's lifetime. Reference materials: "Watari Yoshin Kafu Ryakki," "[Masamune-ki](#/post/shigezane/tyosaku)," "Kyodo Watari Nos. 81, 57, 46," "Teizan-ko Jika Kiroku," "Date Tensho Nikki," "[Kuranosuke Yashiki](http://www.page.sannet.ne.jp/kuranosuke/index.html)," "Date Yoshin Kafu," "Shihon Sendai-han Shi Jiten," "Watari-machi Shi," "Sendai-han Kashinroku," "Genealogies of the Katakura Clan, Lords of Shiroishi Castle, and Their Retainers," "Watari Date Family Documents Research Group Results Report 1: Catalog of Documents from Various Houses of the Watari Date Clan held at Daiyu-ji Temple in Hokkaido, with 'Oshu Soma-shi Nomaoi-zu Byobu' held by Date City." Information provided by: Haru-sama, Tome@Date-otoko-sama

※1 Number from the Watari Yoshin Kafu Ryakki. Represents the rank at the time the Watari Yoshin Kafu Ryakki was compiled.

※2 Distinctions between Bajo (horse), Toko (on foot), Fudan-teppo (non-iron), Shinchi-bajo (new horse), Shinchi-go-toko (new foot), Go-fudan-gumi (non-iron), Go-kachi-ko-me-tsurau-go-kachu (So), and Iwaki-gozen-sama-me-tsurau-go-kachu (Iwa), according to the Warabi Shishido Family Documents (as published in "Kyodo Watari No. 57"). This is said to be a copy made in Genroku 11 from the original of Kan'ei 19.

### Aoki Yamato-no-kami

- Appears in the Tensho Diary as a messenger "from Nihonmatsu (Shigezane)." May have been a direct retainer of Masamune.

### Aoki Genban-no-jo

- A retainer of Toshimune Kakeda. The [Sawajiri clan](#/post/shigezane/kasin) was related to him. In Genki 2, he served under Sanemoto. In Tensho 4, he distinguished himself at the Battle of Kawamata and was granted a letter of commendation by Terumune.

### Aoki Tanetsuna

- Danjo-no-chu. Son of Aoki Genban-no-jo. Played an active role in negotiations with the Tamura clan.

### Tsunahiro Aoki

- Bizen. Son of Aoki Tanetsuna. During the Battle of Hitotoribashi, he served as the castle warden of Obama Castle. When Shigezane fled, he became a direct retainer of Masamune and was granted 200 koku. He resided in Narita Village, Otani-sho, Kurokawa District, as a district magistrate. His descendants were common samurai of the Sendai Domain.
- Participated in the takeover of Kakuda Castle during Shigezane's flight ([Sendai Shiryo "Shigezane Date Fled to Takano"](#/post/shigezane/sendaishiryou-1))

### Shigejiro Asanuma

- Served in the Summer Campaign of the Siege of Osaka (on foot).

### Sokuro Asanuma

Lord of Shinjo Castle in Mogami District, Ushu Province; served Ashikaga Shuri-no-daibu Minamoto no Yoshimori Asomi. Known as Ishikawa Yahei. Son, Mitsutomo, served the Date clan during the Tensho era."

When Sanemoto entered the Uesugi clan, he was assigned to Sanemoto and granted a hikaryo-mon torige-tai-yari and a Bizen nagasaki nagamitsu by Uemune. He played a prominent role despite his advanced age in the [Battle of Hitotoribashi](#/post/shigezane/hitotoribashi), where he was killed in action. Served as a karo.

He never removed the ball for the rest of his life, twisting it as a source of amusement while drinking. He was adopted into Sado and was actually the second son of Horikoshi Noto. He held a fief of 500 koku. When Sanemoto succeeded to the Uesugi clan, he was assigned 30 mounted riders as a samurai commander and was placed under Sanemoto's command. He subsequently became a retainer of Sanemoto.

Later, he was summoned by Masamune for 20 kanmon and changed his name to Mimasaka. He became a senior retainer to Date Hidemune, but due to a falling out, he returned to his home province and changed his name to Echigo. His lineage became extinct in Horeki 9.

### Endo Suruga-no-kami

- In Tensho 16, when Sadatsuna submitted to the Date clan, he accompanied Sadatsuna to Masamune (Jike Kiroku).
- Sent a letter to an acquaintance of the enemy during the standoff at Koriyama.
- The Endo family of the Sendai Domain's main hall records "Endo Suruga" as the head of the house during the Eiroku period. During the time of the Awano Daizen administration, he went to Natori and resided in Kawakami Village for several years. For some reason, his ancestral estate was extinguished; during the Keicho era, Fujizaemon, the heir of Suruga, petitioned the Date main house for service and was granted permission.
- [See Date Masamune Documents 162](#/post/shigezane/162)
- Quoted from [Rikka (Oral traditions of "Shinobu Village," Fukushima City)](http://members.jcom.home.ne.jp/rikka/chimei/chimei_04sinobu_idx.html). The mountain on the border between Oda and Hiraishi is known as either Asahi-kan or Shinchi-kan. It is said that during the time of Terumune Date, Endo Suruga-no-kami, a retainer of the Date clan, lived here; traces such as dry moats still remain in the mountains today. (From "History of Fukushima City," Supplemental Volume IV: Folklore of Fukushima II (Place Names))

### Yasukiyo Okabe

### Naotsugu Tadaki

- Brief Record of the Watari Yoshin Family Genealogy 53: Echigo. Tensho 10 (1582)–Shoho 3 (1646). Served Shigezane. Also known as Naosada. After entering Watari, he became embroiled in an argument with other senior retainers within the castle, which led to his attainder and exile. Three years later, he was recalled; not only were his lands and holdings restored to their former status, but he also received the income he had earned during his exile. Overcome with gratitude, he devoted himself to loyal service as a mounted guard. During the era of great peace, as there were no battles in which his life could be risked, he requested and was granted permission to commit ritual suicide (junshi), and was presented with the sake cup for the oath of ritual suicide (tsuihara go-seiyaku). It is said that Shigezane frequently visited Naotsugu's retirement residence to view his horses. After Shigezane's death, he visited Daiyu-ji Temple three times a day and committed ritual suicide on June 20. His Buddhist name was Kan-o Totetsu. His death poem: "The clouds of my heart have cleared, and I am now truly beholding the light of the moon."

## **Father: Shigezane Date** 1527–1587

Born in Daiei 7 (1527). Commonly known as Togoro. Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade; Hyobu-no-daifu. After taking Buddhist vows, he took the name Seiansai. According to one account, he was initially named Naomoto. His father was Tanemune, the 14th head of the Date clan. His mother was the primary wife from the Ashina clan. However, there are [alternative accounts](#/post/shigezane/nazo) regarding his mother; sources from the Uesugi side identify her as the daughter of Nakajo Sadasuke of the Yohoku-shu. As the third son of Tanemune, he was eight years younger than Harumune.

During the Tenbun era, at the request of his great-great-grandfather Uesugi Shigezane—who had heard he was naturally clever and brave—he was adopted by Shigezane. On this occasion, Shigezane bestowed upon him the character "Sane" and the "sparrow on a bamboo" crest, and he took the name Sanemoto. He underwent his genpuku in Tenbun 9 (1540).

In Tenbun 11 (1542), three days before his departure for the Uesugi clan in Echigo, the "Tenbun Disturbance" broke out, in which his father Tanemune was abducted and imprisoned by his elder brother Harumune. The Uesugi retainers who had come to meet him left Sanemoto behind and returned to Echigo. With nowhere else to go in Echigo, Sanemoto was entrusted with Omori Castle by Tanemune and became its lord. It is said that Omori Castle was briefly seized by Harumune's side, and Sanemoto fled to Yanagawa. Meanwhile, in Echigo, a movement opposing the succession arose, centered around the Yohoku-shu, leading to internal strife.

In Tenbun 17 (1548), the Tenbun Disturbance ended with Tanemune's retirement. Two years later, Shigezane Date died in Echigo, and the Uesugi clan—the shugo of Echigo—came to an end. The shugo-dai, Nagao Kagetora (Uesugi Kenshin), inherited the family name from the Kanto Kanrei, Uesugi Norimasa, becoming the lord of Echigo Province in both name and reality. Incidentally, Uesugi Kenshin was one year younger than Sanemoto. Because the conflict ended in victory for Harumune, Sanemoto became a guest of the then-lord of Omori Castle, Endo Oki, and spent his days enduring hardship. However, Sanemoto apparently enjoyed widespread popularity, and before long, he ousted Endo Oki to become the lord of Omori Castle. For some reason, Harumune also turned a blind eye to this (History of Omori Castle). According to the "Sendai Shiryo," around the time of the conclusion of the Tenbun Disturbance, the sister of Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu became Sanemoto's first wife. Sanemoto's gravestone at Yorin-ji (erected in Keio 3) also identifies his wife as a member of the Hatakeyama clan and his successor wife as a member of the Date clan (Kyosei-in). Following this, Sanemoto played an active role in controlling the Sendai route and serving as a liaison. It was fair to say that among the lords along the Sendai route, there was virtually no one who dealt with the Date clan without going through Sanemoto.

In Tensho 2 (1574), he captured Hachichome Castle. He targeted Nihonmatsu Castle, but since Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu of Nihonmatsu appealed to Terumune through Tamura Takaaki, a peace agreement was reached.

Around Tensho 12 (1584), he ceded the family headship to Shigezane and retired to Hachichome Castle. While his retirement was in name only, there are indications that he continued to engage in various forms of information warfare thereafter. Furthermore, Hachichome Castle served as the frontline base at the southern end of the Date clan's territory.

In Tensho 15 (1587), he passed away in Hachichome at the age of 61. He was buried at Yorin-ji Temple in Ogura Village, Shinobu District. It is said that a pine tree was planted as a grave marker; today, a tree stump remains beside a newly erected gorinto pagoda. His posthumous Buddhist name was Dokusho-in-don Ketsuzan Goei Daikoji.

## **Mother: Daughter of Harumune Date** ?-1591.10.3

Dharma name: Kyosei-in Enshin Myokan Daishi. Her father was Harumune Date, and her mother was Princess Kubo of the Iwaki clan. She was born as the younger sister immediately following Terumune Date. Since she was older than Masakage Rusu, she must have been born sometime between 1545 and 1547. When a husband has only one wife, like Harumune does, it's easier to calculate the children's ages (lol). During the Eiroku era, she married her uncle, Sanemoto Date. In the "Old Castle Tour" section of the Otsuka Yakuho, the marriage is listed as occurring in Eiroku 9, but there is no citation. Assuming she was two years younger than Terumune, she would have been 20 in Eiroku 9. I wonder if Harumune would have just left his daughter alone until she was 20. Oh, if it's Eiroku 9, then the head of the clan would have been Terumune. It seems more likely that Sanemoto took a second wife (History of Sendai City, 1929 edition). Considering Sanemoto's age, that would be more natural. In Eiroku 11 (1568), she gave birth to Shigezane Date. She passed away on October 3, Tensho 19 (1591), likely around the age of 40. It is unclear where she died. In the autumn of that year, Masamune was driven to Iwadeyama, and Shinobu and Omori were ruled by Kimura Yoshikiyo. Chronologically, this would seem to be Kakuda, though it is somewhat uncertain.

## **Wife: Watari clan** 1573–1595.6.4

Dharma name: Gensho-in-dono Jirin Teiho Daishi. Her father was Shigemune Watari, and her mother was the daughter of Moritane Soma. She was the elder sister of Sadamune Date of Wakuya. In the Taiga drama, she was named "Tose," which might be more familiar. Born in Tensho 1 (1573) (calculated backward from the age at death recorded in the "Wakuya Date Documents 11: Tendo Naiki Letters"). She married Shigezane in the winter of Tensho 14 (1586). Incidentally, her father Shigemune was 35 that year. According to the family records, Watari Sanemoto reported the marriage arrangements to Masamune. Sanemoto passed away the following year, in 1586. She is said to have died in Fushimi on June 4, Bunroku 4 (1595) (according to a commemorative publication). Their married life lasted about ten years. She was likely in her mid-twenties? Shigezane is said to have been granted a residence in Fushimi by Hideyoshi, but it does not appear on the Fushimi Castle map. It may have been a section of the Masamune residence. She was buried within the current grounds of Chosen-ji Temple in Kakuda. Until recently, the burial site was referred to as the "Watari Mausoleum," but due to reorganization of the graveyard and other factors, its current location is unknown.

## **Second Wife: Nikaido clan** ?-1620.10.23

Her father was Moriyoshi Nikaido. Her mother was Anan-hime, the daughter of Harumune Date. She was a cousin of Shigezane, and Moritaka Ashina was her full brother. After the death of Moriyoshi Nikaido, her mother, Anan, served as the female lord of Sukagawa, causing Masamune considerable trouble. The Nikaido clan initially married into Iwaki Tsunetaka. In Tensho 18 (1590), Iwaki Tsunetaka died suddenly while en route to the Odawara campaign. Nokamaru (Sadataka) of the Satake clan succeeded him in the Iwaki family. The movements of the Nikaido clan at this time remain unclear. Meanwhile, the Iwaki family had a biological son, Masataka. Iwaki Masataka is described as "the posthumous son of Tsunetaka"; while there are theories that he was either the legal wife or a concubine, the "Historical Materials: Encyclopedia of the Date Clan Retainers of Sendai" adopts the theory that he was the legal wife. In Keicho 12 (1607), Iwaki Masataka came to the Sendai Domain seeking protection and became a retainer. Masamune immediately treated Masataka as a relative, and Masataka was granted a fief in Shimizu, Kurihara District. This became the later Iwayado Date clan. At this time, Masataka came to Sendai with his mother, who, by order, remarried Shigezane Date of Date Awa. This is the Nikaido clan. In Watari, she was called Iwaki Gozen. She passed away on October 23, Genna 6 (1620). Her dharma name was Bussho-in-dono Tengan Myoshin Daishi. Her grave is believed to be on a small elevation behind the mausoleum of Shigezane at the Watari Date family burial site in Daiyu-ji Temple.

## **Wife? The Watari clan**

She does not appear in the official histories. However, according to Mr. Misaburo Shinoki, there is a legend that Shigezane's wife, "Ms. Watari," was from Watari in Fukushima City. This Watari area is located directly across the Abukuma River from Omori, where the legends of Anju and Zushio are preserved. There is a castle site here called Tsubaki-kan (Tsubakiyama-kan), which is said to have been the residence of Shigezane Date (Nihon Jokaku Taikei).

## **Child: Kozomaru 1611–1614, and one other daughter**

Shigezane had two biological children, but both died young. Kozomaru died in 1614 (Keicho 19), on the same day Shigezane departed Watari for the Winter Campaign at Osaka. He was four years old. He had one daughter, but she also died before then.

## **Adopted Son: Shigezane Date** 1613–1665.6.35

Kashokumaru. Jibu-no-daifu. Awa. Ninth son of Masamune. Mother of the Shibata (Shibata) clan. Born in Sendai in 1613 (Keicho 18). Came of age in November 1625 (Kan'ei 2). In 1633 (Kan'ei 10), he married the daughter of Shirakawa Ukyo Yoshizane, lord of the Masasaka territory in Kurihara District. In 1652 (Joo 1), he changed his title from Jibu to Awa. He was said to possess great strength, capable of breaking deer antlers, to be proficient in swimming, and to have mastered the art of firearms under his elder brother, Tadamune. The topic regarding this man is the "Joo Incident." Munemi had fish nets cast at Arahama in Watari District and was taking lunch on a hill. A foot soldier of the Yamagata Domain stationed at Arahama Port happened to pass by and got into a fight with Munemi's page, Shibata Hikobei, who had tried to stop him. Hikobei inflicted a cut on the opponent, but the Yamagata Domain ordered the injured man to commit seppuku. Consequently, the magistrates of Watari argued that Hikobei should also be punished to maintain a balance with Yamagata, but Munemi refused to comply. Left with no choice, he reported the matter to Tadamune, who also supported the punishment, and Hikobei's seppuku was decreed. Following this incident, Munemi attempted to leave Watari, but after being persuaded by those around him, he entered the priesthood at Kokubunji-in. However, perhaps it was merely for show, as he left the temple after a single day. Incidentally, Hikobei was Munemi's maternal cousin. He died on June 5, 1665 (Kanbun 5), at the age of 53. Buddhist name: Ensho-in-don Tetsuzan Ritsu-do Daizenjomon.

Furthermore, documents from the Sendai Date family identify Munemi's wife as the daughter of Shirakawa Kunai Yoshitsuna (father of Ukyo Yoshizane). ([Date Masamune Documents 3220](#/post/shigezane/3220)).

## **Grandson Munenari Date** 1636–1670.6.1

The eldest son of Munemi. Born in Kan'ei 13 (1636), the year of Masamune's death. His mother was Choju-in, a concubine of Munemi. He came of age in Shoho 4. In Manji 3 (1660), he married the daughter of Date Aki Muneshige, the lord of Wakuya Castle. In Kanbun 5 (1665), he became the lord of Watari Castle, but passed away after only five years.

## **Those for whom Shigezane served as the eboshi-oya**

****Kagetsuna Katakura****

Samon, Kojuro. Eldest son of Kagetsuna Katakura. Lord of Shiroishi Castle. No henku is recorded, although the sound "Shige" is the same. Born in Tensho 12 (1584). He distinguished himself during the Summer Campaign of the Siege of Osaka and earned the nickname "Demon Kojuro." At this time, he married Ame, the daughter of Sanada Yukimura, who later became his wife.

****[Tokiwa Kagesada](http://shigezane.info/majime/kasin/kasin.htm#tokiwa-kagesada)****

A close retainer of Shigezane. Since he was granted a character from his name, Shigezane was likely his eboshi-oya, though as he entered service at age 17, it is possible that Shigezane had him change his name.

****[Maeda Sanenobu](http://shigezane.info/majime/kasin/kasin.htm#maeda-sanenobu)****

A close retainer of Shigezane. In Keicho 17, at the age of 13, he underwent genpuku under Shigezane.

****Okochi Family Home****

Gentayu. Member of the Okochi family, summoned to the Sendai Domain. He served as military chief during the reign of Tadamune. It is said that during his childhood, he underwent his coming-of-age ceremony at the residence of Shigezane and was granted a character of his name.

shigezane:kinrin.cover_alt: Illustration from the Reference and Archives
shigezane:kinrin.markdown:
**☆ [Chiba Clan](http://members.jcom.home.ne.jp/bamen/index.htm)**

A comprehensive chronicle of the Chiba clan, descendants of Emperor Kanmu. For references related to the Date clan, we recommend "The Chiba Clan of Oshu" and, among the "Six Chiba Parties," the "[Soma Clan](http://members.jcom.home.ne.jp/bamen1/souma.htm)" and "[Takeishi Clan](http://members.jcom.home.ne.jp/2131535101/takesi.htm)."

**☆ [The Era of the Combined Study of the Four Aizu Houses](http://call-you.sakura.ne.jp/)**

A site featuring a modern Japanese translation of the Combined Study of the Four Aizu Houses. I'm so glad! The meticulous attention to detail in this site's design is wonderful.

**☆ [The History of Aizu from an Archaeological Perspective](http://www17.ocn.ne.jp/~aizua/)**

An incredibly detailed website on the history of Aizu. Packed with specialized content and rich in information.

**☆ [Oku-Aizu Sengoku Fudoki](http://www.geocities.jp/rockfish384/)**

A specialized website on the Sengoku period of Oku-Aizu, a site of little-known fierce battles. The mopping-up operations conducted by the Date clan in Oku-Aizu following the fall of the Ashina clan remain largely unknown.

**☆ [Yamagata Historical Journey](http://www3.omn.ne.jp/~nishiki/)**

A website about Sengoku-period warlords associated with Yamagata. The BGM is awesome! While the Mogami clan is the go-to name for Yamagata, there are also plenty of other daimyo and kokujin in the Okitama region with ties to the Date clan, so be sure to check them out.

**☆ [Yoshimitsu Mogami, Lord of Dewa](http://www.ne.jp/asahi/sengoku/yamagata/)**

A website about Yoshimitsu Mogami, the Ushu Tandai. A reevaluation of Yoshimitsu, who has been subject to various misconceptions.

**☆ [The Rise and Fall of the Nikaido Clan, Sengoku Daimyo](http://www.muratasystem.or.jp/~hideyuki/welcome.html)**

A specialized website on the Sukagawa Nikaido clan. It's great that it even includes details on their retainers. It also provides detailed accounts of the war chronicles of southern Oku.

**☆ [History of Nanao and the Noto Hatakeyama Clan](http://www15.ocn.ne.jp/~nanao/index.html)**

A website about the Noto Hatakeyama clan. It also includes information on the Nihonmatsu Hatakeyama clan.

**☆ [New Chronicle of the Rise and Fall of the Onodera](http://www.kit.hi-ho.ne.jp/m210/sinonoderaseisuiki/)**

A website publishing research and studies on the Onodera clan, which originated in Onodera-go, Shimotsuga District, Shimotsuke Province (Onodera, Iwafune Town, Tsuga District, Tochigi Prefecture).

**☆ [The Roots and History of the Yanai Clan](http://www.ne.jp/asahi/yanai/roots/)**

History and research on the Yanai, Nouchi, and Yanai clans. Includes detailed explanations of the Yanai clan, retainers and subordinates of the Date clan. It's also great that the original historical documents are available for reading.

**☆ [Asaku Land](http://sakazu36.hp.infoseek.co.jp/)**

Local information on Mizusawa Sakuragawa. Currently uploading the roster of retainers of the Rusu clan.

**☆ [M Manufacturing Co., Ltd.](http://umamasi.hp.infoseek.co.jp/)**

In addition to content related to Nobunaga's Ambition and other titles, a special feature article on Harunobu Kasai!

**☆ [Oshu Toraneko-kan](http://toraneko.cside.com/)**

Introduces the history of Mutsu, focusing primarily on three works: *The Tale of the Tono Nanbu Clan*, *History of the Oshu Boshin War*, and *The First Nine Years: The Fourth Generation of the Fujiwara*.

**☆ [Early Modern Documents Museum](http://komonjokan.net/)**

Information site for the Nanbu Domain. Rich in historical materials. Goal.

**☆ [Tono Matsuzaki Jengo II](http://www.tonotv.com/members/bisyamon/)**

The history of the Asonuma clan and Matsuzaki Town.

**☆ [Kitadewa Monogatari](http://www.geocities.jp/kitadewa/)**

Akita's Sengoku-period information site. The go-to source for all things Akita.

**☆ [Ou Chinjufu](http://f21.aaa.livedoor.jp/~chinjufu/)**

A local history website covering the Tohoku region as a whole.

**☆ [Fuun Sengoku-shi: Family Crests of Sengoku Warlords](http://www2.harimaya.com/sengoku/)**

If there's anything you can't figure out from the genealogy or family crests, start here. It covers pretty much everything. Simply incredible...! It has a surname index and a regional index, making it very user-friendly.

**☆ [Comprehensive Encyclopedia of Iwate's Cultural Information](http://www.bunka.pref.iwate.jp/)**

If you're looking into the history and culture of Iwate Prefecture, start right here!

shigezane:kotemori.title: Battle of Kotemori Castle
shigezane:kotemori.summary: August 1585. Having secured the defection of Aoki Shuri, a retainer of Ouchi Ujitsuna, Shigezane reported the matter to Masamune. Masamune immediately launched a military campaign to subdue the Ouchi.
shigezane:kotemori.markdown:
August 23–27, Tensho 13

August, Tensho 13. Having secured the defection of Aoki Shuri, a retainer of Ouchi Ujitsuna, Shigezane reported the matter to Masamune. Masamune immediately launched a military campaign to subdue the Ouchi.

First, Shigezane dispatched Koyanagawa Morimune, Munemi Shiroishi, Kagetaka Hamada, and Munetoki Harada; Shigezane then stationed these four generals at Iino, near Karimatsuda (the castle of Aoki Shuri). Shigezane himself deployed his forces at Tatsukoyama. On August 12, Masamune also rode out to Fukushima. Having obtained a map of Shiomatsu from Aoki Shuri, Masamune moved his camp to Kawamata and met with Tamura Kiyoaki at Bigahira. Together, they attacked Kotemori Castle, where Ouchi Ujitsuna was entrenched. The attack was scheduled to begin on the 23rd, but due to rain, hostilities did not commence until the following day, the 24th.

Now, while the Date and Tamura forces besieged Kotemori Castle, the forces of Ashina and Hatakeyama, who had rushed to reinforce Ouchi, surrounded both armies. The Ouchi forces holed up in the castle and did not step foot outside; thus, the battle initially unfolded between the Hatakeyama and Date forces, who had taken the lead. The Tamura forces pressed from the east and the Date forces from the west, but Mount Oyama lay between them, preventing the two armies from joining forces. Masamune attacked the Hatakeyama forces with his hatamoto and continuous musket fire; while the Date forces gained the upper hand, they withdrew their troops after noon. That night, Ouchi Ujitsuna secretly escaped to Obama. Following this, the defending commanders of Kotemori became Ono Shusui and Arai Hannai. The Date army also withdrew about five ri and took up a field position. They remained vigilant against a night attack, but dawn broke without incident.

The 25th. The day passed with skirmishes. There was a passage between the reinforcements and the castle interior, and it was presumed that this was why the fortress was so secure.

The 26th. The attack on the castle resumed. At Kagetsuna Katakura's suggestion, musketeers fired volleys, but the defenders ignored them. This marked the third night of field encampment, and a military council was held regarding the future course of attack. Shigezane proposed moving his forces to the Take-yashiki south of the castle to link up with the Tamura forces and cut off the passage between the reinforcements and the castle. Masamune expressed concern, stating, "If we move to the Take-yashiki, it will become a battle on two fronts—against the reinforcements and the garrison." However, Shigezane maintained that "priority should be given to linking up with the Tamura army." Shigezane's forces and the Tamura forces would handle the battle on both fronts. Their reasoning was that the enemy reinforcements would be unable to make a significant impact due to the poor terrain. In response, Kyusetsu Harada offered a cautious view, stating, "Even without taking such risks, the castle will fall through a prolonged siege." While both opinions had their supporters, the council failed to reach a consensus, and the meeting adjourned.

The 27th. At dawn, Shigezane moved his camp to the Take-yashiki without Masamune's permission. Masakage Rusu followed suit, and upon hearing the report, Masamune ordered the entire army to move toward the Take-yashiki. At that point, a man named Ishikawa Kageyu from within the castle requested to speak with Shigezane's retainer, [Endo Shimotsuke](file:///C:/Documents and Settings/柏元真理子/My Documents/My Webs/成実2/majime/kasin.htm#endou-simotuke). The two were on close terms. When Shigezane dispatched Endo Shimotsuke, the latter stated, "Now that the path to the reinforcements has been blocked, the fall of the castle is certain. I wish to entrust the castle to Shigezane and withdraw." Upon receiving the report, Masamune responded, "If you surrender to the Date clan, that is fine." However, Ishikawa Kageyu and the other garrison forces insisted on withdrawing to Obama, claiming, "Our withdrawal is not to beg for our lives, but to share our destruction with Ouchi Bizen." Masamune refused. Finding the enemy's request brazen, he judged that they would surrender given their level of prowess and launched an all-out attack. Endo Shimotsuke, who had entered the castle as a messenger, was in a predicament. Amidst the fierce onslaught of his allies, he escaped with desperate resolve, waving a small flag. He barely managed to return to his camp. Afterward, when fire was set to the castle from Shigezane's camp, various parts of the fortress began to burn as it was a windy day. Perhaps for this reason, the garrison unexpectedly quickly lost their resistance, and the castle fell. Masamune ordered a massacre; not only men and women, but even cattle and horses were slaughtered.

shigezane:kurono2.title: Letter from Shigezane Date
shigezane:kurono2.summary: A letter from Shigezane Date. It begins: "If it is deemed appropriate, I shall send someone immediately tomorrow. Since I shall dig tomorrow and arrive early the day after tomorrow, I request that you station musketeers among the laborers mentioned above. ..."
shigezane:kurono2.markdown:
If it is said that this is permissible, I shall send someone immediately tomorrow. Since I shall dig tomorrow and arrive early the day after tomorrow, I shall have the wooden beams ready and the musketeers stationed. — As for you saying it must not be done, you shall also return the muskets. I shall arrive within five or six days, so at that time I shall have the wooden beams ready. I believe the wooden beams should be ready by the 1st, so everyone—even if the rice is not ready—I would like to have it shown to you.

End

Lord Kakubei Kurono

shigezane:masamuneki-index.markdown:
This is based on the "Masamune-ki" contained in the "Date Historical Materials Collection." Or rather, it's a direct copy. Due to copyright issues, I will not post the footnotes from the source on the website.

Text conversion assistance: Kei-sama [慶様 \[sd-script\]-Writing about him-](http://sd-script.hateblo.jp/), who has been examining Shigezane Date, has converted the text and provided a modern Japanese translation on their own site. With Kei-sama's permission, I have reposted the converted portions on this site. The relevant article includes credit to Kei-sama and a link to their site. I hereby express my gratitude.

#### Volume 1

> Matters Concerning Ouchi, Bizen, and Date > Matters Concerning Ouchi's Leave > Matters Concerning the Concern for Nihonmatsu, Military Strategy in Inawashiro > Matters Concerning the Loyalty of Aoki Shuri > The Fall of Kotemori Castle, Aoki Shuri's Substitution as a Witness

#### Volume 2

> [Matters Concerning the Peace Agreement at the Nihonmatsu 8-chome Border](#/post/shigezane/masamuneki2-1) > [The Capture of Yotsumatsu](#/post/shigezane/masamuneki2-2) > [The Murder of Yoshitsugu of Nihonmatsu by His Own Retainers](#/post/shigezane/masamuneki2-3) > [The Battle of Hitotori Bridge at Motomiya](#/post/shigezane/masamuneki2-4)

#### Volume 3

shigezane:masamuneki1-1.title: Matters Concerning Ouchi, Bizen, and Date
shigezane:masamuneki1-1.summary: Thus, around that time, in Oshu, the Satake, Shirakawa, Sukagawa, and Ishikawa clans—all of them in bitter conflict—fought against Masamune, the seventeenth-generation head of the Fujiwara Asomi Date line.
shigezane:masamuneki1-1.markdown:
Thus, around that time, in Oshu, the Satake, Shirakawa, Sukagawa, and Ishikawa of the Sendo region were brutally united and fought against Masamune, the seventeenth head of the Date clan, known as Fujiwara no Asomi. When asked what had triggered the conflict, it came to light that in the eleventh year of Tensho (the year of the Water Goat), when Masamune was seventeen and his father Terumune was forty, he succeeded to the Date house and took up residence in the castle at Yonezawa. However, among the four pine-towns of Sendo in Oshu, there was a lord of Kohama named Ouchi Bizen Sadatsuna. Through certain circumstances, he had come to serve under the Date progenitor since the days of Old Bizen. The reason for this was the malice of Nakano Hitachi. Between the father and son, Uemune and Harumune, an unexpected plot had severed their bond of affection beyond all expectation, and the downfall of the Date house was already imminent. At that time, Bizen also abandoned the Date; since they were neighbors, he sought the help of Tamura Kiyoaki, remaining loyal to him as a single faction. During the war between Tamura and Iwaki one year, Bizen's younger brother Katahira Suke Ishimonro and others, along with Kiyoaki's kin including Tamura Uma-no-kami Ro and others, engaged in a quarrel at a field camp. The Uma-no-kami overstepped his bounds, and though Ouchi repeatedly filed lawsuits seeking the death penalty, Kiyoaki refused to grant it. Consequently, the Ouchi brothers turned their backs on Tamura and plotted with the Satake of Aizu; from the following year, the Ouchi became the vanguard and fought against Tamura for several years. As Masamune was Kiyoaki's son-in-law, he was still young and viewed this matter as a lingering grudge, but as it was still the era of his father Terumune, he could not fully vent his indignation and lived with a longing for the time to come. Thus, perhaps because the house members believed Masamune would become a distinguished and wise general from a young age, when he succeeded to the headship, what did the great officials of the neighboring provinces think? Messengers of congratulations arrived in extraordinary numbers from various places, and there were many letters of secret correspondence and requests for alliances from other nearby lords. Perhaps Ouchi Bizen Sadatsuna also thought his descendants were of great importance, for by this time, congratulatory gifts had arrived in full. The matter regarding Kiyoaki was thus discussed at the Ouchi residence, and it was said: "You have protected the Date for generations; now there is no reason for the line to be broken. Since this is a fortunate occasion, remain under our service as you are." Sadatsuna replied: "Since the days of Old Bizen, it has been my duty to protect the house. Nevertheless, one year ago, due to the treason of Nakano Hitachi, the bond of affection between my ancestors and father and son was endangered; since you sought help from Tamura despite being neighbors, a minor matter caused you to offend Kiyoaki's heart. Therefore, having appealed to the Satake and Aizu, your lands in Yotsumatsu remained secure through the kindness of those two provinces. Now, since you are asked to serve us—which is your original wish—how could I possibly betray you? In that case, I shall have my residence granted to you, and by next spring, I shall move there with my wife and children to reconcile with you and serve you." Accordingly, he was granted a residence. From that October until January of the following year (the twelfth year), he remained stationed at Yonezawa.

shigezane:masamuneki1-2.title: Retirement Grant to Ouchi
shigezane:masamuneki1-2.summary: In the same January, when Masamune was eighteen years old, Ouchi said, "Now that the snow is so deep that construction on the estate cannot proceed, I shall take this opportunity to request leave, make preparations to return to Yotsumatsu, and lead my wife and children with me." Masamune heard this...
shigezane:masamuneki1-2.markdown:
In the same first month, when Masamune was eighteen years old, Ouchi stated, "As the snow is now so deep that construction of the residence cannot proceed, I shall take this opportunity of granting leave, prepare to return to Yotsumatsu, and lead my wife and children with me." Upon hearing this, Masamune replied, "Since you have come of your own volition, there should be no cause for suspicion," and granted leave, sending him back to his ancestral lands in Yotsumatsu. Although the snow had cleared and the end of May had arrived, he never returned. There was no word from him. Consequently, although Endo Yamashiro, a retainer of the Date, admonished Ouchi, Ouchi maintained ties with Satake and Aizu, and thus Masamune did not even consider returning. Accordingly, Masamune immediately deliberated on an expedition to subdue them and had already set out. However, in recent years, Satake, Aizu, Iwaki, Ishikawa, Shirakawa, and Sukagawa had each reached a peace agreement with the Date, and all things had settled into tranquility; now, however, Satake, Aizu, and Ouchi had once again formed an alliance to rebel. Since Masamune was not yet twenty, Terumune—who found this utterly laughable—believed that if Ouchi were to be subdued, starting with the seasoned Satake Yoshishige and the great lords of neighboring provinces, they would become enemies. Terumune, holding a dissenting view, dispatched men and sent two envoys, Miyagawa Ikke and Igarashi Roshu, to Ouchi's residence, stating: "Masamune's resentment toward Tamura is such that he entrusts himself to the Date; if the matter is settled without incident, how could his reputation be tarnished?" Ouchi replied, "Your words are grateful, but having once betrayed them, I am prepared for my ruin." He further dispatched Harada Kyusetsu and Katakura Ikyu, stating, "Your concern is well-founded; therefore, let us settle the matter with hostages and appease Masamune's resentment." They refused, stating that this was also impossible. Furthermore, among the relatives of Bizen, there were men called Ouchi and Nagato, who had been sent to Yonezawa several times as envoys and were known to both father and son; at that time, they had taken the Buddhist name Gasai. To these two envoys, he said, "Regardless of how you proceed, Bizen will not accept it; why do you claim they will not enter? Even if they do not accept it, what can be done? Even if it is the army of the Date, perhaps it is something entirely different." The two envoys grew infuriated and replied, "Either you go to Yonezawa, or you subdue Yotsumatsu; we shall see what happens in the end." However, as there was no further concern thereafter, the two envoys did not proceed. When Kyusetsu and Ikyu returned and reported the matter, Terumune declared, "Masamune must subdue Ouchi and have his head displayed at the military gate," but for certain reasons, he delayed the dispatch of troops. Thus, Masamune summoned the Date retainers Harada Samanosuke Munenaga and Katakura Kojuro Kagetsuna and told them: "Regarding the matter brought by the envoys from Aizu, granting permission to Ouchi and Bizen is my utmost desire. I intend to move to Yonezawa as well, as there should be no complete collapse in Aizu. Now that Ouchi has rebelled, it is entirely the intention of Aizu. Such an act will send resentment and resentment as far as the neighboring provinces. I intend to sever ties with Aizu and initiate a military conflict; neither side will achieve their goals as desired. If there are those who plot a military coup and form a faction in that region, I intend to initiate a war and make my intentions known." Samanosuke asked, "Should I dispatch a certain Yoriki, a retainer of Aizu named Hirata Taroemon, to look into this?" Masamune inquired, "What is his true intention?" He replied, "I do not know the details, but he is usually clever; surely he would not be double-minded in his service." Accordingly, he proceeded; a man called Shibano Danjo, located to the north of Aizu, was intended to be made loyal, and along with him, not a single person from Danjo's faction—all of them—agreed that if Masamune mounted his horse, they would sever ties. Accordingly, on the fifth day of the fifth month of the thirteenth year (the year of the Wood Rooster), Samanosuke passed through, crossing a difficult pass called Mashikura-goe, and arrived at Danjo's place. Since Danjo lived in a residence without a castle, Samanosuke, though cautious, brought a small number of men, fearing he might return in vain. He raised the signal fire to sever ties; the Imatsu forces launched a surprise attack, and while allies came from various directions, there was a mutual suspicion that Aizu was changing its allegiance, and in a state of impatience, the envoy Hirata Taroemon suddenly changed his mind. He informed the enemy camp that the Aizu rebellion was the work of Shibata Danjo alone, and that from the Date, only Harada Samanosuke was present, lacking in numbers. The enemy army, emboldened by this, awaited a single battle. However, it ended in a defeat beyond all expectation; the Yoriki and retainers were all slain, and Samanosuke finally retrieved Danjo along with his wife and children. Then, on the third day of the same month, Masamune dispatched horses to a place called Hibara on the borders of Aizu territory—sixty ri north of Aizu and ten ri from Yonezawa. Hibara was captured immediately, but since this was the first act of rebellion against Aizu, even the troops from Yonezawa were dispatched in secret. Hearing that Samanosuke had been defeated, Masamune issued a summons on May fifth for the entire army to gather at Yarihara. While he waited for the forces to arrive, the Aizu troops barricaded themselves in Oshio, holding the castle firmly. On the eighth day, the Date forces advanced to the mountain above Oshio, but as there was only a single path through the mountains, there was no terrain suitable for a defensive position. Since the rear guard was separated from Hibara by a great mountain, no battle ensued; they withdrew shortly thereafter, sending back the low-ranking retainers and remaining at Hibara himself.

shigezane:masamuneki1-3.title: Matters Concerning the Care of Nihonmatsu, and Further on the Military Strategy of Inawashiro
shigezane:masamuneki1-3.summary: While ties with Aizu had been severed, no such break had occurred with Nihonmatsu, a faction of the Aizu clan, and matters remained peaceful. As for the reason for this, around that time, Shigezane and Chikazane handed over Omori in Shinobu to Shigezane, who then relocated to Hachichome, living secluded from the world.
shigezane:masamuneki1-3.markdown:
While a pact had been broken with Aizu, no such pact had been made with Nihonmatsu, an ally of Aizu, and the situation remained peaceful. The reason for this was that around that time, Shigezane and Chikazane had handed over Omori in Shinobu to Shigezane and moved to Hachichome, living there in seclusion. Consequently, Yoshitsugu of Nihonmatsu maintained secret communications with Chikazane and was on close terms with him. The details were as follows: although the Satake had allied with Aizu, Nihonmatsu and Yohonmatsu—originally positioned to balance the growing power of the Satake, Aizu, or the Sendo region—were in a precarious position of their own. Because Masamune, though young, was wise in governance and a formidable opponent in both literary and military arts, it was the intention that if the Date army were to mobilize this time, Yoshitsugu would rely on Chikazane and surrender. Since Chikazane also agreed, the boundary was successfully settled. The details are set forth below. On May 8, Shigezane departed from his castle at Omori; on the 9th, he arrived at Hibara and appeared before Masamune, who asked, "Regarding the breach with Aizu, how is the boundary with Nihonmatsu?" Shigezane replied, "For now, things are peaceful. Perhaps Yoshitsugu considers your position of authority to be of great importance. Two of his vassals, Yusa and Shimosa, are acquainted with Chikazane and are pleased to be with him; I have frequently sent Shimosa as messengers, and through secret communications, things have remained quiet. The breach of that boundary will be handled according to your instructions." Then, removing those present and speaking in secret, he mentioned the failure of the campaign against Aizu, stating, "Though the plan existed, every point was a stumbling block, and since there was no way to attack at the time, we even had to retreat yesterday. Now, I wish to first settle the boundary with Nihonmatsu; and since there is also a breach with Aizu, what do you think of attacking both fronts at once?" To this, Shigezane replied, "Among the high-ranking vassals of Aizu, Inawashiro Danjo Morikuni has a man named Ishibe Shimosa who is a capable man; shall we prepare the Danjo and see if he can achieve success?" He then summoned Uma-no-suke, who, having heard Shigezane's words, sent a letter stating, "I command you to employ military strategy." He further instructed Kagetsuna Katakura, Hoki (the Seven Officials), and Shigezane to attach accompanying letters, all of whom wrote their responses. Hoki, who had been a ronin in Aizu, had been supported by the Date and had a generous spirit; thus, he remained a trusted ally of Masamune. As he had many acquaintances in Aizu, he forwarded the letter. Furthermore, regarding Kagetsuna Katakura, who had been of humble birth, Masamune had taken him under his wing since his youth and used him closely; his reputation for bravery goes without saying. He was a foremost strategist; while it is common for people to be unable to move forward when contemplating ten plans, Kagetsuna's ten plans were all capable of advancing first. Perhaps it was because Masamune, even from a young age, viewed him as exceptional, even as a member of the household, that the house held him in high regard. Indeed, at the time, he rose from a mere foot soldier to Katakura; he became a man of honor and eventually grew into a high-ranking official who vied with others for position within the house, becoming a vassal and even attaining the rank of vanguard for the Date. The people of all ranks felt this. When such a humble man is promoted, it naturally invites criticism and envy in any province; the rise of a peer is one thing, but when one rises before a lord, jealousy is inevitable. Yet, from a young age, Masamune promoted many people, starting with Kagetsuna; whether they were high-ranking officials or common peasants, he never let slander stand. When he showed deep affection to one person, all the people felt humbled, as if they were his own. Thus, it is said that he was called a great general since ancient times, first because he recognized the people of his own house; surely, Masamune too would be called a great general. When Masamune was nineteen, on the twelfth day of the eighth month of Tensho 13 (the year of the Wood Rooster), he first led his horses to Yohonmatsu in the Sendo region. At that time, his father, Terumune, suffered an unforeseen death. Seizing this opportunity, the seven generals of the Sendo region—including the veteran Satake Yoshishige—prepared their camps at the main post of the Sendo region, intending to seize the Date and challenge the young Masamune. However, as proof of the loyalty of the soldiers who had followed him day after day, not a single man wavered; they achieved victory over a great force, and the seven generals eventually looked back at the nineteen-year-old Masamune. The details are all recorded above. Since those letters were written exactly as they were, Masamune declared, "Send those letters from here to Inawashiro, and leave the reply at Omori. Though the sun has set and men and horses are weary, I am concerned about the boundary of Nihonmatsu; therefore, I shall return quickly and shall have Minbu of Shigeno serve as my guide for the night." He then sent them on their way. "It is a noble cause, but return by night and day," he commanded. Thus, they returned via Yarihara that day. Six or seven days later, when Shikibu Omine and Hoki (the Seven Palace Guards) arrived at Omori and read the reply from Inawashiro, the Danjo was satisfied and pleased, stating that military strategy was of the utmost importance. He left Shikibu and Hoki in a place where no one knew of their identity and instead appointed a monk named Sanzoken, who had originally come from Inawashiro; this time, he sent Tsuchiyu-dori of Shinobu. [The content of that letter](#/post/shigezane/t13-6-11) stated: "Having read the reply sent from Hibara, I am deeply pleased by your loyalty. Should you have any further requests, I shall gladly comply. As Masamune has prepared the seal, I send this reply: 1. Half of the northern part of Aizu shall be granted to you. 2. The people of Aizu, regardless of their loyalty since my time, shall be seated in the seats of Aizu for generations; this shall not apply to the fudai-shu. 3. If you do not mobilize your army and withdraw from Inawashiro, a pardon shall be granted for the three hundred kanmon of your estate." Regarding these three requests, Shikibu and Hoki remained at Omori, and when the Danjo delivered the written instructions, Masamune read them and signed them, stating, "1. Regarding the three requests of the Danjo, there shall be no disorder. Should the castle be abandoned, the three hundred kanmon of Shiba within the domain shall be granted as requested." With this, the written instructions were handed to Shigezane. Since Shikibu and Hoki were going to Hibara, they returned to Inawashiro with Sanzoken carrying the seal. Two or three days later, Morikuni replied, "I have certainly received and accepted your seal. However, as the head of the house, Moritane insists that he must serve Aizu; I shall find a way to settle this and reach a pact." After a day or two, he sent Sanzoken again, urgently requesting a pact. Moritane refused, and the father and son became estranged. Even the children of the house were divided, and the agreed-upon pact failed; thus, the war against Aizu could not be carried out. A new post was established at Hibara, with Goto Magobei appointed as castle warden, while Masamune himself returned to his camp first. Thus, in May, when Masamune was nineteen, he departed from Yonezawa, where he was stationed, and this marked the beginning of his military campaigns. Shigezane was eighteen at the time; to have ventured into another province for military strategy without any foresight—now that it had come to this—was a perilous thing; the news of it reached others and was a disgrace, making my hair stand on end.

shigezane:masamuneki1-4.title: Aoki Shuri Tadatsuseji
shigezane:masamuneki1-4.summary: In the same July, Shigezane sent a messenger to Yonezawa, stating: "I have now received word regarding the inquiry from Inawashiro Danjo and his son; the loyalty we had agreed upon has deviated beyond all expectation, and matters have unfolded contrary to my intentions. Furthermore, as the attempt to sever ties with Aizu has met with various setbacks, I request that you first dispatch horses to Yotsumatsu on the Sendo road..."
shigezane:masamuneki1-4.markdown:
In July of the same year, Munemi sent an envoy to Yonezawa, stating: "This time, I come to request the assistance of Inawashiro Danjo and his son; the loyalty promised has proven to be contrary to my expectations, and as for the failure to conclude the agreement with Aizu, I shall first dispatch horses to Yotsumatsu on the Sendai road to punish Ouchi Bizen Sadaami; if you then proceed along the Sendai road, I shall ensure your success. Should you accept this request, I shall arrange for Sadatsuna's retainers to join your ranks." To this, he replied, "My only concern is that this attempt has ended in failure; though I depart, I would be most pleased if the loyalty of the Ouchi retainers were secured. In that case, I shall arrange the matter." Accordingly, Munemi dispatched two of his retainers—Ouchi no Naibun and Ishii Genshiro—to the residence of Yotsumatsu, for whom he felt a kinship; he sent those four men to Yotsumatsu and spoke with Aoki Shuri, a retainer of the Ouchi clan and lord of Karimatsuda Castle, who expressed his willingness to be loyal. Consequently, Munemi sent a written pledge of reward and expectation. In response, Ouchi turned his back on Tamura and grew anxious, taking hostages from his retainers; he likewise turned his back on Date, harboring further ambitions and treating all ranks of his retainers without distinction. Thus, Shuri had a younger brother named Shintaro, sixteen years old, who later came to Date and was brought under Masamune's direct patronage. Recently, Aoki Sabu had passed away, leaving a five-year-old son to Shintaro, whom he sent to Obama. However, if Shuri were to harbor treason, both hostages would be sentenced to death; even if he were to succeed in life, what profit would there be? He resolved that, no matter what, he would find a way to replace the witnesses. At one time, Shuri went to Obama and spoke to three young men—the sons of three senior retainers: Nakazawa Kuroshiro, Ouchi Shinpachiro, and Okochi Jirokichi—saying, "There are now many pheasant chicks at Karimatsuda; it is the season for chasing birds. Shintaro is not staying here, so come and chase some birds for amusement." Thinking this might be true, the three men came on the 5th day of the 8th month, and on the following 6th, they chased birds, a contest between Masako and her fourteen or fifteen-year-old brother. That night, they prepared a meal and drank heavily until midnight, at which point Shuri said, "It is dangerous to continue drinking after a few cups; let us simply draw our swords and pour more wine." The others replied that it was not a problem, but Shuri, harboring some secret, spoke with wit and deception, seizing the swords. "From now on, we shall drink freely," he said, taking the lead. Believing this to be the truth, they drank heavily and became intoxicated, losing all sense of time. At that time, Shuri and his fourteen retainers, having armored themselves, visited the three men at their beds on the morning of the 7th, saying, "We hold a grudge against Sadatsuna and have pledged our loyalty to Date. As you know, we have left Shintaro and his five-year-old child in Obama; we rely on you three to serve as witnesses. Even if Sadatsuna harbors resentment toward us, how could he abandon the children of three senior retainers? He must obey, for he fears for his life." The three young men were suddenly struck with panic; though they felt their lives were in danger, their swords were seized and they lacked the strength to fight. Furthermore, as their lives were too precious to abandon, all three reluctantly surrendered. Shuri, now at ease regarding the witnesses, set fire to Obama that day, cut ties, and reported the matter to Munemi. When Munemi hurriedly inquired of this at Yonezawa, it was said that it was too late until Munemi himself arrived; thus, four men—Koyanagawa Doriari, Shiroishi Wakasa, Hamada Izu, and Harada Samanosuke—were dispatched as Munemi's retainers and stationed at a place called Iino near Karimatsuda. Munemi established a camp at a place called Tateneyama, and Masamune also dispatched horses to Fukushima in Shinobu on the 12th day of the 8th month. Consequently, Shuri and Munemi took the opportunity to summon him, praising his extraordinary loyalty, and presented him with a sword with a golden hilt, given by Hasebe Kunishige. Afterward, Munemi ordered that a painting of Yotsumatsu be produced; a painter was assigned, and once the painting was completed and presented, Munemi ordered troops to be deployed from the vicinity of Karimatsuda. Before the operation began, he moved his camp to a place called Kawamata in Kote District. Before the operation, he met Kiyoaki for the first time at a place called Warigahira, marking the ninth year since their marriage. On the 23rd, he told Kiyoaki that the operation would begin at Kotemori, but due to heavy rain, it was carried out on the 4th. Meanwhile, reinforcements from Aizu, Sendai, and Nihonmatsu arrived to assist at Obama and came to the vicinity of Kotemori. At Kotemori, Ouchi Bizen himself was entrenched, and while many appeared within the castle, not a single enemy cavalryman appeared despite the allied forces pressing in; furthermore, the allies had no means of attacking. When the enemy's numbers were drawn out, a battle was initiated at the rear where the enemy had emerged; the allied troops repelled them and engaged in combat. The reinforcements from Aizu and Nihonmatsu, acting in coordination from within the castle, fought from the south entrance, while the Nihonmatsu forces led the vanguard. Thus, the Tamura forces attacked from the east, and the Date forces attacked from the north. Nevertheless, due to the great mountain between them, the Tamura forces did not engage in battle and instead acted as a screen for the Date troops. Masamune took the command baton from his waist and, with five or six hundred musketeers and hatamoto, attacked from the east side, cutting through the enemy's line. The enemy were utterly defeated and pushed back toward the gate, where two hundred and sixty-two were beheaded. Although many were slain, the enemy did not enter the gate but fled south of the castle; Masamune attacked them while the Nihonmatsu forces were still engaged, seeing that the allies were about to be overwhelmed, and immediately withdrew. Ouchi returned to Obama that night. The allies withdrew about five ri that night and established a camp at Ueno. Wondering if it would be possible to continue through the night, they sent out scouts along the roads, but found no trouble. On the 25th, they pressed the attack and encountered the enemy; reinforcements from Aizu arrived to assist, but they were stationed at a mountain called Nakukuki, preventing the enemy from entering below. Although there appeared to be a passage into the castle, the enemy did not enter, and thus they withdrew that day without incident, establishing no field camp in enemy territory. Nevertheless, the Tamura forces remained unengaged due to the great mountain. On the following 26th, they again attempted to attack, but were thwarted. Therefore, Kagetsuna Katakura suggested firing muskets to see if the castle's strength could be tested. Munemi agreed and fired at the gate, but the castle was firmly held in the center; thus, he pressed the attack again and established a field camp. This time, there was a bamboo hut south of the castle. "If Munemi moves his camp tomorrow and blocks the passage into the castle, we certainly cannot hold out. If Munemi moves his camp, the allied forces will coordinate; what then?" they asked. Masamune replied, "If he moves to the bamboo hut, the enemy reinforcements will descend and obstruct us; at that point, we shall emerge from the castle and fight a battle at both entrances." Munemi replied, "Even if there are two entrances, if he moves his camp, our encounter with the Tamura forces will be the primary point. If he has already sallied out to Munemi's camp, the Tamura forces and Munemi will be left to their own devices. Furthermore, if we assist the reinforcements stationed to the side, their numbers will obstruct the allied forces; since the terrain is a critical point, a battle would not be easily won. As for how to handle this, even the day before yesterday, when you pushed into the gate, the Nihonmatsu forces fought fiercely, but you withdrew out of concern for the vulnerable point." Harada Kyusetsu replied, "The matter of moving the camp is a serious matter that must be handled with caution; let us simply wait a few days and see how things develop." Everyone agreed that Kyusetsu's reasoning was sound, and some suggested it would be better to let him move, but on that day, they withdrew without further dispute.

shigezane:masamuneki1-5.title: Regarding the Replacement of Witness Aoki Shuri at the Fall of Kotemori Castle
shigezane:masamuneki1-5.summary: As dawn broke, I moved the camp to the bamboo residence I mentioned yesterday—a move that was quite unwelcome; furthermore, while it was prudent to do so without notifying Masamune, I moved it today at the Hour of the Rabbit in order to block the paths of Shiroyama and keep the enemy from observing. Thus, Date Ueno-no-kami Masakage also...
shigezane:masamuneki1-5.markdown:
As dawn broke, I moved the camp to the bamboo residence mentioned yesterday; while this was generally disliked, I moved it without consulting Masamune—though this was a precautionary measure—to block the passage at Shiroyama and allow the enemy to observe the situation. Thus, I moved the camp today at the hour of the Rabbit, and Date Ueno-no-kami Masakage followed suit. Upon hearing this, Masamune declared that the entire army should also relocate. Consequently, the entire force gradually made preparations for the move. While this was happening, a man emerged from within the castle, holding a small flag and beckoning us toward him; when asked what business he had, he identified himself as Ishikawa Kageyu, stating that since Shigezane's retainer Endo Shimotsuke was a close confidant, he had matters to discuss upon meeting him. When Shimotsuke was brought forward and met him, he said, "My request is not for any other purpose than this: the retainers of the Bizen fudai are entrenched in this castle. Among them are Ono Shusui and Arai Hannai, servants close to the Ouchi; they lead the garrison, but since the passage is blocked and the fall of the castle is imminent, I rely on Shigezane to lead the charge and withdraw from the castle." When this matter was reported to Masamune, he declared, "Should we advance the army's front and seize it without incident? Even so, should the enemy army withdraw toward this side, I shall send out an outpost." When this was relayed to Kageyu, he replied, "Those who have come to the house are all pleading for their lives. Even if they request an outpost or a petition, it is because the destruction of Bizen would be unthinkable; they beg that the fudai retainers be withdrawn to Obama, and that the two generations of their descendants be spared." When this request was repeated, Masamune declared that they would not be sent. Furthermore, Shimotsuke was dispatched to convey this message; at that time, a man was led into the second inner gate, and Kageyu went up to the main bailey to deliver the instructions. Then, Masamune spoke to Shigezane, saying, "The men within the castle are speaking of their own accord; they are merely rabble who speak ill of us. If we capture this castle without resistance, even if the main bailey does not fall, the enemy army will withdraw toward this side. In such a case, it would serve to alert the enemy in the surrounding areas." Meanwhile, a notice was sent through the camp to attack swiftly, and hatamoto were dispatched. Accordingly, Shigezane attacked the castle and, after gaining control, opened fire with muskets. Shimotsuke, acting as a messenger, could not emerge from the inner gate and, waving a small flag, slipped into the camp of the enemy; thus, his life was saved. Afterward, Shigezane's camp opened fire, and as the wind happened to be strong and blew in all directions, the enemy's positions were abandoned beyond their expectations. From the hour of the Horse, the attack began, and both the castle and the main bailey fell. Masamune declared, "They shall be cut down," and various inspectors were appointed; not only men and women, but even cattle and horses were slaughtered. The withdrawal took place at the hour of the Rooster. The new castle and Kiyama were enemy territory, but startled by the spears of Kotemori, both castles were burned to the ground that night. The following day, at twenty-two sun, a notice was issued to move to Tsukidate. While we were moving the camp, a lone rider emerged from Tsukidate and beckoned us toward him. Shigezane and his men mounted and, upon asking what was the matter, found a man named Hattori Gennai, a ronin from Yohonmatsu who had been in Shigezane's service for a year. Around that time, Gennai had intended to remain in Tsukidate, but he was dismissed and told, "The enemies within the castle have just withdrawn; hurry and press them to take them." At that point, the allies prepared and pressed the attack, and in the meantime, the enemy withdrew without leaving a single person. Masamune then moved to that castle and let the men and horses rest. Meanwhile, the lord of that place intended to use three men—including Aoki Shuri, as mentioned—as witnesses, and notified Obama to that effect. The Ouchi were regretful that these witnesses were being returned, but since they could not abandon the children of three senior retainers, they had no choice but to set a deadline. Shuri then requested a supervisor from Masamune; the two parties met at a place called Kosegawa, and Shuri exchanged his younger brother Shintaro and a five-year-old child for three young men. The people of the time felt that this was a commendable feat of military strategy. Kan'ei 13, Year of the Fire Rat, an auspicious day in June. Date Awa Shigezane
