shigezane:masamuneki10-1.title: Actions Taken by Shigezane
shigezane:masamuneki10-1.summary: Accordingly, from the beginning of the Kan'ei era, Masamune established a residence three cho square in the vicinity of Kokubun Sendai in Miyagi, dug a moat thirty ken wide along the outer perimeter, constructed embankments over two jo and several shaku, named the area Wakabayashi, and moved there from Sendai.
shigezane:masamuneki10-1.markdown:
Accordingly, from the beginning of the Kan'ei era, Masamune established a residence three cho in all directions near Kokubun Sendai in the Miyagi district; he dug a moat thirty ken wide around the outer perimeter and built embankments over two jo and several shaku, naming the place Wakabayashi and moving there from Sendai. In time, not only the various retainers but even the towns themselves were established, and it reached a point where it was thought he might use it as a place of retirement. Consequently, plans were drawn up for the Shigezane residence, and applications were submitted three or four times. At that time, the young child, titled Hyobu-no-daifu, was frequently presented with Noh performances; thus, a stage was erected at the Shigezane residence, and on the 19th day of the second month of the eleventh year, an application was made to present Noh performances. The former lord held a gathering at the sukiya, and thereafter proceeded to the shoin, where he was granted one kara-ori night robe, ten kosode, and ten scrolls. From this side, a tachi-origami, one hundred silver coins, one black horse, and one hundred bundles of cotton were presented. When Masamune changed the attire to long hakama, the Noh performance began according to the proper etiquette, and the relatives each came to watch. In connection with this, as a token of greeting, he placed his usual attendants by his veranda. Among them was a man from the Kamigata region named Sobaku, who held a fief of one hundred kanmon and had a style of dress befitting a host; he was scheduled to accompany the lord in the shoin that day. However, while Hyobu-no-daifu was performing Noh—as he was young—Masamune was in a particularly high spirits; perhaps Sobaku was under the influence of alcohol, or perhaps it was simply a matter of luck. He became quite intoxicated and praised the performers excessively, even overstepping the bounds of the relatives; some ignored him, while others treated it as a mere diversion. Yet, still intoxicated, he felt it would be wrong not to make the guests weep, and without regard for the eyes of others, he repeated this two or three times. Then, as the color of his skin changed, he took a nearby sword and struck Sobaku on the head with the scabbard, splitting it open by one or two sun and drawing blood across his face. Everyone then left the room, and Masamune, having left his own room, entered the toshi-ma. With his two messengers, Nakajima Kanmono and Sasa Wakasa, he went to the Shigezane residence and said, "After all this construction, whatever anger you may harbor, there is no reason for such things; moreover, as Sobaku has always been my companion, everyone knows the inconveniences that arise. If today things remain gloomy, or if the success of the construction is poor, or if the matter of his neck is handled poorly, how could I possibly endure it? As for us below, we shall wait for the moment; as for those above, unless there is a fitting occasion, it would indeed be improper. Please consider this carefully. Of the several thousand spectators on that white sands, there will surely be people from various provinces, two or three at a time. Even if it is your place, your rank has risen to Chunagon, yet your manners are improper; you fear neither the Imperial Court nor the ridicule of others, yet you fail to observe proper etiquette—this is a disgrace to the ears of people from other provinces. Now, that man, when he returned to his own province and spent a year in Sendai, Oshu, he treated Masamune as a relative, calling him Date Awa, and performed Noh for him; his manners were proper. However, there was a Noh attendant monk of a certain age beside him who spoke as he pleased, acting with utter insolence; it was said that people merely listened, yet it was said they were different. Such sentiments have vanished like bubbles of water since ancient times; your current anger stems from this. Even if you did not remove him, as you are both of a certain age, you ought to complain to your master; therefore, I have withdrawn my seat." Upon hearing this, he was moved to tears and said, "I am grateful for your words, but at that moment, I sent the guests to that seat; your anger is entirely justified. Your words are deeply painful." To this, Masamune replied again, "Since you speak so freely, there is no reason for such ill will; the master should also relax his heart and watch the performance. Let the Noh begin." With no lingering resentment, he rose as night fell. Now, the first point of suspicion was: what had happened to Masamune since that evening? He was constantly anxious that a fire might break out. The master's retainers, perhaps exhausted by their daily toil, told him to earnestly warn them against fire; Nakajima Kanmono, Okuyama Daigaku, Sasa Wakasa, and even the head page conducted a close investigation. It was said that when they checked the hearth in the toshi-ma, someone had dropped a cigarette ember into the trash beneath the veranda. The fire naturally spread to both kitchens, and at the hour of the Tiger that night, one building of the residence was engulfed in flames. While it was still burning, he sent Sasa Wakasa as an envoy, saying, "Though it is laughable, this is a time when losses are inevitable, so do not let it weigh on your mind." After the fire had passed one day, he gave instructions to the shoin and ordered the repair of the partially burned areas, telling Wakasa to carefully report any further deficiencies. Such was his sincere heart; though he forgot the appearance when writing, his pen would not stop. In all, he devoted himself to the matter with all his heart, but as is the way of life in this world, he passed away; that no trace of him remains—regardless of the eyes of others—is a matter of great sorrow for the retainers and all people. Even after that, Sobaku escaped the scene, but his clothing was damaged; perhaps they wondered how he could serve him twice, and after two or three days, both father and son were sentenced to death.

shigezane:masamuneki10-2.title: The Conduct of Masamune Throughout His Life
shigezane:masamuneki10-2.summary: As such, I should have always been well aware of the affairs of the ladies of the house; yet, even in public, there were many times when they did not see me. Since both the private and public matters of the house were open and hidden nothing remained hidden; thus, I have recorded here all that I have seen and heard.
shigezane:masamuneki10-2.markdown:
As such, one would naturally expect him to be well acquainted with matters concerning the inner quarters; indeed, even in public, there were many times when he did not see them. Since both the inner and outer quarters were open to the house, both the good and the bad, I have recorded here all that I witnessed. Upon rising in the morning, he would tie his hair in a single bundle, perform his ablutions, and return to his main bed to request tobacco. The person who rolled and brought the tobacco was fixed to the inner quarters; as for the tobacco itself, he would spread a Chinese leather mat beneath it, place a tool upon it, and have the tobacco rolled and a candle lit—whether three or five pipes, it was always as prescribed. Afterward, he would go out to the public quarters and enter the private room. The private room was a single Kyoto-style room, one square *ken* in size, with three-tiered shelves inside; upon the shelves were an inkstone, writing paper, a writing board, and an incense burner, and besides, a sword rack and various other items were neatly arranged. Whenever he entered the private room, pottery was provided for both morning and evening. Later, when he entered the bathing room, the inner page-boy would bring the morning meal tray from the kitchen; he would correct any details that did not suit his taste and send them to the scribes, who would then produce a clean copy and hand it over. As for taking his bath, he would place his large and small swords in the sword rack and set his nose-paper, inro, drawstring bag, obi, and kosode in a wide lid; even in these details, there was never the slightest deviation. Furthermore, regardless of how the bath was taken or how he was dressed in a yukata to wipe himself, everything was as prescribed. In general, he took two baths, morning and evening; not to mention when traveling, even amidst cold winds and storms, these manners remained constant. After his bath, he would enter the public bedroom, change into the kosode he had received from the inner quarters in the morning, go out to the usual living quarters, and have his hair tied. At this time, he would untie his left side; it was said that because the cords would naturally loosen, he would untie them several times. Regarding the five seasonal festivals, he wore a pair of matching garments; on the 1st, 15th, and 28th of the month, he wore a haori and hakama. Afterward, he would go to the public parlor and call out, "Companions!" At that time, of the two page-boys on duty, one would sit and call out while the other stepped forward; with his own directions to those on either side, he would arrange the parlor and call, "Bring the trays!" When the trays were brought, none were left for the companions; as soon as the trays were delivered, he would straighten his knees, take his chopsticks, and place his hand on his wrist to eat, and likewise, the companions would begin to eat with their chopsticks. Then, as the second tray of side dishes was brought, the page-boys would gather in the shadows, compare the dishes, and serve them one by one. After eating, when he drank sake, he would rinse his mouth, as was customary. However, if even one of the relatives joined him, he would not do so. Normally, he would not drink even large quantities of sake, stating that it depended on the temperament of the person. If one were to circulate it for amusement, thinking Masamune might also drink it, they would gather around and pass it from person to person; even if he himself did not drink, he would wait as long as the matter was not settled, until he saw that a conclusion had been reached, and then he would request "hot water." When the trays were brought and the tea sweets arrived, he would circulate them among the guests and stand to wash his hands; the companions would then follow and wash their hands, and the main guests would say, "Everything is as it should be." At that time, he would face the stand by the tea altar, prepare the tea, and serve the thin tea and sweets. When he picked up the tea cover, the companions would follow and stand; then the officials would enter and attend to various needs. When the eight-bell clock struck, the day's business was concluded, and the evening meal tray was brought; he would arrange it as he had done in the morning, and then enter the inner quarters. The evening meal was consumed in the grand inner quarters, after which he entered the private room and took his evening bath. The manners throughout the day from the morning were as described above; beyond this, there were countless other minute details. Thus, it was said that the inner quarters never passed idle time. While he did not do such things in public, for the amusement of the inner quarters, he would place documents on a viewing stand and read them constantly. Therefore, his calligraphy was large and unmistakable throughout the land; his poetry and song were a companion to those of great status or to monks, and when poetry was exchanged, he would respond with appropriate verses. Moreover, since he had not indulged in military battles from a young age, his scholarship was extensive; while his poetry and song did not manifest openly, it was not seen that he was lacking in them. At that time, he invited poets—Kannyo, his son Kaneyo, his nephew Kanemasu, and others named Kaneya—and took them under his wing, traveling between Edo and Sendai, providing them with service and support. Furthermore, he brought his wife and children and kept them at the castle without interruption for a long time. In a certain year, when Kaneyo and Kanemasu arrived, he gathered the priests of the household to amuse themselves with poetry and song.

shigezane:masamuneki11-6.title: Deer Hunting
shigezane:masamuneki11-6.summary: On the 19th day of the first month of the 13th year of Kan'ei (Year of the Fire Rat), he departed from Wakabayashi and proceeded to an island called Jugohama, fifteen days' journey ahead, where he went deer hunting.
shigezane:masamuneki11-6.markdown:
On the nineteenth day of the first month of the thirteenth year of Kan'ei (the year of the Fire Rat), he departed from Wakabayashi and proceeded to an island called Jugohama, fifteen days' journey ahead, where he went deer hunting. During his journey, he spent his time merely indulging in various excursions here and there. Around that time, his favorite pages—Nan Jirokichi and Kato Jusaburo—told him and all the other pages, "At this stop along the way, there is a landing place called Yokogawa; though it is a small place, its development is not far inferior to that of Sendai. It is a port on the Kitakami River and serves as the inner capital; let us show this to the younger men." And so, they stayed there for the night. Now, that Yokogawa was quite different from how it had been in the past; it was now so desolate that it was unmistakable. When one spoke of Yokogawa, it meant the shrine of Yokogawa, but it no longer retained any trace of its former appearance. Masamune, seeing this, was struck by the change in scenery and said, "How is it that it has become so desolate? Explain the details of this matter." He rigorously investigated the matter, down to the officials and village headmen, growing incensed; and in the following morning's kyoka,

If it be hard, even tabi or ten pairs of straw sandals would be of no use—Yokogawa.

...he composed the poem. On that day, he arrived at a temporary lodge on an island called Nafuri; the following day he rested, and from there he ventured into the mountains for his daily deer hunt. Strangely, in the mountains where he had pursued the deer, three deer—which had not been seen even in the morning's nets—came out and galloped; their whiteness was truly striking. Masamune beheld these deer and declared, "How extraordinary! They are a remarkable sight; I shall capture them as my achievement." Everyone pressed forward, eager to capture them and make themselves prominent, but two escaped, and as it seemed the last one was also slipping away, he himself stopped them—was this perhaps a mysterious omen of good fortune? Overall, he spoke thus while in the mountains, declaring that this would be his final departure to that island and repeatedly speaking of his reluctance to leave. On the evening he departed from that island, it rained and he remained there for one day; the following day passed faster than ever before. In the account of this, everyone listened attentively, and all composed poems as their final farewells. "Since my age is such that this shall be my final departure to this island, I shall compose one poem as a parting word," he declared,

Guided by the moon of a cloudless heart, I clear the darkness of this fleeting world—thus I go.

He composed this poem and passed away; thus, it is truly lamentable that the poem above became his death poem.

shigezane:masamuneki11-7.title: The Journey to Edo
shigezane:masamuneki11-7.summary: From the second and third months of that year, whether on excursions or visiting various places, he would occasionally remark, "This coming spring will surely be difficult to pass; my solace while in the capital shall end here." But when April soon arrived, he said, "I shall depart on the twentieth of that month."
shigezane:masamuneki11-7.markdown:
From the second and third months of that year, he ceased all leisurely outings and visits, occasionally remarking, "This coming spring will surely be difficult to pass; my solace in the capital shall end here." When April soon arrived, he declared, "I shall depart on the twentieth of that month." In the meantime, Masamune had long yearned for the early spring of the cuckoo, and having heard that the cuckoo had always visited every summer, he dispatched messengers to inquire about its whereabouts. Upon receiving word, he immediately opened the shoji screens and rejoiced, saying, "How auspicious!" That summer, too, he declared, "I am too lazy to travel; I shall remain in my home province and not hear a single cry," and though he journeyed to the various mountains, still no word came. Out of sheer frustration, on the night of the nineteenth, he went out into the woods surrounding Sendai Castle and ate his lunch at the site of the mountain of his longing, now the burial ground. "Indeed, this mountain is bordered by a river, situated beneath Sendai and Wakabayashi; one can see all the way to the sea, and the scenery is beyond compare. Even if I were to die tomorrow, this shall be the residence for my second generation. Ensure that Tadamune is well informed of this," he declared. Composing a series of poems, he wrote: "Even if the cuckoo does not sing, what could I possibly grieve over? Even in the twilight of a future evening," and returned at dusk. On the morning of the twentieth, he departed from Wakabayashi. As he had intended, his destination was Iwanuma; as he passed along the coastal road, the cuckoo arrived and rested its wings upon the willows in the alleys. Despite the large retinue, it paid them no mind, merely gazing down at the mounts upon which it perched. Then, without a single sound, it flew away, singing, about fourteen or fifteen ken ahead, roughly one cho to the east of the road. Having heard the cuckoo so frequently of late, his attendants were immensely delighted, exclaiming, "How auspicious is this departure!" Thereupon, Masamune entered Iwanuma Castle and said to those close to him, "Have you all heard of today's cuckoo? I am seventy years old, yet it is rare for me to hear its first cry; moreover, to see the bird so close from within its mount, fourteen or fifteen ken ahead—I cannot even recall such a thing. This shall be a fortunate omen for my departure for Edo; or perhaps it is a sign of misfortune?" Having thus concluded his visit, he stayed the night at Shiroishi in Kata-kurai, the castle of Kojuro Katakura, and retired to bed, exhausted. The next morning, in high spirits, he held a reception before his sake, with Sannosuke—the adopted son and representative of Kojuro—present. Afterward, as Sannosuke was riding his horse, Masamune, who doted on him, said to Nanjiro Kichi, "May I offer you a cup of sake as a token of my goodwill?" Without heeding this, Kichi began various anecdotes; after some time, when Masamune inquired further, he replied, "I shall not speak of such things repeatedly. You both should be mindful; it is not for me, and the cup should not be sent hastily, yet there is a reason why I deliberately refrain. When asked for the details, Kojuro has no son and has appointed his grandson as his son; this is truly an extraordinary inconvenience. Naturally, the retainers will undoubtedly try to push him forward; he is only five or six years old, so it is not an unreasonable request, but during the previous audience, he appeared utterly bewildered. Kojuro's long-standing inconveniences may now suddenly be reversed and become an ordeal. Now, if he is called 'son' and drinks a cup, Kojuro will surely be concerned; moreover, seeing such a sight from the side would be unsightly, and some might say the cup is unsuitable for Kojuro. If that is the case, then even as a provisional measure, it is not a blessing for Kojuro, but rather a misfortune for all." Thus, without giving him the cup, he departed. As he did, he summoned Sannosuke to the front of the mount and, holding the reins himself, said, "Kojuro is a fortunate man; take such a good son and raise him with care." As this was such a profound sentiment, the attendants were deeply moved, and Kojuro, overwhelmed by the grace, cried out and shed tears. Indeed, all things have their fortunes and misfortunes; as he had always been deeply affectionate toward Takano, the attendants were greatly delighted. Then, on that day, as he departed from Wakabayashi, one wonders what the attendants felt. Though they were not in the mood for a grand departure for Edo, they felt a surge of courage; by the evening, everyone wished to return to their own homes. Out of sheer suspicion, they inquired of one another at Shiroishi, and found their hearts in accord—a most auspicious omen. Thus, upon arriving in Edo, in less than a month, he descended upon his corpse; it was truly a marvel.

shigezane:masamuneki12-1.title: Matters of Illness
shigezane:masamuneki12-1.summary: On the 21st of the same month, he departed Shiroishi, and after a day or two of travel, he felt a sense of something unusual.
shigezane:masamuneki12-1.markdown:
On the 21st of the same month, he departed for Shiroishi; the journey felt unusual, as if it were an extraordinary occasion. Nevertheless, as it coincided with the twenty-first anniversary of the death of the Great Chancellor Lord Ieyasu, and as Lord Iemitsu of the Shogunal house was grandly constructing a shrine at Mount Nikko, Masamune proceeded directly to Nikko from his journey. On the 25th, he visited the shrine; the court nobles descended, and as the monkey-dancers began their Noh performances before the deity, Masamune first entered the quarters of the Sojo. Once everything was concluded, he proceeded to the shrine, where he was guided by Itami Harima-no-kami, the chief commissioner for the reconstruction of the hall. While there, the court musicians performed the Kagura, and as Masamune approached the gateway, the court attendants offered three bows of ritual paper and brought a sake flask from the offerings, proceeding to offer the three-three-nine-degree ritual. However, as his spirits grew increasingly subdued, he felt a desire to hurry back down the mountain. But Harima-no-kami said, "I have been appointed as the commissioner for a single hall in this mountain's construction, and since the Shogunal Lord Iemitsu has recently passed away, I trust that your feelings will be granted through my services. Though it is a hardship, I beg you to please visit this mountain; if the Shogunal Lord's wishes are fulfilled, if such a construction is a reward before the deity, then a single word of your appreciation would suffice; if I may be so bold, I shall arrange the details for you." He then guided him to the inner sanctuary. Though his mood remained heavy, he ascended without complaint. As he stepped onto the stone platform in front of the garden, he collapsed. When he was helped up, a small cut appeared beside his right finger and was bandaged; he then stood before the hall and declared, "I shall pray with a quiet heart; you shall descend first." Harima-no-kami immediately descended. Masamune stood in the garden of the hall and said, "From here I shall descend; to have collapsed where one should not is seen as a sign that this shall be the final time I go to Nikko; I shall not go any further to see the sights." Thereafter, he returned to the inn at Imaichi. Strangely enough, a horse he cherished deeply, named Shiga Kurige, was brought out that day to lead him down the mountain. This horse, who had been exceptionally spirited, suddenly neighed twice or three times and collapsed, dying instantly. Medicine was administered and he recovered; by the time he returned to Imaichi at night, there were no signs of illness. Some said that this horse had died because Masamune had ceased eating from the moment he fell ill. Upon arriving at Imaichi again, as he washed himself and had his hair tied, a bird like a dove flew in from behind and rested its wings upon a fir tree in the garden of the room. It was near Nan Jirokichi and Kato Juzaburo; when they noticed it, they remarked that the various colors of its plumage were beyond description—truly a bird of foreign lands. Out of sheer curiosity, they reported the matter to Masamune, who saw it and said, "That is a bustard; it is rare for one to come so close to the village." Before he could finish speaking, the bird flew off toward Nikko. Looking after it, he saw something like smoke trailing from behind Masamune to the fir tree, and from the fir tree, the bird's trail continued. Though they were merely two pages, as those who had served for two generations, they did not utter a word of complaint. After he passed away, they told this as the final tale. On April 28th, he arrived in Edo, and on the 29th, at the hour of the Dragon, Matsudaira Izu-no-kami arrived as an envoy. Hearing that he had been unwell since the start of the journey under a scorching sun, Izu-no-kami remarked that it was laughable and commanded that the illness be duly acknowledged. Upon meeting Izu-no-kami, Masamune said, "My diligence in fulfilling the Emperor's wishes has been considerable; as it has been some time since I have seen your noble countenance, tomorrow is the first day of the month, so I shall enter the castle and offer my thanks." With this request, he entered the castle the following day at the hour of the Rabbit, had an audience, and retired at the hour of the Horse. Then, on that same day, Abe Bungo-no-kami arrived as an envoy and delivered a hawk, stating, "Generally, the daimyo who visit the shrine do so without fail every April; the fact that you ascended while so ill is deeply regrettable. Your spirits are further diminished; for the sake of your recovery, it is essential that you directly appoint Don-an Hoin as your physician and arrange for treatment to begin tomorrow."

shigezane:masamuneki12-2.title: The Shogun's Attendance at the Medical Treatment
shigezane:masamuneki12-2.summary: Accordingly, from the beginning of the Kan'ei era, Masamune established a residence three cho square in the vicinity of Kokubun Sendai in Miyagi, dug a moat thirty ken wide along the outer perimeter, constructed embankments over two jo and several shaku, named the area Wakabayashi, and moved there from Sendai.
shigezane:masamuneki12-2.markdown:
Accordingly, from the beginning of the Kan'ei era, Masamune established a residence three cho in all directions near Kokubun Sendai in the Miyagi district; he dug a moat thirty ken wide around the outer perimeter and built embankments over two jo and several shaku, naming the place Wakabayashi and moving there from Sendai. In time, not only the various retainers but even the towns themselves were established, and it reached a point where it was thought he might use it as a place of retirement. Consequently, plans were drawn up for the Shigezane residence, and applications were submitted three or four times. At that time, the young child, titled Hyobu-no-daifu, was frequently presented with Noh performances; thus, a stage was erected at the Shigezane residence, and on the 19th day of the second month of the eleventh year, an application was made to present Noh performances. The former lord held a gathering at the sukiya, and thereafter proceeded to the shoin, where he was granted one kara-ori night robe, ten kosode, and ten scrolls. From this side, a tachi-origami, one hundred silver coins, one black horse, and one hundred bundles of cotton were presented. When Masamune changed the attire to long hakama, the Noh performance began according to the proper etiquette, and the relatives each came to watch. In connection with this, as a token of greeting, he placed his usual attendants by his veranda. Among them was a man from the Kamigata region named Sobaku, who held a fief of one hundred kanmon and had a style of dress befitting a host; he was scheduled to accompany the lord in the shoin that day. However, while Hyobu-no-daifu was performing Noh—as he was young—Masamune was in a particularly high spirits; perhaps Sobaku was under the influence of alcohol, or perhaps it was simply a matter of luck. He became quite intoxicated and praised the performers excessively, even overstepping the bounds of the relatives; some ignored him, while others treated it as a mere diversion. Yet, still intoxicated, he felt it would be wrong not to make the guests weep, and without regard for the eyes of others, he repeated this two or three times. Then, as the color of his skin changed, he took a nearby sword and struck Sobaku on the head with the scabbard, splitting it open by one or two sun and drawing blood across his face. Everyone then left the room, and Masamune, having left his own room, entered the toshi-ma. With his two messengers, Nakajima Kanmono and Sasa Wakasa, he went to the Shigezane residence and said, "After all this construction, whatever anger you may harbor, there is no reason for such things; moreover, as Sobaku has always been my companion, everyone knows the inconveniences that arise. If today things remain gloomy, or if the success of the construction is poor, or if the matter of his neck is handled poorly, how could I possibly endure it? As for us below, we shall wait for the moment; as for those above, unless there is a fitting occasion, it would indeed be improper. Please consider this carefully. Of the several thousand spectators on that white sands, there will surely be people from various provinces, two or three at a time. Even if it is your place, your rank has risen to Chunagon, yet your manners are improper; you fear neither the Imperial Court nor the ridicule of others, yet you fail to observe proper etiquette—this is a disgrace to the ears of people from other provinces. Now, that man, when he returned to his own province and spent a year in Sendai, Oshu, he treated Masamune as a relative, calling him Date Awa, and performed Noh for him; his manners were proper. However, there was a Noh attendant monk of a certain age beside him who spoke as he pleased, acting with utter insolence; it was said that people merely listened, yet it was said they were different. Such sentiments have vanished like bubbles of water since ancient times; your current anger stems from this. Even if you did not remove him, as you are both of a certain age, you ought to complain to your master; therefore, I have withdrawn my seat." Upon hearing this, he was moved to tears and said, "I am grateful for your words, but at that moment, I sent the guests to that seat; your anger is entirely justified. Your words are deeply painful." To this, Masamune replied again, "Since you speak so freely, there is no reason for such ill will; the master should also relax his heart and watch the performance. Let the Noh begin." With no lingering resentment, he rose as night fell. Now, the first point of suspicion was: what had happened to Masamune since that evening? He was constantly anxious that a fire might break out. The master's retainers, perhaps exhausted by their daily toil, told him to earnestly warn them against fire; Nakajima Kanmono, Okuyama Daigaku, Sasa Wakasa, and even the head page conducted a close investigation. It was said that when they checked the hearth in the toshi-ma, someone had dropped a cigarette ember into the trash beneath the veranda. The fire naturally spread to both kitchens, and at the hour of the Tiger that night, one building of the residence was engulfed in flames. While it was still burning, he sent Sasa Wakasa as an envoy, saying, "Though it is laughable, this is a time when losses are inevitable, so do not let it weigh on your mind." After the fire had passed one day, he gave instructions to the shoin and ordered the repair of the partially burned areas, telling Wakasa to carefully report any further deficiencies. Such was his sincere heart; though he forgot the appearance when writing, his pen would not stop. In all, he devoted himself to the matter with all his heart, but as is the way of life in this world, he passed away; that no trace of him remains—regardless of the eyes of others—is a matter of great sorrow for the retainers and all people. Even after that, Sobaku escaped the scene, but his clothing was damaged; perhaps they wondered how he could serve him twice, and after two or three days, both father and son were sentenced to death.

shigezane:masamuneki12-3.title: Notice of Death Regarding the Second Generation's Submission
shigezane:masamuneki12-3.summary: On the 22nd of the same month (May, Kan'ei 13), all those called the attendants of the second generation submitted their written petitions; upon reviewing them and pressing them against my face, I exclaimed, "My, what a pity!"
shigezane:masamuneki12-3.markdown:
On the 22nd of the same month (May, Kan'ei 13), all those who served as attendants to the second generation submitted written petitions. Upon reviewing them and seeing their faces, he declared, "Ah, what a pity. If such men were to be put to use in the affairs of this world, how could they not be of great help in securing the realm? Some are young, others are vigorous; they would surely be of great service to the lord and Tadamune. Please, find a way to aid them." He then entrusted the matter to Naito Gaiki and Yagyu Tajima-no-kami. Furthermore, although Oi-no-kami and Sanuki-no-kami, acting on private intentions from within the palace, attempted to obstruct the matter in various ways, he firmly decided that, given the urgency of the matter, he must proceed without hesitation. Throughout this time, Masamune appeared deeply distressed, and it was beyond words. Nevertheless, from the onset of his illness until the end, not once did he utter a word of complaint. On the 23rd of the same month, perhaps thinking there was no longer time to waste, he declared, "Clear away all tools and implements, and cast into fire anything that is no longer needed." Beside him was a woman, twice his age, the chief retainer of the ladies-in-waiting, who had been serving him like a mother since days before. Seeing this, she said, "What shall I do? Although it is difficult to say, whether one is high or low, one's illness surely brings many duties. Since you seem to be in good spirits today, I wish to request your guidance, first and foremost, regarding the prayers; what would you say if you were present?" Suppressing her tears, she spoke. "How remarkably you speak. Listen well: the day before yesterday, the Shogun granted you a leave of absence beyond all expectation. While you possess Tadamune, a head of house with over thirty heirs, you have no lingering attachments to this world; everything depends solely on Tadamune. Even if one speaks of leaving instructions, it is not the custom of the old ways. Even as a woman, I shall tell you this: I have instructed the women serving me during my lifetime to grant them leave and send them to their relatives; among those who find no future in that life, I shall provide the sustenance necessary to carry on the lineage so they do not go astray. Even so, the aftermath of my passing is left to Tadamune. Though we are father and son, our hearts are separate; whatever a father may leave behind, whether according to the circumstances of the time or the shifting tides of this fleeting world, discrepancies are commonplace. However, I shall not let Tadamune be led astray; may he find peace even after my death." At this, the close ladies-in-waiting wailed and grieved, their eyes unbearable to behold. On the night of the 23rd, he said, "Tomorrow I shall have fully recovered; from tomorrow, all hardships shall cease. For tonight, remain in deep meditation," and went to sleep. However, he awoke from time to time, asking, "I have stayed awake for one night longer than my usual hundred nights; when is it now?" They replied, "It is the early morning." "Wake up," he commanded. He went out to a place of ten-odd ken, relieved himself comfortably, and then returned, entrusted the sword he wore to those beside him, and lay down upon his bed, where he passed away. It was the hour of the Tiger on the 24th of May, Kan'ei 13, in the year of the Fire Rat. At this time, Sakai Sanuki-no-kami (Tadakatsu) was the envoy, with orders stating, "Tadamune's grief is in accord with the lord's wishes; especially on the anniversary of the death of Chancellor Hidetada, he feels it most deeply. Therefore, send the body to Sendai Castle." Thus, at the hour of the Dog on the 24th, the body departed Edo. The various implements and the attendants proceeded to the destination in great prosperity. At the hour of the Goat on the 25th, Doi Oi-no-kami (Toshikatsu) and Sakai Sanuki-no-kami (Tadakatsu) were appointed as envoys, and following these two orders—"that there be no discrepancy regarding the successor Tadamune, and that he be moved to the upper residence from today"—the matter was carried out according to the imperial decree, and the transfer was made that day. Accordingly, the attendants up to the second generation, regarding the chants used during the journey for the body,

At Nasu-no-hara: Moniwa no Sayome (Kanetsuna) — My body exposed to the air; on the grassy pillows of Nasu-no-hara, on a summer night when no dreams are formed, the moon. At Shirakawa: The same — My journey at Shirakawa now reaches its end; the barrier gates open, and I cross the Matsukawa. The same: Aoki Chugoro (Tomoshige) — At last I depart; shall I linger on the journey of this fleeting world? The barrier at Shirakawa is open. The same: Kato Juzaburo (Yasuji) — As the journey at Shirakawa comes to an end, the barrier gates open and I head toward the shrine. At Asakayama: Moniwa no Sayome (Kanetsuna) — Today is the last day of this presence; I turn the waves of the Asaka marshes of Mutsu into tears. The same: Kanno Shozaemon (Sugano Katsuzaemon Shigenari) — Only today do the shadows of Mutsu's sorrows fall upon the waters of the mountain well of Asaka. At Kunimi Pass: Sato Naizen (Yoshinobu) — Hearing it is Kunimi, my heart is restless; how could I possibly bear the parting tomorrow? Minami Jirokichi (Masakichi) — I had long thought it would decay; will there be anyone who sees the end of this young grass?

All of the above were attendants along the journey. On the first day of the sixth month, at the hour of the Goat, they entered directly into Kakuhan-ji, a temple of the Sekizan sect of Zen Buddhism in Sendai. From the samurai to the foot soldiers, they lamented that the service of all people in this world ended there. Now, as they arrived, they proceeded two or three cho from the temple; having left the castle in April, they had not yet even let two months pass. Thinking, "How could I be replaced by such a humble person?" and wondering what this unexpected visit to the temple was for, they clung to their carriages and, alongside the attendants, burst into sudden, loud wailing that echoed through heaven and earth—a sound beyond all description. The body was brought into the temple. On the third day, a sword with a leather scabbard, like that worn by the Chunagon, was brought in; armor, both large and small, were placed beside it. After nightfall, when the silence had fallen, they placed the body upon the mountain of love, where they had been viewed at the bento site in April. The chanting was by the priest Seigaku of the Sekizan sect (Kakuhan-ji); the sutra chanting was by the head priest To, the first head priest, and the head priest Yo, who served as the vicar. Overall, it was said that Masamune was the reincarnation of a holy man of the baths known as Mankai. The first strange occurrence was that Masamune's mother, Ariyo, became exceptionally anxious and refused to sleep. Terumune, finding this odd, gradually became convinced. When he inquired about the details, she declared that she had been startled by a dream in which she entered Brahman's womb, and thereafter she could not explain the matter. From that month, she became pregnant and gave birth suddenly. According to this account, Masamune was given the childhood name Bonten-maru. Truly, a holy rebirth! They leveled that mountain (Kyogamine), dug a hole over one jo and several shaku, rubbed large stones together to make a space of one and a half ken on all sides, placed the body inside, used the same stones as a lid, raised the area to over four shaku, and built a shrine upon it. When they dug the hole for the body, it was slightly over one shaku thick and over one and a half ken wide; a stone resembling a lid was unearthed from the hole. When it was said that this was most suspicious, an old man recounted, "It is told that the remains of the ancient holy man Bankai (Mankai) were buried there under a wide stone lid; this must be that stone." Continuing with this account, people said, "The holy man Bankai was blind in one eye, and Masamune is also blind in his right eye; furthermore, he has recently desired that mountain to be the seat of a second life, and since that stone now serves as the lid for the burial, there is no doubt that the holy man of the shrine has been reincarnated." Thus, thirty-odd days passed at Kakuhan-ji. During that time, monks from various parts of Mount Koya performed sutra chanting without limit. Meanwhile, those who committed ritual seppuku began doing so at the temple three or four days before the funeral, and some committed seppuku at their lodgings. Their respective circumstances, the dharma names they had been given, and their death poems are as follows.

Shinzawa Dochu Zenjomon, Ishida Shogen (Yojun): The path at the mountain's edge, beneath the clear moon, is cool; the sound of the pine wind drifts. Zenba Shoin Zenjomon, Moniwa Sayome (Kanetsuna): At last, the way of the wandering warrior shines; how wonderful is the descent of Amida. Hotoku Shoto Zenjomon, Sato Naizen (Yoshinobu): Returning to earth, water, fire, and wind—each returning to its own place, I suddenly pierced through the Middle Way of existence. Enshu Ryoki Zenjomon, Aoki Chugoro (Tomoshige): Very well, then, let it be clouded; though it clouds, I shall take the path of the moon of the heart as my guide. Seiin Joko Zenjomon, Minami Jirokichi (Masakichi): Though late, the heart is swift; the sword of the warrior is the descent of Amida. Setsutei Ryosen Zenjomon, Kato Juzaburo (Yasuji): As the clear moon sets, let the shadows move together toward the west. Hoshuku Kyusui Zenjomon, Kanno Shozaemon (Sugano Katsuzaemon Shigenari): From the moment I set out, I know not where to go; may the path of the journey illuminate me—the descent of Amida. Haken Doko Zenjomon, Yanome Ihei (Tsuneshige): The sky is clear and the light of the moon falls upon the path; I shall not lose my way, for I now realize the end. Kirio Chikin Zenjomon, Iryuda San'emon (Motoyasu): Returning to my old home, the dew has cleared; together, you and I walk the path of the origin. Taketomo Suken Zenjomon, Kuwaori Bingo (Tsunanaga): Let the light of the clear moon guide the way; lead me to the Pure Land of Misao. Etsusho Dokan Zenjomon, Kisai: In this world, how could one begrudge a life? Together, you and I, we shall go above the clouds. Ryoso Juin Zenjomon, Ono Nizaemon (Tokimura): The storm rages against the tall pines, and the scattered dew falls upon the undergrowth of Ono. Ishin Doetsu Zenjomon, Kodaira Shuri (Tarozaemon Motonari): Now that the sixty-plus years have passed, I awaken from my dream; together, you and I walk the path of the origin. Tenshin Intoku Zenjomon, Otsuki Kiemon (Teian): Since we are friends who simply seek the light of a lamp, how could we ever be lost at the crossroads of the Six Realms? Ishiun Shintetsu Zenjomon, Watanabe Gonnojo (Shigetaka): Do all people think the days are fading? Look again at the bright day of your return. Until the hour of the Rabbit, the dew flourishes on the grass and leaves; when the hour of the Snake arrives, it returns to its original form.

Also Tsui-fuku: Shogaku Shunzu Zenjomon, under Ishida Shogen; Aoyagi Denzaemon, under Ryoshu Motomune Zenjomon, under Ishida Shogen; Kato San'emon, under Matsumine Jicho Zenjomon, under Moniwa Sayome; Shoji Mohei (Tokaibayashi Shigedenji), under Enkan Kosei Zenjomon, under Moniwa Sayome; Yokoyama Kakubei, under Seiho Jokei Zenjomon, under Naito; Sugiyama Rihei

The fifteen mentioned above, together with those whose abdomens were cut open, total twenty. It goes without saying that their final resolve was unparalleled. Whether it be for future generations or previous ones, it must have been rare; at the time, such reports were widespread even in other provinces.

shigezane:masamuneki12-4.title: Funeral Order and Seven Buddhist Rites
shigezane:masamuneki12-4.summary: The burial site was located below the Rear North Hill of Hachiman Shrine, seven or eight cho west of Kakuhan-ji Temple. The path for the funeral was twelve ken wide; the area was marked with red squares of four sun and enclosed by fences on both sides, with straw mats spread within, and cotton laid atop them; then, from within the four gates, white-washed cotton was spread over the cotton.
shigezane:masamuneki12-4.markdown:
The burial site is located below the Rear North Hill of Hachiman Shrine, seven or eight cho west of Kakuhan-ji Temple. The path for the funeral procession is twelve ken wide; the area is marked with red four-sun squares and fences on both sides, with straw mats spread within, and cotton laid atop them; furthermore, white bleached cotton was spread over the cotton from within the four gates. Outside the fences, the area is slightly over two ken wide and enclosed by bamboo palisades; inside the fences, there are guard posts, and for every ten ken, there is one head-guard and ten staff-bearers, totaling twenty-two head-guards in both directions, spanning eight cho. Between the fences and the boundary, there is one head-guard, ten muskets, and ten spears for every ten ken; this spans eight cho in one direction only. The front hall of the funeral bier is four ken on each side and one jo nine shaku high, with moss-thatched roofing, gold-leaf ridge, and pillars wrapped in red-ground ■-cloth with gold crests. The funeral castle is two cho square; the outer curtains are white bleached cotton and the inner curtains are linn; at one location to the west of the four gates, there are fifty muskets, fifty spears, twenty staff-bearers, and two head-guards each. 1. The bier is covered in brocade on all sides. The eight pillars are wrapped in red-colored brocade, and the ends are adorned with metal ornaments, with both the double borders enclosed. From the ornamental pendants to the floral crowns, there are seven nine-star and bamboo-and-sparrow crests, and red upper wraps on all sides. 1. The offering bier is covered in gold brocade on all sides, with the metal crests as described above. 1. Another offering bier is covered in yellow ■-cloth on all sides.

Seven Buddhist Rituals (Omitted)

Upon completion in this manner, Tadamune had everything—from the burial site to the mausoleum's worship hall, the guardhouses on both sides, and the tea and meal quarters—erected; throughout his tenure, he visited the site every month on the anniversary of his death. Subsequently, he handed over the Hoshun-in temple of Reverend Seigaku Wakabayashi, the guiding priest, to the treasurer, and established a new temple on the altar within the mausoleum, relocating the priest; it is now known as Shoshu-zan Zuiho-den.

June, Kan'ei 19, Year of the Water Horse: Recorded by Shigezane Date of Awa

※■ is the character with the radical 示 and the right component 純

shigezane:masamuneki2-1.title: Regarding the Boundaries of Nihonmatsu 8-chome
shigezane:masamuneki2-1.summary: While there were clashes at the four pine trees, Nihonmatsu and Hachichome remained unscathed. The details are as stated above.
shigezane:masamuneki2-1.markdown:
At that time, although there were conflicts at Yonbonmatsu, Nihonmatsu, and Hachichome, those areas remained unscathed. The details are as stated above. Since Yonbonmatsu and Nihonmatsu were regions where the power of Satake, Aizu, and Iwaki was concentrated—areas where one had to adapt according to the circumstances—Yoshitsugu of Nihonmatsu had sent reinforcements to Yonbonmatsu; however, he resolved that should the Date seek assistance this time, he would surrender, relying on Sanemoto. Around that time, although Sanemoto was ill, he maintained a steadfast resolve to keep the border region quiet at all times. When reinforcements from Aizu and the Sendo region were sent to Yonbonmatsu, Tamura was stationed far away and did not travel to Nihonmatsu. Therefore, if Sanemoto approached Yoshitsugu and kept this border quiet, it would appear that Satake, Aizu, Sendo, and Iwaki had now all aligned with Nihonmatsu; yet, the enemy had reached a peace agreement with Sanemoto, and the border remained secure. Consequently, the four generals mentioned above would likely harbor suspicions toward Yoshitsugu. At that point, if Yoshitsugu had not sided with Masamune, he might have otherwise been cast aside. Overall, from the start of the war, Masamune had felt regret over the Aizu's lack of coordination; thus, he exhausted every military strategy against the Aizu, forcing them to surrender through the spearhead of the Date and bringing the Sendo region under his control. Masamune, though young, was a capable general in both literary and military arts; in the future, the Aizu retainers would likely see their own interests eclipsed by his, and each would seek to win over his side. Sanemoto calculated that by exhausting all his strength against both the minor enemies and his own forces, he could further successfully keep the border with Nihonmatsu quiet. He secretly informed Masamune of these matters, and Sanemoto, noting that though he was but a child, Shigezane had grasped his intentions, replied: "The matter of the peace with Nihonmatsu was not the result of Yoshitsugu's usual prudence, nor was it the result of our own; we kept that border quiet through modest planning. Now, as you are young, I urge you to admonish the young lord and sever ties with this border; as it stands, my own heart is burdened and my ailments have grown severe. I pray that you will settle this matter once and for all." When Sanemoto showed him a written oath, he expressed his hope and submitted the oath twice. Subsequently, as Sanemoto had hoped, after Yonbonmatsu fell to the Date, Yoshitsugu also surrendered. Thereafter, Masamune took control of Aizu and established his castle; however, that event occurred unexpectedly and suddenly, and Terumune suffered an unforeseen death, not to mention that the Date lost their upper and lower leadership. Thus, Tamura Kiyoaki advised Masamune: "In Obama at Yonbonmatsu, there are many reinforcements; if the troops drawn from various directions gather there and become a large army, there will be no particular way to deal with them even if they attack Yonbonmatsu. This time, it would be best to first move toward Tamura, capture the small castle held by the Buzen domain, and then press the attack to take Obama." Following this advice, on September 22, Tensho 13, he established Tsukidate and moved his horses to a place called Kurokago within Tamura's territory, resting there on the 23rd. Meanwhile, reports reached Kagetsuna Katakura that the Date forces had been brought in from among the enemy in Obama and were plotting rebellion against the Ouchi to remain loyal. In response, Kagetsuna, along with Shiroishi Wakasa, Sakurada Uhei, and Shigezane Date, left four men at Tsukidate for military operations in Obama, while he himself moved from Kurokago to a place called Onami on the 24th. Although the Nihonmatsu forces provided reinforcements from within and engaged them in battle, it was not a particularly fierce fight, and he withdrew to Kurokago that day. Upon hearing that the four men left at Tsukidate had moved to Onami, Kagetsuna set out to intercept them at a place called Kosegawa. While Masamune was still slow to act, Kojuro—who at the time had no troops of his own—managed to cross Kosegawa with about two hundred men without prior consultation. He encountered the enemy of Obama and was pursued by Kagetsuna's men, fleeing about five ri to Kosegawa. The remaining three men crossed the river and engaged the enemy in battle; though the enemy numbered five or six hundred cavalry, fearing that Masamune's efforts would be jeopardized, they hastily withdrew. As his own forces were few, they did not attack and took over ten heads from each side, thereby resolving the conflict.

shigezane:masamuneki2-2.title: The Acquisition of the Four Pines
shigezane:masamuneki2-2.summary: On September 25 of the same year, Masamune made a sortie to a place called Iwakado in the district of Yonhonmatsu, surveyed the terrain, and considered whether it would be feasible to establish a nearby garrison or launch an attack; if there were any way to capture this castle, he would first cut off the route from Obama to Nihonmatsu—this was the first step...
shigezane:masamuneki2-2.markdown:
On September 25 of the same year, Masamune went to a place called Iwakado in the district of Yonematsu-no-Matsu to survey the terrain and determine whether a close-quarters assault or an attack would be feasible. He reasoned that if the castle could be taken, he would cut off the route from Obama to Nihonmatsu; this was to be the first order of business, and he intended to move to that location on the 26th. On that day, he withdrew to the aforementioned Kurokago. Meanwhile, in Obama, he held discussions with the senior retainers from Aizu and those providing reinforcements. They agreed that it was not unusual for Masamune to scout Iwakado today and that it should be attacked; they concluded that it would be a close-quarters engagement, and in any case, if Iwakado were captured, it would be unthinkable that Obama could be repelled. They appeared to have exchanged views and reached a mutual understanding. At that time, the Aizu senior retainers, via Ouchi, dispatched two messengers—Nakanome Shikibu and Hirata Owari—from among the reinforcements from Aizu to report the above details. Furthermore, it was mentioned that among the Four Heavenly Kings of the Aizu senior retainers, the position of Matsumoto Tosho-no-suke had become vacant; it was suggested that they request that location and appoint someone to it. Ouchi likely considered the severance of the route to Nihonmatsu to be a grave matter. The fortifications under Bizen's control were also completely breached. On the night of September 25, he set fire to his residence in Obama and retreated to Nihonmatsu that night. Since he intended to head toward Aizu from there, Masamune moved to that castle and took possession of Yonematsu-no-Matsu. Consequently, in Obama, as soon as the flames were seen, he wondered what had become of the main camp at Kurokago and rushed from Narumi-tsukikan. As the attendants went ahead, someone approached him in the darkness; he asked, "Who might you be?" The man replied, "I am Ouchi Gasai. I have failed to hold Bizen Yonematsu-no-Matsu, and tonight I am setting fire to my residence to repel the enemy. As for the castle garrison, it is nighttime, and while I was fleeing, I became lost and was mistaken for a fugitive from Bizen. I have rushed to the camp to request a legal hearing, hoping my life may be spared." Accordingly, three or four men were dispatched and first sent to Gasai's camp. When Gasai went to the main camp, the enemy had already fled and the castle had burned down; Masamune happened to see this. He declared that Ouchi Gasai was a fugitive and, seeking to save his life, had broken into a certain camp. He stated that he had been rushing there and had sent someone to lead the way. Masamune intended to question Gasai starting the next day, but Gasai, like a summer insect, spoke ill of him, saying, "How could one escape such a crime? I shall make you a cow-slayer." Upon hearing this, Masamune sent more men and had the gates locked. Nevertheless, he felt it would be too harsh to immediately sentence someone who had broken in to death. He turned to Kagetsuna Katakura, and after several legal hearings, Masamune decided that sentencing the one who had broken in to death would not only spread the news to all sides but also diminish his own authority among his followers. Thus, he suppressed his anger and declared that Gasai's life would be pardoned. His perilous life was thus saved. He then ordered him to leave, but his whereabouts became unknown and he was lost.

shigezane:masamuneki2-3.title: Yoshitsugu Nihonmatsu's Petition
shigezane:masamuneki2-3.summary: Accordingly, on the 26th day of the same month, at the hour of the Horse, when Masamune was nineteen years old, he moved to Obama Castle.
shigezane:masamuneki2-3.markdown:
Accordingly, on the 26th day of the 9th month, when Masamune was nineteen, he moved to the castle of Obama. In those days, Nihonmatsu Yoshitsugu had relied on Sanemoto, guarding the Date clan for generations and maintaining its stability. However, in recent years, due to the conflicts between Satake and Aizu over Tamura, he had harbored resentment toward Kiyoaki; thus, although the two generals had allied and frequently fought side-by-side, they did not forget their subsequent fate regarding the Date clan. Even during the time Lord Terumune was at Omura's camp one year, they both visited the camp to serve. Seeing this, Sanemoto expressed his gratitude and stated that, as a reward, he wished to have his domain restored. Sanemoto, being ill, was unable to travel to Obama and informed Terumune of this. Terumune then told Masamune: "I have entrusted the affairs of Omura's camp to you; therefore, now that the campaign against the Ouchi is underway, when a battle occurred at the south gate, one of the enemy's units—Yoshitsugu—was the vanguard; likewise, when another unit attacked the inner area of Onami, reinforcements were sent from Nihonmatsu, and the garrison there held out and fought a fierce battle. Since the Ouchi are a formidable enemy, I shall attack Nihonmatsu next; the outcome will depend on our respective victories." However, despite this, Masamune, driven by various pleas and particularly by his father's admonition, felt there was no other choice and replied: "In that case, I shall have the men I serve—who have served me until now—immediately report to you without fail, as I wish to receive this reward." Yoshitsugu replied, "Whether it be the south or the north, I shall take one side and place you there; I wish to receive this reward." But Masamune did not accept this. He then said, "If that is your wish, I shall have the retainers I serve, who have been under my command until now, report to you immediately without fail; though they may have thrown away their lives in lawsuits, those who revere their lord and are willing to offer their precious lives—how could they be treated as beggars or outcasts? I shall have you accept one side, regardless of the cost." Yet, this too was rejected. At that point, Yoshitsugu, seeing there was no other way, suddenly approached Terumune on the 6th day of the 10th month at a place called Miyanomori in the Yohonmatsu district, claiming he had come to surrender. Terumune stayed that night at the kitchen of Obama Castle and gathered the chief retainers to convey Yoshitsugu's surrender to Masamune. Terumune then declared that Shigezane should act as the messenger. As Shigezane was eighteen years old, he asked if it was appropriate for a youth to be such a critical messenger; Terumune replied that since he was the one handling the matter, he would act as the messenger and handle all arrangements, leaving no room for objection. Accordingly, Yoshitsugu told Shigezane: "Though I have relied on Sanemoto and made various pleas, now that I have become an enemy, I cannot be reconciled with you. Accordingly, I shall enter your house and entrust myself entirely to Lord Terumune; if I am not accepted after my surrender, I resolve to commit suicide without hesitation, and this is my intention." When he reported this to Masamune, Terumune replied, "First, while my father is neutral, if there is no peace after my surrender, how could the above be accepted?" He then handed over his son, Prince Kokuo, who was twelve years old, and the matter was settled with a single agreement. Thus, wishing to arrange a reconciliation, Yoshitsugu went to Shigezane's camp at Miyanomori on the 7th day of the 10th month and informed Masamune of this. Masamune replied that they should meet. However, as time passed, they met by candlelight; thereafter, he returned to Miyanomori. On the morning of the 8th, he sent a messenger, saying: "Since my domain was restored solely thanks to Lord Terumune, I shall offer my gratitude to him, return quickly to my castle, and deliver the child agreed upon; please come to me." Accordingly, he went to Miyanomori and appeared before Terumune, who congratulated him on the successful capture of Nihonmatsu. Date Ueno-no-kami Masakage and other Date chief retainers came from Obama and gathered before Terumune. When Yoshitsugu stated his intentions, Terumune immediately sat down; his attendants included Takabayashi Shuzen, Kanokoda Izumi, and Otsuki Nakatsuka, who were the three who accompanied him. Ueno and Shigezane were welcomed into the hall. As Yoshitsugu entered from the outer garden, Kanokoda Izumi stood beside him and asked what was the matter; he nodded twice, and then the four of them entered the hall. Terumune seated Ueno and Shigezane after him. Was this not a sign of good omen? They sat there without speaking to one another. Terumune then stepped out to greet them; during the thanksgiving in the hall, it seemed that since everyone was of his side, his wishes were not granted. Regarding the matter of the camp, he remained in the outer garden and was escorted back by bamboo fences, such that all three could not stand shoulder-to-shoulder. Ueno and Shigezane returned to the hall after Terumune and were seen off by those inside. Yoshitsugu struck his hand and said, "I am deeply grateful for your guidance, yet I have heard that I shall perish," but he did not finish. He grabbed the chest of his kosode with his left hand and drew his wakizashi with his right. Seven or eight attendants, including Ueno and Shigezane, rushed to restrain the Date men and pushed them behind Terumune. However, as it was a narrow path, they leaped aside; though no one could stop them, they called out, "Stop the gate!" but as they rushed out, Terumune pulled them back and led them to Nihonmatsu. The men of the house could not help but follow them. Those who heard the news at Obama rushed forward with their armor ready. Those who emerged from Miyanomori were all in hakama, without exception. However, seeing this, no one dared to fight back; it was simply absurd. They followed for over ten ri to a place called Takada. Among the Nihonmatsu men, those who carried equipment were Hanzawa Gennai, Tsukiken Yusa Magokuro (who carried a bow), and one other; the others all drew their swords, surrounding Terumune and Yoshitsugu and driving them toward Nihonmatsu. The Date men could not follow and killed Terumune, who was forty-two years old. Seeing this, the men of the house raised a war cry and charged all at once; not only the soldiers but even the commoners joined in, and over fifty people were killed. Yoshitsugu was thirty-three; it was heartbreaking that they killed one another. When they rushed in to surrender and joined their ranks, both father and son were thought to be beyond help, but perhaps by some divine calamity, a fierce battle broke out, and the Date men lost their weapons. Looking back at that conflict, when Yoshitsurge came to Obama on the 7th and met Masamune, some of Masamune's men were staying at the inn in Obama town; fourteen or fifteen of them were staying there and playing. When they were quiet, they began swapping their swords and wakizashi, cutting them in half and surrounding each other in a wheel-like formation. Three of Terumune's men from Miyanomori had come to Obama town for business and asked, "What is the meaning of this? Are we in such haste?" They replied jokingly, "We shall cut the two-man group into small pieces tomorrow." The two-man group, whether they were the "two-man group" or the "straight-man" group, were present and heard this. That night, Yoshitsugu returned to Miyanomori and reported it, and they were said to have suddenly become determined. They also wondered if a group from Nihonmatsu had come to ambush them; they speculated that if it was a surrender, it would be impossible, and that they might be targeting Masamune, wondering how such a sudden event could happen. One day, Masamune, saying he was resting, had gone ten or fifteen ri away to the mountains to hunt hawks. When he finished, he informed the hawk-hunting grounds of the conflict. He immediately told them to go to Takada and attack Nihonmatsu from there the next day. The councilors suggested choosing an auspicious day and proceeding accordingly. Thus, on the morning of the 9th, he returned to Obama. The body of Terumune was moved to Obama on the night of the 8th, and on the 9th, he was placed in the Zukifuku-ji temple in Senzan-ha, Zen sect, in Yonezawa; the guiding priest was Master Tokai. During the funeral, Endo Yamashiro and Uchiba Emon II served as attendants. There was also a man named Suda Hoki who, at that time, was a monk named Doku; he committed ritual suicide at a place a hundred ri from Yonezawa. This Doku had no notice of it, and it was rumored that committing suicide at a place was suspicious. Masamune also found it suspicious, but since it was said to be a ritual suicide, everyone accepted it. As for Yamashiro, he was originally Endo Takumi, a prisoner in Kuwaori, Date; he was always fond of poetry and occasionally, in his intoxication, fell from his horse and broke the scabbard of his sword. The next day, he wrote a mad poem: "Though I fell, I grieve that the scabbard broke from the heavy drinking last night." Nakano Hitachi, hearing this, knew he was a man of great wisdom and summoned him. Hitachi, being powerful, frequently brought him before Terumune; when Hitachi was too extravagant to attend, he used Takumi to arrange various matters, and Terumune naturally grew close to Takumi. Thus, Terumune, who had long cherished the affection between Harumune and Terumune, used this opportunity to alienate his father and son. He plotted to overthrow the Date house by exploiting this opportunity, believing the Date house would perish. When Terumune saw that Takumi was under Hitachi's surveillance, Takumi conspired with Sanemoto and persuaded Hitachi to lead Sanemoto from Yonezawa to Obira, the residence of Sanemoto in Yonezawa. After that, Takumi acted as the true advisor, and the Date house would endure forever. Thus, Takumi changed his name to Yamashiro and served as a retainer for two generations, and it was said that there was no equal to him. This was the story of Yamashiro. Masamune then attacked Nihonmatsu without delay on the 15th of October. The three territories of Mihonmatsu, Tamanoi, and Numakawa within Yoshitsugu's domain also gathered at Nihonmatsu on the night of the 8th, with Sanemoto, the twelve-year-old son, as their general, and Yoshitsugu's relative, Shinjo Danjo, as their guardian. Nihonmatsu was besieged. When they attacked the castle, not a single rider emerged from within; the castle was fortified and held firm, so Masamune crossed the Abukuma River and withdrew his main army to Takada, where they set up field camps. Shigezane, however, positioned his camp to the north of Nihonmatsu, separate from Takada. As for the reason, he explained that since the eighth block was the retirement place of Shigezane and Sanemoto, he left it under guard and placed troops at Ibota. Accordingly, to consult on the army's strategy the next day, Shigezane withdrew to Takada and sent his forces to Ibota. They brought out their numbers from within and engaged in a battle, with many on both sides falling dead. Seeing this, the Takada side crossed the river and helped each other, driving back the enemy who emerged from the castle and splitting them apart. Then, from the hour of the Boar on the 15th, a strong wind blew, and from the hour of the Ox, heavy snow fell; it continued day and night for four days until the 18th, when horses could no longer move and fighting became impossible. On the 21st, they retreated to Obama Castle. Since snow had accumulated and it would not last through the year, all personnel from the borders were returned, and he himself rested at Obama. Thus, until July of the 14th, Nihonmatsu remained fortified. The reason for this was that at the time, two places called Takatama and Akugashima were strongholds of the Aizu faction; it was thought that they might be used as auxiliary castles by placing troops there via the paths to Nihonmatsu. However, if that were the case, there were concerns that the three generals—Satake, Aizu, and Iwaki—would advance toward the Asaka front and bypass Nihonmatsu, pursuing the enemy to the Asaka front. Therefore, they refrained from using auxiliary castles and sent troops to block the paths. The enemy could see them from the high mountains, and since there were no paths, when troops entered, they could see through them and pass through, so they were fortified until the following year.
