shigezane:masamuneki2-4.title: Battle of Hitoribashi at Motomiya
shigezane:masamuneki2-4.summary: Meanwhile, the generals of Satake, Iwaki, Aizu, and Sendo had been meeting with the Ouchi since the previous day and were said to be preparing to oppose Date; however, they were no match for Masamune's prowess, and as the Ouchi also withdrew to Aizu, Masamune moved to Obama Castle, leaving each of them filled with regret; and taking advantage of the occasion of Terumune's death...
shigezane:masamuneki2-4.markdown:
Accordingly, the generals of Satake, Iwaki, Aizu, and Sendai had been in league with Ouchi for some time and were now preparing to oppose Date; however, they were unable to withstand Masamune's momentum. As Ouchi also withdrew toward Aizu, Masamune moved his forces to Obama Castle. Feeling a sense of regret, he seized the opportunity when Terumune passed away, intending to seize Date. On the 10th day of the 13th month of that year, Yoshinobu—the son of Satake Yoshishige—his second son Yoshihiro of Aizu, Iwaki Tsunetaka, Ishikawa Yamato-no-kami Akimitsu, and Shirakawa Yoshichika—six generals united and marched out to Sugagawa in Sendai, attacking the castles of Date's allies in the Asaka region; it was further reported that a castle called Nakamura had fallen. Consequently, Masamune rode out to Iwakado and dispatched Tomizawa Omi, Kuwaori Settsu-no-kami, and Ito Hizen, accompanied by three hundred banner-men and firearms, to guard Takakura. To Hongu, he sent Segami Nakatsuka, Nakajima Ise, and Hamada Izu; to Tamanoi, he sent Shirakawa Wakasa. As for Shigezane, he remained at Shibuya for the siege of Nihonmatsu, as he was to be kept on guard for the "eight-cho" area. Meanwhile, since the garrison at Obama was small, Masamune ordered Shigezane to hurry to their position, leaving more than half of his forces at Shibuya and proceeding to Yohonmatsu and Obama. Masamune then rode out to Shigezane's location and said, "Because your forces are few, you have not left any men at Obama's garrison; therefore, hurry to your position." Thus, Shigezane left more than thirty riders, including Aoki Bizen and Uchibaba Hayato, and followed behind, arriving at Iwakado. Masamune then said, "Maeda Sawa Hyobu has now changed his allegiance and is aligned with Satake and Aizu. The enemy will surely attack Takakura tomorrow, or perhaps Hongu; Shigezane, proceed first." Masamune was thus honored. The camp for Shigezane that night was at a place called Nukazawa. Maeda Sawa Hyobu was a traitor; though originally an ally of Nihonmatsu, he had remained loyal to Masamune after the murder of Yoshitsugu, but had now aligned himself with Shigeshige. Seeing that the forces were large, he planned to abandon Date and switch his allegiance to Satake and Aizu, thereby becoming an enemy of Masamune. On the 16th, the enemy established a field camp on the plain south of Maeda Sawa, and on the 17th, they intended to attack Takakura. Based on these plans, Masamune moved his horses from Iwakado to Hongu; if the attack were to come from Takakura, he intended to send the forces from Hongu to the Kannon-do temple there and assist them from there, establishing a camp at Nihonmatsu's West Otawara. At that time, the southern town boundary of Hongu consisted of fields, but there was a stream flowing through it that reached the inner town; furthermore, the Hitori-bashi bridge was located about eight or nine cho west of the current site, south of the Aizu highway from Hongu, in a wooded area. The military camp at that time was not on the current highway. Thus, Shigezane left his men in two locations, totaling only seventy or eighty riders, but in order to assist Takakura, he established a camp beneath the mountain of the highway. Meanwhile, the enemy army, divided into three groups, pressed forward in three directions. The forces garrisoned at Takakura, seeing that Hongu was empty, intended to send out their men to block them. Many claimed the enemy was too large, but Tomizuka Omi and Ito Hizen were pushed back; nevertheless, the soldiers marching toward Hongu declared they would send out their men to block them. Believing this to be the will of the enemy, the forces advanced, and indeed the enemy retreated. However, the enemy also deployed the Iwaki forces, engaging the allies at two points and cutting down twenty or thirty men. Because the enemy was large, the forces from Maeda Sawa clashed with the allies stationed at the Kannon-do, while the forces from Arai engaged Shigezane. It was a battle at two points. Before the battle with Shigezane began, a man named Shimo-Koriyama Uchi-no-ki rode up to a high point facing Shigezane and, seeing a signal flag, noticed three men—Shirakawa Wakasa, Hamada Izu, and Takano Iki—with their equipment. Six or seven armored warriors and over a hundred foot soldiers then approached from that direction. Seeing many following them, Uchi-no-ki wondered who they were, thinking they were enemies. However, noticing a gap of over one cho between their positions and the enemy's boundary, he became suspicious. As expected, he fired a single arrow at that distance. At that moment, Uchi-no-ki recognized the boundary between friend and foe and called out from atop a mountain, "The enemy has reached this point! Raise the small flags!" Everyone then raised their flags. Wakasa, Izu, and Iki passed through Shigezane's camp and went straight to the flag-pole. Meanwhile, the allies left the Kannon-do and established a camp at Ota-no-hara, but were overwhelmed by the large numbers; the Kannon-do was captured, and many, including Shigenatsu Niwa, were slain. However, Shigenatsu was not killed and retreated to the allied camp, but as the banner-men were crushed and appeared defeated, Date Motoyasu, Motomune, his son Mino-no-kami Shigemune, his son Ueno-no-kami Masakage, his cousin Hikokuro Morishige—all relatives of Masamune—as well as Harada Samanosuke Munenaga, Katakura Kojuro Katsunaga, and others who had distinguished themselves, fought alongside the banner-men as they had done since long ago, resulting in no great defeat. Meanwhile, not a single person remained in Shigezane's camp; to the left was the great Abukuma River. From Maeda Sawa toward the Kannon-do, the enemy was defeated after seven cho or more, and from Arai, they pressed toward the Kannon-do. Shigezane engaged the enemy who had come to his aid, but as he was only eighteen years old and lacked experience, he saw a banner-pole raised by Shimo-Koriyama Uchi-no-ki. Shigezane said, "The allies at the Kannon-do are collapsing and are being pushed back; hurry and retreat!" and handed the raised banner-pole to a small man. Because the enemy was large, the allies witnessed the critical moment, but felt that retreating here would be a stain for generations to come. Deciding to fight to the end, they pursued Wakasa, Izu, and Iki, who reached the bottom of the mountain. Shigezane was about to release his men, but the enemy had retreated. Shigezane's retainers, including Iba Toe—who was seventy-three years old and a formidable man—charged forward, striking two enemies and having his retainers take their heads. They pursued them for four or five cho from the south of the mountain to the foot of Hitori-bashi, where they turned them back and drove them back toward the mountain. Meanwhile, Uchi-no-ki, Ueno-no-kami, crossed the boundary between friend and foe, riding around to ensure they did not collapse. A spear-man advanced and attempted to thrust at the horse he was riding, but was countered and thrown back, running forward. He was cut down with a single stroke by a retainer, who then took the head of his retainer and slew another man. They caught up to the point where the battle had begun and fought again. The fellow banner-men, firearm generals Kayaba Genbe and Ushizaka Sakon, each rode into the enemy ranks, striking four enemies each, and drove them back toward the bridge. Kita-Shimotsuke, who charged forward, struck the horses riding the foot soldiers; the Shimotsuke then stood up and retreated. The allies then deployed their men to block the retreat, with Iba Toe riding around to ensure they did not collapse. The rear guard was overwhelmed, and as the leader was too far from the allies—especially since they were warriors wearing armor and unable to move freely—the enemy charged and took two heads, breaking the retreat. The enemy was defeated and driven back to the bridge, where over two hundred and fifty were killed, and thirty-nine of the allies, including common soldiers, were slain. Afterward, the Kannon-do was abandoned, and Shigezane gathered his men and split off to fight, raising a victory cry. Miraculously, without losing a single blade, he achieved victory and returned to the front of the Kannon-do; this was truly in accordance with the divine will and was deeply appreciated. Toe retreated from that spot. As mentioned, Shimo-Koriyama Uchi-no-ki served closely under Terumune; in the past, during the Soma campaign, he had been entrusted with firearms and had earned great praise. However, he had since incurred Masamune's wrath and was stationed at Shigezane's camp. On that day, when the allies were lagging behind, he charged forward and pushed back, striking twice and having his retainers take the heads of two enemies, achieving an unparalleled feat of valor. After the enemy was driven from the Kannon-do, he reorganized his camp at the Takakura highway crossing, believing another battle would occur. Masamune's camp was about five or six cho away, but perhaps because the enemy had withdrawn, nothing happened; since the allies were few, they did not attack and withdrew. This battle took place on the 17th day of the 11th month of the 13th year of Tensho, when Masamune was nineteen years old. On the night of the 17th, he arrived at Iwakado, across the Abukuma River. He received a [handwritten letter](#/post/shigezane/29) sent by a messenger from Yamaji and Awaji: "Today, the battle at the Kannon-do was fought; the enemy, having come from Arai to assist the Kannon-do, was defeated by your small force, achieving an unparalleled victory and honor that has astonished all ears. Due to your conduct, all armies are greatly pleased; it is utterly laughable that so many of my own men were wounded or killed. I hear that tomorrow the enemy army will approach Hongu; if you do not go there, it would be your greatest wish. I have informed Date Ueno Masakage to agree to this. On the 17th day of the 11th month, at the hour of the Boar, Shigezane, Masamune." Awaji, upon hearing this, could not believe he had heard that Hongu was approaching and had mistakenly entered the enemy territory. He believed that tomorrow the enemy would approach Hongu and attempt to break the siege of Nihonmatsu; thus, after a council at the enemy camp, he returned home that night and reported this. Masamune then decided that Hongu should be besieged and that this was essential to their situation. However, they were exhausted by the campaign and could not prepare suddenly; they set out for Hongu at the hour of the Tiger on the 18th, but upon inquiring about the enemy's movements, they learned they had been stationed there since the previous night. They then reported that the enemy had set fire to the camp, suggesting it was a signal. They replied that the signal-fire had spread and the enemy had fled, stating that the field camps of Satake, Aizu, and Iwaki had dispersed. They then showed them Maeda Sawa, and since not a single person remained there, Masamune moved his horses to Hongu and made all necessary arrangements. A man named Nakamura Hachiroemon, who had been at the flag-pole, had charged into the enemy during the battle at the Kannon-do and slain about twenty armored warriors; thus, believing that fifty or a hundred of their men could be saved, Nakamura's sword was damaged beyond repair. When Hamada Izu brought it forward, Masamune, seeing that it had earned honor, granted him an additional four pine trees as a reward. This was a reward for his achievement. Subsequently, Masamune withdrew from Hongu to Iwakado, but the enemy, having prepared a counter-attack, remained at Iwakado for two days. However, as the enemy had all retreated to their castles, Masamune returned to Koba that year and spent the winter there. On an auspicious day in the 6th month of the 13th year of Kan'ei, Date Awa Shigezane.

shigezane:masamuneki3-1.title: The Battle of Shibukawa in Adachi District
shigezane:masamuneki3-1.summary: From the tenth month of Tensho 13 (Year of the Wood Rooster) to the seventh month of Tensho 14 (Year of the Fire Dog), during the siege of Nihonmatsu, as a precaution against attack from a distance of eight cho, Shigezane, then eighteen years old, was stationed at the fortress at Shibukawa.
shigezane:masamuneki3-1.markdown:
From the tenth month of Tensho 13 (Year of the Wood Rooster) to the seventh month of Tensho 14 (Year of the Fire Dog), during the siege of Nihonmatsu, as a precaution for the eight-cho area, Shigezane—who was eighteen years old at the time—was stationed at the fortress of Shibukawa. On November 17 of Tensho 13, after the Battle of Hongu and the various arrangements at Sendo-guchi, Masamune returned to his camp at Yohonmatsu. Accordingly, by December, Shigezane also returned to the aforementioned Shibukawa. However, around the hour of the Monkey on the eleventh of that month, while Shigezane was in his usual quarters, his retainers took the powder box of a musket and set it alight, transferring the fire to the box and burning it to the ground; as a result, everything within the castle was burned, and Shigezane himself was burned beyond measure. To this day, one of his fingers remains stuck together, leaving him crippled for life; at that time, not to mention the ten who died and only one who survived. In the midst of this, on the hour of the Horse on January 1 of Tensho 14, forces attacked from two directions as if charging; first came a single rider in armor, followed by ten-odd foot soldiers, who pursued the water-fetchers at the edge of the camp. When Shigezane encountered them, there was a small hill of brush along the road to Nihonmatsu; as the allies pursued them along a single path, two hundred enemy cavalry and two thousand four or five hundred foot ashigaru were hidden behind that brush. As the enemy rose up, the allied soldiers fought back; not only were they unable to advance along the road, but they were scattered in all directions, making their defeat utterly foolish. Now, the commanders on this side dispatched two men, Shigezane's retainers Shiga Oi-no-zaemon and Yusa Sato-emon. Having heard much of the enemy's Kanokoda-emon and Sato-emon, they did not engage in the fighting but rode up to a high point to watch. Sato-emon, being born in the neighborhood, knew the way well; heading west from the path the allies were pursuing, he overtook the enemy, and within a single field, he and another man took the heads of two or three men. From there, he pursued them and took down another man, eventually catching up to where emon was holding his ground; Kanokoda, unable to hold out, was cornered at a place called Noji. Until then, Shiga Oi-no-zaemon had charged at the front and taken down four enemies; meanwhile, his elder brother Haneda Uma-no-suke went elsewhere and charged swiftly, riding a side-horse to take down five enemies, causing thirty-odd enemies to be beheaded. The allies, who had come to aid from their own eight-cho territory, did not engage in the fighting but crossed the current road to Noji. Thinking that the enemy could be cut off east of Nihon-yanagi, they pursued those who had collapsed further; on the narrow path of Kanokoda-Iido, they drove back those who had crossed in line, achieving a victory unparalleled in honor. Kanokoda, who had been on the verge of collapse, gathered those who had crossed and led them to victory—this was a feat that could not be surpassed. Thus, they took the heads of over three hundred and forty enemy foot soldiers, while over thirty of their own foot soldiers were killed in action. As day began to fade, they separated and raised songs of victory. Yusa Sato-emon, seeing Kanokoda's skill that day, drew his horse with great dexterity; it was truly magnificent—a master of exceptional skill, just as he had heard, and I later heard that he received a reward. Furthermore, when Masamune was in Obama, on the second day of that January, he was exceptionally pleased to present the head of the aforementioned Kanokoda. This battle took place when Masamune was twenty-two years old.

shigezane:masamuneki3-10.title: Eiei Gekkan Shifu Danjo Seishi
shigezane:masamuneki3-10.summary: Gekkan was the son-in-law of Soma Yoshitane; thus, even during the Battle of Osaki Shimo-shinden, Gekkan's troops fired their matchlock guns without ammunition.
shigezane:masamuneki3-10.markdown:
Gekkan was the son-in-law of Soma Yoshitane; thus, during the Battle of Osaki Shimo-shinden, Gekkan and his men fired their guns without ammunition. When Masamune heard of this, he reasoned that the deep valley of his castle bordered Osaki, and since Yoshitane was a relative, his rebellion was grave; consequently, Gekkan was first placed under the custody of a man called Akiu Settsu-no-kami, and later executed. Subsequently, Danjo Chikauji Iesane also fell out with Danjo, and while residing at Nao Castle, he remained loyal to Yoshitaka, cherishing that castle. For this reason, Masamune grew suspicious of Danjo, and his suspicions were fully justified. Nevertheless, believing that a single act of loyalty could be contested and that disloyalty might occur, he submitted several written oaths, which were accepted. Accordingly, he requested a spy to Iwateyama and dispatched Konarita Soemon; before long, Danjo died of illness, and Soemon was instructed to handle all arrangements as if the man were still alive, taking charge of Iwateyama. Konarita Soemon was recently referred to as Yamaoka Shima.

shigezane:masamuneki3-11.title: The Escape of Kurokawa Gesshu from Capital Punishment
shigezane:masamuneki3-11.summary: The inefficiency of the Date forces in the upcoming battle against Osaki is due to the treachery of Kurokawa Gesshu.
shigezane:masamuneki3-11.markdown:
The inefficiency of the Date forces in the upcoming war against Osaki was due to the treachery of Kurokawa Gesshu. Masamune had previously intended to seize Kurokawa, the stronghold of Gesshu, and from there press toward Osaki; however, fearing that if he clashed with Osaki, the likes of Atsugi, Aizu, Iwaki, and Shirakawa would each march out to their original posts and intervene, he delayed the campaign for that year. In the following year, the forces of the Sendo region rose in rebellion once more, and Masamune's side emerged victorious; furthermore, he gained control of Aizu and remained in the castle for a year. Consequently, from then on, he set his sights on the Kanto region and ceased to mention the matter of Osaki. However, when Taiko Hideyoshi departed for Odawara, Masamune confiscated Aizu and granted it to Yonezawa as his original domain; meanwhile, Osaki and Kasai were granted to Kimura Ise-no-kami, and Masamune was granted Natori, Kokubun, Miyagi, and Kurokawa-kiri. Gesshu, his son-in-law, gathered the people and declared, "Please spare my life and safety." When he reported this to Masamune, he stated that the unexpected deaths of various troops at Osaki were due to Gesshu's treachery, and declared that Gesshu's head should be severed as a memorial; he was then sent to Akiu and entrusted to Sakaino Genban. Accordingly, Ueno, upon hearing the matter, stated to Masamune, "That Hamada Izu, Tatesuke Saburo, and Kunai Inaba were able to withdraw unscathed at Osaki was due to Gesshu's integrity; though I shall not speak of this, as I am your senior, I offer a portion of my territory in service, and simply as a token of gratitude, I beg that Gesshu's life be spared." After a hundred pleas, Ueno, citing his uncle's lawsuit, had no choice but to grant the request. Ueno took Gesshu from Genban's hands and returned to Rifu, the castle of Miyagi, his joy being extraordinary. The territory Ueno had requested was also granted without being confiscated, and the matter was successfully concluded. Later, out of gratitude toward Ueno, a small portion of land was granted to Gesshu; subsequently, after taking up residence in Sendai, he received the honor of being summoned by Masamune. It is said that this was solely due to the success with Ueno. Meanwhile, Gesshu's uncle, Hachimori Sagami, had already strongly admonished Gesshu at Kuwaori Castle in Osaki; furthermore, because Gesshu had adopted the crest of the small flag sent by Masamune as his own, Hachimori was deeply concerned and sent him to Oguni to be placed under the care of Koriyama Shikibu; later, both his wife and children were executed.

An auspicious day in the sixth month of the nineteenth year of Kan'ei (Year of the Water Horse) — Shigezane Date of Awa

shigezane:masamuneki3-2.title: Regarding Masamune's Illness and the Departure from the Castle in Nihonmatsu
shigezane:masamuneki3-2.summary: In the second month of the fourteenth year, year of the Fire Dog, five men—Genban Minowa, Shinbei Ujiie, Tanba Yusa, Shimousa of the same name, and Etchu Horie—while besieged in Nihonmatsu, rebelled and conspired with Masamune.
shigezane:masamuneki3-2.markdown:
In the second month of the fourteenth year (Year of the Fire Dog), five men—Minowa Genban, Ujiie Shinbei, Yusa Tanba, Nakashimo Shimosa, and Horie Etchu—who had been besieged in Nihonmatsu, rebelled and conspired with Masamune. As for the circumstances: since the terrain of the Minowa residence was advantageous, it would have been easy for them to seize the castle; thus, the Date forces intended to withdraw to the Minowa residence to remain loyal. As the aforementioned men each presented hostages, the soldiers were dispatched there. Consequently, the remaining four men were unable to maintain even a small number of retainers within the castle town; the four men, along with their wives, children, and servants, had gathered and entrenched themselves at the Minowa residence, rendering the Date forces unable to maneuver their bows and spears. Meanwhile, as Minowa lay between the main castle and Awaka-saku, if Awaka-saku had also remained loyal, the castle would have fallen eventually—though not immediately—and the conspirators, having gathered there, attacked Genban's residence from the hour of the Tiger that day. Unable to repel them, they broke through the screens and forced their way out through the steep terrain; people poured out in crowds from the precarious spots, and forty to fifty men and women were trampled to death, while the castle remained firmly held. At this time, Masamune was ill, and his operations toward Nihonmatsu were delayed. In early April of the same year, he dispatched horses and was thought to be approaching the castle; however, he feared that if that were the case, he might launch an attack from the Asaka front via Satake, Aizu, and Iwaki, as he had done the previous year. Concerned that the castle might be bypassed and that the forces would advance toward Asaka, he refrained from a direct approach and instead conducted operations for five days from the northeast and south. However, although there were two or three skirmishes, the castle was well-defended, making it difficult to attack, and he first withdrew to Obama. Meanwhile, Soma Yoshitane, relying on Sanemoto, declared that those besieged in Nihonmatsu would conduct a sortie, stating that Masamune's messenger should deliver his message. Although Sanemoto had been suffering from a prolonged illness, Masamune's persistent requests were unreasonable; Sanemoto went from the castle at Hachi-chome to Obama and delivered a message of safety. There was no particular dispute, and the siege was lifted; Masamune declared that Nihonmatsu had been taken, and Masamune was satisfied. Accordingly, on July 6 of the same year, he set fire to the main bailey and retreated to Aizu. The retainers then withdrew to various places as they saw fit. Thus, just as it was declared that the castle had been taken over by Shigezane, forces advanced from Shibukawa that day and established a temporary shelter in the main bailey. On the twenty-fourth of the same month, Masamune dispatched horses from Obama, inspected the castle, and made various arrangements. He then returned to Obama and issued the allocation of fiefs to the Date generals and minor retainers as follows: 1. Obama in Yotsumatsu was granted to Shiroishi Wakasa; the remaining lands were granted to minor retainers with increased stipends. 2. Nihonmatsu was granted to Shigezane; the Omori in Shinobu, formerly held by Shigezane, was granted to Kagetsuna Katakura Kojuro; they returned to their camp in Yonezawa in early August of the same year. As for the Asaka front, it had previously been settled, and those passing through were permitted to do so with escorts.

shigezane:masamuneki3-3.title: The Sudden Death of Tamura Kiyoto: Dissension Between Masamune and His Northern Allies
shigezane:masamuneki3-3.summary: In the same eleventh month, Kiyoaki Tamura died suddenly. Consequently, Masamune departed from Yonezawa for Fukushima in Shinobu, dispatched a messenger to Tamura, and immediately returned. As Kiyoaki had no heir, he had frequently declared that, for the remainder of his days, he intended to eventually cede Tamura to Masamune.
shigezane:masamuneki3-3.markdown:
In the same eleventh month, Kiyoaki Tamura died suddenly. Consequently, Masamune departed from Yonezawa for Fukushima in Shinobu and dispatched messengers to Tamura, after which he returned. As Kiyoaki had no heir, he had frequently declared that, during his remaining days, he would eventually cede Tamura to Masamune. Thus, despite his death, Masamune appointed the mother of Kiyoaki as the chief castle warden at Miharu in Tamura, and entrusted various administrative affairs—including the management of Tamura—to four men: Tsukisai and Meisetsu of the Kiyoaki clan, his cousin Uemon, and the senior retainer Hashimoto Gyobu. While this was the arrangement, Masamune's relations with the Northern Lady were poor at the time; the mother at Miharu resented this, and though she secretly harbored rebellious intentions, Tsukisai and Gyobu believed that even if the Northern Lady's relations were poor, they should not turn against Masamune and betray Tamura, and thus continued to protect the Date. Furthermore, Meisetsu and Uemon reasoned that since the Northern Lady was the aunt of Soma Yoshitane, regardless of whether she was a woman, it would be acceptable to side with Soma and turn against Masamune; thus, while they maintained a facade of protecting the Date, their true intentions leaned toward Soma. Because the internal relations among the four men at Tamura were divided in this manner, it became a matter of which side they supported; even among the subordinates, they were split between the Tsukisai and Meisetsu factions, though to the higher authorities, they maintained a facade of loyalty to the Date. Consequently, Masamune remained in discord with the Northern Lady for one year. When Masamune was ten years old, Kiyoaki's nine-year-old daughter, Midori, was betrothed; subsequently, due to a dispute, Masamune personally killed the matchmaker and executed all the remaining wives without exception. Due to this outburst, a rift remained between them. Nevertheless, as the Northern Lady was young at the time, they eventually reconciled, which was a fortunate turn of events. A legitimate daughter was born to her, and thereafter she had two sons—the head of the house, Tadamune; the third son, Settsu-no-kami Munetsuna; and the fourth son, Takematsu. She bore many children and lived a prosperous life for approximately sixty years; when the Northern Lady was sixty-nine, Masamune passed away at the age of seventy. At this time, the Northern Lady was restored to her former status and took the name Yotoku-in; the filial piety shown by the head of the house, Tadamune, was truly remarkable.

shigezane:masamuneki3-4.title: Regarding the Appearance of Okoshi Kii-no-kami
shigezane:masamuneki3-4.summary: Thus, around that time, among the Tamura retainers, there was a member of the Tamura clan known as Okoshi Kii-no-kami—a relative of Soma Yoshitane as well—who held a high rank within the house. He sought to align himself with Soma in an attempt to have Tamura taken over by Yoshitane.
shigezane:masamuneki3-4.markdown:
At that time, among the retainers of Tamura, there was a man known as Okoshi Kii-no-kami, a member of the Tamura clan; he was also a relative of Soma Yoshitane and held a high rank within the house. He conspired with Soma, intending to seize Tamura for Yoshitane's use. Furthermore, among the Tamura retainers were four or five ronin from Soma—distinguished men capable of holding their own castles—and all of them were aligned with Soma. The most prominent figure in Tamura was Tamura Uemon-no-kami, the head of the Umeyuki house and lord of a castle in a place called Ono. He conspired with Kii-no-kami and leaned toward Soma. At one time, Gessai, Gyobu, and Shiroishi Wakasa spoke of Kii-no-kami, stating that his rebellion against Date was manifest and that he wished to be captured alive. When this matter was reported to Wakasa in Yonezawa, Masamune wrote to Shigezane: "I wish to know the details; send one reliable person." A man named Endo Suruga was dispatched; Gessai and Gyobu stated that the matter was futile, yet they feared that if Kii-no-kami were unexpectedly taken into custody, it would be a misdeed on Tamura's part; furthermore, they noted that even if Gessai's side were to rally, it would not be advantageous. When asked for the specifics, it was said that among the four Tamura retainers, two were with Date and the remaining two were with Okoshi; the three were with Soma, their internal affairs split into two factions with rival ambitions, keeping a watchful eye on one another. If the situation became precarious, they would settle the matter at Tamura, even if the distance from Yonezawa was great. Overall, both allies and enemies were to side with the two aforementioned leaders. Regarding the matter of Kii-no-kami, as it was a time when the Date were providing guidance, it was ordered that Kii-no-kami be secretly informed so that no conflict would arise at Tamura. Since Kii-no-kami already had a close relationship with Uchigasaki Uma-no-kami, whenever Shigezane had a matter to attend to, he would always send a relative named Okoshi Bizen to Uma-no-kami's office. Accordingly, this time he requested that Bizen be sent, and Bizen arrived. Shigezane met him and, though he intended to discuss the matter of Masamune, he first inquired in detail about the situation at Tamura, thinking that if Kii-no-kami spoke without ulterior motives, he might then discuss the matter. After hearing various things, Shigezane kept everything to himself and did not speak of it. Finding this a delay, he immediately relayed the matter to Uma-no-kami; Bizen then returned to Kii-no-kami and informed him of this, after which Kii-no-kami ceased his attendance at Miharu and withdrew to his castle in Okoshi. Meanwhile, the four senior retainers of Tamura sent messengers to Kii-no-kami, inquiring why he had ceased his attendance. At first, Kii-no-kami spoke without hesitation, but as the inquiries into the details intensified, he replied, "If I had continued my service at Miharu, I would have been captured alive, as Shigezane informed me." Upon hearing this, the four senior retainers informed Shigezane, asking what this meant. Shigezane replied, "What should I know? Since the house is divided, I find it laughable; I only wished for peace, yet such a matter is a nuisance." The four retainers then informed Kii-no-kami that Shigezane had spoken thus and urged him to hurry and attend. At that time, Uma-no-kami stated that it was certain he would be informed, but since the four retainers repeatedly reported the matter, Uma-no-kami inquired further. He learned that Kii-no-kami was particularly fond of Kishu and had told Bizen that the world spoke of Lord Kii-no-kami as having a rebellious heart, and that if he attended Miharu, he would naturally be killed or imprisoned, as the situation was perilous. Bizen replied, "I cannot agree to what Shigezane says; Kii-no-kami's report is incorrect," and this was conveyed to Tamura. The four retainers then said, "In that case, why not send Uma-no-kami and Bizen to confront him?" Having no other choice, a date was set for early March. Bizen was sent to a place in Tamura called Onikuda. When an inspector from Miharu inquired about the matter, Bizen replied, "There is no such thing." Consequently, Uma-no-kami was not sent; instead, a messenger was sent to Tamura requesting that Uma-no-kami be sent. However, since no inspector was present, they declined, citing a lack of formality. Subsequently, an inspector was attached to Bizen, and at that time, Uma-no-kami was also to be sent. However, out of consideration for the internal relations of the Shigezane household, the inspector refrained from sending him, and only Bizen was sent. Shigezane was pleased by this arrangement, and one inspector accompanied Bizen to both Onikuda and Tamura. There, Okoshi Bizen said to Uma-no-kami, "The report from Shigezane is accurate." To this, Uma-no-kami replied, "I told Lord Kii-no-kami that if his intentions were misplaced, his attendance should be questioned; yet he now ceases his attendance—this clearly shows his double-mindedness. If there were no other way, he would attend this very moment, and there would likely be no disturbance at Miharu." They argued back and forth, with neither side gaining the upper hand. Since the death of Kiyoaki, the Tamura house had generally been in such turmoil; if Shigezane were to speak openly now, it would cause a loss of face for both Masamune and Shigezane. Afterward, during a meeting at Tamura to discuss whether they should protect Date, a man named Tokiwa Iga spoke up: "Since Kiyoaki's lifetime, it has been your constant saying that Tamura should eventually be handed over to Lord Masamune; now that the time has come, to whom should it be assigned? Even so, it depends on the nature of the matter." Just as Iga spoke, the others in the meeting were at a loss for words, and Iga's words were seen as the resolution; while it was initially said to be for Date, the underlying intent was largely toward Soma. The details are as follows: the ronin in Tamura who were openly rebellious were mostly Soma retainers, and they were close with any ronin of their rank. Not only the Soma retainers, but ronin from Satake, Aizu, and Sendo were also close, and since Umeyuki and Uemon had conspired with them, these were the six points of contention. The details of these matters are recorded in this fourth volume. Despite such investigations, Umeyuki and Uemon were in league with Kii-no-kami; furthermore, their involvement with Gessai and Gyobu this time was in connection with the affairs of the Date, and they had also sent word to Shigezane's side.

shigezane:masamuneki3-5.title: Regarding the Osaki Camp
shigezane:masamuneki3-5.summary: In July of the same fourteenth year, Masamune raised an army from the Sendo region and captured the areas up to Yotsumatsu and Nihonmatsu, returning to Yonezawa in early August.
shigezane:masamuneki3-5.markdown:
In the seventh month of the fourteenth year, Masamune raised an army along the Sendo route and captured the areas up to Yotsumatsu and Nihonmatsu; in early August, he returned to his camp at Yonezawa. At that time, the retainers of Osaki Yoshitaka split into two factions and approached Masamune, questioning the true nature of their situation. Around that time, there was a man named Nitta Gyobu who served Yoshitaka and was highly revered by him. However, Gyobu had a habit of telling blatant lies; unlike Yoshitaka's previous conduct, he later began serving a man named Iyo Sohachiro. Consequently, Gyobu was filled with trepidation, and since he had many relatives, those relatives collectively warned him against it. Sohachiro, however, likely viewed this as a grave matter; he sought the assistance of a man named Ujiie Danjo, the lord of Iwate Castle, as a last resort, and requested his help. Danjo promised to lead the effort upon receiving the request. Upon hearing this, Gyobu's relatives feared that if Danjo were to mediate, Gyobu's faction would be resented. At that time, there was a dispute between Osaki and Date regarding the border, and Yoshitaka and Masamune were at odds. Gyobu's faction rejoiced at this, saying, "If reinforcements are sent from the Date, we shall strike down Danjo's faction along with Sohachiro, force Yoshitaka to commit suicide, and easily seize control of Osaki." Masamune declared, "I shall dispatch the necessary number of troops as circumstances dictate." Nevertheless, Gyobu had remained loyal to Yoshitaka until then, stationed at Nasho Castle in Tsukumo. Thus, Danjo told Yoshitaka, "Gyobu's faction has pledged loyalty to Masamune, yet they harbor treasonous intent and are a calamity that may lead to their destruction. Should Gyobu not be punished? Or else, what would become of him in prison?" Yoshitaka replied, "Though it is a past matter, I served him since he was a child, and a death sentence or imprisonment would be inconvenient. I shall simply send him to his current residence in Nitta." Despite various attempts to dissuade him, these efforts were in vain. Consequently, Yoshitaka summoned Gyobu and said, "It is regrettable that you and your faction plotted rebellion, but as a reward for serving me since childhood, I intend to grant you a death sentence. From this moment on, go to your residence in Nitta." Gyobu replied, "Your command is difficult to fulfill, but if I am granted leave and leave the Honmaru, I shall remain concerned and will immediately strike down my peers. Though it is a grave matter, out of gratitude for everything thus far, I would be grateful if you would not take me with you halfway." Yoshitaka, citing the inconvenience, sent him as far as a place called Fushimi within Osaki. Meanwhile, Gyobu's retainers—some twenty or thirty in total—surrounded Yoshitaka from all sides without following him. When Yoshitaka said, "The attendants are unnecessary," they appeared ready to act swiftly and finally escorted him to Fushimi. When told, "Go from here," Gyobu replied, "I alone shall go, but my retainers must surely accompany me to Nitta." When asked what would happen to the attendants, Yoshitaka replied, "I intend to strike down Yoshitaka; therefore, contrary to expectations, I sent him to Nitta and did not send him to the castle in Nasho, but left him there." Meanwhile, Gyobu's relatives—Satomi Kii-no-kami, the lord of Rozuka Castle; Shuzen, the lord of Yachimori Castle; Katsuraoka Tarozaemon, the lord of Miyazawa Castle; Danjo, the lord of Furukawa Castle; Sakyoryo, the lord of Momo Castle; Yagisawa Bizen; Yoneizumi Gon'emon; Miyazaki Minbu; Nakanome Hyogo; Iikawa Osumi; and Kurosawa Jibu—who was the father-in-law of Yoshitaka—all approached Masamune. They plotted to use their influence to strike down Ujiie's faction along with Sohachiro and force Yoshitaka to commit suicide. However, contrary to their expectations, Yoshitaka was captured alive; their original plan was now reversed, and they decided to abandon the Date to protect Yoshitaka and eliminate Ujiie and the Sohachiro. The loyalists informed Yoshitaka, "If Gyobu's relatives have conspired to bring you down, how could you treat your lifelong lord with such neglect? We thought only of Danjo alone and had already made a promise regarding two generations of attendants; now, to attempt to eliminate you would be shameful. However, since you are confined in Nitta and facing litigation, it is only natural that our strength is insufficient."

shigezane:masamuneki3-6.title: The Story of Ujiie Danjo Chusetsu
shigezane:masamuneki3-6.summary: Meanwhile, upon hearing from Danjo that Yoshitaka was facing a lawsuit by the Gyobu faction, he remarked, "This is most alarming. Should the traitors who rebelled against me be plotting their downfall, I would have intended to remain alone in Namago Castle and accompany them to their destruction; yet now they seek to strike me down—such is the way of the world..."
shigezane:masamuneki3-6.markdown:
Meanwhile, when Danjo heard of the lawsuit involving Yoshitaka's faction, he remarked, "This is a grave matter. Should the traitors who turned back their loyalty rebel, I intended to bring myself alone to Naisho-go Castle and accompany them to their destruction, yet now they seek to subdue me—such is the way of the world, for they speak of such things. I shall therefore take matters into my own hands and petition the Date, so as to save my life." With this, he dispatched two retainers, Kagetsuna Katakura and Gyobu Mayama, to Yonezawa, and through Kagetsuna Katakura, he stated: "Nitta Gyobu and his relatives have betrayed Yoshitaka and declared their loyalty to the Date; however, contrary to expectations, they have captured Gyobu alive. Now, there is a plot to renege on that loyalty and bring about my destruction. If you would kindly grant your assistance, I shall easily bring the entire Osaki domain under control and present it to you. What say you?" Masamune declared, "My resentment toward Yoshitaka has endured for years; furthermore, the betrayal of loyalty by Gyobu's faction is a serious matter. I shall dispatch troops to provide assistance." Consequently, the two envoys returned hastily and reported the matter, and the Danjo was greatly pleased. Thus, Yoshitaka was captured alive at Nitta; thereafter, although Naisho was a deserted place, Danjo kept Yoshitaka's northern son, Lord Shozaburo, and the lady of the house, To-no-kata, as hostages at Naisho Castle, with Danjo Chikagawa and Iba Sohachiro assigned to their guard. Danjo intended to send Lord Shozaburo to the Date, but feeling that it would be unthinkable to betray a hereditary lord—let alone send him along—he feared that doing so would defile the divine mandate and bring retribution from the Buddha and the Three Jewels; thus, he sent him to the castle warden of Nitta, Nanjo Shimosa. The northern son, having been separated from Yoshitaka and his son, grieved day and night and contemplated suicide, but as this was impossible, he spent his days and nights in tears. Then, on the sixteenth day of the first month of the fifteenth year (the year of the Fire Pig), although the Date forces were directed toward Osaki, out of concern for the Asaka front, they did not dispatch any samurai generals south of Shinobu, focusing instead only on the personnel of the inner quarters. In response, Masamune dispatched two generals—Unno Ueno-no-kami Masakage and Izumida Aki Shigemitsu of the house—along with Awano Suketaro, Nagai Gekkan, Takashiro Suo, Omatsuzawa Saemon, Miyanai Inaba, and Tate Sukesaburo; the elder retainer Hamada Izu served as military commissioner, and Oyamada Chikuzen as the inspector, with Yamagishi Shuri as the overseer, leading the entire army to Endo Dewa in Matsuyama. Meanwhile, those who had pledged loyalty to the Date from Osaki—Ujiie Danjo, Ichikuri Hyobu, Yuyama Shuri, Ichinosako Izu, Miyano Bungo, and Tomizawa Hyuga of Sannosako—were all fortunately in the vicinity of Iwadeyama. However, since Gesshu was in rebellion against the Date, the point between Yotsukamado and Matsuyama was Kurokawa, the residence of Gesshu; regardless of whether it was Owari or not, this too was impossible. Thus, they each inquired as to where they should strike and what to do. The enemy army, entrenched in Kuwaori and Shiyama Nike Castle, stated that if the Date troops pressed through, they would fight a battle from Nike Castle, but since they were blocked by the river outlet at Sanbongi, it would be difficult to make an effective move. To this, Endo Dewa said, "Kai, the lord of Niinuma Castle, is my brother-in-law and has been loyal to the Date for generations. Therefore, if we place a blockade at Shiyama and pass through to Nakashinden, there should be no issue." Ueno replied, "While that may be true, Nakashinden is more than twenty ri away; moreover, with the enemy castle behind us and the roads to both locations blocked, it would be risky to press through from that place." Shigemitsu then thought: "Since this army was initiated by us, Lord Ueno has said for some time now that there is discord between us; furthermore, Gesshu is my father-in-law, and I suspect he will not cooperate in this campaign." He stated, "Aki and Dewa have spoken; if Ujiie does not face the Date forces, he will lose his support, and the risk of returning loyalty to Yoshitaka becomes grave. It would be best to place a blockade at Shiyama and pass through." Consequently, they had no choice but to proceed with the operation toward Nakashinden.

shigezane:masamuneki3-7.title: Kurokawa Gesshu Haruuji's Rebellious Intentions: Concern for the Justice of His Reputation
shigezane:masamuneki3-7.summary: Thus, when asked about the details of Haruuji's treason against the Date, it came to light that long ago, a man named Kurokawa Shikibu had been sent by Terumune's ancestors to serve under Tsukifune.
shigezane:masamuneki3-7.markdown:
Thus, when asked about the circumstances behind Haruuji's rebellion against the Date, it came to light that long ago, a man named Kurokawa Shikibu had been sent by the Tsukifune family to serve under Terumune Date and his successors. Ukon, the lord of Iizaka Castle in Shinobu District, had entered into a contract to take Shikibu as his son-in-law and entrust him as his representative. However, as the girl was only about ten years old and Shikibu was thirty at the time, the agreement remained unfulfilled and no wedding had yet taken place. Meanwhile, Ukon felt that Shikibu was too old for the girl and that his own retirement was not yet the right time; he reasoned that if he sent the girl to Masamune and, should a child be born of this union, he could claim the girl as his representative—which would be beneficial for the clan. Thus, he broke the contract. Consequently, Shikibu lost face, ceased his service to the Tsukifune family, and immediately withdrew to Echigo. This resentment persisted; although Tsukifune had been the stepfather to Yoshitaka, he had appointed Yoshitaka's younger brother, Yoshiyasu, as the representative, and had given the daughter of Date Motoyasu in marriage to Yoshiyasu. Because Tsukifune remained in Tsukifune's service, he feared for his own fate should Yoshitaka fall, and thus he rebelled. The Danjo, concerned by the situation, noted that while there had been a promise to provide Date forces, no sign of such support had yet appeared; as they were trapped within the enemy territory, passage was impossible. Though he waited and waited, the year drew to a close and the end of the fifteenth year of Tensho arrived. Just as he was anxiously awaiting the arrival of Osaki, on February 2nd, the Date forces from Matsuyama crossed the Sanbongi River; the vanguard pushed through Shiyama, reached Shinnuma, and launched an attack on Nakashinden. Since Shimoshinden was the stronghold of Yoshitaka's faction, the castle lord Kasai Kanmono and the generals providing support—Satomi Kii-no-kami, Yachimori Shuzen, Yagisawa Bizen, Kurosawa Jibu, Yoneizumi Gon'emon, Miyazaki Minbu, and seven other followers—barricaded themselves in Kasai's castle, boldly declaring, "If the Date army pushes through Nakashinden, we shall not let a single soul pass." Yet, given their superior numbers, they passed through despite their words. The generals at Shiyama included Furukawa Danjo, Ishikawa Echizen, Kasai Taroemon, and Ukyo-no-suke, the lord of Momo Castle, along with various other followers. From the river southward toward Kuwaori Castle, Kurokawa Tsukifune barricaded himself, and together with Osumi, the lord of Iigawa Castle, they blocked the roads between the two castles. Date Ueno, Hamada Izu, Tatesuke Saburo, and Miyauchi Inaba led the charge, crossing the Sanbongi River with over four hundred cavalry lined up side-by-side and stationed in the fields south of Shiyama. The vanguard emerged near Nakashinden and advanced four or five cho from the town called Nanjo Shimousa; the advance troops launched a charge, forcing their way inside and sending signal fires from the town walls to two or three baileys, but they broke through into the main castle of Shimousa, which remained firmly fortified. As the enemy forces pressed forward from all sides, the military commissioner Oyamada Chikuzen, concerned for the aftermath, issued orders and arranged for a general retreat and high-level preparations. Upon hearing of this action, Ujiie Danjo—unexpectedly surprised that the Date forces had advanced to Nakashinden—declared that he would join the Date army and charged toward Mount Iwate, intending to join the Date forces. However, as the enemy forces burned and withdrew from all directions, he could not join them, and Danjo retreated in vain. The Date forces, facing deep snow and a single road, had barely reached noon when they hurriedly withdrew, intending to join the enemy forces at Shiyama. Date Ueno and Hamada Izu withdrew quickly; furthermore, the Tada River and the three- or four-ken water canal and bridge were both impassable. Thus, the advance troops turned back toward Shinnuma and launched a battle at Nakashinden, but the main bridge was double-blocked. The allies, concerned by this, were lagging behind, but Oyamada Chikuzen, a man of great honor, repelled the enemy and scattered them. As one foot soldier crossed to the side, Chikuzen pursued him to strike him down; after riding for fourteen or fifteen ken, he entered a deep field where the snow had piled up, appearing like flat land. Unaware of the deep snow, he charged in, causing his horse to fall and knocking Chikuzen off. As he attempted to pull the reins to pull himself back, the enemy counterattacked and attempted to strike Chikuzen. At that moment, Chikuzen let go of the reins and fought with his drawn sword, but as the enemy was numerous, he circled behind him and had one leg severed. Though he fought without abandoning his sword, as he was an old warrior, the strikes were ineffective. Four retainers rushed forward and attempted to strike his head; Chikuzen threw away his sword, seized the retainers, drew the short sword at his waist, and thrust it straight into the center, bringing both of them down on the same pillow. The enemy then came and took their heads. The enemy forces were stationed south of the river, but seeing the defeat of our side, they crossed the river to join the men at Nakashinden. By then, the sun had already begun to set over the mountain edge. Chikuzen, the military commissioner, and many others of our side had been killed, and since the main bridge was blocked, they could not escape; the Date forces became unexpectedly entrenched at Shinnuma. Thus, on the morning Oyamada was killed, perhaps as a mysterious omen, a horse emerged from the stables ten ken or more from the camp, and the drum of the horse he was riding began to say "fast, slow, slow," and the attendants amused themselves by this. It is said that Chikuzen, believing he would win today's battle, turned toward the front. However, after Chikuzen was killed, someone recognized the horse and said, "This horse was a divine steed, brought to the Kannon of Nonotake for Yoshitaka's prayers a year ago." It was said that Yoshitaka also recognized it. Rumor spread that the horse had passed through various hands to reach Chikuzen, and that to die riding that horse was a manifestation of divine power. Furthermore, when Chikuzen gave a token to Mogami Yoshiaki via Yoshitaka, the latter, feeling that his honor had been compromised, had a small white-horse-comb flag on a black background presented to Mount Haguro in Dewa. People of the time felt it was a blessing, believing that his death had brought him such renown.

shigezane:masamuneki3-8.title: The Case of Gesshu
shigezane:masamuneki3-8.summary: Meanwhile, the second line of the Date forces—including those from Ueno and Izu—was stationed in the fields south of Moriyama; the vanguard attempted to push through and draw them back, but were unable to cross the bridge at the critical point.
shigezane:masamuneki3-8.markdown:
Meanwhile, the second line of the Date forces—including those from Ueno and Izu—was stationed in the fields south of Shiyama. When the vanguard attempted to pass and draw them back, they pushed forward to force their way through, but they were unable to cross the bridge at the critical point. Furthermore, the enemy from both Kuwaori and Shiyama castles had them surrounded from all sides; as the sun was beginning to set, passage became even more impossible. Consequently, the second line could not evacuate the area either. A messenger was sent from the direction of Ueno to Haruuji, the father-in-law, requesting that they be allowed to withdraw, to which Haruuji replied, "Allow them to withdraw." Ueno then declared, "I shall fight alone to force my way through; if you allow a single unit of our forces to pass, I shall withdraw; otherwise, I shall fight to the death." At this juncture, a man named Yamori Sagami, an uncle of Tsukifune, urged Haruuji, saying, "First, we must defeat Ueno and his forces one by one to determine the true strength of the army. As for that matter, Osaki is divided into various districts, but Masamune is a man of great power; once he becomes the enemy, it would mean the Date army is aided, and it would be impossible to reclaim them a second time—Tsukifune himself would be sacrificed. The only way is to defeat the enemy here." Nevertheless, unable to bring himself to kill his son-in-law, he withdrew to Ueno, leaving no trace of the Date forces behind and retreating toward Matsuyama. Thus, the vanguard soldiers, unable to break through, were reduced to a force of five thousand men; having taken refuge in Shinnuma, a small settlement, they were already suffering from hunger and thirst. The Date side also dispatched troops to lift the siege, but as the Date army sent a single unit, Haruuji grew anxious regarding the Asaka and Sendo-guchi areas. While they were deliberating whether those besieged should push through Shiyama, cut down the enemy on the other side, and retreat to Matsuyama, Nagai Tsukikan remarked, "The enemy has the south castles of Kuwaori and Shiyama surrounded; it is a prime location to attack and hold them. Furthermore, when they cross the Tamatsukuri River, they will surely be enveloped from behind and left with no way out, certain to die in battle." Indeed, this was the expected outcome. At that time, the Tamatsukuri River flowed through the town of Furukawa, and when it fell toward Shiyama, it turned north and joined there. Meanwhile, two messengers from the enemy side, named Suzuki Iga and Kitago Samanosuke, arrived midway and sent a messenger to Shinnuma, summoning Otani and Kazawa, who were besieged, and stating that if they handed over Izumida Aki and Tsukikan as hostages, the besieged forces would be allowed to leave their castles. The two men returned to the castle first and informed Tsukikan and Aki. Aki's retainer, Yumura Genzaemon, said, "It is expected that many will be cut down and die in battle; however, if the forces are withdrawn and Aki alone is captured at a later date, what greater shame could there be than to be beheaded and die in captivity? Should Aki not fight and accept this?" Tsukikan replied, "Regardless of everything else, Lord Aki's act of saving the forces is the greatest loyalty to Masamune. Now, let us fall into the enemy's hands and hasten to withdraw our allies." Genzaemon added, "I have already fully grasped your true intentions," and they engaged in an intense argument. Aki replied, "Genzaemon's words are useless; I care not for others—I am content to fall into the enemy's hands, even if I am alone, to save the forces," and conveyed this intent to Suzuki Iga and Kitago Samanosuke. Since Tsukikan had already agreed to surrender, on the 23rd day of the second month, both men left the castle of Shinnuma and went to Arigabukuro in Osaki to become hostages; the Date forces then left their castles and withdrew to their side in Matsuyama. Consequently, Hamada Izu, Konarita Soemon, and Yamagishi Shuri returned to Yonezawa and reported the army's affairs to Masamune, who declared, "We have ventured too far into enemy territory without proper reconnaissance and have committed a grave error. Let us consult with the Danjo and attack and seize the castles at Kuwaori and Shiyama."

shigezane:masamuneki3-9.title: Regarding the envoy from Mogami to Osaki
shigezane:masamuneki3-9.summary: Mogami Yoshiaki dispatched his retainer Noto Nobezawa to Arigabukuro in Osaki; upon meeting Tsukikage, what did he say? He returned Tsukikage to Fukaya, and handed over Noto—accompanied by a single man from Aki—to the two castle wardens of Onoda, Genban and Kurozaemon.
shigezane:masamuneki3-9.markdown:
Mogami Yoshiaki dispatched his retainer, Noto of Nobezawa, to Arigabukuro in Osaki. What did he say upon meeting Gekkan? He returned Gekkan to the original deep valley and handed him over to two men—Genban and Kurozaemon, the castle lords of Onoda—with Aki and Noto as his attendants. That night, Noto again came to the Aki post and said, "It is not unusual for you to be brought here; there are already plots by Yoshiaki to coordinate with the Satake, Aizu, and Iwaki factions to launch an army against the Date. Therefore, since Soma Yoshitane should also be involved, a man named Imokubo Mataemon has been sent to Dewa to coordinate matters. Furthermore, if you also conspire within the clan, should you rebel against the Date, you yourself will suffer a dire fate." Aki replied, "I staked my very life in service to my lord; how could I possibly reclaim the merit of leading the troops during the siege? Behead me at once!" Noto remarked, "Ah, what unparalleled words for a samurai," and was thus rewarded. Accordingly, Aki, intending to report this matter to Masamune, sent a secret messenger named Saito Magoemon to Yonezawa to explain the details. While Shiba Yoshiaki was the uncle of Masamune's mother, he had fought frequently during the time of Terumune, but had established peace with Masamune and had recently been on friendly terms. Nevertheless, he was an exceptionally wicked general who had destroyed many high-ranking members of our house and had even sentenced both of his sons to death. Thus, when Masamune captured Yohon-no-matsu and Nihonmatsu, the Satake, Aizu, Soma, Iwaki, Shirakawa, and Sukagawa each turned against the Date; since Yoshiaki was a neighbor, they awaited the right moment to reach a reconciliation and wage war against the Date, longing for the castle of Yonezawa. Moreover, as the Date forces in Osaki were now powerless, and since Yoshitaka had sent the hostage Aki of Izumida to Mogami, he sought to sever ties with Masamune further. There was a man named Ayugu Fujitaro on the border between Yonezawa and Mogami, whom Yoshiaki approached; on the thirteenth day of the third month of the sixteenth year of Tensho, Fujitaro attacked the Date. Masamune declared that he would strike him down without delay. The senior retainers said, "Since Yoshiaki is a wicked general, his military strategies and schemes in the neighboring provinces are beyond suspicion; let us hear his words." "Though each has spoken, how shall we proceed?" they said, and it was decided that the horses should be readied for the attack. However, Ayugu repeatedly requested reinforcements from Mogami, but for some reason, not a single rider came to aid him. Furthermore, upon hearing that Masamune was marching out, Fujitaro withdrew to Mogami. Consequently, peace prevailed throughout Yonezawa.

shigezane:masamuneki4-1.title: Regarding the Desires of Ouchi and Date
shigezane:masamuneki4-1.summary: In the tenth year of Tensho, the year of the Fire Pig, when Masamune was twenty-one, campaigns were waged against Mogami and Osaki, yet the Asaka region remained undisturbed and peaceful for the time being.
shigezane:masamuneki4-1.markdown:
In the tenth year of Tensho, the year of the Fire Pig, when Masamune was twenty-one, campaigns were waged against Mogami and Osaki, but the region around Asaka remained peaceful for the time being. It was then that Ouchi Bizen and Shigezane, from Aizu, sent a message stating: "The fall of Yohon-no-Matsu is no extraordinary matter. Three senior retainers on guard duty from Aizu reported that the stronghold of Yohon-no-Matsu is difficult to breach; as for the details, they asked whether Lord Masamune should be blamed for summoning Iwakado nearby to inspect it. Since he is in close proximity, even if the route to Nihonmatsu is impassable, it would be unthinkable to withdraw from Obama should that place fall. Therefore, it is now evident that the matter has been settled; in that case, Yohon-no-Matsu—the site of the former Matsumoto Tosho-no-suke of Aizu—is vacant land. Since there are those who intend to seize that land to become senior retainers, if one were to withdraw, not only would the matter of one's fief be ignored, but one would not even receive the sustenance required to survive and would starve to death. Thus, I now recall that the Aizu retainers had sought to have me removed; Lord Masamune summoned Iwakado and pressed him as far as Yohon-no-Matsu. If both castles fall, my fate goes without saying, and even the guards would be annihilated. While each would wish to be stationed there, fearing the failure of their mission to Aizu, they admonished me and removed me from the group; thus, it seems the agreement was violated. As for what occurred, my luck has run out and I have gone against Lord Masamune's will, leading to this state of affairs. If, on top of this, you were to grant me a small amount of income from the Date, I would be most grateful. However, this deeply offends me, and I humbly request that you grant me a pardon. I have also pledged my loyalty to my younger brother, Katahira Sukeemon; I therefore earnestly request that a pardon be granted." Upon hearing this, Shigezane, through Kagetsuna Katakura, asked, "Should Ouchi be summoned? What are the details?" To this, Shigezane replied, "Since the death of Kiyoaki, there has been no lord who could firmly hold Tamura; the fragmentation of the Tamura house is well-known. Ouchi Bizen has seized this opportunity. Yohon-no-Matsu is held by the lower-ranking retainers and is a hereditary estate; thus, by manipulating the intentions of the Sendo generals and framing it as an uprising by Bizen's army, he intends to oppose us twice. Next, as for Katahira, the territory of Sukeemon lies south of Takatama Akukashima in enemy territory; if Sukeemon remains loyal, both those lands and Aizu could be secured and withdrawn from us. In that case, Takakura, Fukuhara, and Koriyama were originally under our control; if those three locations are added along with Katahira, there would be no need for war. Therefore, if you summon Bizen and grant him a reward, how should we respond?" To this, Masamune declared, "Ouchi has once become an enemy, and while it is regrettable, I took the opportunity when Terumune died last year to reconcile with Satake, Aizu, and Iwaki; their cooperation up to Motomiya was regrettable. Therefore, this military campaign against the Sendo cannot be achieved without further disturbance. If Sukeemon remains loyal, Ouchi may also be pardoned." Accordingly, a messenger from Bizen's side conveyed this message and returned. Thus, since the withdrawal of Ouchi, Yohon-no-Matsu was granted to Shiroishi Wakasa. When Shigezane told Wakasa that Bizen had surrendered to the Date, Wakasa remarked, "Generally, Yohon-no-Matsu is held by the hereditary retainers of Ouchi; while one is concerned about the residence in Bizen's territory, one's desire for the house is no small joy." Shigezane accepted this, and the matter was settled. However, thereafter, Ouchi from Aizu said, "Your words are troublesome; I have heard everything, and now that Aizu is spreading word of this, my life is already in danger." Shigezane replied, "Why should I speak of it? Although you say that Obama is now the castle of Shiroishi Wakasa, if I hide your desire for the Date from Wakasa, I fear suspicion may arise; thus, I whispered the matter to him. Perhaps he is colluding." Subsequently, Wakasa told Shigezane, "Ouchi says he wishes to rely on me and earnestly requests my help, claiming there is collusion from Aizu. While I believe it is unwise to speak of such matters, since I do not know the truth of Wakasa's collusion, why not speak a little? First, Masamune is deeply attached to Aizu, and that sentiment is widely known; thus, if Ouchi is killed and loyalty to Aizu is severed, I shall have no choice but to endure it for the sake of his loyalty." Shigezane told Wakasa, "Regardless, since it has come to Ouchi's surrender, I must go. Above all, my primary consideration is for the sake of the Date." With that, they parted ways. As for why Wakasa spoke ill of him, Ouchi Bizen was a man of great honor; even when Yohon-no-Matsu was his castle, although Tamura was nearby, he acted as a shield for Kiyoaki, refused assistance from Satake and Aizu, and for several years maintained his own army, winning frequent victories in battle—a feat unparalleled, as Masamune knew. If Bizen surrendered to the Date, he might return his original lands and even Yohon-no-Matsu; since there was no other way, he intended to force a surrender in the south, believing that otherwise Yohon-no-Matsu would not be returned, and otherwise he would be killed in Aizu; this was the reasoning he gave. Because of such circumstances, the surrender to the Date was delayed for that year, and Ouchi, concerned for Aizu, requested a leave of absence for the same month, withdrawing to Katahira.

shigezane:masamuneki4-2.title: Regarding the Ouchi Bizen Hand-Cutting
shigezane:masamuneki4-2.summary: Meanwhile, in the districts of Sendo Asaka—namely Ota, Arai, and Naeshiroda—though separated from Nihonmatsu, they remained part of the Nihonmatsu domain. Consequently, during the turmoil following Yoshitsugu's assassination, the people of these three locations also fled in all directions, leaving the lands desolate.
shigezane:masamuneki4-2.markdown:
At that time, in the Sendo Asaka district—specifically Ota, Arai, and Naeshiroda—though separated from Nihonmatsu, these lands were part of the Nihonmatsu domain. Consequently, during the turmoil following the murder of Yoshitsugu, the people of these three locations fled in all directions, leaving the lands desolate. Later, when Masamune took control of Nihonmatsu and granted lands to Shigezane, he assigned local peasants to those three locations. However, since these two places, Takatama and Akugashima, were enemy territory and close to Naeshiroda, the peasants who had been recalled gathered in the old castle to cultivate the land as a precaution. Then, around the hour of the Ox on February 12, Tensho 16 (the year of the Wood Rat), forces from Katahira, Akugashima, and Takatama mobilized and attacked Naeshiroda, the domain of Ouchi Bizen and Shigezane. They slew over a hundred local peasants from Yorii and even killed a man named Honnai Shusui, who had been appointed as a leader, setting off signal fires and sparking another rebellion. In response, the people of Ota and Arai, no longer having local peasants in their original lands, retreated to a private estate called Tamai. At the end of the same month, Ouchi approached Shigezane, claiming that since he had relied on Shigezane's help last year and had plotted against the Date, his life was now in danger; he sought to report this to Aizu while maintaining a facade of submission, pleading for his life. Upon hearing this, Shigezane, given the success of his efforts, managed to escape all blame and repeatedly petitioned for reinstatement in Yonezawa. However, Ouchi had reversed his previous agreement; to press his claim to a private estate and kill Honnai Shusui was an unprecedented act of treachery. Shigezane could not believe he was being driven out and repeatedly pleaded that others be appointed in his stead, but Ouchi refused. Then, a messenger sent by Ouchi to Shigezane—a relative of Shusui who resided in Shigezane's private estate of Tamanoi—stated, "Tamanoi is close to enemy territory and lies on the border; even the local peasants are loyal to Nihonmatsu, so they were concerned that even if they grazed grass in other domains, they might collude with the enemy. Now that the Katahira brothers have demonstrated their loyalty, there is no doubt that Takatama and Akugashima, the enemy territories, will also be secured and eventually fall into your possession. Furthermore, bringing the Ouchi brothers back into the fold is for the sake of the Date and for the sake of Tamanoi." Following this frequent petition, and since it was primarily for the sake of the Date, Shigezane reported this to Yonezawa. Masamune replied, "It is regrettable that Naeshiroda was attacked, but since your loyalty to this side remains unwavering and you have pleaded for your life, this too is not unreasonable. If Sukeemon remains loyal, I shall summon Bizen as well. Keep this in mind." Accordingly, a request was sent to Bizen, and Sukeemon proved utterly loyal; when Shigezane offered four or five other nearby villages, the situation was successfully resolved, and a document was prepared stating that Ouchi would be granted Hobara. When this was sent to the Ouchi brothers, Sukeemon said, "I am the son-in-law of the Tango representative of Se-no-ue; since that Tango is still under a cloud of resentment following the Nakano-Hitachi turmoil, it would be all the more grateful if this were pardoned." When the matter was brought up, Ouchi replied, "Regarding Hitachi, even my relatives are too precious to spare, but Tango is my grandson; I cannot possibly forgive him." Sukeemon replied, "Your consideration is most generous. Though it is difficult for me, I shall serve as the representative. Once my son's estate is confiscated, I alone cannot escape the resentment of all sides; while I am not entirely disloyal, I have no choice but to submit the written judgment you provide." Hearing this, Masamune remarked, "How kindly you have spoken; the spirit of a samurai is truly remarkable," and granted Tango's pardon. Consequently, while the Bizen brothers were coming this way, Kagetsuna Katakura agreed to wait at Nihonmatsu, the castle of Shigezane, as he had arranged with Shigezane. shigezane:masamuneki4-3.title: Regarding the Land Survey of Shigezane's Territory
shigezane:masamuneki4-3.summary: Thus, it is said in the military lore of Oshu that one might "conduct grass operations," "enter the grass," "lie in the grass," or "rise from the grass"—or rather, "search for an early opportunity." The first, "conducting grass operations," refers to secretly dispatching forces from one's own domain to another; this is called "grass operations."
shigezane:masamuneki4-3.markdown:
Thus, among the military lore of Oshu, there are accounts of "kusa-chogi" (grass raids)—where one enters the grass, lies down in the grass, or rises from the grass—and the practice of "soka o sagasu" (searching for the early morning). The term "kusa-chogi" refers to secretly dispatching forces from one's own territory into another's. Depending on the size of the force, these were divided into "first grass," "second grass," and "third grass," with the number of men assigned in stages; for the first grass, only foot soldiers were sent two or three cho ahead, infiltrating stealthily during the night until they reached the vicinity of the enemy castle—this was called "entering the grass." From there, they would scout for a suitable location and lie in wait; this was called "lying in the grass." Then, once dawn broke, if even a single person emerged from the interior, or if even a few people appeared from the enemy territory, striking them down in the first grass was called "rising from the grass." Precisely at that moment, the people of the enemy territory would realize what was happening and, each taking up their arms, attempt to strike down the first grass; as the grass-raiders fled in disorder, our forces would pursue them in increasing numbers, leading to a clash where two or three grass-raiders fought one another. Once it was known that the grass had entered our territory, our men would be divided into two or three groups and sent in from the flanks to cut through the tracks left by the two or three grass-raiders; then, engaging in battle with those troops, the remaining men would search from the first grass, joining the two or three who had risen and fled. However, as they pressed in from the rear, there were times when the strength of the grass-raiders proved too great and they instead struck down our forces. Even in broad daylight, if a location such as the edge of the mountains was suitable, a grass raid would be conducted as described above; though it was daytime, it was not called "grass," but "daytime raid." On the thirteenth day of the third month of the same year, Shigezane's territory at Tamanoi—specifically a place called Nishihara, located at the edge of the mountains, four or five ri from Tamanoi—was targeted by an enemy raid. The enemy intended to strike down those on the route from Tamanoi at Nishihara, but the people of Tamanoi, realizing this, pursued them from a distance without engaging in battle. The people of Takatama, seeing this, decided to launch a follow-up attack and strike them down; on the night of the twenty-second of the same month, they resolved to send a grass raid to the mountain path from Tamanoi to Takatama at a place called Yazawa. Now, the Ouchi brothers—who, as mentioned, were utterly loyal to Date but had conspired—had not yet cut ties with the enemy side at that time; yet, if they now joined forces with Takatama, they would be revealed as accomplices of Date. Fearing that word of this would reach Aizu and cause a great disturbance, there was no other choice but to have men from Suke-emon’s territory at Katahira and Akugashima join them at Takatama. On the twenty-third, word reached Motomiya, Shigezane’s territory, that a grass raid was coming for Tamanoi tonight. On the morning of the twenty-third, the people of Motomiya and Tamanoi, including Shigezane himself, went out to search, but as not a single person was found, they withdrew, believing it to be a false report. During the daytime of that day, twenty or thirty men appeared near Tamanoi; our forces attempted to engage them but were forced to retreat, eventually cornering them at a place called Dairin-da. As they saw our forces retreating and saw an opportunity to strike them down, they hid over three hundred men in the shadow of a small hill at the aforementioned Yazawa and prepared a follow-up attack. Just as the battle was about to begin, they intended to ambush the enemy, but because the people of Tamanoi had pursued the enemy without consultation, they never dreamed of an ambush. Believing the enemy's footprints had become muddy, they charged forward; as the enemy began to collapse and lose their footing, the enemy in the follow-up attack also waited and advanced quickly. Though they were not overrun, our forces began to collapse and were pushed back to the river, where three or four men were killed. When the enemy fought back at the river, the enemy general, Takatama Taroemon, crossed the boundary of our side and crossed the river to the side. Shigezane, on foot, stationed himself at Shigayama Saburo and waited with a gun at the river-stream; he fired a shot, and it was a fine shot, with one bullet striking Taroemon in the waist. Another bullet struck the horse's shoulder, throwing the horse backward like a folding screen. The enemy's footprints became muddy at the entrance of the ambush. A fierce warrior named Ota Shuzen, who urged his lord to withdraw, had not yet collapsed when Shuzen mounted a horse at Kosaka. Yama Saburo then fired an arrow at him, striking the saddle-ring in two pieces and sending the rider flying. Shuzen fell headlong, drew the small flag he had tucked into his own person, and suffered a severe wound. "If we withdraw from here, we shall surely collapse; you, Shuzen, take over and lead the lord to retreat," he cried. He gave the small flag to his younger brother, Sayome, and rode away from the scene. The people of the time felt how pitiful yet brave a warrior he was. In short, this grass raid was launched following the initiative of Shuzen and Taroemon. Because both had fought as described above, the overall force collapsed, and fifty-three heads were taken in pursuit. Because it was a battle that broke out like an avalanche, many were killed, but many managed to escape through the rugged terrain of the mountain shadows; it was later heard that many enemies did not even return to their lodgings that night. The heads were then presented to Yonezawa for inspection.
