#### About the Noh Play "Surigami"

In the Sendai Domain, where Noh theater flourished, several new Noh plays were created during the Edo period, and "Surigami" is one such work. The author was Hiraga Kurando Yoshimasa, a retainer of the Sendai Domain, who is said to have presented the text to Date Shigemura. The premiere took place several generations later, during the reign of Date Saimune. Because it drew upon the deeds of the domain's founder, there were reportedly strict restrictions on its performance; however, since the Date family of Iwadeyama preserved it within the Shunfuji school and made it a tradition to chant it during the New Year, it seems to have been reasonably well-known. (※[Shunfuji school](http://blog.goo.ne.jp/nuenokai/m/200607): One of the schools of Noh waki roles. The founder is said to be Shunfuji Rokuro Jiro, though other theories exist. It flourished as the affiliated school of the Konparu troupe, but declined after the Meiji era and was abolished in 1945 (Showa 20). by [Yahoo! Dictionary](http://dic.yahoo.co.jp/dsearch?dtype=2&p=%BD%D5%C6%A3%CE%AE)) The author, Hiraga Kurando Yoshimasa, is believed to be the Hiraga Izumo Yoshimasa mentioned in the entry for the Hiraga clan in the "Private Biographical Dictionary of Sendai Domain Retainers." The Hiraga clan was a lineage ranked among the seated retainers with a stipend of 100 kanmon; since they served the Date family since the time of Date Naomune and resided at the Uchibaba Yamaguchi residence, they called themselves the Baba clan until the Enpo era.

The Noh play takes the form of a "katsu-shura mugen-no" (victory-shura dream-vision play), recounting the Battle of Surigami Ue with Munemi as the shite.

(First Act) While returning to Kyoto after participating in the Date clan's annual New Year's Seven-Herb Renga, the Hogen (of the Inawashiro clan) decides to visit Kodaira-gata Tenmangu Shrine in Inawashiro, a place tied to his ancestors. Upon arriving in Inawashiro and gazing at Kurokawa Castle from afar, he recalls Masamune's poem—"Picking the seven herbs, all gathered on a single leaf"—which served as the origin of the Seven-Herb Renga. Just then, an old man appears from nowhere and asks him about the spirit of the poem. When the Hogen replies, "You mean the seven herbs of spring," the old man explains, "That is true, but it is a poem in which Lord Komon (Masamune) subdued enemies from seven different places." The Hogen asks the old man for directions to Kodaira-gata Tenmangu Shrine; guided by him, he arrives safely at the shrine, where the plum blossoms are in full bloom. As they enjoy the blossoms together, the old man points out famous sites along the Way of the Immortals. Eventually, evening falls. When he requests music so they can enjoy the night together, the old man vanishes, blending into the evening mist. (Intermission) (Second Act) As the Hogen plays music just as the old man wished, a splendid warrior appears in the moonlight and identifies himself as Shigezane Date. Shigezane recounts the events of the Battle of Surigami Ue and celebrates the glory of the Sendai Domain.

## Noh Play "Surigami"

"Noh" (from Ryokichi Mihara, *History of Miyagi Prefecture*, Vol. 14: Literature and Performing Arts), Noh play "Surigami"

Author: Hiraga Kurando Yoshimasa, a retainer of the Sendai Domain (during the reign of Shigemura Date); Premiere: February 4, Bunka 12, at the Ninomaru main stage of Sendai Castle. Front Shite: Toko no Okina; Rear Shite: Fujiwara Shigezane (Shigezane Date); Waki: Hogen [name unknown] (Inawashiro clan). Location: Mutsu, Aizu; Season: March

**Waki**

In this reign, the people forget even to bolt their doors. Passing through the [Great Wooden Gate of Seki](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-sitahimonoseki.htm), beyond the traces of the western hall whose name alone remains, in Michinoku, the [Village of Shinobu](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-sinobunosato.htm) with its cedar shoots, two willows adding their green — deep into the [Mountains of Aizu](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-aizune.htm) in spring, we have arrived at Inawashiro. We have arrived at Inawashiro.

**Waki**

**Shite**

Nafunafu—what brings you to compose a renga such as this now?

**Waki**

How strange—in the vast, desolate wilderness, where not a single dwelling is in sight, an old man alone arrives and asks me what the refrain of the current renga poem is; it is indeed most peculiar. Now then, who might you be?

**Shite**

Nay, I too am no stranger; now, as I shall weave seven types into a single leaf, how shall you interpret this?

**Waki**

The seven types referred to are: the Gogyo-utabirako Buddha's seat, bellflower, white turnip, Japanese parsley, and mizuna. These are referred to collectively.

**Shite**

While that was indeed the case, it must still be a matter of profound significance. Long ago, there were seven strongholds of the enemy in this area, but more than half have already fallen. The remaining enemies, too, have largely succumbed; as their songs of submission began to fade, long ago [Shinobu-moji-zuri](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-sinobumotizuri.htm) began to crumble, and as the warriors (mononofu) dreamed upon their horses, using their armor sleeves as pillows and the sea's waves as shields—even the drums of the waves ceased—how long did the still, clear lake endure, or how long did it finally run its course?

**Waki**

I humbly state that our ancestor was a man named Kaneya Inawashiro, a native of this place; he practiced the art of linked verse and passed it down through the generations, and enshrined a deity at Tenmangu. As I have yet to pay my respects at that shrine, I wish to do so; please advise me as to where I may do so.

**Shite**

This is Tenjin of Kodaira-gata; he stands far off by the shores of that lake. If you come to pay your respects, I shall show you the way. Cross over this way. Nafu-nafu—this is indeed Tenmangu; please offer your prayers in peace.

**Waki**

I was born into a family that has followed the path of old, and have long revered this deity. How grateful I am to be visiting this shrine today. Though a garment of moss would be fitting as an offering, I shall offer these flowers to the divine. Ah, the plums are in full bloom.

**Shite**

Indeed, the plum blossoms are in full bloom; if I pluck a blossom and pin it to my hair, the snow of February will fall upon my robes—what a wondrous sight!

**Land**

Though my form may seem like an old pine tree—though my form may seem like an old pine tree—the flowers of my heart shall surely bloom. Here, too, as the pine wind blows through the peaks of Bandai, the flowers bloom in their eternal hue; looking east across the mountains, there are no gaps between the mountains and rivers of the villages along the sacred path; gazing south at the faint mist, the distant mountains seen from afar—what place might they be?

**Shite**

Indeed, when one leaves the capital amidst the mist and hears that the autumn wind is blowing, if one returns to the capital, it shall already be autumn—[Shirakawa Barrier](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-sirakawanoseki.htm)—but then again...

**Land**

North of here, [Adatarayama](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-adatarayama.htm)—where can one see the plains opening to the east of the mountain?

**Shite**

In Michinoku, in Michinoku's [Adachigahara](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-adatigahara.htm) black mound, the demon who dwelt in hiding, long ago—

**Land**

Now, a tranquil spring haze drifts over [Sueno-Matsuyama](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/miyagi/m-suenomatuyama.htm), and what appears slightly elevated within is—

**Shite**

Be mindful of [Asakayama](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-asakayama.htm), renowned for its name, and discern the depths of the heart—even its shadow is visible—at [Yamanoi](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-asakayama.htm).

**Land**

The flowering katsumi of [Asaka Pond](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-asakanonuma.htm)

**Shite**

Young grass beginning to sprout—

**Land**

Even the tree buds of spring

**Shite**

Wakamidori

**Land**

Looking out, plum and willow trees intertwine in the decorative colors of spring; at [Aikuma](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-abukumagawa.htm), where the river winds—a single trickle of water accumulating into a deep pool—its end stretches for a thousand ri. In this bountiful world, living on long into old age, forgetting the waves of aging, let us rejoice together; let us rejoice together. Already, upon the plum branches in the evening glow, the moon has emerged, its light filtering through the blossoms—a pure fragrance and moonlight; in such a wondrous nighttime, I beg you to play music. At that moment, I too shall come, clad in the ceremonial robes (omigoromo) of old days, to dance and play; lost in the evening mist, I shall vanish without a trace, leaving no trace behind.

**(Intermission)**

**Waki**

Raising their voices in Taiheiraku, raising their voices in Taiheiraku, they played that music, tuning their flutes and adding the rhythm of the tsutsumi and drums; they played this music.

**Shite**

What fascinating music! What you are now playing must be the "Relief of the King of Qin from His Camp." I recall how, long ago, when Emperor Taizong of Tang was still the King of Qin, he greatly defeated Liu Wuzhou and established his reign; after the peace that followed, he had this dance of the Seven Virtues composed. It is a sign of a prosperous reign, and as a testament to his rule, the strings and bamboo—

**Land**

His voice, clear and resonant,

**Shite**

Of Mine no Matsukaze Lake

**Location**

Is it heard, like the wind?

**Waki**

How strange—in the clear moonlight where the music's voice resounds, there appears a warrior, clad in armor, as radiant as a flower; who might this person be?

**Shite**

What shall I speak of now? Fujiwara no Shigezane, who lived during the reign of Lord Komon. I have come thus far in order to recount the tales of old.

**Land**

To begin with, this Lord Komon—possessing wisdom, benevolence, and courage—brought order to a chaotic world, laying the foundation for peace for the people and the governance of the state, a legacy passed down through the generations.

**Shite**

It is also said that things have settled down and the unrest is not remembered.

**Land**

Ever since the days of the Onin conflict, the four seas have been in turmoil all at once; the squabbling of the snails' horns has shown no sign of abating.

**Shite**

It was around Tensho 17, at the beginning of Minazuki.

**Land**

Even the summer sky forgot its heat, and hunters pursuing deer saw no mountains; it was heard that, starting with Yoshihiro of Taira, they had pressed their advance as far as the vicinity of [Iwase](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-iwasenomori.htm), an enemy of the neighboring provinces.

**Shite**

You, too, lead forth your horse.

**Land**

Exerting the might of dragon and tiger, they stand their ground, supporting one another.

**Shite**

However, Inawashiro Morikuni

**Land**

Since he declared his intention to side with the lord, Shigezane and Kagetsuna were dispatched. Upon hearing this, Yoshihiro broke camp that very day and hurried back into the province. Upon learning of this, the lord sent a messenger to Shigezane, inquiring if he would urge the horses forward. The two replied that as Yoshihiro was drawing near, it would not be of any consequence; since there were many enemies on all sides, there was no need to abandon the camp and venture this far. Yet, what did my lord think? He hastily made his way that night to [Mount Shinobu](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/fukushima/f-sinobuyama.htm), passing through the secret path of Shiba, across the dew-covered highlands of Akogashima, and over the mountain roads to Inawashiro, entering under the cover of midnight, yet there was no one there to know him.

**Shite**

Since dawn had already broken that night,

**Land**

On the front of Surigami, the allied forces were divided; the main camp was established away from the main camp, in the thickets of the forest at the foot of the renowned Mount Bandai on the Azuma road, with no gaps between them within the sun-bridge. Below, along the riverbank, both forces flew banners of victory, awaiting the approach of the enemy.

**Shite**

Thus, Yoshihiro, leading over three thousand cavalry, pressed forward to this plain of Surigami, where he encountered Kagetsuna Morikuni; they fought fiercely, and Shigezane and Munemi aided one another, breaking through the enemy's vanguard—

**Land**

Seeing this, Yoshihiro—seeing this—reasoned that the enemy possessed only this force; he ordered his forces to divide into two columns, push forward with the archers and cavalry, and envelop the enemy in the center to strike them down, charging forward with zeal to annihilate them all in one sweep. Just as he was making his move, from an unexpected mountainside, a banner was raised and a roar that shook heaven and earth—like the crashing of a thunderbolt—echoed, as the enemy charged straight toward Yoshihiro's main camp; and in the midst of this,

**Shite**

Chikanari Minamoto

**Location**

Tachibana no Nakatsuna was the first to plunge in, scattering the opposing forces across the hooves of his horses as he galloped forward; he pursued them in great numbers as they fought, driving them down the slope of Surigami in a straight line, some casting them aside and others lopping off their heads, driving the disordered masses here and cornering them there. By employing the secret art of "crane-wing flight," Yoshihiro's own refuge seemed to float and sink, as if leaping into the waves. Then, after that, when this lord's prestige spread far and wide—across the singing tides of Shikishima, the verdant hills of Aoba that never sway their branches, and the flourishing [Miyagino](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/miyagi/m-miyagino.htm)—

**Shite**

The spring of a thousand years, when even the plants sway—it has indeed become a blessed era.

Note) Komon-kun, Masamune Date Mutsu-no-kami, Fujiwara Munemi, Date Togoro Shigezane, Kagetsuna, Kojuro Katakura Kagetsuna, Munemi, Shiroishi Uemon Munemi, Yoshihiro, Ashiname Yoshihiro, Morikuni, Inawashiro Danjo Morikuni, Chikanari, Hiraga Izumo Chikanari, Ancestor of the author Hiraga Yoshimasa, Nakatsuna, Omachi Nakatsuna, Kurokawa Castle, Former name of Aizu-Wakamatsu Castle

## Admin's Thoughts

It's quite something how he managed to produce a piece of historical fiction about the domain founder in that era (lol). The author must have been someone who absolutely loved writing this kind of thing. It somehow makes sense that this was written by an amateur rather than a professional. Perhaps they felt hesitant to make Masamune the protagonist, or maybe they were selected because they had written the "Shigezane-ki"—either way, the protagonist is Shigezane. However, based on the text, there is absolutely no necessity for Shigezane to be the protagonist. I feel they introduced a bit too many characters and leaned too heavily into the narrative. It wouldn't be strange for any of the military commanders mentioned in the text to be the protagonist. If they wanted to glorify Masamune, I think it would have turned out cleaner if Masamune had been the protagonist, but I suppose they were just hesitant. Since Shigezane was the key figure who passed down Masamune's story to later generations, I think he was a suitable second-best choice. But because they chose Shigezane, the text of the second act probably drifted toward a "narrative" style... If they had done this (the content of the second act) via interspersed narration, and then ended the second act with text more suited for a captivating kakeri... (← I'm being too greedy!)

The procession and descriptions of famous sites in the first act feature a parade of Mutsu's utamakura, designed so that you can enjoy a trip without even leaving your seat. For Mutsu's utamakura, please refer to this site [“Ezo, Mutsu, Utamakura”](http://www7.plala.or.jp/t-aterui/). I've also included links within the main text.

The famous sites of the Sendo aren't visible from the Aizu Basin, but let's just say it would be tactless to point that out. After all, it explicitly says "crossing the mountains." I wonder if it would be wrong to meet the old man in Inawashiro, rather than on the Sendo, and then have him point out the sights as they travel... (I'm really nitpicking here (＾＾A)). Also, some might point out that since one person cannot play both the drum and the flute simultaneously, a waki-tsure should be brought in; however, since it's rare for waki-tsure to have their own lines, there may have been a proper attendant monk during the performance.

In typical productions, the later shite is a young warrior. And if there's a kogaki where they perform as an old warrior, it really gets me.

## Bonus

By the way, Katsu-shura plays are extremely rare; among the current repertoire, there are "Ebisu" and "Tamura."

"Yashima"

only the third act. Among the Taiko No plays still performed today, the Katsu-shura is only the first act, "Akechi-uchi." See:

Nohgaku Land

Nohgaku Association

Among these, "

Yashima

」is renowned as a masterpiece, but the administrator absolutely loves the closing lines. From the gripping depiction of the naval battle, the mood shifts abruptly to "What appeared to be the enemy were flocks of seagulls..."—a satisfying conclusion befitting its dreamlike reputation.

shigezane:oboegaki60.title: Kimura Uemon Memorandum 60
shigezane:oboegaki60.summary: ※Partial excerpt. Kanji and kana have been rewritten for readability.
shigezane:oboegaki60.markdown:
※Partial excerpt. Kanji and kana have been rewritten for readability.

In the historical accounts, it is recounted that because Lord Terumune was such a formidable man, Lord Nihonmatsu grew increasingly close to him, yet his final moments were so wretched they defy description. As Lord Nihonmatsu spoke of various matters, it was decided that Lord Terumune would remain safe and that Lord Nihonmatsu would visit him at the fortified residence. Since things were tumultuous at the time, it was agreed that should they return to the castle at any time and visit him, they would do so at their leisure. Thus, news suddenly arrived that Lord Nihonmatsu would visit tomorrow, and a provisional feast was arranged on our end. As we were merely residents of the residence, on the morning of Lord Nihonmatsu's visit, word came that four or five wild boars had been slain on the mountain behind us. Since there were guests outside today, it was deemed a fitting opportunity, and the resident attendants and foot soldiers prepared for a boar hunt. As we had no particular reason to slip away, we set out for the mountains with bows, spears, and firearms. Just as the attendants of Lord Nihonmatsu were beginning to find it strange, Lord Terumune and Lord Nihonmatsu were in the drawing room, deeply engrossed in conversation, speaking of how neither could possibly be absent from one another. Suddenly, a commotion broke out; the dining shelves in the kitchen—which were suspended by ropes four or five ken apart—had snapped, and the piled square plates and bowls tumbled down. The sound of a commotion reached the drawing room, and while Lord Nihonmatsu found it mysterious, the attendants grew increasingly suspicious and, believing Lord Nihonmatsu was about to return to him and be struck down midway, thought the young lord must have come out with firearms. Hearing the commotion in the kitchen, they called out to Lord Nihonmatsu, saying he had business to attend to, and whispered something to him; the attendants then stepped outside. Lord Nihonmatsu returned to the drawing room, and they immediately exchanged farewells and departed. Lord Terumune said, "Is this a hasty return? Yet there is still much remaining." He tried to detain him, but as he persisted, they had no choice but to see him to the gate; as they reached the entrance of the great hall and bowed to each other upon the raised platform, Lord Nihonmatsu's attendants locked eyes with him, seized Lord Terumune firmly, and said, "Your recent conduct has been most heartless. We shall accompany you to Nihonmatsu," and led him away. A page named Kutsuki, carrying a sword, clung to Lord Nihonmatsu's sleeve, and together they fled in great numbers, sending a swift messenger to the mountains of the hunting grounds. "How regrettable," they thought in surprise, and pursued them, only to find exactly what they had feared. Looking closer, they saw Lord Nihonmatsu gripping Lord Terumune by the chest and raising him up, thrusting his short sword against him; he was prepared to stab him to death right then and there if anyone approached. Just as everyone was drawing near, Shigezane and others rushed forward, crying, "What? What is this!" Lord Terumune looked back and said, "Unintentionally, my luck has run out, and I am powerless against my daily enemies. While you were shielding me, the territory of Nihonmatsu draws near. If you move across the river, you become my own hostage. It would be a most regrettable outcome. Cast me aside, cast me aside!" Yet, as he was a senior retainer of the clan, no one could say it was right, and they had no choice but to lead him away. They rode their horses back and forth behind him, questioning him of the details, but he gave no answer. As they drew closer to the territory of Nihonmatsu, it seemed a report had been sent, and a great number of men gathered across the river. Just as they thought the situation was hopeless, Shigezane and the clan members all mounted our horses and charged forward, saying, "There is no other way. We have no choice but to abandon him. What shall we do?" When they said, "What a wretched fate, with nothing to rely on," seeing their expressions, the Nihonmatsu men seized him firmly and, out of pity, stabbed Lord Terumune to death. The page carrying the sword clung to the corpse and died from the stab. Every single member of the Nihonmatsu party was beaten to death; furthermore, those who attempted to attack Lord Nihonmatsu were hacked to pieces, one stroke at a time. The corpse was then pierced and gathered with wisteria vines, sewn together, and hung as a banner at that spot to drive away the enemy across the river, proclaiming that the body of Lord Terumune had been recovered.

(Adapted from "Records of the Words and Deeds of Masamune Date: Memoirs of Kimura Uemon" by Yuriko Koigawa, Shinjinbutsu Oraisha, 1997)

shigezane:oomori-dateke.summary: In the "General History of Ancient and Medieval Fukushima City," Seiji Kobayashi notes that since the *Harumune-ko Sai-chi Kashi-roku* contains no mention of Marumori, where Tanemune retired, or Omori, where Sanemoto resided, Tanemune and Sanemoto held independent lordship even during Harumune's reign.
shigezane:oomori-dateke.markdown:
## The Marriage of Date Sanemoto and the Establishment of the Omori Date Clan

In "History of Fukushima City: Ancient and Medieval Periods, General History Volume," Seiji Kobayashi notes that since the "Harumune-ko Sai-chi Kashi-roku" contains no mention of Marumori, where Tanemune retired, or Omori, where Sanemoto resided, Tanemune and Sanemoto held independent lordship even during Harumune's reign. However, there is also an interpretation—while also citing the same "Harumune-ko Sai-chi Kashi-roku"—that the absence of mentions of Marumori and Omori is because these territories were direct holdings of the Date main house.

Now, the wife of Shigezane Date is said to have been Kyosei-in, the eldest daughter of his elder brother, Harumune Date (Date Family Documents, No. 10-3290). To consider the significance of this marriage, let us compare the marital status of Shigezane's brothers and Kyosei-in's sisters.

Satoshi Kuroshima argues that, given the differing political orientations of Harumune and Terumune, among Terumune's children, Kyosei-in and Masuho-hime (wife of Koyanagawa Morimune), who married into Dochu, did so at Harumune's behest, while the marriages of his younger sisters to other families were at Terumune's behest ("The Distant Date Harumune: The Gap Between Contemporary Historical Sources and Early Modern Family Genealogies," Aoyama Shigaku).

The commonality between these two is the age difference between the couple. While Koyanagawa Morimune was born in 1523 and Date Sanemoto in 1527, Kyosei-in and Masuho-hime—assuming that all of Harumune's children were born to his primary wife of the Iwaki clan—were born between 1545 and 1547. (Masuho-hime is said to be the mother of Koyanagawa Muneshige, but Muneshige himself was born in 1545.)

Sanemoto's marriage is said to have occurred around Eiroku 9 (“Kojo Meguri,” Otsuka Yakuho). If this is accepted, it would mean that Sanemoto, like his younger brothers Tessai Sosei and Kensai Socho, had not previously had a wife worthy of mention. (While records of the Tome Date clan state that Tessai Sosei was of the Kuwaori clan, there is no mention of a wife in the materials from the Date main house (Date Family Documents No. 10-3290).)

During the Muromachi and Sengoku periods, the Date clan tended to refrain from establishing branch houses. From the time the 11th head, Mochimune, established the Koyanagawa and Kakeda branches until the 17th head, Masamune, established branch houses for his sons, males other than the eldest son were either adopted or remained as *heyazumi* (resident retainers). Sanemoto, who was intended to be adopted into the Uesugi clan, maintained a certain level of *yoki* (retained cavalry)—primarily the *shu* (attendants) assigned to him for his journey to Echigo—even after remaining in the Date clan due to these circumstances. However, as long as Sanemoto remained in the Date clan, Harumune neither followed the aforementioned custom nor arranged a formal marriage for him. In other words, while Sanemoto had many *yoki*, it is believed that he was treated as *heyazumi*.

This situation began to change during Terumune's tenure as head of the clan. The transfer of leadership from Harumune to Terumune did not proceed smoothly; it is reported that it took place amid discord between father and son.

Shigemoto Date was the lord of Omori, a strategic transportation hub between Nakadori and Yonezawa, while Morimune Koyanagawa was the lord of Takahata. During the Genki Incident, in which Munetoki Nakano fell from power, Morimune Koyanagawa was reprimanded by Terumune for failing to take proactive measures to subjugate Nakano; meanwhile, Shigemoto Date, along with Harumune, became a figure relied upon by Nakano, who had sought a return to the Date clan.

This incident suggests that Shigemoto and Morimune were to some extent close to the former head, Harumune, and his regent, Munetoki Nakano, and that the marriages between the aforementioned daughter of Harumune and Shigemoto and Morimune were arranged to ensure the stability of the clan.

Indeed, records of Shigemoto's activities are concentrated during the reign of Terumune—presumably after the marriage—and Shigemoto, who had been confined to his quarters, effectively established a branch house through his marriage to Kyosei-in, marking the birth of the "Omori Date family."

## The Dissolution of the Omori Date Family

The Omori Date family, established as described above, participated in the Battle of Hitotoribashi in Tensho 13, leading 80 cavalrymen (Date Nikki). Since this figure was reached after leaving half at Shibukawa and 30 at Obama, Shigezane's forces numbered 220 cavalrymen. While the number of men remaining at their home castle, Omori, and at Sanchome—Shigemoto's retirement castle—is unknown, if 30 cavalrymen—the same number as at Obama—remained, the total would be 280 cavalrymen, or perhaps over 1,000 men as a military force.

Furthermore, in the vast province of Mutsu, the territories of daimyo typically spanned only a single district or half a district; however, as noted in the land grant document issued by Masamune to Kojuro Katakura in Tensho 14—which states, "the area south of Sugawa, held by Shigezane in recent years"—the Omori Date family held nearly the entire southern half of Shinobu District. Additionally, Hachome Castle, which Sanemoto had captured from the Hatakeyama clan in Tensho 2, became an outpost under the direct control of the Omori Date family.

With such extensive territory and considerable military strength, the Omori Date family became the most powerful faction within the Date clan and came to wield significant influence within the clan. However, having only recently branched off, the Omori Date family also suffered from a certain vulnerability. As they had only recently established themselves as a branch house, they lacked hereditary vassals; instead, their forces were composed of mounted retainers assigned by the Date main house.

For example, Haneda Umanosuke—who appeared in a Taiga drama as a senior retainer to Munemi—came from the Haneda family, a lineage granted to Sanemoto when he entered the Uesugi clan. However, he was not simply a retainer of the Omori Date family; according to the New Year's greeting diary from January 1584, he visited Masamune for New Year's greetings separately from Munemi. This suggests that he held dual allegiance to both Masamune and Munemi.

While there are records and traditions stating that Masamune's retainers went to Mount Koya to urge Shigezane to return upon his flight, there is no tradition that Shigezane's own retainers did so. Furthermore, at this time, Haneda Umanosuke became isolated within the Shigezane household; during the takeover of Kakuda, all but Haneda Umanosuke remained under the direct control of the Date main house.

In other words, when Kakuda was taken over, many of the Shigezane household's retainers naturally transitioned into retainers directly under the main house; thus, the Omori Date house was dissolved.

## Omori Castle

Omori, [Fukushima City](http://www.city.fukushima.fukushima.jp/), Fukushima Prefecture. It is now Shiroyama Park. A mountain castle located in the southwestern part of the Fukushima Basin. This mountain was apparently once called "Shinobu Mori." Shigezane resided here from birth until his transfer to Nihonmatsu in Tensho 14. During the Bunji era, the clan of Sato Shoji (the family of Sato Tsugunobu and Tadanobu, retainers of Minamoto no Yoshitsune) appears to have established a castle. Their descendants resided there until the Nanboku-cho period, and the site flourished as the administrative center of Shinobu District in Mutsu Province. Later, during the Tenbun era, the Date clan entered the area, and Date Sanemoto became the castle lord. Shigezane was Sanemoto's son. At the time, Omori served as a junction between the Sendo (Oshu Kaido), the Ushu Kaido, and the Aizu Kaido, making it a strategic transportation hub. It is said to have been the largest town in Shinobu and Date districts. The castle consists of the honmaru, the North Wing (corresponding to the ninomaru), and the South Wing (corresponding to the Hime-goten and demaru). From the foot of the mountain, there is a road leading from Minami-ote (meaning "South Main Gate") to the South Wing, and another leading from Kita-ote (North Main Gate) to the North Wing. The road from the south is relatively gentle; however, this was designed so that if an enemy ascended from this route, they could be caught in a pincer attack from the honmaru and the South Wing. A doi (earthen rampart) surrounded the castle, with the samurai residences located inside the rampart and the townhouses outside. Place names such as "Baba," "Tsubaki-kan," and "Ichi-no-gamae" remain within the inner area. Additionally, a dry moat still exists beneath the honmaru. The holdings of Sanemoto and his son Shigezane during their tenure as lords of Omori Castle were "31 villages in Shinobu District and 2 villages in Natori District." Furthermore, in the chigyo-hanmono (land grant document) issued when Kajira Kojuro was granted Omori, the area is described as "the area south of Sugawa, which Shigezane has held in recent years," suggesting that the south half of Shinobu District was roughly the area in question.

## Tsubaki-kan / Kasuga-kan

Tsubaki-kan is located in Watari, Fukushima City, Fukushima Prefecture, on Mount Benten. It sits on the opposite bank of Omori and Sugime (Fukushima), overlooking the Watari ferry. It seems to have served as an outpost for Omori Castle or as a surveillance post along the highway. Legend has it that Iwaki Hangan, the father of "Anju and Zushio," lived here—but isn't the Fukushima Basin Iwashiro rather than Iwaki? The *Nihon Jokaku Taikei* and *Sendo・Aizu Shojo no Kenkyu* describe it as "the residence of Shigezane Date." I wonder if he traveled back and forth between Omori and this place? However, there is also a place called "Tsubaki-kan" at the foot of Omori Castle. Since Omori Castle was a mountain castle, it is likely that the castle lord's residence was also located at the foot of the mountain. Because they share the same name, they may have been confused. On the other hand, the entry for Watari Village in the *Shintatsu Nigun Mura-shi* lists Tsubaki-kan and Kasuga-kan as historical sites. There are no mentions of Shigezane Date associated with Tsubaki-kan, but there is a tradition that Kasuga-kan was the residence of "Watari Awa-no-kami."

## Shibukawa Castle (Tagoya-kan / Tagoya-kan)

Shibukawa, [Adachi Town](http://www.town.adachi.fukushima.jp/), Adachi District, Fukushima Prefecture. A forward base where Shigezane was stationed during the campaign to capture Nihonmatsu. Originally a branch castle of Nihonmatsu Castle, it was abandoned following the death of Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu and occupied by Shigezane. Thereafter, it became Shigezane's own castle, serving as a branch castle of Hachichome.

"Tagoya-kan, also known as Shibukawa-kan, was the castle of Yusa Sato Uemon and his son, retainers of Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu; they surrendered to Masamune Date on May 5, Tensho 13. Later, Date Awa-no-kami Shigezane resided here. It is said that [this land](http://www.seesaa.jp/afr.pl?affiliate_id=157417&keyword=%93y%92n) still does not fly banners during the Boys' Day festival to this day, as it marks the day of surrender." (Adachi District Gazetteer)

"Shibukawa, Tagoya-kan: Yusa Shinzaemon resides here. The old records state, 'Yusa Sato Zaemon, heir Shinzaemon,' and so on. Upon examination, old records state that Yusa Tanba-no-kami and his son, Shimosa-no-kami, resided here. As Yusa's clan was particularly large, it is difficult to determine. ... Yusa Tanba-no-kami was a retainer of Hatakeyama, but after rebelling against Umeomaru and being slaughtered without exception at Minowa-kan, Date Togoro took his place and resided there." (Aioi-shu, Vol. 8; Information provided by Mr. Nozaki)

## Hachichome Castle

Matsukawa, Fukushima City. The retirement castle of Sanemoto, father of Munemi. Hachichome was originally a town that developed along the Mizuhara River—a post town of a thousand houses—but following Tanemune's development of the castle grounds, the entire town was relocated to the castle town. During Tanemune's reign, it appears to have been the residence of Horikoshi Noto.

## Ouchi Nishiyama-kan

Kita-Ide, Ouchi-Ide, Marumori Town. Said to have been Shigezane's camp during the Date-Soma conflict under Terumune. The adjacent Akikoyama Castle is said to have been Masamune's camp.

**Memorandum on the Records of Old Castles in the Sendai Domain**

Nishiyama Castle: 66 ken east-west, 60 ken north-south, 3,960 tsubo. This castle stands on the site of a temporary camp established by Date Awa Shigezane during the conflict with the (Soma) Nagato-no-kami of the (Date clan). The aforementioned Shigezane was Ito Sanemoto, the fourth son of Date Tanemune. He is the great-grandfather of the current Date Chiyomatsu.

**An'ei Fudoki Goyo-kakidashi**

Nishiyama-kan within Meigayama: height over six jo, north-south over 54 ken, east-west over 20 ken. It is recounted that during the Soma marriage arrangement in previous years, this was the camp of Date Awa, an ancestor of Lord Awa, the jito of Watari. However, both locations had since become fields and mountains.

The above is from "Castles and Residences of Marumori Town," compiled by the Marumori Town Board of Education, Miyagi Prefecture, and others (Information provided by Mr./Ms. Nozaki).

## Yorin-ji

Oda, Fukushima City. The family temple of the Date (Sanemoto) clan until their move to Watari. It houses the graves of Sanemoto and Tanemune. Tanemune's grave contains a portion of his remains. The site preserves [legends such as the Zazen Stone and the Monster Stone](http://www.bakebake.com/kaido/fukusima/kenpoku/kp02yori.htm). (Photo courtesy of Mr. Jun Nozaki. From left: Yorin-ji Temple Gate, Grave of Date Tanemune, Grave of Date Sanemoto)

[Shigezane Date's Residence and Castle](#/post/shigezane/sumai)

shigezane:ougi.markdown:
This article,

> On the Kao of the Date Clan during the Sengoku Period—Focusing on Tanemune Date > Naomasa Oishi, Bulletin of the Institute for Tohoku Culture, Tohoku Gakuin University. (No. 20) [1988.08]

Based on this, this is a discussion of the kao associated with the Date clan during the Sengoku period. Unless otherwise noted, the illustrations of the kao are taken from the aforementioned paper. It is said that imitations of kao tend to reflect respect for the individual whose kao served as the model.

## 1. The World of "Uemune's Fan Shape"

| Date Tanemune Kao Type 3 | Date Tanemune Kao Type 4 | Hosokawa Inken Kao | |---|---|---| | | | |

Date Tanemune's kao is divided into six types according to the aforementioned paper by Oishi. This entry focuses on Types 3 and 4 of these. While these are said to be modeled after the kao of Hosokawa Inken, please note the **fan shape in the upper left**. According to the paper, this kao came into use in the early Tenbun period—likely around the time he moved his residence from Yanagawa Castle to Kuwaori Nishiyama Castle—and was used until around Tenbun 14–16, during the Tenbun Disturbance.

| Date Harumune's Kao, Type 1 | Date Harumune's Kao, Type 2 | Date Harumune's Kao, Type 3 | |---|---|---| | | | |

This is the kao of Harumune, who clashed with his father, Tanemune, during the Tenbun Disturbance. The same paper identifies Type 1 and Type 2 of Harumune's kao as imitations of Type 3 and Type 4 of Tanemune's kao, categorizing them as kao of the same Hosokawa lineage. After emerging victorious in the Tenbun Disturbance, Harumune issued land grant documents to his retainers all at once on January 17, Tenbun 22 ("Harumune-ko Sai-chi Kashi-roku"), and at this time, he revised his kao. This is Harumune's Type 3 kao. What stands out in this Type 3 is the "horizon line"—a straight horizontal line drawn at the bottom. This is said to be a kao of the Kamakura Kubo and Koga Kubo lineages. From the Hosokawa style to the Koga Kubo style. The same paper discerns Harumune's resolve from this, while also drawing attention to the fan shape in the upper left. The fan shape inherited from Tanemune remains.

| Terumune Date's kao | Masakage Rusu's kao | Akimitsu Ishikawa's kao | |---|---|---| | | | |

This fan-shaped motif was further passed down to Harumune's sons. The kao of Terumune, Masakage, and Akimitsu all feature the same fan shape. However, the lower portion of Akimitsu Ishikawa's kao is said to closely resemble that of the Satake clan; this is interpreted as indicating Akimitsu's dual affiliations, as he was caught between the Satake and Date powers.

| Kao of Chikataka Iwaki | Kao of Haruuji Kurokawa | |---|---| | | |

The kao of Chikataka Iwaki, the eldest son of Harumune, appears to have something resembling a fan shape, though it is not definitive; it is said to be close to a kao unique to the Iwaki clan. Furthermore, the paper points out a similar fan shape found in the kao of Haruuji Kurokawa, a kokujin of Kurokawa District. The Kurokawa clan was situated between the two major powers, the Date and Osaki. The paper interprets their kao—which shows both their loyalty to the Date clan under their umbrella and their status as independent kokujin—as well as a kao that likens themselves to the Date clan's adoption of a successor, reflecting on the shock and impact that Haruuji Kurokawa's defection in Tensho 16 had on the Date clan.

The above is a brief summary of the fan shape seen in Tanemune's kao, drawn from the Oishi paper mentioned at the beginning. Even among Tanemune's sons, this fan shape is not seen in the kao of Sanemoto Date or Motomune Watari. The paper also examines this point, but I will introduce that discussion in a separate section.

Now, I will present another kao here.

| Kao of Soma Yoshitane | | |---|---| | | Quoted from the flyer for the Miharu Town Museum of History and Folklore's FY2012 Autumn Exhibition Project, "Tamura Gessai and His Descendants" |

This is the kao (stylized signature) of Soma Yoshitane. The eldest daughter of Date Tanemune (Yakata-gozen) married Soma Akitane. Soma Yoshitane was her grandson. After being defeated in the Tenbun Disturbance, Date Tanemune retired to Marumori and deepened his ties with the Soma clan. At the suggestion of Tanemune, who visited Odaka in 1559, Soma Yoshitane married Date Tanemune's youngest daughter (Koshigawa-gozen) the following year at the age of 12 (*Sengoku Soma Sandaiki* by Shizuo Mori). Tanemune passed away after ceding the southern part of Igu District—his own retirement domain—to the Soma clan, sparking a territorial dispute between the Date and Soma clans over Igu District. It is said that Koshigawa-gozen was divorced around this time (ibid.), but the kao of Soma Yoshitane appears to feature the "fan-shaped mark" of Tanemune. It also resembles the first and second types of Harumune's kao.

Around the time the tide of defeat in the Tenbun Disturbance grew increasingly clear, Tanemune changed his kao once again, adopting one that closely resembled that of Konoe Taneie. That fan-shaped mark was no longer visible.

| Shigezane Date's Kao, Types 5 and 6 | Konoe Taneie's Kao | |---|---| | | |

However, Soma Yoshiue used the "Date Shigezane fan-shaped kao." In Mayumi Chiba's series "The One-Eyed Dragon Masamune" in the Kahoku Shimpo Children's Newspaper, there is a scene where Soma Yoshitane addresses the spirit of Date Shigezane, who rests in Marumori Castle, saying, "We too are descendants of your blood." The kao quoted above is from a letter addressed to Tamura Gessai; while the flyer does not provide a date, it feels as though this kao expresses Soma Yoshitane's sentiments.

shigezane:rekishi-shiryou-index.markdown:
This section draws heavily on the lists provided by [“Harumaki”](http://www.katana.cx/~hrmk/) and [“Oku-Aizu Sengoku Fudoki”](http://www.geocities.jp/rockfish384/). I would like to take this opportunity to express my gratitude. There are more collections of tales and military chronicles than primary sources. Many are available online via the National Diet Library's Modern Digital Library. Listed in Japanese alphabetical order.

**Aioi-shu**

Included in the middle volume of the Iwaki Historical Materials Series

**Aizu Ashina-ki**

From the origins to the downfall of the Ashina clan. Included in [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index), Vol. 5.

**Aizu Shika Goko**

Mukai Shinbei Yoshishige, Kanbun 2 (1662). Included in the Modern Digital Library. For a modern Japanese translation, see [“The Era of the Aizu Shika Goko”](http://www17.ocn.ne.jp/~you/).

**Aizu Kassenki**

I have received a copy of the historical document. It is published in "Aizu Shiryo Sosho Vol. 3" and is included in the Modern Digital Library. See [“Oku-Aizu Sengoku Fudoki > Aizu no Sen'eki > Aizu Kassenki”](http://www.geocities.jp/rockfish384/tatakai/tatakai14.htm).

**[Ashitate Family Documents](http://px.a8.net/svt/ejp?a8mat=O6BQH+XCANM+5WS+C28PV&a8ejpredirect=http%3A%2F%2Fitem.rakuten.co.jp%2Fbook%2F1728686%2F)**

Record of the Ayugai Family of the Sendai Date Clan

**Ihoku Gunki**

Includes Masamune's campaign in Oku-Aizu. See [“Oku-Aizu Sengoku Fudoki > Aizu Campaigns”](http://www.geocities.jp/rockfish384/tatakai.htm).

**Inan Gunki**

Includes Masamune's campaign in Oku-Aizu. See [“Oku-Aizu Sengoku Fudoki > Aizu Campaigns”](http://www.geocities.jp/rockfish384/tatakai.htm).

**Inan Kassenki**

Includes Masamune's campaign in Oku-Aizu. See [“Oku-Aizu Sengoku Fudoki > Aizu Campaigns”](http://www.geocities.jp/rockfish384/tatakai.htm).

**[Goka Nenpyoroku](http://www.mars.dti.ne.jp/~h2r9m2c1/nenpyouroku-B.html)**

A chronology of the Ichinoseki Tamura family, from the first generation, Muneyoshi, to the fifth generation, Murataka.

**[Ou Eikei Gunki](http://www.mumyosha.co.jp/hist.html#gunki)**

Published by Jinbutsu Orai-sha. A military chronicle written in clear, accessible prose. It has been reprinted.

**The Military Tale of Aizu Hibara in Oshu**

The Rise and Fall of the Anazawa Clan. Includes Masamune's Battle of Hibara. See [“Oku-Aizu Sengoku Fudoki > Aizu Campaigns”](http://www.geocities.jp/rockfish384/tatakai.htm). Included in the Aizu Materials Series. Available at the Modern Digital Library.

**Oshu Kasai-ki**

Included in [Iwate Prefecture](http://www.seesaa.jp/afr.pl?affiliate_id=157417&keyword=%8A%E2%8E%E8%8C%A7) Sengoku Period Documents II

**Oshu Kasai Jikki**

Compiled by Masanobu Kasai, second son of Harunobu Kasai, in Bunroku 2. Included in *Shintei Zoho Shiseki Shuran*, Sequel 8.

**Okuso Chawaki**

A tale of Soma. Included in the second volume of the Iwaki Historical Materials Collection.

**Onko Chishinki**

Events in the Aizu-Inan region from Tensho 17 to Genroku are listed in bullet points. See [“Oku-Aizu Sengoku Fudoki > Aizu Campaigns”](http://www.geocities.jp/rockfish384/tatakai.htm).

**Kasai-Osaki Seisui-ki**

The Rise and Fall of the Kasai and Osaki Clans. Included in [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index), Vol. 7.

**Katakura Daidai-ki**

Included in the History of Shiroishi City.

**Kimura Uemon Memorandum**

Published by Shinjinbutsu Orai-sha as [Records of the Words and Deeds of Masamune Date: Kimura Uemon Memorandum](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4404024630?ie=UTF8&tag=oysannohitori-22&linkCode=as2&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4404024630). Masamune's first-person narrative is particularly intriguing. Shigezane also appears.

**Excerpts from the Records of Great-Great-Grandfather Terumune, Great-Grandfather Masamune, and Grandfather Tadamune**

**Kodan Fudenjo**

**Onagoshu**

A record of Masamune's words and deeds. Included in Volume 1 of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index). An affordable edition, recompiled by Tomio Takahashi from Hobundo, titled "Date Masamune Genkoroku — Masamune-ko Meigoshu" (http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/ASIN/4832301950/oysannohitori-22), is now available.

**Chawaki Isetsu Kaisenshu**

A lost entry from the Okuso Chawaki. Included in the second volume of the Iwaki Historical Materials Series.

**Shigezane-ki**

Written by Shigezane Date. A military chronicle spanning from Tensho 12 to Keicho 5. Included in Volume 3 of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index).

**[Jozan Kidan](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/scrpt/jgmWeb.dll?DispUrl?si=0&jp=40016167&vol=00000&koma=1&tp=0)**

A collection of tales of military prowess.

**[Jinkai-shu](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/scrpt/jgmWeb.dll?DispUrl?si=0&jp=40022584&vol=00000&koma=1&tp=0)**

Included in [“A Study of the Date-ke Jinkai-shu”](#/post/shigezane/ronbun). Laws of the Date clan.

**Shinpen Togoku-ki**

The rise and fall of the various eastern powers such as the Satake, Ashina, Date, Iwaki, and Mogami. See [“Oku-Aizu Sengoku Fudoki > The Aizu Campaigns”](http://www.geocities.jp/rockfish384/tatakai.htm).

**Shintatsu Ittoshi**

Included in Iwaki Shiryo Sosho, Vol. 1

**Izumi Tadaki**

Includes Masamune's campaign in Oku-Aizu. See [“Oku-Aizu Sengoku Fudoki > Aizu Campaigns”](http://www.geocities.jp/rockfish384/tatakai.htm).

**[Section on Treasures: Register of Sendai Family Swords (Sendai Family Sword Registry; Record of the Lineage of the Date Family Treasure Swords)](http://webarchives.tnm.jp/dlib/detail/228;jsessionid=0B74D9BD25F19E998746A2D89A332400)**

Available for viewing on the Tokyo National Museum Digital Archive.

**Sendai Kojoki**

An introduction to the ancient castles of the Sendai domain. Included in Volume 4 of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index).

**[Sendai Shikan](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/757632/1)**

By Kenzo Yano. May 1900

**[Sendai Shiryo](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/cgi-bin/img/BIImgFrame.cgi?JP_NUM=40007315&VOL_NUM=00001&KOMA=1&ITYPE=0)**

1892, Senjin Oka. Biographies of figures from the early Sendai Domain. It's debatable whether this qualifies as a historical source, but I'll include it here anyway.

**[Sendai Shiden](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/cgi-bin/img/BIImgFrame.cgi?JP_NUM=40016279&VOL_NUM=00000&KOMA=1&ITYPE=0)**

By Shozo Suzuki. Dec. 1892.

**[Biographical History of Sendai](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/scrpt/jgmWeb.dll?DispUrl?si=0&jp=40016280&vol=00000&koma=1&tp=0)**

Written by Toraiwa Dosetsu, compiled by Kiyoaki Nami and edited by Bunsuke Ashitate. Sendai Bunko Series, Vol. 4, Meiji 29.1

**Record of Retainers of the Sendai Domain**

**[Biographies of Figures of the Sendai Domain](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/cgi-bin/img/BIImgFrame.cgi?JP_NUM=53009889&VOL_NUM=00000&KOMA=1&ITYPE=0)**

Miyagi Prefecture. 1908

**[Sendai Domain Founders' Records](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/scrpt/jgmWeb.dll?DispUrl?si=0&jp=40018593&vol=00000&koma=1&tp=0)**

Written by Takedo (Kaoru) Saito, Seiundo, Nov. 1881

**[Historical Records of the Founders of the Sendai Domain](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/scrpt/jgmWeb.dll?DispUrl?si=0&jp=40018594&vol=00001&koma=1&tp=0)**

Edited by Shuji Shimo-Iizaka and Eiji Tanno, Meiji 17.8

**[Deeds of the Founder of the Sendai Domain in Honor of the Emperor](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/scrpt/jgmWeb.dll?DispUrl?si=0&jp=40018595&vol=00000&koma=1&tp=0)**

Written by Kenzo Yano, May 1899

**Sendai Bukan**

Written by Nobuyoshi Sato. A biography of Masamune. Included in Volume 3 of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index) supplement.

**Registers of Officials of Sendai Domain**

The stipends of the Sendai domain retainers are listed in alphabetical order. Included in Volume 6 of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index).

**Sendoki**

A military chronicle of the Sendo region centered on Masamune. Included in the Battles section of Volume 22, Part 2 of the *Zoku Gunsho Ruiju*.

**Date-ke Kyuki**

A transcribed copy is held at the Historiographical Institute of the University of Tokyo.

**Records of the Date Family Administration**

The official history of the Date clan. Seizan (Terumune) is included in the Jinbutsu Orai-sha Sengoku Shiryo Sosho ["Date Shiryo-shu"](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index). There are also volumes covering two generations: Seizan (Terumune) and Teizan (Masamune). The complete set was published by Hobundo. As the administrator living in the Kansai region, I scrambled to find a library that possessed this set and was willing to lend it.

**Date-ke Seshin Kafu**

Genealogical records and family rosters of the Date clan, included in the subsequent volumes of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index)

**Supplement to the Genealogy of the Date Clan Retainers**

Included in the [Sendai Series](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index) subsequent volumes

**[Brief Genealogy of the Date Clan](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/cgi-bin/img/BIImgFrame.cgi?JP_NUM=40017556&VOL_NUM=00000&KOMA=1&ITYPE=0)**

Written by Kibun Tanabe et al., Meiji 29.9 (Sendai Bunko Series; Vol. 7)

**[Biographies of the Date Clan Retainers](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/cgi-bin/img/BIImgFrame.cgi?JP_NUM=40016334&VOL_NUM=00000&KOMA=1&ITYPE=0)**

Written by Kibun Tanabe, edited by Shozo Suzuki, Sendai Sosho, Vol. 7, Sendai Sosho Publishing Association, June 1914.

**[Date-ke Seshinroku](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/cgi-bin/img/BIImgFrame.cgi?JP_NUM=40017555&VOL_NUM=00000&KOMA=1&ITYPE=0)**

Written by Hirotada Sazawa, Koun Seisha, Meiji 38

**Diary of Shigezane Date**

Included in the *Gunsho Ruiju*, Battles section. Nearly identical to the *Shigezane-ki*. A landmark historical document—the first "historical source" the administrator ever encountered. It was in the high school library.

**Date Clan Genealogical Record**

**[Study on the Genealogical Lineage of the Date Clan](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/scrpt/jgmWeb.dll?DispUrl?si=0&jp=40017557&vol=00001&koma=1&tp=0)**

Compiled by Tsunamura Date: The Official History of the Date Clan, Part 1. Sendai Bunko Series, Vol. 9

**[Study of the Genealogical Lineage of the Date Clan](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/scrpt/jgmWeb.dll?DispUrl?si=0&jp=40017558&vol=00001&koma=1&tp=0)**

Compiled by Tsunamura Date, edited by Bunsuke Ashitate and Kiyoaki Sakanami. Included in the Sendai Bunko Series, Vol. 10, and the Jinbutsu Orai-sha Sengoku Historical Materials Series ["Date Historical Materials Collection" (#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index)]. The official history of the Date clan prior to Harumune.

**[Brief Record of the Date Clan Genealogy](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/scrpt/jgmWeb.dll?DispUrl?si=0&jp=40017556&vol=00000&koma=1&tp=0)**

Written by Kibun Tanabe, supplemented by Kisei Tanabe, and further expanded by Kiyoaki Sakanami, Sept. 1894, Sendai Bunko Series, Vol. 7

**Diary of Terumune Date**

Diaries from around Terumune's circle in Tensho 2. Included in "[Date Family Documents](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index)" and "History of Fukushima Prefecture, Vol. 7."

**Date Tensho Diary**

Included in the Jinbutsu Orai-sha Sengoku Historical Materials Series ["Date Historical Materials Collection"](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index). It's interesting that the weather is recorded.

**Date Hikan**

A military chronicle of Ou centered on the Date clan. Included in Volumes 17 and 18 of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index). I wonder how much of it can be trusted.

**Date Benranshi**

Written by Dogan Sakuma. Covers the period from Asamune to Tsunamura. Included in Volume 3 of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index).

**Record of the Posthumous Memoirs of Taketoku Date**

Written by Tomonao Hori. Article on Masamune. Included in [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index), Vol. 10.

**Collected Poems of Lord Masamune Date**

Included in Volume 1 of the Sendai Sosho. A collection of poems by Masamune.

**Historical Materials on the Biography of Lord Masamune Date**

A wonderful book that compiles various historical materials in chronological order to chronicle Masamune's life. I found this one at a secondhand bookstore in Sanjo Kawaramachi, Kyoto. It was deeply moving to realize that there are others in the Kansai region who own it as well.

**Chronology of Lord Masamune Date**

Written by Dogan Sakuma. A chronology of Masamune. Included in [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index), Vol. 1.

**[Date Ryakukei](http://kindai.ndl.go.jp/scrpt/jgmWeb.dll?DispUrl?si=0&jp=40017560&vol=00000&koma=1&tp=0)**

Written by Kiyoaki Sakunami. Included in Vol. 1 of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index), Sendai Bunko Sosho, Vol. 1.

**Tamura Hyosenki**

Included in the second volume of the Iwaki Historical Materials Collection

**Too Gunki**

Included in the Battles section of Volume 22, Part 2 of the *Zoku Gunsho Ruiju*. Focuses on the Nanbu clan. Also contains entries on the Waga Uprising.

**Too Roko Monogatari**

Accounts of Sendai Castle and military affairs. Included in Volume 8 of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index).

**Togoku Taiheiki**

A military chronicle held by the Tanno family, retainers of the Watari Date clan. While the term "Togoku Taiheiki" generally refers to the work depicting the so-called "Sekigahara of the North," this volume begins with Terumune's campaign against Igu in Tensho 10 and concludes with entries from Meireki 3. The colophon reads, "Written in mid-winter of Meiji 25, Year of the Water Monkey, by Shuryo Sato." Below are the PDF files, provided with the permission of the Tanno family. Each is approximately 30MB. ・[Togoku Taiheiki Vol. 1](http://shigezane.info/majime/siryou/bunken/tougokutaiheiki/tougokutaiheiki1.pdf) ・[Togoku Taiheiki Vol. 2](http://shigezane.info/majime/siryou/bunken/tougokutaiheiki/tougokutaiheiki2.pdf) ・[Togoku Taiheiki Vol. 3](http://shigezane.info/majime/siryou/bunken/tougokutaiheiki/tougokutaiheiki3.pdf)

**Register of Family Genealogies of the Retainers of the Tome Date Clan**

**Record of Land Grants by Lord Harumune**

Included in [“A Study of the Date-ke Jinkatsu-shu”](#/post/shigezane/ronbun). It's quite an interesting historical source if you take a close look at it.

**Fujiba Seisui-ki**

A military chronicle of the Nikaido clan, lords of Sukagawa Castle. Included in the Battles section of Volume 22, Part 2 of the *Zoku Gunsho Ruiju*.

**Bujo Kanjoki**

A collection of military anecdotes. It was included after the Jozan Kidan.

**[Buhen Tokigaki](http://www.konan-wu.ac.jp/~kikuchi/buhen/buhaki.htm)**

A collection of military anecdotes. It includes the origin of the bamboo-and-sparrow crest and Usami Nagamitsu's sword. It also covers the siege of Fukushima Castle from the Uesugi perspective. (Stories 109 and 110)

**Masamune-ki**

Written by Shigezane Date. A military chronicle spanning from Tensho 12 to Keicho 5. Included in Volume 11 of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index). Also included in the Jinbutsu Orai-sha Sengoku Shiryo Sosho ["Date Shiryoshu"](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index).

**The Tale of Mogami Yoshimitsu**

A military chronicle concerning Mogami Yoshimitsu. Included in the Battles section, Volume 22, Part 2 of the *Zoku Gunsho Ruiju*.

**The Tale of Yamaguchi Dosai**

A military chronicle of Yamaguchi Dosai, a retainer of the Hatakeyama clan of Nihonmatsu. Included in Volume 3 of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index).

**Yamanouchi Tenshoki**

The Rise and Fall of the Yamanouchi Clan in Oku-Aizu. Includes Masamune's campaigns in Oku-Aizu. See [“Oku-Aizu Sengoku Fudoki > Aizu Campaigns”](http://www.geocities.jp/rockfish384/tatakai.htm).

**Roo Kikigaki**

Sendai Sosho Besshu, Vol. 3. Entries on the Katakura Family

**Rojin Denbunki**

Military accounts centered on Masamune. Included in Volume 6 of the [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index).

**Chronicle of the Waga Uprising**

Included in the Battles section of Volume 22, Part 2 of the *Zoku Gunsho Ruiju*. A military chronicle from the Nanbu clan's perspective.

**Watari Family Records**

Chronicle of the Wakuya Date (Watari) clan. Included in [Sendai Sosho](#/post/shigezane/rekishi-shiryou-index), Vol. 9.

**Brief Genealogy of the Watari Yoshin Family**

A roster of retainers of the Watari Date clan, including their biographical histories.

> Search by historical source name: Shiga Documents—Documents passed down through the Shiga family, senior retainers of the Watari Date clan. Warabi Shishido Family Documents—Documents passed down through the Shishido family, retainers of the Watari Date clan. Portions (?) have been transcribed in "Kyodo Watari No. 57."

**Aizu Historical Materials Collection**

Aizu Materials Preservation Society, 1917-1920; Hinohara Gun Monogatari (Kensuke Kikuchi); Machi Orai (Author unknown); Dogimura Nikki (Author unknown); Aizu Kassenki (Author unknown); Aizu Sooki (Author unknown); Ashina-ke Yuisho Kosho (Tadatake Sekiba); Kaihan Hennenryaku (Compiled by Anrin Shiryu Tan'en, revised by Tadajun Takeura Sato); Tsugiki-sho (Collected by Seiryu Ogawa, supplemented by Shigemasa Kikuchi); Tsugiki-sho Sakusha Burui (Compiled by Shigemasa Kikuchi); Kitai Hyakuei (Composed by Shunryu Hosokawa, revised by Shigemasa Kikuchi); Aizu Kyuji Zakko, Vols. 1-9 (Compiled by Yoshishige Mukai); Shingu Zasshoki (Naomasa Watanabe); Ennichi-ji Engi (Sanpei Miyagi); Kodairagata (Written by Setsuo Mori)

**[Aizu Jin Monogatari](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4585051163&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

Kunieda Seiken, Minoru Matsuda (Modern Japanese translation). Completed in Enpo 8 (1680). This is a version edited by Kunieda Seiken, based on a record of the events of the Aizu Campaign that Sakai Tadakatsu had ordered his subordinate, Sugihara Chikikiyo, to compile.

**[Ashitate Family Documents](http://px.a8.net/svt/ejp?a8mat=O6BQH+XCANM+5WS+C28PV&a8ejpredirect=http%3A%2F%2Fitem.rakuten.co.jp%2Fbook%2F1728686%2F)**

Record of the Ayugai Family of the Sendai Date Clan

**Iwaiwa Historical Materials Collection**

Volume 1: Shindachi Ittoshi / Fukushima-jo Soden / Okuyo Sendo Hyokan / Aizu Takako-den / Aizu Zoku Tadataka-den / Aizu Sozakura Hyokan Volume 2: Aioi-shu / Bunka Genko-nen Sen Fudoki / Asakawa Sodo Kenbunki / Hongu Minamimachi Yurai-ki Volume 3: Iwaki-shi / Iwaki Fudoki / Iwaki Daidai Keizu / Oku-ai Chawa-ki / Chawa-ki Isetsu Kaisen-shu / Too Hyoyo-ki / Tamura Heisenki / Minamoto Tada-ko Gojogyo-ki / Senzai no Matsu / Ubarin Minamoto-ko Den

**[Ou Eikei Gunki](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4895443884&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

Yoshitaka Imamura, Jinbutsu Orai-sha, June 15, 1966. A military chronicle of Ou. The writing is accessible, making it an enjoyable read.

**Commentary on the Medieval Rusu Family Documents**

Mizusawa City Library S54.3.31

**Documents Related to Kojuro Kagetsuna Katakura**

Shiroishi City Cultural Property Research Report Vol. 47, December 2013. Transcriptions and collections of documents related to Kojuro Kagetsuna Katakura, arranged in chronological order. Includes the "Katakura Daidai-ki: Kagetsuna-fu," "Gochigyo Kudasare Gocho: Kojuro Katakura," "Date Yoshin Kafu: Katakura," and "Fujiwara-sei Katakura-shi Keizu."

**Zoku Gunsho Ruiju**

Hanawa Hokiichi, Vol. 22, Part 2, Battles section: "Sendoki," "Toyo Seisui-ki," "Too Gunki," "Waga Ikki Shidai," "Mogami Yoshimitsu Monogatari"

**[Koyaroku - Bantora-shu - — Edition held by Kakuhan-ji Temple, Sendai](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4839348022&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

Written by Koya Soetsu. Kakuhan-ji Temple has transcribed the *Bantora-shu*, a collection of sayings by Priest Koya.

**[Sendai City History Materials: Masamune Date Documents](http://www.city.sendai.jp/kyouiku/museum/kankou/kankou04.html)**

Sendai City has gathered an overwhelming collection of Masamune's letters. Reading through them in detail brings a smile to your face.

**[Sendai City Museum Collection Catalog VII: Materials on Sendai Domain Retainers (Family Divisions)](http://www.city.sendai.jp/kyouiku/museum/kankou/kankou01.html)**

The Sendai City Museum catalog from March 31, 1994, is also quite interesting.

**[Sendai City Museum Catalogue 1: Materials Related to the Keicho Embassy to Europe](http://www.city.sendai.jp/kyouiku/museum/kankou/kankou01.html)**

S63.8.12

**Sendai City Museum Catalogue 3: Letters of Masamune Date**

Dec. 25, 1990

**Chronicle of the Founders of the Sendai Domain**

Saito, Chikudo. Sendai: Seiundo, Nov. 1881. Included in the Modern Digital Library.

**Historical Sites of the Founding Lords of the Sendai Domain**

Edited by Shuji Shimo-Iizaka and Eiji Tanno. Sendai: Han'emon Shiraki, August 1884. Included in the Modern Digital Library.

**Sendai Sosho**

Published in 1922. Reprinted by Hobundo in 1974. A volume that exhaustively compiles historical materials from the Sendai domain. It is divided into Main, Supplementary, and Continuation volumes. Included in the Modern Digital Library. Available materials can be found here (under preparation).

**Sendai Sosho: Supplementary Volume**

Continuation of the Sendai Sosho. Details to follow.

**[Records of the Ayugai Family of the Sendai Date Clan: Ashitate Family Documents](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4872940342&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

Written by Mitsuyuki Ashitate.

**Documents of the Ishimoda Family, Senior Retainers of the Sendai Domain**

Tosui Shobo, Feb. 1981. Documents preserved by the Ishimoda family, senior retainers of the Sendai Domain. While many relate to domain administration, several letters concerning Shigezane are also included.

**Date Family Documents: Japanese Historical Documents, Division 3, Date Family Documents. You can also access these by clicking [here](http://www.hi.u-tokyo.ac.jp/ships/shipscontroller) and searching for "Date."**

Date Family Documents No. 1 [Date Family Documents No. 2](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4130910426&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211) [Date Family Documents No. 3](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4130910434&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211) Date Family Documents No. 4 [Date Family Documents No. 5](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4130910450&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211) [Date Family Documents No. 6](http://px.a8.net/svt/ejp?a8mat=O6BQH+XCANM+5WS+C28PV&a8ejpredirect=http%3A%2F%2Fitem.rakuten.co.jp%2Fbook%2F484776%2F) [Date Family Documents No. 7](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4130910477&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211) [Date Family Documents No. 8](http://px.a8.net/svt/ejp?a8mat=O6BQH+XCANM+5WS+C28PV&a8ejpredirect=http%3A%2F%2Fitem.rakuten.co.jp%2Fbook%2F484778%2F) Date Family Documents No. 9 [Date Family Documents No. 10](http://px.a8.net/svt/ejp?a8mat=O6BQH+XCANM+5WS+C28PV&a8ejpredirect=http%3A%2F%2Fitem.rakuten.co.jp%2Fbook%2F484779%2F)

****

****

**[Historical Records of the Date Clan](http://www.konp.co.jp/publication/list/index.php?page=2&rows=19)**

Kunimune Date, Konno Printing, February 3, 2001. A family history written by the 15th head of the Sendai Date clan. Table of contents [here](#/post/shigezane/datekasisoudan).

**Catalogue of Date Family Documents**

A catalogue of historical documents held by the Date City Pioneering Museum. It was previously housed at the Prefectural Nakanoshima Library, but perhaps because it was compiled in haste, the contents seem to contain a fair number of errors. Compiled by the Date City Board of Education. A treasure trove for researching the Date family of Watari.

**Date Historical Materials Collection**

Seiji Kobayashi, Jinbutsu Orai-sha, February 15, 1967, Sengoku Historical Materials Series. Included materials: "Seizan-ko Jike Kiroku," "Masamune-ki," "Date Tensho Nikki," and "Date Shoto Seijiko."

**[Records of the Words and Deeds of Masamune Date—Notes of Uemon Kimura](http://www.amazon.co.jp/gp/product/4404024630?ie=UTF8&tag=oysannohitori-22&linkCode=as2&camp=247&creative=1211&creativeASIN=4404024630)**

Masamune's firsthand account is fascinating. Shigezane also appears.

**Shirattsuki (Complete) — Tome Date Traditions Record —**

Tome Domain Historical Materials, Vol. 2, 5,000 yen (tax included), Contact: Toyama Promotion Public Corporation Co., Ltd. (6 Sakurakoji, Teraike, Tome-machi, Tome-gun, Miyagi Prefecture 0220-52-2496), published November 25, 2004. 567 pages, A5 size.

**[Collection of Domain Law Historical Materials 〈3〉 Sendai Domain](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/redirect?link_code=as2&path=ASIN/4423780534&tag=oysannohitori-22&camp=247&creative=1211)**

Contains the "Hyojosho Kakushikicho" and nine other historical documents from the Sendai Domain (Date clan).

**History of Fukushima Prefecture, Vol. 7: Ancient and Medieval Materials**

An astonishingly vast mountain of historical materials. Primarily letters.

## Books

Shinsho books are "for general readers," and selected titles are listed here.

As stated above, following the repeated defeats of the Tamura forces, Masamune Date and Kiyoaki personally took charge; they launched a simultaneous attack on Shiomatsu from both Terumune and his son Kiyoaki, resulting in the fall of Shiomatsu Castle. Ouchi Bizen retreated and barricaded himself in Wakamatsu. Terumune succeeded in capturing Shiomatsu as he had desired, and both father and son entered it as their residence. From there, they clashed with Yoshitsugu of Nihonmatsu. In Yoshitsugu's view, since Terumune and his son possessed such formidable power, they could ultimately not prevail; nevertheless, he felt profound resentment that the lands which had served as the hereditary domain for generations had been unjustly handed over to Terumune, and that Terumune was to be treated as a mere retainer. He constantly ground his teeth in frustration. As his inner wife had a distinguished lineage with Terumune, he privately proposed a peaceful settlement, suggesting that Yoshitsugu should enter Terumune's service as a token of gratitude. However, as Masamune refused to agree, the inner wife made various representations to Terumune, and a meeting was arranged. When Yoshitsugu reached Obama without even summoning his cavalry, relying solely on his personal attendants, Terumune was particularly pleased; he provided various feasts, drank several cups of sake, and after paying his respects, stepped out to the entrance. Terumune also went out to the veranda to see him off, but Yoshitsugu, pretending to be composed, exchanged a knowing glance with a man named Kanokoda Izumi who was accompanying him; then, he seized Terumune by the collar, drew his short sword, and struck him. Kanokoda simultaneously grabbed him from behind, pulled him down from the veranda into the garden, and dragged him out by the force of his grip. Terumune's close attendants and outside samurai were so panicked that there was no way to stop him; they rushed after him and finally cornered the two men at a place called Awasu within Suzuishi Village. Meanwhile, Masamune had gone to the nearby area of Takano. Upon hearing the news suddenly, he rushed to the scene, but neither he nor his retainers could find a way to intervene and were utterly bewildered. Nihonmatsu was separated by a single river called the Abukuma River, and word of this soon reached Nihonmatsu; they dispatched their forces. Seeing this, Masamune pursued them fiercely and called out to strike Terumune and his retainers, but as expected, none of the retainers dared to intervene. However, as the situation grew urgent, Yoshitsugu stabbed Terumune to death with the short sword he had used and committed suicide with that same blade. He called out to all his elders and retainers, telling them to serve their lord, and each of them committed suicide. Masamune immediately pressed his advance toward Nihonmatsu, but a retainer named Shinjo Danjo held the castle firmly; Masamune, exasperated, withdrew to Shiomatsu.

Genna 8, final day of the month, Shiomatsu, Obama Village: Toemon (66), Genzaemon (70), Izumi (70)

1. Yoshitsugu of Nihonmatsu initially entered into an agreement with Terumune Date and his son; furthermore, as his primary wife had a lineage tracing back to Terumune, when Terumune marched on Soma, Nihonmatsu dispatched 50 mounted riders and 100 muskets as reinforcements. Gradually, the Date clan grew increasingly powerful; not only did they capture the small castles of their neighbors, but they also successfully stormed and captured the strongholds of generals numbering two or three thousand, and all eventually became retainers of the Date clan. Consequently, signs emerged that they might also move against Shiomatsu in Nihonmatsu; thus, for mutual benefit, they arranged a marriage between the daughter of Ouchi Bizen and Yoshitsugu's eldest son, Yoshifusa (Tsuna), and they became close both internally and externally. 1. The Date father and son marched against Shiomatsu on September 24, Tensho 12—38 years prior to that year—at which time Shiomatsu fell. Subsequently, the Date clan severed ties with Nihonmatsu. 1. Although Yoshitsugu passed away, a senior retainer named Shinjo Shin'an protected Yoshitsugu's wife and children until July 15 of the following year; though their provisions, bows, and muskets had all been exhausted, the wife and children safely relocated to Aizu.

(The rest is omitted)

Genna 8, Nihonmatsu: Elderly man Taian Ouchi (70), Priest Shuma (60)

shigezane:ryakureki.title: Brief Biography of Shigezane Date
shigezane:ryakureki.summary: Born in 1568 (Eiroku 11), likely at Omori Castle in Shinobu District. One year younger than Masamune. Childhood name: Tokimunemaru. Common names: Togoro, Hyobu, and Awa.
shigezane:ryakureki.markdown:
[View the "Shigezane Date Timeline" by scrolling horizontally here](https://oosawak.github.io/neo-shigezane-zanmai/nenpyou-timeline.html)

Born in 1568 (Eiroku 11), likely at Omori Castle in Shinobu District. He was one year younger than Masamune. His childhood name was Tokimunemaru. His common names were Togoro, Hyobu, and Awa. "Togoro" was the same as his father Sanemoto's common name. The "To" was derived from the Fujiwara clan. Until he left Masamune's service, he consistently went by "Togoro." In documents, he is often referred to simply as "Goro." "Hyobu" was his common name for a short period after returning to service in 1600 (Keicho 5) and before moving to Watari. Prior to moving to Watari, he had already used the name "Awa," which he continued to use until his death. These names—"Awa" and "Togoro"—became the hereditary common names of the Date clan in Watari.

Some records state that his coming-of-age ceremony took place in 1579 (Tensho 7). According to the "Tokiwa Sadaken Documents," Terumune served as his eboshi-oya, and the ceremony was held at Omori Castle. The timing of his first battle is unknown. According to one account, he presented a treasured sword during Masamune's coming-of-age ceremony. Around 1584 (Tensho 12), coinciding with Masamune's succession to the headship of the clan, Shigezane also likely became the lord of Omori Castle. He was probably around 17 years old. Since this was based on the traditional Japanese age reckoning, he would have been a second-year high school student by modern standards.

He reportedly achieved great feats in the battles of Hitotoribashi, Kotemori, Kubota, and Surigami, and is said to have described himself as "unparalleled in bravery and martial prowess." He contributed to various stratagems during Masamune's conquest of the Sendo region, distinguishing himself in both wisdom and courage. In 1586 (Tensho 14), following the capture of Nihonmatsu, he became the lord of Nihonmatsu Castle. In 1590 (Tensho 18), during Masamune's campaign in Odawara, he served as the governor of Aizu and suppressed a small-scale rebellion. Following Hideyoshi's Oshu Shioki, Masamune was transferred to Iwadeyama, and Shigezane moved with him to Kakuda. He participated in the Bunroku Campaign and crossed to Korea alongside Masamune and others. In 1595 (Bunroku 4), when Toyotomi Hidetsugu fell from power, Masamune was also suspected of complicity. At that time, he submitted a written oath signed by 19 of Masamune's senior retainers to Hideyoshi; Shigezane's name was listed second, following Ishikawa Yoshimune. Around the time of Hideyoshi's death, he fled Masamune's side. He entered Mount Koya and is said to have later lived in humble quarters in Kasuya, Sagami. Masamune confiscated Kakuda, Shigezane's castle. During this incident, retainers who resisted were killed in action.

In 1600 (Keicho 5), coinciding with the Battle of Sekigahara, the Uesugi clan of the Toyotomi faction and the Date clan of the Tokugawa faction clashed in the Ou region. During the siege of Shiroishi Castle, he returned to service at Ishikawa Akimitsu's camp. In 1602 (Keicho 7), he became the lord of Watari Castle. He participated in the Winter and Summer Campaigns of Osaka. When the Mogami clan of Yamagata was stripped of its domain, he marched out and took possession of Nobezawa Castle. This marked his final military campaign. He supervised the construction of the stone walls in the Ninomaru of Edo Castle. In his later years, he wrote biographies of Masamune. Works such as the *Shigezane-ki*, *Masamune-ki*, and *Masamune-ko Gomyogo-shu* are attributed to him. When presenting a report of gratitude to the Edo shogunal house, he was permitted to use a palanquin within the castle, where he recounted the affairs of the Ou army to Shogun Iemitsu through a bamboo screen. In 1646 (Shoho 3), he retired and passed away at the age of 79. His Buddhist dharma name was Yuzan-ji-dono Kyuzan Tensho Daikoji (he later changed the honorific title to Daiyu-ji-dono).

Death Poem: In a year rare since ancient times, even the lingering moments here were but within a dream.

He adopted Shigezane Date, the ninth son of Masamune.

He had two children, but they died young.
