shigezane:s4-sendaisisi.title: *History of Sendai City (1929 Edition)*, Vol. 1, Part 3, Biographies, Domain Retainers: Shigezane Date
shigezane:s4-sendaisisi.summary: Shigezane Date, known by the childhood names Fujigoro and Hyobu, and later as Awa, took Sanemoto, a son of Lord Tanemune, as his ancestor. His mother was a daughter of Lord Harumune. Shigezane was a man of character, possessing great wisdom and strategic acumen.
shigezane:s4-sendaisisi.markdown:
Shigezane Date, known by the childhood names Fujigoro and Hyobu, and later as Awa, traced his lineage to Sanemoto, a son of Lord Tanemune. His mother was a daughter of Lord Harumune. Shigezane was a man of exceptional wisdom and strategic brilliance, renowned as peerless in courage and martial prowess. In Tensho 13, during the Battle of Hitotoribashi, Shigezane's unit broke away from the main force and established a position while the enemy army was encircling them, achieving great merit. Lord Masamune bestowed a letter of commendation upon him. In Tensho 14, following the fall of Nihonmatsu Castle, Shigezane was granted the castle. Consequently, he held 38,000 koku across thirty villages in Adachi District. In Tensho 16, during the Battle of Koriyama, and in Tensho 17, during the various engagements at Surigami and Sukagawa, he rendered distinguished service. In Tensho 18, during the Battle of Osaki, Shigezane went out and became a hostage in the camp of Gamo Ujisato. He returned to Nihonmatsu when Ujisato departed for Kyoto. In Tensho 19, he was granted sixteen villages in Igu District and one village in Shibata, and moved to Kakuda Castle. In Bunroku 2, he participated in the Korean Campaign. In April, he accompanied the Lord to Fushimi and then proceeded to Koya in Kishu. While Shigezane's achievements surpassed those of other retainers, his rank and stipend were lower than theirs; this led to growing discontent, which culminated in this action. Masakage Rusu attempted to persuade him, but he did not listen. The Lord ordered Yashiro Kageyori to take control of Kakuda Castle, stating, "If he does not obey, strike and seize it." Over thirty men, including Shigezane's retainer Haneda Sanekage, died in battle. Later, Uesugi Kagekatsu summoned him with 50,000 koku, but he did not comply. That autumn, Lords Akimitsu, Masakage, and Kagetsuna summoned him by official order. Shigezane eventually arrived. During the Battle of Shiroishi, he stayed at Akimitsu's camp. Saito Hyobu, a general of the Uesugi clan, admiring Shigezane's reputation, led five thousand soldiers from Shinobu District and requested to join him. In Tensho 7, he was granted Watari. In Genna 1, he participated in the Battle of Osaka. In Kan'ei 15, Shigezane visited Edo on official business. He was seventy-one at the time. He entered the gates by imperial carriage and was granted meals at Chiyoda Castle. At this time, Iemitsu, discussing military affairs in the Ou region, heard him speak across the barrier and greatly praised his courage and strategy; he was granted twenty robes for formal occasions and ten outer robes. He passed away on June 4, Shoho 3, at the age of seventy-nine. His Buddhist name was Kyuzan Tensho, and he was titled Yuzan-ji. He was buried at Daiyu-ji in Kotsutsumi Village, Watari District. His death poem reads: "Since ancient times, in rare years, even the surplus of horns here existed within my dreams." (Sechizen-den, Tohan Shiko)

shigezane:sanemoto-sebyouki.title: Record of the Mausoleum of Kessan-kun
shigezane:sanemoto-sebyouki.summary: This is the epitaph for Sanemoto's grave, as recorded in the "Sendai Kinseki-shi" included in the Sendai Sosho.
shigezane:sanemoto-sebyouki.markdown:
This is the epitaph for Sanemoto's grave, as recorded in the "Sendai Kinseki-shi" included in the Sendai Sosho.

Received from Mr. Nozaki. (Reading: Musui)

---

> His name was Sanemoto. He took Date as his clan name. His childhood name was Tokimunemaru. He was already granted the title of Togoro. Sane was the fifth son of Lord Tanemune. His mother was the daughter of Taira Moritaka, the Aizu Ashina Shuri-no-daibu. He was born in a certain month of the Great Eiei 6, Year of the Fire Rabbit. In Tenbun, Year of the Water Tiger, he was sixteen years old. His maternal great-grandfather, Uesugi Sadazane, had once agreed to make him an adopted son, and thus bestowed upon him a henki (personal name). He was also granted a treasure sword cast by Nagamitsu and the bamboo-and-sparrow crest. In the sixth month of summer, the Shuri-no-daibu was dispatched to welcome him. At that time, treacherous retainers such as Kuwatori Nakano conspired to bring about disorder. When the plot was discovered, the retainers rioted; consequently, the plan was not carried out. Later, he eventually resided at Omori Castle in Shinobu, holding eleven villages and two villages in Natori. In Tensho, Year of the Wood Dog, by order of Lord Terumune, he attacked Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu and captured eight of its affiliated castles, after which he resided there. In Year of the Fire Pig, he was granted the Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, and appointed Hyobu-no-daifu, after which he retired shortly. He shaved his head and took the name Seiansai. He passed away on the 16th day of the fourth month of Year of the Fire Rabbit, at the age of sixty-one. He was buried at Yorin-ji Temple in Ogura Village, Shinobu District. The monk added the posthumous name Dokusho-in Kessan Goei Daikoji. Sane was the son of Lord Tanemune and the younger brother of Lord Harumune. His descendants held fiefs within the province for generations; thus, they were the masters who, for a hundred generations, did not deviate from the rites of propriety. However, at the time the laws of warfare were first established, they could not follow the ancient codes and prepared the rites accordingly. For several generations, they largely followed the old ways and ceased to do so. Consequently, they could not extend the system of propriety far into the future. Now, in the year of Tenpo, Year of the Fire Monkey, exactly two hundred and fifty years have passed since your passing. > Your twelfth-generation descendant, Muneyoshi, was truly devoted to the rites of honoring the ancestors and followed the path of filial piety with utmost sincerity. Thus, he consulted with his son, Munetsune, to carefully examine the rites and determine the propriety of the times. They selected a site beside the ancestral grave and established a shrine. At appropriate times, they gathered the clan members to piously perform the rites, ensuring that they never fell into decline, so as not to bring shame upon their lineage and to avoid being counted among the descendants. I record this matter to be passed down to my descendants. Alas, the path of honoring the ancestors and filial piety is such that those who lead the way are the ancestors; thus, the return of public virtue is inevitable. This is the foundation of state administration and the source of social transformation. May I not fail to do so? shigezane:sanemoto-sendaishiryou.title: Biography of Shigezane Date from the Sendai Shiryo
shigezane:sanemoto-sendaishiryou.summary: Shigezane Date. Sixth son of Lord Naoyama (Tanemune). Mother: daughter of Ashina Moritaka. In Tenbun 11, just as he was about to depart for Echigo to be taken under the care of the Uesugi clan, he encountered Nakano Hitachi, who was plotting against him; the two lords, Naoyama Hozan (Harumune) and his son, exploited the rift between them.
shigezane:sanemoto-sendaishiryou.markdown:
Shigezane Date. Sixth son of Lord Naoyama (Tanemune). Mother: daughter of Ashina Moritaka. In Tenbun 11, just as he was about to depart for Echigo to be taken under the care of the Uesugi clan, he encountered Nakano Hitachi, who plotted against him; Lord Naoyama Hozan (Harumune) and his son created a rift between them. On June 20, the followers took up positions at Nishiyama; Shigezane, supporting Lord Naoyama, went into battle and lost the initiative. He retreated to Date-Yanagawa. Ultimately, unable to reach Kamakura, he wandered with a few retainers. At this time, Endo Oki, lord of Omori Castle in Shinobu, and Horikoshi Noto, lord of Hachichome Castle, spoke together, saying, "Shigezane is wandering and has no home. He is most pitiful. Let us join forces to aid him." The two lords welcomed Shigezane, and for about half a year, he stayed with both households. Oki preferred bravery and had no wife or concubines. He indulged in wine (?) and lived dissolutely, and people did not follow him. However, Shigezane was of noble lineage and loved others with benevolence. Many people jokingly thought they would support Shigezane. Upon hearing this, Shigezane felt it was indeed a worthy cause. Some said, "I survive by the grace of Oki. I do not wish to become his subordinate." Retainers such as Uchizaki Uma-no-kami, Endo Suruga, Haneda Uma-no-suke, Endo Shimotsuke, Mayanagi Naga■, Funasako Shinza, Ibano Totomi, Ushizaka Sado, Kayaba Hizen, and Hishinuma Ise conspired with the Oki retainers. Oki's close retainer, Genzo, seized his sword and broke free while Oki lay drunk. Ibano Totomi was skilled in the use of the naginata. The others entered first. Oki, holding a secondary sword hanging from a pillar, rose to block them. Totomi was wounded in the chest and fled with two swords. Oki's strength was unmatched by his enemies; taking advantage of the night, he fled to Soma. Through this, he seized Omori. Noto was greatly enraged and refused all communication. Shigezane's influence grew stronger by the day. Hachichome also returned to Shigezane. Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu, at Yonihonmatsu Castle, gave his sister to Shigezane as a wife. Subsequently, Lord Naoyama and his son reconciled. Upon the death of his wife from the Hatakeyama clan, Lord Hozan desired a harmonious household and gave his daughter to Shigezane. In Eiroku 11, Shigezane gave birth to Shigezane. In Tensho 11, Shigezane grew old at Hachichome Castle and took the name Seian. Shigezane, aged 16, succeeded him. He passed away on the 16th day of Tensho 15. He was buried at Yoan-ji in Omori, aged 61.

shigezane:sanriku-jishin.title: 1611 Keicho Sanriku Earthquake
shigezane:sanriku-jishin.summary: March 11, 2011, the Great East Japan Earthquake. It was known that M7-class major earthquakes occur along the Pacific coast of the Tohoku region roughly every 30–40 years.
shigezane:sanriku-jishin.cover_alt: Illustration of the Keicho Sanriku Earthquake
shigezane:sanriku-jishin.markdown:
March 11, 2011: The Great East Japan Earthquake. It was known that M7-class major earthquakes occur along the Pacific coast of the Tohoku region roughly every 30–40 years. The 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake was a trench-type earthquake caused by the Pacific and North American plates, but the rupture that began in Sanriku propagated several hundred kilometers southward, causing immense damage.

In the past, the Jogan tsunami was known as a large-scale tsunami earthquake; the 2011 disaster struck just as disaster prevention plans based on this knowledge were about to be formulated.

Now, it seems relatively little is known that, even during the era of **Masamune Date**, there was a similar major tsunami earthquake—the Keicho Sanriku Earthquake and Keicho Sanriku Tsunami—which this site covers. I had read the articles myself, but I had hardly given it much thought.

October 28, Keicho 16 (December 2, 1611). Masamune (aged 45) was in Sendai.

## Course of the 1611 Keicho Sanriku Earthquake

- A series of earthquakes began in the morning. The mainshock occurred around 10:00 a.m. The seismic intensity was reportedly around 4, with 2–3 in Otsuchi; no records of earthquake damage have been found. A tsunami struck at 8:00 p.m. ([Central Disaster Management Council](http://www.bousai.go.jp/jishin/chubou/kyoukun/rep/1896-meiji-sanrikuJISHINTSUNAMI/1896-meiji-sanrikuJISHINTSUNAMI_05_chap1.pdf))

## Damage from the 1611 Keicho Sanriku Earthquake

- Many Ainu drowned on the southeastern coast of Hokkaido ([Aomori Prefecture Disaster Prevention Website](http://www.bousai.pref.aomori.jp/jisinsouran/ippan/ye1600/p00016.html))
- Nanbu and Tsugaru: "Over 3,000 laypeople, horses, etc., by the seashore drowned, or so it is said" (Teizan-ko Jike Kiroku)
- 50 people drowned in Imaizumi (Rikuzentakata City), and most houses were swept away. ([Japan Meteorological Agency](http://www.jma-net.go.jp/sendai/jishin-kazan/higai.htm))
- 800 deaths in Usumi and Otsuchi, 50 in Funakoshi, and 330 in Yamada, Tsugaruishi, and Miyako ([Central Disaster Management Council](http://www.bousai.go.jp/jishin/chubou/kyoukun/rep/1896-meiji-sanrikuJISHINTSUNAMI/1896-meiji-sanrikuJISHINTSUNAMI_05_chap1.pdf))
- In Miyako, too, every single house was swept away by the waves. ([Japan Meteorological Agency](http://www.jma-net.go.jp/sendai/jishin-kazan/higai.htm))
- Sendai Domain territory: "1,783 people drowned, and 85 cattle and horses drowned" (Teizan-ko Jika Kiroku), "Upon descending to the villages, not a single house remained" (ibid., separate entry)
- Soma Domain: "Approximately 700 people died in the tsunami" (Soma Domain Century, [according to a Fukushima Minpo article](http://www.minpo.jp/pub/topics/jishin2011/2011/04/post_921.html))

## Tsunami inundation area of the 1611 Keicho Sanriku Earthquake

The entry for November 30, Keicho 16, in the Jike Records, contains a description from which the location reached by this tsunami can be inferred. It states that while at sea, an earthquake occurred and the person was swept away by the tsunami, eventually washing ashore along with their boat at "Sengan-matsu."

According to a footnote, "Sengan-matsu"—the site where the boat is said to have washed ashore and been moored—is a pine grove in the mountains of Sengan Village, Natori District. "Sengan-matsu" was reportedly a pine grove at the summit of Mount Sengan (the mountain behind Greenpia Iwanuma, elevation approx. 180m) and served as a navigational landmark. The southern end of the mountain, on the Abukuma River side, is quite steep. Perhaps the boat washed ashore even among the pines at the foot of the mountain.

One of the origins of the place name "Iwanuma" is described in the *Miyagi-ken Chimei-ko* as follows: "Izumida Aki Shigemitsu, a retainer of the Date clan, built a castle on this site and named it 'Ugasaki Castle.' The moats surrounding this castle formed 'marshes,' and since there were ten such marshes, a section of the castle and the marshes together were reportedly called 'Iwanuma'" ([Iwanuma City Chamber of Commerce and Industry](http://iwanuma.in-shoko.com/shiru/mukashi.html#3)). Indeed, topographic maps show that the Iwanuma city area is somewhat low-lying. It is believed that the Keicho tsunami crossed this low-lying area and reached at least the 5-meter elevation line at the foot of the mountains.

A simulation of the inundation extent of the Jogan tsunami is featured in "Reconstructing the Giant Tsunami Seen by People of the Heian Period—The Jogan Tsunami of 869 AD," published in the annual report [“AFERC NEWS No.16”](https://selectra.jp/sites/selectra.jp/files/pdf/no16.pdf) (September 2010) of the Active Fault and Earthquake Research Center, National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (p. 9, Figs. 12, 13). While fine details cannot be discerned due to the scale, it appears that areas with an elevation of approximately 10 meters or less were inundated.

Regarding the geological records of the Keicho Sanriku earthquake, there have been reports of sand layers atop the Towada tephra; however, because these layers are thin, it seems difficult to trace correlations across a wide area. (As a layperson, I am also curious as to why they are so thin.) [Regional Variations in Run-up Heights during the Great Sanriku Tsunami](http://sakuya.ed.shizuoka.ac.jp/rzisin/kaishi_24/HE24_041_048_03HatoriSanriku090409.pdf) mentions the tsunami reaching Kasumeme in Wakabayashi Ward, and Namiwake Shrine in Kasumeme, Wakabayashi Ward, also preserves traditions of both the Jogan and Keicho tsunamis. During the Great East Japan Earthquake, the Sendai Eastern Road—constructed with embankments—served as a seawall, and tsunami damage was relatively minor west of the Eastern Road, including Kasumeme Airfield. However, water reached as far as the vicinity of Kasumeme Airfield. ↓ Click for photo.

[Great East Japan Earthquake, near Kasumenome, Wakabayashi Ward, Sendai City. Photo: Asia Air Survey Co., Ltd.](http://www.ajiko.co.jp/bousai/touhoku2011/_GYO1702-kasuminome.jpg)

If the records of the family archives are to be believed, then even during the Keicho Sanriku earthquake—as with the Jogan earthquake—it is reasonable to assume that areas in Sendai Bay with an elevation of approximately 5 meters or less, and in some places even 10 meters, were certainly inundated.

While the History of Watari Town mentions only Iwanuma regarding the Keicho tsunami, tsunami damage occurred across a wide area stretching from the southeastern coast of Hokkaido to Minamisoma ([Japan Meteorological Agency](http://www.jma-net.go.jp/sendai/jishin-kazan/higai.htm)). The report from the National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology mentioned above also contains descriptions of sand layers suggesting this, but the conclusion is that detecting such layers over a wide area is difficult, making it impossible to determine which specific sand layer is responsible. Geologically, several tsunami events have been observed prior to the Jogan earthquake, with major tsunamis occurring at intervals of 400 to 800 years.

Looking at the historical sites, one notices that they are concentrated in the hilly areas rather than in the more accessible plains. In Watari, this includes not only the Kotsutsumi Castle ruins, but also the Sanjusangen-do Kanga site and Jingu-ji. The Higashi Kaido, the main highway prior to the Edo period, also runs considerably further inland compared to the Edo-hama Kaido. In this area, besides military and political reasons, the impact of floods, storm surges, and tsunamis may also have been significant. (Prior to the early modern period, all rivers in the plains were prone to flooding.) Even today, looking at topographic maps of the Watari area, one can see that farmland is relatively abundant up to about 1 km from the coastline; I suspect this is because the terrain is primarily sandy.

## The 1611 Keicho Sanriku Earthquake and the Early Sendai Domain

In Wakabayashi, near Kasumeme—an area that likely suffered flooding even during the Keicho tsunami—Masamune established his residence in his later years. The era in which Masamune lived was likewise a time of frequent earthquakes (even eruptions in Karita and Zao occurred).

- November 1608: Earthquake and tsunami in Sendai
- October 1611: Keicho Sanriku Earthquake
- July 1616: Major earthquake and massive tsunami in Sendai. Stone walls collapsed.
- 1627: Major earthquake in Iwaki and Katta districts. Permission to build Wakabayashi Castle granted the same year.
- November 1628: Wakabayashi Castle completed
- October 1633: Great Earthquake
- May 1636: Death of Masamune
- March 1646: Major earthquake. Sendai Castle stone walls collapse.

While the presence and scale of the tsunami remain unknown, one cannot help but wonder how Masamune managed to establish Wakabayashi Castle under such circumstances. However, Wakabayashi Castle sits atop a natural levee and is at a higher elevation than Kasumeme Airfield (Kasumeme Airfield = 5m, Wakabayashi Castle = 10m). The nearby [Tomizuka Kofun](http://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%81%A0%E8%A6%8B%E5%A1%9A%E5%8F%A4%E5%A2%B3) is a Kofun-period site that has remained well-preserved despite repeated earthquakes and tsunamis. Alternatively, Masamune may have judged that the tsunami would not reach this far and viewed the site as part of a redevelopment effort.

According to the *History of Sendai City (Heisei Edition)*, Early Modern Period I, the development of new fields in tsunami-affected areas began during the Shoho era, 30 years after the Keicho Sanriku Earthquake. (It is unclear whether there were fields there prior to that.) Furthermore, according to local tradition recorded in "[Sendai Temple and Shrine Tour](http://www3.plala.or.jp/gameticket/32takasago.html#tsurumaki-okada)," the Okada district of Miyagino Ward "suffered severe damage from the great tsunami caused by the earthquake of December, Keicho 16 (1611), which reportedly reached as far as the vicinity of Arai, but was revitalized through the Sendai Domain's encouragement of new field reclamation from the Genna era (1615–) through the Kan'ei era (until 1644)." It also states, "During the Genna era, a domain retainer named Yoshida Gonroku Shigetomo held a stipend of over 800 koku here; he encouraged the reclamation of wasteland, opening over 700 koku of paddy fields and coming to hold a total stipend of 1,500 koku. Subsequently, through the Kan'ei era, the reclamation of fields in Okada and Niihama also flourished" ([http://www.stks.city.sendai.jp/sgks/WebPages/miyaginoku/13/13-05-06.htm#rekisi](http://www.stks.city.sendai.jp/sgks/WebPages/miyaginoku/13/13-05-06.htm#rekisi)). At this time, survivors of the Keicho Sanriku Earthquake should still have been alive, but perhaps because the imperative of increasing food production took priority, the development of new fields in low-lying coastal wetlands and the subsequent establishment of new villages were actively pursued.

## Tsunami-Related Historical Sites and Tradition Sites in the Sendai Plain

- Namifuki Shrine (Kasumeme, Wakabayashi Ward): Legend has it that the tsunami stopped here during the Keicho Sanriku Earthquake. The current Namifuki Shrine is said to have been moved approximately 500 meters inland.
- Takoyakushi (Taihaku-ku Nagamachi 4-chome). According to local historian Yukiyoshi Iinuma, this is the location where both an octopus and Yakushi Nyorai were washed ashore during the Keicho tsunami [(Kahoku Shimpo, April 5, 2011, evening edition)](http://www.kahoku.co.jp/news/2011/04/20110405t13050.htm). (However, there appear to be various theories regarding its origin.) The elevation here is also 5–10 m. It is further from the coastline than Wakabayashi Castle.
- Towada tephra was detected in the southern outer ditch of the Sendai-Koriyama Government Office Site. The presence of a Jogan tsunami sand layer beneath it remains unconfirmed.
- Gamo Nenbutsu-da Jizo-son (Gamo Nenbutsu-da, Miyagino Ward): When Okada and Gamo were submerged in seawater for eight days following the great tsunami caused by the earthquake of December, Keicho 16 (1611), the residents gathered on the eastern plateau (present-day Aza Nenbutsu-da) to chant Nenbutsu and pray to the gods and Buddhas for the seawater to recede. To commemorate how the waters finally receded thanks to this divine blessing, a Jizo statue was later erected at this site where the Nenbutsu had been chanted (from [Sendai Temple and Shrine Tour](http://www3.plala.or.jp/gameticket/32takasago.html#gamou jizo-son)).

## Records of the Teizan-ko Family: Entry for October 28, Keicho 16

Shortly after the hour of the Snake, a great earthquake struck the domain and a tsunami struck. 1,783 people drowned in the domain, and 85 cattle and horses drowned.

## Teizan-ko Jike Kiroku, Entry for November 30, Keicho 16

The Lord presented the first cod to the Great Deity. Lord Honda Uenosuke Masazumi was granted an audience. Furthermore, it was reported that a tsunami had struck Masamune's territory, resulting in 50 drownings. Goto Shozaburo further reported that at the time the tsunami was expected, he had instructed two retainers of the Masamune house to procure fish; when the fishermen set out in their boats, they said, "Today the color of the tide is unfavorable and the weather is also poor; it is not the time to set sail." Consequently, one of the two replied, "Indeed," and did not go, while the other said, "To fail to follow my lord's orders would be to deceive him," and summoned six or seven fishermen and set sail. After rowing out for several dozen cho, a great wave suddenly arose. Nevertheless, the boat remained afloat on the waves and did not sink. The fishermen reached the mountains near their dwellings. There, they tied the boat to a pine tree—a pine known as the Sengan-matsu. After the waves receded, the boat was caught in the treetops. When the fishermen descended to the village, not a single house remained; the retainers who had stayed behind and the other fishermen all drowned.

(Omitted)

At that time, it is said that over 3,000 coastal laypeople, horses, and men from Nanbu, Tsugaru, and other areas also drowned.

This account is recorded from this volume of political records. The so-called Sengan-matsu is not a single pine tree. Thousands of trees stand in a row from the foot of the mountain to the summit. Eventually, this became the name of the mountain. It is located in Natori District. Since the banks of the Aikuma River are nearby, the ripples of the sea tide flow into this river and overflow; perhaps boats were once moored to the pines at the foot of the mountain. Tradition says that in ancient times, boats were moored to the cedars atop this mountain. Today, those old cedars still remain.

Footnote) Sengan-matsu: Pine stumps arranged in rows along the mountain ridge in the Sengan area of present-day Iwanuma Town, Natori District. They served as a landmark for maritime navigation, and it is said that boatmen considered their existence to be worth a thousand kan, hence the name Sengan-matsu.

shigezane:sanuma.summary: The Battle of Sanuma was one of the engagements fought during the Osaki-Kasai Uprising, which broke out between Tensho 18 and Tensho 19.
shigezane:sanuma.markdown:
The Battle of Sanuma was one of the engagements fought during the Osaki-Kasai Uprising, which broke out between Tensho 18 and Tensho 19.

On June 27, Tensho 19, the Date forces began their advance toward Sanuma Castle. On the 28th, they ordered a siege. Masamune's main camp was on Sunagoyama, a hill west of Sanuma Castle; Oniba Tsunamoto's camp was between the marsh and the river; and Kagetsuna Katakura's camp was to the east. An informative monument marking Shigezane's camp now stands on the grounds of Sanuma Junior High School. According to records such as the "Kimura Uemon Memorandum," Shigezane appears to have served as the commander of the main assault alongside Harada Munetoki.

View [Battle of Sanuma](https://maps.google.co.jp/maps/ms?msid=205399149311139861661.0004c981b68fe8d3f208e&msa=0&hl=ja&brcurrent=3,0x5f893e3cbff0183f:0x63c6f89be1058522,0&ie=UTF8&t=m&ll=38.696262,141.189079&spn=0.011723,0.018239&z=15&source=embed) on a larger map

The castle held out through the 28th and 29th, but during the general assault on July 1, all areas except the inner bailey were abandoned. On July 3, Harada Munetoki and Goto Nobuyasu scaled the inner bailey's gateposts and stone walls to break through the gate, and at the hour of the Tiger, the full force stormed inside. There were over 500 rebels and more than 2,000 peasants and others within the castle, all of whom were slaughtered.

While the massacre of 800 people during the Battle of Kotemori is well-known as a massacre carried out by Masamune, the Battle of Sanuma also saw a massacre on a scale of 2,000 people.

shigezane:sendaishiryou-1.title: Biography of Shigezane from the Sendai Shiryo: Shigezane Date Retreats to Takano (Vol. 2)
shigezane:sendaishiryou-1.summary: ※The original text is in Classical Chinese, but the administrator has provided a reading version. ※Parts where characters were blurred and unreadable have been marked with ■. Please bear with me, as I will correct them once they are deciphered.
shigezane:sendaishiryou-1.markdown:
※ The original text is in Classical Chinese, but the administrator has provided a reading version. ※ Some characters were too blurred to read and have been marked with ■. Please bear with me—I will correct them once they are deciphered.

Lord Nagon built a castle at Iwadeyama. Shigezane Date was granted Kakuda. Following the laws of the Toyotomi clan, the marquises and counts of the lineage all resided in Osaka. Shigezane retained Uchizaki Uma-no-kami, Haneda Uma-no-suke, and Endo Shuke to guard Kakuda. Haneda and Endo made an agreement and took turns heading west. Uma-no-kami decided the affairs of the domain. A certain samurai, leading his wife and twenty retainers, lived as a wanderer. He petitioned for inclusion in the civil registry. Enraged by the samurai's presumption, Uma-no-suke confiscated his assets and banished him. The samurai reached Iwadeyama and presented his petition. Yashiro Kageyu personally interrogated him. The samurai said, "My assets were confiscated, and I have come to this place as a beggar." He then summoned Uma-no-suke to press him on his reasoning. Kageyu said, "Your son has become the head of the house, yet he is ignorant of propriety. Is this why you have come to this state?" He then returned the confiscated assets. Uma-no-suke was filled with shame. The crowd further asked, "With what face do you stand above others?" Uma-no-suke left after leaving a letter. His father, Koyuki, was over eighty years old. Greatly shocked, he went to the capital and appeared before Shigezane, saying, "This wretched son shall have the head of the old retainer severed." Shigezane comforted and admonished him, saying, "Uma-no-suke knows Kuwashima Manki. He will surely reside in that house. Manki is the veterinarian of the Tokugawa clan. Invite him and return this son. Do not let this cause you concern." He sent a messenger to return him. At this time, Shigezane returned from Korea and lost his wife, of the Watari clan. He did not enter the domain. Lord Nagon said, "The fief has been reduced; it is not as it was yesterday." He informed Shoko and Kagetsuna of this and plotted the matter. Uma-no-suke came from Edo to meet him. In private conversation, he said, "Manki will report your poverty to Lord Tokugawa." The Lord said, "Though Shigezane is young, his martial prowess is unparalleled; for the sake of the domain, he subsists on a mere twenty or thirty thousand koku, which is lamentable. If he serves me, I shall grant him one hundred thousand koku." Hearing this, Shigezane was greatly pleased. Uma-no-suke said, "This matter must be plotted without fail. I shall travel east, enter the domain, secure a residence, assign a stipend, collect funds, and send them to you to cover these expenses." They agreed on a date, and upon arriving, he praised Shigezane's intentions and collected funds from all directions. Subsequently, Shigezane fled to Koya. He sent a messenger to notify Uma-no-suke. Endo Shuke learned of this and secretly reported it. Lord Nagon praised his loyalty and said, "This matter must not be initiated by me." He observed Shigezane's movements and ordered Yashiro Kageyu to make this prisoner. Upon receiving news that Uma-no-suke had fled to Koya, he feigned great shock. Shuke took a letter and threw it in his face. He exposed the conspiracy and publicly rebuked him for misleading his lord. He reported the matter to Iwadeyama. Kageyu ordered Marumori, Koya, and Iki to attack Uma-no-suke. Uchizaki Uma-no-kami, Endo Shuke, Aoki Bizen, Sasa Gohei, Yusa Kurado-no-kami, Kondo Shichihei, Ishikawa Yahei, Shiranezawa Tanba, Koya Kurado, Takahashi Shinano, Suzuki Ma■, Kurosawa Shizunai, Henmi Hayato, Otosuke-jo Kawamura Mago-u, Koyanagawa Jinnai, Endo Yoichi, and Uma-no-suke surrounded the residence. Uma-no-suke committed suicide with his wife. His mother, younger brother Genshichi (13), eldest son Tomizawa ■ (19), and second son Takamori Hikoshichi were entrusted to him. Wearing military attire and holding a cross-spear, he stepped out into the garden. He clashed spears with Ishikawa Yahei. Yahei's spear broke. Shiga Sanza fired a cannon from atop the wall. It pierced both thighs and ■ him. Shigezane was in Koya, awaiting news of Uma-no-suke. Shigezane sat there. Koka lived as a wanderer in all directions. Aoki Tota, Shiga Yashichi, Haneda Kokichi, Sugiyama Kuza, Tokiwa Hayato, and Oka Hanbei accompanied him.

shigezane:sendaishiryou-2.title: Biography of Shigezane from the Sendai Shiryo: Shigezane Date Expresses Gratitude (Vol. 2)
shigezane:sendaishiryou-2.summary: ※The original text is in Classical Chinese, but the administrator has provided a reading version. ※Parts where characters were blurred and unreadable have been marked with ■. Please bear with me, as I will correct them once they are deciphered.
shigezane:sendaishiryou-2.markdown:
※ The original text is in Classical Chinese, but the administrator has provided a reading version. ※ Some characters were too blurred to read and have been marked with ■. Please bear with me—I will correct them once they are deciphered.

In the 14th year of Kan'ei, a great flood struck the domain. In the 15th year, the shogunate granted 5,000 kan of silver. Shigezane journeyed west to express his gratitude. He entered ■ on May 27. He was 71 years old at the time. He proceeded to the second gate and was escorted. Sayhei Kiyono and Kuradosuke Tokiwa accompanied him. He informed the two Naito Gaiki that he was permitted to assist the elder in entering the palace. Sanshu Sakai, Mameshu Matsudaira, and Toyoshu Abe appeared and offered their heartfelt consolation. The Shogun conveyed his intentions. Tea was served at the resting place. As the assembled nobles were not awaiting a formal ceremony, they were granted water, utensils, and meals. Tajima Yagyu and Naito Gaiki sat in attendance. When the meal ended, tea was served. The three gentlemen—Sakai, Yagyu, and Naito—said, "We wish to hear of the strategic details of the battles fought in the interior in former times; we request that you discuss those broad outlines." Daring to ask if their aged bodies could be troubled, Shigezane replied, "Five or seven days' worth of wartime accounts cannot possibly be fully recounted. I request that we speak of only fragments of them." He then explained the two battles of Hongu and Hitotoribashi. The assembly all clapped their hands and praised him. The requests continued unabated. He then explained the battle of Surigami-hara at Inawashiro, saying, "Ashina Morishige led a great army, departed from the main castle, and took up a position at Surigami-hara. Upon engaging the enemy, he moved. Fearing the ferocity of our army, he retreated and took refuge at the foot of the forest. After suffering a great defeat, he returned to the main castle. He and a dozen or so retainers fled, shielding themselves from the snowfall. Our army immediately made the main castle its headquarters." The assembly all marveled at his prowess and forgot their weariness. By imperial decree, he was granted twenty layers of curtains and ten overcoats. The elders rose to escort him. Gaiki and Tajima escorted him to the outer palace and reported, "His Highness is within the inner screens of the palace. He personally wishes to hear the accounts of the wartime experiences of his son."

shigezane:sendaishiryou-3.title: Biography of Shigezane from the Sendai Shiryo: Shigezane Date (Volume 2)
shigezane:sendaishiryou-3.summary: ※The original text is in Classical Chinese, but the administrator has provided a reading version. ※Parts where characters were blurred and unreadable have been marked with ■. Please bear with me, as I will correct them once they are deciphered.
shigezane:sendaishiryou-3.markdown:
※ The original text is in Classical Chinese, but the administrator has provided a reading version. ※ Some characters were too blurred to read and have been marked with ■. Please bear with me—I will correct them once they are deciphered.

In April of Tensho 16, Lord Nagon Hatakeyama was defeated. Nihonmatsu Castle was granted to Shigezane, who held a fief of 38,000 koku. In June, Satake Yoshishige, along with the Ashina, Iwaki, and Ishikawa clans, invaded with 14,000 troops. Lord Nagon, upon seeing them, stationed 600 cavalry at Fukuhara and deployed his generals. Shigezane said, "There is a plain north of Kubota. We shall engage the enemy there." Komori Shigezane held his ground firmly and did not advance. Suspecting the enemy's strategy, they retreated. Shigezane dug a pond and built two layers of ramparts. The next day, he expanded them to a height of 8 shaku. He surrounded the area with palisades, making it like a fortress. The enemy, seeing it, regarded it as a divine fortress. In front of the ramparts were rice fields. Soldiers from Aizu—Okuma and Inaba—led 300 troops and used the ditches as paths. Shigezane ordered his skilled archers to shoot at them. Inaba was wounded and retreated. The enemy built two forts between the mountains of Kubota and Koriyama, cutting off all reinforcement routes. The Lord ordered a fort to be established at the Kubota River to resist them, and had the generals draw lots to assign guard duties. Kagetsuna Katakura and Muneaki Tamura were assigned guard duty. Kagetsuna requested to engage in battle with Shigezane. The various units spoke among themselves, saying, "Two heroes are clashing; surely something will be achieved." Shigezane said, "If we cannot initiate a battle and the reinforcement routes are blocked, Koriyama is in grave danger. We must fight. Shall we simply sit and watch the days pass? Are we not cowardly?" Kagetsuna replied, "The enemy's numbers are far superior. We must not fight rashly." The enemy general, Shinkoku Sadamichi, passed in front of the ramparts with over 100 cavalry. Shigezane rejoiced greatly and said, "The opportunity has arrived!" He dispatched Fujiza Katakura to pursue them. Fujiza pushed deep into the enemy lines and was in great peril. Two generals emerged to reinforce him. The two ramparts raised their troops and came out to fight. Eventually, they defeated the enemy. They advanced, broke through two palisades, and took over 200 heads. The four clans finally found themselves unable to fight and requested a peace settlement and withdrawal. On this day, the forces faced off at Koriyama. In September of Tensho 19, Lord Nagon was transferred to Iwateyama. He was granted Kakuda Castle and 16 villages in Igu. In Bunroku 2, he participated in the Korean Campaign and returned in triumph. Shortly thereafter, an incident occurred involving the Kanpaku Hidetsugu. Ishida Mitsunari slandered the Lord and accused him of being a tyrant. The Kanpaku was greatly incensed. The Lord was filled with anxiety and fear. Shigezane hurried to the Lord's side and personally explained his innocence. He said, "Hesitation has delayed us, and the opportunity has already passed. Should the unexpected happen, I, your retainer, shall defend this castle with the generals and soldiers, resist the Western Army, and die in battle." The Lord then departed for the west, and no incident occurred. In Tensho 3, he remained at the Fushimi residence. In Tensho 4, for certain reasons, he left Fushimi and went to Mount Koya. He dispatched Komori Sessai, Ishikawa Akimitsu, Kuwaori Tenryo, and Arisaka Tanba to repeatedly admonish him, but he would not respond. Eventually, his whereabouts became unknown. Later, he resided in Kasuya Village, Soshu. Lord Tosho granted him 100 units of rice. When various lords visited to pay their respects, he did not respond. During the Battle of Sekigahara, Uesugi Kagekatsu summoned him with a fief of 50,000 koku. Sessai, Akimitsu, and Kagetsuna sent people to reason with him from all angles. Only then did he return. The Lord waited for him, treated him with great generosity, and granted him 100 units of rice. In October of Tensho 7, he was granted Watari Castle. In May of Genna 1, he achieved merit during the Siege of Osaka. In Tensho 14, floods struck the Kitakami and Abukuma regions. The water in the plains reached a depth of 5 jo. Rice fields and huts were all swept away. The Shogunate granted him 5,000 kan of silver. Lord Gizan (Tadamune) granted Shigezane an audience to express his gratitude. He was 71 years old at the time. The Shogunate specially waited for him and, as a mark of respect, granted him food and drink from the senior councilors. They inquired about military affairs. Shigezane was eloquent and clear, responding fluently. From troop movements, formations, and camp setups to combat, strategy, and victory or defeat—everything was laid out before him. Those who heard it praised him. Across the palisades, the Shogun heard the news. He looked to his left and right. In recognition of his great virtue, he was granted 10 sets of formal attire and two overcoats. He bowed in gratitude and departed. The senior councilors rose to see him off. He was permitted to use the palanquin within the camp gates. In Tensho 20, his fief was increased. He held 20,000 koku. Shigezane desired few children and was stingy with his wife and concubines; thus, he had no children. He adopted Lord Nagon's ninth son, Munezane, as his heir.

(※Brief biographies of Munemi and his successors omitted)

Shigezane joined the army at the age of 13. He attacked the Soma clan and fought valiantly. For nine years, he served in the army and fought, achieving feats unmatched by any other. However, Ishikawa Akimitsu and Takamori Sessai held higher ranks and stipends than he did. His spirit was utterly unsatisfied. He thus fled to Mount Koya. The Lord Nagon dispatched Kuwaori Tenryo and Arisaka Tanba to persuade him from all sides. Shigezane remained obstinate and would not yield. Consequently, Haneda Uma was dispatched to lead the Kakuda family ■ in an attempt to flee to Dewa. The Lord declared, "This plot is nothing more than serving Lord Toyotomi and claiming to be my equal." He ordered Iwateyama Rusuyashiro Kageyu to attack Kakuda Castle. Thus, 2,000 soldiers and officers launched an assault. Uma, along with Ishikawa Yahei, Iba Kojiro, and over 100 others—including Endo, Kanazawa, Uchizaki, Shiranezawa, Kayaba, and Ushizaka—repelled them. All claimed they would not bring shame upon their lord's name through cowardice; they fought fiercely and died without yielding. Thirty men remained; they closed the castle and killed 30 women of their own accord, then cast off their armor and helmets to commit suicide. These men—both Jitsumoto and Shigezane, father and son—had devoted themselves to military loyalty. They ■ the house and lived off their stipends. All were included in the letters of commendation issued by the Lord Nagon and his son. Yet, in a single morning, they met this tragedy. The people all viewed this as a wrong. Upon hearing of this, Shigezane was greatly incensed and retired to Shimogori in Odawara. Upon hearing this, Lord Tosho granted him a stipend of 100 koku. The Lord informed Lord Tosho that he wished to cease this. Later, as years passed, Ishikawa, Takamori, Rusu, and Katakura—the four clans—persuaded him from all sides. Shigezane's anger subsided somewhat, and he eventually declined the invitation of the Uesugi clan and returned. In Keicho 5, he joined the Ishikawa clan and fought at Shiroishi and Fukushima. The Lord again granted him special treatment. He was granted 30,000 koku in Watari District (Eikei Gunki).

shigezane:sendaishiryou-4.title: Biography of Shigezane from the Sendai Shiryo: Shigezane Date (Volume 2)
shigezane:sendaishiryou-4.summary: ※The original text is in Classical Chinese, but the administrator has provided a reading version. ※Parts where characters were blurred and unreadable have been marked with ■. Please bear with me, as I will correct them once they are deciphered.
shigezane:sendaishiryou-4.markdown:
※ The original text is in Classical Chinese, but the administrator has provided a reading version. ※ Some characters were too blurred to read and have been marked with ■. Please bear with me—I will correct them once they are deciphered.

Shigezane Date, courtesy name Togoro, was known as Awa. He was the son of Hyobu-no-daifu Sanemoto. His mother was the daughter of Lord Hoyama (Harumune). He possessed great courage and strategic acumen. In Tensho 13, Ouchi Sadatsuna rebelled. The Lord, Nagon, sought to attack Aizu to seize its stronghold. He had a certain Hirata invite Shibano Danjo, a retainer of the Ashina clan, to surrender. Danjo, unable to decide the matter on his own, leaked the information and fled. Shigezane said, "My retainer, Haneda Sanekage, has an old acquaintance with Inawashiro Morikuni, Ishibe Shimosa. I shall have Morikuni join our cause." The Lord had Sanekage invite Morikuni to surrender. Morikuni's son, Moritane, disagreed, and the plan did not come to fruition. Shigezane said, "Aizu cannot yet be attacked." He first requested that Sadatsuna be removed. He then invited Aoki Shuri, a retainer of Sadatsuna, to serve as a guide and attacked Kotemori Castle. Aizu and Nihonmatsu dispatched troops to reinforce them, and the enemy was unable to break through. Shigezane said, "I shall emerge from behind the castle and cut off the supply lines."

shigezane:sendaishiryou-5.title: Excerpt from Sendai Shiryo: Old Documents of Kuninari Date
shigezane:sendaishiryou-5.summary: Shigezane Date received the family estate in Tensho 11. He ceded the estate of Seizan-ko (Terumune) to Nagon-ko. October 8, Year 13. He attacked Nagon-ko Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu, avenging an ingratitude that had gone unrewarded.
shigezane:sendaishiryou-5.markdown:
Shigezane Date received the family estate in Tensho 11. He ceded the family estate of Seizan-ko (Terumune) to Nagon-ko. On October 8, Tensho 13, he attacked Nagon-ko Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu, avenging an insult he had suffered. He advanced to plot against Nihonmatsu. In July of Tensho 14, at the request of Soma Yoshitane, he released the castle garrison. Shigezane was granted Nihonmatsu Castle and held 33 villages. Kagetsuna Katakura moved to Omori, holding a castle for the first time. In Tensho 19, at Iwadeyama Castle, Nagon-ko granted Shigezane 17 villages in Igu District and 1 village in Shibata District. He built a castle in Kakuda. The Toyotomi clan decreed that all members of the marquessate lineage reside in Osaka. Shigezane led his family and headed west. In Bunroku 4, Shigezane fell out with Nagon-ko and fled to Mount Koya. He was 28 years old. Aoki Tota, Shiga Yashichi, Tokiwa Hayato, Haneda Kokichi, Sugimura Kuza, Oka Hanbei, Oka Kyuichi, and Ogata Oribe accompanied him. He plotted to enter service through Asano Danjo-shin and Shindo Hiko-u. Danjo approved this. On August 18, Keicho 3, Lord Toyotomi passed away. Okubo Tadanari, a retainer, and Shirahata Yoshiu's younger brother, Sobei, plotted to serve the Tokugawa clan. Upon meeting Nagon-ko's daughter, who married the Shosho of Echigo, things did not go well. Tadanari was welcomed to Odawara and took up residence at a temple in Kasuya-go. In April of Keicho 5, Naoe Kanetsugu and Yusa Sato-u were dispatched to request Shigezane as their adopted son. Tadanari departed Odawara in secret; Tadanari was greatly surprised and, having been denied entry, left the castle. Forced by circumstances, he took up residence in Ota. Ishikawa Akimitsu and Kagetsuna Katakura, following Nagon-ko's instructions, dispatched envoys to bring him back. Tadanari welcomed Shigezane, presented him with armor, and gave his retainer Tokiwa Hayato a golden robe. Ishikawa Yoshimune arrived in Ota and welcomed him into Kakuda. On July 23, he appeared before Nagon-ko at the Shiroishi military camp. He was 33 years old. He was granted a fief of 100 koku. In Keicho 7, he was granted 20 villages in Watari District. Droughts occurred year after year. In Keicho 15, he requested a land survey and was further granted 200 kan of new land. In Shoho 2, at age 78, he requested retirement and established a hermitage in the new land, though it was not yet completed. On June 4, Keicho 3, he died of illness.

shigezane:sesindenki-narumi.title: Biography of Shigezane Date from the Date Yoshin Denki
shigezane:sesindenki-narumi.summary: Shigezane Date Fujiwara, initially known as Togoro, was the legitimate son of Hyobu-daifu Sanemoto. His mother was the daughter of Lord Harumune, the 15th head of the house. A member of the house's clan (the house's noble lineage; since ancient times, there has been no designation of "clan" other than that of the single house).
shigezane:sesindenki-narumi.markdown:
Shigezane Date, also known as Fujigoro, was the eldest son of Hyobu-daifu Sanemoto. His mother was the daughter of Lord Harumune, the 15th head of the house. He was a member of the house's clan (the house's noble lineage; since ancient times, it had held the title of "Ichimon," and no separate "clan" designation existed. It was not until the time of Lord Masamune that the title of "Ichimon" was first decreed, distinguishing them as a distinct family line). He was a man of great talent, decisiveness, and ambition—an unparalleled and valiant general. During the reign of the 17th head, Lord Masamune, he achieved military distinction in the Aizu-Sendo campaign and various other engagements. He initially resided at Omori Castle in Shinobu District. After the fall of Nihonmatsu Castle, he was granted Nihonmatsu Castle and relocated there, later moving to Kakuda Castle in Igu District. The details of his conduct are not recorded with precision. Based solely on the accounts in the family records, on the 17th day of the 11th month of Tensho 13 (Year of the Wood Rooster), during the Battle of Hitotoribashi, Shigezane led over 1,000 soldiers and took up a position on a small hill by the roadside between Takakura and Hongu. The enemy approaching from Takakura headed toward Shigezane's camp. In front of the camp was a slightly elevated area. When the Naiki of Shimo-Koriyama mounted his horse and looked out, he saw the banners of three men—Munemi Shiroishi, Kagetaka Hamada, and Chikakane Takano—with approximately 6–7 riders and 140–150 foot soldiers galloping from the direction of Takakura. Subsequently, a larger force pressed forward. Suspecting their identity, he fired his musket about one cho away. Thinking this was the boundary between friend and foe, he turned his horse back and called out, "The enemy is coming! Quickly raise your banners!" All the men raised their banners and waited for one another. The three men rushed into Shigezane's camp and immediately charged through the main camp. At this time, the battle at Hitotoribashi in front of the Kannon-do was in progress. Consequently, the Naiki turned back to Shigezane's camp and said, "The enemy has cut through the gap between the forces at the Kannon-do and ours. Retreat immediately!" He then drew a banner from his horse and handed it to the foot soldiers. Hearing this, Shigezane said, "Even if we retreat, we are certain to be killed in battle. We shall fight to the death here," and remained his ground, issuing orders to his soldiers to again raise the banner and wait. The enemy soon pressed forward to the foot of the mountain. They engaged in a fierce battle, pursuing and being pursued, fighting several rounds. A retainer, Ibano Totomi, a 73-year-old man of great strength, was eventually killed in action. Once the battle at the Kannon-do ended and the enemy withdrew, Shigezane also withdrew his troops. The Lord also received a written commendation praising Shigezane's actions today—that he had fought between two great armies, separated by the main camp, and yet had not been defeated, a feat unheard of and unparalleled in previous generations. On the first day of the first month of Tensho 14 (Year of the Fire Dog), the Nihonmatsu forces came to Shigezane's camp at Shibukawa and fought; over 260 heads were taken. On the 23rd day of the third month of Tensho 16 (Year of the Dog), a consultation regarding Kusatori took place at Tamai, Shigezane's territory. Shigezane pursued the enemy to a place called ■Wada and fought a battle; the leader, Takatama Taro Saemon Yoshinao, was wounded by a musket, and a man named Ota Shuzen was also killed in action. The head of Tamai Hyuga was taken, and over 150 heads were captured.

shigezane:sesinkahu-narumi.title: Biography of Shigezane from the Date Family Genealogy
shigezane:sesinkahu-narumi.summary: ※The original text is in Classical Chinese, but the administrator has provided a reading version.
shigezane:sesinkahu-narumi.markdown:
※ The original text is in Classical Chinese, but the administrator has provided a reading version.

Shigezane, son of Sanemoto (originally named Fujigoro, later known as Hyobu). In the 13th year of Tensho, during the reign of Lord Teizan, Ouchi Bizen Sadatsuna, lord of Shiomatsu Castle, rebelled. Shigezane conspired with the Lord to attack him. In the winter of that year, three generals—Aizu Morioki, Satake Yoshishige, and Iwaki Tsunetaka—camped together in front of the Sendo Honmyo. When the Lord formed his battle lines, Shigezane broke away from the group and positioned himself among the fierce enemy troops. Already in a perilous situation, he fought valiantly and achieved great military merit. This is known as the Battle of Hitotori Bridge. In the 14th year, Nihonmatsu Castle fell. Shigezane moved there and held it. He governed Nihonmatsu in Adachi District and 8-chome 33-mura in Shinobu District. In the 6th month of the 16th year, Satake Yoshishige and Aizu Yoshihiro camped in Iwadeyama. From then until the 18th year, he achieved several military merits. In the 6th month of the 17th year, the Lord fought Aizu Ashina Heishiro Yoshihiro at Surigami-ue; Yoshihiro was defeated and fled to Shirakawa. Consequently, the Lord moved his castle to Aizu Kurokawa. In the 18th year, the Lord had an audience with Kanpaku Hideyoshi at Odawara. He appointed Shigezane as the caretaker of Kurokawa Castle. That year, the Osaki-Kasai Uprising broke out. Gamo Hida-no-kami Ujisato and Asano Danjo Shohitsu Nagayoshi attacked it. The Lord served as their vanguard. Someone within the Lord's circle slandered Ujisato; Ujisato became suspicious and placed Shigezane under his command, stationing him in Ujisato's camp. Ujisato pursued him to the capital and escorted him back to Nihonmatsu, where Shigezane finally returned. In the 9th month of the 19th year, when the Lord moved to Iwadeyama Castle (having previously been in Yonezawa), he was granted 16 villages in Igu District and moved to Kakuda Castle. In the 2nd year of Bunroku, he participated in the Korean campaigns. Upon returning to Japan, he resided at the Fushimi residence. In the 4th year, due to certain circumstances, Shigezane left the Fushimi residence and retired to Mount Koya in Kishu. Masakage Rusu, Ishikawa Akimitsu, and others dispatched Kuwaori Tenryosai and Arisaka Tanba to repeatedly urge him to return, but he would not listen. Consequently, he ordered his senior retainer, Hata Umasuke Sanekage, to have Shigezane's retainers leave Kakuda. Shigezane's whereabouts were unknown. The Lord then ordered Yashiro Kanageyu Hyoe Kagenori (then the castellan of Iwadeyama Castle) to have Shigezane's retainers leave Kakuda, stating that if they did not obey, he would be struck down. Kagenori led troops to Kakuda. Sanekage took refuge in his own residence and resisted. More than 30 people died. Shigezane fled, overwhelmed by the authority of Kagenori. It is said that Kagenori eventually seized Kakuda Castle. Later, Shigezane retired to Soshu Odawara-koya Village. He was granted 100 *koku* of rice (some say 10,000 *koku*) by the Tosho-byo (Emperor Ieyasu). The Lord appealed against this, and thus the matter was settled. In the 5th year of Keicho, during the Battle of Sekigahara, Uesugi Kagekatsu, with 50,000 *koku* (some say 300,000 *koku*), invited Shigezane to join him, intending to pit him against the Lord. Shigezane declined and did not accept. In the 7th month of that year, Ishikawa Akimitsu, Masakage Rusu, Katakura Kagetsuna, and others persuaded him to return. It was in this month that Shigezane had an audience with the Lord. There was the Battle of Shiroishi. Acting on orders, he belonged to the army of Ishikawa Akimitsu. At this time, he was granted 100 *koku* of rice. In the 3rd month of the 6th year, the Lord received a [letter](#/post/shigezane/1120) and ordered Shigezane and Watari Mino Shigemune to command the troops under their authority. In the 12th month of the 7th year, the Lord again received a [letter](#/post/shigezane/1199) and granted him Watari Castle (the former castle of Katakura Bitchu Kagetsuna). He moved there the following year. In the 6th month of the 11th year, the Lord's first daughter (known as Gorohachi-hime) married Echigo Shosho Tadateru. Acting on orders, Shigezane escorted her and had an audience at the Taitoku-byo (Emperor Hidetada). He was granted a sword (Kunimitsu) and seasonal attire from the shogunal court. In the 5th month of the 1st year of Genna, he participated in the Osaka Campaign; acting on orders, he commanded the firearms unit (Tosho-koshi-gumi) and captured 7 heads. In the 5th month of the 2nd year, the heir (known as Gizan-ko) received a letter. In this month, Shigezane presented horse medicine and books on horsemanship. In the 9th month of the 3rd year, acting on orders, he was in charge of the heir's wedding. Three days after the wedding, he accompanied the heir to the residence of Bizen Saisho Terumasa-kyo. Terumasa-kyo granted him a sword. In this month, the Lord and the heir had an audience with the Shogunal House upon the completion of the wedding. Shigezane accompanied them. He had audiences at the Taitoku-byo (Emperor Hidetada) and the Daiyu-byo (Emperor Iemitsu) and was granted seasonal attire (some say 10 *kosode* and 2 *haori*). In the 5th month of the 5th year, the Lord attended repairs at Edo Castle and sent an envoy to Edo in his stead (at this time, Ojo Saneyori assisted him, along with several others). At this time, he was granted five layers of *kabuta*. In the 6th month, Shigezane and Saneyori accompanied the heir to an audience with the Shogunal court. The court granted them courteous words of gratitude. In the 9th month, the Lord received a personal letter and fish. In the 11th month, he had an audience with the Shogunal court and was granted seasonal attire. In the 2nd month of the 7th year, he was ordered to send an envoy to Edo (prior to this, the Shogunal House had granted him Shirokane; thus, the Lord sent Shigezane to express his gratitude. It is not yet clear whether Shigezane actually departed). In the 9th month of the 8th year, he witnessed the fall of the Mogami clan. Leading 600 men, he seized the residence of the Nobezawa clan. In the 5th year of Kan'ei, he was granted an additional 2,000 *koku* of rice (10 villages within Uta District). In the 1st month of the 10th year, through Ichibo-dazen Muneyori, he presented a document recording the number of troops and horses, stating there were approximately 1,169 infantry and 155 horses. In the 2nd month of the 11th year, the Lord hosted him at a villa in Wakabayashi. Shigezane requested the Lord to let him pick flowers, cutting narcissus and long plum blossoms, and presenting them in short lengths. The Lord recited that the mountain alum was his younger brother and the plum was his elder brother, and cut the narcissus into short lengths. He then took the plum blossoms, cut them long, and inserted them as flowers. There was also a Noh performance. The Lord granted him 10 *koku* of seasonal attire and 1 *koku* of nightwear. Shigezane presented one black horse, 100 *tan* of white cotton, and 30 pieces of boardwork. That night, Shigezane's residence caught fire and was completely destroyed. The Lord received a letter and had a study constructed. (The family tradition says that on the day of the banquet, a miracle occurred. During the time of Kanzan, Shigezane acted on orders to record the event. It is said that thereafter, the Lord also recounted what he had heard). In the 14th year of Kan'ei, during the reign of Gizan-ko (Tadamune), the domain suffered from flooding. The Shogunal House granted 5,000 *kanme* of Shirokane, which was distributed. In the 5th month of the following year, Shigezane, on behalf of the retainers, sent an envoy to Edo to express gratitude. He was 71 years old at the time; the Shogunal House treated him with particular kindness, seating the senior officials and providing him with a meal. After the event, the senior officials requested to discuss the battles in the military. After several moments, everyone praised him. The Shogunal House granted him 20 *koku* of seasonal attire and 10 *haori*. Shigezane expressed his gratitude and was about to depart. The senior officials rose and escorted him a few steps. On this day, the Shogunal court (Daiyu-byo) wished to hear the news. They heard it through a screen and praised him deeply. In the 2nd month of the 3rd year of Shoho, he announced his old age. Shigezane achieved numerous military merits, which are too numerous to list. The details are clear in the *Masamune-ki* (a record of the battles of Lord Teizan, later presented for Lord Kanzan's review) written by Shigezane himself. Prior to this, during the Tensho era, he achieved the greatest merit at the Battle of Hitotori Bridge. The Lord received a letter and expressed his appreciation. In the 7th month of the 14th year, he was granted Nihonmatsu Castle (prior to this, he had been granted Omori Castle in Date District; it is said that Omori Castle was later granted to Katakura Kojuro Kagetsuna). His stipend was 38,000 *koku*. In the 12th month of the 10th year, the Lord received a [personal letter](#/post/shigezane/1199) granting him a residence in Watari District (located over 7 *ri* from the capital), and granting him mountains, fields, and beaches (estimated at about 180 *koku*), leaving the remaining land as surplus (said not to be included in the main stipend). Shigezane earnestly requested that his main stipend of 108 *koku* be paid to the government and that the surplus land be included in his main stipend, requesting a vermilion seal. The Lord ordered him, "Do not dare refuse." Shigezane requested again, "How shall future generations of descendants prove this and preserve the grace of my Lord? I humbly request that it be as previously requested." The Lord granted the request. Accordingly, Shigezane presented a sword (Usami Nagamitsu) to express his gratitude. In the 5th year of Kan'ei, he was granted another 2,000 *koku* of new land (located over 13 *ri* from the capital). He was also granted mountains and fields (estimated at 16 *koku* and 5 *to*), which became surplus land. In the 1st month of the 2nd year of Jokyo, during the reign of Lord Kanzan, he paid the surplus land (from the Watari and Uta districts) to the government. Shigezane's grandson, Shigeuji, grieved this and sent a detailed petition to the government. Upon the death of the heir of Katayama (Lord Kanzan's first son, Sencho-kun, who died prematurely on August 23, Jokyo 2, at the age of 5; his Buddhist name was Katayama Genkyu Korin-in, and he was buried at Zuisei-ji Temple in Shirokane, Edo), the request was not fulfilled. In the 20th year of Kan'ei, during the reign of Gizan-ko, his rice holdings were increased, and surplus land from the tax boundaries was added, bringing his total stipend to 20,000 *koku*. Shigezane had previously studied the Tenryu swordsmanship under his retainer Arakawa Hyuga Shushu and mastered the art. It is said that the number of gifts Shigezane received was too numerous to list. (Lord Teizan once hosted a tea ceremony for Shigezane. The Lord said to Shigezane, "It is difficult for an old man to use porcelain; I shall give you fine tea utensils." Later, he searched the back storehouses of Iwaki Bunrin for tea utensils and had a certain Sasa Wakasa grant them to him. Shigezane firmly declined, saying, "The treasures of the back storehouses are not something my retainer should touch." Wakasa responded, "I shall present several precious items for your use," and added, "I, Shigezane, am of the same age as you. Our talents in martial prowess and bravery are equally matched. Why should I monopolize the wealth and nobility without sharing them? Let us share the treasures; this is my wish. Do not refuse." Afterward, the Lord attended a tea ceremony hosted by Shigezane. In the 12th month, the Lord visited the tea room and used the tea utensils he had first granted. Shigezane presented a prized horse worth 100 gold pieces and 30 pieces of Shirokane, to express his gratitude for the lord's grace. After Shigezane's death, his son, Munezane, presented those tea utensils and a sword to Gizan-ko. The sword was a relic of Lord Teizan, which he had been granted by Gizan-ko.) Shigezane had no children and adopted the 9th son of Lord Teizan as his heir.

shigezane:sesinndenki-sanemoto.title: Biography of Date Sanemoto from the Date Kasei Shinden
shigezane:sesinndenki-sanemoto.summary: Date Hyobu-no-tasuke Fujiwara Sanemoto was the third son of Tanemune, the 14th head of the house. His mother was the daughter of Ashina Shuri-no-daibu Taira Moritaka, lord of Aizu. During the Tenbun era, his maternal great-grandfather, Fujiwara Sadazane, lord of Echigo and Hyogo-no-kami, left no heir.
shigezane:sesinndenki-sanemoto.markdown:
Shigezane Date, known as Fujiwara Sanemoto, was the third son of the 14th head of the house, Tanemune. His mother was the daughter of Ashina Shuri-no-daibu Taira Moritaka, the lord of Aizu. During the Tenbun era, his maternal great-grandfather, Fujiwara Sadazane—the lord of Echigo and Hyogo-no-kami—left no heir. Consequently, arrangements were made for an adopted heir. He was granted the character "Sane" and presented with the tachi of Usami Nagamitsu, a treasure passed down in the family, as well as banners (feathered bamboo and sparrow crests). However, these arrangements were ultimately not realized. He held 31 villages in Shinobu District and 2 villages in Natori District of Oshu, residing in Omori Castle in Shinobu District. In the early Tensho era, by order of the 16th head, Terumune, he attacked and captured the Hachichome branch castle of Hatakeyama Shuri-no-daibu Minamoto Yoshitsugu, the lord of Nihonmatsu. Thereafter, he ceded the house to his eldest son, Fujigoro Shigezane, and retired to Hachichome Castle, where he took Buddhist vows and took the name Seiansai. At this time, through the strategic planning of Seiansai, the borders of Nihonmatsu remained peaceful and free from conflict. The reason was that while Nihonmatsu Yoshitsugu had aided the Ouchi, he had originally aligned himself with the powerful and relied on their strength; thus, given the strength of this house's archers and spears, he intended to seek peace. Furthermore, Seiansai reasoned: "The reinforcements moving from the Aizu Sendo to Shiomatsu cannot easily pass through Tamura as it is enemy territory; they must travel via the lands of Nihonmatsu. If I am cordial toward Yoshitsugu, those reinforcements will not suspect him and will be unable to pass." Accordingly, he treated Yoshitsugu with particular kindness. This matter was secretly reported to the lord, but not to his son, Shigezane. He was merely told that if this border were to go to war, it would cause trouble, and he was required to swear an oath twice. Alas, though he was a capable general possessing both wisdom and courage, his deeds were not fully passed down. Through the few records that remain, one can only glimpse a glimpse of his bravery and intellect. He passed away on the 16th day of the 4th month of Tensho 15, the year of the Fire Pig. He was 61 years old, and his Buddhist name was Kessan Eigo Dokusho-in.

shigezane:shigezaneki-1.title: 1. Lord Terumune's successive generations..
shigezane:shigezaneki-1.summary: Throughout the generations of Lord Ikki Mune, those of Satake, Aizu, Iwaki, and Ishikawa have all maintained a half-hearted relationship, and things have remained in this state. The aforementioned have, for several years, launched arrows at Tamura, leaving Lord Kiyoaki at his wit's end.
shigezane:shigezaneki-1.markdown:
1. Throughout the successive generations of Lord Terumune, the Satake, Aizu, Iwaki, and Ishikawa clans all maintained a half-hearted relationship with him, and affairs remained stagnant. Each of these clans had spent several years firing arrows at Tamura, leaving Lord Kiyoaki at his wit's end. Although he was Lord Masamune's father-in-law, as it was the era of Lord Terumune, there was no other recourse. However, in October of Tensho 12, when Lord Masamune succeeded to the lordship, messengers arrived from various quarters bearing congratulatory gifts. Among them were the lord of Shiomatsu and Ouchi Bizen; upon hearing that the Ouchi clan had relied on the Date clan for generations, Lord Masamune declared that since this had not been the case in recent years, they should henceforth reside permanently in Yonezawa. The Ouchi clan replied, "We are deeply grateful for your kindness," and stated, "Since our parents' generation, we have served you; however, in recent years, regarding the affairs of the Date domain, we have relied on Tamura. Because a minor matter has offended your grace, we subsequently relied on the Aizu and Satake clans, and have sustained our livelihoods through their patronage. Therefore, from this moment forward, we shall reside permanently in Yonezawa and serve you; we request to be granted a residence and for my wife and children to relocate." Accordingly, they spent the winter of that year in Yonezawa.

shigezane:shigezaneki-10.summary: On the 25th, he conducted a reconnaissance of Iwakado, surveying the terrain; it was decided that if he were to attack from nearby or seize the area, the route to Nihonmatsu would become obstructed, and that he should move elsewhere the following day; upon this decision, he returned to Kurokago.
shigezane:shigezaneki-10.markdown:
> 1. On the 25th, he conducted a reconnaissance of Iwakado, surveying the terrain; it was decided that if he were to attack from nearby or seize the area, the route to Nihonmatsu would become obstructed, and that he should move elsewhere tomorrow; upon this deliberation, he returned to Kurokago.

shigezane:shigezaneki-11.title: 1. The supporters in Obama..
shigezane:shigezaneki-11.summary: At Kohama, those seeking assistance consulted one another, stating, "If the Iwakado is taken, it should not be removed." The men from Aizu advised Ouchi Bizen, saying, "Today, Lord Masamune has viewed the Iwakado."
shigezane:shigezaneki-11.markdown:
> 1. Regarding the consultation among the relief forces in Obama, > they stated, "Should Iwakado be taken, it should not be removed." > When the men of Aizu advised Ouchi Bizen, > they said, "Today, Lord Masamune viewed Iwakado. It is evident that he intends to take that castle." > In response, > "Since it should not be removed under any circumstances, it should be removed tonight. In Aizu, the site formerly held by Matsumoto Tosho-no-suke is now vacant; please have it handed over and delivered to the senior retainers of Aizu." > As this was proposed, they strongly advised that it be removed, and sent Nakame Shikibu and Hirata Owari to urge the matter; Ouchi Bizen, valuing the route, had no remaining castles in Obama and removed it to Nihonmatsu that night, and the Shiomatsu portion was handed over.

shigezane:shigezaneki-12.title: 1. On the 26th of the same month……
shigezane:shigezaneki-12.summary: On the 26th day of the month, as Lord Masamune was transferring his horse to Obama Castle, Nihonmatsu Yoshitsugu conveyed the following message to our lord Shigezane: "Though we have relied on the Date clan for generations and stood by them, in recent years, Aizu, Satake, Iwaki, and Tamura have turned their bows and arrows against us."
shigezane:shigezaneki-12.markdown:
> 1. On the 26th of the same month, when Lord Masamune moved his horses to Obama Castle, Nihonmatsu Yoshitsugu conveyed the following request to our Chikazane Moto: > "For generations, we have relied on the Date and maintained friendly relations, yet in recent years, Aizu, Satake, Iwaki, and Tamura have directed their arrows against us. We also harbor resentment toward Lord Kiyoaki and wish to seek the alliance of Aizu and Satake. We request that you join us at the same castle and, until the final outcome, place Lord Terumune at your disposal. > When the arrows are directed toward Soma, we intend to visit your camp twice and render our service; we ask that you treat us without prejudice." > Upon receiving this request, Chikazane Moto conveyed the above to Lord Terumune, who took note of it. Furthermore, > "During the recent campaign to subdue Ouchi and Bizen, in the battles at Kotemori Ryoguchi, one unit served as Yoshitsugu's vanguard. During the operation within Oba, when Nihonmatsu's garrison was deployed and the initial skirmishes took place, the enemy was no different from Ouchi." > As he deemed this to be the case, he ordered that operations be carried out at Nihonmatsu. Nevertheless, regarding various apologies, > "If that is the case, you shall cede the area up to Nangu and Sugitagawa, and be confined to five villages in the center. Furthermore, your son shall be sent to Yonezawa as a hostage." > This was the order given. Yoshitsugu offered an apology, stating, > "Whether to the south or the north, we ask that you seize one side for us," > but as this was not granted, on October 6, he stormed the camp of Lord Terumune at a place called Miyamori.

shigezane:shigezaneki-13.title: I. On the evening of October 6..
shigezane:shigezaneki-13.summary: On the evening of October 6, Lord Terumune visited the camps of Lord Masamune, summoned the chief retainers to the kitchen, and held a hearing regarding Yoshitsugu's apology and the lawsuit.
shigezane:shigezaneki-13.markdown:
> 1. On the evening of October 6, Lord Terumune visited the camp of Lord Masamune and summoned the chief retainers to the kitchen to inquire about the circumstances of Yoshitsugu's apology and to discuss the lawsuit. Although we were inexperienced, we were summoned as personal messengers. > "You shall serve as messengers to Yoshitsugu," > Lord Terumune commanded. We stated, > "We are inexperienced and lacking in all capacities. To be commanded as messengers for such a serious matter is a burden." > When we repeatedly stated this, > "Since the matter has been handled by Sanemoto, you shall serve as messengers. Lord Terumune shall handle all arrangements," > he commanded; thus, we had no choice but to follow his will. Regarding the lawsuit Yoshitsugu brought against us, we apologized as follows: > "Whether in the north or the south, we beg that you grant us leave." > As this was unavoidable, > "If that is the case, it would be a burden if the retainers we have kept until now were left to beg for food. While we state that we should receive our original fiefs and be employed, we resolve that even if we must commit seppuku, we shall not betray your will; we beg that you grant us your permission," > we stated, and our request was granted. Yoshitsugu said, > "I am deeply grateful for your forgiveness, and I wish to appear before you," > and so he commanded. When we reported this, he agreed that we should attend. Yoshitsugu and his party arrived at our camp at the hour of the eighth day on the 7th; as time passed and the candles burned down, we met and spoke before returning to Nihonmatsu. On the morning of the 8th, we received a messenger from Yoshitsugu: > "We intend to go to Miyamori. We wish to offer our apologies using Lord Terumune's earnings. We also wish to announce our preparations for patrols," > he commanded. When we visited Lord Terumune's camp, Date Ueno and many other chief retainers had gone to Miyamori. > "We wish to visit Nihonmatsu," > they reported to Lord Terumune. Since this was a convenient opportunity, we reported the intent Yoshitsugu had conveyed to us: > "We should urge you to depart immediately," > he commanded. As we reported this, Yoshitsugu went to Lord Terumune's camp. Yoshitsugu's party—Takamori Naizen, Kanokoda Izumi, and Okoshi Nakatsukasa—were summoned to the reception room. When Izumi arrived, he whispered something to Yoshitsugu; upon entering the room, Lord Terumune was present, along with Ueno and ourselves. As there was no small talk, he stepped forward to escort the guests and offered his thanks inside. The retainers of the inner quarters were present. As there was no way to capture them, they proceeded to the front garden; there was a single path flanked by bamboo fences on both sides, leaving no way to pass through, until they reached the garden. Ueno and I stepped out into the garden, but there was no way through; as we stood behind them, Yoshitsugu struck the ground with his hand and cried, > "I feel that the hospitality shown to us this time has been excessive. In that case, I understand that we shall be killed," > he commanded. He seized Lord Terumune's chest with his left hand and drew his short sword. As it seemed they had coordinated in advance, seven or eight of Yoshitsugu's party, who were close behind, moved around Lord Terumune and pushed Ueno and us aside. There was no way to pass by his side, > "Block the gate!" > they called, but as this was impossible, they rushed forward; thus, we had no choice but to follow behind them. Those who had come from Obama immediately charged forward with weapons. Those who had accompanied him from Miyamori were without armor, wearing their bare skin. No one said they should fight them; instead, they surrounded him in astonishment and accompanied him for over ten ri to a place called Takada. Since Lord Masamune had gone to Takano and was away, we reported the matter to him and returned. The equipment-bearers from Nihonmatsu consisted of one man named Hanzawa Gennai and one bow-bearer named Yusa Magokuro. All others were unarmed and surrounded Lord Terumune and Yoshitsugu. Then, from among those surrounding them, a shot was fired. No one said they should fight them, but the entire group attacked, killing over fifty people from Nihonmatsu, and Lord Terumune was also killed. Lord Masamune also departed for Takada that night. The chief retainers stated, > "First, we should withdraw to Obama, and on an auspicious day, launch an attack on Nihonmatsu," > and so he returned to Obama in the early hours of the 9th. Lord Terumune's body was accompanied to Obama that night, and the funeral rites were performed at Shifuku-ji in Nagai. Endo Yamashiro and Uchibaba Uemon committed ritual suicide. On the evening of the 8th, Yoshitsugu was questioned and his limbs were severed; he was tied with wisteria and hanged outside Obama Town, with numerous guards posted around him. The lands held by Yoshitsugu—Motomiya, Tamanoi, and Shibukawa—were withdrawn to Nihonmatsu on the evening of the 8th. It was commanded that he be sent as a hostage to Yonezawa; his twelve-year-old son, called Koku-den, was guarded by hereditary retainers, and Yoshitsugu's cousin, Shinjo Danjo, was one of those who had known him since long ago. That man became the commander and held out in a castle.
