shigezane:shigezaneki-14.title: I October 15……
shigezane:shigezaneki-14.summary: 1. October 15. Although they made an advance toward Nihonmatsu, they encountered strong resistance from within; thus, they launched an attack without incident, crossed the river to Takada, with the entire force withdrawing and establishing a field camp.
shigezane:shigezaneki-14.markdown:
> 1. October 15. We marched toward Nihonmatsu, but as the enemy held their ground firmly and did not emerge from within, we launched an attack without incident, crossed the river to Takada, with the entire force withdrawing and establishing a field camp. We were to receive a council of war the following day, so we also proceeded to Takada. The camp site for that night was called Hoda (Ioda); it was north of Nihonmatsu and in a location distinct from Takada. It was within the eighth block, and a lookout was stationed there. As our forces advanced north, the enemy emerged from the castle and engaged us in battle. Many on both sides were killed in combat. As the forces at Takada also repelled us, those who had emerged from the castle pushed in as far as the distant arrows and engaged in a final battle. From around midnight on the 15th, a great wind blew, and from dawn, heavy snow fell; it continued to fall day and night from the 16th to the 18th. Consequently, as horses could no longer keep pace and operations became impossible, all forces at the border repelled the enemy and took rest.

shigezane:shigezaneki-15.title: 1. Around the 10th of Shimotsuki..
shigezane:shigezaneki-15.summary: Around the 10th day of the first month, Lords Yoshishige Satake, Yoshihiro Aizu, Tsunetaka Iwaki, Akimitsu Ishikawa, and Yoshichika Shiraishi, acting in concert, marched to Sukagawa and conducted operations against the castles served by the Date clan in the Asazumi area, where they attacked and captured the castle known as Nakamura.
shigezane:shigezaneki-15.markdown:
> Around the 10th day of the 11th month, Lord Satake Yoshishige, Lord Aizu Yoshihiro, Lord Iwaki Tsunetaka, Lord Ishikawa Akimitsu, and Lord Shirakawa Yoshichika were summoned and marched to Sukagawa, where they conducted operations against the castles served by the Date clan in the Asazumi area and captured a castle called Nakamura. As this news arrived suddenly at Obama, Lord Masamune marched to Iwakado; at Takakura, Tomizuka Omi, Kuwaori Settsu-no-kami, Ito Hizen, and 300 hatamoto musketeers were stationed there. At the main castle, Segami Nakatsukasa, Nakajima Ise, Hamada Izu, and Sakurada Uhei were stationed. At Tamai Castle, Shiroishi Wakasa was stationed. Since we were besieged in Nihonmatsu, troops were stationed at a castle called Shibukawa for the defense of the Hachi-chome area. > "The troops stationed at Obama are all few in number, so they should proceed immediately." > As this order was issued, more than half of the troops at Shibukawa were left behind; they moved toward Shiomatsu and proceeded to Obama, where Lord Masamune promptly marched out. Since no troops were left behind while Obama was vacant, it was ordered that our forces should remain. Thus, Aoki Bizen, Uchibaba Hyuga, and about 30 cavalrymen were left behind; when we appeared before him at Iwakado, he stated: > "Maeda Sawa Hyobu has also changed his allegiance to serve Aizu; tomorrow he will surely conduct operations at either Takakura or Motomiya, so he should proceed." > Following this order, we camped that night at a place called Nukazawa (糠沢). That Maeda Sawa Hyobu was a former retainer of Nihonmatsu; when Yoshitsugu committed seppuku, he had served the Date clan, but now that Lord Satake had marched out, he had changed his allegiance. On the 16th of the same month, the enemy established a field camp at Minami-no-hara, south of Maeda Sawa. > "This will surely be the occasion for an operation against Takakura." > Upon receiving this report, Lord Masamune also moved from Iwakado to Motomiya. At that time, Motomiya consisted merely of fields and farmland with no inhabitants; there was a small stream, and only the area within the town walls was inhabited. > "We should launch an operation against Takakura." > Following this, to assist the troops, we sent a force to Kannon-do in Motomiya and, as soon as they arrived, prepared a defense at the foot of the highway at Takakura to reinforce them. The enemy, numbering over 50 cavalrymen, pushed through in three lines. The men besieged in Takakura said: > "Motomiya is unmanned, so we wish to send troops to hold it." > They said this, and while some replied, > "That cannot be done," > Tomizuka Omi and Ito Hizen stated: > "Even if they are pushed in, if we can hold the troops passing through Motomiya, it will not be a problem." > Both men said this and sent troops; as they pushed the enemy back, Iwaki's troops switched positions and closed in, driving them in from both ends and killing 20 to 30 men. Because the enemy was numerous, the troops pushed from Maeda Sawa fought against those coming out of Kannon-do. Furthermore, the troops pushing from Arai fought on both sides of the engagement. (Before) the fight, Shimo-Koriyama Naiki, looking toward Takayama, saw about 6 to 7 cavalrymen and 140 to 150 ashigaru approaching Motomiya from the direction of Takakura. A large number of troops followed. Thinking they were not the enemy, he suspected them of being allies; however, it appeared to be the boundary between friend and foe, with a gap of over one cho. Finding this suspicious, he watched, and when a single musket was fired from that gap, he realized it was the boundary between friend and foe. He rode back from the mountaintop and called out: > "The enemy has arrived! Raise the small flags!" > At that moment, he raised the small flags and waited; then Wakasa, Izu, and Iki rushed toward us and proceeded directly to the banners. These troops from Kannon-do were stationed at Ota-hara, but because the enemy army was large, they could not hold them; they were defeated, pushed back from Kannon-do, and retreated near the banners. Over 50 men were killed, including Moniwa Satsuki. Satsuki's head was not taken. Date Motoyasu, Mino, Ueno, Hikokuro, Harada Samanosuke, Kajitsura Kojuro, and others fought back, so there was no great defeat for our forces. Not a single one of our allies remained; we retreated to the Okawa, over 7 cho behind the enemy. We were 18 years old and had no idea what was happening; Shimo-Koriyama Naiki mounted a horse and, from atop the horse, pulled out a small flag and said: > "The men of Kannon-do have been routed and pushed back, so hurry and clear the way!" > He then handed the small flag to the pedestrians. We thought: > "Even if we clear the way, we will be killed, so we should die here." > With this in mind, we did not pull the flag back. Consequently, the enemy drove away Shiroishi Wakasa, Takano Iki, and Hamada Izu; as the enemy reached the bottom of the mountain, we began to let our troops go, but the enemy pushed them back. Here, Iwano Totomi, a man of great merit with 73 achievements, was the first to charge in and kill two of the enemy; he had one man take the head and drove the enemy back about 5 cho south of the mountain to the bridgehead. Haneda Umanosuke, riding through the boundary between friend and foe, rode his horse back and forth, pushing the enemy back so they would not collapse; then a spear-bearer stepped forward and struck Umanosuke, but as he turned back and tried to run forward, Umanosuke struck him with a single blow and killed him; the man was also killed by his own retainers, and one of his own retainers was also killed, and they were driven back to the starting point of the engagement. From there, Kayaba Genbe, the musket captain, and Ushizaka Sakon both charged into the center of the enemy and struck two cavalrymen on horseback, but they could not break through because of the armor; it was the enemy's exit point. They were then driven back to the original bridgehead, and as Kita-Shimotsuke mounted his horse, a foot soldier ran forward and struck Shinsuke's horse; Shinsuke was also unable to withstand it and was pushed back, becoming the enemy's exit point. Iwano Totomi acted as the rearguard to ensure the allies did not collapse, turned back, and became too far from the allies. That day, saying, > "With armor on, the old man cannot see," > he charged out in a sudden rush; the enemy mounted and struck his head with two blows, but he could not withstand it and was pushed back. The allies were then driven back to the original position. Consequently, the engagement at Kannon-do ended, and the enemy withdrew. We did not push back, but instead moved the supporting troops around and fought, ending the engagement; as for Kannon-do, whoever was stationed there, it happened on a different line, so I do not know. Totomi turned back and was killed. By the mysterious providence of heaven, not a single act was staged, and it was ended like the engagement at Kannon-do. I do not speak of the defeated army, but among the retainers of our house, over 10 men, including Iwano Totomi and Kita-Shimotsuke, were killed. We also took 9 enemy heads. I do not record the details of the battle in detail. I shall write them down now. Once the enemy at Kannon-do withdrew, our forces withdrew to the allies. Afterward, the enemy withdrew from Kannon-do and returned to their positions at the Takakura highway river crossing. > "Shall we fight?" > Thinking this, perhaps because Lord Masamune's forces were about 5 to 6 cho away, we launched an attack without incident. Since our forces were also few, we did not push them back; that man called Shimo-Koriyama Naiki had served closely to the former Lord Terumune and had been appointed musket captain during the time of the Soma bows and arrows. At that time, he had been disowned and had come to rely on us. On that day, when our allies were lagging, he rode his horse back and forth to support them and push the enemy back; when he charged at the front, he struck the enemy twice and had his retainers take the heads, achieving unparalleled success.

shigezane:shigezaneki-16.title: 1. On the evening of the 17th, Lord Masamune……
shigezane:shigezaneki-16.summary: On the evening of the 17th, Lord Masamune also retired to Iwakado; around midnight, Yamaji Awaji came as a messenger to my place and presented a handwritten letter, stating in his remarks, "Today's treatment is beyond compare."
shigezane:shigezaneki-16.markdown:
I. On the evening of the 17th, Lord Masamune also withdrew to Iwakado. Around midnight, Yamaji Awaji was dispatched as a messenger to my residence, delivering [a letter in his own hand](#/post/shigezane/29). In his address, he stated: "The conduct of today is without parallel. To have fought behind the enemy's lines and not be taken prisoner by the defeated army is unprecedented. Precisely because of you, many men have been saved. Surely there will be numerous wounded and dead. In particular, I have heard that tomorrow the enemy will advance close to the main castle. Whoever wishes to be sent, as there is no one available to me, I shall enter the main castle, albeit against official orders. Date Ueno has been dispatched." Thus he commanded. Furthermore, Awaji reported: "How many allies were there in today's battle? As it was impossible to bring them along, the two of us had no choice but to blend in with the enemy. The enemy was unaware of the situation. Upon consultation, we agreed that the main castle should be approached and that the forces besieging Nihonmatsu should be removed; having heard the details, we finally escaped the enemy camp at dusk. Now that you have been commanded thus, and since the main castle is to be besieged, I shall make the necessary preparations." However, as this was sudden, I could not prepare myself in time, and I entered the main castle in the early hours of the 18th. When I asked, "Since my arrival was late, have you sent out lookouts?" he replied, "I have left them in place since nightfall." Seeing the fires, I thought, "Have they moved their camp?" Just then, a lookout horse arrived and reported, "The Satake, Aizu, and Iwaki forces have been removed, and eventually, Maedazawa was also cleared." Upon this, I sent men to Maedazawa to investigate, and they withdrew without a single person remaining. When Lord Masamune arrived at the main castle and issued his orders, Hamada Izu stated before him: "In yesterday's battle, Nakamura Hachiroemon performed an unparalleled feat. Because of Hachiroemon, fifty or sixty allies were saved." At that time, Hachiroemon, having no intention of doing so, drew his sword and cut down twenty enemy cavalrymen; seeing that he had missed every strike, the Lord decreed that he should be granted an increase in his fief. Furthermore, the Lord stated, "Should the enemy perform any further feats, it shall be unforgivable." Thus, although he remained at Iwakado for two days, as nothing further occurred, he returned to Obama and spent the New Year there.

shigezane:shigezaneki-17.title: 1. In Tensho 14, at Shibukawa..
shigezane:shigezaneki-17.summary: In the 14th year of Tenten, while we resided at Shibukawa, on New Year's Day, word arrived from Nihonmatsu requesting that we set out around midday; accordingly, one mounted rider and about ten foot soldiers arrived ahead and rode up to the water-drawing area at the edge of the camp...
shigezane:shigezaneki-17.markdown:
1. In Tensho 14, while we were stationed at Shibukawa, on New Year's Day, word arrived from Nihonmatsu requesting that we set out around midday. One mounted rider and about ten infantrymen arrived first and rode toward the end of the camp at the water-drawing station; as they drove the water-drawers about, they encountered the enemy from within and engaged in battle. On the highway to Nihonmatsu, there was a small hill of brush; as they pursued the enemy along a single path, about 100 mounted riders and over 1,000 ashigaru were stationed behind the brush and pushed them back. Not only was the path blocked, but they were also scattered to the sides; Kayaba Genbei, Imaizumi Kanmono, Yokoyama Hikoshiro, and Naraba Toshiro were killed in action. Kanokoda Uemon thought, "Sato Uemon is a man I have heard of before. I shall see how he fares." With this in mind, Uemon rode up to a slight elevation; as Uemon was born nearby and knew the way, he withdrew westward from the path they were pursuing. Once the enemy had passed, three men engaged them within a single field and took two heads; from there, they pursued the enemy, and Uemon engaged another man, eventually catching up to where Uemon was. Uemon, unable to withstand the onslaught, fought a desperate stand and was driven into the open fields. Shiga Oi Saemon charged in first and took four heads. Haneda Umanosuke went elsewhere and arrived late, charging in from the side and taking five heads, taking about 30 heads there. From then on, the enemy's mobility was impaired, and those who had come to their aid from Hachichome crossed the open fields, pushing through the current highway toward Nihonyanagi. The battlefield lay east of Nihonyanagi, and knowing they would be pushed back, they broke the Nihonmatsu forces and pursued them further. Kanokoda Uemon halted his horse at the narrow path of Iidoi, pushed back those who had fled, and brought about a decisive conclusion to the fight. As it was, the sun was already setting; our forces withdrew, taking 263 heads, and reported to Obama on the 2nd. Kanokoda Uemon returned and later reported, "Sato Uemon is a skilled horseman; I have heard of him."

shigezane:shigezaneki-18.title: 1. February of the same year. At the siege of Nihonmatsu..
shigezane:shigezaneki-18.summary: February of the same year. While besieged in Nihonmatsu, five men—Gemban Miwa, Shinbei Ujiie, Tanba Yusa, Shimousa Yusa, and Etchu Horie—held a consultation.
shigezane:shigezaneki-18.markdown:
1. February of the same year. While besieged at Nihonmatsu, five men—Miwa Genban, Ujiie Shinbei, Yusa Tanba, the same from Shimosa, and Horie Etchu—held a consultation. They reported to Lord Masamune, saying, "Having rendered our services, we request that the castle be taken; therefore, troops should be stationed at Genban's residence, as the terrain is favorable." Having thus reported, the five aforementioned men provided hostages. Troops were dispatched in the middle of the night. As four of the men were stationed at the castle and there was no place to house them, they were moved to Genban's residence; however, those in the vicinity flocked only to Genban's residence, leaving no room to deploy many men or fire their muskets. Furthermore, regarding the Kuriga-saku fence, had they been reinforced, it would not have been easily breached; however, as the Kuriga-saku was firmly fortified, and since Genban's residence lay between the main castle and the Kuriga-saku, it could not be held. At dawn, an attack was launched from within the castle upon Genban's residence; as the exits had been blocked and the main entrance was crowded with men, it was impossible to advance, so they broke through the walls. People piled up and tumbled down from the steep slopes, and approximately 40 to 50 men and women were trampled to death; the castle interior remained firmly fortified.

shigezane:shigezaneki-19.title: 1 Lord Masamune is somewhat displeased..
shigezane:shigezaneki-19.summary: As Lord Masamune was somewhat displeased, the campaign to Nihonmatsu was postponed and carried out in early April.
shigezane:shigezaneki-19.markdown:
1. As Lord Masamune was somewhat displeased, he postponed the campaign to Nihonmatsu and instead carried out operations in early April. Although he privately wished to maintain a close garrison, he considered that if he were to proceed as he had last year, departing from Aizu Mountain Castle for Asaka, he might end up storming the castle; accordingly, despite conducting operations for five days from the north, south, and east, not a single person emerged from within. Even after two attempts at siege walls, the castle remained secure, making it difficult to attack, and thus he withdrew to Obama. Meanwhile, a messenger arrived from Soma Yoshitane; although we were relatives, as Yoshitane had requested it, we proceeded to Obama and ensured his safe passage. Furthermore, as there was no specific order, we handled the matter by ensuring the siege of Nihonmatsu was lifted. On July 16 of the same year, the Honmaru was burned down, and the forces withdrew to Aizu, while the subordinates dispersed as they pleased. Since we were commanded that "the castle shall be taken over," we established a temporary shelter in the Honmaru until that day. On July 26, Lord Masamune arrived at Nihonmatsu and returned the same day.

shigezane:shigezaneki-2.title: 1. January, Tensho 13..
shigezane:shigezaneki-2.summary: In the first month of 1585, Ouchi Bizen reported, "As the snow is deep and construction is difficult, I humbly request leave to return home, bring my wife and children, and make the necessary preparations before reporting back."
shigezane:shigezaneki-2.markdown:
1. In the first month of Tensho 13, Ouchi Bizen reported as follows: "As the snow is deep and construction is difficult, I request leave to return and bring my wife and children with me to make preparations. Furthermore, I wish to accept the rewards for the Satake and Aizu campaigns of the past few years. I desire to express my gratitude." Accordingly, leave was granted; however, although the snow subsequently melted, he did not return. Consequently, despite repeated dispatches from Endo Yamashiro, instructing him that he should return, he remained absent. Eventually, he declared, "Regardless of your intentions, I shall not report to you." Since the subjugation of the Ouchi involved the Aizu, Satake, Iwaki, and Ishikawa forces—all of whom had been appointed in recent years and were part of the same faction—Lord Terumune found it laughable that the man had become an enemy. He deemed it appropriate to advise that the Ouchi should be reported to him. Thus, he dispatched two envoys, Miyagawa Ikkeisai and Igarashi Roshusai, stating that, per his orders, he should return; and that following the success of the campaign against Tamura, such was his command, so he should not worry in the least regarding his own life or fief. Lord Terumune was told to accept this, but replied, "Your intentions are excessive, but having spoken thus, even should I perish, I shall not report to you." Furthermore, two envoys, Katakura Ikyusai and Harada Kyusetsusai, were dispatched, stating that the matter was indeed worthy of concern; they advised that if this were the case, hostages should be provided, and that even if he did not return in person, a lawsuit should be filed against Lord Masamune. However, he declared, "Regardless of your intentions, I shall not provide hostages." Among the Ouchi relatives was a man named Ouchi Nagato, who frequently came to Yonezawa as an envoy; both father and son were acquainted with him. He was later known as Gasai. This man, addressing Kyusetsu and Ikyu, spoke disparagingly of Lord Masamune's subjugation of the Ouchi, saying it was entirely unexpected; the two envoys became incensed and returned, saying, "Will you go to Yonezawa, or will you subjugate them? We shall see the outcome." This matter was then reported. Both father and son felt great resentment. Meanwhile, Lord Masamune summoned Harada Samanosuke and Katakura Kojuro, stating that if the envoys from Aizu were to grant a pardon to Ouchi Bizen and send him to Yonezawa, there would be no need for assistance on this side. Furthermore, he heard that the envoys had spoken with hidden motives from Aizu, yet he wondered why the Ouchi alone should bear the burden of the enemy. Feeling regret over the double dealing in Aizu, he declared that he wished to sever ties with Aizu. Additionally, since there were critical positions in all directions, he ordered that not a single person serving in Aizu be allowed to serve under him. Samanosuke replied, "I understand the envoys from Aizu are particularly earnest and find it suspicious that Ouchi Bizen was dismissed; perhaps this was spoken with hidden motives from Aizu. It must be unavoidable. We should arrange to send even a single person from among the Aizu prisoners to serve." Lord Masamune asked, "Is there anyone with such resourcefulness?" To which Samanosuke replied, "I do not know the hidden motives, but I am a man of capable resourcefulness for the moment. Furthermore, as this concerns service, I shall not act out of mere flattery." Upon hearing this, the Lord said, "If so, I shall assign the task," and sent the envoys. Among them was a man named Shibano Danjo from the north of Aizu, who stated, "I shall serve." There were two or three others who agreed, saying, "If the campaign proceeds toward our side, we shall serve." Thus, on May 2, Harada Samanosuke crossed the difficult pass known as Sarukura-go and was sent to Danjo's place. Danjo did not possess a castle but lived in a small residence where he kept a few retainers; Samanosuke crossed the pass and set fire to the place, causing the Aizu forces to fall into great confusion. Troops arrived from various directions to assist, but all were concerned, asking, "Are they taking my place?" At that moment, Tarozaemon, the messenger for the arrangement, rushed to the Aizu forces and declared, "The one taking the place is Danjo alone; Samanosuke has crossed without a single companion." Just as the Aizu forces felt their hearts settle and prepared to fight, Samanosuke was defeated; several of the yoriki and retainers were killed, and Danjo was forced to flee, taking his wife and children with him. On the 3rd, Lord Masamune marched to Hibara and immediately took possession of it. However, as it was a secret operation, he brought only the men from Nagai and did not bring the full force. While awaiting the arrival of the full army, he issued orders and, on the 8th of the same month, launched an attack at Oshio. The full Aizu force was stationed at Oshio Castle, holding it firmly; they operated daily at the critical point atop Mount Oshio. As there was no terrain that would allow them to descend and attack, they remained entrenched in the castle; though they attacked frequently, there was no terrain to secure the troops, as there was only a single path through the great mountain. Consequently, those who did not retreat were turned back and remained stationed at Hibara.

shigezane:shigezaneki-20.title: 1. The castle of Nihonmatsu, from last year until this July..
shigezane:shigezaneki-20.summary: Regarding the circumstances surrounding the castle of Ichi-Nihonmatsu from last year until this July: Takatama and Yasukogashima were assigned to service in Aizu and made their way to Nihonmatsu via the deep mountains.
shigezane:shigezaneki-20.markdown:
1. Regarding the castle of Nihonmatsu, the circumstances under which it was held from last year until this July are as follows: Takatama and Yasukogashima were sent to serve in Aizu and made their way to Nihonmatsu via the deep mountains. Privately, it was desired that "the castle be closed off to the path," but this was not done out of consideration for the departures of Yoshihiro, Yoshishige, and Tsunetaka. Furthermore, as it appeared from Takayama that the path should be blocked, troops were deployed to prevent passage. When there were no troops present, the path was left open, and a few people, including I-ki, were able to pass through; thus, it was held until July of this year.

shigezane:shigezaneki-23.title: 1. In Tensho 14, following the fall of the Nihonmatsu and Shiomatsu clans..
shigezane:shigezaneki-23.summary: In the 14th year of Tensho, after the retainers of Nihonmatsu and Shiomatsu had settled their affairs and delivered their horses to Yonezawa in August, the retainers of Osaki Yoshitaka split into two factions. The root of the matter that was reported to Lord Masamune was that a man named Niida Gyobu, a page serving Yoshitaka at the time, had made an extraordinary appearance.
shigezane:shigezaneki-23.markdown:
I. In Tensho 14, after the retainers of Nihonmatsu and Shiomatsu had settled their affairs and delivered their horses to Yonezawa in August, the retainers of Osaki Yoshitaka split into two factions and petitioned Lord Masamune. The root cause of this was a man named Niida Gyobu, a page serving Yoshitaka at the time, who took an unusually bold stand. Consequently, a man named Ibano Sohachiro was soon brought into service; Gyobu became fearful (of him?) of Sohachiro, and since Gyobu had many relatives, all of those relatives also became fearful (of him?). Meanwhile, Sohachiro reasoned, "We are but a solitary man and have no one to rely on; I shall propose a plan and seek the assistance of the lord of Iwadeyama, a man named Ujiie Danjo." Having thus decided, he approached Danjo and made his request in full detail; Danjo agreed and pledged his cooperation. Thereupon, the relatives of Niida Gyobu reasoned, "With Danjo's mediation, we shall surely be brought into trouble. Now that the dispute between Osaki and Date is at its peak, we shall petition Lord Masamune for aid, defeat Danjo's faction and Sohachiro, and force Yoshitaka to commit seppuku." They reported this to Lord Masamune, who agreed and declared that whenever they requested it, he would dispatch the necessary number of men. Until then, Gyobu had served Yoshitaka and was stationed at Nao Castle. However, Ujiie raised an objection to Yoshitaka, stating, "Gyobu and his associates are plotting rebellion and have petitioned Lord Masamune; therefore, Gyobu should be ordered to commit seppuku. He should be confined." Yoshitaka replied, "Since those around him are plotting rebellion, I shall find it most regrettable. Though I would normally order seppuku, as I have served him since childhood, I shall spare him. I shall have Niida come at once." Gyobu replied, "While I am grateful for your kindness, my peers all hate me; if I were to leave the main castle, they would claim I am acting against your will and surely strike me down. Though I hesitate to speak much, I humbly beg that, given the grace you have shown me thus far, you would take me with you as far as Fushimi." Yoshitaka found this reasonable and declared, "If that is the case, I shall take you as far as Fushimi and release you; I shall have you accompany me." He then brought two horses into the courtyard—one for Yoshitaka and one for Gyobu. Leaving Gyobu behind, Yoshitaka took the reins of his horse and told the attendants that they were not needed. He then acted swiftly, looking to his left and right, and declared, "From here, we proceed to Niida." Gyobu replied, "I intend to go alone, but I beg that the retainers take me as far as Niida." Yoshitaka replied, "There should be no objection," but Gyobu protested, "I must accompany you." He argued that if there were no attendants, he would be in a position where Yoshitaka himself would be struck down; thus, insisting that they must go to Niida, he kept Gyobu at Niida without returning to Nao. The members of Gyobu's faction—Satomi Kii-no-kami, lord of Okamizuka; Yagisawa Bizen, lord of Yachimori; Yoneizumi Gon'emon; Miyazaki Minbu; Ishikawa Echizen, lord of Takashimizu; Katsuraoka Tarozaemon, lord of Miyazaki; Momo Sakyosuke, lord of Momo; Nakanome Hyogo; Iikawa Osumi; and Kurosawa Jibu—who were Yoshitaka's brothers-in-law—were all plotting rebellion. They intended to rely on Lord Masamune and use his authority to defeat Ujiie's faction and Ibano Sohachiro, and to force Yoshitaka to commit seppuku. Unexpectedly, however, Yoshitaka was captured alive and held at Nitta. While they were there, their minds changed; they abandoned Date and supported Yoshitaka, resolving to defeat Ujiie Danjo and Ibano Sohachiro. These men reported to Yoshitaka, "Gyobu and his associates have caused great trouble; if we support Yoshitaka, who could possibly harbor ill will toward him? If Ujiie Danjo alone is defeated, all of Osaki will be satisfied." They thus made their petition. Yoshitaka, having heard that those men were plotting rebellion and relying on Date, replied that since he had considered Ujiie Danjo as his sole retainer, he should accompany him in seppuku. He did not intend to defeat Danjo, but as they remained at Niida and petitioned him, he eventually relented, saying, "That is reasonable."

shigezane:shigezaneki-24.title: 1. In the records of Ujiie Danjo..
shigezane:shigezaneki-24.summary: In the account of Ujiie Danjo, it is written: "Now, in this ever-changing world, while the Osakabe faction relied on the Date and plotted rebellion against Yoshitaka, I resolved to serve solely and prepared to take refuge in Namio Castle..."
shigezane:shigezaneki-24.markdown:
1. According to the account of Ujiie Danjo: "Now, in this ever-changing world, while the Osaka party had placed their trust in the Date and plotted rebellion against Yoshitaka, I resolved to serve solely and prepare to hole up in Namio Castle; thus, I intended to move to Mount Iwate to accompany him in his seppuku. However, contrary to my expectations, Yoshitaka has devised a plan to subjugate us, and this situation is unavoidable. From here on, we intend to place our trust in the Date, subjugate Yoshitaka, and thereby save our own lives." He then dispatched men named Kajitsuna Katakura and Shikibu Mayama from among Danjo's retainers to proceed to Yonezawa, and informed them of the details regarding his request to Kojuro Katakura, stating: "I have informed the relatives of Osaka Osaka that they have plotted rebellion against Yoshitaka and intend to place their trust in Yonezawa; unexpectedly, Osaka has captured Yoshitaka alive and has betrayed his oath of service to the Date, intending to install Yoshitaka in his place. As I am now in a position where my ruin is imminent, if Lord Masamune were to render assistance, Osaki could easily fall into Lord Masamune's hands." When Kojuro reported this, Lord Masamune remarked that the matter had long been a source of resentment for Yoshitaka, and that the relatives of the Osaka party felt great regret over the breach of their loyalty. Consequently, an order was issued that Ujiie Danjo should lead the effort. Kojuro immediately conveyed the instructions to Danjo's messengers, Shikibu; both messengers were delighted and hastened to Iwadeyama to report as Danjo had requested, and Danjo was exceedingly pleased.

shigezane:shigezaneki-26.title: 1. Regarding Danjo's intentions..
shigezane:shigezaneki-26.summary: In the account of Ichidan Shozo, it says that having betrayed his hereditary lord through an unforeseen turn of events and entered the service of the Date, he felt the heavens themselves were outraged; thus, he brought along his lord's son, Shozaburo, and went before Lord Masamune to serve as a retainer—a matter the heavens also found grievous...
shigezane:shigezaneki-26.markdown:
1. In the account of Danjo, he lamented that he had betrayed his hereditary lord through an unforeseen turn of events to serve the Date; fearing the wrath of the heavens, he felt it only right to escort Lord Masamune, bringing along Lord Shozaburo—the son of his lord—to serve as an attendant. Feeling that the heavens would also be indignant and that he should be cast out by the Triple Gem of Buddha and God, he escorted Lord Shozaburo to the residence of Nanjo Shimosa in Nakashinden. Both men were cast out by Yoshitaka and Lord Shozaburo; though they grieved day and night and contemplated suicide, they ultimately could not bring themselves to do so, and could do nothing but weep.

shigezane:shigezaneki-27.title: 1. January 16, Tensho 15……
shigezane:shigezaneki-27.summary: On the 16th day of the first month of the 15th year of Tentensho, orders were issued to Osaki; Date Uenosuke and Izumida Aki were appointed as commanders of the troops, while Awano Suketaro, Nagai Gekkan, Takashiro Suo, Omatsuzawa Saemon, Miyanai Inaba, Tate Sukesaburo, and Hamada Izu were appointed as military commissioners...
shigezane:shigezaneki-27.markdown:
1. On January 16, Tensho 15, orders were issued for Osaki. Date Uenosuke and Izumida Aki were appointed as commanders of the troops; additionally, Awano Suketaro, Nagai Gekkan, Takashiro Suo, Omatsuzawa Saemon, Miyanai Inaba, Tate Sukesaburo, and Hamada Izu were appointed as military commissioners, and Oyamada Chikuzen was appointed as the deputy commander. Konarita Soemon, Yamagishi Shuri, and other forces were stationed at Dewa Castle in Endo. They proceeded to take up positions in Matsuyama. Those serving Date in Osaki were Ujiie Danjo, Yuyama Shuri, Ichikuri Hyobu, Ichisako Izu, Miyano Bungo, and Miyasako no Miya Hyuga—all of whom were men from the vicinity of Iwadeyama. From Matsuyama, they were stationed at Tegoshi, and there was no terrain suitable for adding to these forces. As for the service for Date Uenosuke, Hamada Izu, Izumida Aki, and others at Matsuyama, a council was held, and it was decided that if service for the Osaki archers and Tsukifune were requested this time, Koshi-kamado Owari would also be called upon; since Iwadeyama was nearby, it should have been the case that the forces would advance there. However, it was agreed that if Kurokawa Tsukifune acted contrary to orders and entered the castles of the district, pushing through the Date forces, the men holed up in the mountains should engage and repel them; thus, the council deliberated on the arrangements for the operation. Endo Dewa stated, "Uenosuke Kai, the lord of Niinuma Castle, is my son-in-law and a man of loyalty to this house; therefore, even if a garrison is placed at Shiyama and they push through to Nakashinden, there should be no issue." Uenosuke replied, "Even if that were the case, the road to Nakashinden is 20 ri. I worry about pushing through while leaving the enemy's castle behind to the north and south." To this, Izumida Aki stated, "Lord Uenosuke has long been with us. Furthermore, regarding this plan for the Osaki archers, if we report it and the troops are dispatched, Tsukifune is Lord Uenosuke's father-in-law. Whether it be him or the other, I believe the archers will not be fully committed this time. I believe what Dewa says is correct. If Ujiie Danjo remains in Iwadeyama Castle and does not see the vanguard of the Date forces, his morale will drop, and it will be difficult for him to serve Yoshitaka; therefore, a garrison should be placed at Shiyama and they should push through." Thus, the matter was settled, and the operation was limited to that of Nakashinden.

shigezane:shigezaneki-28.title: I. The true intent behind Kurokawa Gesshu's contrary intentions was..
shigezane:shigezaneki-28.summary: The underlying intent behind Kurokawa Gesshu's opposition was that Gesshu's uncle, a man named Kurokawa Shikibu, had served during the reign of Lord Terumune.
shigezane:shigezaneki-28.markdown:
1. The underlying intent behind Kurokawa Gesshu's rebellious actions was that Gesshu's uncle, a man named Kurokawa Shikibu, had served during the reign of Lord Terumune. It had been agreed that Shikibu would marry the daughter of a man named Ukon-no-tasuke, the lord of Iizaka Castle, and be entrusted as the representative; however, by the time the daughter was about ten years old, Shikibu had entered his senior years, and it was likely that his retirement would come soon. Having also been given as a concubine to Lord Masamune and having conceived a child, Gesshu had proposed that he be appointed as the representative, believing this to be for the best for the clan's interests. However, as the matter was handled differently, Kurokawa Shikibu felt greatly aggrieved. He ceased all communication with Gesshu. Furthermore, Gesshu's resentment stemmed from the fact that he was the adoptive father of Osaki Yoshitaka. When Yoshitaka's younger brother, Yoshiyasu, was appointed as Gesshu's successor as representative—and since Yoshiyasu had become the son-in-law of Date Motoyasu—he was placed ahead of Gesshu. Consequently, believing that if Yoshitaka were to fall, he would henceforth prioritize his own safety, he began to plot a rebellion.

shigezane:shigezaneki-29.title: 1 Ujiie Danjo, ……
shigezane:shigezaneki-29.summary: Ujiie Danjo: While the Lord intends to dispatch Date troops, even now there is not the slightest sign of the forces securing the village, and as the roads remain impassable, no word has reached us from anywhere; we have been waiting day after day, and as the New Year has already begun, we have been anxious morning and evening...
shigezane:shigezaneki-29.markdown:
1. Ujiie Danjo was instructed to dispatch Date forces; however, as no sign of the advance troops could be seen and the routes were obstructed, no reports arrived from any quarter. Waiting day after day, and with January already past, he remained anxious morning and evening. Then, on February 2, the forces from Matsuyama set out, crossed the river, and the vanguard gradually advanced past Shiyama, reaching Niinuma and engaging in combat at Nakashinden. At the castle called Shimoshinden, Katsuraoka Kanmono served as the castle lord; other supporting generals included Satomi Kii, Yagisawa Bizen (the younger brother of Yachimori Shuzen), Yoneizumi Gon'emon, Miyazaki Minbu, and Kurosawa Jibu. These men were stationed there, and Ujiie Danjo declared that if the Date forces pushed through to Nakashinden, not a single person would be allowed to pass. However, as the opposing force was too numerous to resist, they pushed through without establishing a blockade. Behind them, at Shiyama Castle, generals Furukawa Danjo, Ishikawa Echizen, Katsuraoka Tarozaemon, and Momo Sakyoryo were stationed. South of the river, at Kuwaori Castle, Kurokawa Gesshu was stationed. The castle lord was a man named Iikawa Osumi. Since the two castles were separated by the road, Date Ueno, Hamada Izu, Tate Sukesaburo, and Miyauchi Inaba—over 400 cavalry—took up positions in the wide fields of Shiyama. While the vanguard was pressing in from the vicinity of Nakashinden, a man named Nanjo Shimosa led four or five cho of town fortifications; the vanguard engaged him in battle, forced him inside, and set fire to two or three fortified town blocks. He then retreated into the Shimosa honmaru and held it firmly. As many enemy castles were breached, Ujiie Danjo, concerned by the noise, ordered Oyamada Chikuzen to withdraw all forces and establish a gradual defensive line. Ujiie Danjo, acting on sudden orders, did not intend to advance as far as Naka-Arada; he simply set out, seizing whatever he could, forced his way in, burned various places, and withdrew, without pressing the Date forces. At that time, the days were short and there was deep snow, leaving only a single path; thus, the Date forces could not withdraw hastily, and it was not until 7 o'clock that they withdrew. Even when the Naka-Arada forces reported that they were unable to pass, Ujiie Danjo did not heed them and drove his troops through. Just as he intended to attack the Ueno and Hamada Izu forces, he withdrew from the rear; since he had pulled back the bridge over the double irrigation moat, they could not pass and retreated to Niinuma. After engaging the Naka-Arada forces there, he heard that the bridge at Kiridokoro had been pulled. Although the coordination of the various forces was poor, Oyamada Chikuzen was a trusted man; he fought back, and thus there was no major collapse. Chikuzen fought back and scattered the enemy; seeing a single foot soldier flee to the side, he pursued him and rode up beside him at a distance of 14–15 ken. There, snow had piled up over the deep rice fields, making it look like flat land; he rode his horse forward and the enemy horse overturned, causing Chikuzen to strike him 2–3 ken and throw the horse away. Chikuzen threw the horse away and attempted to withdraw, but was unable to do so. Seeing this, the enemy turned back and attempted to strike Chikuzen; Chikuzen released the reins, drew his sword, and they clashed. It was not just one or two men, but a great number; the enemy pressed in from behind, cut one leg, and brought the opponent down, causing him to fall immediately. Nevertheless, the enemy did not abandon their swords and continued to fight. As they were veteran warriors, the battle was prolonged; as their breath grew short and their sword strikes weakened, four young retainers rushed forward, attempting to take the head. Ujiie Danjo threw away his sword, pulled them back, drew his wakizashi, and thrust it through the center, bringing both men down; those who followed from behind then took their heads. The enemy forces remained stationed south of the river, but having been defeated and unable to even cross the river, they saw that their side was losing and crossed the river to join the Naka-Arada forces. As dusk fell, Chikuzen was killed in action, and the allied forces were defeated, with many slain. As the bridge at Kiridokoro was pulled and the forces retreated to Niinuma, they barricaded themselves inside the castle.

shigezane:shigezaneki-3.title: 1 To Aizu..
shigezane:shigezaneki-3.summary: While the route to Aizu had been cut off, the border of Nihonmatsu remained open. At Hachichome, where my elder brother Shigezane Moto had retired, I received a dispatch from Yoshitsugu Nihonmatsu and spoke with him warmly.
shigezane:shigezaneki-3.markdown:
Although the border with Aizu had been settled, there was no settlement regarding the border with Nihonmatsu. At Hachichome, where my elder father, Motomoto, had retired, I received a dispatch from Nihonmatsu Yoshitsugu and spoke with him in great sincerity. The details were as follows: while Aizu and Satake were on our side, Nihonmatsu and Shiomatsu had originally recruited soldiers for Tamura, Aizu, and Satake; since we were in a position of great dependence, he expressed his wish that if the Date were to recruit this time, we should entrust our elder father to the Date and serve them, as Yoshitsugu held this view in good faith. Therefore, as there was no settlement regarding the border, on the 8th we departed from Omori, and on the 9th we personally visited Lord Masamune's camp to report. Upon inquiry, he asked, "How is the situation regarding the Nihonmatsu border?" I replied, "First and foremost, things remain quiet. Yoshitsugu also views this with great care. There are those who constantly harass our elder father—men called Yusa and Shimosa—but since we have been close friends for a long time, we have entrusted them with dispatches and also act as couriers. As for that border, we shall settle it according to your will." Upon hearing this, he dismissed the attendants and informed me of the details of the settlement with Aizu, recounting how Harada Samanosuke had been defeated in battle. Since there were no men serving in Aizu and that area was a strategic point, there was no way to resolve the matter; thus, he ordered that the troops be withdrawn and that a reply be sent by yesterday. He then stated, "The Nihonmatsu border must first be settled. How is the settlement of the two entrances?" We replied, "Even if there are no men serving in Aizu, we shall have Inawashiro Danjo observe the situation." He replied, "Is there a plan?" To this, we stated, "A man called Haneda Umanosuke has a close relationship with the Inawashiro elder, a man called Ishibe Shimosa; they are particularly close. We have brought him along for this visit." Immediately, Umanosuke was summoned, and upon hearing that "Inawashiro has a good rapport with him," he was ordered, "Prepare a letter and deliver it." We drafted the letter in his presence. We were ordered that Kojuro Katakura and Shichimiya Hoki should also attach their letters; accordingly, all sent their letters. Since this letter was 30 ri from Hinohara to Inawashiro, any reply sent from there would be forwarded to Omori; thus, we were ordered to return immediately. I stated, "Today the men and horses are exhausted and the day is drawing to a close; I wish to return tomorrow." Since he felt uneasy regarding the Nihonmatsu border and as we were staying nearby with no official business, he ordered that we return as quickly as possible. We returned to Omori on the same day. Shichimiya Hoki had been a longtime Aizu ronin and was usually among the attendants; since all the Aizu retainers knew him, he was brought along. Four or five days later, Mine Shikibu and Shichimiya Hoki were dispatched from Hinohara as messengers to Omori; as for the letter from Inawashiro, it was understood that it would be opened and accepted. Since we were staying at that entrance, two men were sent from there to arrange the matter. They arranged an inn where no one was present, and a man called Sanzoken, who had come from Inawashiro, was dispatched as a messenger, crossing the Deyu-dori road. The wording of the [letter](#/post/shigezane/t13-6-8) was: "I have received the reply sent from Hinohara. I am satisfied that we shall serve Masamune. If there are any further requests, I shall accept them. I shall present Masamune's seal." Accordingly, Danjo sent the [written document](#/post/shigezane/t13-6-11) containing the following requests: "1. That the northern half be granted as a fief. 2. That those of us who serve thereafter be placed in the seat of authority in Aizu, as is customary. 3. That if the bows and arrows are not provided as desired and Inawashiro is withdrawn, a pardon of 300 kan be granted within the Date domain." As there were no further requests beyond these three points, the document was sent. Shikibu and Hoki remained in Omori, and only the written document was sent back to Hinohara. Lord Masamune reviewed it and, stating that there should be no discrepancy from the document, placed the Danjo's written document before him and ordered that the pardon for the withdrawal be issued promptly; he designated the lands of Karita and Shibata, wrote 300 kan, and sent the seal. Shikibu and Hoki handed the document to us and returned to Hinohara. We then sent the seal to Inawashiro via Sanzoken. Two or three days later, we returned. "I have delivered the seal. However, as my son Moritane must serve in Aizu, I shall urge him accordingly and settle the matter." After a day or two, we sent Sanzoken and told him, "Please hasten the settlement," but Moritane did not fully understand and became divided within the household, making it impossible to settle the matter. As the bows and arrows at the Aizu entrance were not provided, a new fort was built at Hinohara, and Goto Magobe was stationed there.

shigezane:shigezaneki-30.title: I. The Morning Oyamada Chikuzen Fell in Battle..
shigezane:shigezaneki-30.summary: On the morning that Oyamada Chikuzen fell in battle, a mysterious omen occurred. Mounting his horse at the inn, he rode out about ten ken; then, the horse he rode spoke, saying, "The drum of time—already late, already late," which awakened those accompanying Chikuzen.
shigezane:shigezaneki-30.markdown:
1. On the morning that Oyamada Chikuzen fell in battle, a mysterious omen occurred. Riding his horse from the inn, he had ridden out about ten ken when the horse spoke, saying, "The drum of time—already late, already late." This awakened the spirits of those accompanying Chikuzen. Upon hearing this, Chikuzen declared, "Today's battle is a victory. Rejoice!" After he fell in battle, the horse was captured by the enemy, and those who had known it declared, "This horse was, for one year, drawn by the divine horse to the Kannon of Nodake for Yoshitaka's prayers." When Yoshitaka heard of this and brought the horse back to examine it, he saw that it was indeed a horse drawn by a divine steed. He declared that the way Chikuzen had ridden and fallen in this battle was a manifestation of the great power of the divine. Upon being told of the reputation of this renowned figure, he ordered that a white horse with a comb-ornament on a black background be presented to Mount Haguro in Dewa as a token of divine grace.

shigezane:shigezaneki-31.title: 1. The number of Uenosuke and Hamada Izu..
shigezane:shigezaneki-31.summary: 1. I intended to draw in the forces of Uenosuke and Hamada Izu, but the day has already set.
shigezane:shigezaneki-31.markdown:
1. He wished to withdraw the forces of Uenosuke and Hamada Izu, but the day had already grown dark. Believing that should they cross the river and prepare their defenses to the north and emerge from Kuwaori Shiyama, they would be unable to be repelled, he sent a messenger from Ueno to Tsukifune, stating, "I intend to withdraw from this location. I request that you proceed with the withdrawal without objection." In response, Tsukifune replied, "Indeed, you alone should withdraw. None else may do so." Ueno then stated further, "How could I alone possibly withdraw, abandoning Hamada Izu and his fellow retainers? If you insist on letting us pass, I shall also be forced to withdraw. If this is not permitted, I shall meet my end in battle." Upon hearing this, Yamori Sagami—Tsukifune's uncle—strongly voiced his dissent, saying, "You should first strike down Lord Ueno and prove the efficacy of your bow and arrow. Osaki is riddled with hollows. As Lord Masamune is a high-ranking lord, there is no reason to jeopardize Tsukifune's safety. If you refrain from your duty, your ruin is certain." However, Tsukifune, feeling it was pitiful to have his son-in-law struck down, replied, "If that is the case, those preparing for that purpose shall all be struck down by Ueno's allies." Accordingly, as he withdrew toward Matsuyama, forces from Nakashinden attacked and burned the bridge, forcing him to take refuge in Shinnuma, contrary to his expectations.

shigezane:shigezaneki-32.title: 1. The forces besieged in Niinuma..
shigezane:shigezaneki-32.summary: 1. As the forces besieged at Niinuma number as many as 5,000, they are on the verge of starvation, as there is no food even in the small area of Niinuma. Lord Masamune intended to dispatch his own private retainers to evacuate them, but due to the Sendo's consideration, this was not done.
shigezane:shigezaneki-32.markdown:
1. The forces besieged at Niinuma number 5,000; as there is no food in the small area of Niinuma, they are on the verge of starvation. Lord Masamune intended to dispatch his own private retainers to evacuate them, but due to the concerns of the Sendo, this was not done. The men of Niinuma argued, "We should push through Shiyama, cut down the enemies in our way, and withdraw to Matsuyama." However, Fukaya Gekkan advised, "The openings at both Kuwaori and Shiyama are narrow. Even if we did so, provided the terrain is favorable, it would not be difficult. If we cross the great river and engage from both sides, we would be caught off guard and perish in vain; therefore, we should first observe the situation." Upon hearing this, they desisted.

shigezane:shigezaneki-33.title: 1. Suzuki Iga of Momo..
shigezane:shigezaneki-33.summary: 1. Suzuki Iga of Momo and Kita-Ezamaryo of Furukawa went aside, sent a messenger to Niinuma, and summoned Otani Kazawa, stating, "If both Izumida Aki and Fukaya Gekkan are handed over as hostages, the various forces shall withdraw." He thus reported.
shigezane:shigezaneki-33.markdown:
1. Suzuki Iga of Momo and Kita-Ezamaro of Furukawa departed midway, sent a messenger to Niinuma, and summoned Otani Kazawa, stating: "If both Izumida Aki and Fukaya Gekkan are handed over as hostages, the various forces shall be withdrawn." This was agreed. Upon Otani Kazawa's withdrawal and this announcement, a man named Yumura Genzaemon, a retainer of Izumida Aki, said: "We have already slain many and are prepared to die in battle. If the various forces are withdrawn and Aki alone is left alive to be beheaded, it would be a profound disgrace after death; therefore, Aki must not agree to this." This was agreed. Gekkan said: "Since both of us are witnesses and will assist the various forces in serving Lord Masamune, we must certainly act as witnesses. What are your thoughts, Lord Aki?" Genzaemon replied: "I can only imagine your feelings." As they argued, Aki said: "There is no need for Genzaemon to speak. We shall not concern ourselves with others; even a single one of us should be handed over as a hostage." This was agreed. Both left Niinuma on February 23 and went to a place called Arigabukuro, at which point the various forces were withdrawn to Matsuyama. Hamada Izu, Konarita Sozaemon, and Yamagishi Shuri reported to Yonezawa and stated the status of the Osaki bows and arrows; the command was that, having acted too deeply and overstepped bounds this time, they should consult with Ujiie Danjo, seize the two castles at Kuwaori Shiyama, and add them to Danjo's holdings.

shigezane:shigezaneki-34.title: 1. From Mogami to Yoshiaki……
shigezane:shigezaneki-34.summary: 1. Yoshiaki (Yoshimitsu) of Mogami dispatched men known as Nobezawa Noto to Arigabukuro; Noto met with Tsukikan of Nagai. What did they discuss? Tsukikan returned to Fukaya, and Aki Izumida alone accompanied him to Onoda.
shigezane:shigezaneki-34.markdown:
1. From Mogami, Yoshiaki (Yoshimitsu) and a man named Nobezawa Noto were dispatched to Arigabukuro. Noto met with Tsukikan of Nagai; what did they discuss? Tsukikan returned to Fukaya, and Aki Izumida alone was sent to Onoda. Aki was handed over to both Genban and Kurozaemon, the lords of Onoda Castle. That night, Noto and Aki visited the inn and said, "It has been agreed among Aizu, Soma, Satake, and Iwaki that you shall take up arms against Lord Date; accordingly, a messenger from Soma named Tochikubo Mataemon has been dispatched. You and your retainers should unite and harbor treason." To this, Aki replied, "We shall lay down our lives in the service of our lord and take refuge in Niinuma. We shall support the various forces. Regarding the matter of arms and arrows, we know nothing of it. We beg that our heads be taken immediately." Noto then said, "What Aki has stated is without parallel," and granted him a reward. Aki thought, "I wish to report this to Lord Masamune," and accordingly, he sent a shinobi messenger named Saito Magoemon to Sendai to report the matter in detail.

shigezane:shigezaneki-35.title: 1. Lord Yoshiaki Mogami..
shigezane:shigezaneki-35.summary: 1. Lord Yoshiaki Mogami, though Lord Masamune's uncle, frequently took up the bow and arrow during the reign of Lord Terumune. In recent years, however, he has been particularly cordial.
shigezane:shigezaneki-35.markdown:
1. Lord Yoshiaki Mogami was Lord Masamune's uncle, yet he frequently took up arms during the reign of Lord Terumune. In recent years, however, he had been particularly cordial. Nevertheless, Lord Yoshiaki was a man of great importance—having forced both brothers of his house to commit seppuku—and thus one must not let one's guard down. Lord Masamune maintained a strong military presence in Nihonmatsu and Shiomatsu, and since Satake, Aizu, Iwaki, Ishikawa, and Shirakawa were all his enemies, he consulted with the aforementioned generals, intending to launch an offensive against the Date and seize Nagai. Ultimately, however, the Date forces were defeated at Osaki, and as a hostage of the region, Izumida Aki was to be handed over to Mogami. Believing that the situation in Yonezawa had reached a breaking point, he arranged a meeting with a man named Ayugai Totaro on the Mogami border; on March 13, Tensho 15, Ayugai Totaro delivered the agreement. Upon hearing this, Lord Masamune decreed that the matter must be settled immediately without further delay. The senior retainers advised, "Reinforcements may arrive from Mogami. Furthermore, others may approach Mogami; therefore, we should be mindful of the situation before proceeding." To this, he replied, "While your advice is most reasonable, if that is the case, I shall not leave Yonezawa; thus, we must settle the matter at Ayugai." Having received this order, he immediately set out. As not a single rider from Mogami provided assistance, Totaro repeatedly urged Mogami to "dispatch reinforcements," but none were sent. Furthermore, upon receiving word that Lord Masamune was departing Yonezawa, Totaro immediately withdrew to Mogami; thus, there were no further complications in Nagai.

shigezane:shigezaneki-36.title: 1. The Fukaya Gekkan is..
shigezane:shigezaneki-36.summary: 1. Fukaya Gekkan served as the brother-in-law to Soma Nagato. Lord Masamune heard that Gekkan had fired a musket without a ball even at Shimo-shinden, and remarked, "Such things may indeed happen."
shigezane:shigezaneki-36.markdown:
1. Fukaya Gekkan served as the brother-in-law to Soma Nagato. Lord Masamune heard that Gekkan had fired a musket without a ball even at Shimo-shinden, and remarked, "Such things may well happen. Fukaya lies on the border with Osaki. Since it is also adjacent to Lord Soma, it is hardly surprising that he would harbor such rebellious intentions." Accordingly, he was placed under the custody of a man named Akiu Settsu-no-kami and ordered to commit seppuku.

shigezane:shigezaneki-37.title: 1. Ujiie Danjo Chika Mikawa……
shigezane:shigezaneki-37.summary: 1. Ujiie Danjo Chika-Mikawa, unlike his children, served Osaki Yoshitaka and resided at Nao Castle, where he held the castle and served Yoshitaka.
shigezane:shigezaneki-37.markdown:
1. Ujiie Danjo Chika-Mikawa, unlike his children, served Osaki Yoshitaka and resided at Nao Castle, managing the castle while serving Yoshitaka. When Lord Masamune grew suspicious of Ujiie Danjo, he stated, "As he serves Yoshitaka, I find this entirely reasonable. Nevertheless, I have repeatedly submitted written oaths stating that I hold no objections, and since these have been duly heard, I ask that you grant him leniency." Accordingly, Konarita Soemon was dispatched to Iwadeyama; however, Ujiie Danjo died of illness, and Konarita Soemon was entrusted with all affairs as if he were the lord of Iwadeyama Castle. When the Kanpaku Hideyoshi departed for Odawara and the Osaki, Kasai, and Kimura Ise-no-kami were granted fiefs, Konarita Soemon also ascended from Iwadeyama.

shigezane:shigezaneki-38.title: I. Kurokawa Gesshu's Rebellious Heart..
shigezane:shigezaneki-38.summary: 1. As Gesshu Kurokawa had turned against us and Masamune had set his sights on Osaki's bows and arrows, yet none were available as he had desired, he privately resolved to subdue Gesshu; however, having dispatched forces to Satake, Aizu, Iwaki, and Ishikawa and advanced as far as Motomiya...
shigezane:shigezaneki-38.markdown:
1. Because Tsukishu Kurokawa had committed treason, Lord Masamune had summoned the forces of Osaki; however, as none arrived as desired, he privately resolved to subdue Tsukishu. Yet, as forces from Satake, Aizu, Iwaki, and Ishikawa had marched out and reached as far as Motomiya, he deemed it appropriate that the aforementioned parties also proceed, and thus refrained from action. The following year, when peasants gathered at Naeshiroda in Ouchi Bizen, he dispersed them and dealt with the rebellion; consequently, following another disturbance of forces along the Sendo region, those forces reached as far as Aizu, and Lord Masamune deemed them the forces of the Kanto region, failing to mention the matter of Osaki. However, upon Lord Hideyoshi's departure for Odawara, these forces were recalled as far as Aizu. As Osaki, Kasai, and Kimura Ise-no-kami had been granted fiefs and had descended, Ueno—being Tsukishu's son-in-law—petitioned that his life be spared, requesting that the forces be withdrawn. When Ueno reported this to Lord Masamune, the latter commanded: "During the time of the Osaki conflict, Tsukishu committed treason and several of his retainers were killed in battle; therefore, Tsukishu's head must be taken immediately." Despite Ueno's repeated petitions, these were not granted, and he was instead handed over to Genban of Akino-Sakai. Ueno went to Yonezawa and petitioned persistently: "During the time of the Osaki conflict, Tsukishu was granted rewards through Hamada Izu, Tate (Tade) Sukesaburo, Miyauchi Inaba, and ourselves; thus, our lives were spared. This is not mentioned in my current petition. As you know, Tsukishu was my superior; therefore, I request that a fief be granted to us. As for Tsukishu's life, I beg that you spare it." To this, the Lord replied that while he found the matter of Tsukishu utterly regrettable, Ueno's life would be spared. Ueno received Tsukishu from Genban and returned to Rifu, feeling profoundly satisfied. Thereafter, Tsukishu was granted a measure of leniency following his petitions, was granted a residence in Sendai, and occasionally visited the Lord. Upon hearing that Yamori Sagami and Kuwaori had strongly voiced dissent against Tsukishu, and further that Tsukishu had adopted the crest of Lord Masamune's personal small flag as his own, the Lord felt great resentment; consequently, he sent his wife and children to Oguni and placed them under the custody of Minbu Kamikoriyama, ultimately sentencing them—including Sagami and his wife—to death.

shigezane:shigezaneki-39.title: 1. In Tensho 15, although Mogami and Osaki were armed with bows and arrows..
shigezane:shigezaneki-39.summary: 1. In Tensho 15, although Mogami and Osaki were under military threat, the Asaka region remained safe for the time being, and nothing of consequence occurred. The three locations of Naeshiroda, Ota, and Arai were under our jurisdiction.
shigezane:shigezaneki-39.markdown:
1. In Tensho 15, although Mogami and Osaki were engaged in archery and warfare, the area around Asaka remained safe, and nothing of consequence occurred. The three locations of Naeshiroda, Ota, and Arai were under our jurisdiction. Despite being near enemy territory, as they were safe, we returned the peasants to their respective homes. In Naeshiroda, being near the enemy territory of Ago-ga-shima (Asako-ga-shima) and Takatama, we gathered the peasants at the old castle and granted them land. Ouchi Bizen came to us and said, "Due to unforeseen circumstances, I have defied the will of Lord Masamune and ended up in such a state. When I was dispatched from Obama, two senior retainers from Aizu expressed differing views, stating that it would be impossible to retain Shiomatsu. The reason is that I heard Lord Masamune had summoned the lands of Iwakado and inspected the terrain. It seems he is wondering whether he will be reprimanded or if he will be stationed nearby. If that is the case, even if he is stationed nearby, the route to Nihonmatsu will be blocked. However, if that were the case, it would be impossible to withdraw from Obama. Since the lineage of the Aizu senior retainer Matsumoto Tosho-no-suke had ended, I requested that this land be granted to me as vacant territory, and I stated that the Aizu senior retainer should serve me. However, not only was the matter of the fief ignored, but even the provisions for my sustenance were not provided, leaving me in a state where I would starve to death. I humbly petition Lord Masamune and beg that we (Shigezane) be granted a small amount of land and employed in his service. Nevertheless, as I fear that even if I speak thus in defiance of his will, it may not reach his ears, I propose that my younger brother, Katahira Sukeemon, serve him, and in exchange, we ask that you grant us a pardon." In response, I, Katakura Kojuro, stated, "Regarding Ouchi Bizen, he should be employed. As for the details, since Lord Kiyoaki's departure, Tamura has been without a master, and I have heard that things are handled privately. I believe Bizen wishes to serve his lord; if that is the case, what do you think? Furthermore, the lands of Katahira are south of Takatama and Asako-ga-shima; if Katahira Sukeemon serves, he cannot hold both of those lands and must withdraw to Aizu. Therefore, Takakura, Fukushima, and Koriyama are the lands he should serve; since he is well-suited for archery and warfare, Bizen should be summoned." Having stated this, his will was that while he felt regret over Ouchi's situation, around the time Lord Terumune passed away last year, the Satake, Aizu, and Iwaki forces had consulted and acted upon it at Motomiya. Since he felt regret over this disposition and intended to rebel again, he believed that while Bizen should be pardoned if Katahira serves, he wished to discuss this matter in detail. Therefore, I shall have the messenger mentioned above send various items to Bizen in due course. I mentioned this, but if I failed to inform Shiroishi Wakasa, I believed I would incur resentment; thus, I told Wakasa. Wakasa replied, "That is only natural. The peasants of Shiomatsu are Bizen's retainers; since I have looked after them in every way, it would be a great blessing if you could come here." We felt the same. I spoke of reporting this to Yonezawa. However, Bizen replied, "It is a nuisance that this matter was leaked. I am currently making the rounds in Aizu without concealment. If this becomes known, it would be impossible for me to commit seppuku." I replied, "I shall not speak of this to others. Shiroishi Wakasa is currently in Obama. It would be improper not to tell him of your service, so I told Wakasa. Will you inform him as well?" Afterward, Wakasa told us, "Bizen has sent word that he is relying on us; this is according to Wakasa's account. That is only natural. If anyone were to step forward, it would be for your own benefit." In Wakasa's view, Bizen was someone he recognized. Since Tamura was nearby, for several years, without the assistance of Satake or Aizu, he had taken up arms and won many battles; Lord Masamune was aware of this. Therefore, he felt that it would be impossible to have Wakasa return Shiomatsu to him, and he believed that if Wakasa did not serve, Bizen would be forced to commit seppuku in Aizu. For this reason, he stopped Ouchi from departing during last year. At the close of that year, Bizen looked after us, Aizu left, and Katahira was entrusted with the duties.

shigezane:shigezaneki-4.title: 1. Early July, Tensho 13..
shigezane:shigezaneki-4.summary: In early July of Tensho 13, I dispatched an envoy to Yonezawa, stating, "Regarding the matter of Inawashiro, a discrepancy has arisen, and I find it most troublesome."
shigezane:shigezaneki-4.markdown:
In early July of Tensho 13, I dispatched an envoy to Yonezawa, stating: "Regarding the matter of Inawashiro, there has been a discrepancy, and I find it most troublesome. As there is no official arrangement with Aizu, should you deem it appropriate to subjugate Ouchi Bizen, I propose that not a single person among the retainers of Bizen be dispatched to serve you. How shall this be handled?" Upon hearing this, your lordship acknowledged that there was no official arrangement with Aizu and withdrew his horses. He then decided that he should proceed to Shiomatsu. Since it was only proper that those serving him be dispatched, he ordered that arrangements be made immediately. Among our retainers, there was a man named Ouchi Naibun, also known as Ishii Genshiro, who had come from former Shiomatsu. I dispatched these two to Aoki Shuri, the lord of Karimatsuda Castle; they agreed that they should serve you and requested fiefs, so I had their official seals prepared. Hostages had long been taken from the lords of castles between Ouchi Bizen and the Tamura border. Whenever Lord Masamune's will was defied, hostages were taken from every lord in Shiomatsu. I took Aoki Shuri's younger brother, Shintaro (who was then known as Aoki Sabu), and a five-year-old child, and delivered the two of them to Obama as hostages. Shuri stated, "Since I serve in Yonezawa, I find it troublesome to abandon those hostages; I wish to request a change of hostages." Accordingly, I sent letters to the sons of the Ouchi Bizen elders—Nakazawa Kuroshiro, Ouchi Shinpachiro, and Okochi Jirokichi—stating, "As it is currently the season for bird-hunting, you should proceed." Since they were all young men and lacked discretion, they proceeded to Karimatsuda on the night of August 5. On the morning of the 6th, they went bird-hunting, caught 14 or 15 pheasants, cooked them, and drank heavily until midnight. Aoki Shuri then said, "Everyone is too drunk; we are in a state of delirium. Hand over your swords and short swords." The three men replied, "It is not a problem at all." However, Shuri had an ulterior motive. Being a man of no drink, he forcibly took the short swords, placed them in a chest, and spent the night without noticing that the three men had fallen asleep. Shuri then summoned about ten retainers, dressed them in armor, and while the three men lay there, he forced them awake. Shuri declared, "I harbor a grudge against Lord Ouchi Bizen and have thus rebelled to serve in Yonezawa. As you know, I have placed my brother Shintaro and my children as hostages in Obama; please do not concern yourself with the request for a change of hostages." The three men replied that they had no choice but to comply, but they were unable to do anything as their swords and short swords had been taken; they remained in Karimatsuda as hostages. That month, Shuri raised an army toward Obama and was defeated; he reported this to us, and I immediately sent a messenger to Yonezawa to report the matter. Your lordship decided that it would be too late for a military campaign and dispatched Koyanagawa Dorihata, Shiroishi Wakasa, Harada Samanosuke, and Hamada Izu. I then sent the two aforementioned men to encamp at Iino near Karimatsuda, while I encamped at a place called Tatsukoyama. Lord Masamune marched to Fukushima in December and dispatched Aoki Shuri and me to Fukushima. Upon our appearance, he expressed great pleasure at our service, bestowed upon us official insignia, and ordered that a map of Shiomatsu be completed. He sent the map-drawer to our lodgings, and once it was largely finished, he reviewed the map and deemed it suitable for operations near Karimatsuda. Since we were coming from Tamura, he ordered that we be stationed with Lord Kiyoaki, and further ordered that we operate at Kotemori. He moved his horses to Kawamata and met with Lord Kiyoaki at a place called Warabigahira on the 23rd, before ordering an operation at Kotemori on the 24th. However, due to heavy rain, the operation was postponed. On the 24th, during the operation at Kotemori, reinforcements from Aizu, Sendo, and Nihonmatsu arrived and reached the vicinity of Kotemori. Ouchi Bizen himself remained at Kotemori, appearing to be firmly entrenched in the castle. Although we attacked shortly thereafter, no one emerged from within, and many were seen inside the castle. There was no way to attack from this side, so as we were being repelled, we sent men from the rear to initiate a battle. The total force was repelled, and a battle ensued. The Aizu reinforcements also broke through, and it appears they coordinated from within the castle, launching an attack from two directions; the Nihonmatsu forces were the first to engage. Tamura attacked from the east, and the Date forces attacked from the north. Between them was a large mountain, making the Tamura forces useless in the battle. Lord Masamune, accompanied by about 500 musketeers from his hatamoto, pushed forward from the eastern mountainside, forcing their way in sideways. The men emerging from the castle were defeated, pushed into the palisade, and 50 heads were taken. Although many were killed, they fled south. The attendants fought with the Nihonmatsu forces and drove them back; the reinforcements were then pushed back and killed in small numbers. Ouchi Bizen returned to Obama that night. That night, he withdrew five ri and established a field camp. Fearing an overnight attack, he placed guards at every crossroads, but nothing happened. On the 25th, he pressed the attack, but no one emerged from the castle. The Aizu forces came to save him, but he prepared a defense at a spot called Nakakuki and pushed down into the passage toward the castle, though a few did not make it. At that time, he was repelled, and the field camp was moved slightly closer. Consequently, there was no clash with the Tamura forces. On the 26th, he attacked again, but no engagement occurred internally. To observe the situation inside, Kojuro Katakura suggested, "We should deploy muskets." Accordingly, about 700 to 800 muskets were deployed against the inner palisade, but the castle remained firmly entrenched; they were repelled, and the field camp was moved slightly closer. I suggested, "Tomorrow, we shall move our camp to the bamboo estate to the south and block the passage; therefore, we should close the main camp." Your lordship replied, "If that is the case, the reinforcements should retreat and block it." He further stated, "If that is the case, there will be no trouble. If we move the camp to the bamboo estate, we will clash with the Tamura forces; the Tamura forces will surely come to our camp, and we are likely to be caught between the Tamura forces and ourselves. Since the reinforcements and the main force will fight, there should be no concern regarding a clash from two directions. Furthermore, even if the reinforcements are defeated, the terrain is at a strategic point, so a battle will not be easily won. Even the day before yesterday, we pushed into the castle, and although the Nihonmatsu forces attacked fiercely, the castle was cleverly defended and withdrawn." To this, Harada Kyusetsu replied, "Moving the camp is utterly unnecessary. Since the battle is important, it shall be handled at a later date." He said this. Some argued that he should have forced us to move, and Kyusetsu's argument was considered reasonable; thus, that day, no battle took place and we remained at our camp.

shigezane:shigezaneki-40.title: 1. February 12, Tensho 16……
shigezane:shigezaneki-40.summary: 1. On February 12, Tensho 16, forces from three locations—Katahira, Yasukogashima, and Takatama—stormed Ouchi Bizen and Naeshiroda before dawn, slaughtering approximately 100 peasants residing in the old castle, and took a man named Honnai Shusui to be their leader...
shigezane:shigezaneki-40.markdown:
1. On February 12, Tensho 16, forces from three locations—Katahira, Yasukogashima, and Takatama—stormed Naeshiroda in the early hours of the morning. They slaughtered approximately 100 peasants residing in the old castle and forced a man named Honnai Shusui to commit seppuku; as they then set fire to the area and incited further unrest, the people of Ota and Arai also withdrew to Tamai. At the end of February, Ouchi Bizen approached us, stating repeatedly: "The agreement made last year has been exposed, and I am in a position where I must commit seppuku; as I find this a burden, I beg your forgiveness regarding my conduct in your domain. Should you grant me further pardon, I intend to enter service in Yonezawa, so please mediate on my behalf." To this, we replied: "Do not seek pardon anywhere; seek it in our own fiefs. Since Honnai Shusui has committed seppuku, we shall not be permitted to mediate. Who is there whom we may turn to for help?" Upon hearing this, a messenger from Ouchi Bizen, a relative of Honnai Shusui, was dispatched. Those relatives were all stationed at Tamai, on the border. When they filed a lawsuit with us, they stated: "The peasants of Tamai are hereditary vassals of Lord Ukyo of Nihonmatsu; we were concerned whether we should notify them even if they were planting grass. Furthermore, since Katahira Sukeemon is in service, this matter is of some importance. As Yasukogashima and Takatama are beyond our control, the Bizen brothers should provide assistance." Having thus stated this, we again sent Kojuro to Yonezawa, to which the reply was: "While it is regrettable that Naeshiroda was scattered, since it has been said that Katahira Sukeemon shall enter service, he shall be summoned. If Sukeemon does not enter service, Ouchi alone shall not be summoned." As this was the will of the lord, we conveyed it accordingly. Once Sukeemon had entered service, four or five nearby villages were designated as recipients; when this was reported to Yonezawa, Hobara was assigned to Bizen, and a seal was granted to Sukeemon, and Kojuro was dispatched. Subsequently, Sukeemon stated: "Although Segami Tango has been disowned, I have taken him as a son-in-law and promised to hand over the representative title; therefore, I beg your forgiveness." When this was reported, the reply was: "Since even the relatives of Nakano Hitachi are regretted, they shall not be summoned." Thus it was commanded. When this was conveyed, Sukeemon stated: "If that is the case, I shall not enter service. Even if I have received the seal, I shall return it." As this was stated, the matter was delayed for about twenty days, until finally the matter with Segami Tango was settled before the lord; Kojuro returned to Nihonmatsu, and we agreed to wait for Bizen and Sukeemon to depart.
