shigezane:shigezaneki-41.title: 1. Around February 12–13, Tensho 16..
shigezane:shigezaneki-41.summary: 1. Around February 12–13, Tensho 16, at a place under our control called Tamai, upon reaching the mountainside from Takatama—a place called Nishihara, four or five ri away from Tamai—we crossed the true grass, and the men of Tamai, lacking military discipline, drove them far away...
shigezane:shigezaneki-41.markdown:
1. Around February 12–13, Tensho 16, at a place under our control called Tamai, we encountered a group called Nishihara, who had been positioned at the mountain edge of Takatama—separated from Tamai by four or five ri. Seeing them cross the brush, the people of Tamai, lacking military discipline, drove them far away. Observing this, we resolved to strike them down and seize them, employing a clever tactic. On March 23, we consulted that we should plant a trap at a place called Yazawa, located near the vicinity of Tamai, along the mountain path toward Takatama. Until that time, Bizen and Sukeemon had also been assigned to our service, but as no word had been given regarding their side, the men from Katahira and Yasukogashima were stationed at Takatama on the night of the 22nd. We had previously agreed that if a trap were set in enemy territory, we would have to report it; accordingly, on the night of the 22nd, we went to the main camp and reported that a trap would be set at Tamai tonight. We then set out, and with the forces from the main camp and Tamai, we waited from the morning of the 23rd. However, no trap was set, and they asked, "Are you lying?" and withdrew. During the day, 20–30 men approached the vicinity of Tamai; we encountered them and withdrew 20–30 men in return. We caught up with them at a place called Taihata and engaged them in battle. Having observed their advance the previous day, we had hidden about 200 men at Yazawa and prepared for a strike. From the moment the battle began, we intended to withdraw, and the enemy gradually began to retreat. Believing the people of Tamai to be cunning, we forced our withdrawal; the enemy collapsed and broke ranks. The men from the strike were impatient and advanced quickly, so they were not struck down, but the allies collapsed and were pushed back to the riverbank where the battle had begun, and 2–3 men were slain. While we were repelling the enemy at the river, Takatama Tarozaemon was riding his horse sideways between the enemy and us. A man named Shigayama Saburo—a foot page of ours who had previously shot at them with a gun—waited for the two sides to fire their guns. As Tarozaemon rode his horse back sideways across a small stream, we fired two bullets; one struck him in the shoulder, and the other struck Tarozaemon in the thigh. He immediately leaped back from his horse and charged; the enemy also withdrew, but without collapsing. As they climbed a small slope, Yama Saburo struck the rear wheel of the saddle with a spear, and with two bullets, we struck the remaining parts. Shuzen looked down, drew his small flag, and gave it to his younger brother, Uneme, saying, "If we are repelled, they will surely collapse; therefore, you take my place as Shuzen, serve as the rearguard, and ensure a decisive victory." He then charged forward and was killed. The trap was a ruse by both Takatama Tarozaemon and Ota Shuzen; once the two were repelled, the enemy collapsed. We took 153 heads during the pursuit. Although we intended to take many more, the terrain in the mountain valley was poor. They fled in disorder, so we took only a few. I later heard that some did not return to the camp that night. The above heads were decapitated, their noses scraped, and salted, then sent to Yonezawa.

shigezane:shigezaneki-42.title: 1. On March 23 of the same year..
shigezane:shigezaneki-42.summary: 1. On March 23 of the same year, upon returning from the Battle of Tamai, Kojuro was instructed to wait for Ouchi Bizen and Katahira Sukeemon, who had gone out; accordingly, he proceeded to Nihonmatsu and remained there. On the night of April 5, a man named Kajiuchi Danjo...
shigezane:shigezaneki-42.markdown:
1. On March 23 of the same year, after the Battle of Tamai, upon returning, Kojuro was informed that Ouchi Bizen and Katahira Sukeemon had departed and that they should wait for them. Accordingly, he proceeded to Nihonmatsu and remained there. On the evening of April 5, a man named Kajiuchi Danjo—a nephew of Ouchi Bizen—visited the residence of Katakura Kojuro and said, "Bizen is proceeding to the main castle tonight. Tomorrow, Katahira Sukeemon shall be executed." Upon hearing this, Katakura Kojuro and Katahira Sukeemon (Takemizu's note: possibly a clerical error for Ouchi Bizen), along with their retainers, proceeded to the main castle. When they met Bizen on the morning of the 6th, Bizen stated, "Although we have firmly agreed that Sukeemon shall also serve, due to a minor incident that occurred between brothers, he has been ordered to commit seppuku; therefore, we have finally arranged this." Upon hearing this, Kojuro resolved that Sukeemon should not serve; however, for the sake of Bizen's own standing, Bizen likely said, "Sukeemon shall serve," and asked whether, once Ouchi arrived, Sukeemon would eventually serve, or whether Katahira's land would be exchanged for that of Aizu. As things stood, this could not be left as is. The bond between brothers was severed; after consulting with Kojuro, he reported the matter to both men. When Ouchi departed, they agreed that even if they were few in number, they would not act without first performing a feat; thus, they agreed to launch an operation at Yasukogashima. Shiroishi Wakasa, Katakura Kojuro, and ourselves—three men in total—proceeded to Yasukogashima, but not a single person from within emerged. As there was no way to force them to serve, we withdrew. The following day, when we attempted another operation, a man named Ishikawa Danjo, who resided within Shiomatsu, transferred to Soma and was executed within the fief of Shiroishi Wakasa; as signs of fire appeared, Wakasa returned midway through the operation. We and Kojuro carried out the attack, but nothing happened. Kojuro returned to Omori on the 8th, and Ouchi Bizen requested an audience at Yonezawa; as he wished to be granted an audience, we, among the retainers, accompanied him, accompanied by a man named Endo Suruga, and escorted him to Yonezawa.

shigezane:shigezaneki-43.title: 1. Regarding Ishikawa Danjo, on April 15..
shigezane:shigezaneki-43.summary: 1. On April 15, at the time of Danjo Ishikawa, the castle said to be held by Wakasa Shiroishi was overgrown with grass; Danjo himself had also gone out and was staying in the enclosure. Early in the morning, two men emerged from within and were cut down by the grass; as they encountered them from within the castle, Danjo and his companions came to their aid...
shigezane:shigezaneki-43.markdown:
1. Regarding the castle said to be held by Shiroishi Wakasa, as of April 15, Ishikawa Danjo had planted grass and himself had gone out to prepare for the siege. Early in the morning, two men emerged from within and were cut down by the grass; as they encountered them from within the castle, Danjo assisted them, drove back those who had emerged from within, seized the castle, and pressed the attack. As the sound of musket fire was heard frequently, Danjo saw Shiroishi Wakasa assisting them and drew his sword to engage in a battle, whereby Wakasa emerged victorious. Approximately 20 heads were taken. We also received musket fire at Nihonmatsu and immediately fired back, but due to the distance, our response was delayed, and we charged in as Wakasa was returning. Wakasa was delighted and escorted us to Miyamori, returning with exceptional hospitality. The man called Danjo was originally Kukichi, the lord of Shiomatsu, and was a member of the general retainer corps. He was a peer of Bizen. As Kukichi's conduct was unsatisfactory, the retainers consulted and removed him. Bizen-oya had at that time entered the service of the Date. Danjo-oya had entered the service of Lord Tamura Kiyoaki. Thereafter, during the period when the Date were procuring bows and arrows, Bizen also entered the service of Lord Kiyoaki and resided nearby; thus, he rendered service to them. Furthermore, during the time when the retainers of Katahira Sukeemon and Iwaki—who were retainers of Tamura Uma-no-kami—were engaged in quarrels in the field, a request was made that the retainers of Uma-no-kami be punished; however, as no agreement was reached, he held a grudge, and from the following year, he entered the service of Aizu and Satake, rendering service to Tamura for several years. Ishikawa Danjo continued to serve Tamura in the same manner. Nevertheless, Lord Masamune took possession of Shiomatsu. Danjo's fief was within Shiomatsu. Since there had been a promise that if Lord Masamune, acting as the representative, were transferred to the Tamura side, Danjo would also transfer to Tamura and serve him, Danjo was assigned to the Date by the will of Lord Kiyoaki to serve Lord Masamune. Additionally, there were four or five others from the former Shiomatsu, including Moriyayama-jo and Ouchi Noto. Those who had removed Kukichi's retainers to serve Tamura were all assigned to the Date. Those men were assigned to Shiroishi Wakasa as the lord, while Ishikawa Danjo alone was employed directly. His original fief was returned to him as before.

shigezane:shigezaneki-44.title: I. November, Tensho 14. Since Lord Kiyoaki's departure
shigezane:shigezaneki-44.summary: 1. November, Tensho 14. Since Lord Kiyoaki's departure, His Lordship has resided at the main castle in Miharu, accompanied by his ladies. However, all affairs are managed by four men: Tamura Gessai, Tamura Baisetsu, Tamura Uemon, and Hashimoto Gyobu.
shigezane:shigezaneki-44.markdown:
I. November, Tensho 14. Since Lord Kiyoaki's departure, the Lord of the Main Castle in Miharu has been occupied by the Lady of the North and her ladies. Nevertheless, all affairs are managed by four men: Tamura Gessai, Tamura Baisetsu, Tamura Uemon, and Hashimoto Gyobu. At that time, Lord Masamune and his wife were in an uneasy state. Privately, the Lord of the North harbored resentment. Gessai and Gyobu reasoned that even if the couple were in an uneasy state, they should not rely on Lord Masamune, for that would be contrary to the house's standing. Baisetsu and Uemon reasoned that since the Lady of the North was the aunt of Soma Yoshitane, they should support her—even if she were a lady—and rely on Soma, as it would be acceptable for Tamura to commit a breach of loyalty toward Lord Masamune; thus, they proposed relying on the Date, as their true intention was to win over Soma. The intentions of Gessai's faction and Baisetsu's faction were thus divided, though generally they agreed to serve the Date. However, there was a man named Okoshi Kii-no-kami, who was a member of the Tamura house and a cousin of Soma Yoshitane; he held the second-highest rank in the Tamura house. This man coordinated with Soma and devised a private scheme. Furthermore, there were four or five Soma ronin within the Tamura house who held castles, so they were all aligned with Soma. The most prominent among them was Baisetsu's son, Tamura Uma-no-kami, the lord of Ono Castle. These two men coordinated with Soma. At one point, Gessai and Gyobu told Shiroishi Wakasa, "We have coordinated with Okoshi Kii-no-kami, and his rebellion is evident; we wish to bring him under our service." They reported this to Yonezawa. Subsequently, Lord Masamune sent a letter to us and commanded that a messenger be dispatched. When we sent one, Gessai and Gyobu reported that the Lord wished to bring Okoshi Kii-no-kami under his service. The Lord replied that this was unnecessary, but felt that if he were not brought under service, it would lead to an emergency for the Tamura house. Gessai's faction was concerned by this. Tamura wished to elevate two men and believed they should be brought under service. Thus, the Lord commanded, "Since Kii is requesting your service, inform him so that he does not let his guard down." Among our retainers, there was a man named Monzaki Sama who had been on close terms with Kii for a long time. A messenger from Kii, a man named Okoshi Bizen, visited Uma-no-kami previously and mentioned that he had some business and that Bizen should be sent over. When Bizen arrived, he inquired about the state of the Tamura house and spoke candidly, believing that Lord Masamune would speak as he had requested. When he met Bizen and inquired about the state of the Tamura house, Bizen kept everything to himself, fearing that speaking directly of such grave matters would be inappropriate; therefore, he had Uma convey the story. After Bizen returned, Kii stopped attending to Miharu and remained secluded in his castle. The four elders of the Tamura house sent a messenger to Kii, saying, "For what reason have you not come out? If you know the reason, please tell us everything." Kii initially hesitated, but after persistent questioning, he replied, "Since Shigezane is attending to Miharu, I shall be brought under service; therefore, I shall not come out." The four men of the Tamura house then reported back to us, saying, "Okoshi Kii is requesting service and wishes to be brought under our care; since we were told not to come out, we did not do so. How did you hear of this and report it to Kii?" We replied, "How could we have spoken of such things? Since the Tamura house's affairs are so difficult, we believe this must be settled. There is no need to report such difficult matters." The four men then told Kii, "Since we have explained it to Shigezane, he will surely not speak of it in such a manner; therefore, he should have attended." When Kii replied that Uma would certainly inform him of this, we received further word from Kii. We then told the Tamura men, "Having heard the details from Uma, we maintain that we have been on close terms with Lord Kii for a long time, but the world speaks of Lord Kii as having changed his heart; if that is your understanding, attendance at Miharu is unnecessary. Whether you are harmed or brought under service is beyond our comprehension." We expressed our differing view. Since Shigezane had said so, we argued that there must have been a misunderstanding regarding Okoshi Bizen. We replied accordingly to the Tamura house. The four men of the Tamura house then said, "Uma and Okoshi Bizen should both come out and face him." We replied, "If Bizen comes out, Uma should be sent along." In early February, a messenger was sent to a place called Oni-uda, stating that Okoshi Bizen had come out. When asked, "Has an inspector come from Tamura?" the reply was, "No inspector has come." We then said, "If there is no inspector, Uma should not be sent." Consequently, Okoshi Bizen returned. Afterward, a messenger was sent to Tamura, stating, "We heard that Uma was sent out recently, but no inspector was sent; therefore, he has not come out. He should be sent out again, accompanied by an inspector." The Tamura men were satisfied, and two inspectors were sent, and they proceeded to Oni-uda; Uma also accompanied them. Regarding the confrontation, Bizen said, "Based on that, I inform Shigezane that he should not attend Miharu." Uma replied, "If that is your understanding, we state that attendance is unnecessary; if you do not attend, it will appear to be a plot of rebellion. If you truly do not misunderstand, you shall attend Miharu. There shall be no dispute in Miharu." With that, he returned without further conflict. Because the arrangement was so difficult, we consulted among ourselves on whether to rely on the Date or how else to handle the situation. A man named Tokiwa Iga was the first to speak, saying, "There is no need for consultation. While Lord Kiyoaki was alive, Lord Masamune succeeded him as the representative, so there is no need for further deliberation. However, each should act according to their own judgment." Since no one else offered a different opinion, it seemed that Iga's words were the most reasonable. Nevertheless, the higher authority leaned toward the Date, while privately they leaned toward the Soma side. The details were that among the prominent ronin of the Tamura house, many were Soma retainers. Baisetsu and Uemon privately coordinated with Soma, claiming that the Soma ronin were their peers and were on close terms; thus, they were very close with Soma, as were Sendo Satake and the ronin of Aizu. Ishikawa Danjo was a peer of Baisetsu and Uemon and was aware of this. As mentioned previously, even if they served Lord Masamune for the time being in accordance with Lord Kiyoaki's wishes, it would be a matter of great importance for their future standing. Furthermore, since the Lady of the North was the aunt of Soma Yoshitane and the Lord of the North and his wife were in an uneasy state, Lord Masamune would likely harbor resentment. Danjo, aware of this, informed Soma, and on April 7, the matter was settled.

shigezane:shigezaneki-45.title: 1. The preceding section details the circumstances of Ishikawa Danjo's treason..
shigezane:shigezaneki-45.summary: 1. The preceding section details the treachery of Ishikawa Danjo. It records the circumstances of the Tamura tribute.
shigezane:shigezaneki-45.markdown:
I. The section above details the circumstances regarding the treason of Ishikawa Danjo. It records the proceedings of the Tamura military preparations. Regarding the matter at Asaka, on the night of April 5th, Ouchi Bizen launched a surprise attack; consequently, the Aizu and Asaka forces were dispatched to the Asaka contingent. Upon hearing that the Sukagawa forces were coordinating their actions, Kagetsuna Katakura, who was stationed at Omori, was informed of the matter and immediately proceeded to Nihonmatsu. He announced that the warriors of Shinobu should promptly mobilize, but as the news was sudden, not a single person arrived. Only Katakura and our party proceeded to Motomiya. Reports indicated that a force had been gathered at Takakura, but as there was no one to oversee them, we—the retainers of the Hachi-chome district—stationed about 20 cavalrymen and 50 muskets at Takakura. On April 17th, Takakura Omi arrived at Motomiya. As he was a veteran of the Nihonmatsu lineage and was well-versed in the affairs of Aizu and Asaka, he inquired, "Where will the action tomorrow be directed?" He was told, "It will be solely the Aizu and Sukagawa forces; it will not exceed 1,000 cavalrymen. The Sukagawa forces and the men from the Tamura border shall not participate, so there will not be a large number of troops. Most likely, they will push through and conduct operations as far as Motomiya." If this were the case, our forces would, depending on the enemy's movements, push up toward the Kannon-do and assist them at Takakura. This would depend on the outcome of the engagement. Should they again attempt an operation toward Motomiya, our forces would withdraw and not emerge; in that event, the enemy would surely establish a defensive line at the Kannon-do. If they were to lower their forces, it would be only natural. In that event, we would send a small number of men from within to engage the enemy, draw them toward the town entrance, and begin the battle. In such a case, we would deploy the forces of Haneda Umanosuke as the vanguard, with Katakura's forces providing support, while our own men would move without engaging in combat to push up the western flank toward the Kannon-do; this would surely disrupt the enemy's advance. If this did not happen, we would cut through from Takakura. A great victory would be certain. Since Takakura Castle is high, any movement toward a certain direction would be visible; thus, if forces were heading toward Takakura, the castle garrison would raise signal flags. It was agreed that if they moved toward Motomiya, we would push them east; Takakura Omi responded in kind. Consequently, on the 18th, signal flags were raised to the west of Takakura Castle, and it was said, "It appears they are moving toward Takakura." When forces were deployed down to the Kannon-do, signal flags were again raised to the east. It was said, "Are they moving toward Motomiya? We must withdraw our forces." Upon hearing this, we resolved to fight as we were and established our defenses. When Katakura and I launched an attack toward the Kannon-do, the enemy forces advanced in waves. Kanokoda Uemon broke through first, leading 40 to 50 ashigaru. I ordered Ishikawa Yahei, "You must engage Kanokoda." As he advanced smoothly, we intended to withdraw downward; I told him that if he continued, we would engage the forces at Motomiya. I dispatched the forces of Haneda Umanosuke and over 30 ashigaru, and after a musket exchange, Yahei charged through, breaking through the boundary between friend and foe, and withdrew. Uemon and his party were alone at first, but later about ten cavalrymen and over 100 ashigaru arrived. Katakura and I pushed the Kannon-do down, and the enemy—Umanosuke's men and Ishikawa Yahei's—were driven back and reached the Kannon-do; as we released our forces, the enemy collapsed. Umanosuke had a page named Bunkuro, who was 16 years old; when Bunkuro struck at the upper guard, Umanosuke turned him back and cut him down, returning two or three foot soldiers and taking their heads. Umanosuke then charged forward and engaged the two foot soldiers, driving the enemy back. The forces that had crossed from Hitotori Bridge toward here, having been overwhelmed by the defenses, fled across Hitotori Bridge and attempted to attack in some manner; however, they established a defensive line opposite the bridge and were pushed back again. Then, a man named Maedagawa Suketaro—a page to Lord Masamune who had been disowned and was relying on us—turned his horse and drove the enemy away. As he turned his horse sideways, a spear-bearer rushed back and struck the horse's belly, but simultaneously, musket fire and shoulder clashes broke out, and the spear-bearer was shot back. Sukegoro stood down, cast off his armor and equipment, entrusted himself to the retainers, took up a hand spear, became a foot soldier, knocked one rider off his horse, and immediately took the head, showing it to us. They were then driven back to the Kannon-do, where Ushizaka Sakon, Haneda Umanosuke, and Ishikawa Yahei engaged in a duel of cavalry. From there, the enemy was pushed back and driven back to Hitotori Bridge, where 43 heads were taken. Three of our party were killed, and the battle ended. If we had acted as discussed on the 17th, we would have slain them all, but because the signal flags were raised incorrectly, we did not achieve a great victory, which remains a regret to this day. Later, when inquiring about the signal flags, I was told that flags had been raised to the west to announce the success of today's operation. "I learned of that yesterday; it was unnecessary," I replied, but it was too late. I heard later that the Aizu forces, believing they had achieved an operation, took the elderly mother of Katahira Sukeemon as a hostage and returned home. I suspect they came from Aizu primarily to take hostages and acted without such intent. Having suffered a defeat, they withdrew to Wakamatsu; Katakura remained at Motomiya until the 21st, but the Aizu forces withdrew. When they arrived, he returned to Yonezawa on the 22nd.

shigezane:shigezaneki-46.title: 1. The Tamura retainers, and those who had reached an agreement with Soma..
shigezane:shigezaneki-46.summary: 1. The retainers of Tamura, those who had reached an agreement with Soma, and even those in the service of Date—all of whom have since rebelled—have committed treason; while it is believed that Lord Masamune should take the field, there has been no official word whatsoever. Accordingly, relying on Tamura Gessai, Hashimoto Gyobu, and Shiroishi Wakasa...
shigezane:shigezaneki-46.markdown:
1. Regarding the Tamura retainers, those who had reached an agreement with Soma, and those serving the Date—all of whom had committed treason through Ishikawa Danjo—it was believed that Lord Masamune should march forth. However, as no official order had been issued, Tsukisai of Tamura, Gyobu of Hashimoto, and Wakasa of Shiroishi were entrusted with the matter and reported to Yonezawa, stating: "Since Danjo has committed treason, we believe you should march forth and subdue him, yet no such action has been taken. While more than half of Tamura have reached an agreement with Soma, they are hesitant about Lord Masamune's march and have not severed ties; furthermore, Danjo has severed ties in order to draw out Soma Yoshitane. Therefore, we urge you to march forth." The Lord's response was that while it was only proper to march forth now that Ishikawa Danjo had committed treason, he possessed the finest bows and arrows. Although daimyo were stationed along the borders in various places, Nagai had only low-ranking retainers stationed along the Mogami border; thus, the Lord was concerned about leaving Yonezawa to march forth. Moreover, not a single piece of land held by Danjo had been granted to him, and since he had only been permitted to ride a horse for one or two engagements, the Lord expressed his displeasure and stated that the matter would be delayed. Tsukisai and Gyobu further pleaded, "No such arrangement exists in this world. The Tamura retainers know that no horse is resting; they should all align with Soma. No bow or arrow possesses such skill; thus, prolonged stays on horseback are impermissible. We urge you to march forth immediately, perform a single engagement, and ride a horse. Out of fear of your march, the men of Tamura have not yet severed their ties. If such measures are not taken, there is no doubt that the two of us will commit seppuku." Following these persistent pleas, a military order was issued, and the Lord marched to Omori on April 14, stayed there for five days, and moved to Shiomatsu Tsukidate on the 20th. The land held by Ishikawa Danjo was Chikuyama, his own castle. The castle of Kotemori—that land had come into the possession of Shiomatsu and was a castle granted to Danjo. The castle called "Todoroki" was on the Soma border, where Oya and Settsu resided. Since Kotemori was near Tsukidate, when an operation was carried out at Kotemori, Soma Yoshitane, having heard of Lord Masamune's march, arrived at Chikuyama one day prior. Ishikawa Danjo himself remained entrenched at Kotemori. Chikuyama was held by the Soma retainers. Lord Masamune, wishing to survey the terrain of Kotemori, passed from north to south and fired muskets from the inside, but the retainers accompanying him did not fire back and passed through. That day, nothing happened. As we were concerned about the southern route, we returned to Nihonmatsu that night. Although the weather was poor the following day, upon arriving at Tsukidate, we requested a delay in the operation and returned home. We continued to visit day after day, but the weather remained bad and no operation could be carried out; thus, on the 25th, we remained entrenched at Omori. Tsukisai and Gyobu were surprised by this and, relying on Wakasa of Shiroishi and themselves, stated: "Though you speak of a single engagement, we believe you should perform four or five days of work; yet, claiming it is due to the weather, you remain entrenched for one day. It seems you are overly concerned about the Mogami border. If the Tamura retainers realize this, those who until recently relied on the Date may change their minds. Therefore, since there is no horse-keeping at Omori and no unforeseen circumstances in either Tamura or Nagai, we believe you should strike quickly; we wish you to be aware that you remain entrenched at Omori." Finding this statement unavoidable, Wakasa accompanied them to Omori, and together with Harada Kyusetsusai, Moriya Shuhaku, Ito Hizen, and Katakura Kojuro, they reported as Tsukisai and Gyobu had said. Ito Hizen stated, "Your plea is reasonable, but as you know, there is not a single daimyo in Nagai. Only low-ranking retainers are stationed at the borders. Even if you say you should strike quickly, the Mogami border extends 200 ri from Omori, so it would be of little use. How do you feel about remaining here on horseback?" Wakasa of Shiroishi replied, "Do you have such a grandiose view of the situation in Tamura? Since Tsukisai and Gyobu have committed themselves to your service, we first intend to crush them; if you withdraw to Omori, neither of them will be of any use. It is difficult to foresee how things will turn out." Then Hizen added, "Even if you wish to keep Tamura under your care, if an emergency arises in Nagai, it would ultimately be futile; therefore, we wish to ensure that no emergency occurs." Kojuro stated, "This discussion is pointless. Please report this to your lord as you see fit." Having said this, they departed and reported the matter. The Lord's response was that while the two had spoken reasonably, he found it unavoidable; that this time, due to the weather, they had failed to act and had withdrawn to Omori; and that since they were remaining here on horseback and could strike quickly in any direction, Tsukisai and Gyobu should be at ease. Upon receiving this order, they returned, and Wakasa of Shiroishi reported the matter, to which Tsukisai and Gyobu were satisfied.

shigezane:shigezaneki-48.title: 1. At Tamura, there are various private grievances..
shigezane:shigezaneki-48.summary: 1. There are various private grievances in Tamura. Gessai and Gyobu stated, "Lord Masamune is staying at Omori, and Yoshitane is at Tsukiyama."
shigezane:shigezaneki-48.markdown:
1. Various private grievances have arisen in Tamura. Gessai and Gyobu stated, "Lord Masamune is stationed at Omori, and Yoshitane is at Tsukiyama. As for admitting people from both sides, how should that be handled? Neither the Date nor the Soma forces should be allowed to serve in any capacity." This was noted. Umeyuki and Uemon were informed of the situation, and consultations were held with other officials; however, all responded that "it is only appropriate," and neither of them conveyed this internally to Kojuro Katakura, nor did they send a messenger to do so.

shigezane:shigezaneki-49.title: 1. Soma Yoshitane, residing at Tsukiyama, ……
shigezane:shigezaneki-49.summary: 1. Soma Yoshitane was residing at Tsukiyama, during which time the retainers of Tamura convened, and it appears they held private discussions with him regarding the matter of the Northern Lord.
shigezane:shigezaneki-49.markdown:
1. Soma Yoshitane was residing at Tsukiyama; meanwhile, the Tamura retainers held consultations, and it appeared they were plotting a private meeting with the Northern Lord. On May 11, word arrived that Yoshitane had sent a messenger; a man named Shindate Yamashiro and Nakamura Sukeemon, both senior retainers of the Soma house, proceeded to Miharu and remained in the town that night. The common folk among them declared that neither the Date nor the Soma forces should be allowed to enter Miharu; they circulated among the people that if both men were present, they would appear tomorrow as if to pay a visit to Yoshitane and seize the castle. Nevertheless, early on the 12th, both Yamashiro and Sukeemon returned to the castle. Hashimoto Gyobu, believing that seppuku was inevitable, arrived before dawn and, after reporting to the inner quarters, served sake to the ladies of the house. Five men from Gyobu's side, three each, entered the castle carrying firearms, bows, spears, and armor. Gessai, Baisetsu, and Uemon did not attend. Yamashiro and Sukeemon also entered the castle with about 50 men, but they carried no equipment. Regarding the report that Soma Yoshitane had arrived, those who had entered were dressed in official attire. Baisetsu ascended to the castle at that time. The ladies of the house sent Gyobu out, and Yoshitane was soon summoned to the castle town. From the evening, a force led by Ogoshi had positioned themselves in a deep valley within the woods east of the castle, numbering about 700 to 800, armed with firearms, bows, and spears. However, while Soma Yoshitane was residing at Tsukiyama, Gyobu and Baisetsu conspired, stating that the Date forces should not be allowed in. They asked whether Yoshitane should be admitted, but Baisetsu replied that no, he must not be let in. Baisetsu had previously agreed that they should march out and seize the castle, but since Gyobu was a man of great merit, he argued that if Yoshitane were admitted, he should be struck down; thus, he maintained that Yoshitane must not be let in. Gyobu gave the order, and they donned their armor. All those who entered the castle carried armor and declared that Yoshitane must not be admitted. When they attempted to fire their firearms, Yoshitane seized about half of the castle and fired his guns and shot his bows, obstructing them. About 30 riders accompanying Yoshitane were present, but as they were all wearing only hakama, nothing could be done. In particular, a firearm hit Yoshitane in the neck; from there, they marched toward the eastern exit, but that exit was also blocked. Furthermore, as the terrain was poor, they attempted to advance with over 200 riders in armor, carrying bows and broken firearms, but they were too late to be of use; they did not return to Tsukiyama and immediately withdrew to Soma. Ogoshi Kii went out and said, "Please stop by," but they did not stop and returned. Shindate Yamashiro and Nakamura Sukeemon, fearing they might be slain within the castle, reported that since there was no such urgency, it would be unnecessary to proceed. Thus, they set out quickly, stating that Yoshitane's appearance was unnecessary, but Gyobu's men thrust their spears at them. Gyobu stopped them, declaring it was unnecessary, and pushed them forward, stating they should hurry and report that it was unnecessary; thus, the castle was held firmly. Word of the situation was sent from Tamura to Shiroishi Wakasa, and a messenger was dispatched to Omori; word reached them shortly after five o'clock at night. Consequently, Lord Masamune launched a swift attack and summoned Shiroishi Wakasa to his castle at Miyamori at five o'clock the following day, deploying forces from the Date and Shinobu domains to attack Tsukiyama over two days. As it was deemed difficult to deploy troops to Tamura, we remained at Shiroishi on the 12th and did not serve as attendants for those two days. On the 16th, an attack was launched on Kotemori, and as orders were given to attend, we proceeded to Kotemori and were summoned to observe the assault; we were stationed at Tsukiyama as reinforcements, while other troops, including the hatamoto, advanced and attacked, causing the castle to fall and everything to be set on fire. This time, there was no order to slaughter everyone; instead, we were ordered to scatter the enemy. We advanced through Miyamori, and the next day, we attacked a castle in Tamura called Okura, where a man named Hikoshichiro, the younger brother of Tamura Uemon, resided. There were many who had changed their allegiance, but they did not break ties. Since Hikoshichiro had mediated between Tsukiyama and Miharu at various times and served as an attendant during the transition, an attack was launched on Hikoshichiro's castle. A small breach was made and the town was cleared, and about ten houses were burned down, but not a single rider emerged from within, nor were there any reinforcements from the side. We approached a monk in Tamura named Bokuun, who had previously been requested to assist; we asked Gessai to intervene and apologized, intending to summon him, but as night fell, we returned to Miyamori. The total force was stationed in a field camp at Nishi. The following day, orders were given for the Soma forces to encamp at Ishizawa and launch an attack. However, as Tamura Hikokuro's arrival was delayed, orders were given to prepare for the defense of Okura and that any who failed to emerge from Okura should be punished. At that point, Hikoshichiro appeared and was ordered to lead the advance to Ishizawa. Ishizawa is a small area within Tamura, but the castle was clearly visible. Since the Soma forces were supporting them and appeared numerous, orders were given to station troops nearby. That night, orders were given to station horses at a small exit in a castle called Nishi, held by Shiroishi Wakasa; however, as there were no suitable houses, a field camp was suddenly established on the eastern mountain. At that moment, a great thunderclap struck, disturbing the troops in the field camp, and fires appeared at Tsukiyama. Despite the thunderclap, when scouts were sent, it was reported that Tsukiyama had been cleared and not a single person remained. Accordingly, it was decided that Ishizawa should also be cleared, and troops were dispatched, but none arrived. Ishikawa Danjo Chikaori had already cleared the area. The fighting was fierce, and the remaining lands held by Danjo fell. The castle was secured in two locations within Tamura, and forces were dispatched to drive them back to Miyamori.

shigezane:shigezaneki-5.title: 1 On the following 27th, yesterday..
shigezane:shigezaneki-5.summary: The following day, the 27th. Yesterday, I stated, "I intend to move my camp to the bamboo residence and cut through the path," and while half agreed, saying "that seems right," the other half did not concur.
shigezane:shigezaneki-5.markdown:
I. On the following 27th. Yesterday, I stated, "I intend to move my camp to the Bamboo Residence and cut through the passage." Half of the assembly agreed, saying, "That seems right," but they did not offer any objections. As the road was not particularly rough, I did not press the matter; however, since I had moved my camp to the Bamboo Residence before dawn, Date Ueno ordered that our camp be moved there as well, stating, "All camps shall be brought together." Accordingly, I transported the camp equipment. The total number of personnel worked as usual, taking their positions and facing the soldiers. Just then, a man emerged from within and waved a small flag toward our camp; upon sending someone to inquire, it was reported that members of our retainers had met him at Toyama and Nonoyama. The man was Ishikawa Kageyu; as I had been on cordial terms with him for some time, I crossed Shimotsuke to meet him. Kageyu stated, "In this castle, many men—including Ono Shusui and Arai Hannai, as well as Ouchi Bizen—are serving in person. Once the passage is cut, there is no way the castle will fall; therefore, I wish to apologize, surrender the castle, and be escorted to Obama." He requested my assistance, so I sent a messenger to report, "I have filed such a petition. Should I be summoned?" The Lord, deeming it appropriate to summon me, ordered my attendance. However, he decreed that those within the castle must not be sent to Obama. He wished for me to surrender to Date; thus, I summoned Ishikawa Kageyu and reported as requested. Kageyu then emerged and said, "The men within the castle state that surrendering to Date is a plea for mercy. Since Ouchi Bizen would not commit seppuku, we wish to offer a sacrifice of our own lives and have thus filed this petition; this is something we have long intended. As stated above, we request to be sent to Obama." Upon hearing this, the Lord ordered it exactly as stated: they shall not be sent to Obama, but shall be escorted back to Date. At that time, I crossed to Shimotsuke and Kawa-futae to report on the situation. The Lord sent another messenger, stating that since the men within the castle had not acted treacherously, he wished to proceed with the attack. He decreed that if the inner bailey did not fall, the men of the castle would be escorted back to Date; thus, he ordered the general assault. I finally stormed the castle. Those from Shimotsuke eventually emerged from within. As our forces set fire to the area, we immediately blew the flames up at the mountain castle, spreading them in all directions and pressing the enemies in; we set fire to every location. Unexpectedly, some of the inner retainers left their posts; the attack began at the hour of the Horse, and by the hour of the Dog, the inner bailey fell. The Lord ordered a wholesale slaughter; he stationed lookouts in various places and cut down not only the men, but even the wives, cattle, and horses, withdrawing at dusk. Those who managed to blend in with our side were treated as enemies and slaughtered without exception. That night, we moved to the New Castle and Kikoriyama enemy territories. Both castles were set on fire and destroyed. In the early hours of the 28th, an order was issued to move to Kikoriyama. As I went to take my position at the camp and called for the men, a man named Hattori Gennai—a former retainer of mine who now served at Shiomatsu—approached me and said, "Now that the Tsukidate has been destroyed, we must pursue them immediately." Following his lead, I pursued them, quickly destroyed the fortifications, and entered the castle. I reported this to the Lord, who then returned his horse to Tsukidate and rested for twenty-two or twenty-three days.

shigezane:shigezaneki-50.title: Not to mention Ichigetsusai and Gyobu..
shigezane:shigezaneki-50.summary: Needless to say, Ichigatsusai and Gyobu—as well as Baisetsu, Uemon, and the other samurai who had reached an agreement with Soma—reported that those who had ventured slightly outward had gone to Miyamomori to attend court, that Ishikawa Danjo had been subdued, and that Tamura was now firmly secured and a cause for celebration.
shigezane:shigezaneki-50.markdown:
Not to mention Ichigetsusai and Gyobu...

1. Not to mention Ichigetsusai and Gyobu... Baisetsu, Uemon, and the other samurai who had reached an agreement with Soma—those who had been somewhat prominent—reported to Miyamomori and stated that Ishikawa Danjo had been subdued and that Tamura was now firmly secured. Among them, Tokiwa Iga also reported. While these matters were being discussed, it was openly stated that the Date should be relied upon; upon hearing that all were in accord with this, the Lord was greatly pleased and bestowed upon them waist-sashes adorned with gold noshi.

shigezane:shigezaneki-51.title: 1. Tamura Gessai, Tamura Baisetsu, Tamura Uemon, Hashimoto Gyobu…
shigezane:shigezaneki-51.summary: 1. Tamura Gessai, Tamura Baisetsu, Tamura Uemon, and Hashimoto Gyobu attended Miyamori, and together with Kojuro Katakura, Hizen Ito, and Kyusetsu Harada, the three stated, "Since the commencement of the Okoshi Kii affair, we have not served Tamura; and since the onset of Tamura's current plot of rebellion..."
shigezane:shigezaneki-51.markdown:
1. Tamura Gessai, Tamura Baisetsu, Tamura Uemon, and Hashimoto Gyobu attended at Miyamori and reported to Kojuro Katakura, Ito Hizen, and Harada Kyusetsu, stating: "Since the commencement of the Okoshi-Kii affair, we have not served Tamura; and since the onset of Tamura's treasonous plot, that man has remained secluded; therefore, we request that you seize that castle." The Lord, having heard the details of the Okoshi-Kii affair, found it particularly regrettable. However, he felt that a single operation would not be sufficient to bring the castle to fall. Therefore, as he had heard that Satake Yoshishige would soon march to the Asaka front, he reasoned that if the troops were kept occupied in that area while Yoshishige marched, the castle could be captured; thus, he advised that no single operation should be undertaken. He requested that a campaign be conducted. However, as it had been stated that if Lord Satake's march was certain, a nearby garrison would be unnecessary, the Lord decreed that a deputy should carry out the operation. Since we were residing at the main castle, we were ordered to attend at Miyamori. The Lord stated that the Tamura forces had filed a complaint regarding the operation against Okoshi. As he had heard that Satake Yoshishige would soon march to the Asaka front, he ordered that the deputy carry out the operation against Okoshi. I replied, "I have not heard of Lord Yoshishige's march from the Asaka route. Who is reporting this?" The attendants were dismissed, and I reported, "I heard this from Suda Mino of Sukagawa." I replied, "This is unexpected. I have heard that Mino serves Satake without equal. I wonder if he has come to report this to us." Two messengers were sent; the first report was poor, and I expressed my concern. I then stated that if the Lord wished to proceed, I should report the matter and mention Satake Yoshishige's march. Around that time, Lord Ishikawa Yamato dispatched a mountain ascetic named Yashiro as a courier. When questioned, that ascetic reported the march. The Lord noted that there was no such report from Washu. I then returned immediately, made preparations over the next two days, went to Funakoshi, and carried out operations at Omori. As I was in charge of the 2-3 sections of the town fortifications, there was no further action to be taken from my side, and I withdrew. Lord Masamune also departed in secret. Meanwhile, the forces from Ono and Shikamata attacked from the east. Regarding the withdrawal of the other Date forces, they encountered the Shikamata forces and fought, firing their muskets frequently; the opposing forces immediately repelled them and pushed them back, scattering them in various directions and withdrawing with about 30 heads. The following day, Lord Masamune returned to Miyamori, and the troops also withdrew.

shigezane:shigezaneki-7.title: 1 Thus, while Shiomatsu was a skilled archer..
shigezane:shigezaneki-7.summary: Thus, while Shiomatsu was skilled with the bow and arrow, our kin resided in Hachichome, and the border of Nihonmatsu remained uncontested.
shigezane:shigezaneki-7.markdown:
1. Thus, while Shiomatsu was a force in arms, our kin resided in Hachichome, and the border of Nihonmatsu remained uncontested. The details are as recorded above: since they had established their position in a formidable stronghold, it seemed that even if Yoshitsugu were to assist Ouchi Bizen, should the Date take up arms, it would be appropriate to apologize to the Date. Furthermore, regarding the judgment of Oya Sanemoto, he reasoned, "The forces of Aizu and the Sendo region are aiding Shiomatsu. As for Tamura, the enemy is the enemy, but since they pass only through the Nihonmatsu domain, I harbor suspicions regarding Yoshitsugu," and thus he settled the border. He reported these matters to Lord Masamune, but as we were still juniors, he was not informed. Had this border dispute been settled, it would likely have become a troublesome and intense conflict; therefore, to ensure that no dispute would arise, he required us to swear oaths twice, and the border between Hachichome and Nihonmatsu was thus kept peaceful.

shigezane:shigezaneki-9.title: 1. From the Black Basket, the 24th..
shigezane:shigezaneki-9.summary: On the 24th, from Ichikuro-kago, an expedition was launched against a castle called Kara-no-uchi. The Nihonmatsu forces assisted in that operation.
shigezane:shigezaneki-9.markdown:
1. On the 24th, from Kurokago, an expedition was launched against a castle called Kara-no-uchi. The Nihonmatsu forces assisted in that location. A small number of men were dispatched from within to engage them, but as they were not strong, a military engagement was concluded, and on that day, nothing further occurred and the forces withdrew to Kurokago. Four men stationed at the fortifications also moved toward a place called Kosegawa; Lord Masamune took action, and Kojuro Katakura, with only a handful of men and a force of about 200, advanced as far as the vicinity of Obama. The forces of Obama pressed forward and pursued them for about five ri to Kosegawa. The four men crossed the river and engaged in battle. Although the Obama forces brought 500 to 600 cavalry, they withdrew hastily, mindful of Lord Masamune's actions. As our forces were few in number, they did not press the attack, and both sides took about ten heads each.

shigezane:shigezaneki-bunrui1.title: Classification of Various Versions of the "Shigezane-ki": Along with a Study on the Origin of the so-called "Hitotoribashi Kanjo"
shigezane:shigezaneki-bunrui1.summary: There are various versions of the "Shigezane-ki" and "Masamune-ki" written by Shigezane Date. I have attempted to classify them. I have also included an analysis of the "Origin of the Hitotoribashi Letter of Commendation."
shigezane:shigezaneki-bunrui1.markdown:
## There are various versions of the "Shigezane-ki" and "Masamune-ki" written by Shigezane Date. I have attempted to classify them. I have also included an analysis of the "Origin of the Hitotoribashi Letter of Commendation."

---

There is a copy of a letter from Masamune Date, often cited as a "letter of commendation" granted to Shigezane Date by Masamune during the Battle of Hitotoribashi. [History of Sendai City, Masamune Date Documents 29. Watari Date Family Historical Materials 1 (70)](#/post/shigezane/29). While it is also featured on this site as linked, I will quote it here once more.

> Now, regarding the battle at the Kannon Hall today: with your small force, you engaged the enemy—who had their backs turned and were reinforced by the great army from Arai—and achieved an unparalleled victory, gaining such immense advantage that it defies all expectation. I am deeply gratified that you, through your own personal efforts, were able to assist the various armies. Nevertheless, it is utterly laughable that there must be so many dead and wounded among your retainers. I have heard that tomorrow, you shall advance close to the enemy camp at the main shrine. If you can indeed reach that location, it would be my greatest wish. I have also conveyed this intent to Date Ueno-no-kami Masakage. With utmost respect and humility. > > (Tensho 13) November 17, Hour of the Boar — Masamune > Messenger: Yamaji Awaji-dono > ※ In the "Watari Date Family Historical Materials" (the original of Masamune Documents 29 held by Date City, Hokkaido), the closing phrase is "Kyoko Kingen." The reading above follows the entry in the History of Sendai City, Masamune Documents 29.

The substance of this letter is also recorded in various editions of the *Shigezane-ki* (*Masamune-ki*), a biography of Masamune written by Shigezane Date; these fall into three main lineages. The following quotations are from Jin-san's [\[sd-script\] Personal Archive of Materials Regarding Shigezane Date, a Retainer of the Date Clan](https://sd-script.hateblo.jp/). My thanks to Jin-san. Among the various editions of the *Shigezane-ki* (*Masamune-ki*), the relatively accessible transcriptions are the <Sendai Sosho "Shigezane-ki">, the <Gunsho Ruiju "Date Nikki">, and the <Jinbutsu Sosho Date Materials Collection "Masamune-ki">; each has distinct characteristics, and the editions currently extant can be classified into a group common to one of these three.

### ① The <Sendai Sosho "Shigezane-ki"> group

The section corresponding to the substance of Masamune Document 29 states "also in the oral account," and it is notable that it is presented not as a letter, but as the oral account of Awaji Yamaji.

> I dispatched Awaji Yamaji as a messenger to my quarters. He provided a handwritten letter* and an oral account.* > Today's engagement was unparalleled; we fought against the enemy and did not suffer defeat—*an unprecedented occurrence*. Ultimately, because of your actions, many were wounded and killed. In particular, I was informed that the enemy is approaching the main castle tomorrow. While you wished to send someone, as there is no one else available to me, I must, regrettably, enter the main castle myself. I have been instructed that Date Ueno has been dispatched. > Furthermore, Awaji stated: "What shall we do regarding our side in today's battle? We cannot possibly accompany you. Both of us have no choice but to blend in with the enemy. I do not know the situation on the enemy side, but according to our discussions, the main castle is to be used as a nearby stronghold, and arrangements were made to withdraw the forces besieged at Nihonmatsu; as I was informed that they would eventually flee the enemy camp," he reported. Since orders have been issued in this manner and the main castle is to be besieged, he stated that he would handle the necessary preparations.

This group includes the Morioka Central Community Center's "Masamune-ki," the Miyagi Prefectural Library's "Masamune-ko Go-gunki," the Kokushi Sosho Gunki-rui San's "Masamune-ko Gunki," and the National Diet Library's "Chunagon Masamune-kyo Go-gunki." Of particular note are the Date Jike Records compiled by the Sendai Date family, as well as the "Watari Petition"—a petition from the Tenwa era submitted to the Sendai Domain by the Watari Date family, who were on the brink of extinction due to a lack of an heir. The Tenwa petition was filed some thirty-odd years after Shigezane's death. At that time, there may still have been people who knew Shigezane or Masamune personally. The fact that this was adopted as an official record during such a period is noteworthy when considering the relationship between the various versions of the Shigezane-ki. Additionally, a characteristic feature is the description of Shigezane's achievements as "unprecedented."

Among these various versions, the Morioka Central Community Center's "Masamune-ki" and the Miyagi Prefectural Library's "Masamune-ko Go-gunki" end their accounts at Keicho 5; however, the National Diet Library's "Chunagon Masamune-kyo Go-gunki" and the Sendai Sosho's "Shigezane-ki" include the sentence "The above passages were likely written by Date Awa Shigezane," followed by chapters serving as supplementary materials or anecdotes. This suggests that the section following "The above passages were likely written by Date Awa Shigezane" was not written by Shigezane, but was an addition. Versions without this addition are designated as "Group ①-1," while those with it are designated as "Group ①-2." "Group ①-1" consists of the Morioka Central Community Center's "Masamune-ki" and the Miyagi Prefectural Library's "Masamune-ko Go-gunki," while "Group ①-2" consists of the National Diet Library's "Chunagon Masamune-kyo Go-gunki" and the Sendai Sosho's "Shigezane-ki."

### ② Group of 〈Gunsho Ruiju "Date Nikki"〉

The relevant section of the Gunsho Ruiju "Date Nikki."

> In the dead of night, as I was escorting Awaji along the mountain path, he personally penned this letter. > Upon hearing that we were not defeated in the battle today while pursuing the enemy, *without any report being passed along, the circumstances were truly extraordinary and beyond description*. Through my own efforts, many others were aided. It is certain that there must be numerous wounded and dead among the retainers. As it has been decreed that we shall take up positions near the main castle tomorrow, I shall—though it is a great undertaking—proceed to the main castle. As I am the only one authorized to do so, I have been instructed. The wording states that Date Ueno shall also accompany me. > Awaji stated that while two men who had become allies to us were currently mingled with the enemy, tomorrow the main castle would be approached, and the forces besieged at Nihonmatsu would be withdrawn. As the sun set, I reported that I had fled the enemy camp and was thus instructed. Since the main castle is to be besieged, I was told to make the necessary preparations.

Regarding the section corresponding to the intent of Masamune Document 29, the explanation that it is a "formal statement" is removed. Additionally, the description of Shigezane's actions changes from "an unprecedented occurrence" to "a matter so extraordinary that nothing has been passed down, and it must be described as truly remarkable." The Kaga City Library's "Date-ki" and the Kyo-Otani Village Library's "Date Nikki" belong to this group.

### ③ Group of 〈Biographies Series: Date Materials Collection "Masamune-ki"〉

Here is the relevant section of the *Jinbutsu Sosho: Date Shiryoshu "Masamune-ki"*. While Group ① and Group ② seen above are written in the form of a single written document, this one is written in the narrative style of archaic prose.

> I received a handwritten official decree sent by Awaji Yamaji as a messenger. > "To begin with, today a battle took place at the Kannon Hall; a large force—having been rescued from Arai and returning to the Kannon Hall—engaged in combat with your small force. In an instance of unparalleled circumstance, you instead achieved a great victory and a feat of unmatched honor, astonishing all who heard the news. Due to your personal conduct, the various armies are immensely pleased; though it be so, the fact that there must be many wounded and dead among your retainers is utterly laughable. I have heard that tomorrow the enemy army is to take up positions near the Main Shrine; should you be able to proceed to that location, it would be your greatest wish. I have also conveyed this to Masakage Date of Ueno, who concurred. November 17, at the hour of the Boar, Shigezane, Masamune." > This is what was written. > As for what Awaji recounted: having heard that the main camp was at the Main Shrine, he had ventured into enemy territory; since the enemy was to take up positions near the Main Shrine tomorrow and withdraw the siege of Nihonmatsu, a council was held at the enemy camp. The two of them, having heard the news, fled back to this side at night and reported the matter; this is why the decree was issued. Starting tomorrow, the Main Shrine will be under siege; it is vital to keep this in mind, he stated.

The relevant section in [History of Sendai City: Masamune Date Documents 29; Watari Date Family Historical Materials 1 (70)](#/post/shigezane/29), which I first examined, is almost identical in wording to the "Masamune-ki" in the *Jinbutsu Sosho: Date Materials Collection*. There are more expressions reflecting Masamune's emotions, whereas Group ① and Group ② leave a more businesslike impression by comparison. Furthermore, the anecdotal section in Group ①—which begins after "The above passages were likely written by Date Awa Shigezane"—appears later in the latter half without particular explanation, further increasing the number of anecdotes.

### "Relationships Between the Various Versions of the Shigezane-ki (Masamune-ki)"

I have organized the findings discussed thus far into a diagram. Based on Jin-san's [\[sd-script\] Personal Archive of Materials Regarding Shigezane Date, a Retainer of the Date Clan](https://sd-script.hateblo.jp/), it is known that the start time of the Battle of Kotemori varies across different versions of the *Shigezane-ki*, so I have also included this in the diagram. The horizontal axis represents the presence or absence of the anecdotal section following "The above passages were likely written by Date Awa Shigezane" in the texts up to Keicho 5; the vertical axis represents the presence or absence of the formal wording in the "Hitotoribashi Commendation."

The various manuscripts in Group ② at the bottom left lack the anecdotal section following "The above passages were likely written by Date Awa Shigezane," suggesting they may have diverged and been transmitted earlier than those in Group ①-2 at the top right. Furthermore, as these manuscripts reached their destination from a distance relative to Sendai, their titles are neither "Masamune" nor "Shigezane," but rather "Date-ki" or "Date Nikki." Within this group, only the "Date-ki" at the Kaga City Library identifies the start time of the Battle of Kotemori as the "Hour of the Horse," a point shared with the various manuscripts in Group ①-1, suggesting that this version was established early on within this group.

The pseudo-classical text group ③ at the bottom right may have been established in parallel with, or based on, that at the top right, as it contains common anecdotes. While the formal address of the "Hitotoribashi Kanjo" is absent, this is considered a change accompanying the transformation into a pseudo-classical narrative form—a development independent of that in Group ② at the bottom left.

Assuming that the descriptive expressions in the Tenna petitions/Date family administrative records and the two "Hitotoribashi Kanjo" from the early Edo period represent the official view of the Watari Date family at the time, the descriptive expressions in Group ① at the top left—specifically the "Masamune-ki" at the Morioka Central Community Center and the "Masamune-ko Gogunki" at the Miyagi Prefectural Library—align with these. The use of the phrase "go-kuchijo ni" is also appropriate for military dispatch and communication on the battlefield; thus, I judge that Group ①.1 is the closest to the original "Shigezane-ki" among the various manuscripts extant today.

On the other hand, among the episodes recorded in the Group ③ pseudo-classical texts are anecdotes—such as those regarding Tamanoi Kusachogi and the New Province of Kazusa at Aizu-Kurokawa—that are not present in the other groups and would be difficult to write by anyone other than Shigezane Date. This cannot be represented on the vertical and horizontal axes of the figure above; thus, the formation process of Group ③ will likely need to be considered separately from those of Group ① and Group ②. However, since the descriptions of the "Hitotoribashi Kanjo" in this group contain the points noted below, there may be room for interpretation regarding how to define "episodes that would be difficult to write by anyone other than Shigezane Date."

### A Study on the Formation of the "Hitotoribashi Kanjo (Copy)"

A copy of a letter from Masamune Date, often presented as a "letter of commendation" granted by Masamune to Shigezane Date during the Battle of Hitotoribashi, [History of Sendai City, Masamune Date Documents 29; Watari Date Family Historical Materials 1 (70)](#/post/shigezane/29). Upon examining this document, which is currently preserved in Date City, Hokkaido, one gets the immediate impression that the paper is "new." Furthermore, the closing phrase—referred to in the History of Sendai City as "kyokyo kingen"—is written as "kyoko kingen." Masamune would not have used "kyoko kingen" when addressing Shigezane. Additionally, this is not a letter of commendation; the content of the letter is an administrative communication from the battlefield. However, for an administrative communication, it contains an unnaturally high amount of emotional expression, and includes a great deal of place names and other information that should have been omitted if they were on the same battlefield. It is strangely concrete and explanatory for the reader. As described in Group ①, it would be more natural for administrative communication of this era to involve a messenger bringing a concise letter from Masamune and conveying the details through a "detailed oral account." This copy of Masamune Date's letter (Masamune Documents 29) is itself highly narrative. One gets the impression that it is structured such that the relationship between the domain founder Masamune and Shigezane, the first head of the Watari Date family, can be explained through this document alone.

In fact, as seen in the first half of this paper, this copy of Masamune Date's letter (Masamune Documents 29) is almost identical to the account in the Group ③ pseudo-classical style.

Since this is an administrative communication document, its priority for preservation was considerably lower than that of letters of commendation for the recipient; thus, the original document that Shigezane Date received from Masamune during the Battle of Hitotori Bridge may have been lost at an early stage. This was likely when Shigezane fled.

As is already evident in the "Watari Petition," Shigezane's military achievements in the "Battle of Hitotori Bridge" served as the pillar supporting the Watari Date clan. To boost morale, it is possible that this extant copy of a letter from Masamune Date (Masamune Documents 29) was "reconstructed" by selecting descriptions from various texts—specifically those in pseudo-classical military chronicles—that possessed a strong emotional appeal. I believe this occurred around the Bakumatsu and Meiji periods. The Watari Date clan faced crises requiring them to bolster their own narrative on two occasions: during the Tenna petition and around the Bakumatsu and Meiji periods; since Group ① was employed at the time of the Tenna petition, this is consistent with the relatively recent date of the paper.

shigezane:shigezanekinonazo.title: The Mystery of the Shigezane-ki
shigezane:shigezanekinonazo.summary: There are three main variants of the "Shigezane-ki": the "Shigezane-ki," the "Shigezane Date Nikki," and the "Masamune-ki."
shigezane:shigezanekinonazo.markdown:
There are three main variants of the *Munemi-ki*: the *Munemi-ki*, the *Shigezane Date Nikki*, and the *Masamune-ki*. According to the commentary in the *Date Shiryoshu*, while it is generally considered that the *Masamune-ki* is the final compilation of the *Munemi-ki* and the *Shigezane Date Nikki*, all three contain sections that appear to be additions to their structure.

While some parts of the latter half of the *Masamune-ki*—covering Masamune's daily life, character, and the appointment of retainers—appear to have been written by those serving Masamune, the pride in his own origins—evident in passages such as his attendance at banquets with the shogunal family and his admiration for the appointment of figures like Kagetsuna Katakura, noting that he "appointed those uncounted among men, and moreover, his judgment was unclouded"—provides ample confidence that the work was penned by Shigezane.

The military records of the *Munemi-ki* end roughly before Munemi's flight—specifically, up until the fall of Toyotomi Hidetsugu. Even thereafter, events in which Munemi could have written military accounts as a party involved include Sekigahara (which is mentioned briefly), the siege of Shiroishi, the Battle of Fukushima, the Siege of Osaka, and the Mogami campaign, yet these are barely recorded. Furthermore, there are no entries pertaining to domain administration. Regarding the Siege of Osaka, detailed notes by Katakura Shigetsuna remain in the Date family archives, and the entries in the *Jike-kiroku* largely follow these. Munemi would naturally have kept detailed notes for each battle (which is why the *Munemi-ki* could be written later), so the fact that no notes at all remain for the battles following his return to service... the fact that they are not recorded in the *Jike-kiroku* suggests that they were already missing at the time the *Jike-kiroku* was compiled.

Why did Shigezane stop writing his military chronicles at the fall of Hidetsugu? I feel that here lies a profound key to uncovering Shigezane's true nature.
