shigezane:shigezanetokassen.title: Battle with Shigezane Date
shigezane:shigezanetokassen.summary: "Shigezane was a man of character, possessed of wisdom and strategic brilliance. For a time, he was hailed as peerless in courage and martial prowess." This is the description of Shigezane Date's character as recorded in the *Tohan Shiko*, a historical record written by Sakunami Kiyoaki, who served the Date clan of Sendai.
shigezane:shigezanetokassen.markdown:
"Shigezane was a man of character, possessing both courage and strategic brilliance. For a time, he was hailed as peerless in martial prowess." This is the description of Shigezane Date as recorded in the *Tohan Shiko*, a historical record written by Sakunami Kiyoaki, who served the Date clan of Sendai. Within the Date clan, Shigezane was a symbol of martial prowess. However, no anecdotes of individual heroism such as those associated with Kato Kiyomasa are known regarding Shigezane. What, then, was the nature of Shigezane's "martial prowess"? I would like to examine this by introducing the battles and military actions that serve as the basis for this "martial prowess," drawing primarily from his own writings: the *Masamune-ki* (included in the *Sengoku Shiryo Sosho*) and the *Date Nikki* (included in the *Gunsho Ruiju*). Please understand that the near-total absence of primary sources is due to limitations in the author's capabilities.

## ■Battles of Shigezane Date

Shigezane Date succeeded to the headship of the Date clan in Tensho 12, coinciding with Masamune Date's ascension, and took over the "Omori Date house," which had been the foremost among the clan's relatives. There are no surviving records of Shigezane's first battle; thus, verifiable accounts are limited to those following his assumption of the headship. When discussing battles, people often refer to a single engagement—for example, a single pitched battle such as the Battle of Sekigahara or the Battle of Surigami. However, a pitched battle is, needless to say, merely one process resulting from various political and military developments leading up to it. This paper introduces the military actions undertaken by Shigezane prior to the Date clan's subordination to the Toyotomi clan. The military actions covered are as follows: ① May, Tensho 13: Battle of Hibara ② Summer–Autumn, Tensho 13: Campaign to capture Yotsumatsu ③ Autumn, Tensho 13–Summer, Tensho 14: Siege of Nihonmatsu ④ Summer, Tensho 15–April, Tensho 16: Stratagems against Ouchi Sadatsuna ⑤ Late Tensho 14–Tensho 16: Tamura Disturbance ⑥ Summer, Tensho 17: Conquest of Aizu ⑦ Autumn, Tensho 17: Battle of Sukagawa For further details regarding the political situation of this period and the broader diplomacy surrounding the battles, see Seiji Kobayashi, *A Study of Masamune Date*—Chapter 5, "Masamune's War and Peace: Focusing on the Battle of Koriyama in Tensho 16, etc." (Yoshikawa Kobunkan). The dates and other information in this paper are based on Shigezane's writings, supplemented by the aforementioned paper by Kobayashi and the family records.

### ① May, Tensho 13: Battle of Hibara

Immediately after assuming the headship, Masamune Date planned an attack on Aizu via the Hibara route. In response to his summons, Shigezane departed Omori on May 8 and arrived at Hibara the following day, May 9. Because Masamune, concerned about the borders of Nihonmatsu, ordered him to return to the castle that same day, Shigezane did not participate in the battle. However, at Hibara, at Shigezane's suggestion, arrangements were made to induce the defection of Inawashiro Morikuni, a senior retainer of the Ashina clan. This was based on the connection between Shigezane's chief retainer, Haneda Sanekage, and Inawashiro Morikuni's chief retainer, Ishibe Kanmono. Although this did not materialize at the time, it was later realized and became a factor in the Date clan's acquisition of Aizu.

### ② Summer–Autumn of Tensho 13: The Campaign to Capture Shiomatsu

#### 【Aoki Shuri's Defection】

The reason Masamune Date planned the aforementioned attack on Aizu was the defection of Ouchi Sadatsuna, who had requested and been granted permission to serve Masamune the previous autumn. "Recently, a messenger arrived from Aizu stating that Ouchi had been pardoned and was sending word that he would provide assistance from Aizu; furthermore, it was heard that Ouchi had shown internal intentions and refused to grant permission for our clan to enter" (Jike Kiroku). It was concluded that this sudden change in Ouchi's attitude was orchestrated by the Ashina clan of Aizu. However, as the internal cooperation of Inawashiro Morikuni failed to materialize, Shigezane proposed a direct attack on Ouchi Sadatsuna of Shiomatsu. Furthermore, Ouchi Sadatsuna had frequently engaged in battle with Tamura Kiyoaki, Masamune's father-in-law, and the Tamura clan had also requested the subjugation of Ouchi. Shigezane stated, "We must arrange for even one or two people within the Ouchi retainers to serve us" (Date Nikki), and sought to create defectors within the Ouchi retainers. Among Shigezane's retainers was Ishii Genshiro, a former hereditary retainer of Shiomatsu; they succeeded in winning over Aoki Shuri, the lord of Karimatsuda Castle. Karimatsuda was a border castle on the Shiomatsu side, adjacent to Date territory. In August, once Aoki Shuri severed ties with Ouchi Sadatsuna, Masamune immediately dispatched Shigezane, Koyanagawa Morimune, Shiroishi Munemi, and Harada Munetoki to reinforce Karimatsuda, and Masamune received Aoki Shuri at Sugime.

#### 【The Battle of Kotemori and the Subjugation of Shiomatsu】

Upon learning that Aoki Shuri had severed ties, Ouchi Sadatsuna fortified his position by withdrawing into Kotemori. Kotemori was a strategic point leading from Kawamata through the Shiomatsu territory toward Tamura. Tamura Kiyoaki, who had requested the subjugation of the Ouchi, also marched out; the Date and Tamura forces attacked Kotemori Castle together, but were unable to coordinate due to the presence of the great mountain between them. They began the siege on the 24th, but by nightfall on the 26th, the castle had not yet fallen. During a military council on the night of the 26th, Shigezane proposed that his forces move to the "Take-yashiki" south of the castle to block the passage of reinforcements to the castle. The reason for this proposal was that such a move would allow Shigezane's forces and the Tamura forces to coordinate. However, because there was a risk of being caught in a pincer attack by both the castle garrison and the reinforcements, the proposal was not accepted, and the council concluded. In the early hours of the 27th, Shigezane moved to the Take-yashiki without Masamune's permission, and Masakage Rusu followed him. Upon noticing this, Masamune moved his entire force, completely cutting off all passage between the castle and the reinforcements. At this point, negotiations for surrender were initiated by the castle garrison. A man named Ishikawa Kageyu, who emerged from the castle, designated Shigezane's retainer Endo Shimotsuke, stating, "As we have shared a close relationship, I wish to speak with you in person" (Masamune-ki). Ouchi Sadatsuna had withdrawn to Obama on the night of the 25th, and his wish was that since he was opening the gates, everyone in the castle should also withdraw to Obama. After several rounds of negotiations, Masamune refused to allow the castle garrison to withdraw to Obama and launched an attack while Endo Shimotsuke was still inside the castle. His judgment was that even if the main bailey did not fall, threatening them with attack would make them abandon their attempt to withdraw to Obama and instead retreat to the Date side. After Endo Shimotsuke barely escaped with his life and returned to camp, Shigezane's forces set fire to the castle. Due to a strong wind at the time, Kotemori Castle was completely burned down and fell, and a massacre was carried out. Upon learning of the fall of Kotemori, Shinjo and Shozan Castles also burned themselves and fell into the hands of the Date forces. On the following day, the 28th, Shigezane, who had headed for Tsukidate by Masamune's order, encountered a lone warrior emerging from the castle. This was Hattori Gennai, a Shiomatsu ronin who had previously served Shigezane and had now returned to Shiomatsu, taking refuge in Tsukidate. Hattori Gennai declared, "Since Tsukidate has also been evacuated, I shall pursue them immediately" (Date Nikki). When Shigezane's forces surged toward the castle, it turned out that the Shiomatsu forces had indeed all been evacuated. Subsequently, Masamune, using Kurokago as his base, and Shigezane, Kagetsuna Katakura, Munemi Shiroishi, and Motochika Sakurada, using Tsukidate as their base, subdued the Shiomatsu territory. On September 25, Ouchi Sadatsuna burned Obama and fled to Aizu. That night, upon seeing the fire in Obama, Shigezane rushed from Tsukidate to see what was happening, at which point Ouchi Gasai, who had become separated from Ouchi Sadatsuna, rushed in seeking Shigezane's help. Through Shigezane's plea for clemency, Ouchi Gasai was spared the death penalty.

### ③ Autumn of Tensho 13 – Summer of Tensho 14: Siege of Nihonmatsu

#### 【The Awanosu Incident and the Siege of Nihonmatsu】

Following Masamune's subjugation of the Shiomatsu territory, Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu of Nihonmatsu—who had provided reinforcements to the Ouchi—began peace negotiations with the Date clan. The Omori Date family—father and son Date Sanemoto and Shigezane—acted as intermediaries in these negotiations; however, on October 8, the "Awanosu Incident" occurred, in which both Terumune Date and Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu met untimely deaths. For details, please refer to "The Awanosu Incident—Various Accounts Surrounding the Death of Terumune" on the website "Shigezane Zanmai." As a result of this incident, the Hatakeyama clan and the Nihonmatsu territory—which were supposed to have become vassals of the Date clan (under military subordination) during the subjugation of Shiomatsu—became completely hostile to the Date clan. Having lost Yoshitsugu, the Hatakeyama clan installed their surviving son, Kokuomaru, as head of the house and appointed their chief relative, Shinjo Moritsugu, as commander; they then withdrew to Nihonmatsu Castle, drawing troops from surrounding branch castles. On October 15, Masamune established a camp at Takada, near Awanosu, and began the siege of Nihonmatsu. Shigezane's camp was located at Ioda, on the border between the Omori and Nihonmatsu territories. While Shigezane was away from Ioda for a military council, an attack was launched by the castle garrison, resulting in numerous casualties on both sides. As heavy snow fell starting that night, Masamune abandoned the attack for the year on the 21st and withdrew to Obama.

#### 【Battle of Hitotori Bridge】

November 10. Upon receiving information that the Satake, Ashina, Iwaki, Ishikawa, and Shirakawa forces had advanced to the Asaka area to relieve Nihonmatsu, Masamune was forced to respond. Masamune dispatched troops to Iwakado; to Takakura, Tomizuka Munetsuna, Kuwaori Masanaga, and Ito Shigenobu; to Motomiya, Segami Kageyasu, Nakajima Munemoto, Hamada Kagetaka, and Sakurada Motochika; and to Tamai, Munemi Shiroishi, to establish a defensive line. However, the Date forces were outnumbered against the allied army. Having abandoned the siege of Nihonmatsu for the remainder of the year, they had returned much of their strength to their local domains. While it is commonly said that the allied army numbered 30,000 and the Date army 8,000, there is no basis for these figures in Shigezane's writings or the family records. Nevertheless, to secure Nihonmatsu Castle, Masamune ordered Shigezane, who was stationed at Shibukawa: "Since we are outnumbered, you have not left any troops at Obama; therefore, leave your forces at Obama and hurry here" (*Masamune-ki*). The fact that Masamune had to mobilize troops from the Nihonmatsu-Omori border and also deploy all his forces from Obama—which served as his base at the time—only underscores the disparity in military strength between the two sides. Shigezane left over thirty cavalry at Obama and met with Masamune at Iwakado on November 16. At this time, the allied army was expected to set up field camps in the "plains south of Maeda-zawa" and move toward Motomiya or Takakura the following day. Shigezane moved to Nukazawa that night, and Masamune moved his camp to Motomiya, establishing a position at "Ota-hara (Aota-hara) west of Motomiya" as reinforcements for Takakura. On the following day, November 17, Shigezane also established a position at "below the mountain on the Kaido" to provide reinforcements for Takakura. The allied army divided its large force into three groups, pressing the Date forces in rotation. Tomizuka and Ito of Takakura Castle sallied out in an attempt to stall the enemy despite their inferiority, but were instead pushed back into the castle. The enemy forces from Maeda-zawa engaged in battle with Masamune's main body at Kannon-do. When Shigezane's retainer, Shimo-Koriyama Naiki, ascended to Oyama, he saw three banners—those of Shiroishi, Takano, and Hamada—along with six or seven enemy cavalry and over a hundred ashigaru heading toward Motomiya. The three—Shiroishi, Takano, and Hamada—passed through Shigezane's defenses toward the main camp, while Shigezane's forces remained to intercept them. The phrase "the force pressing from Arai fought against Shigezane" (*Masamune-ki*) likely refers to this contingent. According to Shigezane himself, because he had left troops at both Obama and Shibukawa, only seventy to eighty cavalry remained. The main camp of Masamune at Aota-hara and Kannon-do could not hold out, and the tide of defeat grew increasingly severe; however, thanks to the efforts of Watari Motomune and his son Shigemune, Masakage Rusu, Kokubun Morishige, Harada Munetoki, and Kagetsuna Katakura, they avoided a total defeat. The remaining Shigezane forces became isolated. To their left was the great river of the Abukuma. Their nearest allies were engaged in battle with the enemy at Aota-hara, a distance of over seven *cho*. Shimo-Koriyama Naiki seized Shigezane's small flag and urged him to retreat, but Shigezane held his ground, declaring: "If I were to retreat from here, it would be a stain upon my lineage for generations to come; I shall fight to the end and die in battle" (*Masamune-ki*). This is the episode passed down in later military chronicles as a testament to Shigezane's bravery. The exploits of Shigezane's retainers during the struggle for Hitori-bashi—located "about four or five *cho* below the south of the mountain" where Shigezane had established his camp—are omitted here, but while Shigezane's forces held out, the enemy at Kannon-do withdrew, and the enemy engaged with Shigezane's forces also retreated. "By a mysterious providence, not a single blade of grass was cut" (*Masamune-ki*). Shigezane's forces successfully defended their camp in this battle. Shigezane recorded that they took the heads of over 250 enemies, while thirty-nine of their own were killed in action (*Masamune-ki*). After the allied army withdrew, they reestablished their defenses at "Takakura Kaido Kawakiri," about five or six *cho* from Masamune's main camp; Masamune remained vigilant, fearing another battle, but the day ended without incident, and Masamune withdrew to Iwakado. The letter of commendation that Masamune issued to Shigezane that night subsequently became one of the symbols of the Watari Date family and was carefully preserved. Another episode involving Shigezane's retainers, who had blended into the enemy camp, reported that the allied army would attack Motomiya the next day; consequently, Masamune ordered Masakage Rusu and Shigezane to move toward Motomiya. When Shigezane headed for Motomiya the following morning, a lookout reported that the allied army had disbanded and withdrawn. As another episode involving Shigezane, the *Kimura Uemon Oboegaki* records a story where Masamune attempted to let his horse drink river water, only to be attacked by the enemy and rescued by Shigezane. This is a moment where Masamune's admiration for Shigezane shines through, with Masamune praising him as "a reliable general to whom I can entrust one side." However, in Shigezane's own writings, it cannot be read that Shigezane himself left the camp, nor that Masamune came near Shigezane's position. It should be noted here that the Date forces used the southern border of Adachi District as their front line. The Nihonmatsu territory of Adachi District was controlled by the Date family, except for the main castle of Nihonmatsu. By entering winter while maintaining this front line, the Date family's control over Adachi District was first solidified.

#### 【Battle of Shibukawa】

After the Battle of Hitori-bashi, Shigezane returned to Shibukawa Castle. Shibukawa Castle was a branch castle of Nihonmatsu and served as a frontier castle guarding the Date family's Omori territory. Following the death of Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu, the castle lord, Yusa Shimosa, withdrew to Nihonmatsu, and the Date family took possession of the now-empty castle. Yusa Shimosa had acted as an intermediary between Hatakeyama and Date Sanemoto, and later conspired with the Date family. Among Shigezane's retainers, Yusa Sato Emon—described as being "born in the neighborhood"—can be confirmed at this time (*Masamune-ki*). On December 11, Shibukawa Castle was completely destroyed by fire, but as it was one of the frontline castles guarding Nihonmatsu Castle, it is believed that restoration was carried out promptly. Shigezane suffered severe burns to his right hand in this fire. At noon on January 1, the Hatakeyama forces, led by Kanokoda Emon, attacked Shibukawa Castle. A single mounted warrior and over ten foot soldiers chased the castle's water-fetchers, leading to a skirmish as the castle garrison also deployed troops. As they pursued the retreating enemy, approximately 200 Hatakeyama cavalry and 2,500 foot ashigaru, who had been lying in ambush on a small hill along the road, appeared, and the castle garrison was defeated. Consequently, Shigezane dispatched Shiga Oi Saemon and Yusa Sato Emon, and Haneda Umanosuke, who had been deployed elsewhere, also joined the battle. With the arrival of reinforcements from Hachichome, the tide of battle turned, and Kanokoda retreated, gathering his crumbling troops.

#### 【The Fall of Nihonmatsu】

In February of Tensho 14, five senior retainers of the Hatakeyama clan—Minowa Genban, Ujiie Shinbei, Yusa Tanba, Yusa Shimosa, and Horie Etchu—colluded with the Date clan. Among them, Minowa Genban's Minowa Castle was a strategic location that formed one of the baileys of Nihonmatsu Castle. These five attempted to lure the Date forces into Minowa Castle and coordinate a coup at Kurigasaku, another branch castle within the same bailey, but the attempt failed. Facing a counterattack from the castle garrison, the large number of men trapped within the narrow castle walls left them unable to move, prompting the five and the Date forces to retreat outside the castle. Due to the rugged terrain, forty to fifty men and women fell into the valley and were trampled to death during this process. The siege of Nihonmatsu was prolonged because Masamune fell ill; the Date clan did not deploy troops again until early April, after Masamune had recovered. However, wary of the deployment of various commanders from the Sendo region as had been the case in November of the previous year, they limited the attack to five days. The castle garrison essentially did not engage, focusing instead on strengthening their defenses. While the Date clan controlled the Nihonmatsu territories outside the main castle, they received supplies from Aizu via a route crossing the mountains from Takatama and Asakogashima, making it difficult to force the castle's fall. Nevertheless, as the Hatakeyama side had no clear breakthrough strategy, it is believed they began to consider surrendering. At this point, Soma Yoshitane stepped in to negotiate peace terms as a mediator between the Date and Hatakeyama clans. Relying on Date Sanemoto, Soma Yoshitane negotiated the conditions for the surrender of Nihonmatsu Castle and the departure of the castle's inhabitants. The proposed terms were the surrender of the castle and the acquisition of the Nihonmatsu territories by the Date clan. Masamune had no objections, and on July 6, the main bailey of Nihonmatsu Castle was burned to the ground; the Hatakeyama forces retreated to Aizu, while their subordinate retainers withdrew to various locations. Shigezane was the one who took possession of the castle. The Nihonmatsu territories were initially granted to Kagetsuna Katakura, but this was revoked. Ultimately, the Nihonmatsu territories were granted to Shigezane, the Omori territories to Kagetsuna Katakura, and the Shiomatsu territories to Munemi Shiroishi.

### ④ Summer of Tensho 15 – April of Tensho 16: Date Naitsuna's Stratagems

Summer of Tensho 15. Ouchi Sadatsuna, who was in Aizu, approached Shigezane to express his desire to submit to Masamune. Ouchi Sadatsuna eventually met with Shigezane and others on April 5, Tensho 16, and submitted to the Date clan. The process of these diplomatic negotiations is detailed in Yuriko Endo's "The Diplomacy of the Date Clan and Kagetsuna Katakura during the Tensho Period," so it will be omitted here, and the focus will be narrowed to the battle, which is the subject of this paper.

#### 【Night Attack on Naeshiroda】

A letter from Masamune dated September 29, Tensho 15, mentions the "Ouchi correspondence." Shigezane, after consulting with Munemi Shiroishi—who had been granted Shiomatsu, the former territory of the Ouchi—had been mediating negotiations for submission through Kagetsuna Katakura; however, this matter was leaked from Munemi Shiroishi to Aizu. Consequently, Ouchi Sadatsuna's position in Aizu became extremely precarious, and it became "difficult even to commit seppuku" (Date Nikki), leading the negotiations to be temporarily shelved. To provide a justification to Aizu, in the early hours of February 12, Tensho 16, Ouchi Sadatsuna attacked Naeshiroda in the Nihonmatsu domain. Because Naeshiroda had also been subjected to a night attack in July of the previous year by those believed to be remnants of the Nihonmatsu and Shiomatsu forces, the peasants had gathered in the old castle, where a man named Honnai Shusui served as the guard captain. As a result of Ouchi Sadatsuna's attack, approximately one hundred peasants in the old castle were killed, Honnai Shusui committed seppuku, and the old castle at Naeshiroda was set on fire. Since Ouchi Sadatsuna had had no choice but to sever ties in order to provide a justification to Aizu, he requested that Shigezane continue to mediate the negotiations, but Shigezane refused, stating, "We shall not act as intermediaries" (Date Nikki). However, a messenger from Sadatsuna to Shigezane—who was a relative of Honnai Shusui—along with other relatives residing in Tamai, all pleaded for Ouchi Sadatsuna to enter the service of the Date clan; thus, Shigezane once again found himself mediating the negotiations for Ouchi Sadatsuna's submission.

#### 【Tamai Sochogi】

Shigezane writes that in the military parlance of Oshu, sending troops stealthily into enemy territory is referred to as "kusa-chogi," "kusa o ireru," or "kusa o fusu." From Takatama and Yasukogashima, a road led along the Yazawa River through the mountains to Tamai. On March 13, Tensho 15, enemy forces emerged from Takatama-cho in Nishihara, four to five ri from Tamai, and attempted to strike those traveling to and from Tamai; however, troops from Tamai emerged and drove them back. Takatama Taroemon of the Aizu side planned another expedition. By this point, the submission of Ouchi Sadatsuna and Katahira Chikatsuna to the Date clan had already been decided, but since ties with Aizu had not yet been severed, the Ouchi and Katahira brothers contributed troops to this expedition on behalf of the Aizu side. Simultaneously, on the night of the 22nd, Takatama came to Motomiya and notified Shigezane that an enemy force would enter Tamai from Takatama on the night of March 23. In response, on the morning of March 23, the forces from Motomiya and Tamai, as well as Shigezane himself, set out to search for the enemy but found none, leading them to believe the report was false. However, at midday, they discovered twenty to thirty men in the vicinity of Tamai; they pursued them as they withdrew and caught up with them at a place called Dairin-da, where a skirmish ensued. The Aizu forces deliberately appeared to be at a disadvantage to lure the Date forces in, then launched a pincer attack with two hundred ambushers hidden behind the small hills of Yazawa. As a result, the Date forces began to collapse and were pushed back to Kawakiri, where three or four men were killed. At this moment, Shigezane's foot page, Shiga Saburo, spotted the Aizu commander, Takatama Taroemon, passing between friend and foe. As Shiga Saburo was skilled with firearms, he secured his gun to a kawayanagi (river-willow) and fired at Takatama Taroemon as he rode back across the small stream. Sure enough, of the two shots, one hit his horse and the other struck Takatama Taroemon in the thigh. This prompted the Date forces to counterattack, and the Aizu forces began to retreat. The rearguard for the Aizu forces was another commander, Ota Shuzen, who maintained his formation and retreated well; however, while climbing a small slope, he was likewise shot by Shiga Saburo. Severely wounded, Ota Shuzen handed his small flag to his younger brother to take over the rearguard, and he died after the retreat. With the retreat of Takatama Taroemon and Ota Shuzen, the rest of the Aizu forces collapsed, and the Date forces ultimately took fifty-three heads. Shigezane had the noses of these heads cut off and sent them to Masamune in Yonezawa.

April, Tensho 16. The appointment of Odate Naitsuna and Katahira Chikazuna as officials was finalized, and Katakura Kagetsuna—who had been handling negotiations with the Ouchi alongside Shigezane—arrived at Nishihara to welcome them. April 5. Katakura Kagetsuna's nephew, Kajinai Danjo, arrived at Kagetsuna's residence and informed him that Naitsuna would break ties with Aizu that night and proceed to Motomiya. It was also conveyed that Katahira Chikazuna was scheduled to break ties on the 6th. Consequently, Shigezane and Kagetsuna went to Motomiya and met with Odate Naitsuna on April 6. However, Katahira Chikazuna—perhaps due to a difference in opinion with his elder brother Naitsuna—attempted to strike a blow against Naitsuna himself; as a result, Naitsuna alone became subordinate. While Shigezane and Kagetsuna were not leading a large force, they felt it would be unsightly to undertake no military action after Odate Naitsuna had submitted. Thus, on the same day, Shigezane, Kagetsuna, and Shiroishi Munemi attacked Anekojima Castle. The castle forces did not respond, so they withdrew that day. It was planned to attack again the following day, but because Iwashi Danjo of Hyakumeki had colluded with Soma to break ties with the territory of Shiroishi Munemi, the attack on the 7th was carried out by Shigezane and Kagetsuna alone. Again, the castle forces did not respond, and Shigezane and Kagetsuna withdrew. Kagetsuna also returned to Omori on the 8th. 【Iwashi Danjo's Incursion】 April 15, Tensho 16. Iwashi Danjo, who had joined the Soma side, entered the territory of Shiroishi near the western edge and personally took the field. Shiroishi Munemi rushed to the scene and a battle ensued, with Munemi emerging victorious. Shigezane heard the sounds of firearms from this battle and rushed to the scene, but he was too late to join the fight. Overjoyed, Shiroishi Munemi hosted a feast for Shigezane at Miyamori. 【The Battle of Motomiya】 Odate Naitsuna's submission to the Date clan was soon reported to Aizu, and word reached them that the forces of Ashina in Aizu and the forces of Nikaido in Sukagawa were cooperating to operate in the Asaka area. Shigezane relayed this to Katakura Kagetsuna, who immediately departed Omori and issued orders from Nishihara to the forces of Shinobu. However, because the arrival was so sudden that almost no one gathered, Shigezane and Kagetsuna moved toward Motomiya alone. They had intended to bring reinforcements from Takakura, but due to their small numbers, they urgently summoned ten-odd cavalrymen and fifty firearms from Hachijome to intercept them. Takakura Omi, the lord of Takakura Castle, also arrived at Motomiya on April 17, and Shigezane, Kagetsuna, and Takakura Omi held a military council. Takakura Omi was originally a hereditary retainer of the Nishihara Hatakeyama clan. Since neither Aizu nor Sukagawa could move their troops from the other border, Takakura Omi predicted that the combined forces of both armies would number fewer than 1,000 cavalrymen and that the enemy's attack tomorrow would not reach Motomiya, remaining at Takakura. Accordingly, Kagetsuna and Shigezane devised a plan: "If the enemy attacks Takakura, our allies shall sally forth to the Kannon Hall and assist Takakura. However, this depends on the enemy's movements. If the enemy moves toward Motomiya and our allies do not respond, the enemy will prepare at the Kannon Hall. We shall send a small force to lure the enemy, draw them toward the town entrance of Motomiya, and engage them; Shigezane's retainer, Hata Umasasuke, shall lead the charge, with Kagetsuna and Umasasuke responding. Shigezane shall proceed to the Kannon Hall without concern for that battle, thereby splitting the enemy force. Then, troops from Takakura shall also be dispatched to cut off the enemy's retreat." Because Takakura was a mountain castle, the enemy's movements were clearly visible. They agreed that if the enemy attacked from Takakura, they would raise signal fires to the west of the castle; if the enemy attacked from Motomiya, they would raise signal fires to the east. Takakura Omi then returned to Takakura Castle. On the dawn of the 18th, signal fires were lit to the west of Takakura Castle. Judging this to be an attack on Takakura, Shigezane and Kagetsuna sallied forth to the Kannon Hall. However, upon reaching the base of the Kannon Hall, signal fires were lit again, this time to the east of the castle. Thinking the enemy had moved toward Motomiya, Shigezane said they should return their troops, but Kagetsuna argued that returning troops who had already moved would affect morale; thus, Shigezane and Kagetsuna prepared at the Kannon Hall as they were. The enemy gradually closed in, but among them was Kadokoda Uemon, a former member of the Hatakeyama clan, who led forty to fifty light infantry. Shigezane ordered his retainer, Iwashi Yahei, to lure Kadokoda to the base of the Kannon Hall. Iwashi Yahei, Hata Umasasuke, and over thirty light infantrymen fired their firearms and, splitting the line between friend and foe, successfully lured Kadokoda toward the Kannon Hall. By this time, Kadokoda's forces had grown to over ten cavalrymen and over a hundred light infantrymen. At this point, the forces from the Kannon Hall descended from the mountain to drive the enemy back, and as planned, the enemy collapsed and fled through the Hitotori Bridge. The enemy forces on the other side of the bridge attacked the Kannon Hall in turn, and the Date forces were pushed back as far as the Hitotori Bridge, but Hata Umasasuke, Ushizaka Sakon, and Iwashi Yahei counterattacked and drove them back to the Hitotori Bridge. Together with the common soldiers, they killed fifty-six enemies, while the Date forces suffered fourteen fatalities. Alongside this battle, the Aizu forces had taken the mother of Katahira Chikazuna as a hostage. While their original goal was the acquisition of the hostage, Shigezane later judged that it would have been unsightly to operate without military action had they not done so. ⑤ Tensho 16: The Tamura Disturbance In November, Tensho 14, Tamura Kiyoaki died suddenly, and the Tamura clan split into the Soma faction—consisting of Kiyoaki's widow (the Soma clan), Tamura Umeyuki, and Tamura Uemon—and the Date faction—consisting of Tamura Tsukisai and Hashimoto Keibu—leading to continued tension. Between the Soma and Date clans, the conflict deepened over the Tamura territory. 【Okoshi Kii-no-kami's Visit】 Okoshi Kii-no-kami was a cousin of Soma Yoshitane. At one point, Tamura Tsukisai and Hashimoto Keibu consulted Shiroishi Uemon Munemi, the lord of Miyumori Castle, stating, "Okoshi Kii-no-kami is in league with the Soma, and his rebellion is evident; we wish to take him alive." When Shiroishi Munemi informed Masamune, Masamune instructed Shigezane to dispatch someone knowledgeable to the area. Shigezane then sent Endo Suruga to Yonezawa. Masamune judged that the alignment between the Soma and Date factions would lead to the stability of the Tamura territory and opposed the consultation between Tamura Tsukisai and Hashimoto Keibu. However, fearing that if they acted rashly, things might go wrong, he instructed Shigezane, who served as the Date side's liaison to Okoshi Kii-no-kami, to inform him of this. Shigezane's retainer, Uchigasaki Umasagashira, was close to Okoshi Kii-no-kami, and Okoshi Kii-no-kami frequently visited Uchigasaki Umasagashira's residence, accompanied by a relative named Okoshi Bizen. Shigezane then summoned Okoshi Bizen to meet with Shigezane. Shigezane first inquired in detail about the situation in Tamura, intending to convey Masamune's words after gaining their trust, but Okoshi Bizen refused to discuss the Tamura situation. Later, through Uchigasaki Umasagashira, Shigezane conveyed this to Okoshi Kii-no-kami; thereafter, Okoshi Kii-no-kami ceased attending the Nishihara court. Upon being questioned by four senior retainers—Tamura Umeyuki, Tamura Uemon, Tamura Tsukisai, and Hashimoto Keibu—Okoshi Kii-no-kami replied, "Shigezane informed me that if I attended the Nishihara court, I would be taken alive." The four retainers protested to Shigezane, but Shigezane remained adamant. When the four retainers conveyed this to Okoshi Kii-no-kami, Okoshi countered, "Shigezane informed me through Uchigasaki Umasagashira." Shigezane replied, "Upon confirming with Uchigasaki Umasagashira, he stated that he had given his personal opinion to his close associate Okoshi Bizen, and had not said this was from Shigezane." To resolve this discrepancy, it was decided to pit Uchigasaki Umasagashira against Okoshi Bizen to determine whose account was correct. Because no official envoy was sent, the situation stalled; they reorganized and faced off, but the matter remained unresolved. 【Iwashi Danjo's Defection and Masamune's Departure】 April 7, Tensho 16. Iwashi Danjo, the lord of Tsukiyama Castle, defected from the Date side to join the Soma side. Iwashi Danjo had been under the military command of Tamura, but following the conversion of the Adachi district to Date territory, he had come under the command of Date Masamune. As mentioned earlier, the Tamura clan was in tension, split between the Date and Soma factions, and there was a widespread rumor that Masamune would depart to subdue Iwashi Danjo. However, at that time, Masamune was engaged in fronts along the Mogami and Osaki borders and could not move easily. Tamura Tsukisai and Hashimoto Keibu, who were part of the Date faction, petitioned Masamune through his liaison, Shiroishi Munemi, stating that while most of Tamura was close to the Soma, their refusal to break ties with the Date was due to their fear of Masamune. Masamune agreed and departed Yonezawa on April 29, arriving at Tsukidate on May 4. In contrast, Soma Yoshitane remained at Tsukiyama, and Iwashi Danjo remained at Kotetsumori, preparing for Masamune's attack. May 6. Masamune went out to scout Kotetsumori. Shigezane had also arrived at Tsukidate, but was sent back to Nishihara to ensure safety in the Asaka area. Due to bad weather during the rainy season, Masamune returned to Omori on the 7th. Shigezane, dissatisfied with the fact that he had returned only for scouting, sent Shiroishi Munemi and Shigezane through him, stating, "A single day of effort suggests the Mogami border is more important than Tamura. May I interpret this as the Date faction now changing their minds? May I assume that your presence at Omori is because you can quickly move to Tamura or the Mogami border?" Masamune replied that this was correct and that they should rest assured. Thus, with Masamune at Omori and Soma Yoshitane at Tsukiyama, the two sides faced off over Tamura. Upon this, the four senior retainers of Tamura agreed that neither the Date nor Soma forces were allowed to enter Tamura. On May 12, Soma Yoshitane planned to enter Nishihara, but was driven back by the aforementioned agreement of the Tamura forces and returned to Soma. Shiroishi Munemi, upon being informed of this by Tamura, immediately reported it to Masamune. Masamune departed immediately, arrived at Miyumori on the 13th, and conducted an attack on Tsukiyama over the following two days. By Masamune's order that Tamura might need reinforcements, Shigezane stationed troops at a place called Uchi-shiraiwa in Tamura and did not participate in this attack. On May 16, Kotetsumori was attacked and fell. Shigezane was in charge of holding Tsukiyama during this siege. This prompted the Soma forces remaining in the Tamura territory to withdraw, and three castles that had leaned toward the Tamura side returned to Masamune's hands. Upon returning to Miyumori, Masamune's four senior retainers, along with the Soma-faction Tamura forces, visited him to express their gratitude for the subjugation of Iwashi Danjo. 【Attack on Okoshi Kii-no-kami and Rumors of Satake Yoshishige's Departure】 The four senior retainers of Tamura requested Masamune to subdue Okoshi Kii-no-kami, as his failure to enter Nishihara during the attempted invasion of Nishihara was a plot by Okoshi Kii-no-kami, who refused to attend the Nishihara court. Masamune refused, citing rumors that Satake Yoshishige was departing for the Asaka area, but at the plea of the four retainers—who asked for at least a single sortie—he decided to dispatch Shigezane as the deputy governor to Okoshi. Shigezane departed for Funabiki and attacked Okoshi, but the castle forces did not respond and withdrew that day. When Masamune departed under cover, he and the Tamura forces, who were attacking together, clashed with the castle forces in the rear; the Date forces also joined them. The enemy was routed, and over thirty heads were taken, ending the engagement. Regarding the rumor of Satake Yoshishige's departure for the Asaka area, Shigezane, who was in charge of Asaka, was unaware. When Shigezane asked Masamune, Masamune cited the messengers of Sugawara Mino-no-kami and Iwashi Akimitsu from Sugawara as the source of the information. 【Koriyama Standoff】 As the rumor had suggested, a combined force of over 8,000 men—consisting of Satake Yoshishige and his son Yoshinobu, Ashina Yoshihiro, Shirakawa Yoshichika, Iwashi Akimitsu, Nikaido, and Iwaki—departed for the Asaka area. On June 1, Masamune received this information from Shiga Amantsurai Takeji, a pro-Date member of the Iwaki clan, and had dispatched troops toward the Asaka area around the 7th (see previous paper by Kobayashi). Masamune judged that the combined force would move toward Takakura or Honmiya; as a reinforcement for Honmiya, he departed Miyumori Castle on the 11th and moved his horses to Sugita. At the time, the Date clan, in addition to the tension with the Soma over the Tamura territory, faced fronts toward the Mogami and Osaki regions; the number of people they could mobilize for Asaka was barely six hundred cavalrymen. The combined force attacked the area around Koriyama, where Masamune was following them. Masamune judged that Honmiya was not an immediate target and, using Takakura as a base, conducted scouting operations toward Kunoyama and Joanyama on June 12 and 13. At this time, Koriyama Castle Lord Koriyama Tarozaemon also met with Masamune. Masamune dispatched thirty-odd cavalrymen and two hundred foot soldiers as reinforcements to Koriyama Castle. Upon receiving information from Koriyama Tarozaemon, Masamune ordered a formation at Joanyama. Nineteen people, including Shigezane, were involved: the accompanying party of Sohanzo Socho and Koryogawa Morimune, the senior retainers Hamada Kagetaka, Harada Munetoki, Tomizuka Munetsuna, and Endo Munenobu, as well as Harada Kyuseisai, Shiroishi Munemi, Ito Shigenobu, and Katakura Kagetsuna. In the council on the 14th, Sohanzo Socho and others expressed opposition to this standoff, but on the 15th, Masamune raised the Hinomaru small flag and deliberately conducted a scouting operation to make it conspicuous. In the council that day, he stated, "The enemy knows of Masamune's small flag; it would be shameful for the house to abandon the standoff and let Koriyama fall so recklessly. It is not uncommon for one to perish due to victory or defeat in battle. I strongly desire a standoff." Koryogawa Morimune feared that the Soma faction of the Tamura clan might break ties, but Masamune argued that a break with the Tamura clan—separated by the Abukuma River—would have little effect, that the castles of Koriyama, Kunoyama, Fukuhara, and Takakura were allies and had taken hostages, and that the distance to Honmiya in Shigezane's territory was short and easy to retreat to, thereby asserting his strong will for a standoff. Some still opposed it, but Masamune decided that the honor of the house was more important than fighting to perish and resolved to proceed with the standoff. Since reinforcements had been dispatched to Koriyama, he sent Iizaka Muneyasu, Omine Nobuyasu, Segami Kageyasu, and Ojo Munenao as deputies to the Kunoyama, Fukuhara, and Takakura castles, with the respective castle lords joining Masamune's army in succession. Ito Shigenobu stated, "This standoff is for the relief of Koriyama Castle; therefore, we should not force a battle, but prioritize defense." This became the primary policy of the Date forces. Masamune's position was chosen based on terrain and a favorable exit point, specifically the area between Kunoyama Castle and Fukuhara Castle. Accordingly, a standoff began for over forty days regarding Koriyama Castle. On the night of the 15th, Masamune returned to Honmiya and entered the camp on the 16th. Considering that Kunoyama, being water-fortified, was difficult to attack, Masamune ordered Shigezane to deploy forces at Joanyama. Shigezane deployed at Joanyama and arranged the defense so that it was easy to respond; however, contrary to expectations, the combined forces advanced between Koriyama and Kunoyama and approached Joanyama from there. Due to their inferior numbers, Masamune followed the policy of caution and did not engage; instead, he proceeded with the construction of the camp while remaining vigilant against the enemy. He postponed the establishment of the camp and utilized the irrigation ditches in front, building two layers of earthen embankments over five shaku within that day. On the 17th, construction continued, and the previous embankments were further reinforced to over eight shaku, with double ditches surrounding the camp. In front of the rice fields of Kunoyama, Tamura Muneaki, Tamura Tsukisai, and Katakura Kagetsuna deployed, while the other allies deployed behind Shigezane's camp. On June 18, while Shigezane's forces continued their construction, the enemy took action. A man named Okuma Inaba from Aizu was leading over three hundred men, filling the irrigation ditches at the edge of the mountain to create a path. Shigezane ordered them to return without regard for the enemy's resistance and dispatched seven or eight rifles; the shots struck Okuma's arm.

shigezane:shintatuittousi.markdown:
His personal name was Shigezane, and he later took the title of Awa-no-kami. He was the son of Motozane Date, known as Hyogo-no-kami. He was born in Shiroyama, Omori Village, Shinobu District. A peerless hero, he captured forts and castles in various places, besieged the castle of Nihonmatsu, and took the fort of Kotemori. His other feats of arms are too numerous to count. He passed away in the ninth year of Kan'ei, the year of the Water Monkey, at the age of sixty-four. When Lord Masamune was transferred to Sendai, Shigezane also built a residence and settled in Watari Village, Igu District. His grandson flourishes to this day and is the head of the Date clan. It is said that as Shigezane had no children, he adopted the youngest son of Lord Masamune to succeed his house, and himself retired to a place called Kashima Village, on the site of a castle, where he enjoyed a life of peace.

---

**※Shintatsu Ittoshi**

A gazetteer of the Shinobu and Date districts written in Tenpo 12 by Masanori Shida of the Fukushima Domain. It is included in the *Iwaiwa Shiryo Sosho* (Rekishi Toshosha, 1971) of Fukushima Prefecture.

As these are all my own personal interpretations, there may be errors. I would appreciate it if anyone who spots a mistake could let me know. I have added "free translations" to those I felt inclined to do. These are also my own personal interpretations, so please do not rely on them too heavily.

shigezane:shouhyou.summary: Below is a list of registered trademarks featuring bamboo and sparrows, arranged by registration date. Some may be omitted from this list. The rights holders are listed in the heading, with the design, registration number, and registration date provided.
shigezane:shouhyou.markdown:
Below is a list of registered trademarks featuring bamboo and sparrows, arranged by registration date. Some may be omitted from this list. The rights holder is listed as the heading, with the design, registration number, and registration date provided. Trademark rights extend only to the scope of the designated services. Please refer to the Japan Patent Office website for specific details. Among the various registered bamboo-and-sparrow trademarks below, some have overlapping designated services. These have been recognized as distinct trademarks from one another.

Since trademarks are commercial trademarks, they are generally unrelated to their use in family crests, articles in books, magazines, or newspapers, academic papers, manga, and the like; they are rights distinct from copyright.

In the pre-modern era, when the "house" was the primary entity, family crests could be considered a type of trademark. Now that the "house" system has disappeared, it is common to view family crests and trademarks as distinct entities.

Terms like "Zuigan-ji" and "Kojuro Katakura" are also registered trademarks, but people use them all the time in discussions about tourism and history, or in fan art. This is because they aren't being used as trademarks.

If you're wondering what trademark infringement entails, what to do if you're accused of it, or what a trademark licensing agreement looks like, please see here.

- On this site: [Approach to Trademark Rights](#/post/shigezane/shouhyouken)

shigezane:shouhyouken.title: Concepts of Trademark Rights
shigezane:shouhyouken.summary: The following are Takesui's personal views. I assume no responsibility. While I believe I have done my research, intellectual property law is complex. Please let me know if you spot any errors.
shigezane:shouhyouken.markdown:
The following are Takesui's personal views. I assume no responsibility. While I believe I have done my research, intellectual property law is complex. If you spot any errors, please let me know. I will correct them. For further details, please consult a lawyer or patent attorney.

## What is a trademark? What is trademark infringement?

A trademark is a business trade mark—a mark, brand name, or brand logo used to ensure that one's own products are not confused with those of others. Therefore, as a general rule, it should be used for one's own products.

Occasionally, counterfeit goods from brands like Gucci or Chanel are sold. This is a clear example of trademark infringement. Doing something that could lead to the products being mistaken for those of others constitutes trademark infringement. This applies regardless of whether it was done intentionally or not.

Under Japanese trademark law, you register the trademark for your product and the types of goods or services (known as "services") to which that mark applies. From the date of registration, you have the exclusive right to use that mark for the registered goods or services. It does not matter who started using them first; priority is given to whoever registered first (or, if there is overlap, whoever filed the application first). This is the legal criterion for determining who committed the confusing act.

However, even if you use the same name or symbol as a registered trademark for the same goods as the designated services, it cannot be said that you are infringing on rights, provided that the use is not such that it could be mistaken for another person's goods.

A trademark holder who had registered the words "POPEYE" alongside a manga for the product "clothing" sued a vendor who sold undershirts featuring the words "POPEYE" prominently on the chest. The court ruled that this "did not constitute an infringement of trademark rights." Consumers do not buy these shirts thinking, "I'll buy this because it's from this company"; rather, they buy them because they like the design. Therefore, this is an example where the mark does not function as a trademark to indicate which company the shirt belongs to, and thus does not constitute trademark use. Had the mark been used on a tag rather than the chest design, it would likely have constituted an infringement of trademark rights, as tags typically bear the manufacturer's or brand name. ("Popeye Undershirt Case," 1974 (Wa) No. 393) The same applies to titles of books, CDs, and the like. ("Yosui Inoue (Under The Sun Case, 1994 (Wa) No. 6280, etc.)")

A trademark must be used as a trademark.

I will quote [the section on the concept of trademark infringement](http://www.ishioroshi.com/biz/kaisetu/shouhyou/index/singai_shouhyousiyou/) from [the Craftman Law Firm website](http://www.ishioroshi.com/biz/).

> Generally, it is recognized that the primary function of a trademark is to serve as a "mark" to distinguish one's own goods from those of others (the function of distinguishing one's own goods from those of others, and the function of indicating origin). > Therefore, even if identical characters or figures are used, the use of such marks cannot be said to infringe upon the trademark right unless they are used in a manner that provides the functions of distinguishing one's own goods from those of others, indicating origin, etc. > For example, if such marks are used in a brochure for one's own products, but such use is clearly nothing more than a description or explanation referring to the products of another party, that use cannot be said to possess the function of indicating origin—the original function of a trademark—and, in substance, does not constitute the use of a trademark.

## What if you're accused of trademark infringement?

As stated above, even if a name, design, or product overlap, it does not constitute trademark infringement as long as the function of the trademark is not infringed.

As long as the use of a mark does not cause your own products to be confused with those of another party (the trademark holder), it does not constitute trademark infringement.

- Mere description/explanation
- Purely decorative use
- Cases where an item bearing a mark cannot be considered a product
- Excerpts from articles, scenes from manga, movies, etc., and backgrounds

These are examples of cases that do not constitute infringement.

I believe it would be sufficient to confirm that the use of the mark or name is not as a trademark (i.e., for distinguishing your own goods or services from those of others), and to state as much.

Note that trademark rights and copyrights are distinct rights. It is possible for a case to constitute copyright infringement without constituting trademark infringement, or vice versa.

## Trademark License Agreement

A trademark license agreement is a contract in which a trademark holder permits another party to use the trademark they have acquired. It is also referred to as a licensing agreement. The consideration for a trademark license agreement can be specified—namely, the so-called "brand fee" or "license fee."

Trademark license agreements are entered into in cases such as allowing affiliated subsidiaries to use a trademark, outsourcing the manufacture of one's own products to a licensee based on license negotiations, or expanding a franchise chain.

If a registered trademark and the trademark in use are not identical, the trademark holder cannot grant a license. This is because the scope of use the trademark holder can authorize is limited to the scope of the exclusive right to the registered trademark.

This means that parody products—such as the "Shiroi Koibito vs. Omoshiroi Koibito" mentioned below—cannot be covered by "trademark use" license agreements. (There are various other examples as well, such as parody T-shirts.) Therefore, when a trademark holder and a user reach an agreement—including for parodies or similar uses—they enter into an agreement "regarding the non-exercise of the trademark holder's right to prohibit use."

- "Even if you use something similar, it wouldn't be called trademark infringement!" (Non-exercise of the right to prohibit trademark use)

Such an agreement,

- "You can use my trademark!" (Trademark License)

So that's separate from that agreement, isn't it? (Of course, it's possible—and indeed common—to include both sets of terms in a single contract.)

> Quoted from [White Lover vs. Funny Lover—A Dispute Over Parody](http://www.jpaa-tokai.jp/activities/media/detail_344_0_2012.html). > [Japan Patent Attorneys Association, Tokai Branch](http://www.jpaa-tokai.jp/index.html) In the article above by patent attorney Daisuke Maeda, it states: > > Would consumers who see the packaging designs of both Ishiya Seika and Yoshimoto Kogyo perceive each confectionery as a product provided by the same entity or by interrelated entities? If such a perception does not arise and consumers can distinguish between the products by looking at these words and packaging designs, then no confusion as to the source occurs, and the trademarks are not similar. In such a case, neither trademark infringement nor violations of the Unfair Competition Prevention Act would be established. (Omitted) Is there any problem with not regulating at all the act of others free-riding on the goodwill acquired by "White Lover"? > While this prompts us to consider the issue of free-riding, it also makes us think about freedom of expression and cultural diversity in cases where trademark rights are not infringed. This case ultimately reached a settlement, with Yoshimoto Kogyo changing the design and limiting the sales regions.

A "non-exercise of the right to prohibit trademark use" agreement is also used when a trademark holder—who is not currently using the mark but has kept it registered—reaches an agreement with a user regarding the use of a similar trademark.

[“Drafting Trademark License Agreements”](http://www.jpaa.or.jp/activity/publication/patent/patent-library/patent-lib/200402/jpaapatent200402_037-056.pdf) — also cited from Toshio Asai, a member of the Japan Patent Attorneys Association.

> When X wished to use Trademark A, X discovered Trademark B—a registered trademark of Y—that was similar in appearance; consequently, X may negotiate with Y and obtain permission to use Trademark A. Since Y does not currently use Trademark B and has no concrete plans to use it in the near future, Y considered it more advantageous to grant a paid license to others to recover even a portion of the application and registration costs, rather than simply registering it as a stock trademark (hereinafter, such a license is referred to as a “non-exercise-of-prohibitory-right license”). Strictly speaking, a non-exercise-of-prohibitory-right license is not a grant of a right of use under the Trademark Act (Articles 30 and 31 of the Act). This is because, under the Trademark Act, exclusive and non-exclusive rights of use are “the right to use a registered trademark for the designated goods or designated services” (Article 30, Paragraph 2 and Article 31, Paragraph 2 of the Act), and can only be established within the scope of an exclusive right; they are not rights to use the trademark within the scope of a prohibitory right—that is, within the scope of similarity to the registered trademark. However, in actual corporate activities, such trademark licenses are common, and under the principle of freedom of contract, there is no reason to deny the validity of such agreements.

## Dormant Trademark

A dormant trademark is one that remains registered but is not being used by the right holder. People keep them as potential product names when launching new products. They may have no intention of using them for their own products, but they do not want others to use them without permission. They figure they can sell them to anyone who wants to use them. For these reasons, dormant trademarks remain. Since dormant trademarks also carry legal rights, they cannot be used without authorization.

However, since trademarks are brand names and brand marks, their value lies in their actual use. Therefore, a "trial for cancellation of non-use of a trademark" can be filed against dormant trademarks.

If a trademark has not been used at all for any period of up to three years preceding the filing of the request for trial, the trademark registration will be cancelled and the trademark right will be extinguished. The party filing the request for cancellation does not need to prove that the trademark has not been used for three years (i.e., that it is dormant); to avoid cancellation, the holder of the trademark right must prove its use. However, even if the trademark holder is not using it, it constitutes "use" if a licensee is using the trademark under a trademark license agreement.

## Mount Koya

This is where Shigezane is said to have first headed after leaving Fushimi. Masamune's grave is also located in the mountain grounds. Additionally, [Kitamuro-in](http://www.shukubo.jp/jpn/syuku/jiin/a/a38.htm) is revered by the Sendai Date, Uwajima Date, and Yamagata Mogami families, among others, and Masamune's memorial tablet is also enshrined there. Soji-in is also said to have close ties to the Sendai Date family.

## Kasuya

It is said that, under the patronage of the Okubo family—senior retainers of the Tokugawa clan—he resided at a Zen temple in Kasuya, Sagami (present-day Isehara City, Kanagawa Prefecture).

shigezane:shuppon1.title: Shigezane's Flight
shigezane:shuppon1.summary: Following the Bunroku Campaign, Shigezane, who had been residing in Fushimi, suddenly vanished from Masamune's side. The exact date remains uncertain.
shigezane:shuppon1.markdown:
※ Under revision. This is why the text is awkward.

Following the Bunroku Campaign, Shigezane, who had been residing in Fushimi, suddenly disappeared from Masamune's side. The exact date is uncertain. However, since his name appears on the oaths sent by senior retainers to Hideyoshi after the fall of Toyotomi Hidetsugu in Bunroku 4 (1595), it is certain that this occurred after that time. The *Date Masamune-kyo Denki Shiryoshu* adopts the theory that this took place in Keicho 3 (1598), but the family records serving as the source state "date unknown." Meanwhile, the *Seshin Kafu* records his departure in Bunroku 4. In any case, it appears he left Masamune's side sometime after the resolution of the Hidetsugu incident and before Hideyoshi's death.

While there are various theories regarding the reasons and developments, I will introduce them in order, citing supporting sources wherever possible.

## Reasons for Departure

The reasons cited for his departure are as follows. I will present them in order.

1. Due to dissatisfaction with land holdings and rank
2. Because he aspired to become an independent daimyo
3. To orchestrate a plot to help Masamune seize control of the realm
4. Reprimanded for his debts
5. At the suggestion of Haneda Umanosuke, he sought to enter the service of the Tokugawa clan.

### Due to dissatisfaction with his fief and rank

The prevailing view for now: it is said that he was dissatisfied with receiving little reward despite his many achievements.

One reason cited is that he was dissatisfied with the meager rewards he received for his achievements in Masamune's conquest of the southern interior. Masamune rejected numerous suitors and granted Nihonmatsu to Shigezane (Date Masamune Documents), entrusting him with future affairs during his campaign at Odawara. During the Odawara campaign, [a letter from Iwaki Tsunetaka received while Kurokawa was in charge](#/post/shigezane/huku-94-7) addressed him as "Lord Nihonmatsu," using the formal style of correspondence reserved for independent daimyo. Until this point, there were few grounds for dissatisfaction regarding Shigezane. Following Masamune's transfer to Iwadeyama, Shigezane moved from Nihonmatsu to Kakuda. While a direct comparison is difficult, the "33 villages of Nihonmatsu" became "16 villages of Kakuda," so it was undoubtedly a reduction in fief. However, since the entire Date domain was being reduced, Shigezane must have fully understood that this was an unavoidable measure. The only person presumed to have seen almost no reduction at this time was likely Kagetsuna Katakura. However, because Shigezane's Nihonmatsu territory had been acquired before the Date clan received the Edict of General Peace, the fate of Nihonmatsu remained unsettled during the Ou Administration. It is imagined that Shigezane undertook considerable efforts to ensure the confirmation of his holdings in Nihonmatsu, and that the associated expenses were substantial. Around this time, Masamune conducted temporary levies for the forces from the Kamigata region arriving in Ou, but only Shigezane and Tamura Muneaki complied in full (Kobayashi Seiji, "Hideyoshi's Ou Administration"). Shigezane and Tamura Muneaki, through Masamune, and Ishikawa Yoshimune, through Ishida Mitsunari and others, launched campaigns to confirm their respective holdings, but none of these proved successful.

What draws attention here is "honor" as a reward. While Masamune promoted capable retainers regardless of their rank, he increased their lands and stipends while keeping their status within the Date clan low. In contrast, Shigezane appears to have held a strong conviction that "I alone am the head of the Date clan." Serving as the caretaker of Kurokawa likely served to greatly bolster Shigezane's prestige. By Bunroku 4 at the latest, Shigezane's rank became second, following the Ishikawa clan. In a joint-signature document by senior retainers in August of Bunroku 4, Ishikawa Minbu-no-tasuke Yoshimune was listed first, and Shigezane was second. Thereafter, regarding the honor of "rank," Shigezane—and the Watari Date clan—would become intensely conscious of the Ishikawa clan. The "Manji 3 Report" contained in the *Sendai Bukan, Vol. 1* states, regarding the origin of the Watari Date clan becoming the second-ranking branch of the clan: "Because Sanemoto could not go to Echigo due to the Tenbun Disturbance, he became the first-ranking member of the Date. Now, the Ishikawa Yamato family holds a higher position than ours because, due to various circumstances regarding the prisoners, they became guests starting in Shigezane's generation" (paraphrased). Furthermore, there is a tradition that when Masamune attempted to grant the "Date" surname to the Ishikawa clan, Shigezane opined, "If I were to bear the name 'Date,' I cannot accept it unless I am the first-ranking member," suggesting he felt strong dissatisfaction with having to be subordinate to the newly arrived Ishikawa clan. Moreover, while it might have been acceptable if the head of the joint-signature document had been his uncle Akimitsu, the fact that it was his son Yoshimune likely wounded Shigezane's pride.

Furthermore, in terms of blood relation to Masamune, Masakage Rusu (third-ranking member of the Mizusawa Date clan) was also an uncle, as was Akimitsu Ishikawa. While the exact reason why Masamune placed the Ishikawa clan at the top remains unclear, the preferential treatment regarding rank—as a consideration for blood ties—is also seen in the subsequent treatment of Iwaki Masataka. What the Ishikawa and Iwaki clans had in common was their impoverishment at the time they sought Masamune's patronage. Masakage Rusu, Shigezane, and Masamune's great-uncle Shigemune Watari (fourth-ranking member of the Wakuya Date clan) possessed not only the influence of blood ties, but also substantial landholdings and military forces. This may have been a policy intended to keep their positions in check based on their familial connections.

### Because he aspired to become an independent daimyo

This is recorded in the Ou Eikei Gunki, following the "theory of dissatisfaction with landholdings and rank." Since this is a military chronicle based on hearsay, it is better to view it not so much as a record of credibility, but rather as the reflections of the people of Ou upon hearing the story that "Shigezane had left the Date clan."

### As part of a plot to enable Masamune to seize control of the realm

The theory presented in "Kyodo Watari No. 60," "'Kyokyo Jitsujitsu': Lord Shigezane's Flight" by Yoshio Fujikura. The flight was intended to travel through various provinces to plot his course. According to Wikipedia, the "Gamo Gunki" also contains an account to this effect.

### Reprimanded for his debts

Adopted by Sohachi Yamaoka in "Masamune Date."

### At the suggestion of Umanosuke Haneda, he sought to enter the service of the Tokugawa clan.

A theory found in [“Sendai Shiryo: Shigezane Date Fled to Koyasan”](#/post/shigezane/sendaishiryou-1).

## Shigezane's movements around the time of his flight

According to the *Seshin Kafu*, Shigezane was in "Fushimi" upon returning from Korea. However, prior to Hidetsugu's fall from power, the stronghold of both the Date and Toyotomi clans was "Juraku," where Hidetsugu resided. Masamune also held his New Year's festivities at the Date residence in Juraku at the time, and Endo Bunshichiro, who died while a guest in Kyoto, passed away at an inn in "Muromachi," located near Juraku. Shigezane should therefore have also been in Juraku. Yet, neither Shigezane nor his wife (Gensho-in) lived in the castle town of "Fushimi"—Hideyoshi's retirement castle—after their return to Japan. Shigezane was not in Kyoto. (Though the journey took less than a day, Fushimi was not referred to as "Kyoto" at the time.) From here,

- Masamune—Hidetsugu
- Shigezane—Hideyoshi

One can imagine such a line.

Next is the timing of the flight; as mentioned previously, there are theories suggesting either Bunroku 4 (1595) or Keicho 3 (1598). The basis for the Bunroku 4 date is the *Seshin Kafu*, and Shigezane's trail likely ends after the joint-signature letter from senior retainers in August of Bunroku 4. The basis for the Keicho 3 (1598) date is likely the entry for Keicho 3 in the *Jike Kiroku*, which mentions the Ishikawa clan being granted Kakuda and states that Shigezane's flight occurred "prior to this." Another clue is that the *Shigezane-ki* contains a record of the Keicho Fushimi earthquake on the 13th day of the intercalary 7th month of Bunroku 5 (Keicho 1). While there is a description of seismic measures taken when Hideyoshi rebuilt the castle at Kohatayama—suggesting he witnessed or heard about it firsthand—there is no mention of the damage to the Date residence, which he would naturally have experienced had the flight occurred before then.

There are various theories regarding where he was after his flight, but the generally accepted view is

- First, hiding at Mount Koya
- Attempted to enter the service of the Tokugawa clan, but was thwarted by Masamune and failed to do so.
- Having been in Kasuya, Sagami Province
- That prior to the Battle of Sekigahara, he declined an offer of 50,000 koku from Uesugi Kagekatsu.

. He returned to service in Keicho 5 (1600). He participated in the siege of Shiroishi Castle from Akimitsu Ishikawa's camp and also had an audience with Masamune at that time.

Based on materials recorded in "Kyodo Watari No. 51," here is a summary of Shigezane's activities following his flight:

＜Fled in Bunroku 4. His companions included Aoki Tota, Shiga Yashichi, Tokiwa Hayato, Haneda Kokichi, Sugimura Kuzaemon, Oka Hanbei, Oka Kyuichi, and Ogata Oribe. He first became a guest of Asano Danjo. After Hideyoshi's death, he sought to enter the service of Tokugawa Ieyasu through Okubo Tadanari, but this proved impossible as marriage negotiations were already underway between Masamune's daughter (Princess Gorokuhachi) and Ieyasu's son (Tadateru). Consequently, Okubo Tadanari sheltered Shigezane at a temple in Kasuya, within his own domain of Sagami Province. In Keicho 5, just before the Battle of Sekigahara, Naoe Kanetsugu adopted Shigezane; Shigezane then fled Kasuya, but was unable to leave the province because Okubo Tadanari hastily closed the gates. Left with no choice, he remained in Ota, where Ishikawa Akimitsu and Kagetsuna Katakura arrived to welcome him at Masamune's secret request; Okubo Tadanari then gave Shigezane his armor as a parting gift.＞

Since there is no mention of the original source, it's unclear what kind of document this is, but judging from other materials, the "Watari Monogatari" said to exist in Date City appears to be the original. There are certainly some points to nitpick—like why of all people, Asano Nagamasa? Since Asano had severed ties with Masamune around this time, perhaps he sheltered Shigezane out of spite?

To be honest, I am not particularly fond of the author, Shito's, novelistic narrative style, but this book contains less "narrative" and "fiction" compared to other works by the author. shigezane:sibukawa.title: Battle of Shibukawa Castle
shigezane:sibukawa.summary: Following the Battle of Hitotori Bridge, Shigezane spent the turn of the year at Shibukawa Castle (Shibukawa, Adachi Town), which served as an outpost of Hachichome Castle, while maintaining frontline vigilance.
shigezane:sibukawa.markdown:
January 1, Tensho 14 (1586)

Following the Battle of Hitotori Bridge, Shigezane spent the turn of the year at Shibukawa Castle (Shibukawa, Adachi Town), which served as an outpost of Hachichome Castle, while maintaining frontline vigilance. Although Shibukawa Castle had been completely destroyed by a fire on December 11 of the previous year, it maintained its function as a frontline base through expedited construction (presumably).

At that point, the Nihonmatsu forces led by Kanokoda Izumi emerged as scouts. Perhaps emboldened by the fact that it was the New Year, the foot soldiers of Shibukawa Castle engaged them haphazardly without being armed, only to find an ambush waiting behind a small hill. Naturally, they were quickly overwhelmed, and upon learning the situation, Shigezane hastily dispatched proper troops to their aid. Haneda Umanosuke happened upon this battle while returning from a mission in the vicinity and joined the fray. His younger brother, Shiga Daisozaemon, also fought valiantly, and the Nihonmatsu forces retreated. Shigezane presented the heads he had taken at this time to Masamune.

shigezane:sobo.title: Who was Shigezane Date's grandmother??
shigezane:sobo.summary: The question of who Shigezane's grandmother—that is, Sanemoto's mother—was. Almost all sources from the Date side identify Sanemoto's mother as Lady Ashina, the wife of Uemune.
shigezane:sobo.markdown:
The question of who Shigezane's grandmother—that is, Sanemoto's mother—was. Almost all materials from the Date side identify Sanemoto's mother as a member of the Ashina clan, the wife of Uemune. However, according to materials from the Uesugi side, Sanemoto's mother is said to have been the younger sister of Nakajo Fujisuke of the Yohoku-shu. The Date-side source is the "Date Family Documents" No. 10-3290, "Letters Regarding the Children of Tanemune," but for the Uesugi side, this has become the accepted view despite the original source remaining unknown. (That said, doubts regarding the provenance of the document persist on the Date side as well. This document is accompanied by a wrapping paper claiming it was written by the High Priest Daiyu of Tosho-ji, a son of Tanemune, but the date is "January 20, Kan'ei 12 (1635)." Wait a minute—High Priest Daiyu was already dead... (died 1618).) Regarding the issue of Sanemoto's succession, it seems things became complicated partly because "other members of the Yohoku-shu, wary of the Nakajo clan's influence becoming too strong, strongly opposed it," but if his mother were of the Ashina clan, this reason would not hold up. The Date-side materials do not mention the Nakajo clan as Uemune's wife. However, considering Sanemoto's position within the Date family, his mother's lineage is important. Sanemoto took his niece (the daughter of Harumune) as his wife, but if Harumune and Sanemoto were half-brothers, the blood connection would be tenuous even in an uncle-niece marriage. Furthermore, regarding the entry in the "Shoto Seiji-ko" stating that the primary wife of the 13th head, Naomune, was the daughter of Uesugi Sadazane, age inconsistencies have been pointed out early on. This is because Sadazane and Tanemune were of the same generation. Consequently, Shin Hasegawa, in "Allied Relationships between Shugo and Kokujin in the Southern Ou Region: The Cases of the Echigo Uesugi and Date Clans," and in "The Echigo Tenbun Disturbance and Date Tanemune: Various Powers in the Southern Ou Region during the Sengoku Period Regarding the Date Tokimune Maru Succession Issue," identifies the "Uesugi clan member as the wife of Date Naomune" as "the elder or younger sister of Uesugi Sadazane, who was the adopted daughter of Uesugi Fusasada."

shigezane:sumou.title: Shigezane Date Enjoys Gambling Sumo
shigezane:sumou.summary: It seems that gambling sumo was sometimes enjoyed in the castle town of Omori. However, this was the Sengoku period, and sumo was a life-or-death affair... Perhaps summoned by Shigezane, the opponent for the gambler from elsewhere was Abe Mino, renowned in Sahara Village for his great strength and stature.
shigezane:sumou.markdown:
It seems that gambling sumo was sometimes enjoyed in the castle town of Omori. However, this was the Sengoku period, and sumo was a life-or-death affair... Perhaps summoned by Shigezane, a gambler from elsewhere arrived to face Abe Mino, who was renowned in Sahara Village for his great strength and stature. Mino casually lifted his opponent overhead, and upon a command from Shigezane, who had grown excited, he slammed the wrestler to the ground. The wrestler died as a result. Overjoyed, Shigezane rewarded Mino and bestowed upon him the epithet "Dai-Mino."

From "Konomi no Katami" by Kunio Hashimoto, contained in the "Oshu Shinobu-gun Sahara-mura Nemoto-ki"

## The Great Strength of Okisaka Omino

In Okisaka of Sahara Village, there lived a man named Abe Mino. He was large in stature and possessed great strength; he would seize women and children from other places, tie them to the great pine trees in the shrine groves, and put them up for sale. He also drove the hatchets he used into the eyes of great trees in the deep mountains, and no one was able to pull them out. He possessed such strength that he could carry the furnishings of a three-ken residence on his back all at once from Genbei of Sakuramoto Hakusui. Around the Tensho era, when Shigezane Date was at Omori Castle, he carelessly handed over a gambler from elsewhere; by Shigezane's order, the gambler was driven into the ground and killed, and Mino received a reward for his victory, at which time he was granted the name "Omino." Furthermore, at Kami-no-Sakaguchi within the Yariai area of Shono Village, seventy-five people from Okino Village were pulling a large wooden pillar, but they had pulled it into a hollow in the slope and were at a loss when Abe Mino of Sahara happened to pass by and pulled the pillar out all by himself. For this reason, it is said that he became renowned as the strength of seventy-five men. It is also said that to ensure that the women and children he had seized from elsewhere would be sold readily, he kept them tied to large trees every day, causing them to suffer as long as they were not sold.

## Original text

At Ogisaka, there was a man named Abe Mino who was exceptionally strong and large in stature. It is said that he seized women and children from other places, tied them to the great pine trees in the shrine groves, and put them up for sale. Furthermore, this man would drive the hatchets he used into the eyes of great trees in the deep mountains, and no one had the strength to pull them out. He possessed such strength that he could carry the furnishings of a three-ken house in a single load from the place of Genbei of Sakuramoto Hakusui. During the Tensho era, in the time of Lord Date Awa-no-kami of Omori, he carelessly thrust a sumo wrestler who had come from elsewhere; by Lord Awa-no-kami's order, the man was driven into the ground and killed, and he received a reward for his victory. From then on, he was given the name "Omino." Additionally, at Kami-no-Sakaguchi within the Yariai area of Shono Village, seventy-five people from Okino Village were pulling a large wooden pillar and had drawn it into a hollow in the slope, leaving them at a loss; then Abe Mino of Sahara happened to pass by and pulled the large pillar up all by himself. Consequently, it became rumored that he possessed the strength of seventy-five men. It is also said that to ensure that the women he had seized from other places would eventually be sold, he kept them tied to large trees every day until they were sold.
