shigezane:suriagejara-kassen.title: Battle of Surigami-ue
shigezane:suriagejara-kassen.summary: On June 1, Tensho 17, Inawashiro Morikuni—with whom Shigezane Date had been resuming negotiations for internal collusion since the beginning of the year—was killed by Ashina. In response, Masamune dispatched Nitta Yoshitsuna and Harada Munetoki to Hibara, and Shigezane Date and Kagetsuna Katakura to Inawashiro.
shigezane:suriagejara-kassen.markdown:
June 5, Tensho 17

On June 1, Tensho 17, Inawashiro Morikuni—with whom Shigezane Date had been resuming internal negotiations since the beginning of the year—was killed in action by Ashina. In response, Masamune dispatched Nitta Yoshitsuna and Harada Munetoki to Hibara, and Shigezane Date and Kagetsuna Katakura to Inawashiro. At the time, Ashina Morishige was stationed at Sukagawa, plotting an invasion of the Tamura territory alongside Iwaki, Satake, and Soma; however, upon receiving urgent news of Inawashiro Morikuni's defection, he rushed back to his base at Aizu-Kurokawa on June 3. The Soma forces had previously lost Komagamine and Minokubi castles on the northern frontier in mid-May and were unable to move freely, while Satake Yoshishige remained in Nakadori and Iwaki Tsunetaka in Hamadori, maintaining a posture of keeping the Date army's main force in check. The day after his return, Ashina Morishige departed for Inawashiro, targeting the Inawashiro, Shigezane, and Katakura forces gathered in the Inawashiro Basin at the foot of Mount Bandai. Unless the Date army provided reinforcements, the Inawashiro sector army would be isolated and annihilated; conversely, if reinforcements were sent, they would be at risk of being caught in a pincer attack by the Satake forces in Nakadori. Masamune attempted to send reinforcements to Inawashiro, but was opposed not only by his close senior retainers but also by the crucial Inawashiro sector army (Shigezane and Katakura). However, Masamune disguised the Inawashiro sector army's objections as a "request for reinforcements" and, in the dead of night on June 4, forcibly moved himself and the main force to Inawashiro to provide reinforcements. He left only a small garrison at the castles on the Tamura border, pressed by the Satake and Iwaki forces.

The battle began on the morning of June 5. Initially, the Ashina army held the advantage, and the vanguard—the Inawashiro unit—and the second line—the Katakura unit—were defeated.

shigezane:t13-10-6.title: 1. On the evening of the 6th, Lord Terumune
shigezane:t13-10-6.summary: 1. On the evening of the 6th, Lord Terumune visited Lord Masamune's camp, summoned the senior retainers to the lady-in-waiting's quarters, and consulted with them regarding the manner of offering an apology to Yoshitsugu.
shigezane:t13-10-6.markdown:
> 1. On the evening of the 6th, Lord Terumune visited the camp of Lord Masamune and summoned the senior retainers to the lady-in-waiting's quarters to discuss the manner of offering an apology to Yoshitsugu. Although we were inexperienced, Lord Terumune commanded that we serve as messengers to Yoshitsugu, stating that we were the ones who should carry out the task. We offered various arguments regarding the propriety of serving as messengers for such a serious matter, but as his will was firm, we had no choice but to obey. He further commanded that, should Yoshitsugu later require us to accompany him—whether to the south or the north—we were to do so; however, as this was impossible, we requested that the retainers be summoned according to their original stipulated landholdings. He further remarked that it was pitiful that those who had served him until now were now treated as beggars, but as this too was unacceptable, we resolved to commit seppuku upon reporting to him. He was pleased to state that everything was at his discretion. Since Yoshitsugu was humbled by our service, he expressed a desire to have an audience with us; upon our earnest request, he agreed that we should certainly meet. On the 7th, at the hour of the eighth, Shigezane arrived at the camp; as time passed, he lit a candle to meet us and then returned to Miyamori. On the 8th, early in the morning, we received a messenger from Shigezane, informing us that he was coming to Miyamori. We accepted this with gratitude. We also wished to offer many expressions of sympathy; having been told that it was acceptable to return home and make preparations to send the children to Yonezawa, we proceeded to Lord Terumune's camp. Lord Date Ueno and many other senior retainers went to Miyamori and reported to Lord Terumune that it would be auspicious to settle in Nihonmatsu. Shigezane told us that it would be humbling to visit Lord Terumune, and when we reported this, he commanded us to depart immediately; thus, Shigezane went to Lord Terumune's camp. Among the attendants, Takabayashi Naizen, Kanokoda Izumi, and Otsuki Nakatsukasa were summoned to the reception room. When Izumi arrived, he whispered something to Shigezane, who then entered the room. Lord Terumune was present, as were Ueno and we. We rose without further idle chatter. We stood by the gate to see them off. Gratitude was expressed inside. Since the inner attendants were gathered around, it was not possible to seize them; as we stood by the gate to see them off to the front garden, there was no path through the bamboo fences, so they were blocked off, and gratitude was expressed. Shigezane thrust his hand to the ground and cried out, > "I have heard that, despite your generous hospitality this time, you intend to kill us!" > With that, he seized the cloth at Lord Terumune's chest with his left hand and drew his short sword with his right. As previously agreed, seven or eight of Shigezane's attendants moved behind him, and Ueno and we remained behind, preventing their passage. As they pushed through, he cried out, > "Block the gate!" > but as they did not comply, he followed them. Those who had come from Obama drew their weapons in haste. Those from Miyamori, unable to don their armor, surrounded him in shock, mostly bare-skinned, and followed him for over ten ri to a place called Takada. Lord Masamune had gone to the hawk grounds and returned after hearing the news. The Nihonmatsu group, Hanzawa Gennai, carried moon-swords, and Yusa Magokuro carried a bow. Others, drawing their swords, surrounded Lord Terumune. Among the allies surrounding him, a single musket was fired; without further command, the entire force attacked, and over fifty members of the Nihonmatsu group were killed, not a single one remaining. Lord Terumune was also killed. Lord Masamune also departed for Takada that night. The senior retainers were first ordered to return to Obama and await an auspicious day for an attack; thus, they returned to Obama in the early hours of the 9th. Lord Terumune's body was escorted to Obama that night and sent to Shifukuji in Nagai on the 9th. During the funeral rites, Endo Yamashiro and Uchibaba Shichiemon committed ritual suicide. Suda Hoki also committed ritual suicide at a residence 100 ri away. On the evening of the 8th, Shigezane's body was cut into pieces, strung together with wisteria, and hung outside Obama Town. The lands held by Shigezane—Motomiya, Tamanoi, and Shibukawa—were transferred to Nihonmatsu on the evening of the 8th, and he was ordered to serve as a hostage in Yonezawa. On the 12th, he appointed his son, who spoke of the King, and a man he had long known, Shigezane's cousin Shinjo Danjo, as his leader and they held out in a castle.

shigezane:t13-6-11.title: Letter from Morikuni Inawashiro, June 11, Tensho 13
shigezane:t13-6-11.summary: Letter from Inawashiro Morikuni, June 11, Tensho 13. The opening reads: "Having perused your letter, should there be any requests, I have received your kind permission to state them. Accordingly..."
shigezane:t13-6-11.markdown:
Having reviewed your letter, should there be any requests, I have received your kind permission to state them. Accordingly,

1. Should Aizu be secured, it shall be granted as a northern fief. Should the bow and arrow not be as you desire, I shall withdraw from Inawashiro; in such an event, a pardon of 300 kanmon shall be granted within the Date domain.

1. From my time forward, should those from Aizu enter service, I request that you place me in the seat of honor.

Aside from the above, I have no further requests; I therefore humbly request that you convey this as appropriate. With utmost respect and deference.

June 11, Tensho 13

Inawashiro Danjo Morikuni (seal)

Lord Togoro Date

## References

**[Masamune-ki: "Concerns Regarding Nihonmatsu, with Addendum on the Military Strategy of Inawashiro"](http://shigezane.info/majime/tyosaku/masamuneki/masamuneki1-3.htm)**

"Upon reviewing the reply sent from Hibara, I was deeply gratified by the assurance of your loyalty. Should you have any further requests, I shall gladly accommodate them; as you stated that you would prepare a seal for Masamune, I replied: 'Should your loyalty be further strengthened and you undertake the administration of Aizu, please include the following items: 1. Within Aizu, the northern half shall be granted to you. 2. The people of Aizu, regardless of their loyalty to me since my time, shall be seated in their respective positions for generations in Aizu; this shall not apply to the fudai-shu. 3. Should you fail to mobilize your forces and withdraw from Inawashiro, a pardon shall be granted for the three hundred kanmon of your house.'"

**[Shigezane-ki "1. To Aizu..."](#/post/shigezane/shigezaneki-3)**

"1. The northern half shall be granted to you. 1. Those who shall serve us hereafter shall be seated in your presence in Aizu, as is customary. 1. If there are no bows and arrows as you desire, and if you withdraw from Inawashiro, you shall be granted 300 kan in leniency within the Date domain. Aside from these three points, I have no further requests; I have written this accordingly..."

shigezane:t13-9-26.title: 1. On the 26th, Lord Masamune to Obama Castle…
shigezane:t13-9-26.summary: 1. On the 26th, when Lord Masamune transferred his horse to Obama Castle, Yoshitsugu Nihonmatsu wrote to Sanemoto: "Though we have relied on the Date clan for generations and maintained our standing, in recent years, Aizu, Satake, and Iwaki have directed their arrows toward Tamura."
shigezane:t13-9-26.markdown:
> 1. On the 26th, while Lord Masamune was transferring his horses to Obama Castle, Yoshitsugu of Nihonmatsu sent a message to Sanemoto, stating: "Though we have relied on the Date clan for generations and maintained our ties, in recent years, Aizu, Satake, and Iwaki have directed their arrows toward Tamura. We, too, hold a grudge against Lord Kiyoaki and have conspired with Aizu and Satake. Nevertheless, as each of us understands the circumstances, we visited Lord Terumune's camp twice during his campaign against Soma to serve him; therefore, we beg that our positions be maintained without further incident." Accordingly, Sanemoto conveyed the above to Lord Terumune. Lord Masamune replied that he had taken note of the conspiracy against Soma. However, this time, having conspired with the Ouchi, they had launched a preemptive strike at Kotemori and also concentrated their forces within Ouha, leading to a battle. As they were enemies akin to the Ouchi in the provinces, he commanded that a decisive battle be fought. Nevertheless, due to various apologies, it was ordered that the lands be ceded—from Sugitagawa-kiri in the south to Aburaiyagawa-kiri in the north—and that a settlement be reached within the five intervening villages. Furthermore, it was ordered that his son be sent to Yonezawa as a hostage. Yoshitsugu repeatedly pleaded, requesting that either the south or the north be granted to him as a compromise, but as this was not granted, on October 6, Yoshitsugu personally visited Lord Terumune's camp at Miyamomori.

shigezane:t18-5-27.title: Teizan-ko Jike Kiroku, entry for May 27, Tensho 18 (Summary)
shigezane:t18-5-27.summary: Excerpt from the Teizan-ko Jike Kiroku, entry for May 27, Tensho 18. The opening reads: "27th, Day of the Fire Rabbit. A letter arrived for Lord Fujigoro from Tsukisai Seikyu Tamura and Gyobu Akinori Hashimoto, retainers of Tamura Magoshichiro Muneaki. The gist is..."
shigezane:t18-5-27.markdown:
27th, Day of the Fire Rabbit. A letter arrived for Lord Fujigoro from Gessai Seikyu Tamura and Gyobu Akinori Hashimoto, retainers of Magoshichiro Muneaki Tamura. The substance was as follows:

"We did not happen to cross paths on the road; I understand that Shuhakusai has departed for Odawara. Whether there will be further explanations thereafter remains uncertain. Therefore, regarding a letter forwarded to Muneaki from a man called Ishida Jibu-shofu, it has been delivered from Niiyama. I forward this letter for your perusal. As for the matter of responding to Jibu-shofu, all arrangements on our end have been left to Lord Masamune; how could we possibly do so without seeking his private instructions? For this reason, Muneaki has not provided a reply. Since Lord Masamune has fortunately joined the campaign, we send our greetings, asking that you coordinate with him. Though we have mentioned this many times, we empathize with the great hardship of your absence."

## Miyagi Prefecture

**☆ [Atago Shrine](http://www.atago.org/top/index.htm)**

Sendai City. Relocated from Yonezawa to follow Masamune.

**☆ [Osaki Hachimangu](http://www.okos.co.jp/oosaki/)**

Sendai City. A combined shrine of Osaki Hachimangu, revered by the Osaki clan, and Narushima Hachimangu, revered by the Date clan.

**☆ [Kameoka Hachimangu](http://hachimanguu.org/)**

Sendai City. Enshrined by Asamune, the first head of the Date clan. Relocated along with the Date clan.

**☆ [Kogan-ji](http://kouganji.or.jp/index.htm)**

Sendai City. The family temple of Takematsumaru, the eighth son of Masamune. It enshrines the memorial tablets of Aihime and Takematsumaru. During the domain period, it played a role in temple affairs as the head of [Rinno-ji](http://www.rinno-ji.or.jp/index.shtml).

**☆ [Sengaku-in](http://homepage2.nifty.com/sengakuin/)**

The administrative temple of Sendai Toshogu Shrine. It houses a wooden statue of Tadamune.

**☆ [Sendai Toshogu Shrine](http://www.sendai-toshogu.or.jp/)**

Sendai City. Enshrined by Tadamune.

**☆ [Zuigan-ji](http://www7.ocn.ne.jp/~zuiganji/)**

Matsushima Town, Miyagi District. A Zen temple in Matsushima deeply revered by Masamune. It is also famous for being the place where Masamune resolved to meet his end should he ever clash with the shogunate.

**☆ [Tosho-ji](http://www.asahi-net.or.jp/~cd4a-yme/tosyoji/index.htm)**

A temple where Oyu Koho, a son of Tanemune, served as chief priest. One of the Five Mountains of Kitayama.

**☆ [Rinno-ji](http://www.rinno-ji.or.jp/index.shtml)**

Commissioned by Masamune's ninth wife. It houses the grave of Aihime's mother and that of Takematsumaru, Masamune's eighth son.

## Fukushima Prefecture

**☆ The Path of KOHAku (Hoshaku-ji) (Under Renovation)**

This is a website about Japanese culture managed by the family, rather than the temple's own site. Of course, it also includes an introduction to the temple. Kohakuzan Hoshaku-ji, located in Funaba-cho, Fukushima City, Fukushima Prefecture, is the burial site of Terumune Date.

## Iwate Prefecture

## Yamagata Prefecture

**☆ [Shoden-an](http://www3.omn.ne.jp/~imanari/)**

Yonezawa City. The family temple of Genbanmaru, son of Tanemune.

## Hokkaido

**☆ [Kotoni Shrine](http://www.geocities.co.jp/HeartLand-Momiji/1970/)**

Sapporo City. Enshrined at the site of the Watari Date clan's settler colony. Shigezane Date and Masayuki Hoshina are enshrined as the deities.

**☆ [Daio-ji](http://homepage1.nifty.com/daiouji/index.htm)**

Date City. The family temple of the Watari Date clan.

A sub-temple of Tofuku-ji in Kyoto. Houses a portrait of Masamune.

shigezane:terumune-deth.title: The Awanosu Incident—Various Accounts Surrounding the Death of Terumune 1
shigezane:terumune-deth.summary: An overview of the Awanosu Incident—in which Terumune Date was abducted by Yoshitsugu Hatakeyama at Miyamori Castle and both were killed by Date forces who attacked them at Awanosu (Hiraishi Takada, Nihonmatsu City)—has already been documented on this site under Battle Records > Awanosu Incident.
shigezane:terumune-deth.markdown:
An overview of the Awanosu Incident—in which Terumune Date was abducted by Yoshitsugu Hatakeyama at Miyamori Castle and both were killed by Date forces who attacked them at Awanosu (Hiraishi Takada, Nihonmatsu City)—has already been documented on this site under [Battle Records > Awanosu Incident](#/post/shigezane/awanosu).

> 〈Awanosu Incident Map〉 Created using Electronic National Land. Black areas represent rivers.

The question of "who killed Terumune" is what sparks discussions about this incident—often driven by a sense of curiosity—and serves as a highlight in works of fiction.

Who killed Terumune, and why did such a grave incident—the simultaneous deaths of two daimyo—occur? I would like to examine these questions using various sources. I must first note that no primary sources regarding this incident are known, and that I must rely on military chronicles, military anecdotes, and oral traditions. Regarding this incident, as a recollection by those involved,

- Recollections of Shigezane Date: "Masamune-ki," "Shigezane-ki," and their variants: "Masamune-ki" (Sengoku Historical Materials Series), "Shigezane-ki" (Sendai Series), "Date Nikki" (Gunsho Ruiju), "Masamune-ko Gogunki" (National History Series)
- Recollections of Masamune Date: "Kimura Uemon Memorandum"
- Recollections of Yamaguchi Dosai, Retainer of Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu: "The Tale of Yamaguchi Dosai"
- Memories of Local Villagers: "Notes of an Elderly Man from Genna 8"

exist. In this section, I have conducted a comparative examination focusing primarily on these.

I have uploaded readings and comparison tables for each source, so please refer to them via the links listed under "References" at the end of this section.

## Terumune and Masamune in the Prelude to the Incident

Following their acquisition of Shiomatsu, Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu of Nihonmatsu proposed a peace settlement to the Date clan. Although the Date side initially refused, they eventually accepted the terms after several pleas from Yoshitsugu.

The dynamic between the young Masamune—who stubbornly refused peace and sought to resort to force—and his father, Terumune, who admonished him, has become an established image since the taiga drama *Dokuganryu Masamune*, and many subsequent fictional works have followed this pattern. The basis for this dynamic is believed to be the *Masamune-ki* written by Shigezane. The proposal for peace was passed from Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu to Date Sanemoto, then to Terumune, and finally to Masamune; while Terumune provided advice and admonitions to Masamune, the final decision-making authority rested with Masamune. However, a comparison between different versions of the *Masamune-ki* and *Shigezane-ki* reveals inconsistencies regarding whether Terumune or Masamune was the decision-maker, as seen in the accounts of Shigezane himself or the copyists and compilers. Specifically, in the *Shigezane-ki*, it can be read that Terumune was the one making decisions throughout, and the "confirmation of tenure for only five villages"—described as a harsh peace condition—was also Terumune's idea. In the *Date Nikki* and *Masamune-ko Gogunki*, both Terumune's decisions and Masamune's decisions are recorded.

Now, let us examine the decision-makers within the Date clan who led to the conclusion of the peace settlement, from the perspective of Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu. The *Yamaguchi Dosai Monogatari* is the memoir of Yamaguchi Dosai, a retainer of Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu. Dosai did not accompany Yoshitsugu on his final farewell visit, and his accounts—from the abduction of Terumune to the deaths of Yoshitsugu and Terumune—largely mirror the variant versions of the *Shigezane-ki* and *Masamune-ki*. However, the descriptions within Nihonmatsu Castle leading up to the peace settlement, as well as the accounts from the deaths of Yoshitsugu and Terumune to the siege of Nihonmatsu Castle, are unique. According to these records, it was Terumune who proposed the terms of the peace settlement.

What about local tradition? The *Genna 8-nen Rojin Oboegaki* states that Yoshitsugu pleaded earnestly with Terumune, but Masamune did not grant his request.

At the time, the succession of the family headship from Terumune to Masamune had only just taken place within the Date clan. While the succession between Terumune and Masamune is commonly understood to have occurred without a period of dual rule, does the inconsistency in the description of this decision—found in the writings of none other than Shigezane Date—not suggest that Terumune had not yet fully relinquished actual power? Masamune himself, in the *Kimura Uemon Oboegaki*,

> "Since we are merely attendants..." > "The attendants grew increasingly suspicious; no doubt they intended to return to Nihonmatsu and strike them midway—when I thought the young lord must have come out with a gun..."

His recollection—as if he had not yet succeeded to the headship of the house—likely stems from a desire to evade his own responsibility, yet it is also intriguing in that it seems to reflect Masamune's own perception at the time. Furthermore, while Shigezane served as the envoy for the Date side during the peace negotiations, it was Terumune who had ordered him to do so; when Shigezane declined, citing his youth, Terumune declared that he would take the lead, stating, "Terumune shall handle all matters (Masamune-ki)." Indeed, on the day of the incident, senior retainers of the Date clan had crowded into Terumune's "camp at Miyamori" to celebrate the conclusion of the peace agreement.

## Outbreak of the Incident

It was the day of the incident. As mentioned previously, senior retainers of the Date clan, including Masakage Rusu, had crowded into Terumune's camp at Miyamori to celebrate the conclusion of the peace agreement (*Shigezane-ki*, *Masamune-ki*, etc.). While there is no record of whether these senior retainers were present for the meeting between Terumune and Yoshitsugu, Masakage Rusu was present.

Regarding the meeting itself, Shigezane records that "they stood without exchanging any words" (*Masamune-ki*; *Shigezane-ki*: "there was no idle chatter either"). While the *Yamaguchi Dosai Monogatari* describes a sake-sharing ceremony—presumably part of the meeting protocol—the claim that there was no idle chatter likely follows Shigezane's own account. On the other hand, the *Genna 8-nen Rojin Oboegaki* states, "Terumune was particularly pleased, and various delicacies were served, with several cups consumed." Masamune's recollections in the *Kimura Uemon Oboegaki* also suggest a feast took place: "It was said that Lord Nihonmatsu would visit tomorrow, so a preliminary feast was arranged here as well"; "While Lord Terumune and Lord Nihonmatsu were conversing in the guest room, speaking of how there should be no lingering attachment between them, it happened suddenly that the dining trays were suspended by ropes across four or five bays by the kitchen."

While the meeting proceeded without incident, it was not without occurrences that foreshadowed the tragedy to follow.

- As they entered the room, Kanokoda Izumi whispered to Yoshitsugu. (Shigezane)
- The incident that sparked the commotion—a tray shelf hanging in the kitchen falling—prompted the attendants to whisper to one another, and Yoshitsugu took his leave. (Masamune)

And while the timing differed, a record exists of a whispered to Yoshitsugu. Shigezane had witnessed the incident on the spot, but since Masamune was out falconing, he likely gathered accounts from those involved later. In any case, it was likely this whisper that led Yoshitsugu to decide to abduct Terumune.

> "...Please proceed to the garden. We—Ueno and I—stepped out into the garden, but as there was no path to follow, we remained behind. Yoshitsugu struck the ground with his hand and declared, 'I find the various hospitality shown to me this time to be excessive. Accordingly, I have heard that I shall be killed.' He then seized Lord Terumune by the chest with his left hand and drew his wakizashi. As it seemed they had prearranged this, Yoshitsugu's retainers—seven or eight of them who were nearby—circled behind Lord Terumune and pulled Ueno and me out, blocking the way." > (Shigezane-ki)

Furthermore, while this passage conveys nearly the same sentiment in the *Date Nikki*, in the *Masamune-ki*—which is believed to have been compiled later—the account is altered to suggest that Masakage and Shigezane saw them off from within the room, stating, "Ueno and Shigezane returned to the Terumune hall, and as they stepped out, those inside saw them off."

## Background of the Decision to Abduct

In the *Shigezane-ki*, Yoshitsugu says:

> "We have received word that we shall be killed."

Under the guise of a peace settlement, the Date side attempted to kill Yoshitsugu. This line of thinking served as Yoshitsugu's motive. According to investigations conducted by Masamune and Shigezane after the incident,

> "Looking back at the events of that disturbance, when Yoshitsugu was in Obama on the seventh day and met with Masamune, some of Masamune's retainers were staying at an inn in the town of Obama. Fourteen or fifteen of them were gathered there in one room, playing; and while they were in a state of relaxation, they began to sharpen the blades of their swords and short swords, filling the carriage-room with water and surrounding it with half-cut blades, each rushing to draw and clash them with one another. At that moment, three or four of Terumune's retainers, who had come to Obama on official business from Miyamori, happened to pass by and asked, 'Why are you in such a hurry?' The retainers, seemingly unaware of the matter, replied jokingly, 'Tomorrow, we shall use this to slice the two-sword-bearers into small pieces.' The two-sword-bearers, wondering whether they were being mocked or if there was some other reason, stood by and heard this. That night, when Yoshitsugu returned to Miyamori, it was reported that he had suddenly changed his mind." > (Masamune-ki) > "...Since we had no particular means of infiltrating, we set out for the mountains with bows, spears, and firearms. The attendants of Lord Nihonmatsu found the situation most suspicious..." > "The sound of people commotionally making a fuss was heard loudly in the guest room; while Lord Nihonmatsu found it strange, the attendants grew increasingly suspicious and, without hesitation, resolved to return to Nihonmatsu and strike them down midway. Thinking that the young lord must have come out with firearms..." > (Kimura Uemon Memorandum) > "The lowly retainers of Yoshitsugu went to the stables, and upon looking, they found one attendant with the blade of his short sword sharpened. A fellow attendant asked, 'What are you doing? Today, Lord Nihonmatsu has returned in peace; there are no bows or arrows, and it is a fine occasion for all ranks; it is said there is a banquet in the guest room.' When asked, 'Are you doing something improper?' the attendant replied, 'Do you not know? When Lord Nihonmatsu returned, there was a secret order to kill every single person without exception. I have been making preparations, aspiring to become a renowned warrior.' When the lowly retainers of Yoshitsugu heard this, they were exceptionally surprised. When they reported this to the samurai, they lamented the regret of having been betrayed and plotted to be struck down. They first summoned Kanokoda and informed him of every detail, and the lowly retainers declared that they had made full preparations. Izumi also informed Yoshitsugu, and he took appropriate measures." > (Yamaguchi Dossai Monogatari)

If we hypothetically synthesize all the accounts: on the night before the incident, one of Masamune's foot soldiers jokingly declared, "Tomorrow, we shall slice the two-sword-bearers into small pieces," and someone from the Nihonmatsu group happened to overhear this. On the day of the event, the Nihonmatsu group spotted Masamune's party heading out, carrying bows, spears, and firearms. Even at the stables, an attendant made a lighthearted remark: "There is a secret order that when Lord Nihonmatsu returns, every last one of them must be shot dead." Just as suspicions were deepening, a commotion broke out—. Masamune must have set out to strike down Yoshitsugu, who was returning to Nihonmatsu. Rather than be killed so needlessly, Kanokoda said to Yoshitsugu.

> "Please exercise your discretion." > (The Tale of Yamaguchi Dosai)

With that whisper,

> "He deliberately did not even summon cavalry, reaching Obama with only his personal attendants." > (Notes of an Elder, Genna 8) > "Among the Nihonmatsu retainers, only Hanzawa Gennai and Tsukiken Yusa Magokuro carried swords; all others drew their blades." > (Masamune-ki)

Though Yoshitsugu and his companions were not armed in any meaningful sense, they took a desperate gamble by abducting Terumune.

I would like to delve a bit deeper into the circumstances that led Yoshitsugu and the others to believe the flippant remarks of a low-ranking retainer—a ruse that defies common sense.

Before the conflict with the Date clan broke out, Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu engaged in peace negotiations. The Date side initially took a hardline stance, declaring, "We cannot forgive you for aligning yourself with Ouchi Ujitsuna. We will attack Nihonmatsu." Seeking to avoid war, Yoshitsugu pleaded further. The Date clan proposed peace terms: "Provide the heir as a hostage, and guarantee the tenure of only five villages between the Sugita and Aburai Rivers." Yoshitsugu negotiated further, arguing that this would not suffice for his livelihood and demanding that half of the Nihonmatsu territory be confiscated—or, if that were impossible, that at least his retainers be granted guaranteed tenure—but his requests were ignored. Cornered, Yoshitsugu, virtually unarmed, made a "sudden incursion" (fuzu-kakeiri) into Miyamori (according to the *Masamune-ki*), surrendering completely and stating that he would comply with any orders, even if he was ordered to commit seppuku. (Here, I wish to emphasize once again that Miyamori was Terumune's camp). An incursion is an act of seeking protection, and there is a custom where the party receiving the intruder protects them—a practice seen in institutions such as *kakekomi-dera* (temples for refugees). I wish to point out the similarity between this and the fact that Yoshitsugu suddenly "intruded" into Miyamori. As a result of this "incursion," following a consultation between Terumune and Masamune, Yoshitsugu's safety was guaranteed the day after the incursion. The peace terms were

> "He handed over a son, His Majesty the King, aged twelve, and the matter was settled with a single article." > (*Masamune-ki*)

The terms had been relaxed to a single condition: the provision of the heir as a hostage. Did this abrupt shift from the Date side's hardline stance bring only relief to Yoshitsugu's mind? Or might it have also brought anxiety—? This is mere speculation.

In the "Yamaguchi Dosai Monogatari," the narrative unfolds somewhat differently from the Date family records mentioned above. In addition to "providing the heir as a hostage and guaranteeing the tenure of only five villages between the Sugita and Aburai Rivers," Terumune first proposed the "guarantee of the ancestral lands of the retainers." Yoshitsugu initially refused and considered battle, but from senior retainers such as Shinjo Shin'an,

> "It is rumored that both the high-ranking and low-ranking retainers of the hereditary line have grown fond of the Date. Furthermore, the castles under our control are utterly at a standstill. Terumune has repeatedly issued instructions: that five villages—from the Sugita River in the north to the Aburai River in the south—be taken as guest lands, while those holding castles or residences shall remain in their castles and residences as is now, and serve the Date by taking a stipend of one *koku*; provided this is carried out successfully, they should be granted the same status. As they still hold a deep affection for Aizu, they have not only refrained from sending witnesses, but are effectively under the banner of Aizu."

Persuaded in this manner, he accepted the terms set forth by Terumune and offered his surrender to the Date. However, Terumune's terms had not been presented with Masamune's consent; after Yoshitsugu had offered his surrender, Terumune had to persuade Masamune. Once Masamune had given his approval, Yoshitsugu—

> "Delighted, at the hour of the Goat on the 7th day of the 10th month of the 13th year of Tensho (Year of the Rooster), he unexpectedly moved from Nihonmatsu to Obama and proceeded to the camp of Date Awa-no-kami."

He expresses his gratitude to Shigezane, who served as the messenger, and states that he also wishes to thank Terumune. The fact that Yoshitsugu's destination was Shigezane's camp in Obama differs from Shigezane's account. Furthermore, it feels odd that Yoshitsugu himself visited Obama "unexpectedly," despite this being a thank-you visit made after the arrangements had been finalized.

## The Death of Terumune

Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu, having abducted Terumune, headed from Miyamori toward Nihonmatsu. Masakage and Shigezane, caught off guard, sent an urgent message to Masamune and pursued Yoshitsugu's party. However, with Terumune held hostage, they could not easily intervene.

The Date side had seized control of the Shiomatsu territory, and the border with the Nihonmatsu territory lay along the Abukuma River. Before Yoshitsugu's party could cross the Abukuma River, Terumune had to be recovered—action had to be taken. At the time, there was a boat crossing at Takada on the Abukuma River (Yamaguchi-do Saito Monogatari). Additionally, Takada Castle stood overlooking the crossing.

It is thought that some catalyst existed for them to take action. Examples include geographical factors such as leaving Miyamori Castle, passing through the castle town of Obama, crossing a mountain pass, or reaching a river crossing point. In fictional works, including Taiga dramas, the geographical factors of crossing the Abukuma River are often highlighted, with the scenes of Terumune and Yoshitsugu's deaths frequently depicted on the banks of the Abukuma. The place names recorded as the locations of these scenes are

- Works of Shigezane (from Miyamori): Takada, over 10 ri away
- "The Tale of Yamaguchi Dosai": Within Ohira, a place called Awanosu (just under one ri from Obama)
- "Memoranda of an Elderly Man, Genna 8": A place called Awasu in Suzuishi Village

Thus, accounts vary depending on the source. The 10 ri mentioned by Shigezane refers to rural ri, where 1 ri = 6 cho ≈ 654 m. Masamune,

> "As they proceeded, they drew near the Nihonmatsu territory; apparently having received word, a great number of men rushed to gather across the river." > (Kimura Uemon Memorandum)

...leaving behind words suggesting that the river was visible from the site. However, the site currently regarded as the "Awanosu Old Battlefield" is located one small hill east of the Abukuma River, and the river is not visible. If the current "Awanosu Old Battlefield" is indeed the site, no particular geographical factors warrant special mention; if there were a catalyst for the action, it would be Masamune's arrival on the scene. Regardless of whether the site was the banks of the Abukuma River or the "Awanosu Old Battlefield," Masamune's arrival—which Shigezane left vague in his writings—was, Masamune himself

> "Surprised, I rushed over to look, and there it was." > (Kimura Uemon Memorandum)

As these words suggest, it seems certain.

Shigezane writes of Terumune's death as follows:

> "However, from among those who had gathered around him, a single shot was fired. Though no one claimed to have finished the kill, the entire group charged in and cut down over 50 members of the Nihonmatsu group, and Lord Terumune was also slain." > (Shigezane-ki)

While no one had specifically given the order, triggered by a shot fired spontaneously, the Date forces launched an attack on Yoshitsugu's party. As a result, Terumune and over 50 members of the Nihonmatsu group, including Yoshitsugu, were killed.

The sound of this gunshot could be heard even at Nihonmatsu Castle.

> "While Shinjo Danjo was on duty at Nihonmatsu Castle, two gunshots were suddenly heard." > (Yamaguchi Dosai Monogatari)

Becoming anxious, Shinjo Danjo (Shin'an) and others armed themselves and proceeded to the Takada ferry to meet Yoshitsugu, where they encountered foot soldiers panting, reporting that Yoshitsugu and his companions had been killed in action. It is said that upon sending lookouts across the river and observing the scene from the lookout stone atop Mount Takada, they saw the Nihonmatsu troops slain as if their counting rods had been thrown in disorder.

Masamune's recollections contain no mention of firearms.

> "As events unfolded and we drew closer to the Nihonmatsu territory, it seemed a report had been sent, for a vast number of men rushed to gather across the river. Just as I thought the situation was hopeless, Shigezane and all the clan members mounted before our horses and charged forward; there was no other way but to abandon the effort. Just as I was asking, 'What shall we do?', they remarked, 'What a wretched fate, with nothing to rely on,' and seeing their expressions, the Nihonmatsu forces were deeply moved and, in their pity, stabbed Lord Terumune to death." > (Kimura Uemon Memorandum)

To Shigezane and the others, who asked, "We have no choice but to abandon him. What shall we do?", Masamune replied, "It cannot be helped." Sensing an impending attack, the Nihonmatsu forces stabbed Terumune to death.

The stabbing of Terumune is also mentioned in the "Genna 8 Elder's Memorandum."

> "Word of this matter soon reached Nihonmatsu, and troops were dispatched; however, Masamune witnessed this, pursued them relentlessly, and called out for Terumune to be struck down along with them. As expected, none of the retainers dared to intervene. Yet, as the situation grew urgent, Yoshitsugu stabbed Terumune to death with the short sword he had been carrying, and then committed suicide with that very blade." > (Genna 8 Elder's Memorandum)

The elder of Obama who recounted this was 70 years old in Genna 8. The incident occurred when he was 33. Masamune ordered, "Strike down Terumune and all," but the retainers hesitated. However, when it seemed they were finally about to strike, Yoshitsugu stabbed Terumune to death and committed suicide. Terumune had not been shot by a musket; he had been stabbed to death.

shigezane:terumune-deth2.markdown:
## The Position and Actions of Date Sanemoto

Now, it appears that Date Sanemoto and his son Shigezane acted as intermediaries between Terumune and Masamune—father and son—and Yoshitsugu during the peace negotiations between Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu and the Date clan. This father-son duo, who held the Omori territory on the southern border of the Date clan, was composed of Shigezane—who, like Masamune, had only just succeeded as head of the house—at the main castle of Omori, and his father Sanemoto, who had retired to Hachichome, a castle on the southern border. The Omori territory bordered Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu's Nihonmatsu territory directly. The border castle on the Date side was Hachichome, while that on the Hatakeyama side was Shibukawa. Hachichome Castle had once been a Hatakeyama stronghold, but in Tensho 2, Date Sanemoto captured it; as a condition of the peace agreement, Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu provided 50 cavalrymen to assist the Date forces engaged in the Soma campaign. From then on, it appears that Date Sanemoto served as an advisor and liaison for Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu. (Sengoku Shi Kenkyu No. 65, "The Development of the Date Domain and the Father-Son Pair Date Sanemoto and Shigezane," Takahiro Sato, 2013). Furthermore, while the conquest of Hachichome is recorded as the first instance of negotiation between Sanemoto and Yoshitsugu in the Date-ke Jike Records, Sanemoto's use of Omori as a base dates back to the Tenbun era, and negotiations with the lords of the Sendo region must have begun during the Tenbun Disturbance.

Regarding the peace negotiations that triggered the Awanosu Incident, the first person Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu turned to was Date Sanemoto, who served as his advisor.

> When Lord Masamune moved his horses to Obama Castle, Nihonmatsu Yoshitsugu conveyed the following message to our lord Sanemoto: > "Though we have relied on the Date clan for generations and maintained close ties, in recent years they have directed their arrows against Aizu, Satake, Iwaki, and Tamura. We too hold a grudge against Lord Kiyoaki and wish to align ourselves with Aizu and Satake. We beg that you join us in the same castle and, until the final outcome, have Lord Terumune act as our guide. Should the arrows be directed toward Soma, we shall visit your camp twice and render our service; we ask that you treat us without prejudice." > In response to this request, our lord Sanemoto conveyed the above to Lord Terumune. > (Shigezane-ki)

It is also suggested that the representative on the Hatakeyama side was Yusa Shimosa, the lord of Shibukawa Castle on the border.

> This Sanemoto was on close terms with Yoshitsugu, and there was constant correspondence between the two. As for Yusa Shimosa, he had been long on friendly terms with Hyobu-no-daifu (Sanemoto), and was frequently dispatched as a messenger. > (Yamaguchi Dosai Monogatari)

This Yusa Shimosa would later become one of the five who returned to their allegiance to the Date during the siege of Nihonmatsu Castle. As previously mentioned, Shinjo Shin'an stated,

> "It is rumored that both the high-ranking and low-ranking retainers of the hereditary line have grown fond of the Date." > (Yamaguchi Dosai Monogatari)

became a reality. That aside, in the preceding stages of the Awanosu Incident in the autumn of Tensho 13, it could be said that negotiations initially began via the route: Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu—Yusa Shimosa—(a retainer of Sanemoto)—Sanemoto—Terumune. Let us summarize the relationships between the various daimyo at this point.

**Date–Ouchi**

Vassalage → Defection/Severance.

**Ouchi–Hatakeyama**

Alliance. Due to deteriorating relations between Hatakeyama and Tamura, Hatakeyama—as a countermeasure against Tamura—had formed an alliance with the Ouchi through a marriage tie.

**Date–Hatakeyama**

Military subordination (uma-uchi). However, due to the deteriorating relationship between the Hatakeyama and the Tamura, the Hatakeyama have distanced themselves from the Date—who have close ties to the Tamura—and are drawing closer to Ashina.

For ten years following the peace settlement of Tensho 2, relations between the Date and Hatakeyama remained stable; however, as noted above, the deteriorating relationship between the Hatakeyama and Tamura brought about a change in the situation. While the course of events is omitted here, the Tamura and Ouchi were in hostilities, and Tamura Kiyoaki's request for the Ouchi to be subdued—having struggled with Ouchi Sadatsuna's attack on the Miharu territory—was one of the factors leading to the severance of ties between the Date and Ouchi. Before the Date and Hatakeyama reached a direct break in relations, Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu had initiated peace negotiations; however, since the Hatakeyama forces had served as the vanguard for the Ouchi forces that had fought the Date forces during the campaign to conquer the Shiomatsu territory, the Date side viewed this as the de facto severance of ties.

> This time, in league with the Ouchi, they took the initiative at Kotemori and also deployed forces into Ouha, leading to a battle. As they were enemies no different from the Ouchi in the provinces, it was ordered that a decisive engagement be fought. > (Date Nikki) > During the recent campaign to subdue the Ouchi of Bizen, in the battles at both Kotemori entrances, one side was led by Yoshitsugu. During the operation into Oba, while a skirmish was underway with the garrison at Nihonmatsu, it was deemed that they were enemies no different from the Ouchi; thus, it was ordered that an operation be carried out against Nihonmatsu. > (Shigezane-ki)

As noted at the outset, the territory bordering Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu's Nihonmatsu domain was the Omori domain held by the father and son, Date Sanemoto and Shigezane. Incidentally, Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu was not the only one sending reinforcements to the Ouchi. The Aizu-Ashina—upon whom the Hatakeyama and Ouchi relied—as well as the various generals of the Sendo region under their influence, also sent reinforcements to the Ouchi. Since the Hatakeyama and Ouchi were in a coalition against Tamura, they could not pass through the Tamura domain; instead, they passed through the Nihonmatsu domain (with the full cooperation of Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu) and entered the Shiomatsu domain. Despite these circumstances, Date Sanemoto maintained peace between the Omori and Nihonmatsu domains and made no attempt to sever ties.

> Thus, while Shiomatsu was under siege by arrows, our kin resided in Hachichome, and the situation at the Nihonmatsu border remained unresolved. > (Shigezane-ki)

According to Shigezane, Sanemoto's view was as follows.

> As for the underlying intent behind keeping the border quiet at all times, when reinforcements were sent from Aizu and the Sendo region to the four pines, Tamura—since it was enemy territory—proceeded toward Nihonmatsu. Therefore, Sanemoto approached Yoshitsugu and urged him to keep the border quiet, reasoning that while Satake, Aizu, Sendo, and Iwaki were now aligned against Nihonmatsu, the enemy would reconcile with Sanemoto and the border would remain secure; subsequently, the four aforementioned generals would likely harbor suspicions toward Yoshitsugu. > (Masamune-ki)

The argument was that despite the severance of ties between the Date and Ouchi, if the relationship between Sanemoto and Yoshitsugu—that is, the relationship between the Date and Hatakeyama—did not collapse, the Aizu, Ashina, and other Sendo generals relied upon by the Ouchi and Hatakeyama would view Yoshitsugu with suspicion. If he could no longer rely on Ashina, Yoshitsugu would be forced to rely on the Date. Sanemoto reasoned thus and pacified the border, having also discussed the matter with Terumune and Masamune, father and son. However, Shigezane only learned of Sanemoto's reasoning after the fact. Shigezane himself had intended to sever ties and attack Nihonmatsu. If the head of the Omori clan (who was Shigezane at the time)—who had previously been in charge of the Nihonmatsu liaison—had advised severing ties, it would have carried significant weight. To prevent this, Sanemoto twice demanded written oaths from Shigezane, yet he never revealed his own intentions to him.

> Although we informed Lord Masamune, as we were juniors, we were not permitted to speak. If this boundary dispute were to be settled, it would only lead to further trouble; thus, we did not dare speak of it. We submitted written oaths twice, and as a result, the boundary between Hachichome and Nihonmatsu was settled without incident. > (Shigezane-ki)

In other words, Terumune and Masamune accepted Shigemoto's views and actions, yet in the actual peace negotiations, they signaled their intent to "move against Nihonmatsu," citing the engagements with the Hatakeyama forces—acting as reinforcements for the Ouchi—at Kotemori and other locations, thereby exerting pressure on Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu. Furthermore, at Kotemori, Shigezane's Omori forces and the Nihonmatsu forces did indeed engage in combat.

Terumune, Masamune, and Shigezane leveraged the Omori Date clan's position as intermediaries to employ a shrewd form of double diplomacy in an attempt to corner Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu.

## The Tie Between Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu and Terumune Date, and Yoshitsugu's "Inner Wife"

Now, in this section, we are comparing the historical sources mentioned at the outset regarding the Awanosu Incident; I would like to introduce an intriguing tradition concerning the negotiation route—or "te-suji"—between Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu and the Date clan.

> As the consort had a distinguished lineage through Terumune, a private request was made that a settlement be reached and that she attend the service of Terumune and his son, Yoshitsugu, to express her gratitude. However, as Masamune would not agree, the consort made various representations to Terumune, and the matter was thus arranged for a meeting. > (Genna 8, Elder's Memorandum, Shiomatsu Obama Village)

> Nihonmatsu Yoshitsugu initially entered into close ties with Terumune Date and his son; furthermore, as the consort had a distinguished lineage through Terumune, > when Terumune marched against Soma, Nihonmatsu dispatched 50 mounted riders and 100 muskets as reinforcements. > (Genna 8, Elder's Memorandum, Nihonmatsu Elder)

Yoshitsugu's consort is generally said to be the daughter of Shinjo Naotsugu of the Hatakeyama clan (Wikipedia). However, the "Genna 8 Elder's Memorandum" states that "the consort has a lineage tracing back to Terumune," suggesting she was a relative of Terumune.

The role of women in diplomatic channels is also exemplified by the case of Hoshun-in (wife of Terumune Date). For further details on Hoshun-in's diplomatic activities, please refer to "The Activities of Hoshun-in in the Ou Region during the Sengoku Period: Peace Maintenance and Women in the Sengoku Period" (Yuriko Endo, Nihonshi Kenkyu (486), 2003.2).

If it is true that Gitsutsugu's wife was a relative of Terumune, the catalyst may have been the capture of Hachichome in Tensho 2 and the subsequent peace settlement; however, no such description can be found in the "Diary of Terumune Date," which records the events of the year Tensho 2.

On the other hand, the "Yamaguchi Dosai Monogatari" depicts the "second wife of Hatakeyama" during the siege of Nihonmatsu, where she "wore armor, a headband of white cloth, let her hair fall loose, and carried a naginata at her side," encouraging the senior retainers by serving them sake and directing the ladies-in-waiting to cast musket balls. It is said that upon the surrender of Nihonmatsu Castle, she withdrew to Aizu.

However, glimpses of Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu's connections to the Date territories—particularly the Omori domain—can be found in the temple-related traditions described later, making it easy to infer that there was some lineage or relationship that had vanished from the official history of the Date clan.

## Yoshitsugu's Family Temple and Omori

This section presents temple-related traditions suggesting a connection between Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu and the Date territories, particularly the Omori domain.

The Nishimatsuyama Shonen-ji, a temple of the Hatakeyama family of Nihonmatsu, is the family temple. The *Yamaguchi Dosai Monogatari* consists of the "Ken" volume, which covers military chronicles, and the "Kon" volume, which focuses primarily on Shonen-ji; from these, the following excerpts regarding Omori and Shonen-ji are provided.

> In the 12th year of Tensho (the year of the Wood Monkey), Hatakeyama Inaba-no-kami Yoshitsugu was killed in battle against Masamune Date. Following that conflict, the resident priest at the time, along with the Hatakeyama memorial tablets and other sacred treasures, moved to a place called Omori in the Shinobu domain, where they established a thatched hermitage and named it Omori Shonen-ji. > (Yamaguchi Dosai Monogatari, Kon, Nihonmatsu Shonen-ji Enki) > During the fall of Nihonmatsu in the Tensho era, the resident priest of Shonen-ji, fearing an enemy attack, temporarily relocated the sacred image and the imperial plaque. Out of compassion, the lord of Omori in Shinobu District donated a small plot of farmland in an area called Uchimachi, ensuring that the Hatakeyama lineage would not be extinguished and allowing Shonen-ji to be rebuilt. (Omitted) Later, as generations passed, Shonen-ji in Omori also fell into decay, and the abbot of Shonen-ji relocated the sacred image hall and the sacred treasures to Horin-ji in Yanagimachi, Fukushima. > (Yamaguchi Dosai Monogatari, Kon, Nihonmatsu Shonen-ji Enki)

The matter regarding Horin-ji in the latter section also appears in the "Shintatsu Ittoshi."

> Gyojuzan Horin-ji, Ji-shu > This temple houses the memorial tablet of Hatakeyama Shuri-no-daibu Yoshitsugu, the former lord of Nihonmatsu Castle. The reason is that after Yoshitsugu left Nihonmatsu, he established a temple in Omori Village, Shinobu District, and named it Shonen-ji. It never ceased in later generations (omitted). It is said that in the present age, his virtuous legacy was transferred to this temple to enshrine the spirit of the Hatakeyama clan. > (Shintatsu Ittoshi, Fukushima-mura)

The "Yamaguchi Dosai Monogatari, Volume 2: The Relocation of Shonen-ji to Omori Village, Shinobu District" records the following regarding the funeral of Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu:

> When Yoshitsugu was assassinated, the Date forces immediately surrounded Nihonmatsu and took up a position; consequently, Yoshitsugu's funeral could not be held at Shonen-ji. The priest of Toda-ji in Kawamata requested Yoshitsugu's remains, which had been in Obama, and held the funeral at Toda-ji. From then on, the Nihonmatsu family of Sanshu is said to have converted from the Ji-shu sect to the Soto sect. > (Yamaguchi Dosai Monogatari, Volume 2: The Relocation of Shonen-ji to Omori Village, Shinobu District)

According to the Kawamata Town website, Toda-ji Temple on Keisoku Mountain in Kawamata (2 Aza-Toda-ji, Iizaka, Kawamata Town) is

> Keisoku-zan Toda-ji is a Zen temple founded in Hotoku 1 (1449) by the priest Saimatsu Seigyu, a native of Kumamoto in Kyushu. At the time, it was a subsidiary temple of Tanryu-in—a Soto Zen temple affiliated with Soji-ji in Kokuwa, Yonezawa City. Through missionary activities spanning the second through the twelfth generations, it expanded to include 17 subsidiary temples, reaching as far north as Hobara, east to Kusano, and west to Tatsukoyama, rivaling Yorin-ji in Hirata, Fukushima City. While repeated fires have left no trace of its former appearance, the name of Date Tanemune remains prominent as the temple's founding patron. > ([http://www.town.kawamata.lg.jp/soshiki/9/bunkazai-zudaji.html](http://www.town.kawamata.lg.jp/soshiki/9/bunkazai-zudaji.html) )

It says.

Additionally, the *Shindachi Ittoshi* contains an account of a legend linking the Omori domain to Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu.

> While there is a theory that Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu resided in Omori-mura after the fall of Nihonmatsu, the personal names of Nagura Yoshitsugu and Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu coincide. Could it be that he changed his name from Hatakeyama to Nagura? > (*Shindachi Ittoshi*, entry for Daihi-do, Jitoku-ji Temple, Hokyu-zan, Sahara-mura, Sugawa Nansugi-tsuma-sho)

The same entry states that Nagura Yoshitsugu, or Nagura Mori-yoshitsugu, was the third generation of the "Jitoku-ji-dono, ancestors of Shinobu" who established the Daihi-do, and that he carried out restoration work on the Daihi-do. Regarding Nagura Yoshitsugu, the author of the *Shindachi Ittoshi* himself writes, "I have not heard the official title Nagura Mori; as for what kind of person he was, his name and surname remain uncertain," and while suggesting an identification with Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu, he writes this in the form of a question, leaving one with the impression that the connection is a forced one. (Furthermore, according to the catalog of the *Shindachi Ittoshi*, Nagura-sho was located within Shinobu District, and Omori also belonged to Nagura-sho.) The theory that "Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu resided in Omori-mura after the fall of Nihonmatsu" is likely a variation of the account regarding the relocation of Shonen-ji to Omori.

Since Sahara-mura is referred to as "Sugawa-minami," it is believed to be within the broader Omori territory. Furthermore, Jitoku-ji, where the Daihi-do is located, is a subsidiary temple of Ogura Yorin-ji—the family temple of the Omori Date clan where the graves of Uemune and Sanemoto still exist—and is the site where Terumune Date was cremated. While the *Shindachi Ittoshi* does not mention the relationship between Jitoku-ji and Terumune Date, the fact that it was written with reference to the "theory that Hatakeyama Yoshitsugu resided in Omori-mura after the fall of Nihonmatsu" is a curious coincidence.

shigezane:terumune-deth3.title: Various Matters Concerning Terumune's Funeral, Burial, and Gravesite
shigezane:terumune-deth3.summary: Following the incident, Masamune marched to Takada that same day and expressed his intention to attack Nihonmatsu, but at the urging of his senior retainers, he returned to Obama in the early hours of the 9th (Teizan-ko Jike Kiroku).
shigezane:terumune-deth3.markdown:
Terumune's remains were interred in Obama on the evening of October 9.

More than a day had passed since the tragedy.

Following the incident, Masamune marched to Takada that same day and expressed his intention to attack Nihonmatsu, but at the urging of his senior retainers, he returned to Obama in the early hours of the 9th (Teizan-ko Jike Kiroku). This suggests that Terumune's remains must have been at the camp in Takada from the 8th until the afternoon of the 9th.

> On that night, the remains of His Highness were brought to Obama Castle. Finally, they were cremated at Jutoku Zenji in Sahara Village, Shinobu District. Zen Master Koya of Shifuku-ji served as the presiding priest. He was known as Kakuhan-ji-dono. The remains were interred at Jiun-ji Shifuku Zenji in Natsugari Village, Nagai-sho, Okitama District, Ushu Province. The date is unknown. > (Teizan-ko Jike Kiroku, entry for October 9, Tensho 13) > They were cremated at Jutoku Zenji in Sahara Village, Shinobu District, and a mausoleum was constructed at Jiun-ji Shifuku Zenji in Natsugari Village, Nagai-sho, Okitama District, Ushu Province, where the remains were enshrined. Zen Master Koya of Shifuku-ji served as the presiding priest. The tea offering and Buddhist rites were conducted by Reverend Shoshitsu of Jutoku-ji. > (Seizan-ko Jike Kiroku, entry for October 8, Tensho 13)

It is recorded that he was cremated at Jutoku Zenji in Sahara Village, Shinobu District (Fukushima City), and his remains were interred at Shifuku-ji in Natsugari (Takahata Town).

※Click to enlarge. Adapted from GSI Maps.

## Jutoku-ji and Jitoku-ji Temples, Sahara, Fukushima City

Jutoku-ji, the temple where Terumune was cremated, is located approximately 40 km from Obama Castle. It is situated at the foot of the mountains just before reaching Mount Azuma, along the Tsuchiyu Road leading from Omori to Inawashiro. It would likely have taken two days to transport the remains. Perhaps the decision to avoid the ritual bathing at Obama was because the site had only recently been captured. The reason why this location—off the route to Yonezawa and far from Yonezawa itself—was chosen as the cremation site remains unknown. If it were a temple associated with the Date clan, other options such as Zuda-ji in Kawamata or various temples in Date District, both closer to Obama, could have been considered, but none were selected. While no records of Terumune's funeral survive, the *Seizan-ko Jike Kiroku* includes the *Heikyo Hogo* of Reverend Kosai of Shifuku-ji and the *Tencha Hogo* of Reverend Shoshitsu of Jutoku-ji; based on this, it is believed that the funeral associated with the cremation was likely held at Jutoku-ji. If Reverend Kosai had to travel from Shifuku-ji in Natsugari to Jutoku-ji in Sawara, this would also have required several days. Jutoku-ji moved to Iwadeyama with Masamune, and later to Sendai. At that time, Masamune designated Terumune as the founding patron and invited Reverend Kishu Sen'o, the eighth head of Shoon-ji, to establish the temple. Terumune's memorial tablet is enshrined at Jutoku-ji in Sendai. As noted above, since Reverend Shoshitsu of Jutoku-ji served as one of the presiding priests for Terumune's funeral, it is certain that Terumune had been a generous patron of Jutoku-ji during his lifetime. However, there is no mention of Jutoku-ji in the New Year's rituals of the "Date Terumune January Events." Regarding Terumune's cremation, conspiracy theories are often attributed to the unusual nature of his death, but cremation was by no means rare at the time. Terumune's cremated remains were likely placed in an urn and buried.

After the relocation of Jutoku-ji, the temple, which had fallen into disuse, was restored during the Kanbun era. It is Jitoku-ji, located at 9 Sahara-dera-mae, Fukushima City. It serves as a subordinate temple of Yorin-ji. Currently, at Jitoku-ji in Sahara, a gorinto (five-ringed tower)—consisting only of the upper portion—remains, known as the head mound of Terumune. According to "History of Fukushima City: Primitive, Ancient, and Medieval Periods,"

> However, the records of Jitoku-ji make no mention whatsoever of such a temple history. It states that while it had once been a Shingon sect temple founded by the Lord of Jitoku-ji in Shinobu, it had fallen into decline and remained without a resident priest; then, during the Kanbun era, Ikkuun Ura-sho, a priest from Rinsen-ji—a Soto sect temple in Yonezawa, Ushu—restored it, converted it to the Soto sect, and it became a subordinate temple of Yorin-ji. > Why is it that Jutoku-ji, which moved to Sendai, does not explicitly state that it is this temple? Is this not a prime example of deliberately concealing the relationship with the former lord?

Now, was the connection to Terumune temporarily forgotten? That does not seem to be the case. Let us examine the traditions recorded in the gazetteers of the Shinobu and Date districts written during the Edo period.

- "Shintatsu Ittoshi," Tenpo 12 (1841), included in the "Fukushima City History Materials Series Vol. 30," "Iwaiwa Historical Materials Series," etc.
- Included in "Oshu Shinobu and Date Two Districts Brief Chronology," An'ei 2 (1773), and "Kogo no Bokei-mi," Kunio Hashimoto (self-published), Showa 59.
- "Oshu Shinobu-gun Sahara-mura Nemoto-ki," Tenmei 8 (1788), included in "Kogo no Bokei-mi" by Kunio Hashimoto (self-published), Showa 59. The related work "Mutsu-no-kuni Shinobu-sato Sahara-mura Nemoto-ki" is included in "Fukushima-shi Shi Shiryo Sosho Vol. 15." ※Both "Oshu Shinobu/Date Ni-gun Ryaku Nendaiki" and "Oshu Shinobu-gun Sahara-mura Nemoto-ki" were authored by Seiuemon Konno.

The texts used are the "Shindachi Ittoshi" contained in the Iwaiwa Shiryo Sosho, as well as the "Oshu Shinobu-Date Ni-gun Ryaku Nendaiki" and "Oshu Shinobu-gun Sahara-mura Nemotoki" contained in the Kogo no Bokei-mi.

The entry for Jitoku-ji in the "Shindachi Ittoshi" contains no mention of its connection to Terumune.

The "Oshu Shinobu-Date Nigun Ryaku Nenki" contains the following entry:

> After fleeing to Masamune, he buried the remains of his father, Terumune, at a temple in Sawara, Shinobu. > In former times, there was a temple in Ohata below. It is said that at this time, the stone pagoda for Terumune of the Date clan was erected on the ground. The memorial tablet is said to be enshrined at Yorin-ji. > It is reported that inquiries from Lord Sendai regarding the ancient burial site, as well as those from the retainers' clans and relatives, arrived frequently up until the Hoei and Kyoho eras. However, as there were no marks whatsoever, they were not put to use.

The "Oshu Shinobu-gun Sawara-mura Nemoto-ki" contains slightly more detailed accounts.

> Masamune had no heir; he brought the remains of his father, Masamune, to Sawara and had them buried at a temple. Nineteen retainers were present for the funeral. The family's elders promptly planted plum trees. > Four large stone pagodas were erected, and while the remains were initially placed there, later, when the Reverend Unpo, the head priest, restored the temple and built the temple grounds, these stone pagodas were buried according to the topography, and the remains were reportedly transferred to Yorin-ji in Ogura Village. > Thereafter, from the Shotoku, Kyoho, and Genbun eras, assorted foot soldiers frequently visited to inquire about the remains. They stated that frequent visits would be costly, and that the remains should be transferred to Yorin-ji under the Reverend Unpo. Incidentally, during the Kanpo era, a man named Rokurobei of Fujita-machi sent a letter stating that he had a request from Lord Sendai; upon inquiring about the stone hall in Sendai, four or five people from the temple's staff dug at two or three locations—including a place called Karau-ume in the fields belonging to Seiuemon, south of the temple—but as there was plenty of charcoal and large stones and no sign of the stone hall, he replied to Rokurobei that the matter mentioned was entirely unfounded. Since previous years, there had been rumors that a temple branch from Sawara existed within Sendai Castle. > Furthermore, while it was said that the Lord of Sendai's burial place was south of the temple, no one knew for certain.

While tradition holds that Terumune's burial site exists, its location is unknown. It is said that the temple was moved to the mountain to the north during its restoration, and that Terumune's stone pagoda was buried. Consequently, one might assume that Terumune's burial site was to the south of the current temple; upon excavating two or three spots, charcoal and large stones suggestive of a site were unearthed, but no stone hall was found. It is written that Terumune's memorial tablet was enshrined at Yorin-ji, but this passage reads as if it were a mere pretext used by the Reverend Unpo.

What is currently identified as the "Grave of Terumune Date's Head" is a large stone located behind the Atago-do, next to the main hall of Jitoku-ji Temple. The information board states,

> At the site of the cremation, what is believed to have originally been a five-ringed tower now stands only as a two-ringed tower. The jewel is engraved with the Date family's simplified crest, "sparrow on bamboo." This is a memorial tower that people have traditionally referred to as the "Head Mound." > An auspicious day in June 2001, Soho Ichino, Twenty-fifth Abbot of Hojuzan Jitoku-ji Temple

It states. In the Jitoku-ji pamphlet "Welcome to the Mountain Temple of Sawara" (November 2012 edition, Kazuyuki Kunii, obtained on June 28, 2014, in front of the main hall),

> The cremation of the remains took place at Jitoku-ji. The Date clan erected two pairs of stone lanterns. The Uesugi clan, defeated at Sekigahara, had their fief reduced to Yonezawa. Fukushima and Nobuo were Uesugi territories. The Date clan, having moved to Sendai, buried the lanterns. When burying the final lantern, they left the upper one and placed the lower one on a massive rock beside the Atago-do hall. It bears a simplified version of the Date clan crest, "Sparrow on Bamboo."

It states. This differs from the tradition found in local gazetteers, which place it "to the south of the temple." It feels incongruous that the "simplified crest of 'sparrow on bamboo'" is engraved on a wind-wheel and is also a diamond crest. Kunio Hashimoto, who edited the gazetteer cited at the beginning—"Kokyo no Bokei-mi" (1984)—was the 24th chief priest of Jitoku-ji and provided detailed notes; however, he makes no mention of the current "head mound" behind the Atago-do, nor is there any reference to Terumune in the entry for Sahara Village in the Meiji-era gazetteer "Shintatsu Nigun Mura-shi." On the other hand, in "History of Fukushima City, Vol. 1," published in 1970,

> At Jitoku-ji in Sahara, there is a site said to be the head mound of Terumune Date.

It is recorded as such.

Just below the main hall of Jitoku-ji Temple stands an old cherry tree known as the "Tanemaki-zakura." The information board from 1970, when it was designated as a Natural Monument, listed its age as 200–250 years, but the board from 2009 states that it is over 300 years old. Quoted from [Kaze no Hito: Shin's Musings (An Adult's Attempt at Comprehensive Life Learning)](http://kazenoshin.exblog.jp/)-[Seasonal Notes: 2012 Cherry Blossom Season ⑤ — Jitoku-ji's "Tanemaki-zakura"](http://kazenoshin.exblog.jp/15262812/).

> The difference in content is that the tree's age was previously listed as 200–250 years, but it is now stated to be over 300 years. Indeed, approximately 40 years have passed since 1970. > On the Fukushima City website, this age is listed as 450 years, and a related explanation appears on the new information board. It seems that, under the assumption "if it were brought from Kohama Castle, where the remains of Terumune Date were laid in state for one night," it would be 450 years.

The location of the "Karau-ume" is mentioned only as "south of the temple" in the *Oshu Shinobu-gun Sahara-mura Nemoto-ki*, but in 2009, an information board identifying the "karo" as Motonobu Endo was installed at the site of the former Sahara Elementary School (the former Kido-guchi of Rinsen-ji). Furthermore, according to [Satobatake // Satobatake 〈since1749〉 Jitoku-ji "Karo no Ume" (site of Rinsho-in Kido-guchi)](http://blogs.yahoo.co.jp/tendomaru2000/25873195.html), the plum tree no longer exists. The author also visited on June 28, 2014, but found only cherry blossoms and no plum tree in sight.

※ Kunio Hashimoto, who transcribed and self-published the *Oshu Shinobu-Date Nigun Ryaku-nenki* and *Oshu Shinobu-gun Sahara-mura Nemoto-ki*, is a local historian who served as the 24th chief priest of Jitoku-ji and as an elementary school teacher. ※ The text for the information boards for the "Terumune Date Head Mound" (2001) and the "Karo no Ume" (2009) was written by Kazuyuki Kunii (Kazuyuki Soho), the 25th chief priest of Jitoku-ji. ※ In writing this entry, I referred to the following website. I express my gratitude.
