- [Shigebe](http://sigechannohe.blog.fc2.com/) [Delusions Regarding the Head Mound of Terumune Date](http://sigechannohe.blog.fc2.com/blog-date-20110801.html)
- [Michinoku Leisurely Mile Counter: The Karo's Plum](http://www.pacs.co.jp/hist_walk/walk_fukusima01/fukusima_karou_ume/index.html)
- [Satobatake // Satobatake 〈since 1749〉 Jitoku-ji "Karo's Plum Tree" (Site of the former Kidoguchi of Rinsho-in)](http://blogs.yahoo.co.jp/tendomaru2000/25873195.html)

## Shifuku-ji, Natsukari, Takahata Town

The family records cited at the beginning state that Terumune's remains were interred at Shifuku-ji in Natsugari. The date of the burial is unknown. While spirit houses in the style of ancestral shrines—such as the Zuiho-den—originated with Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Toyokuni Shrine, it is unlikely they were adopted for Terumune's burial; however, in the Seizan-ko family records,

> A mausoleum was constructed at Shifuku-zenji to house the remains.

Could this be influenced by the funeral records of Masamune and Tsunamune?

At the site of Shifuku-ji Temple in Natsukari, in addition to the grave of Terumune, there are gorinto (five-ringed towers) believed to be the graves of the ninth-generation head, Masamune Date (Gizan), his primary wife of the Ki clan, and Motonobu Endo, who committed ritual suicide following Terumune. Looking at the photographs, all of these are gorinto on flat ground without mounds, surrounded by stone fences and with a stone lantern in the foreground. Since the styles of the stone fences and lanterns are very similar, I believe they were installed around the same time. At the very least, when these stone fences and lanterns were installed, the gorinto of Terumune and Motonobu Endo were likely established with the intent of serving as memorial towers, just as those of the ninth-generation head and his wife were. It feels only natural for a memorial tower for a major patron to be located within a temple.

Regarding Terumune's gorinto, I shall quote the detailed account found in the [“18th Emishi Culture Seminar Materials Collection: Miscellaneous Notes on Stone Gorinto in Yamagata Prefecture”](http://www.emisi.com/material/18_2007.9/18semi_kawasaki2-6.htm) (Toshio Kawasaki 2007 [Emishi Society](http://emisi.com/)).

> Among these, the one said to be the grave of Terumune stands 88 cm tall; its water ring is spherical and made of andesite, while the other parts are made of tuff. Unusually, there is no wind ring; instead, a hole is provided at the top of the fire ring to receive the spherical void ring as it sinks deeply into it, and the fire ring is thin, with a noki width of 3 cm, exhibiting an extreme inversion. A similar inversion of the cap is seen in the tiered tower at Joko-ji Temple in Ayugai, Shirataka Town, dated Tensho 7 (1579). Terumune met an untimely death in Tensho 13 (1585). > Figure 7: The purported grave of Terumune Date in Natsukari, Takahata Town (quoted from [the aforementioned Kawasaki report](http://www.emisi.com/material/18_2007.9/18semi_kawasaki2-6.htm)) > As seen in this tower, extreme inversion of the cap appears to be common among stone towers from the latter half of the 16th century to the first half of the 17th century. This gorinto is also estimated to date from that period, albeit in a modified form (Figure 7).

Although not mentioned in the Kawasaki report, the grave of Motonobu Endo in the same location also appears to exhibit the characteristic inversion of the cap of the fire ring, judging by the photographs. Furthermore, while a wind ring is present, some photographs show the void ring to be missing while others do not; perhaps the void ring is not fixed. In fictional works such as novels, there are frequent depictions of Motonobu Endo committing ritual suicide before Terumune's grave, but the *Seizan-ko Jike Kiroku* merely states that he was "buried beside the mausoleum of Kakuhan-ji-dono."

Additionally, besides the graves of Masamune Gizan and his wife located at the site of Shifuku-ji Temple in Natsukari, another was discovered in 1904 at Notekura Tonomine, 443 Takemori, Takahata Town, Higashi-Okitama District ([Takahata Town Tourism Association website Mahoroba no Sato Takahata](http://takahata.info/) > Sightseeing Spots > [Grave of Lord Masamune Gizan (Notekura Burial Site)](http://takahata.info/detail/?no=2192)). The gorinto (five-ringed tower) of Masamune Gizan and his wife at this Notekura burial site is also mentioned in the aforementioned Kawasaki report.

Shifuku-ji in Natsukari, to which Terumune was deeply devoted, was a renowned temple counted among the Ten Great Temples of Kanto and served as a temple fortress. It featured double earthen ramparts and double moats spanning two cho on each side; it is said that when plot maps and archaeological remains are overlaid, the moat and rampart patterns align well. The Date family burial ground, where the graves of Terumune and others are located, is situated at the southwestern end and is separated from the temple grounds by an inner moat. While the *Seizan-ko Jike Kiroku* states, "a mausoleum was constructed at Shifuku-zenji," it remains unclear whether a mausoleum building was included. To the west of the Shifuku-ji residence, the Natsukari residence was situated almost adjacently, and the two residences are said to have shared a close relationship. (Yamagata Prefecture Medieval Castle and Fortification Site Survey Report, Vol. 1: Okitama Region)

## Kakuhan-ji, Toyama, Yonezawa City

In the following year, Tensho 14, Masamune established Kakuhan-ji in Toyama Village as the family temple for Terumune. Toyama is located at the eastern foot of the Shahei Hills, where Tateyama is situated. Ascending the mountain leads to Mount Atago and Mount Hayama; in addition to the abandoned Kakuhan-ji, numerous other temples have existed or still exist there.

> For the benefit of Lord Seizan, a temple complex was established in Toyama Village, Nagai-sho, Okitama District. It was named Kakuhan Zen-ji, and the mountain was called Toyama. Specifically, the priest Koya (whose name was Soetsu), the former abbot of Shifuku-ji, was invited to serve as the founding head priest. > (Records of the Seizan-ko Family, Tensho 14, entry for this year) > Lord Masamune, for the benefit of his father Lord Seizan, built a temple in Toyama Village, Nagai-sho, Okitama District, Ushu, and named it Toyama Kakuhan Zen-ji, inviting the priest Koya of Shifuku-ji to serve as the founding head priest. Within the temple grounds, Ikoku-in, Chogetsu-an, and Hofuku-an were built, serving as the memorial sites for the three who committed ritual suicide. > (Records of the Seizan-ko Family, Tensho 15 entry)

Kakuhan-ji was relocated to Iwadeyama and subsequently to Sendai following the transfer of the Date clan's fief. The Kakuhan-ji in Yonezawa has since fallen into ruin, and excavation surveys were conducted in 1987–1988. The following presents the results of these surveys, based on the "Yonezawa City Buried Cultural Properties Survey Report, Vol. 26: Kakuhan-ji" (Yonezawa City Board of Education, 1989).

In this excavation survey, the place names "Kakuhan-ji," "Monzen," and "Oise-bayashi" were identified as the site of Kakuhan-ji. There are six flat areas within the survey area—sites A through F—where buildings are believed to have existed. Among these, site F, the largest in scale, is presumed to be the site of the main hall and kuri; however, detailed excavations were conducted at three sites: A, B, and D.

<Modified figure from p. 5 of "Yonezawa City Buried Cultural Properties Survey Report, Vol. 26: Kakuhan-ji"> Click to enlarge (Please return using your browser)

At Site A, a depression—likely a mark from the removal of foundation stones—was detected, forming a hexagon approximately in the center of the flat area. This suggests a hexagonal hall with sides of about two ken (3.6 m). At Site B, a burial pit, a group of foundation stones, and a ditch believed to be a rainwater runoff channel were detected near the center of the flat area. A building (burial hall) with a gable-style roof, measuring nine shaku square, is presumed to have stood atop a circular earthen burial pit. Descending the stone steps at the front of the burial hall leads to an approach path believed to lead to Site A. A burial pit is located at the southwest corner of Site D. The platform is a square mound with a lens-shaped earthen pit at its center. A large quantity of charcoal and cremated remains were excavated from this site. However, there are no firing marks in the surrounding soil, indicating that the remains were interred after being cremated elsewhere. On the southern edge of Site D, there is a single-character, single-stone sutra mound. Multiple handwriting styles are visible, among which one resembles the handwriting of Reverend Koya, held by Kakuhan-ji Temple in Sendai.

Based on these results, this report posits that Site A may be the memorial site of Terumune Date, Site B that of Motonobu Endo (Ikoku-in), and Sites D and E those of Hoki Suda (Chogetsu-an) and Uchibaba Uemon (Hofuku-an). If this inference is adopted, given that a burial pit was detected at Site B and marks from the removal of foundation stones are present at Site A, it would be possible to interpret the record of the Seizan-ko family as referring to Kakuhan-ji rather than Shifuku-ji, stating that Motonobu Endo was "buried beside the mausoleum of Kakuhan-ji-dono."

(In that case, regarding the "Five-Ring Pagodas of Gizan Masamune and His Wife" at Natsukari Shifuku-ji, in terms of the number of pagodas alone, it wouldn't be far-fetched to consider them to be Hoki Suda and Uchibaba Uemon, rather than Gizan Masamune and his wife... Well, they are all just "traditional accounts," after all...)

shigezane:touhannsikou-narumi.summary: His childhood name was Fujigoro, also known as Hyobu. Later, he was called Awa. shigezane:touhannsikou-narumi.markdown:
His childhood name was Togoro, and also Hyobu. Later, he was called Awa. (Omitted) Shigezane became a man of great courage and strategic brilliance. For a time, he was praised as peerless in martial prowess. In Tensho 13, during the Battle of Hitotobashi, Shigezane's unit broke away from the main force and achieved merit amidst the fierce fighting of the enemy army. It is said that his retainers—Ibano Totomi, Haneda Umanosuke, Kayaba Genbei, and Kita-Shimotsuke—were the most distinguished. (Ibano received two wounds and died during the night.) Lord Teizan bestowed a letter of commendation upon him. In Tensho 14, Nihonmatsu Castle fell; it was granted to Shigezane. Consequently, he held 33 villages and 38,000 koku in Adachi District. In Tensho 16, during the Battle of Koriyama, and in Tensho 17, during the various engagements at Surigami and Sugahara, he achieved merit. In Tensho 18, during the Battle of Osaki, Shigezane went out and became a hostage in the camp of Gamo Ujisato. When Ujisato arrived in the capital, Shigezane returned to Nihonmatsu. In Tensho 19, he was again granted 16 villages in Igu District and one village in Shibata District, and moved to Kakuda Castle. In Bunroku 2, he participated in the Korean campaigns. In Bunroku 4, Shigezane accompanied the Lord to Fushimi, but left for certain reasons and went to Mount Koya. This was because Shigezane's achievements surpassed those of other generals, yet his rank and stipend could not keep pace. Thus, discontent grew, leading to this outcome. (In Bunroku 4, Shigezane fled to Mount Koya, aged 28. Aoki Tota, Shiga Yashichi, Tokiwa Hayato, Haneda Kokichi, Sugimura Kuzaemon, Oka Hanbei, Oka Kyuichi, and Kosugi Oribe accompanied him. Shindo Hikoemon, a retainer of Asano Danjo, plotted to have him enter service. Danjo approved this. On August 18, Keicho 3, the Taiko passed away. Shigezane conspired with Sobei—the younger brother of Shirahata Giemon, a retainer of Okubo Tadanari—to enter the service of the Tokugawa clan. When Lord Teizan married his daughter to the Shosho of Echigo, the matter did not go well. Tadanari welcomed him to Odawara, where he stayed at a temple in Kasuya Village. In April of Keicho 5, Naoe Kanetsugu dispatched Yusa Satoemon to request Shigezane as his adopted son and departed Odawara privately. Tadanari was greatly surprised, left the gates, and went into public view. Forced by circumstances, he stayed in Ota. Ishikawa Akimitsu and Katakura Kagetsuna reported the Lord's intentions and dispatched messengers to bring him back. Tadanari welcomed Shigezane and presented him with armor. Ishikawa Yoshimune went to Ota to welcome him, and he entered Kakuda.) At this, Masakage urged others to persuade him to stop, but he did not listen. The Lord ordered Yashiro Kageyori to take possession of Kakuda, stating that if he still refused, he should be attacked and taken. Shigezane's retainers, including Haneda Sanekage and over 30 others, died in battle. The rest either surrendered or fled. Shigezane then resided in Kasuya Village, Odawara. He was summoned by Lord Tosho and granted a stipend of 100 koku. The Lord declined the offer. In Keicho 5, Uesugi Kagekatsu and Ishida Mitsunari plotted a rebellion and widely recruited prominent figures. Kagekatsu invited Shigezane with a grant of 50,000 koku. Shigezane replied, "My father, Sanemoto, has already become the adopted son of Uesugi Sadazane. Furthermore, Kagekatsu is the enemy of my former lord. To entrust my hostage to him is not in accordance with my principles." Ultimately, the offer was not accepted. In the autumn of that year, Akimitsu, Masakage, Kagetsuna, and other generals invited him by the lord's command. Shigezane then arrived. During the Battle of Shiroishi, his troops were few and he could not form a unit. He stayed within Akimitsu's camp. Later, Saito Hyobu, a subordinate of the Uesugi clan, admired Shigezane's reputation and led 5,000 soldiers from Shinobu District, requesting to join him. In Keicho 7, he was again granted Watari Castle, with a stipend of over 20,000 koku. In Genna 1, he participated in the Siege of Osaka. In Genna 5, the stone walls of the Great Castle in Edo were repaired. Shigezane was ordered to oversee the work. In September of Genna 8, upon the fall of the Mogami clan, he followed the lord's orders and led 600 men to seize the castle of the Nobezawa clan. In Kan'ei 15, Shigezane again petitioned the Lord to visit Edo. He was 71 years old at the time. The Tairo permitted him to enter the gate of the imperial carriage. He was also granted ■ in the Great Castle. Sakai Sanuki-no-kami, Matsudaira Izu-no-kami, Ii Saburo-no-kami, Doi Oi-no-kami, Abe Bungo-no-kami, and Yagyu Tajima-no-kami attended him. He was further ordered to discuss military affairs of the Ou region. Lord Taiyu, hearing of this, expressed great admiration. He was granted 20 robes and 10 outer robes. He passed away on June 4, Shoho 3, aged 79. His Buddhist name was Kyuzan Tensho Yuzan-ji. He was buried at Daiyu-ji in Kotsutsumi Village, Watari District. (His death poem: "In a year rare since ancient times, nine years remained—yet they dwell within my dreams.") Four of his retainers committed ritual suicide: Tokiwa Hayato Motoyasu (Buddhist name Shoan Shigen), Tanaki Echigo Naosada (Buddhist name Kan-o Totetsu), Maeda Tosho Sanenobu (Buddhist name Gyoku ■■), and a certain Ogawa Gohei. Shigezane once compiled the *Masamune-ki*, recording the events of his military campaigns. He also studied the swordsmanship of the Tenryu school under his retainer Arakawa Hyuga Akihide and mastered its traditions. Lord Teizan once visited Shigezane's residence and hosted him for tea. The Lord said, "It is difficult for me to use porcelain in my old age. I shall give you some fine tea utensils." Later, he searched for tea utensils from Iwaki Bunrin in the Later Capital and had Sasa Wakasa grant them to him. Shigezane firmly declined, saying, "The treasures of the Later Capital are not a place for me." Wakasa replied, "I grant them to you for the sake of your service." He added, "I, Shigezane, am of the same rank as you, and our martial prowess and talent are comparable. Our loyalty and integrity are also unmatched. Why should I monopolize wealth and honor instead of sharing these treasures with you? Your intentions are as clear as mine. Do not decline." Thereafter, the Lord hosted Shigezane for a tea gathering. The Lord entered the tea room and used the utensils he had just granted. Shigezane then presented a prized horse, 100 gold pieces, and 30 pieces of silver to express his gratitude. Shigezane then led his son Shigezane and presented the tea utensils and ten swords to Lord Gizan. The swords were relics of Lord Teizan, which Lord Gizan had granted to Shigezane. Shigezane had no children. Lord Teizan requested his son, Shigezane, to be his heir. When Shigezane first fled, his retainers Kanasunai-ki, Ishikawa, and Shiranezawa all came out to serve him. During the time of Lord Gizan, Shigezane recommended Shiranezawa to be the unit commander. The Lord felt that Shigezane did not mind the previous events. Shiranezawa...

> > (I transcribed this at a library about 15 years ago, but it's cut off halfway through. Did I not transcribe the rest???)

shigezane:touhanyajyou.title: Biography of Shigezane from the "Tohan Yajo" (included in the Sendai Sosho, Vol. 8)
shigezane:touhanyajyou.summary: Lord of Watari, Lord of Watari, Lord Shigezane Date. Originally named Togoro, and later Awa. He was the eldest son of Hyobu-daifu Sanemoto. His courage and strategy were unparalleled, and he possessed a great fondness for the arts and letters. He was one year younger than Lord Teizan.
shigezane:touhanyajyou.markdown:
From "Tohan Yajo," Volume 1 (original Classical Chinese text transcribed into Japanese)

Lord of Watari, Lord of Watari, Lord Shigezane Date. Originally named Togoro, he later took the name Awa. He was the eldest son of Hyobu-daifu Sanemoto. His courage and strategy were unparalleled, and he possessed a great fondness for literature and the arts. He was one year younger than Lord Teizan. He accompanied him in every campaign. He rendered the greatest service during the campaign in Aizu. Heavily entrusted with many matters regarding the founding of the domain. He resided in Kakuda Village, Igu District. In the second year of Keicho, he defied the will of his lord and fled. The Lord dispatched Yashiro Kageyori to govern the village. The remaining retainers surrendered. Only the chief steward, Haneda Uma-no-suke, refused and fought. More than thirty people from the household perished. The Lord went into hiding in Kasuya Village, Odawara, in Soshu. Uesugi Kagekatsu summoned him. He refused, citing his 50,000 koku fief. Tosho-ko granted him 100 units of granary rice as a stipend. Ishikawa Akimitsu, Date Masakage, Kagetsuna Katakura, and others confirmed his sincerity. The Lord also relented. In the fifth year of Keicho, he was recalled. Later, his fief was transferred to Watari District, where he held 28,000 koku. In the fifteenth year of Kan'ei, Lord Taiyu granted him 5,000 kan of silver. The Lord entered the castle for an audience. Lord Taiyu said, "Those who once wore armor and wielded sharp blades are now few and far between. You should discuss the strategies of days gone by, for I wish to hear them." At the time, Izu-no-kami Matsudaira Nobutsuna, Saburo-no-kami Ii Naotaka, Oi-no-kami Doi Toshikatsu, and various other lords were present. The Lord spoke, captivating the assembly and leaving them deeply impressed. He was further granted several gifts of clothing. He passed away on the 4th day of the 6th month of the third year of Shoho, at the age of seventy-one. He had no children. Lord Teizan designated his ninth son, Lord Shigezane, as his successor. Shigezane's son, Munenari, died of smallpox in the second year of Tenna, leaving no heir. Lord Gizan ordered the reduction of his fief, granting 10,000 koku to the second son, Motoatsu [Lord of Wakuya Village], to succeed him. At that time, Shigezane's wife was still alive. She refused to obey the order and, after gathering the assembly, argued, "Our house is the bulwark of the domain. The founding was the achievement of Munenari. The previous lord was powerful; how can his heir be cut off simply because he died young? Furthermore, the wounds of the various retainers have not yet healed, and there is no place for hasty burial. I cannot bear this; I submit a memorial to request that if this be granted, I shall simply accept my death." The assembly agreed. Thus, Shiga Rokurobei, Tadano Saburoemon, Tokiwa Hayato, Ohori Mokunoshin, and others jointly signed several articles detailing Shigezane's achievements, petitioning for the preservation of his fief and selecting a close relative as his successor. Their writing was clear and logical, deeply moving the people. The Lord, realizing the truth, finally granted the request. He then designated the second son, Date Munetoshi [Lord of Iwadeyama], as his successor. The domain remained as it was. The writing is still recited to this day. It is called the Watari Petition.

shigezane:tyosaku.title: Works of Shigezane Date
shigezane:tyosaku.summary: I will be uploading each work in turn. Please follow the links. When uploading, I have made the following modifications. Please refer to the original texts for the exact details.
shigezane:tyosaku.markdown:
I will be uploading each work in turn. Please follow the links. When uploading, I have made the following modifications. Please refer to the original texts for the exact details.

- I have provided a reading version.
- Variant characters have been replaced with standard characters.
- Punctuation has been added for readability.
- That said, there are inconsistencies in the notation due to difficulties in reading the text accurately or a lack of overall proofreading.

Here are the works currently uploaded. All of them are still in progress.

- Included in "[Masamune-ki](#/post/shigezane/masamuneki-index)," Jinbutsu Orai-sha, Sengoku Historical Materials Series 10, "Date Historical Materials Collection, Vol. 1."
- [“Shigezane-ki”](#/post/shigezane/shigezaneki-mokuji) Included in Volume 3 of the Sendai Sosho. Republished by Hobundo in 1974.
- "[Date Nikki](#/post/shigezane/datenikki)" is included in Volume 21 of the Battles section of the Gunsho Ruiju.

### Waka

Masamune left behind many poems and songs, but what about Shigezane? All the administrator knows of is the death poem.

"Since ancient times, in a rare year, nine remaining—such things have occurred only in dreams."

only one poem. There is also a theory that the original poem for the folk song "Sansa Shigure" below is a waka composed by Shigezane; in the [section on "Sansa Shigure"](http://senketu2112.hp.infoseek.co.jp/komonjyo_haikei.html) of [Atsushi Takakura's Miyagi Local History](http://senketu2112.hp.infoseek.co.jp/index.html),

Shigemune Watari's "Without a sound, the night drizzle of Chino arrives, and my sleeves are likely getting soaked" and Shigezane Date's "Without a sound, a storm sweeps across the pines, and the drizzle of the grasslands is likely wetting me."

It is mentioned that there is a theory that this serves as the original poem.

### Folk song

Is it a passing shower, or rain in Chino? Even the sound reaches me, and I'm getting drenched—shongaina.

The folk song "Sansashigure" is traditionally said to have been composed during Masamune's conquest of Aizu, but in addition to the theory that it was written by Masamune, there is also the theory that it was written by Shigezane. There is also a theory that it was a collaborative work, in which Masamune refined Shigezane's waka.

### Map

There is an ancient map called "Sendo no Zu," which is said to have been created by Shigezane and presented to Masamune. (To be precise, I believe he "had it made," though.)

shigezane:uesugi.title: Genealogy of Kao 2
shigezane:uesugi.summary: On the Kao of the Date Clan during the Sengoku Period—Focusing on Date Tanemune. Tohoku Gakuin University Institute for Tohoku Culture Bulletin (No. 20) [1988.08]
shigezane:uesugi.markdown:
This article,

> On the Kao of the Date Clan during the Sengoku Period—Focusing on Tanemune Date > Naomasa Oishi, Bulletin of the Institute for Tohoku Culture, Tohoku Gakuin University. (No. 20) [1988.08]

Based on this, this is a discussion of the kao associated with the Date clan during the Sengoku period. Unless otherwise noted, the illustrations of the kao are taken from the aforementioned paper. It is said that imitations of kao tend to reflect respect for the individual whose kao served as the model.

## 2. Uesugi and Date

| Date Tanemune Kao Type 1 | Date Tanemune Kao Type 2 | Uesugi Sadazane Kao | |---|---|---| | | | | | Uesugi Fusasada Kao | Uesugi Norisada Kao | Uesugi Akisada Kao | | | | |

Date Tanemune's kao (stylized signature) is divided into six types according to the aforementioned paper by Oishi. This entry focuses on Type 1 and Type 2. Type 2, in particular, closely resembles that of Uesugi Akisada. This is the kao of the Uesugi style; it is said that all members of the Echigo Uesugi clan during this period used similar signatures. Uesugi Akisada was of the Kanto Kanrei house, but he was adopted into the Echigo Uesugi family. Uesugi Akisada fought and was defeated and killed by Nagao Tamekage and Uesugi Shigezane; it is suggested that this conflict was an attempt by Akisada to restore the legitimate line of the Echigo Shugo Uesugi family, and that Tanemune may have sought to project himself onto Akisada. The kao of Uesugi Shigezane—the Shugo of Echigo who was intended to be Sanemoto's adoptive father—has a different shape, but there is no mention of an interpretation regarding it. Tanemune used this kao roughly until the time of his move from his castle in Yanagawa to Kuwaori Nishiyama, or until his appointment as Shugo of Mutsu. Until then, regardless of his actual power, Tanemune's position was that of a mere kokujin lord.

Among Tanemune's sons, some inherited and continued to use this Uesugi-style kao: Date Sanemoto and Watari Motomune.

| Date Sanemoto's Kao (Reference) | Date Sanemoto's Kao | Watari Motomune's Kao | |---|---|---| | | | |

> ※Date Sanemoto's kao (reference) is cited from the "List of Kao" in *History of Fukushima Prefecture, Vol. 7*.

According to the same paper, Date Sanemoto's kao is a variation of Type 1 of Date Tanemune's kao, while Watari Motomune's kao closely resembles Type 2 of Date Tanemune's kao. The paper notes that Sanemoto's kao is of the Uesugi type because he was slated for adoption into the Uesugi family, the shugo of Echigo, and that Motomune's kao may reflect his strong feelings regarding the fact that the cause of the Tenbun Disturbance lay in the issue of Sanemoto's adoption. Both Sanemoto and Motomune continued to use these kao even after the conclusion of the Tenbun Disturbance (※Motomune also had a different type of kao).

| Watari Motomune's Kao (Reference) | |---| | |

Quoted from "List of Kao" in "History of Fukushima Prefecture, Vol. 7"

Quoting from the same paper.

> "It appears that Tanemune expressed his political aspirations in the form of kao (stylized signatures) at each stage of his life, and may have had his sons share this role and use them as honorific titles, thereby seeking to express and realize his ideal as the King of Oshu as a whole. > Furthermore, Sanemoto, Motomune, and others did not change the form of their kao even after the Tenbun Disturbance—neither under the Harumune administration nor during the tenure of Terumune—and Harumune himself, as will be discussed in the next section, inherited a portion of his father's kao. I believe this suggests that Tanemune's ideals, as described above, were not entirely rejected after Harumune, but continued to be carried forward."

What was the "ideal" that Sanemoto and Motomune shared? I cannot conceive of a message as clear as "Tanemune's Fan Shape." Or perhaps it was not an "ideal," but rather a "warning" against plunging the Dochu into great turmoil?

Return to [1. The World of "Uemune's Fan Shape"](#/post/shigezane/ougi)

shigezane:usami.title: The Mystery of "Nagamitsu Usami"
shigezane:usami.summary: Various thoughts on the mystery pointed out by Mr. Nozaki on the forum.
shigezane:usami.markdown:
Various thoughts on the mystery pointed out by Mr. Nozaki on the forum.

"Usami Nagamitsu," a family treasure of the Watari Date clan sent by the Uesugi clan along with the bamboo-and-sparrow crest when Sanemoto entered Echigo. It is still held as an Important Art Object at the Date City Pioneering Memorial Museum. While this sword is generally classified as a "tachi," a closer examination of the records reveals that "koshigatana" had somehow become "tachi" over time.

## "Memorandum of Unknown Names," Date Family Documents 10-3230, History of Yanagawa Town 5, Materials Volume 2, 537

> One Yachiyake-kiri tachi, one Nakamitsu, one sword from Usami-no-Tono, one sword from Yoshimune, Moriie-tona-tsuke, Mumon, Shakuto, Chitori... (omitted) ...one tachi from Uesuki-dono, Kikiyau-tsukuri, Kunitsuna, one tachi from Ichi-okuma-hizen-no-Tono... (the rest omitted)

The *Shimei Mikaku Kakigaki* is an inventory of swords and armor. The names of individuals appearing in the inventory—such as Usami, Nagao, Nakajo, Uesugi, Okuma-hizen, Watari, Miyota Hoki, Makino Shuri-no-suke, and Yoshimune (Kakeda Yoshimune?)—suggest that it is related to Uesugi Sanemoto's succession into the family. While there is no mention of whether these were gifts to Sanemoto, the entry "Nagamitsu, a sword from Lord Usami" is recorded. In this inventory, waist swords are referred to as *katana* and tachi as *tachi*; **"Nagamitsu, a sword from Lord Usami" is a waist sword**. Meanwhile, it notes "a tachi from Lord Uesugi, kikyo-zukuri, Kunitsuna," and **the tachi gifted by the Uesugi family is not Nagamitsu**. Could Kunitsuna be Awataguchi Kunitsuna?

## *Date Tanemune and Harumune: Records of the Children*, Date Family Documents 10-3290, History of Yanagawa Town 5, Materials Volume 2, 537

> ……Lord Sanemoto: The Uesugi representative was dispatched, bearing the bamboo-and-sparrow crest, the Nagamitsu waist sword, and the character "Sane" from Sane's name, accompanied by a messenger named Dairaku-dono, ……

The text states that it was written on January 20, Kan'ei 12. Here, **the item presented by the Uesugi family was the "Nagamitsu waist sword." There is no mention of "Usami."** Since "waza no mono" can refer either to a waist sword or a sword in general, it could be interpreted as either a tachi or a katana. It remains unclear whether this was a gift separate from the "tachi from Lord Uesugi" mentioned in the *Shimei Mikaku Oboegaki*, or whether it has been conflated with the "sword from Lord Nagamitsu Usami." The author is said to be the priest Daiyu, but as he was already deceased by Kan'ei 12, it remains unknown who wrote it.

## "Masamune-ki, Vol. 11: Masamune Monoheki-goto"

> ...Now, as for the major and minor ones: Habaki Kuniyuki, Rai Kunimitsu, Usami Nagamitsu, Niji Kunitoshi, ...

June, Kan'ei 19: A colophon by Shigezane Date of Awa. Here, **"Usami Nagamitsu" appears for the first time**. "Daisho" appears to be used as a general term for swords and blades. If the colophon is taken at face value, it means that Shigezane himself referred to him as "Usami Nagamitsu." However, there is also a theory that the anecdotal sections in the latter half of the *Masamune-ki* contain additions by another person.

## "Watari Petition"

> The ancestors, Sanemoto, had received the promise of succession from Lord Sadazane Uesugi; the crest of a sparrow on a bamboo branch, the sword worn by Usami Nagamitsu, the character "Sane," and various other items were presented...

The "Watari Petition" dates to Tenwa 2 (1682). For details, see this site's [“The Achievements of Date Sanemoto as Documented by the Watari Petition”](#/post/shigezane/watarisojyou-mimoto). Regarding the "sword worn at the waist," see above.

## *Date Shoto Seijiko*, Volume 9: Lord Tanemune Date

> ○June, Tenbun 11 (Year of the Water Tiger). Two envoys, Naoe Dairaku, were dispatched from Echigo to welcome Lord Goro, the heir. They were presented with the sword Usami Nagamitsu Take-suzume, passed down through generations, and granted the character "Sane." He was to be adopted as the heir to Uesugi Hyogo-no-kami Shigezane. Accordingly, Shigezane was dispatched on the 23rd of June. However, on the 20th, an internal rebellion unexpectedly broke out, and the mission ultimately failed.

The "Date Shoto Seiji Ko" was compiled during the Genroku era. Here, **"Usami Nagamitsu was a hereditary retainer of the Uesugi clan and a waist sword."**

## "Date Jike Kiroku," Teizan-ko Jike Kiroku, Volume 2

> ○ (Tensho 15, April) 16th, Yi-hai: Fujiwara Sanemoto (Nyudo Seiansai), Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, Hyobu-no-daifu, passed away at Hachichome Castle in Shinobu District, Oshu. Age 61. His dharma name was Yuzan Eigo Dokusho-in. ... In Tenbun 11, he was appointed head of the Uesugi Hyogo-no-kami line in Echigo Province by Fujiwara Sadazane. Sadazane was the maternal grandfather of Lord Tanemune. From Sadazane, he was granted the character "Sane" from his personal name, the ancestral sword Usami Nagamitsu, and the family crest of a sparrow on a bamboo stalk, among others.

The "Date Jike Kiroku" was compiled during the Genroku era. Although it was compiled during the same period as the "Date Shoto Seijiko," it states here that **"Usami Nagamitsu was a hereditary retainer of the Uesugi clan and a tachi."**

## "Date Seishin Kafu"

> His maternal grandfather, Uesugi Hyogo-no-kami Shigezane, arranged for Yo to become the heir; presented a tachi (Usami Nagamitsu), a bamboo-and-sparrow crested curtain... (omitted) ... > Thereupon, Shigezane presented a sword (Usami Nagamitsu) to express his gratitude... (the rest omitted)

The "Date Yoshin Kafu" was compiled during the eras of Munemura and Shigemura. It records events up to the Meiwa era. The sword that Shigezane presented to Masamune upon receiving the Watari fief is identified as "Usami Nagamitsu." Since it is referred to as a "sword," it is **"the tachi of Usami Nagamitsu."**

## [“Buhen Wakigaki 110”](#/post/shigezane/buhen110)

> Shigezane Usami presented the Bizen Nagamitsu tachi to Shigezane. This sword was of extraordinary size and particularly robust; its possession by Usami brought Shigezane boundless delight. Consequently, it was renamed "Usami Nagamitsu" and kept as a treasure. Later, after the unrest in Echigo was settled, Uesugi Shigezane had a daughter but no son; he arranged for his son-in-law, Date Hyobu—the second son of Date Uemune, aged sixteen—to be adopted as Shigezane's grandson, as it was said he was exceptionally gifted. At that time, Shigezane sent a character from his own name along with a bamboo curtain depicting a sparrow and a bird, accompanied by the Bizen Nagamitsu tachi, to express his congratulations.

"Buhen Watari Kikigaki" is a work of martial tales from the early Edo period. It is a record of martial stories that circulated among the common people. In [the same 111 stories](#/post/shigezane/buhen111), the origin of Usami Nagamitsu is described. "Usami Nagamitsu" is said to have been the sword worn by "Usami Sadayuki," a man of great martial prowess among the 25 generals of Uesugi. [※Usami Sadayuki is a fictional character](http://www2.harimaya.com/uesugi/k_busyo.html) He is a creation of Usami Teisuke, a military strategist from Kishu in the 17th century.

## "Register of Swords and Other Armor of the Sendai Family, Treasures Section," held by the Tokyo National Museum

The Tokyo National Museum holds a copy of "O-homotsu no Bu: Sendai-ke Go-koshimono no Cho," compiled in the late Edo period, which is available via the Digital Library. It is a catalog of swords and other weapons held by the Sendai Date clan during the late Edo period. The list proceeds from Moriie Sayu-maki Otachi → Bizen Kagehide → Watari Raikunimitsu → Hagai Kuniyuki, followed by Usami Nagamitsu; the fact that it was received from Shiyama Yoshimura upon Tadatsuyama Munemura's entry into the domain suggests that it was carefully preserved even after it passed into the possession of the Sendai Date clan.

> 1 Usami Nagamitsu > August 3, Genroku 3; 20 gold pieces > > Inscription: Length 2 shaku 4 sun 5 bu > Referred to as Gizan-sama's; alternatively said to be Teizan-sama's, though currently unknown > The genealogy records: April 5, Enkyo 1; Tadatsuyama-sama succeeded as head of the house > It is said that upon entering the domain, Shiyama-sama was presented with it, etc. > The aforementioned sword by Nagamitsu was originally a sword of the Uesugi family; it was presented to Date Hyobu-no-dasuke, son of the 14th head, > Tadamune-sama, by Uesugi Sadazane, > with the single character "Jitsu" from the Takee crest; it was the sword of Usami Nagamitsu. > The records state: > However, the aforementioned sword was presented to Tadatsuyama-sama, Date Awamura Jitsu-sama ■ > It was presented to someone during the reign of ■ and was granted to two people ■■■■; as for the Takee crest, > it was presented to Harumune-sama, the 15th head, during the reign of Jitsumoto; Usami > Nagamitsu's sword was presented to Gizan-sama by Awa Munemi > It is reported that the sword was presented to Gizan-sama by Uesugi Sadazane. > The above points are contained in one document and a separate sheet. > > Tomizuka Takayoshi, regarding the tradition of the Usami Nagamitsu tachi: > Usami Suruga-no-kami Sadayuki was the ancestor of the fifth generation, Usami Saemon-no-jo > Masatoyo; in Kansho 3, when Hatakeyama Uma Yoshinari was besieged at Kintai-ji Castle in Kawachi Province, > forces from various provinces attacked it. > The Shogun, Jisho-in Yoshimasa-ko, appointed Masatoyo to lead the vanguard, > and as he possessed great renown, he bestowed the tachi of Bizen Nagamitsu. > It was passed down through the generations and presented to Uesugi Sadazane; Sadazane admired it > and named it Usami Nagamitsu, later passing it to Sadazane's > maternal grandson, Date Hyobu-no-shosuke Jitsumoto; Jitsumoto passed it to his son, > Munemi; Munemi presented it to Chunagon Masamune-ko, and it remains to this day > as one of the treasures of the Sendai house. > > Upon careful consideration, the theory recorded by Tomizuka Takayoshi ■ states that the sword of Usami Nagamitsu > was presented to Teizan-ko by Date Shigezane, and that Awa Munemi was presented to Gizan-ko > at the residence of the Awa family; the correct account has not yet been verified. > ※ I tried my best to read this after checking the Digital Library, but please let me know if there are any mistakes...

## The extant tachi of "Usami Nagamitsu"

Currently, the "Tachi of Usami Nagamitsu," a family treasure of the Watari Date family, is housed at the Date City Pioneering Memorial Museum. It was designated as an Important Art Object by the national government in 1940 and is attributed to "Usami Nagamitsu." This "Usami Nagamitsu" is a tachi. It is recorded that in 1892, two swords were presented to the House of Count Date in Sendai, and in exchange, the tachi of Usami Nagamitsu—which had been presented previously (according to the Date Family Genealogy, at the time of the Watari grant)—was returned (Date Family Related Materials Catalog 756, 15-1, "Supplementary Notes to the Catalog"). While "Nagamitsu" was a swordsmith of the Bizen Osafune school, no swordsmith named "Usami Nagamitsu" actually existed.

"Usami Nagamitsu" from Figure 50, p. 21, "Masamune Date and His Retainers," Sendai City Museum

## "Usami Nagamitsu" as a Symbol

Since the Usami clan were local lords of Echigo Province, it is natural to interpret the common name "Usami Nagamitsu" as "Nagamitsu associated with the Usami clan." Tachi were sometimes used with uchigatana mountings, or polished down to serve as waist swords. The reference to "Nagamitsu, a sword from Lord Usami" in the "Memorandum of Unknown Names" likely indicates that the mountings and handling at that point were those of a "tachi."

The entries "Nagamitsu, a sword from Lord Usami" and "Tachi Kunitsuna from Lord Uesugi" in the *Memorandum of Unknown Names*. Juxtaposing the descriptions in these documents, it appears as though the two gradually became conflated. Since "Nagamitsu" was a well-known swordsmith with many attributed works, it is possible that there was another "Nagamitsu passed down from the Uesugi family" besides the one in this memorandum—and that this may be the "Nagamitsu waist sword" mentioned in the *Record of Children of Date Tanemune and Harumune*.

For the Watari Date clan, the fact that Sanemoto was the heir to the Uesugi clan, the shugo of Echigo, and Shigezane's martial prowess were the bedrock of the house. The gift of a "tachi" from the Uesugi clan, the gift of a "Nagamitsu" passed down through the Usami family, and the legends of the martial prowess of the Echigo kokujin Usami Sadayuki—these elements combined to create the "Tachi of Usami Nagamitsu," which served as a fitting symbol of both the "connection to the Uesugi clan, the shugo of Echigo" and "Shigezane's martial prowess," and likely functioned as the spiritual pillar of the Watari Date clan.

Then, during the Meiji period, a single tachi inscribed "Nagamitsu" was returned from the House of Count Date in Sendai (the Sendai Date clan) to the House of Baron Date in Usu (the Watari Date clan) as "Usami Nagamitsu."

Then, during the Meiji period, Usami Nagamitsu was returned from the House of Count Date in Sendai (the Sendai Date clan) to the House of Baron Date in Usu (the Watari Date clan), who had sought a new frontier in Hokkaido.

## Addenda and What May Be Considered Discussions

Right off the bat, let me offer an apology: I am completely ignorant when it comes to Japanese swords. While I am curious about which of the two—"Nagamitsu" or "Kunitsuna"—was the higher-grade item according to the values of the time when the Uesugi clan gifted them to the Date clan, I do not know. (Comparing the Kyogen [“Nagamitsu”](http://www.tarokaja.com/wiki.cgi?page=%C4%B9%B8%F7) and [“Awataguchi”](http://www.tarokaja.com/wiki.cgi?page=%B0%C0%C5%C4%B8%FD), I get the feeling that Kunitsuna was the higher-grade item.)

Regarding the matter of Shigezane "presenting Usami Nagamitsu upon receiving the Watari grant," I have not confirmed this in any sources other than the *Seshin Kafu* (or rather, prior to that). At the time, it was customary to present a tachi as a token of gratitude for greetings, so I believe it would have been perfectly natural to present a tachi upon receiving the Watari grant—and he likely made such presentations on other occasions as well. If the "Nagamitsu" was among the tachi presented by Shigezane to Masamune... (perhaps there were several). It is easy to imagine that when the Date clan of Sendai organized their sword collection, if there was a "Nagamitsu presented by Shigezane to Masamune," they would have identified it as "Usami Nagamitsu"; and if an inquiry regarding the "Usami Nagamitsu presented by Shigezane" were made by the Watari Date clan during the Meiji period, that specific blade would likely be selected.

There seem to be several surviving inventories of swords held by the Date clans of Sendai and Watari, but I haven't read them. Since I can't read the cursive script, I haven't even checked to see if microfilms are available ^^; I've included a list below; if anyone is familiar with them, I would appreciate it if you could let me know.

- Catalogue of Materials in the Sendai City Museum: Weapons and Armor, Revised Edition, Plate 143 "Register of Imperial Treasures"
- "Record of Personal Armor, Keio 3" — Catalogue of Date Family-Related Materials held by the Date City Pioneering Memorial Museum (090・98-1). Several other records of personal armor are also included in this catalogue.

Now, there is an anecdote about Masamune involving the "Furiwake-gami Masamune." He essentially fabricated a "Masamune" sword. Even today, Japanese swords are frequently forgeries, fakes, or copies. Even in my own family's farmhouse, there are a few swords that seem to have been purchased back when we were doing well; the names engraved on the blades alone are impressive. Since there were appraisers even in Masamune's time, it suggests that, conversely, authentic and fake pieces were so intermingled that appraisers could actually make a living. Probing whether a surviving "Usami Nagamitsu" truly came from the Uesugi clan, or whether it is truly a "Nagamitsu," is inherently a pointless pursuit; what matters is that the "Usami Nagamitsu" of the Watari Date clan is a symbol of the house—beginning with Jitsumoto and Shigezane—and continues to serve that function to this day. My interest lies less in whether the "Nagamitsu" is authentic, whether there are contradictions between the extant object and its provenance, or whether the provenance is true, and more in the process of how that provenance was established.

※The strikethroughs in the above article are due to revisions made in December 2021, when a description regarding the "Register of Sendai Family Swords, Treasure Section" held by the Tokyo National Museum was added to the main text.

shigezane:watari-01-06.title: Letter from Shigezane Date, January 6, date unknown
shigezane:watari-01-06.summary: Letter from Shigezane Date, January 6, date unknown. The opening reads: "Suddenly, I instructed Ichizaemon and Heibei, and they reported that it was as requested. I am satisfied. Although Lord ◾️ Goro arrived this morning, as there is a hawk before me and it is a difficult matter, I have no..."
shigezane:watari-01-06.markdown:
Suddenly, I instructed Ichizaemon and Heibei, and they replied that it was as requested. I am satisfied. Since Lord ◾️goro arrived this morning and there is a pressing need for hawks, I understand that if none are available, it cannot be helped; if one or two are desired, I shall arrange for their arrival. Regarding yesterday's letter, there were one or two items. As for Jirozaemon, the falconer, he reported that there are approximately five young hawks and fifty mountain hawks. Jirozaemon-no-jo stated that those arriving here in November are primarily hawks and should be available. I have been informed that this should be communicated to the subordinates; accordingly, I shall arrange for Ichizaemon to arrive as appropriate. The following day, he shall report to me. As there is currently no boat, it is difficult to arrange the transport. As for the hawks, I was told they should be sent up immediately. Respectfully and humbly, January 6th, Shigezane, Lord Shiga Bingo.

Furthermore, the kosode sent to Ichizaemon has been delivered; Heibei requested a payment of 1,500 mon as the goods to be handed over. Since two pieces were sent to Ichizaemon, Heibei should receive 1,000 mon. That amount shall not be deducted. Please inform Magoemon accordingly and hand over the goods. As for those in private, it has been suggested that a small amount of money be provided in advance to obtain hawks, and that the general condition of the hawks be ascertained before receiving them. Should they come to this location, that amount shall be paid; however, as it would be difficult if forgotten, I mention this now. It would be appropriate to arrange this with those sent this time. Since this is in Sagami, I wish to have as many hawks as possible; I would like to have three mountain hawks and five young hawks. That is all. I will mention this again. As for the laborers, since they mentioned bait and the like, they should be brought in. Although it was said that Ryoan would come, in reality he does not, so I believe only two people will be needed; the matter of the laborers should be handled accordingly. That is all.

## Casual reading

Upon being suddenly instructed regarding Ichizaemon and Heibei, I replied that it was most appropriate. I am satisfied. This morning, Lord ■ Goro visited; as it is difficult to ascertain whether there are hawks on hand, if none are available, it cannot be helped. If there are, I understood that if one or two were desired, I should inform you accordingly. In yesterday's letter, you stated that there were one or two. As for the falconers, Jirozaemon reports that there are about five young hawks and fifty mountain hawks. Jirozaemon-no-jo stated that those who sent them here in November reported that hawks had arrived and that it would be fine as long as they were available. I have been instructed to notify you before the personnel are dispatched; therefore, Ichizaemon shall proceed accordingly. As everything has been agreed upon, I shall inform you that the personnel will visit here the following day. As there is currently no boat, it is difficult to ascertain the timing of their arrival. You have been instructed that if the hawks are available, they shall be sent immediately. With utmost respect. January 6th, Shigezane, Lord Shiga Bingo

Furthermore, the kosode sent to Ichizaemon has arrived. I shall deliver it. He stated that he wishes to borrow one kan and five hundred mon from Heibei. Since I have provided two pieces to Ichizaemon, I should provide one kan to Heibei. I shall not make a loan; I shall simply provide the funds. I shall inform Magoemon as stated above and deliver it to him. Someone well-informed privately suggested that I provide a small amount of money in advance and inquire about the condition of the hawks before accepting them; should they visit me, I shall inform them of that amount, but if it were difficult to remember, I should first inform them. It would be appropriate to arrange this with those sent this time. As this is in Sagami, I wish to have them send up hawks in any manner. I wish to have two or three mountain-returning young hawks sent up. That is all. I shall report again. As for the laborers, since they will enter to buy bait and the like, they should do so. Although Ryoan stated that he would come, in reality he will not; I believe there will be only about two people, so as for the laborers, it should be arranged accordingly. That is all.

## Rough translation

When I suddenly instructed Ichizaemon and Heibei, they agreed, and I am satisfied. This morning, Lord ■Goro visited and informed me: "I do not know if there are hawks at Matsumae; if there are none, it cannot be helped. However, he says he desires either one or two pairs, so if that is the case, please let him know." In yesterday's letter, it was stated that there were one or two pairs. When Jirozaemon inquired of the falconer, he replied that there were about five young hawks and fifty mountain-returning hawks. Jirozaemon stated that those who sent them here in November said that hawks were appearing frequently, and that this was likely the case. Since I was instructed to notify them before sending personnel, Ichizaemon is to come as soon as word is received. As various arrangements have been made, I shall instruct him to come here the day after I notify him. As there are currently no boats, it is difficult to imagine how slow the travel will be. He commanded that if hawks are present, they be sent up immediately. With utmost respect.

January 6, Shigezane

Lord Shiga Bingo

Furthermore, the kosode sent to Ichizaemon has arrived, so please deliver it. Heibei has expressed a desire to borrow one kan and five hundred mon in payment. Since two kiri were provided to Ichizaemon, it would be appropriate to provide one kan to Heibei. This is not a loan; please provide it as such. Tell Magoemon as stated above and have him deliver it. Tell someone you know well in private to lend a small amount of money in Matsumae and ask them to obtain a good hawk, or to hear about the condition of the hawks. If Bingo comes here, I will mention the matter, but since I must not forget it, I am writing this first. Please coordinate with those being dispatched this time. As things have become contentious with Sagami, I want to find some way to have them send up hawks. I would like to have two or three mountain-returning young hawks sent up. That is all. Also, a postscript. Regarding the laborers, will they be brought in to feed the birds during the ascent? Ryoan said they would come, but that is not the case. I expect only about two people for the ascent, so please keep that in mind regarding the laborers. That is all.

shigezane:watari-03-18.title: Letter from Shigezane Date, March 18, date unknown
shigezane:watari-03-18.summary: Letter from Shigezane Date, March 18, date unknown. The opening reads: "Regarding the matter of the investigation into the construction of the original weir, it is appropriate; as for the various general affairs, shall they be settled? If so, I shall return; should there be any issues, albeit a grave matter, I shall remain for two or three days..."
shigezane:watari-03-18.markdown:
Regarding the matter of the investigation into the construction of the original weir, that seems appropriate; perhaps there are gaps in the general arrangements. If that is the case, I shall return. Should there be any issues, despite it being a great undertaking, it would be appropriate to remain for two or three days. I have been informed that Ichiga Hikozaemon has captured Okumagawa in Soma; since Lord Izumi Kuradosuke has ordered that a letter be sent from that side, I shall reply accordingly. As for the matter of formal greetings, I have been told that they have been placed in a basket; therefore, the letter should be sent without delay. Furthermore, as for the matter of courtesy and such, how should I proceed? I have forgotten. In any case, I shall send a letter to Shirobei-dono and consult with him; as this is for mutual benefit, I shall send the request while observing proper etiquette. Regarding matters such as the sword, it has been agreed that the Soma party shall present them; therefore, I believe such matters should not be mentioned. Nevertheless, as this is for mutual benefit, I wish to request that any specific matters be replied to; it is difficult to determine what should be conveyed. I shall consult with him immediately. As for the details, I shall inquire of Moheiji. Respectfully and humbly.

March 18, Shigezane, to Lord Shiga Bingo

Furthermore, it appears that the seedbeds here have been completed; as for the original matter, it should be handled as Yaza-sama suggests—that a Kageyu residence should be constructed and presented—but I forgot to mention this and failed to notify you. I have sent word to the Gagaku-no-jo, intending to have him handle the matter, and have instructed him to come to see Tadaemon tomorrow.

## Casual reading

Regarding the weir construction, I understand the situation is settled; that is as it should be. Should there be any matters to attend to, I shall make myself available. If that is the case, I shall return. Should there be any complications, even if it is a great inconvenience, I shall remain for two or three days. I have received word that Ichi Kahikozaemon has been captured at Kumagawa in Soma. Lord Izumi Kuradosuke has stated that if a letter arrives from you, it shall be returned; as he has placed it in a basket, I advise you to send your letter accordingly. As for the matter of formal courtesy and such, how has it been? I have forgotten. In any case, I have sent a letter to Shirobei-dono to arrange a consultation; as it is for our mutual benefit, it shall be sent and received, even as a formal courtesy. Regarding the matter of the swords, I have stated that those who pursue them shall be dealt with by the people of Soma; therefore, I believe such matters should not be mentioned. Nevertheless, as it is for our mutual benefit, I wish to request that any separate holdings be returned. It is difficult to know how to handle the matter of such persons. I shall report the consultation immediately, and that shall be as it should be. As for the circumstances, I shall inquire of Mohei-ji. Respectfully and humbly.

March 18, Shigezane, to Lord Shiga Bingo

Furthermore, as for the seedbeds, it appears we have now settled the matter. That, too, should be handled accordingly. I had intended to build and advance the Kageyu residence, but I forgot to do so; I have now dispatched word to the Gagaku-no-jo. I believe it would be best to have them carry out the work, so I have instructed them to visit Tadaemon tomorrow.

## Rough translation

It seems the construction on the weir there has been completed, which is only natural. I trust your various affairs have been settled. If they have, please return. If anything remains unfinished, I apologize for the trouble, but please stay for two or three days. I hear that a report from Ichiga Hikozaemon was intercepted at Kumagawa in Soma. Lord Izumi Kuradosuke stated that if he received a letter from you, he would return it; as it is said to be kept in a basket, please send a letter. As for the matters of formal etiquette and such, how have things been? I had forgotten. In any case, please send a letter to Lord Shirobei to consult with him; as it is for mutual benefit, please send and receive whatever formalities may be required. Regarding the swords and other items, those who followed after you claimed they would deliver them to the people of Soma, but I believe it is better not to say such things. However, as it is for mutual benefit, I wish to instruct you to return the separate holdings. As it is difficult to guess what kind of person may have been involved, please consult with him immediately. Regarding the situation, please inquire with Moheiji. With utmost respect and humility.

March 18, Shigezane, to Lord Shiga Bingo

Furthermore, the seedbeds here are mostly finished. Please do the same there. I had intended to instruct Kageyu to handle the household construction, but I forgot and have not yet done so. I have sent word to the Gagaku-no-jo. Intending to have Hyuga handle the after-care, I have instructed him to appear before Tadaemon tomorrow.

shigezane:watari-04-05.title: Letter from Shigezane Date, April 5, date unknown
shigezane:watari-04-05.summary: Letter from Shigezane Date, April 5, date unknown. The opening reads: "Indeed, as stated. The above account is also for Genbei."
shigezane:watari-04-05.markdown:
Regarding the matter of the New Land Land Clearance Register, the chief officials have stated there is no change. Bizen has likely prepared it so that as many land clearances as possible may occur as soon as they begin. As for the finer details, the chief officials may not be fully aware; should the matter be transferred to this office, we shall borrow the main register and conduct the correspondence. It is only natural that the correspondence be conducted from here. Since Genbei has also come, I believe the register should be prepared as a clean copy. As for Lord Wakasa's, I shall report it in his diary. I believe Shiroishi Tarobei should be notified, so I intend to have the register presented to Tarobei. That is the purpose. As for Genbei's departure for Sendai, I shall notify him. Regarding the register, I intend to borrow it from Iwanuma Tokuda and bring it with me. Respectfully submitted.

April 5, Shigezane

Furthermore, I have not heard that he has come for Kaian medicine. The pain in his leg also persists. Since yesterday, the pain in his leg has only worsened. I suspect it is beriberi. When he is burned, it hurts in another location. Beriberi is (6 characters unknown)

Lord Mokusuke Ushizaka

## Casual reading

​Regarding the matter of the registers for the initial clearing of the new land: the chief officials have stated that there is no need for any changes. To ensure that the number of registers increases as the work progresses, I shall have Bizen forge them. The finer details are likely beyond the knowledge of the chief officials. Should you come this way, I shall borrow the main register and present it to you. It is only fitting that the register be drawn up in ink. As for the register mentioned above, Genbei shall visit and have it drawn up; therefore, I believe it should be prepared as a clean register. I shall submit this to Lord Wakasa in his initial diary. I believe Tarobei Shiroishi should deliver it, so I believe the register should be shown to Tarobei. This is for that purpose. Genbei shall travel to Sendai to have it drawn up. As for the register, I shall borrow it from Tokuda Iwanuma and bring it with me. Respectfully submitted.

April 5, Munemi

Furthermore, I have not heard any word regarding the Kaian medicine. The pain in my shoulder also persists. Since yesterday, the pain in my shoulder has worsened. I suspect it may be beriberi. When I apply heat to the painful area, another spot begins to ache. Beriberi is (6 characters unknown)

Lord Mokusuke Ushizaka

​

shigezane:watari-jidai.cover_alt: Illustrations of the residence and castle town
shigezane:watari-jidai.markdown:
## Watari Castle

Watari-aza Kyukan, [Watari Town](http://www.town.watari.miyagi.jp/), Watari District, Miyagi Prefecture. Also known as Gogyu Castle. It was built in the early 14th century by the Takeishi clan, a branch of the Chiba clan (as Kotsutsumi Castle). During the Tensho era, Watari Motomune relocated the castle to the east. Kotsutsumi Castle became Yuzan-ji (now Daiyu-ji), the family temple of the Watari Date clan. However, Yuzan-ji was founded by Shigezane, who invited monks from Yorin-ji in Ogura, Fukushima City. In Tensho 19, Kagetsuna Katakura became the castle lord, but in Keicho 7, he moved to Shiroishi, replacing Shigezane. Shigezane finally settled here and passed away in Watari in Shoho 3; thereafter, it served as the residence for successive generations of the Watari Date clan. The castle featured two masugata (square-shaped baileys) in the honmaru, ninomaru, and sannomaru. Under the Tokugawa shogunate's "One Castle per Province" edict, it was referred to as the Watari Fortress. The surrounding area was once wetlands, which served as natural moats. Due to being divided by town roads and the development of shops and residences, little remains of the original appearance of the castle site. In the honmaru, Watari Shrine was established in the Meiji era, where Shigezane Date is enshrined. The deity's name is Takehaya Chio-no-Mikoto.

[Miyagi Prefecture > Historic Road Scenes > Edohama Kaido and Watari Town Area](http://www.pref.miyagi.jp/kohou/kenseidayori/200503/kodo/kodo.htm)

Photo courtesy of Mr./Ms. Shimizu

Photo courtesy of Mr./Ms. Nozaki

→[Records from the Heartland of the Great East Japan Earthquake](http://shigezane.info/majime/Earthquake/0311top.html)

## Yachigoya Fort

Fukushima Prefecture, [Shinchi Town](http://www.shinchi-town.jp/), Yachigoya, Aza-Furuyashiki. Built during the Eiroku era by Soma Moritane and Yoshitane. However, after about a year, the castle was moved to Minokubi Castle (Shinchi Castle, Yachigoya, Aza-Tatemae) to the west. On May 20, Tensho 17, it passed into the hands of Masamune and was granted to Watari Shigemune. While the identity of the lord of Shinchi after Shigemune's move to Wakuya remains uncertain, by Kan'ei 5 (1628), it became part of the fief of Munemi, along with Fukuda. Munemi renovated the original Yachigoya fortifications and appointed a deputy governor. Paired cherry trees stood in front of the main southern gate, and the site was referred to as "Sakura-no-Yakata" or "Oyashiki." It is a flatland castle consisting of two baileys, north and south.

→[Records from the Heart of the Great East Japan Earthquake](http://shigezane.info/majime/Earthquake/0311top.html)

## Sendai

[Sendai City](http://www.city.sendai.jp/). The Sendai residence of the Watari Date clan. Starting from the era of Tadamune, departure banquets were held here whenever the domain lord departed for Edo. (During Masamune's reign, it was the residence of Tsunamoto Moniwa). Image sourced from Rakuten. Links to Sendai travel information. References > [Summary of Academic Research Results from the Sendai Castle Site](http://www.city.sendai.jp/kyouiku/bunkazai/gakuzyutu/index.html) [Status of Sendai Castle Excavation Surveys](http://www.city.sendai.jp/kyouiku/bunkazai/castle/index.html)

## Wakabayashi

[Wakabayashi Ward, Sendai City](http://www.city.sendai.jp/). Shigezane's residence was also located in Wakabayashi (now Miyagi Prison), which was intended to be Masamune's retirement castle. On the night of the housewarming celebration for which Masamune had been invited, the building was completely destroyed by a fire of unknown origin. It is said that this day was unsettling, marked by supernatural occurrences and bloody incidents.

## Osaka

Since Shigezane campaigned in both the summer and winter campaigns of the Siege of Osaka, he will be featured here. Here is a brief overview of the lands and historical sites associated with the Date clan during this time.

**Kawachi Kokubun**

Kokubun, Kashiwara City. Campsite during the Summer Campaign.

**Near Domyoji**

Around Kokubun and Tamate in Kashiwara City, Domyoji in Fujiidera City, and Konda in Habikino City. A site of fierce fighting where Kagetsuna Katakura's valiant exploits are recounted.

**Chausuyama**

Domyoji's postwar advance.

**Nanba**

Domyoji's postwar advance.

**Tachiuribori**

Tachiuribori, Nishi Ward, Osaka City. Legend has it that Masamune established a camp here (Settsu Meisho Zue Taisei).

**Gansen-ji**

Ooka, Naniwa Ward, Osaka City. Donated the hall and tea room as guest quarters during the Siege of Osaka. Destroyed by air raids.

Display description on hover

## Daiyu-ji

The family temple of the Watari Date clan. It houses the mausoleum of Shigezane, as well as the burial grounds of the Watari Date family. Detailed research on the Watari Date family burial grounds can be found in ["On the Transition of Burial Sites for High-Ranking Retainers in the Sendai Domain: Burial Sites of the Watari Date Family, Retainers of the Sendai Domain"](http://www2.nkansai.ne.jp/users/monmuse/wataridateke/top-mokuji.htm). Although not indicated on the information board, there is a theory that the slightly elevated area behind Shigezane's mausoleum is the burial ground for the successor wife, of the Nikaido clan. Shigezane's mausoleum was renovated and restored between 1997 and 1999. Prior to the renovation, the mausoleum featured tiles arranged atop the corner ridge and an onigawara (ogre-faced tile) at the ridge end; these were added during a renovation in the early Showa era. With this latest renovation, it has returned to its original form without the decorative tiles. The three-tiered tomoe on the right of the door was painted during the restoration as a divine crest. The tomoe crest on the frog-shaped base above was originally absent, but was reportedly added during the restoration at the suggestion of a shrine carpenter. (Information provided by: Yamabiko-sama) The mausoleum is open to the public twice a year, on January 16 and August 16. The area around Daiyu-ji is the site of Kotsutsumi Castle, the residence of the Takeishi Watari clan. During the Tenbun era, Watari Motomune moved his base to Watari Castle, and the castle was abandoned.

shigezane:watarisojyou-mimoto.markdown:
In Tenwa 2 (1682), the head of the Watari Date clan died suddenly at a young age. The domain appointed a late-adopted heir and adopted a policy of halving the fief. The clan members resisted this, requesting a different adoptee and insisting that all their lands be fully confirmed. Listing the loyal services of Sanemoto and Shigezane,

"With all these achievements, don't reduce the fief (ToT). I'd prefer Nakamura Izu as the successor."

And so, below is an excerpt from the section detailing Sanemoto's achievements in the "Watari Petition (published in the transcription of the History of Watari Town)."

---

> The ancestors, Sanemoto, had received the promise of succession from Lord Sadazane Uesugi; they were granted the bamboo-and-sparrow-curtain crest and the item worn at the waist by Nagamitsu Usami, as well as the character "Sane," and various other tokens. As they were already preparing to relocate to Echigo and had set a deadline, there arose those who acted contrary to the will of the lord. Since the relationship between Lord Tanemune and Lord Harumune, father and son, was strained, no mediator came to Echigo to arrange a reconciliation; thus, the reconciliation was achieved, and I believe it is an act of loyalty and filial piety that they remained within the retainer house for generations to come.

shigezane:watarisojyou-narumi.title: Shigezane's Achievements as Documented in the Watari Petition
shigezane:watarisojyou-narumi.summary: In Tenwa 2 (1682), the head of the Watari Date clan died suddenly at a young age. The domain appointed a late-adopted heir and adopted a policy of halving his landholdings. shigezane:watarisojyou-narumi.markdown:
In Tenwa 2 (1682), the head of the Watari Date clan died suddenly at a young age. The domain appointed a late-adopted heir and adopted a policy of halving his landholdings. The clan members resisted this, demanding a different adoptee and insisting that all their lands be fully confirmed.

Listing the loyal services of Sanemoto and Shigezane, he said, "With achievements like these, don't reduce the landholdings (ToT). I'd prefer Nakamura Izu as the successor."

By the standards of the time, it felt like a pretty brazen request... (^^ゞ. Plus, the head of the house died while he was still petitioning for adoption as a late-life heir, so in reality, he was adopted posthumously.

This incident is known as the "Tenwa Petition," and the petition filed by the Watari Date clan is called the "Watari Petition." It took place roughly 35 years after Shigezane's death. There were likely still people who knew the "living Shigezane." It is fascinating to get a glimpse of how Shigezane was perceived by the clan at the time.

And so, here is an excerpt from the section on Shigezane's achievements in the "Watari Petition" (published in the transcription of the History of Watari Town).

---

> Now, as for the matter of Shigezane's service, it goes without saying that during the Battle of Sendo, Shigezane achieved victory through his military prowess; furthermore, I have heard accounts that he frequently stepped in on behalf of Lord Teizan (Masamune). I hereby report the following. > > 1. During the Battle of Ninto-hitoribashi, Aizu Yoshihiro, Satake Yoshishige, Iwaki Tsunetaka, Ishikawa Akimitsu, and Shirakawa Yoshichika joined forces. The forces of these five houses surged forward like clouds and mist, driving the defeated army back as far as Lord Teizan's banners. Numerous men, beginning with Moniwa Sagetsu, were slain in action, and Lord Teizan himself appeared to be in grave danger. At that moment, Shigezane left his allies, disregarded his own life, and charged into the heart of the enemy. Although many of his retainers also fell in battle, Shigezane's exceptional military skill enabled the enemy to scatter. Lord Teizan was deeply impressed by Shigezane's prowess and appointed Yamaji Awaji as a messenger, stating that today's performance was unparalleled—that he had fought behind the enemy lines without allowing the defeated army to escape—an occurrence unprecedented in history. In short, it was because of him that many were saved; it is recorded in his own handwritten letter that there must surely be many who were wounded, a point I have also noted in Shigezane's memorandum. > > 1. During the Battle of Surigami, Shigezane employed his military strategy to bring Inawashiro Danjo to his side; thus, Lord Teizan's reputation was enhanced, and the twelve districts of Aizu were secured. Shigezane was rewarded for his military merit. Furthermore, regarding the acquisition of Shiomatsu, Shigezane frequently consulted and coordinated matters through his strategic ingenuity; there is no concealment in this. Beyond these, his loyal service on several other occasions goes without saying. > > 1. During the era of the Taiko, when Gamo Ujisato descended to Oshu, Ujisato had both loyal and treacherous retainers, and Lord Teizan faced great hardship in his governance. Shigezane, disregarding his own life, became a hostage and crossed over to Ujisato; thus, Ujisato's suspicions were dispelled, and Lord Teizan escaped the aforementioned hardship. Furthermore, when Kanpaku Hidetsugu committed seppuku, the Taiko also harbored suspicions toward Lord Teizan, and it was a grave matter. Shigezane stated, "Since you are residing in the province, it would not be appropriate to report your defiance; therefore, you should promptly ascend to Fushimi and declare that you have no rebellious intent. Should it come to seppuku, I shall take charge of the affairs of the province. I shall persuade the retainers to fight a single battle and achieve your ultimate wish; therefore, please ascend." Upon his departure from Iwadeyama, close associates informed him along the way that Masamune was sympathetic to Hidetsugu; thus, he believed that if he ascended, he would surely be forced to commit seppuku. However, as the investigation proceeded and he visited Yakuin (Seyaku-in Zenshu), he was told, "Now then, you have gone so far as to ascend; please proceed to Osaka immediately and first come to our residence." Upon visiting Yakuin and being granted various gifts, the Taiko thought, "If Masamune were rebellious, he should not have ascended so rashly," and his previous suspicions were dispelled. From then on, things proceeded increasingly favorably. The Taiko's consideration, forgiveness, and assurance were repeatedly granted to Lord Teizan and Shigezane; I have heard from Shigezane's account that regarding the matter of Fushimi, it was solely through his own prudence that he escaped the hardship and received the grant of hands. > > The above details show his repeated loyal service and that his merits were recognized by the high authorities, as is well-known to the world. When Lord Tadamune granted 5,000 kanme of silver in Kan'ei 15, the entire household went to the capital to express their gratitude. They were granted palanquins as far as the Ni-no-mon gate, were granted many ceremonial robes, and were further granted seats in private rooms, with Matsudaira Izu-no-kami, Ii Sabu-no-kami, Doi Oi, and others being seated alongside them. Shigezane was granted the special privilege of serving in matters of bow and arrow, and he was even granted a seat within a single shoji screen of the Shogun, allowing him to hear the Shogun's words. Moreover, the Shogun was impressed by Shigezane's military prowess and held him in high regard, which served as a decoration for the house.

shigezane:yakedo.title: Burn on the right hand
shigezane:yakedo.summary: I hadn't seen any books mentioning this—even though it's written so clearly in the "Masamune-ki." Or so I thought, until I found it in the "Shin-Ou Eikei Gunki: Aizu Volume."
shigezane:yakedo.markdown:
I hadn't seen any books mentioning this—even though it's written so clearly in the "Masamune-ki." Or so I thought, until I found it in "[Shin-Ou Eikei Gunki: Aizu no Maki](http://www.amazon.co.jp/exec/obidos/ASIN/4897574439/oysannohitori-22)."

It was the hour of the Dog on December 11, Tensho 13 (around 8:00 p.m.). Following the Battle of Hitotori Bridge, Shigezane was on guard duty for Nihonmatsu at the forward base, Shibukawa Castle. In the room where Shigezane usually stayed, a close retainer accidentally dropped a spark onto a gunpowder box. Since he dropped the spark directly onto the powder, it was catastrophic. The fire spread through the castle in an instant, and Shibukawa Castle was completely burned to the ground. Shigezane narrowly escaped being burned to death, though he suffered severe burns to his right hand. These burns were so severe that, although they healed, all the fingers of his right hand became fused together—a condition that apparently never healed for the rest of his life. He ended up in a state exactly like Hideyo Noguchi's left hand. ...Still, the fact that he kept ammunition in the room where he usually slept and woke is quite something. I guess that's just how it is.

Now, how did these burns affect Shigezane, a man of great martial prowess? If even his thumb was stuck together, the things he could do with his right hand would be extremely limited. Conversely, if his thumb had been spared, while fine work might have been impossible, he might have still managed to hold a sword or a brush. Chopsticks, however, would likely be out of the question. Letters written in Shigezane's own hand also survive, but as the administrator—who has only seen them in print—I cannot tell whether he wrote them with his right or left hand. (I probably wouldn't be able to tell even if I saw them in person, either.) Below is a quotation from the "Masamune-ki."

> From [“Masamune-ki, Volume 3: The Battle of Shibukawa in Adachi District”](#/post/shigezane/masamuneki3-1) > Thus, when December arrived, Shigezane also returned to the aforementioned Shibukawa. However, around the hour of the Dog on the 11th of the same month, in the parlor where Shigezane was staying, his retainers set fire to the gunpowder box and transferred the flames to the box itself, burning it to the ground; as a result, the entire castle was consumed, and Shigezane himself was burned beyond measure. To this day, his fingers remain fused together, leaving him crippled for life; at the time, not to mention the ten who died and only one who survived.

It was a blessing in disguise that there was no enemy attack taking advantage of the fire. Given that a forward base had been burned to the ground in the dead of winter during wartime, I imagine it must have been quite dire. Furthermore, regarding a mystery concerning the burns, there is a record stating that Shigezane had attained full mastery of Tenryu swordsmanship (Seshin Kafu). While I find it hard to believe that he could wield a sword like an able-bodied person, perhaps it was not a problem as long as he was in good health.

Addendum: April 6, 2009. In the overview of the scrolls introduced in Akemi Takahashi's "On the Collection of Instructional Documents Passed down by Masamune Date" (included in Sendai City Museum Research Report No. 11), there are two scrolls (B-16, B-26) titled "Namu Goju Gunma Shugosho," with a colophon reading "Attributed to Terufusa / Aragawa Matazaemon / Shigezane / Tensho 12, Year of the Wood Monkey, October." "Attributed to Terufusa" likely refers to Saito Denkibo, the founder of Tenryu. Saito Denkibo died in Tensho 15, so there is no contradiction. According to the author, this is a "Tenryu (naginata school) license granted to Shigezane Date." If so, it would mean he obtained the license at a very young age, before sustaining his burns and injuries.

But this burn has really become well-known lately....

The original site, "Shigezane Zanmai," features a section called the "Dojin Translation Project," where volunteers translate historical materials into modern Japanese. The focus is on *The Love of Masamune Date*, with translations progressing for each of Masamune's concubines and associated figures.

The translation will not be included; instead, this page will link to the original site.

shigezane:intro-novels.summary: This is the introduction page for the "Novels" section of the original site, "Shigezane Zanmai." It provides links to 47 historical novels about Shigezane and Masamune written by the site administrator.
shigezane:intro-novels.markdown:
The original site "Shigezane Zanmai" features a historical fiction section called "Novels," curated by administrator TAKEMI Shigino. It is a compelling section featuring short and medium-length stories centered on Shigezane and Masamune, depicting battles, family, and retainers.

Since the novels are works of fiction, the main texts are not incorporated into Neo Shigezane Zanmai; instead, this page links to the original site. Please start by visiting "Personal Novels" (the section's entry point).

shigezane:intro-takesuzume.cover_alt: Illustration introducing the Take-suzume Crest Gallery
shigezane:intro-takesuzume.markdown:
The "Sparrow on Bamboo" is known as the family crest of the Date clan. The original site, "Shigezane Zanmai," features a gallery of Bamboo-and-Sparrow crest designs found in various regions, as well as an explanatory page regarding these designs.

Images will not be embedded; instead, this page will link to the original site. Note that while these two pages are listed under "Report" on the original site, their content is primarily image-based, so Neo Shigezane Zanmai has treated them as a combination of introductions and links.
